title: Superposition — Study Notes
content:
Superposition

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 2 (WPH12), sat at AS.

Principle of superposition

When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Constructive interference occurs where the waves are in phase; destructive interference occurs where they are in antiphase.

Stationary waves

  • A stationary wave forms when two progressive waves of the same frequency, amplitude and wavelength travel in opposite directions and superpose.
  • Nodes are points of zero amplitude; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes (or antinodes) are separated by λ/2.
  • On a string fixed at both ends, the fundamental frequency is f = v/(2L), so the wavelength is λ = 2L.

Interference

For coherent sources (same frequency and a constant phase difference) with slit separation a and screen distance D, the fringe spacing is Δx = λD/a.

Diffraction

Diffraction is the spreading of a wave after it passes through a gap or round an edge. It is greatest when the gap width is comparable to the wavelength.

Diffraction grating

For a grating with slit spacing d, the angle θ of the nth-order maximum satisfies nλ = d sin θ. A grating with more lines per metre gives a smaller d and larger angles of diffraction.

Worked example: light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two slits 0.30 mm apart, with a screen 1.5 m away. Fringe spacing Δx = λD/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5) ÷ (3.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.0 mm.

Exam tips: convert nm and mm to metres before using Δx = λD/a. Check the order n when using a grating. Coherence is a requirement for interference, so state it.

The diffraction grating equation

A diffraction grating has many closely spaced slits. Light of wavelength λ leaves the grating at angle θ to form bright maxima when d sin θ = nλ, where d is the slit spacing and n is the order of the maximum. Each order is sharper and more widely separated than a double slit, because the many slits reinforce the bright positions. The number of orders visible is limited by the condition that sin θ cannot exceed 1.

Exam tip: convert the slit spacing to metres before using the grating equation, and note that the central maximum is n = 0.

Two-source interference: a worked calculation

Two coherent loudspeakers emit sound of frequency 680 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, so λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. A listener walks along a line parallel to the line joining the speakers. At a point where the path difference is 0.75 m, the waves arrive in antiphase, because 0.75 is an odd multiple of λ/2 (0.25 m). The listener hears a minimum there.

Use the path difference, not the distance from one source, to decide the outcome. Path difference = nλ gives a maximum; path difference = (n + ½)λ gives a minimum. Writing the test as a multiple of λ, and not as a raw distance, is the step examiners look for.

Phase difference and path difference

A phase difference of 360° (2π radians) corresponds to a path difference of one wavelength. A phase difference of 180° corresponds to a path difference of λ/2. In general, phase difference = (path difference / λ) × 360°. Questions often give one and ask for the other, so be ready to convert between them.

  • Coherence needs a constant phase difference, which is why two independent light bulbs do not produce a stable fringe pattern.
  • Monochromatic light is needed for sharp fringes, because each wavelength produces its own fringe spacing and the patterns blur together.
  • Fringe spacing is directly proportional to wavelength and to screen distance, and inversely proportional to slit separation. Halving a doubles the spacing.

Stationary waves: harmonics on a pipe

An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so its fundamental wavelength is 2L and its harmonics are f, 2f, 3f and so on. A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so its fundamental wavelength is 4L, and it produces only odd harmonics: f, 3f, 5f.

Example: a pipe of length 0.85 m, open at both ends, with speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹. The fundamental is f = v/(2L) = 340/1.7 = 200 Hz, and the second harmonic is 400 Hz.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the slit spacing a where the question gives the slit-to-screen distance D, or the reverse. Read the labels in the diagram before substituting.
  • Stating that a stationary wave transfers energy along the string. It does not: energy is confined between the nodes, and the wave transfers no net energy along the medium.
  • Calling the points between two adjacent nodes "in phase" without qualification. Particles between the same two nodes are in phase; particles either side of a node are in antiphase.

title: Exam technique: Integration
content:
### What earns the marks
For indefinite integrals, each term raised correctly plus the constant earns full marks. For definite integrals, the antiderivative quoted earns one mark and the correct upper-minus-lower evaluation earns the next. For area and curve-finding, the limits or the given point used earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: constant of integration omitted. Correction: +c always for indefinite. Error: limits subtracted backwards. Correction: upper minus lower. Error: power rule inverted on roots. Correction: root x is x to the half, integral goes up.
### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.
### Worked example
Find the integral of 6x² − 4x⁻³. Raise each power by one and divide by the new power: 6x² becomes 2x³, and −4x⁻³ becomes 2x⁻² because (−4)/(−2) = 2. Add the constant: 2x³ + 2x⁻² + c. Check by differentiating: 6x² + (−4)x⁻³, which matches the original.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate geometry of circles

Level note: circles are Pure 2 (WMA12) in Edexcel, sat at AS; this note is the detailed treatment and the AS Coordinate Geometry note covers the same ground.

At A2, coordinate geometry centres on the circle: its equation, tangents, normals and the interaction with straight lines.

Circle equations

  • Centre (a, b), radius r: (x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2.
  • General form x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (-g, -f) and radius sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c).
  • Always complete the square to find centre and radius.

Tangents and normals

  • The tangent at a point is perpendicular to the radius at that point: gradient of tangent = -1 / (gradient of radius).
  • The normal at a point passes through the centre (it is the radius line extended).
  • For the circle x^2 + y^2 = r^2, the tangent at (x1, y1) is x x1 + y y1 = r^2.

Line and circle

  • Substituting a line into the circle gives a quadratic: two roots = two intersections (secant), one repeated root = tangent, no real roots = no intersection.
  • Tangency condition: the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line equals the radius.
  • Distance from (x0, y0) to ax + by + c = 0 is |ax0 + by0 + c| / sqrt(a^2 + b^2).

Tangent from an external point

The length of a tangent from an external point P to a circle is sqrt(d^2 - r^2), where d is the distance from P to the centre.

title: Waves — Study Notes
content:
Waves

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 2 (WPH12), sat at AS.

Progressive waves

  • A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter. Its speed is v = fλ, where f is the frequency and λ the wavelength. Period T = 1/f.
  • Phase difference: two points separated by one wavelength are in phase. Points separated by half a wavelength are in antiphase.

Transverse and longitudinal waves

  • Transverse: the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. light, waves on a string).
  • Longitudinal: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (e.g. sound in air, compressions and rarefactions).

Doppler effect for sound

When a source moves towards an observer, the observed frequency is higher and the wavelength is shorter. When it moves away, the observed frequency is lower and the wavelength is longer. The speed of sound in the medium does not change.

Electromagnetic spectrum

All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. In order of increasing wavelength: gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves. Frequency increases in the reverse order.

Polarisation

Only transverse waves can be polarised. Polarisation restricts the oscillations to a single plane. Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.

Worked example: a wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 6.0 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 50 × 6.0 = 300 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: learn the spectrum order in terms of wavelength, not frequency. For the Doppler effect, state which way the source moves relative to the observer. Only transverse waves can show polarisation.

Polarisation and the Doppler effect

Only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations can be restricted to one plane. A polariser passes only the component of the oscillation along its transmission axis. Light from a sky or a reflection is partly polarised, which is why polarising filters reduce glare. The Doppler effect for a moving source gives an observed frequency f' = f v/(v ± vs), where the upper sign applies when the source moves away from the observer and the lower sign when it approaches.

Exam tip: longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised, so say so explicitly if a question asks about it.

Worked example: wave speed from frequency and wavelength

A sound wave has frequency 680 Hz and wavelength 0.50 m. Using v = fλ, the speed is 680 × 0.50 = 340 m/s, close to the speed of sound in air. For an electromagnetic wave in a vacuum the same relation applies, with v = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Take the wavelength from a displacement–distance graph and the period from a displacement–time graph, then use f = 1/T before substituting.

Exam method: reading wave graphs

On a displacement–distance graph, the wavelength is the distance between two adjacent points in phase, such as two successive crests, not the distance between a crest and a trough. On a displacement–time graph, the period is the time for one complete oscillation at a fixed point. Mark the values on the axes carefully, because many lost marks come from reading half a wavelength or half a period.

title: Exam technique: Continuous Random Variables
content:
### What earns the marks
For pdf constants, total area equals 1 stated earns the method mark. For probabilities, the integral with correct limits earns each mark. For mean and variance, E(X) and E(X squared) - E(X) squared each earn credit stepwise.
### Traps
Error: point probabilities given positive values. Correction: points have zero area. Error: mean mistaken for median. Correction: solve the half-area equation for medians. Error: variance sign reversed. Correction: E(X squared) minus mean squared.
### Worked example
A pdf is f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area is 1, so the integral of kx from 0 to 2 gives 2k = 1 and k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) is the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2, which is [x²/4] from 1 to 2 = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The mean is the integral of x · x/2 from 0 to 2, which is 8/6 = 4/3.

A pdf is f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area is 1, so the integral of kx from 0 to 2 gives 2k = 1 and k = 1/2. Then P(X > 1) is the integral of x/2 from 1 to 2, which is [x²/4] from 1 to 2 = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4. The mean is the integral of x · x/2 from 0 to 2, which is 8/6 = 4/3.

title: Algebra — Inequalities — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Inequalities

Mathematics — OL. solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

  • 1. Solving
  • 2. Integer solutions
  • 3. Double inequalities
  • 4. Shading regions

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

Solve 2x − 3 < 7. Add 3 to both sides to get 2x < 10, then divide by 2 to get x < 5. If x is an integer and −2 ≤ x < 5, the integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. The bounds are inclusive on the left and exclusive on the right, so the endpoint −2 is included and 5 is not.

Common mistakes

  • Reversing the inequality sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number, for example in −3x > 6, which gives x < −2.
  • Using a solid line for a strict inequality. Use a dashed line for < or >, and a solid line for ≤ or ≥.
  • Shading the wrong side. Test a point such as (0, 0) and shade the region that makes the inequality true.

title: Exam technique: Hardware & Architecture
content:
### What earns the marks
For the fetch-execute cycle, each stage in order earns stepwise credit. For CPU parts, control unit versus ALU roles stated earn one mark each. For sensors, the named sensor matched to its use earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: RAM and ROM roles swapped. Correction: RAM is working memory, ROM holds boot code. Error: control unit claimed to compute. Correction: the ALU computes, the CU coordinates. Error: stages given out of order. Correction: fetch, decode, execute, store.### Worked example
The execute stage is where the instruction is carried out. For arithmetic or logic the ALU does the work and the result goes to a register or memory; the control unit sends the signals that make this happen. Before that, the PC holds the next address, the MAR receives it, the MDR receives the instruction and the CIR holds it while it is decoded. Give the sequence and what each part does, not just the names.
### Recall check
Describe what happens between the PC being loaded and the instruction being decoded. Explain why the PC is incremented after each fetch, in one sentence.

title: Circular Motion and SHM — Study Notes
content:
Circular Motion and SHM

Edexcel International A Level Physics, A2: circular motion in Unit 4 (WPH14) and simple harmonic motion in Unit 5 (WPH15).

Uniform circular motion

A particle moving in a circle of radius r at constant speed has a constantly changing velocity, because its direction changes. Angular speed ω is the rate of change of angle in radians per second: ω = 2π/T = 2πf. The linear speed is v = ωr.

Centripetal acceleration and force

The acceleration is directed towards the centre: a = v²/r = ω²r. The resultant force providing it is F = mv²/r = mω²r, also towards the centre. This force does no work, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity, so the kinetic energy stays constant.

Example: a particle on a 0.40 m radius with T = 2.0 s has ω = π rad s⁻¹, v = 1.26 m s⁻¹ and a = π² × 0.40 ≈ 3.9 m s⁻².

Simple harmonic motion as projected circular motion

The displacement of a point moving on a circle, projected onto a diameter, is x = x₀ sin ωt (or cos ωt). Its acceleration is a = −ω²x, always opposite to the displacement, so the defining condition for SHM is that acceleration is proportional to and opposite to displacement.

Solutions: x = x₀ sin ωt starts at the centre; x = x₀ cos ωt starts at an extreme. Time period T = 2π/ω.

Velocity and acceleration:

  • v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); v_max = ωx₀ at the centre
  • a_max = ω²x₀ at the extremes; a = 0 at the centre

Example: a pendulum with x₀ = 0.02 m and f = 0.5 Hz has a_max = (2π × 0.5)² × 0.02 ≈ 0.20 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM

The total energy is E = ½mω²x₀², constant. It is exchanged between kinetic energy (maximum at the centre) and potential energy (maximum at the extremes). Kinetic energy is at a maximum when displacement is zero, not when acceleration is largest.

Damping and resonance

Damping removes energy from the oscillator. Light damping gives slow decay of amplitude; critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating; heavy damping is slower still. A system driven at its natural frequency resonates, giving maximum amplitude (playground swings, microwave ovens, bridges that must avoid the wind frequency).

Exam tips: quote a = −ω²x as the defining condition in SHM questions. Time-period questions often need only T = 2π/ω. State which energy is at a maximum and where.

Worked example: a mass on a string

A 0.50 kg mass on a string of length 0.80 m moves in a horizontal circle at 4.0 m/s. The tension supplies the centripetal force, so T = mv²/r = 0.50 × 4.0² / 0.80 = 10 N. If the same mass is swung in a vertical circle, the tension is least at the top. The minimum speed at the top occurs when the tension falls to zero, giving v = √(gr). Here that is √(9.8 × 0.80) ≈ 2.8 m/s. Below this speed the string goes slack and the mass no longer follows the circle.

Exam method: SHM equations

Use x = A sin(ωt) or x = A cos(ωt), depending on the point at which timing starts. The maximum speed is v₀ = Aω and the maximum acceleration is a₀ = Aω². Use ω = 2π/T, and convert any frequency in hertz by multiplying by 2π before you substitute, because ω is in radians per second. For a simple pendulum at small angles, the period is T = 2π√(L/g) and does not depend on the amplitude.

title: Geometry — Angles and Polygons — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Mathematics — OL. angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

  • 1. Core angle facts
  • 2. Polygons
  • 3. Circle theorems (Extended)
  • 4. Algebra with angles

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Worked example

The interior angle sum of a polygon with n sides is (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular octagon, n = 8, so the sum is 6 × 180° = 1080°. Each interior angle is 1080 ÷ 8 = 135°, and each exterior angle is 360 ÷ 8 = 45°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon always add up to 360°.

Common mistakes

  • Using 360° for the interior sum instead of (n − 2) × 180°.
  • Confusing the angle at the centre with the angle at the circumference. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference when both subtend the same arc.
  • Writing a reason without naming the theorem. Name it, for example "angles in the same segment" or "opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°".

Worked example

title: Trigonometry — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Trigonometry

Mathematics — AS (9709). Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

Key areas to revise

  • Exact Values
  • Key Identities
  • Solving Equations
  • Graphs and Transformations
  • Using Identities

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

Solve 2 sin x = −1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°. Rearrange to sin x = −1/2. The reference angle is 30°, and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, so x = 180° + 30° = 210° and x = 360° − 30° = 330°. Both answers go in the final line, because a question that asks for "all solutions in the interval" loses marks when one is missing.

Common mistakes

  • Stopping at the calculator value and missing the second solution in the interval.
  • Giving answers in degrees when the question asks for radians, or the reverse. Check the units against the question before writing the final answer.
  • Dividing both sides of an equation by a trig expression that could be zero, which loses solutions. Factorise and set each factor to zero instead.

Worked example

Solve 2 sin x = −1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 360°. Rearrange to sin x = −1/2. The reference angle is 30°, and sine is negative in the third and fourth quadrants, so x = 180° + 30° = 210° and x = 360° − 30° = 330°. Both answers go in the final line, because a question that asks for "all solutions in the interval" loses marks when one is missing.

title: Algebra — Equations — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

Solving linear equations step by step

Collect the unknown on one side and the numbers on the other, undoing operations in the reverse order to BODMAS. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. When brackets are present, expand first, then collect like terms. Fractions are cleared by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator.

Simultaneous equations

Two linear equations in x and y can be solved by elimination (make the coefficient of one unknown equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or by substitution (rearrange one equation for one unknown and put it into the other). Check the answer in both original equations. Examiners award method marks for a correct, clearly shown elimination even when arithmetic slips later.

Rearranging formulae

Treat the subject letter as the unknown and apply inverse operations. Where the subject appears twice, gather every term containing it, factorise, then divide. Square roots or squares are undone with a square and a root, applied to both sides.

Worked example: equations with fractions

Solve 3(x − 2)/4 = x + 1. Multiply both sides by 4 to clear the denominator: 3(x − 2) = 4(x + 1), so 3x − 6 = 4x + 4, which gives −10 = x. Check by substitution: left side 3(−12)/4 = −9 and right side −10 + 1 = −9. Both agree, so x = −10.

Examiners award the method mark for clearing the fraction correctly, so write the line where every term is multiplied by the denominator before you expand.

Unknowns on both sides

Solve 5x + 3 = 2x − 9. Subtract 2x from both sides to get 3x + 3 = −9, then subtract 3 to get 3x = −12, so x = −4. Keeping the unknowns on the side where the coefficient stays positive avoids negative-sign slips.

Quadratics and the discriminant

For ax² + bx + c = 0, the discriminant b² − 4ac decides how many real roots there are. If it is positive there are two distinct real roots, if it is zero there is one repeated root, and if it is negative there are no real roots.

Example: 2x² + 3x − 5 = 0 has discriminant 9 + 40 = 49. The formula gives x = (−3 ± 7)/4, so x = 1 or x = −2.5. Check x = 1: 2 + 3 − 5 = 0.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Dividing both sides of an equation by a variable, which can lose a solution (for example x² = 4x has solutions 0 and 4).
  • Applying the quadratic formula with the wrong sign on b, for example writing −3 when b = +3 in the formula.
  • Stopping at a rearranged formula without isolating the subject, or leaving a square root unsimplified when the question asks for an exact answer.

title: Exam technique: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For electromagnets, turns plus current plus soft iron core earns each mark. For transformers, the turns ratio equation quoted earns the method mark. For induction, rate of change of flux linked to emf size earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: steel chosen for electromagnet cores. Correction: soft iron; steel suits permanent magnets. Error: Fleming hands swapped. Correction: left for motor, right for generator. Error: step-up confused with step-down. Correction: more secondary turns means step-up.
### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.
### Worked example
A transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. The primary is supplied at 240 V. The turns ratio gives Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 240 × 100 / 2000 = 12 V. More secondary turns than primary turns means a step-up transformer, so the output voltage rises.

title: Waves — Quick Revision Summary

Quick revision: Waves

  • Doppler Effect

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A wave on a rope has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Its speed is v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m s⁻¹. The same equation applies to sound and light, but the speed of light in a vacuum is 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and does not depend on the source. Intensity falls with the inverse square of distance from a point source, so doubling the distance cuts the intensity to one quarter.

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up frequency and wavelength in v = fλ, or leaving wavelength in centimetres while using metres per second.
  • Saying waves carry matter. A wave carries energy, and the particles of the medium oscillate about fixed positions.
  • Assuming polarisation applies to longitudinal waves. Only transverse waves can be polarised.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Units 4 and 5 (WPH14, WPH15), sat at A2.

The nucleus

The nucleus holds protons and neutrons, collectively nucleons. Nuclide notation ᴬZX gives Z protons and A nucleons, so N = A − Z neutrons. Isotopes share Z and differ in N. Nuclear densities are about 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³, so nearly all the mass of an atom sits in a tiny volume.

Mass defect and binding energy (23.1)

The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its separate nucleons. This difference is the mass defect Δm. Energy equivalent to Δm, given by E = Δmc², is the binding energy: the energy released when the nucleus is assembled from separate nucleons, and the energy needed to separate it. In nuclear work, 1 u = 931 MeV.

Example: a mass defect of 0.0300 u corresponds to E = 0.0300 × 931 ≈ 27.9 MeV.

The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, the most tightly bound nucleus. Energy is released when the nucleons move toward this peak, by fission of heavy nuclei or by fusion of light ones.

Radioactive decay (23.2)

Decay is random and spontaneous. The effect of each type on the nucleus and its penetration are:

TypeWhat changesStopped by
alphaZ − 2, A − 4paper
beta-minusZ + 1, A unchangeda few mm of aluminium
gammano change to Z or Athick lead

The activity A = λN is the rate of decay, in becquerel (Bq). The decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by λ = ln 2 / t½. The number of nuclei left after time t is N = N₀e^(−λt).

Example: a sample with t½ = 10 days has 1/8 of its original activity after 30 days, since three half-lives have passed.

Example: with t½ = 5.0 h = 1.8 × 10⁴ s, λ = 0.693 / 1.8 × 10⁴ ≈ 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹.

Fission and fusion

Heavy nuclei split (fission) into lighter nuclei of greater binding energy per nucleon, which releases energy in reactors. Light nuclei merge (fusion), which releases energy in stars.

Exam tips: balance Z and A on both sides of every decay equation. Convert the half-life to seconds before finding λ. Use A = λN, not guesswork with halves, when the number of nuclei is needed.

Worked example: binding energy per nucleon

Carbon-12 has six protons and six neutrons. Adding their masses gives about 12.096 u, while the carbon-12 nucleus has a mass of about 11.997 u once the electrons are removed. The mass defect is therefore about 0.099 u. Using 1 u = 931.5 MeV, the binding energy is about 92 MeV, which is about 7.7 MeV per nucleon. Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56 at about 8.8 MeV. Fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy nuclei both move products toward that peak, and that shift is why both processes release energy.

Exam method: nuclear equations

Balance the nucleon number and the proton number on each side of the equation separately. Alpha emission lowers the nucleon number by 4 and the proton number by 2. Beta-minus emission (an electron) leaves the nucleon number unchanged and raises the proton number by 1, because a neutron becomes a proton. Write the full symbol with its nucleon and proton numbers so the marker can check both conservation laws.

title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism

Physics — A2. F = BIL sin θ (Fleming's left hand: field-index, current-first-finger, force-thumb).

Key areas to revise

  • Force on a Current
  • Force on a Moving Charge
  • Fields from Currents
  • Electromagnetic Induction

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A straight wire of length 0.40 m carries a current of 2.5 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.12 T. The force is F = BIL sin θ = 0.12 × 2.5 × 0.40 × sin 90° = 0.12 N. Fleming's left hand gives the direction: the field points from the first finger (north to south), the current points along the second finger, and the force is the thumb.

Common mistakes

  • Using θ = 0° when the wire is at right angles to the field. The force is zero only when the wire is parallel to the field.
  • Mixing up the left and right hand rules. The left hand is for motors (force), and the right hand is for generators (induced current).
  • Forgetting that the force on a charge moving in a field is F = BQv, not BIL, unless you convert the current first.

title: Exam technique: Probability (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For conditional probability, the restricted sample space stated earns the method mark. For independence checks, P(A)P(B) compared with P(A and B) earns both marks. For Bayes-style updates, the tree fractions multiplied along branches earn stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: mutually exclusive assumed independent. Correction: test, never assume. Error: given-condition ignored. Correction: shrink the denominator first. Error: branches added instead of multiplied. Correction: multiply along, add across.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.
### Worked example
Event A has P(A) = 0.5 and event B has P(B) = 0.4. Given that A and B are independent, P(A and B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20. If the question instead gives P(A and B) = 0.3, then the events are not independent, because 0.3 does not equal 0.20. The conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B) = 0.3 ÷ 0.4 = 0.75.

title: Exam technique: Poisson Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For lambda scaling, the rate times the interval stated earns the first mark. For probabilities, e^-lambda lambda^x / x! with values earns the method mark. For approximations, the condition named (n large, p small, lambda = np) earns credit.
### Traps
Error: unscaled lambda over a new interval. Correction: scale first. Error: binomial coefficients inside Poisson work. Correction: Poisson formula only. Error: mean and variance treated as different. Correction: both equal lambda.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Worked example
Calls arrive at a rate of 3 per minute, so over 2 minutes λ = 6. The probability of exactly 2 calls is P(X = 2) = e⁻⁶ × 6² / 2! = 18e⁻⁶ ≈ 0.0446. The mean and the variance both equal λ, so the mean number in 2 minutes is 6.
### Check the Poisson conditions
Confirm that events occur singly, at a constant average rate and independently in the interval. Then write the model as X ~ Po(λ) with λ stated for the correct interval length.

### Scale the parameter to the interval
If the rate is given per minute and the question asks about five minutes, multiply the rate by five before you use the tables. Writing this step explicitly earns the method mark.

### Use the tables for cumulative probabilities
Read P(X ≤ r) from the table, and find P(X ≥ r) as 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1). Check the inequality direction in the question before you choose the value to subtract.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Series
content:
### What earns the marks
For AP terms, a + (n-1)d with the brackets evaluated earns the mark; sums use n/2(2a + (n-1)d) quoted. For GP work, the ratio found by division earns one mark and the formula applied earns the next. For sum to infinity, the |r| < 1 check stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: n used instead of (n-1) in terms. Correction: first term needs zero gaps. Error: infinity sums with |r| >= 1. Correction: check convergence first. Error: differentiating S_n for the nth term. Correction: subtract S_{n-1}.
### Worked example
An arithmetic progression has a = 5 and d = 3. The 20th term is a + 19d = 5 + 57 = 62. The sum of the first 20 terms is S₂₀ = (20/2)(2a + 19d) = 10 × 67 = 670. A geometric progression with terms 2, 6, 18 has r = 3, so S₅ = 2(3⁵ − 1)/(3 − 1) = 242. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, so for r = 1/2 with a = 8 the sum is 8 / (1 − 1/2) = 16.

title: Acid-base Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes
content:
Acid-base Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry

Edexcel International A Level Chemistry WCH14 Topic 14 Acid-base Equilibria builds upon GCSE and AS concepts by exploring proton transfer, the quantitative treatment of strong and weak acids and bases, pH scales, buffer solutions, titration curves, and acid dissociation constants.

Bronsed-Lowry Theory and Conjugate Pairs

Acid-base reactions involve the transfer of protons. A Brnsted-Lowry acid is defined as a proton donor, and a Brnsted-Lowry base is defined as a proton acceptor. When an acid donates a proton, it forms its conjugate base. When a base accepts a proton, it forms its conjugate acid. These species form conjugate acid-base pairs that differ by a single proton (H+).

  • Brnsted-Lowry acid: a proton (H+) donor.
  • Brnsted-Lowry base: a proton (H+) acceptor.
  • Conjugate acid-base pair: two species related by the gain or loss of a single proton, written as acid / conjugate base or base / conjugate acid.
  • In the reaction between ethanoic acid and water, CH3COOH and CH3COO- form one pair, while H3O+ and H2O form the other pair.

pH Scale and Calculations

The term pH is defined as the negative logarithm to the base 10 of the hydrogen ion concentration in aqueous solution, expressed mathematically. A ten-fold change in hydrogen ion concentration causes a change of one pH unit.

  • pH definition: pH = −log10[H+]
  • Hydrogen ion concentration from pH: [H+] = 10^(−pH)
  • Ionic product of water, Kw, is defined as Kw = [H+][OH−] with a value of 1.0 × 10^(−14) mol2 dm−6 at 298 K.
  • pKa is defined as −log10(Ka) and pKw is defined as −log10(Kw).
  • For strong bases, calculate pOH = −log10[OH−] and use pH = 14.00 − pOH at 298 K, or use [H+] = Kw / [OH−] before finding the pH.

Worked Example: Calculate the pH of 0.050 mol dm−3 sodium hydroxide at 298 K.

  • Step 1: Identify [OH−] = 0.050 mol dm−3 because NaOH is a strong base and dissociates completely.
  • Step 2: Calculate pOH = −log10(0.050) = 1.30.
  • Step 3: Calculate pH = 14.00 − 1.30 = 12.70.

Strong and Weak Acids and Experimental Analysis

A strong acid dissociates completely in water, meaning the concentration of hydrogen ions equals the concentration of the acid. A weak acid dissociates only partly in water, establishing an equilibrium. The degree of dissociation is much lower for weak acids than for strong acids.

  • Strong acid: dissociates completely, so [H+] = [acid]. For 0.010 mol dm−3 HCl, [H+] = 0.010 mol dm−3 and pH = 2.00.
  • Weak acid: dissociates partially, represented by HA ⇌ H+ + A−.
  • Acid dissociation constant expression: Ka = [H+][A−] / [HA].
  • Experimental analysis involves measuring the pH of a variety of substances, including equimolar solutions of strong and weak acids, strong and weak bases, and salts. Strong acids have much lower pH values than weak acids of the same concentration.
  • Comparing the pH of a strong acid and a weak acid after dilution 10, 100, and 1000 times shows that diluting a strong acid by a factor of 10 increases its pH by 1 unit, whereas diluting a weak acid by a factor of 10 increases its pH by less than 1 unit due to partial re-dissociation of the weak acid.

Worked Example: Calculate the pH of 0.100 mol dm−3 propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH, given that Ka = 1.35 × 10^(−5) mol dm−3.

  • Step 1: Write the expression Ka = [H+]2 / [HA], assuming [H+] = [A−] and [HA]equilibrium equals initial [HA] because dissociation is very small.
  • Step 2: Rearrange to [H+] = √(Ka × [HA]) = √(1.35 × 10^(−5) × 0.100) = √(1.35 × 10^(−6)) = 1.16 × 10^(−3) mol dm−3.
  • Step 3: Calculate pH = −log10(1.16 × 10^(−3)) = 2.93.

Core Practical 11 and Determining Ka from Experimental Data

Core Practical 11 involves finding the Ka value for a weak acid by measuring the pH of solutions of known concentration, or by using titration methods and half-equivalence points.

  • To calculate Ka for a weak acid from experimental data given the pH of a solution containing a known mass of acid, first calculate the concentration of the acid in mol dm−3.
  • Use [H+] = 10^(−pH) to find the hydrogen ion concentration.
  • Substitute [H+], [OH−] approximations, and remaining undissociated acid concentration into Ka = [H+]2 / [HA].
  • In weak acid-strong base or strong acid-weak base titrations, at the exact point where half the acid is neutralised, [HA] = [A−], which simplifies the buffer equation to pH = pKa, allowing Ka to be determined directly from the pH reading at that volume.

Titration Curves and Indicators

Titration curves plot pH against volume of titrant added. They cover all combinations of strong and weak monoprotic and diprotic acids with bases.

  • Strong acid and strong base curve starts low, has a steep vertical section from pH 3 to 11 at the equivalence point of pH 7.
  • Weak acid and strong base curve starts higher (around pH 3), has a buffer region, and a steep vertical section from pH 7 to 11 with an equivalence point above pH 7.
  • Strong acid and weak base curve has a steep vertical section from pH 3 to 7 with an equivalence point below pH 7.
  • Weak acid and weak base curves show no sharp vertical pH change, making titrations difficult without a pH meter.
  • Diprotic acids show two distinct equivalence points corresponding to the donation of two protons per molecule.
  • Indicator selection: choose an indicator whose pH range falls entirely within the steep vertical section of the titration curve. Phenolphthalein (pH range 8.3 to 10.0) is suitable for weak acid-strong base titrations. Methyl orange (pH range 3.1 to 4.4) is suitable for strong acid-weak base titrations.

Buffer Solutions

A buffer solution is a system that minimises changes in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added. An acidic buffer consists of a weak acid and its salt (providing the conjugate base), such as ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate.

  • Buffer action: when H+ is added, it reacts with the conjugate base (A−) to form undissociated weak acid (HA), removing excess H+. When OH− is added, it reacts with H+ ions (or HA directly) to form water, pulling the equilibrium to the right to replace the H+ ions.
  • Buffer pH calculation formula: pH = pKa + log([A−] / [HA]).
  • To calculate concentrations required to prepare a buffer solution of a given pH, rearrange the buffer formula using target pH, known Ka, and ratio of salt to acid.
  • Biological importance: buffers in cells and in blood, specifically the carbonic acid-hydrogencarbonate system (H2CO3 / HCO3−), maintain blood pH strictly between 7.35 and 7.45.
  • Importance in foods: buffers and acidulants prevent deterioration due to pH changes caused by bacterial or fungal activity, preserving texture and safety.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Assuming weak acids dissociate completely. Correction: Always use Ka expressions and make the standard weak acid approximation [HA]start equals [HA]equilibrium.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that Kw varies with temperature and treating 1.0 × 10^(−14) as universal at all temperatures. Correction: Use 1.0 × 10^(−14) mol2 dm−6 strictly for 298 K unless specified otherwise.
  • Mistake: Selecting methyl orange for a weak acid-strong base titration. Correction: Methyl orange changes colour below pH 7, whereas the equivalence point of a weak acid-strong base titration is above pH 7; use phenolphthalein instead.
  • Mistake: Confusing conjugate acid-base pairs by omitting charges or hydrogen atoms. Correction: Check that pairs differ by exactly one H+ ion.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: Define a Brnsted-Lowry acid. Answer: A proton donor. Step: State the definition clearly for credit.
  2. Question: Calculate the pH of 0.0200 mol dm−3 hydrochloric acid. Answer: [H+] = 0.0200 mol dm−3, so pH = −log10(0.0200) = 1.70. Step: Recognise complete dissociation of strong acid and apply pH formula.
  3. Question: Write the expression for the acid dissociation constant, Ka, for propanoic acid. Answer: Ka = [H+][CH3CH2COO−] / [CH3CH2COOH]. Step: Include all equilibrium concentrations correctly.
  4. Question: Explain why the pH of a weak acid changes less than that of a strong acid upon 10-fold dilution. Answer: Diluting a weak acid shifts the equilibrium to the right, causing further dissociation which partially compensates for the added water volume. Step: Mention equilibrium shift and partial dissociation.
  5. Question: State the buffer pair present in blood plasma. Answer: H2CO3 and HCO3−. Step: Name carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate ions.

Use these notes alongside past paper practice questions for Edexcel IAL Chemistry Topic 14. Ensure all formula manipulations for Ka and buffer calculations are practiced thoroughly before moving on to Topic 15 Energetics II.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Weak acid pH, applied to 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ethanoic acid with Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵: [H⁺] = √(Ka × c) = √(1.74 × 10⁻⁶) = 1.32 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, so pH = 2.88. The square-root shortcut is valid only when dissociation is under about 5%; check that before you use it.
  • Buffer pH, applied to an equimolar ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate buffer: pH = pKa + log([A⁻] ÷ [HA]). With equal concentrations, pH = pKa = 4.76. Doubling the base raises the pH by log 2, about 0.30 units. Say which ratio you have used.
  • Indicator choice: a strong acid with a strong base needs an indicator that changes within the steep part of the curve, such as methyl orange or phenolphthalein. A weak acid with a strong base ends above pH 7, so phenolphthalein is the usual choice. Methyl orange changes too early for that titration.
  • Mark-scheme phrasing: a weak acid is only partly dissociated, so [H⁺] is much less than the stated acid concentration. State that the dissociation is small before you simplify the expression.

title:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 2 Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression. It covers membrane structure and properties, osmosis and the different kinds of membrane transport, the structure of proteins and how they are built from amino acids, the structure of DNA and RNA and how DNA replicates, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation, mutations and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as an example of a gene mutation in humans, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cell membranes and the fluid mosaic model

The cell surface membrane (plasma membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer; each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, and the heads face out and in while the tails face each other, making a barrier to charged and water-soluble substances. The fluid mosaic model is the accepted interpretation: the membrane is fluid — the phospholipids and proteins can move laterally in the layer — and mosaic because it contains a variety of proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer, including channel proteins and carrier proteins for transport, receptor proteins for signalling, and proteins for cell recognition. The model is an interpretation of data — it was built from evidence such as electron micrographs and the ability of membranes to fuse and to self-seal — and it explains the structure and properties of cell membranes and how they control what enters and leaves the cell. Cholesterol in the membrane reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid at low temperatures.

2. Core Practical 3 — investigating membrane properties

Investigate membrane properties including the effect of alcohol and of temperature on membrane permeability. A typical method uses beetroot cylinders, which contain the red pigment betalain in their vacuoles; as the membrane is damaged, pigment leaks out and the colour of the surrounding solution deepens. Cut cylinders to the same length, wash off surface pigment in distilled water, then place them in water at a range of temperatures or in different concentrations of alcohol for a fixed time, remove the tissue and measure the concentration of pigment in the solution with a colorimeter. As temperature rises or alcohol concentration rises, the membrane proteins denature and the lipid bilayer is disrupted, so permeability increases and more pigment leaks out; a control at room temperature or in distilled water shows the baseline. Record the colorimeter reading for each tube, plot a graph of permeability against temperature or against alcohol concentration, and explain the trend in terms of the effect on membrane proteins and lipids.

3. Osmosis and how water moves across membranes

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient — from higher water potential to lower water potential. Water potential is the tendency of water to move; adding a solute lowers it, so a concentrated solution has a more negative water potential than a dilute one, and pure water has the highest (zero) water potential. If a cell is placed in a solution of higher water potential than its contents, water enters by osmosis and the cell swells; if it is an animal cell it may burst (haemolysis); if it is a plant cell the cell wall prevents bursting and the cell becomes turgid, which supports the plant. In a solution of lower water potential, water leaves and the cell shrinks — animal cells crenate and plant cells become plasmolysed, with the membrane pulling away from the wall. A recommended additional practical is to investigate tissue water potentials using plant tissue (for example potato or onion epidermis) and graded concentrations of a solute: place tissue in solutions of different molarity, note the change in length or mass, and find the concentration at which there is no change — that concentration has the same water potential as the tissue.

4. Passive transport, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis

Passive transport needs no energy input because substances move down their concentration gradient. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration; small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer, while ions and large polar molecules cannot. Facilitated diffusion is the movement of specific particles down their concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins — channel proteins form water-filled pores for ions, and carrier proteins change shape to carry molecules across. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and needs energy directly from ATP; carrier proteins use ATP to pump substances across, as in the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell inside a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane; phagocytosis takes in solid material and pinocytosis takes in fluid. Exocytosis is the reverse — material is moved out of the cell in a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane, as in the secretion of proteins and neurotransmitters. Carrier and channel proteins are involved in facilitated diffusion and active transport; the key difference is that active transport needs ATP and moves substances against their gradient.

5. Protein structure: from amino acid to three-dimensional shape

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure of an amino acid is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group all attached to a central carbon, with a hydrogen on the remaining bond. There are around 20 amino acids found in proteins, differing only in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein is its primary structure. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and then polypeptides; a polypeptide chain is a protein's primary structure and it determines everything about the protein. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it gives the protein its specific shape and therefore its function. Globular proteins are roughly spherical and usually soluble and active — haemoglobin is the classic example, with four polypeptide chains and a haem group each carrying one oxygen molecule, and it shows quaternary structure (several polypeptides together) plus the importance of the three-dimensional shape for its oxygen-carrying function. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and structural — collagen is the example, made of three polypeptide chains wound into a rope-like triple helix, giving strength for tendons, ligaments and skin. The shape of a protein determines its function, so a change to the primary structure can alter the folding and disable the protein.

6. DNA structure and replication

A DNA molecule is made of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a base — either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T). The two strands run antiparallel and are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and C pairs with G (three hydrogen bonds). RNA is similar but has ribose instead of deoxyribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. The two strands are complementary, so knowing one strand tells you the other, and the two strands separate at replication. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, and free nucleotides pair with their complementary bases; DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides into a new strand. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl's experiment supported this: they grew bacteria in a medium with a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N), then moved them to a 14N medium and examined the DNA by centrifugation; the first generation was a single hybrid band (not one heavy and one light, which would be conservative replication), and later generations showed a mixture of hybrid and light bands — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.

7. The genetic code and how it works

The genetic code is the set of rules translating the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a protein. It is a triplet code — three bases (a base triplet on DNA, a codon on mRNA) code for one amino acid; it is non-overlapping — each base is read once in order; and it is degenerate — more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, which is why many mutations change a base but not the amino acid. Part of the code is a stop codon that signals the end of translation; there is no amino acid for it. A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In transcription, the gene is copied into a complementary mRNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase, using the DNA template (antisense) strand; the mRNA is complementary to the template strand and the same as the coding (sense) strand except with uracil in place of thymine. mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to ribosomes in the cytoplasm; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome, each with a three-base anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon, so the ribosome joins the amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the order of the codons until a stop codon is reached.

8. Mutations: the changes and their effects

A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another — it may do nothing, change one amino acid, or, rarely, create a stop codon that shortens the protein. An insertion adds one or more bases and a deletion removes one or more; because the code is read in triplets, an insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation and usually destroying the protein's function. Mutations are the only source of new alleles, and most have no observable effect — they may be in non-coding DNA, or a degenerate codon and amino acid may stay the same, or the changed protein still folds and works. Some mutations give rise to cancer (if they affect control of the cell cycle) or to genetic disorders. Ionising radiation such as X-rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, can increase the rate of mutation by damaging DNA.

9. Patterns of inheritance: monohybrid crosses, pedigree diagrams and sex linkage

A gene can have different alleles; the genotype is the alleles an organism has, the phenotype is the observable feature. Dominant alleles show in the phenotype even when heterozygous; recessive alleles only show when homozygous. A monohybrid cross is the inheritance of one gene with two alleles; the typical ratios are a 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, but only if the alleles are completely dominant and the gene is autosomal. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene on the X chromosome — because males have only one X, a recessive allele on it shows in their phenotype even though they are effectively hemizygous; red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are human X-linked conditions that are more common in males. Pedigree diagrams record which family members show a trait and are used to work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked. Codominance is when both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, as in the ABO blood group system where IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive, giving the four blood groups A, B, AB and O.

10. Cystic fibrosis: a mutation that affects three systems

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for a chloride ion channel protein; in the most common form a deletion of three bases removes a single amino acid from the protein, so the channel does not work properly. As a result, chloride ions and water cannot move properly across cell membranes, and the mucus and other secretions become abnormally thick. In the gaseous exchange system the thick mucus blocks the airways and makes it hard to breathe and to clear infections; in the digestive system the pancreatic duct is blocked so digestive enzymes from the pancreas cannot reach the gut, so food is not digested and absorbed properly, and the person may be malnourished; in the reproductive system the vas deferens is often absent or blocked in males, causing infertility. Treatments include physiotherapy and antibiotics for the lungs, and enzyme supplements with meals for digestion, and newer treatments aim to correct the underlying defect.

11. Genetic screening: what it can do and the issues it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of recessive alleles (people who have one normal allele and one faulty allele and are unaffected but could pass the allele on), and prenatal testing can check a fetus: amniocentesis takes a sample of amniotic fluid at around 15–17 weeks, and chorionic villus sampling takes a sample of placental tissue at 8–12 weeks. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is used with IVF to test embryos before implantation and select unaffected ones. Each raises ethical and social questions — the safety and reliability of the test, the risks of miscarriage with invasive prenatal testing, the right to know or not to know, who decides which conditions to test for, the possible choice to terminate a pregnancy, anxiety and guilt, and the risk that screening could be used to select non-medical traits. Students should be able to identify and discuss these from religious, moral and social viewpoints and to evaluate the implications of prenatal genetic screening.

12. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can draw a cell membrane from the fluid mosaic model and label the phospholipid bilayer, the proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; state the difference between diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport, and give an example of each; outline the steps of DNA extraction (a simple practical with strawberries or onions is useful to remember); and carry out a genetic cross with a Punnett square and interpret the ratios. Revise by drawing protein structure from amino acid to tertiary, then drawing the DNA double helix and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson–Stahl evidence. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development, because the same DNA and protein-synthesis processes control cell differentiation and the cell cycle.
content:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI11 Unit 1, Topic 2 Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression. It covers membrane structure and properties, osmosis and the different kinds of membrane transport, the structure of proteins and how they are built from amino acids, the structure of DNA and RNA and how DNA replicates, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation, mutations and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as an example of a gene mutation in humans, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cell membranes and the fluid mosaic model

The cell surface membrane (plasma membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer; each phospholipid has a hydrophilic head and two hydrophobic tails, and the heads face out and in while the tails face each other, making a barrier to charged and water-soluble substances. The fluid mosaic model is the accepted interpretation: the membrane is fluid — the phospholipids and proteins can move laterally in the layer — and mosaic because it contains a variety of proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer, including channel proteins and carrier proteins for transport, receptor proteins for signalling, and proteins for cell recognition. The model is an interpretation of data — it was built from evidence such as electron micrographs and the ability of membranes to fuse and to self-seal — and it explains the structure and properties of cell membranes and how they control what enters and leaves the cell. Cholesterol in the membrane reduces fluidity at high temperatures and prevents the membrane from becoming too rigid at low temperatures.

2. Core Practical 3 — investigating membrane properties

Investigate membrane properties including the effect of alcohol and of temperature on membrane permeability. A typical method uses beetroot cylinders, which contain the red pigment betalain in their vacuoles; as the membrane is damaged, pigment leaks out and the colour of the surrounding solution deepens. Cut cylinders to the same length, wash off surface pigment in distilled water, then place them in water at a range of temperatures or in different concentrations of alcohol for a fixed time, remove the tissue and measure the concentration of pigment in the solution with a colorimeter. As temperature rises or alcohol concentration rises, the membrane proteins denature and the lipid bilayer is disrupted, so permeability increases and more pigment leaks out; a control at room temperature or in distilled water shows the baseline. Record the colorimeter reading for each tube, plot a graph of permeability against temperature or against alcohol concentration, and explain the trend in terms of the effect on membrane proteins and lipids.

3. Osmosis and how water moves across membranes

Osmosis is the net movement of free water molecules through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient — from higher water potential to lower water potential. Water potential is the tendency of water to move; adding a solute lowers it, so a concentrated solution has a more negative water potential than a dilute one, and pure water has the highest (zero) water potential. If a cell is placed in a solution of higher water potential than its contents, water enters by osmosis and the cell swells; if it is an animal cell it may burst (haemolysis); if it is a plant cell the cell wall prevents bursting and the cell becomes turgid, which supports the plant. In a solution of lower water potential, water leaves and the cell shrinks — animal cells crenate and plant cells become plasmolysed, with the membrane pulling away from the wall. A recommended additional practical is to investigate tissue water potentials using plant tissue (for example potato or onion epidermis) and graded concentrations of a solute: place tissue in solutions of different molarity, note the change in length or mass, and find the concentration at which there is no change — that concentration has the same water potential as the tissue.

4. Passive transport, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis

Passive transport needs no energy input because substances move down their concentration gradient. Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration; small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer, while ions and large polar molecules cannot. Facilitated diffusion is the movement of specific particles down their concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins — channel proteins form water-filled pores for ions, and carrier proteins change shape to carry molecules across. Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient (from low to high concentration) and needs energy directly from ATP; carrier proteins use ATP to pump substances across, as in the sodium–potassium pump. Endocytosis is the bulk movement of material into the cell inside a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane; phagocytosis takes in solid material and pinocytosis takes in fluid. Exocytosis is the reverse — material is moved out of the cell in a vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane, as in the secretion of proteins and neurotransmitters. Carrier and channel proteins are involved in facilitated diffusion and active transport; the key difference is that active transport needs ATP and moves substances against their gradient.

5. Protein structure: from amino acid to three-dimensional shape

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure of an amino acid is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group all attached to a central carbon, with a hydrogen on the remaining bond. There are around 20 amino acids found in proteins, differing only in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein is its primary structure. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and then polypeptides; a polypeptide chain is a protein''s primary structure and it determines everything about the protein. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between the peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it gives the protein its specific shape and therefore its function. Globular proteins are roughly spherical and usually soluble and active — haemoglobin is the classic example, with four polypeptide chains and a haem group each carrying one oxygen molecule, and it shows quaternary structure (several polypeptides together) plus the importance of the three-dimensional shape for its oxygen-carrying function. Fibrous proteins are long, insoluble and structural — collagen is the example, made of three polypeptide chains wound into a rope-like triple helix, giving strength for tendons, ligaments and skin. The shape of a protein determines its function, so a change to the primary structure can alter the folding and disable the protein.

6. DNA structure and replication

A DNA molecule is made of two nucleotide strands twisted into a double helix. Each nucleotide is made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a base — either adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T). The two strands run antiparallel and are linked by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) and C pairs with G (three hydrogen bonds). RNA is similar but has ribose instead of deoxyribose, uracil instead of thymine, and is usually single-stranded. The two strands are complementary, so knowing one strand tells you the other, and the two strands separate at replication. DNA replication is semi-conservative: the double helix unzips, each strand acts as a template, and free nucleotides pair with their complementary bases; DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides into a new strand. The result is two identical DNA molecules, each with one old strand and one new strand. Meselson and Stahl''s experiment supported this: they grew bacteria in a medium with a heavy isotope of nitrogen (15N), then moved them to a 14N medium and examined the DNA by centrifugation; the first generation was a single hybrid band (not one heavy and one light, which would be conservative replication), and later generations showed a mixture of hybrid and light bands — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.

7. The genetic code and how it works

The genetic code is the set of rules translating the base sequence of mRNA into the amino acid sequence of a protein. It is a triplet code — three bases (a base triplet on DNA, a codon on mRNA) code for one amino acid; it is non-overlapping — each base is read once in order; and it is degenerate — more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, which is why many mutations change a base but not the amino acid. Part of the code is a stop codon that signals the end of translation; there is no amino acid for it. A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. In transcription, the gene is copied into a complementary mRNA molecule by the enzyme RNA polymerase, using the DNA template (antisense) strand; the mRNA is complementary to the template strand and the same as the coding (sense) strand except with uracil in place of thymine. mRNA leaves the nucleus and attaches to ribosomes in the cytoplasm; transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry amino acids to the ribosome, each with a three-base anticodon that pairs with the mRNA codon, so the ribosome joins the amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the order of the codons until a stop codon is reached.

8. Mutations: the changes and their effects

A mutation is a change in the DNA base sequence. A substitution replaces one base with another — it may do nothing, change one amino acid, or, rarely, create a stop codon that shortens the protein. An insertion adds one or more bases and a deletion removes one or more; because the code is read in triplets, an insertion or deletion not in a multiple of three causes a frameshift, changing every amino acid after the mutation and usually destroying the protein''s function. Mutations are the only source of new alleles, and most have no observable effect — they may be in non-coding DNA, or a degenerate codon and amino acid may stay the same, or the changed protein still folds and works. Some mutations give rise to cancer (if they affect control of the cell cycle) or to genetic disorders. Ionising radiation such as X-rays and ultraviolet light, and some chemicals such as those in tobacco smoke, can increase the rate of mutation by damaging DNA.

9. Patterns of inheritance: monohybrid crosses, pedigree diagrams and sex linkage

A gene can have different alleles; the genotype is the alleles an organism has, the phenotype is the observable feature. Dominant alleles show in the phenotype even when heterozygous; recessive alleles only show when homozygous. A monohybrid cross is the inheritance of one gene with two alleles; the typical ratios are a 3:1 phenotype ratio in the F2 of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes, but only if the alleles are completely dominant and the gene is autosomal. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene on the X chromosome — because males have only one X, a recessive allele on it shows in their phenotype even though they are effectively hemizygous; red-green colour blindness and haemophilia are human X-linked conditions that are more common in males. Pedigree diagrams record which family members show a trait and are used to work out whether a trait is dominant or recessive and whether it is autosomal or sex-linked. Codominance is when both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote, as in the ABO blood group system where IA and IB are codominant and i is recessive, giving the four blood groups A, B, AB and O.

10. Cystic fibrosis: a mutation that affects three systems

Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation in a gene that codes for a chloride ion channel protein; in the most common form a deletion of three bases removes a single amino acid from the protein, so the channel does not work properly. As a result, chloride ions and water cannot move properly across cell membranes, and the mucus and other secretions become abnormally thick. In the gaseous exchange system the thick mucus blocks the airways and makes it hard to breathe and to clear infections; in the digestive system the pancreatic duct is blocked so digestive enzymes from the pancreas cannot reach the gut, so food is not digested and absorbed properly, and the person may be malnourished; in the reproductive system the vas deferens is often absent or blocked in males, causing infertility. Treatments include physiotherapy and antibiotics for the lungs, and enzyme supplements with meals for digestion, and newer treatments aim to correct the underlying defect.

11. Genetic screening: what it can do and the issues it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of recessive alleles (people who have one normal allele and one faulty allele and are unaffected but could pass the allele on), and prenatal testing can check a fetus: amniocentesis takes a sample of amniotic fluid at around 15–17 weeks, and chorionic villus sampling takes a sample of placental tissue at 8–12 weeks. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is used with IVF to test embryos before implantation and select unaffected ones. Each raises ethical and social questions — the safety and reliability of the test, the risks of miscarriage with invasive prenatal testing, the right to know or not to know, who decides which conditions to test for, the possible choice to terminate a pregnancy, anxiety and guilt, and the risk that screening could be used to select non-medical traits. Students should be able to identify and discuss these from religious, moral and social viewpoints and to evaluate the implications of prenatal genetic screening.

12. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can draw a cell membrane from the fluid mosaic model and label the phospholipid bilayer, the proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins; state the difference between diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport, and give an example of each; outline the steps of DNA extraction (a simple practical with strawberries or onions is useful to remember); and carry out a genetic cross with a Punnett square and interpret the ratios. Revise by drawing protein structure from amino acid to tertiary, then drawing the DNA double helix and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson–Stahl evidence. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development, because the same DNA and protein-synthesis processes control cell differentiation and the cell cycle.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Osmosis, applied to a potato cylinder placed in a sugar solution: water moves from the higher water potential to the lower one, down a gradient, through a partially permeable membrane. A cylinder that loses mass has been placed in a solution of lower water potential than its cells. Give the direction of water movement and the reason in the same sentence.
  • Monohybrid cross, applied to two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa): the offspring are 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so the phenotypic ratio is 3 : 1. Write the parental genotypes, the gametes and the Punnett square, then state the ratio. A ratio alone earns less than the full working.
  • Sex linkage, applied to X-linked haemophilia: a carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) and a normal father (XᴴY) have a 50% chance of a son with haemophilia, but a daughter cannot be affected unless her father is affected. Use the X and Y chromosomes explicitly in the genotypes.
  • Mutation effects: a substitution may have no effect because the genetic code is degenerate, while a frameshift changes every codon after the mutation. Name the type of mutation and state whether the change alters the amino acid sequence.
