title: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data — Study Notes
content:
Simulation, Sensors and Real Data

Syllabus note: 9618 has no separate simulation-and-sensors section; this material supports practical work (data logging, modelling, sensor input), including Paper 4.

Simulation and Modelling

A simulation is a program that models a real system to test scenarios safely and cheaply: weather models, traffic flows, epidemic spread. Models use abstractions — chosen variables and equations — with a time step. Advantages: no real-world risk, repeatable, faster or slower than real time. Limitations: only as good as the model; rare events may be missed.

Sensors and Signals

Sensors measure physical quantities: temperature (thermistor), light (LDR), pressure, humidity, sound. Most output analogue signals varying continuously; computers need digital values, so an ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) samples the signal. Resolution depends on bits — an 8-bit ADC gives 256 levels. A DAC converts digital output back to analogue for actuators or speakers.

Monitoring vs Control

  • Monitoring: sensors feed data to the computer, which only records, displays or raises alarms — no action taken on the environment.
  • Control: the computer acts via actuators (motors, valves, heaters) based on sensor input — the classic feedback loop.

Real-Time Considerations

Control systems are often real-time: late output can be wrong output. Sampling rate must exceed twice the highest signal frequency (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.

Exam tips: distinguish monitoring from control with a named example; describe the role of ADC and DAC in a greenhouse system; explain one limitation of a simulation.

Exam method: using simulation output with real data

Sensor readings are noisy, drift over time and can contain missing or impossible values. Before using them, check each reading against a sensible range, remove or flag outliers, and decide how to handle gaps, for example by ignoring them or interpolating between neighbouring readings. State which cleaning step you chose.

A simulation is only as reliable as its assumptions and its inputs. In an exam answer, state one assumption the model makes, explain how it could make the output differ from reality, and suggest a way to test the model against measured data.

Exam cue: When asked to evaluate a simulation, give a specific limitation tied to the scenario in the question rather than a general comment that simulations are approximate.

Worked example: comparing simulation output with real data

A simulation predicts a mean room temperature of 24.0 °C. Sensors in the real room record a mean of 25.3 °C. The difference is 25.3 minus 24.0, which is 1.3 °C. The percentage error is the difference divided by the real value, so 1.3 divided by 25.3 gives about 5.1 per cent. State the direction of the error as well as its size: the model underestimates the real temperature.

Then suggest a cause that the model could plausibly miss, such as heat from windows, occupants or equipment. A good evaluation names one assumption in the simulation and says how changing it would move the output closer to the real data.

Why real-time systems differ from batch simulations

  • A real-time system must respond within a fixed deadline, so a late result is a failure even when it is correct.
  • A batch simulation can run to completion and be checked afterwards, whereas a control system acts on each reading as it arrives.
  • Sampling rate matters: sample too slowly and fast changes are missed entirely, which is an aliasing risk.

title: Networking & Communication — Study Notes
content:
Networking & Communication

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): transmission modes, serial/parallel, packet switching, protocols, LAN/WAN, hardware, security layers.

1. Transmission basics

  • Serial: one bit at a time — reliable over distance, cheaper cable.
  • Parallel: several bits at once — faster over short runs; skew/crosstalk limit distance.
  • Simplex / half-duplex / full-duplex direction; bandwidth (bits/s) vs bit rate.

2. Packets

Header (sender/receiver addresses, sequence number) + payload + trailer (checksum). Packet switching: routes vary, packets reassembled at destination; checksum failure → re-request. Benefits: robustness, shared lines; delays/reassembly overhead.

3. Protocols

TCP/IP stack layers (application, transport, network, link). HTTP/HTTPS (TLS encryption), FTP (with login + commands), email: SMTP send, POP3/IMAP retrieve. Bluetooth/Wi-Fi for WPAN/WLAN.

4. Network types & hardware

LAN (site) vs WAN (internet). Router (joins networks, IP), switch (MAC frames within LAN), gateway (protocol translation), NIC, WAP. MAC address (burned-in, layer 2) vs IP address (assigned, layer 3).

5. Security in transmission

Encryption scrambles plaintext → ciphertext (key needed); HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; firewall packet filtering by port/IP; authentication (user+pass, 2FA); access levels.

Exam tips: explain why skew limits parallel over distance; compare MAC vs IP in a table; protocol questions want "rules for communication", not acronyms alone.

Packet switching and protocols

In packet switching, a message is divided into packets. Each packet carries a header with its source and destination addresses and a sequence number, so it can travel by any available route. The packets are reassembled in the correct order at the destination. Packet switching makes efficient use of the network, because no dedicated connection is held open for the whole transmission.

A protocol is an agreed set of rules that devices follow to communicate. TCP/IP is the set of protocols used on the internet. TCP splits data into packets and checks that they arrive, while IP handles addressing and routing between networks.

Exam tip: explain a protocol as a set of rules, and give one example of what it governs, such as addressing or error checking.

Worked example: working out a subnet

A device has the IP address 192.168.1.10 with the subnet mask 255.255.255.0. Applying the mask with a bitwise AND gives the network address 192.168.1.0. The first usable host address is 192.168.1.1 and the last is 192.168.1.254, because the all-zeros address is the network and the all-ones address is the broadcast. Question setters often ask for the broadcast address, which here is 192.168.1.255.

Packets, protocols and layers

  • A message is split into packets. Each packet carries a header with the source and destination addresses and a sequence number so the receiver can rebuild the message in order.
  • Protocols define the rules for each layer. TCP checks for lost packets and requests a resend, while UDP sends without that checking, which suits live video and gaming.

title: Kinematics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Kinematics

Physics — AS. Sign convention matters: take up as positive and g = −9.81 m s⁻² for falling objects.

Key areas to revise

  • Definitions
  • Graphs
  • SUVAT (uniform acceleration only)
  • Projectiles

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked example

A ball is dropped from rest and falls 20 m. Taking down as positive, u = 0, s = 20 m and a = 9.81 m s⁻². Then v² = u² + 2as = 392.4, so v ≈ 19.8 m s⁻¹. Using the sign convention with up positive instead gives s = −20 m and a = −9.81 m s⁻², which gives the same answer with the signs consistent.

Common mistakes

  • Using SUVAT for a case with non-uniform acceleration, such as a body with increasing air resistance.
  • Mixing signs, for example taking up as positive but using g = +9.81 m s⁻².
  • Reading a displacement–time gradient as velocity only when it is a straight line. The gradient gives instantaneous velocity at any point on a curve.

title: Statistics — Probability — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Probability

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): probability scale, combined events, tree diagrams, conditional probability, relative frequency.

1. Basics

P(event) = favourable/total; 0 ≤ P ≤ 1; P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Probabilities of a complete set sum to 1 — use to find a missing probability.

2. Combined events

  • Independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • With replacement ⇒ independent; without replacement ⇒ denominators shrink.

Example: bag 4 red, 6 blue; two draws without replacement: P(both red) = 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15.

3. Tree diagrams

Multiply along branches; add between outcome paths. Label end products like 4/10 × 6/9 = 4/15.

4. Conditional probability

P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). From tree diagrams it is the "given the first branch happened" re-weighting.

5. Relative frequency (experimental)

Relative frequency = successes ÷ trials. More trials → closer to theoretical probability; compare with expected counts (n × P).

Exam tips: always reduce fractions for final answers; in tree diagrams write the multiplication line before the product — that is where the marks are.

Probability scale and notation

Probabilities lie between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), and may be written as fractions, decimals or percentages. The probabilities of all outcomes in a sample space add up to 1, so the probability of an event not happening is 1 minus the probability it happens.

Combined events and tree diagrams

For independent events, multiply the probabilities along the branches. For events without replacement, the second probabilities change, so recalculate the denominators on the second set of branches. Add the probabilities of separate routes that give the required outcome.

Expected frequency

Expected frequency is the probability multiplied by the number of trials. For example, if a coin is tossed 200 times the expected number of heads is 200 × 0.5 = 100.

Worked example: drawing without replacement

A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two counters are taken without replacement. P(red, red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10. P(blue, blue) = 2/5 × 1/4 = 1/10. P(one of each) = 1 − 3/10 − 1/10 = 6/10 = 3/5. The probabilities of all the outcomes must add up to 1, so use this as a check.

With replacement and at least one

If the first counter is replaced, the second draw has the same probabilities. P(at least one red) is quicker through the complement: 1 − P(no red) = 1 − (2/5 × 2/5) = 21/25. Use the complement whenever the phrase "at least one" appears.

Mutually exclusive and independent events

  • Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen, so P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • Independent events do not affect each other, so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Test independence by checking whether P(A and B) equals this product.
  • Probabilities always lie between 0 and 1 inclusive. An answer outside this range signals an error.

Exam point: give probabilities as exact fractions unless the question asks for a decimal, and round only the final answer, to the accuracy the question requests.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Study Notes
content:
Hypothesis Testing

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 2 (WST02), sat at A2.

The Framework

The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Test for a Binomial Proportion

With X ~ B(n, p₀) under H₀, compute the probability of results at least as extreme as the observed count in the direction of H₁.

Example: H₀: p = 0.3 against H₁: p > 0.3, observed 10 successes in n = 20. Compute P(X ≥ 10) under B(20, 0.3). If that tail probability is below α, reject H₀.

One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed

One-tailed tests take the whole α in one direction. Two-tailed tests split α across both tails: compare against α/2 on each side, or equivalently check whether the observation falls in the extreme 2.5% (for α = 5%). Choose the tails from the wording of H₁, not from the data.

Critical Regions

The critical region is the set of values of the test statistic that would lead to rejection. Its boundary is the critical value. For B(20, 0.3) at the 5% level with H₁: p > 0.3, find the smallest k with P(X ≥ k) < 0.05 — that k opens the critical region.

Conclusions in Context

Never just say "reject H₀". Conclude in the language of the problem: "there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the proportion has increased". State the significance level, the direction, and the real-world quantity.

Exam tips: define H₀ and H₁ with symbols AND words. Verify which tail the observation sits in before computing. If the observed value lies in the critical region, evidence supports H₁; otherwise there is insufficient evidence — never "prove H₀ true".

Exam method: hypotheses and critical regions

The null hypothesis H₀ states that there is no change or no difference, and the alternative H₁ states the claim being tested. Choose H₁ with a one-tailed test when the question states a direction (greater than or less than), and with a two-tailed test when it asks whether the value has changed.

At the 5% significance level a one-tailed test uses the critical value z = 1.645 for an upper test, and a two-tailed test splits 5% between two tails, giving z = 1.96. Compare the test statistic with the critical value, and reject H₀ when the statistic lies in the critical region.

For a sample mean, the test statistic is z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n), using the population mean stated in H₀. When the sample is large, the Central Limit Theorem lets you use the normal distribution even if the population is not normal.

State the conclusion in the context of the question, for example: there is sufficient evidence at the 5% level to suggest that the mean has increased.

Exam cue: Always state H₀ and H₁ in terms of the population parameter, not the sample statistic, and give a conclusion in words.

title: Artificial Intelligence
content:
Artificial Intelligence

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 18 (Artificial intelligence), examined in Paper 3.

AI Characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation.

Machine Learning

  • Supervised: learns from labelled data (spam detection)
  • Unsupervised: finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering)
  • Reinforcement: learns by reward signals (game agents)

Training/evaluation loop: fit on training data, test on unseen data to avoid overfitting. Neural networks adjust weights via backpropagation.

Ethics of AI

Bias in training data → unfair outputs; opaque decisions → accountability gaps; job displacement; autonomous weapons.

An AI system learns from its training data. If that data over-represents some groups or reflects past prejudice, the system's outputs can be biased, and it may treat people unfairly without anyone intending it. Developers can reduce this by checking the training data and testing the system on a wide range of cases.

Worked example: a bias scenario

A facial recognition system is trained mostly on photographs of one group of people. When it is tested on a different group it misidentifies people far more often. The cause is sampling bias: the training data did not represent the people the system would be used on. The fix is to collect a training set that reflects the full user population, to test the system on each group separately, and to report the error rate for each group rather than one overall figure.

Bias can also come from the people who label the data. If labellers apply their own assumptions, those assumptions are learned by the model. Name the source of bias in your answer, because marks are given for identifying where the bias enters, not just for saying that it exists.

title: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Trigonometry — Sine and Cosine Rules

Mathematics — OL. area formula, sine rule, cosine rule, multi-step bearing and 3-D problems (Extended).

  • 1. Area of a triangle
  • 2. Sine rule
  • 3. Cosine rule
  • 4. Bearing problems
  • 5. 3-D trigonometry

Formulas to learn

  • Area of a triangle: one half of a b sin C.
  • Sine rule: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C.
  • Cosine rule: a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc cos A, and cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) / (2bc).

Worked example

In a triangle with sides 7 and 9 and included angle 40 degrees, the area is one half of 7 x 9 x sin 40, about 20.2. The angle opposite the side 9 is then found by the sine rule, so check the answer against the cosine rule before you finish.

title: Exam technique: Algorithms & Programming
content:
### What earns the marks
For trace tables, every variable column updated stepwise earns the marks; the final OUTPUT row earns the last one. For validation versus verification, one named example of each earns one mark each. For test data, normal plus abnormal plus extreme or boundary stated earns full marks.
### Traps
Error: dry-running only the final values. Correction: fill every row of the table. Error: validation and verification swapped. Correction: validation checks input, verification checks transfer. Error: one test type only. Correction: name all three kinds.### Worked example
A trace table for a loop that totals numbers has one column per variable and one row per pass. Record each variable after every line that changes it, and tick the loop condition on each pass. Most mark schemes lose the final OUTPUT mark when the last row is missing, so check the final row against the stated output before you finish.
### Recall check
Give a normal, an abnormal and an extreme test for an input that must be a percentage from 0 to 100. Say which fault each abnormal or extreme value is designed to expose, because a bare list of values earns less than values with reasons.

title: Exam technique: Abstract Data Types
content:
### What earns the marks
For ADT choice, the access pattern stated earns the mark: LIFO for stacks, FIFO for queues, keyed jumps for BSTs. For traversals, the visit order written (root-left-right for preorder) earns each mark. For linked structures, pointer relinking described earns the insertion mark without any shifting claim.
### Traps
Error: queues for undo. Correction: undo is LIFO, so stack. Error: inorder claimed as root-first. Correction: preorder is root-first. Error: arrays claimed best for mid-list churn. Correction: shifting costs every insert.
### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.
### Worked example
Trace a stack. Push A, push B, push C, then pop, then push D, then pop. After the three pushes the top is C, so the first pop returns C. Pushing D leaves the stack as A, B, D, so the second pop returns D and B is left on top. A stack is last in, first out, so the top item always leaves first.

title: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

1. Bearings

  • Measured clockwise from north; three figures: 065°, 128°, 300°.
  • Back bearing = front bearing ± 180°.
  • Draw a north line at both points; north lines are parallel, giving Z-angles.

Example: B is on bearing 070° from A → A is on bearing 250° from B.

2. Scale drawings

1 cm : 500 m style scales; measure, convert, and quote distances/bearings from your drawing to the accuracy allowed.

3. Constructions

  • Perpendicular bisector of a segment: equal arcs from both ends, join the crossings.
  • Angle bisector: equal arcs from the vertex arms.
  • 60° and 90° constructions with compasses; leave all arcs visible.

4. Loci

Fixed distance from a point = circle; from a line = parallel lines with rounded ends; equidistant from two points = perpendicular bisector; from two lines = angle bisector.

Example: a goat tied by a 5 m rope to a corner of a 4 m × 6 m shed: the reachable region is ¾ circle radius 5 m + two ¼ circles radius 1 m where the rope wraps.

Exam tips: state "clockwise from north" in bearing definitions; shade/label locus regions clearly; use a ruler for construction lines too.

Three-figure bearings

A bearing is measured clockwise from north and written with three figures, so 045° is north-east and 250° is south-west. To find the back bearing, add or subtract 180°. Draw a north line at the starting point and measure the angle carefully with a protractor.

Scale drawings and distance

Use the scale given to convert a map distance to a real distance, and convert back when drawing. Scale 1:50 000 means 1 cm on the map represents 50 000 cm, or 0.5 km. Use Pythagoras or trigonometry to find distances where a direct measurement is not possible.

Loci

The locus of points at a fixed distance from a point is a circle. Points equidistant from two points lie on the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them. Points equidistant from two lines lie on an angle bisector. Shade a region by combining the loci and stating the condition clearly.

Worked example: the back bearing

An aircraft flies from A to B on a bearing of 118°. To find the bearing of A from B, add 180° because the north line at B is parallel to the north line at A: 118° + 180° = 298°. If the sum is greater than 360°, subtract 360°. Draw the north line at the point from which the angle is measured, because the marks depend on the angle being taken from the correct point.

Exam method: loci and constructions

The locus of points at a fixed distance from one point is a circle. The locus of points equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them. The locus of points equidistant from two lines is an angle bisector. Show every construction arc, because the marks are given for the arcs as well as the final line, and do not erase them.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For energy, mass defect times c squared with units earns both marks. For decay, ln2 over half-life quoted earns the method mark; activity as lambda N earns the second. For radii, the cube-root rule applied to ratios earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: half-life used as the decay constant. Correction: divide ln2 by it. Error: fission named for the Sun. Correction: fusion powers stars. Error: radius scaled linearly with A. Correction: cube root of nucleon number.
### Worked example
A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.

A nucleus has a half-life of 8 days. The decay constant is lambda = ln 2 / 8, which is about 0.087 per day. If the sample holds N = 2.0 x 10^10 nuclei, the activity is A = lambda N, about 1.7 x 10^9 decays per day. Quote the unit with the answer, because the mark depends on it.

title: Astronomy and Cosmology — Study Notes
content:
Astronomy and Cosmology

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 5 (WPH15), sat at A2.

Luminosity and Intensity

Luminosity L is total power radiated (W). Intensity at distance d: I = L/(4πd²) — the key to distances.

Standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known L, so measuring I gives d.

Example: the Sun: I = 1370 W m⁻² at d = 1.5 × 10¹¹ m gives L ≈ 3.9 × 10²⁶ W.

Stellar radii (25.2)

A star radiates as a black body of surface temperature T, so L = 4πR²σT⁴. Rearranged, R = √(L / 4πσT⁴). Luminosity therefore depends on both radius and temperature.

Example: with L = 3.9 × 10²⁶ W and T = 5800 K, R = √(3.9 × 10²⁶ / (4π × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 5800⁴)) ≈ 7.0 × 10⁸ m.

Doubling the temperature at fixed radius multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16. A cool red giant can be far more luminous than the Sun because its radius is very large.

Wien and Stefan–Boltzmann

  • Wien: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K — hotter stars are bluer
  • Stefan: L = σAT⁴, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸

Hubble's Law

Galaxies recede with v = Hd, H₀ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Redshift z = Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for small z.

Example: a galaxy at 100 Mpc recedes at v = 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 100 × 3.09 × 10²² ≈ 6800 km s⁻¹.

The Big Bang

Evidence: Hubble expansion, cosmic microwave background (2.7 K), hydrogen/helium abundance. Age estimate: t ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years. The fate question: critical density, Ω.

Exam tips: convert Mpc to metres (×3.09 × 10²²) before Hubble arithmetic; distinguish redshift of light from distance ladder methods.

Standard candles and the cosmic distance ladder

A standard candle is an object whose luminosity is known, such as a Type Ia supernova or a Cepheid variable star. Comparing its known luminosity with its observed brightness gives its distance, using the inverse-square law. Stellar radii can be found in the same way: the luminosity L = 4πR2σT4 links radius, surface temperature and output power.

Exam tip: state which assumption you are making, such as that the star radiates as a black body, before you calculate the radius.

Worked example: distance from parallax

A star has a parallax angle of 0.25 arcseconds when observed from opposite sides of the Earth's orbit. The distance in parsecs is d = 1/p = 1/0.25 = 4.0 pc. One parsec is about 3.26 light-years, so the star is roughly 13 light-years away. Parallax is the most direct distance method, and it works only for nearby stars.

Inverse-square law for brightness

The apparent brightness of a star falls as the inverse square of its distance. A star that is four times as far away appears 4² = 16 times fainter, for the same luminosity. This is why luminosity, which is intrinsic, must be distinguished from apparent brightness, which depends on distance.

Hubble's law and the expanding universe

  • Hubble's law states that v = H₀d, where v is the recession speed and d is the distance.
  • With H₀ ≈ 70 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, a galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at about 7000 km s⁻¹.
  • Redshift shows that most galaxies are moving away from us, which is evidence that the universe is expanding.

Exam point: the Big Bang model gives an age for the universe of about 13.8 billion years, consistent with the cosmic microwave background, which is the faint, nearly uniform radiation left from the early universe.

title: Oscillations and Waves II — Study Notes
content:
Oscillations and Waves II

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 5 (WPH15), sat at A2: oscillations and SHM. The superposition recap at the end is AS Unit 2 (WPH12) revision.

Simple harmonic motion (17.1)

A body oscillates with simple harmonic motion when its acceleration is proportional to its displacement x and directed towards the equilibrium position: a = −ω²x. The angular frequency is ω = 2πf, and the displacement is x = x₀ sin ωt, where x₀ is the amplitude.

The velocity is v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²), and the maximum acceleration is a₀ = ω²x₀. Velocity is zero at the extremes and maximum at equilibrium. Acceleration is maximum at the extremes and zero at equilibrium.

Example: amplitude 0.030 m and frequency 2.0 Hz give a₀ = (2π × 2.0)² × 0.030 ≈ 4.7 m s⁻².

Energy in SHM (17.2)

Kinetic energy is greatest at the equilibrium position, where speed is greatest. Potential energy is greatest at the extremes. The total energy is constant: E = ½mω²x₀², and it is shared between kinetic and potential energy as the body oscillates.

Example: a 0.20 kg mass with ω = 10 rad s⁻¹ and x₀ = 0.050 m has E = ½ × 0.20 × 10² × 0.050² = 0.025 J.

Damping, forced oscillations and resonance (17.3)

Damping removes energy from an oscillator. Light damping gives decaying oscillations. Critical damping returns the system to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating. Heavy damping is also non-oscillatory but slower.

A forced oscillator is driven by a periodic force. When the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, the amplitude is at its maximum, which is resonance. Greater damping lowers the peak and broadens the resonance curve.

Exam tips: state which quantity is maximum or zero at each point of the cycle. For resonance, always name the driving frequency relative to the natural frequency.

Waves: the superposition ideas

Progressive vs Stationary

Progressive waves transfer energy; stationary waves store it in loops. Stationary patterns arise from two identical waves travelling in opposite directions (reflections on strings, air columns).

PropertyProgressiveStationary
Amplitudesame for all pointsvaries: nodes zero, antinodes max
Phasevaries along wavesame within a loop, π flip across nodes
Energytransferredtrapped

Harmonics

A string fixed at both ends: f₁ = v/2L, then 2f₁, 3f₁… Closed pipes resonate at odd multiples; open pipes at all multiples.

Superposition Applications

  • Young's double slit: x = λD/a — evidence light is a wave
  • Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ — resolution of spectra
  • Noise-cancelling headphones: destructive interference of antiphase sound

Polarization Applications

Polaroid sunglasses cut glare from horizontal surfaces; stress analysis in plastics; LCD screens control light with twisted polarizers. Malus' law I = I₀cos²θ.

Exam tips: 'explain' marks want the physics: path difference, phase, node/antinode conditions — not just formula substitution.

title: Exam technique: Information Representation
content:
### What earns the marks
For two complement, inversion plus one stated earns the method mark before the value. For floating point, mantissa plus exponent roles stated earn one mark each. For normalisation, the leading-bit rule quoted earns the precision mark.
### Traps
Error: sign bit ignored in range. Correction: an n-bit signed range tops at 2^(n-1) - 1. Error: larger exponent read as more precision. Correction: exponent sets range, mantissa sets precision. Error: normalised form guessed. Correction: mantissa starts with 0.1 or 1.0 pattern per the scheme.
### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.
### Worked example
Write -45 in 8-bit two's complement. First write 45 in binary: 00101101. Invert every bit to get 11010010, then add 1 to get 11010011. Check: the sign bit has weight -128, so the value is -128 + 64 + 16 + 2 + 1 = -45, which matches.

title:
Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI14. It stays in the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise detail, not to replace the notes. The topic splits into four blocks: the biochemistry of photosynthesis and energy currency, the way energy moves through trophic levels, the ecology of populations and communities and the evidence for climate change, and the wrap-up in metabolic rate and evolution.

Photosynthesis and energy currency

Photosynthesis is the pathway that captures light energy and stores it in chemical form by using that energy to split water, combine the hydrogen with carbon dioxide, and release oxygen. The overall equation is the shorthand: carbon dioxide and water, with light, yield glucose and oxygen. The important conceptual point is that the energy is not just “used” by the plant; it is stored in the bonds of the product, and the water-splitting step is the one that makes oxygen.

  • 5.1 The overall reaction needs light energy to split the strong bonds in water, storing hydrogen in glucose by combining it with carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen to the atmosphere. This is the source of the atmospheric oxygen we breathe and the entry point for energy into ecosystems.
  • 5.2 The immediate energy currency is ATP. Photophosphorylation uses light energy to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, and the hydrolysis of ATP provides a fast, small packet of energy for endergonic processes. This is why the light-dependent and light-independent reactions are linked through ATP and reduced NADP rather than through glucose directly.
  • 5.3 The light-dependent reactions happen on the thylakoid membranes. Light excites electrons in chlorophyll; those electrons are passed down an electron transport chain; their energy is used to make ATP and to reduce NADP to reduced NADP; and water is split by photolysis, releasing oxygen, protons and replacement electrons. Cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation are both used, and the difference matters: non-cyclic produces ATP, reduced NADP, and oxygen, while cyclic makes ATP only and does not produce reduced NADP or oxygen.
  • 5.4 (i) The light-independent reactions, the Calvin cycle, happen in the stroma. The key enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide onto ribulose bisphosphate, RuBP, forming glycerate 3-phosphate, GP. GP is then reduced using ATP and reduced NADP to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, GALP. Some GALP leaves the cycle to make glucose and other products; some is used to regenerate RuBP so the cycle can continue.
  • 5.4 (ii) The products of the Calvin cycle are simple sugars used in respiration and in the synthesis of new biological molecules — polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. The link between photosynthesis and the rest of metabolism is that the carbohydrates made here are the raw material for everything else the organism builds.

Chloroplast structure and the pigment basis of photosynthesis

Structure and function are linked in the chloroplast. The thylakoids provide the membrane surface for the light-dependent reactions, the stroma holds the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, and the double membrane isolates the biochemical machinery. The pigments are the reason different wavelengths matter, and their separation by chromatography is both a practical skill and a way to understand absorption and action spectra.

  • 5.5 The chloroplast structure matches the function: thylakoids give a large surface area for light absorption and for the pigment arrays and electron transport chain; the stroma contains the enzymes, including RuBisCO, that run the Calvin cycle; and the envelope keeps the internal conditions separated from the cytoplasm.
  • 5.6 The absorption spectrum shows how much light of each wavelength a pigment absorbs; the action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. In an ideal case they track each other because the wavelengths a pigment absorbs are the ones that drive photosynthesis, but the two are not the same concept: one is about the pigment, the other about the whole process.
  • 5.7 Chloroplast pigments can be separated by paper or thin-layer chromatography. The distance each pigment moves compared with the solvent front gives the Rf value: Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front. The Rf value helps identify the pigment — chlorophylls, carotenoids and xanthophylls all have characteristic Rf values.
  • 5.8 Core Practical 10 investigates the effects of light intensity, light wavelength, temperature and carbon dioxide availability on the rate of photosynthesis using a suitable aquatic plant, measuring oxygen bubbles or gas volume. It is a classic rate experiment, and the point is to see that photosynthesis is affected by more than one factor and that one of them will be limiting at any moment.

Energy transfer between trophic levels

Once light energy is fixed by producers, it moves through the ecosystem when organisms eat one another. The key idea is that energy transfer is inefficient, and the inefficiency is why food chains are short and why top predators are rare. Gross primary productivity and net primary productivity make the accounting explicit.

  • 5.9 (i) Gross primary productivity, GPP, is the total chemical energy fixed by photosynthesis in a given area and time. Net primary productivity, NPP, is GPP minus the energy lost in plant respiration, R. So NPP = GPP − R. NPP is the energy actually available to the next trophic level because it is what remains after the plant has used some of the fixed energy itself.
  • 5.9 (ii) The calculation of NPP is a simple subtraction, but the important understanding is that respiration is the loss and that plants are not perfectly efficient converters of light energy into stored chemical energy, either. A forest can have a high GPP but much of that is respired away, so NPP is what matters for the consumers.
  • 5.10 The efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels is calculated as (energy or biomass transferred to the next level ÷ energy or biomass received at the previous level) × 100%. The typical figure is well below 100%, often around 10% as a rough guide, because energy is lost in respiration, in egested material, in uneaten parts, and in the energy used by the level itself. This inefficiency is why biomass and energy fall sharply up the trophic levels.

Worked example: if a producer level contains 15000 kJ m−2 year−1 and the primary consumer level contains 1400 kJ m−2 year−1, the transfer efficiency is (1400 ÷ 15000) × 100 = 9.33%. The number itself is not memorable; what matters is that the calculation shows how small the fraction is and why the higher levels get progressively smaller.

Ecology: populations, communities, habitats and niches

Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with each other and with their environment. The basic vocabulary here is the foundation for the rest of the topic, and the specification wants you to know what each term means and how they relate.

  • 5.11 A population is a group of interbreeding individuals of the same species in a habitat; a community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in a habitat; a habitat is the place where an organism lives; and an ecosystem is a self-sustaining system of living organisms interacting with their non-living surroundings. The ecosystem is larger than the community because it includes the abiotic part too.
  • 5.12 The numbers and distribution of organisms are controlled by biotic factors such as competition, predation and disease, and by abiotic factors such as temperature, pH, light intensity and moisture. Which factor limits a population depends on the organism and the environment; in one place it may be food, in another it may be temperature or water.
  • 5.13 The niche concept explains distribution and abundance: a niche is the role of a species in its ecosystem, including the conditions it tolerates, the resources it uses and the interactions it has. Two species cannot indefinitely occupy exactly the same niche, because one will outcompete the other; this is competitive exclusion, and it is one reason species partition resources and why communities can be diverse.
  • 5.14 Core Practical 11 is the fieldwork snapshot: use quadrats to sample abundance and transects, belt or line, to sample distribution, and record abiotic factors at the same time. The point is not just to count organisms but to relate their distribution to the environmental gradient being surveyed. Random sampling is used for abundance where the habitat is uniform; systematic sampling along a transect is used where there is a gradient such as trampling, exposure or moisture.

Succession and communities over time

Communities do not stay the same. After a disturbance or on newly available substrate, a predictable sequence of change occurs, and the endpoint is often a stable community. This is succession, and it matters because it shows that ecosystems are dynamic and that the species present at one time reflect the history of the site, not just the current conditions.

  • 5.15 Succession is the sequence of change from colonisation by pioneer species to a climax community. Pioneer species colonise bare or hostile substrate, change the abiotic conditions — for example by building soil or adding shade — and make the environment less hostile for later species. The community passes through seral stages of increasing complexity and biodiversity until a climax community forms, which is relatively stable and dominated by species adapted to the conditions at that stage.
  • The dynamic point is that succession is not random. It is directional and partly predictable, because the early species modify the environment in ways that favour later ones. The climax community is not a permanent fixed end in every case; if the environment changes, the community can move again. The exam point is that pioneer species are adapted to hostile conditions and later species are adapted to the conditions the pioneers helped create.

Climate change: evidence, causes and modelling

Climate change is the big applied part of this topic, and the specification treats it carefully: it asks for the evidence, the causes, the limitations of models, and the distinction between correlation and causation. This is one of the places where exam questions reward a precise, sceptical answer rather than a confident but vague one.

  • 5.16 Evidence for climate change comes from several independent sources. Atmospheric carbon dioxide records such as the Mauna Loa curve show a rising trend; temperature records show a warming trend; pollen preserved in peat bogs gives information about past vegetation and so past climate; and dendrochronology, tree-ring analysis, gives year-by-year information about growth conditions. The key skill is to recognise that correlation does not prove causation, and that each line of evidence has limitations and possible confounding factors. A rising temperature and a rising CO2 curve can be correlated without the student yet having explained the mechanism; the mechanism is asked for separately.
  • 5.17 The causes of anthropogenic climate change include the release of greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour — from human activities. These gases absorb and re-radiate infrared radiation, increasing the amount of energy retained by the atmosphere. This is the enhanced greenhouse effect: the natural greenhouse effect is what makes Earth warm enough to live on, and the enhanced effect is the additional warming from the extra greenhouse gases. To answer well, name the gases and describe the mechanism, not just say “humans cause it”.
  • 5.18 Knowledge of the carbon cycle is used to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide. Methods include reforestation and afforestation, which increase the removal of CO2 by photosynthesis; protecting peatlands and other carbon-rich ecosystems; reducing fossil fuel combustion; and carbon capture and storage. Each method works by changing the size or direction of a carbon flux, and each has limitations: trees take time to grow and can be lost again, peatlands can be damaged, and capture and storage is not yet universally practical or cheap.
  • 5.19 (i) Data can be extrapolated to make predictions, and models of future climate change are built from such extrapolations and from our understanding of the system. Models are useful precisely because they let us explore the consequences of different scenarios.
  • 5.19 (ii) Models have limitations. The system has complex feedback loops, including cloud cover and ice albedo, that are hard to quantify; historical data are incomplete; and future human behaviour — policy, technology and emissions — is itself unpredictable. A good answer says that models are the best tool available, not that they are perfect, and explains the nature of the uncertainty.
  • 5.20 The effects of climate change include changing rainfall patterns and changes in seasonal cycles, which affect the distribution of species, their development and life cycles. Temperature affects enzyme activity, so it can affect metabolism and development directly as well as shifting the ranges of species. Phenological changes — timing of flowering, breeding, migration — are evidence of these effects. The point is that climate change is not just a temperature story; it is a biology story because organisms are sensitive to the conditions.

Metabolic rate, temperature and evolution

The final block pulls the topic together with two ideas that cut across biology: temperature affects enzyme-controlled metabolism, and evolution is a change in allele frequency. Both are specification points and both are general enough to appear in questions about other topics too.

  • 5.21 Temperature affects enzyme activity up to an optimum; beyond the optimum, enzymes denature because their tertiary and quaternary structures are disrupted by the breakage of hydrogen and ionic bonds. The Q10 temperature coefficient is a way to express how much the rate of a reaction changes with a 10 °C rise: Q10 = rate at T + 10 °C ÷ rate at T. It is not a universal constant; it is a measure that applies to a particular reaction under particular conditions. A common error is to say that high temperature breaks peptide bonds or destroys the primary structure; it does not — it disrupts the higher-order structure that holds the active site in shape.
  • 5.22 Core Practical 12 investigates the effect of temperature on the development of organisms, for example seedling growth rate or brine shrimp hatch rate, while taking into account the ethical use of organisms. The practical point is to measure a rate or a development outcome at different temperatures and to relate it to the effect of temperature on enzyme activity, while using the organisms ethically.
  • 5.23 Evolution is a change in allele frequency in a gene pool over time, brought about by gene mutation creating new alleles and natural selection increasing the frequency of advantageous ones. The important definition is the allele-frequency one: evolution is not “an individual changing during its life”; it is a change in the genetic composition of a population across generations. Mutation provides the variation; selection changes the frequencies.
  • 5.24 Isolation reduces gene flow between populations, allowing them to diverge genetically. Allopatric speciation happens when a physical barrier separates populations so that gene flow stops; sympatric speciation happens in the same habitat through reproductive isolation — differences in timing, behaviour, or genetics that prevent interbreeding. The key difference is the role of a physical barrier: allopatric needs one, sympatric does not. In both cases, the outcome is that populations become so different that they can no longer produce fertile offspring, and they are then distinct species.
  • 5.25 Scientific conclusions about controversial issues can be influenced by who is reaching them. Funding, political agendas and stakeholder motives can affect what conclusions are emphasised or how evidence is interpreted. This is not a claim that science is arbitrary; it is a reason to look at the evidence, the method, and the possible biases, and to distinguish a conclusion that follows from the data from one that is shaped by interests.
  • 5.26 Reforestation and the use of sustainable resources such as biofuels are examples of managing the conflict between human needs and conservation. They try to meet human needs while limiting harm to the environment, and they are practical applications of the ideas in the topic — that ecosystems provide services, that carbon can be kept out of the atmosphere by vegetation and soil, and that trade-offs matter. The point is that conservation is not only about protecting species; it is also about managing the relationship between people and the environment.

Worked examples to practise

These are the sorts of short calculations and comparisons the topic rewards. They are not decoration; they are the most likely exam material from this part of the syllabus.

  • Photosynthesis rate: if an aquatic plant releases 24 bubbles per minute at one light intensity and 48 bubbles per minute at double the intensity, the rate has doubled. The point is to be clear what is being measured and how a change in the independent variable is reflected in the dependent variable. Oxygen production is a proxy for photosynthesis rate; it is not the same as measuring carbon fixed, but it is workable if stated clearly.
  • Efficiency: if producers contain 12000 kJ m−2 year−1 and primary consumers 1500 kJ m−2 year−1, the efficiency is (1500 ÷ 12000) × 100 = 12.5%. Round numbers make the method clear; the actual value does not need to be exactly 10%.
  • Q10: if a reaction rate is 4.0 units at 20 °C and 8.0 units at 30 °C, Q10 = 8.0 ÷ 4.0 = 2.0. The interpretation is that the rate doubles for a 10 °C rise in this case. The method is the same whichever numbers are given.
  • Allele frequency: if a population of 200 individuals has 60 individuals with a recessive phenotype and the trait is controlled by a single gene with complete dominance, the frequency of the recessive phenotype is 60 ÷ 200 = 0.30, which is q2 in the Hardy–Weinberg context; the allele frequencies follow from that. This is a bridge to the genetics topic, and it shows that evolution is tracked as a change in allele frequency.

How the pieces fit together

The topic is really about two movements of energy: into ecosystems through photosynthesis and then up through the trophic levels with losses at each step, and the parallel movement of carbon through the carbon cycle. The ecology part places organisms in their populations, communities and environments and explains why they are where they are. The climate change part uses the same system idea — flows, stores, feedbacks — to ask what happens when the energy balance of the planet changes, and what we might do about it. The final part, metabolism and evolution, is the reminder that organisms are constrained by their biochemistry and by their genetics, and that both constraints shape how they respond to the environment.

  • Start with the energy: light captured by the pigments of the chloroplast, used to make ATP and reduced NADP, used to fix carbon in the Calvin cycle, ending as sugars that feed respiration and biosynthesis.
  • Move to the transfer: GPP to NPP to the next trophic level, with an efficiency calculation that explains why chains are short.
  • Move to the ecology: populations and communities, biotic and abiotic factors, niche and succession, and the fieldwork methods used to measure them.
  • Move to the change: evidence for climate change, the greenhouse mechanism, the carbon-cycle methods for mitigation, the limits of models, and the biological effects of a warmer, more variable climate.
  • End with the basics that apply everywhere: temperature affects enzyme activity and development, Q10 measures the thermal sensitivity, and evolution is a change in allele frequency driven by mutation and selection, with isolation enabling speciation.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying the light-dependent reactions make glucose: they make ATP and reduced NADP and oxygen; glucose comes from the Calvin cycle.
  • Confusing absorption spectrum and action spectrum: one is about what the pigment absorbs, the other about the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength.
  • Using the wrong Rf formula: Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front. A common variant is to invert it.
  • Treating GPP and NPP as the same thing: NPP is GPP minus respiration, and it is the energy available to consumers.
  • Forgetting to say that transfer efficiency is a percentage and giving the raw fraction alone.
  • Stating that evolution is an individual changing during its lifetime rather than a change in allele frequency in a population.
  • Saying that sympatric speciation needs a physical barrier: it does not; that is allopatric speciation.
  • Saying high temperature breaks peptide bonds or destroys the primary structure of an enzyme: it disrupts the higher-order structure, not the primary sequence.
  • Treating correlation as causation in climate evidence without saying so, or without mentioning the mechanism.
  • Using a single climate indicator as if it proved everything: the evidence is multiple and each line has limitations.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe the roles of the light-dependent and light-independent reactions of photosynthesis and state where each occurs. Answer: The light-dependent reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes; they use light energy to excite electrons, make ATP and reduced NADP by non-cyclic photophosphorylation, and split water to release oxygen. The light-independent reactions occur in the stroma; they use ATP and reduced NADP to reduce carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle, producing triose phosphate that can be used to synthesise glucose and other organic molecules. (5 marks)
  2. Explain how gross primary productivity and net primary productivity are related and why net primary productivity is the more important figure for consumers. Answer: GPP is the total energy fixed by photosynthesis; plant respiration uses some of it; NPP is GPP minus respiration, so NPP = GPP − R. NPP is the energy available to the next trophic level because it is what remains after the plant has covered its own respiration, so consumers depend on NPP, not GPP. (4 marks)
  3. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer if a producer trophic level contains 18000 kJ m−2 year−1 and the primary consumer level contains 1620 kJ m−2 year−1. Answer: Efficiency = (1620 ÷ 18000) × 100 = 9.0%. (2 marks)
  4. Describe how you would investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using an aquatic plant, and state one control variable. Answer: Place the aquatic plant in water at a fixed temperature and carbon dioxide concentration; vary the light intensity; count the bubbles of oxygen released per minute or measure the volume of gas collected in a fixed time; keep temperature, carbon dioxide concentration and plant species constant as control variables. (5 marks)
  5. Explain the difference between allopatric and sympatric speciation. Answer: Allopatric speciation occurs when a physical barrier separates populations so gene flow stops and they diverge; sympatric speciation occurs in the same area without a physical barrier, with reproductive isolation such as differences in breeding time or behaviour preventing interbreeding. In both cases the result is that populations become reproductively isolated and form new species. (4 marks)
  6. Describe the evidence for climate change and explain why correlation between two variables is not proof of causation. Answer: Evidence includes rising atmospheric carbon dioxide records, rising temperature records, pollen in peat bogs showing past vegetation, and tree rings. Correlation alone does not prove causation because the two variables could both be affected by a third factor, or the trend could be coincidental; to show causation you need a plausible mechanism and evidence that linking the variables is not better explained by something else. (5 marks)
  7. Explain the effect of temperature on enzyme activity up to and beyond the optimum, and define the Q10 temperature coefficient. Answer: Enzyme activity increases with temperature up to the optimum because molecules have more kinetic energy, but beyond the optimum the enzyme denatures as hydrogen and ionic bonds break and the active site is lost; the primary structure remains intact. Q10 is the factor by which the rate increases when the temperature rises by 10 °C, calculated as rate at T + 10 °C ÷ rate at T. (5 marks)
  8. Describe how reforestation can reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide and state one limitation of this approach. Answer: Trees take up carbon dioxide by photosynthesis and store the carbon in their biomass and in the soil, so planting trees increases the removal of CO2 from the atmosphere and holds it there. Limitation: newly planted trees take time to grow and store significant carbon, forests can be lost to fire or disease, and the land may compete with other uses. (4 marks)

Energy Flow, Ecosystems and the Environment — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI14. It stays in the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise detail, not to replace the notes. The topic splits into four blocks: the biochemistry of photosynthesis and energy currency, the way energy moves through trophic levels, the ecology of populations and communities and the evidence for climate change, and the wrap-up in metabolic rate and evolution.

Photosynthesis and energy currency

Photosynthesis is the pathway that captures light energy and stores it in chemical form by using that energy to split water, combine the hydrogen with carbon dioxide, and release oxygen. The overall equation is the shorthand: carbon dioxide and water, with light, yield glucose and oxygen. The important conceptual point is that the energy is not just “used” by the plant; it is stored in the bonds of the product, and the water-splitting step is the one that makes oxygen.

  • 5.1 The overall reaction needs light energy to split the strong bonds in water, storing hydrogen in glucose by combining it with carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen to the atmosphere. This is the source of the atmospheric oxygen we breathe and the entry point for energy into ecosystems.
  • 5.2 The immediate energy currency is ATP. Photophosphorylation uses light energy to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, and the hydrolysis of ATP provides a fast, small packet of energy for endergonic processes. This is why the light-dependent and light-independent reactions are linked through ATP and reduced NADP rather than through glucose directly.
  • 5.3 The light-dependent reactions happen on the thylakoid membranes. Light excites electrons in chlorophyll; those electrons are passed down an electron transport chain; their energy is used to make ATP and to reduce NADP to reduced NADP; and water is split by photolysis, releasing oxygen, protons and replacement electrons. Cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation are both used, and the difference matters: non-cyclic produces ATP, reduced NADP, and oxygen, while cyclic makes ATP only and does not produce reduced NADP or oxygen.
  • 5.4 (i) The light-independent reactions, the Calvin cycle, happen in the stroma. The key enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide onto ribulose bisphosphate, RuBP, forming glycerate 3-phosphate, GP. GP is then reduced using ATP and reduced NADP to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, GALP. Some GALP leaves the cycle to make glucose and other products; some is used to regenerate RuBP so the cycle can continue.
  • 5.4 (ii) The products of the Calvin cycle are simple sugars used in respiration and in the synthesis of new biological molecules — polysaccharides, amino acids, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. The link between photosynthesis and the rest of metabolism is that the carbohydrates made here are the raw material for everything else the organism builds.

Chloroplast structure and the pigment basis of photosynthesis

Structure and function are linked in the chloroplast. The thylakoids provide the membrane surface for the light-dependent reactions, the stroma holds the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, and the double membrane isolates the biochemical machinery. The pigments are the reason different wavelengths matter, and their separation by chromatography is both a practical skill and a way to understand absorption and action spectra.

  • 5.5 The chloroplast structure matches the function: thylakoids give a large surface area for light absorption and for the pigment arrays and electron transport chain; the stroma contains the enzymes, including RuBisCO, that run the Calvin cycle; and the envelope keeps the internal conditions separated from the cytoplasm.
  • 5.6 The absorption spectrum shows how much light of each wavelength a pigment absorbs; the action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength. In an ideal case they track each other because the wavelengths a pigment absorbs are the ones that drive photosynthesis, but the two are not the same concept: one is about the pigment, the other about the whole process.
  • 5.7 Chloroplast pigments can be separated by paper or thin-layer chromatography. The distance each pigment moves compared with the solvent front gives the Rf value: Rf = distance moved by pigment ÷ distance moved by solvent front. The Rf value helps identify the pigment — chlorophylls, carotenoids and xanthophylls all have characteristic Rf values.
  • 5.8 Core Practical 10 investigates the effects of light intensity, light wavelength, temperature and carbon dioxide availability on the rate of photosynthesis using a suitable aquatic plant, measuring oxygen bubbles or gas volume. It is a classic rate experiment, and the point is to see that photosynthesis is affected by more than one factor and that one of them will be limiting at any moment.

Energy transfer between trophic levels

Once light energy is fixed by producers, it moves through the ecosystem when organisms eat one another. The key idea is that energy transfer is inefficient, and the inefficiency is why food chains are short and why top predators are rare. Gross primary productivity and net primary productivity make the accounting explicit.

  • 5.9 (i) Gross primary productivity, GPP, is the total chemical energy fixed by photosynthesis in a given area and time. Net primary productivity, NPP, is GPP minus the energy lost in plant respiration, R. So NPP = GPP − R. NPP is the energy actually available to the next trophic level because it is what remains after the plant has used some of the fixed energy itself.
  • 5.9 (ii) The calculation of NPP is a simple subtraction, but the important understanding is that respiration is the loss and that plants are not perfectly efficient converters of light energy into stored chemical energy, either. A forest can have a high GPP but much of that is respired away, so NPP is what matters for the consumers.
  • 5.10 The efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels is calculated as (energy or biomass transferred to the next level ÷ energy or biomass received at the previous level) × 100%. The typical figure is well below 100%, often around 10% as a rough guide, because energy is lost in respiration, in egested material, in uneaten parts, and in the energy used by the level itself. This inefficiency is why biomass and energy fall sharply up the trophic levels.

Worked example: if a producer level contains 15000 kJ m−2 year−1 and the primary consumer level contains 1400 kJ m−2 year−1, the transfer efficiency is (1400 ÷ 15000) × 100 = 9.33%. The number itself is not memorable; what matters is that the calculation shows how small the fraction is and why the higher levels get progressively smaller.

Ecology: populations, communities, habitats and niches

Ecology is the study of how organisms interact with each other and with their environment. The basic vocabulary here is the foundation for the rest of the topic, and the specification wants you to know what each term means and how they relate.

  • 5.11 A population is a group of interbreeding individuals of the same species in a habitat; a community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in a habitat; a habitat is the place where an organism lives; and an ecosystem is a self-sustaining system of living organisms interacting with their non-living surroundings. The ecosystem is larger than the community because it includes the abiotic part too.
  • 5.12 The numbers and distribution of organisms are controlled by biotic factors such as competition, predation and disease, and by abiotic factors such as temperature, pH, light intensity and moisture. Which factor limits a population depends on the organism and the environment; in one place it may be food, in another it may be temperature or water.
  • 5.13 The niche concept explains distribution and abundance: a niche is the role of a species in its ecosystem, including the conditions it tolerates, the resources it uses and the interactions it has. Two species cannot indefinitely occupy exactly the same niche, because one will outcompete the other; this is competitive exclusion, and it is one reason species partition resources and why communities can be diverse.
  • 5.14 Core Practical 11 is the fieldwork snapshot: use quadrats to sample abundance and transects, belt or line, to sample distribution, and record abiotic factors at the same time. The point is not just to count organisms but to relate their distribution to the environmental gradient being surveyed. Random sampling is used for abundance where the habitat is uniform; systematic sampling along a transect is used where there is a gradient such as trampling, exposure or moisture.

Succession and communities over time

Communities do not stay the same. After a disturbance or on newly available substrate, a predictable sequence of change occurs, and the endpoint is often a stable community. This is succession, and it matters because it shows that ecosystems are dynamic and that the species present at one time reflect the history of the site, not just the current conditions.

  • 5.15 Succession is the sequence of change from colonisation by pioneer species to a climax community. Pioneer species colonise bare or hostile substrate, change the abiotic conditions — for example by building soil or adding shade — and make the environment less hostile for later species. The community passes through seral stages of increasing complexity and biodiversity until a climax community forms, which is relatively stable and dominated by species adapted to the conditions at that stage.
  • The dynamic point is that succession is not random. It is directional and partly predictable, because the early species modify the environment in ways that favour later ones. The climax community is not a permanent fixed end in every case; if the environment changes, the community can move again. The exam point is that pioneer species are adapted to hostile conditions and later species are adapted to the conditions the pioneers helped create.

Climate change: evidence, causes and modelling

Climate change is the big applied part of this topic, and the specification treats it carefully: it asks for the evidence, the causes, the limitations of models, and the distinction between correlation and causation. This is one of the places where exam questions reward a precise, sceptical answer rather than a confident but vague one.

  • 5.16 Evidence for climate change comes from several independent sources. Atmospheric carbon dioxide records such as the Mauna Loa curve show a rising trend; temperature records show a warming trend; pollen preserved in peat bogs gives information about past vegetation and so past climate; and dendrochronology, tree-ring analysis, gives year-by-year information about growth conditions. The key skill is to recognise that correlation does not prove causation, and that each line of evidence has limitations and possible confounding factors. A rising temperature and a rising CO2 curve can be correlated without the student yet having explained the mechanism; the mechanism is asked for separately.
  • 5.17 The causes of anthropogenic climate change include the release of greenhouse gases — carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and water vapour — from human activities. These gases absorb and re-radiate infrared radiation, increasing the amount of energy retained by the atmosphere. This is the enhanced greenhouse effect: the natural greenhouse effect is what makes Earth warm enough to live on, and the enhanced effect is the additional warming from the extra greenhouse gases. To answer well, name the gases and describe the mechanism, not just say “humans cause it”.
  • 5.18 Knowledge of the carbon cycle is used to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide. Methods include reforestation and afforestation, which increase the removal of CO2 by photosynthesis; protecting peatlands and other carbon-rich ecosystems; reducing fossil fuel combustion; and carbon capture and storage. Each method works by changing the size or direction of a carbon flux, and each has limitations: trees take time to grow and can be lost again, peatlands can be damaged, and capture and storage is not yet universally practical or cheap.
  • 5.19 (i) Data can be extrapolated to make predictions, and models of future climate change are built from such extrapolations and from our understanding of the system. Models are useful precisely because they let us explore the consequences of different scenarios.
  • 5.19 (ii) Models have limitations. The system has complex feedback loops, including cloud cover and ice albedo, that are hard to quantify; historical data are incomplete; and future human behaviour — policy, technology and emissions — is itself unpredictable. A good answer says that models are the best tool available, not that they are perfect, and explains the nature of the uncertainty.
  • 5.20 The effects of climate change include changing rainfall patterns and changes in seasonal cycles, which affect the distribution of species, their development and life cycles. Temperature affects enzyme activity, so it can affect metabolism and development directly as well as shifting the ranges of species. Phenological changes — timing of flowering, breeding, migration — are evidence of these effects. The point is that climate change is not just a temperature story; it is a biology story because organisms are sensitive to the conditions.

Metabolic rate, temperature and evolution

The final block pulls the topic together with two ideas that cut across biology: temperature affects enzyme-controlled metabolism, and evolution is a change in allele frequency. Both are specification points and both are general enough to appear in questions about other topics too.

  • 5.21 Temperature affects enzyme activity up to an optimum; beyond the optimum, enzymes denature because their tertiary and quaternary structures are disrupted by the breakage of hydrogen and ionic bonds. The Q10 temperature coefficient is a way to express how much the rate of a reaction changes with a 10 °C rise: Q10 = rate at T + 10 °C ÷ rate at T. It is not a universal constant; it is a measure that applies to a particular reaction under particular conditions. A common error is to say that high temperature breaks peptide bonds or destroys the primary structure; it does not — it disrupts the higher-order structure that holds the active site in shape.
  • 5.22 Core Practical 12 investigates the effect of temperature on the development of organisms, for example seedling growth rate or brine shrimp hatch rate, while taking into account the ethical use of organisms. The practical point is to measure a rate or a development outcome at different temperatures and to relate it to the effect of temperature on enzyme activity, while using the organisms ethically.
  • 5.23 Evolution is a change in allele frequency in a gene pool over time, brought about by gene mutation creating new alleles and natural selection increasing the frequency of advantageous ones. The important definition is the allele-frequency one: evolution is not “an individual changing during its life”; it is a change in the genetic composition of a population across generations. Mutation provides the variation; selection changes the frequencies.
  • 5.24 Isolation reduces gene flow between populations, allowing them to diverge genetically. Allopatric speciation happens when a physical barrier separates populations so that gene flow stops; sympatric speciation happens in the same habitat through reproductive isolation — differences in timing, behaviour, or genetics that prevent interbreeding. The key difference is the role of a physical barrier: allopatric needs one, sympatric does not. In both cases, the outcome is that populations become so different that they can no longer produce fertile offspring, and they are then distinct species.
  • 5.25 Scientific conclusions about controversial issues can be influenced by who is reaching them. Funding, political agendas and stakeholder motives can affect what conclusions are emphasised or how evidence is interpreted. This is not a claim that science is arbitrary; it is a reason to look at the evidence, the method, and the possible biases, and to distinguish a conclusion that follows from the data from one that is shaped by interests.

title: Networks and the Internet — Study Notes
content:
Networks and the Internet

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 14 (Communication and internet technologies), examined in Paper 3.

The TCP/IP Stack

Four layers: Application (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport (TCP reliable, connection-oriented with sequence numbers and acknowledgements; UDP fast, connectionless), Internet (IP addressing and routing), Link (physical delivery on the local network). Layering separates concerns so each layer can change independently.

Switching

  • Circuit switching: a dedicated path is held for the call (traditional telephone) — wasteful if idle.
  • Packet switching: data split into packets routed independently; each carries source/destination addresses and a sequence number, reassembled at the destination. Efficient and fault-tolerant; packets may arrive out of order (TCP fixes ordering).

Addressing and Subnetting

IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, written dotted decimal, split into network + host portions by the subnet mask. ANDing an IP with the mask yields the network ID. 192.168.4.0/26 means the first 26 bits are network, leaving 6 host bits: 64 addresses, 62 usable. NAT maps private addresses to one public IP.

Models and Protection

Client-server centralises services (web, email, files); peer-to-peer shares directly (torrents, small LANs). Firewalls filter traffic by rules; proxy servers sit between clients and the internet, caching and filtering; ports identify services (80/443 web, 25 SMTP).

Exam tips: compute usable hosts from a given prefix; trace a packet through the four layers naming one protocol per layer; explain one advantage of packet over circuit switching.

Protocols and switching

A protocol is a set of rules that devices follow to communicate. TCP/IP is the suite used on the internet, and protocols define how data is addressed, formatted and checked for errors.

In circuit switching a dedicated path is set up for the whole call, as in the traditional telephone network. In packet switching the message is split into packets, each carrying a header with source and destination addresses and a sequence number. Packets can take different routes and are reassembled at the destination.

Exam tip: packet switching uses the network efficiently because no path is reserved, but packets can arrive out of order.

Exam method: dividing a network into subnets

Take 192.168.1.0/24 and split it into four equal subnets. A /24 prefix leaves 8 host bits, so borrowing 2 bits gives a /26 prefix and 6 host bits, which means 64 addresses per subnet. The four networks are 192.168.1.0, 192.168.1.64, 192.168.1.128 and 192.168.1.192. In each subnet the first address is the network address and the last is the broadcast address, so the usable hosts are 62 per subnet.

Always work out the block size first: 256 minus the last octet of the subnet mask gives the step between subnet addresses. For a mask ending in 192, the step is 64.

Common errors in networking questions

  • Forgetting that the network and broadcast addresses cannot be assigned to hosts, so the usable count is 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2.
  • Confusing packet switching with circuit switching. Packet switching splits data into packets that may take different routes; circuit switching reserves a fixed path for the whole call.
  • Stating that a router works at the data link layer. Routers forward packets using IP addresses, so they operate at the network layer.

Formulas to learn

Worked example

A cumulative frequency curve has its points plotted against the upper class boundary. Reading the curve at 25 percent of the total gives Q1, at 50 percent gives the median, and at 75 percent gives Q3. The IQR is Q3 minus Q1, and it is less affected by outliers than the range.

title: Exam technique: Dynamics
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultant force, subtract opposition before applying F = ma to earn both marks. For collisions, total momentum before equated to total after earns the method mark. For rebounds, the sign change included earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: friction ignored in acceleration. Correction: use the resultant, not the push alone. Error: rebound treated as stopping. Correction: add the speeds with the sign flip. Error: kinetic energy claimed conserved generally. Correction: momentum always, kinetic only when elastic.
### Worked example
A car of mass 800 kg has a driving force of 2400 N and a resistance of 400 N. The resultant force is 2400 - 400 = 2000 N, so a = F/m = 2000 / 800 = 2.5 m/s^2. Subtract the opposing force before you divide by the mass.
