title: Ethics, Security & Impact — Study Notes
content:
Ethics, Security & Impact

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): ethics & professional codes, security threats, malware, online safety, environmental/employment impact.

1. Ethics and codes

ACM/IEEE-CS/BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, privacy. Applying: identify the principle → apply to scenario → stakeholders affected → consequences.

2. Threats

  • Malware: virus (attaches, replicates via host), worm (self-spreads), trojan (disguised), spyware, ransomware.
  • Social: phishing (fake emails/sites), pharming (DNS/hosts redirect), shoulder surfing, brute force.
  • Technical: interception (packet sniffing), SQL injection (malicious input into queries), DoS (flooding services).

3. Cyber security

Cyber security protects data, systems and users from attack. A vulnerability is a weakness an attack can use; a threat is what exploits it.

  • Vulnerabilities: default or weak passwords, unpatched software, misconfigured access rights, unsecured or public Wi-Fi, removable media (memory sticks), insider threat, unencrypted data in transit.
  • Malware: virus (needs a host file and replicates when that file runs), worm (self-spreads across a network), trojan (disguised as useful software), spyware (records activity), ransomware (encrypts files and demands payment), adware.
  • Social engineering: phishing (fake email or site asks for details), pharming (malicious redirect via DNS or the hosts file), blagging (invented story), shoulder surfing, brute-force and dictionary attacks.
  • Technical attacks: interception / packet sniffing on an unsecured network, SQL injection (malicious input typed into a query field), denial of service and DDoS (flooding a service so it cannot respond), session hijacking.

Protection: strong unique passwords plus 2FA; biometric authentication (fingerprint, face); encryption so intercepted data is unreadable (plaintext is turned into ciphertext with a key — HTTPS/TLS does this on websites); firewalls filtering traffic by IP address and port; anti-malware that scans, blocks and quarantines; patching and updates; user access levels so staff reach only what they need; regular backups; user training; penetration testing to find holes first.

Answer shape: name the threat precisely (pharming is not phishing), then give the matched defence — pharming → keep DNS servers and hosts files secure and check HTTPS certificates.

4. Digital currency

A digital currency exists only in electronic form. A cryptocurrency (for example Bitcoin) is a decentralised digital currency secured by cryptography and recorded on a blockchain.

  • Blockchain: a distributed ledger — every node holds a copy. Transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block stores the hash of the previous block, so altering an old record breaks the chain and is rejected by the network.
  • Keys and wallets: the owner holds a public key (the address others pay to) and a private key (proves ownership and signs a payment). A wallet stores these keys — lose the private key and the money is gone.
  • Transactions: broadcast to the network, checked by nodes and added to a block; the verifier (miner) is rewarded. No bank or central authority is involved.

Advantages: quick international transfers, low transaction fees, no central authority to fail or censor, a transparent ledger, and coins cannot be counterfeited. Disadvantages: the value is very volatile, payments are irreversible, mining uses large amounts of energy, it appeals to criminals and ransomware demands, it needs internet access and technical care, and there is little consumer protection if a wallet is lost or stolen.

5. Defences

Antivirus/antispyware (scan, quarantine), firewalls (port/IP filtering), 2FA + biometrics, strong passwords + managers, encryption (HTTPS, VPN), access levels, patches/updates, user training.

6. Online behaviour

Digital footprint, cyberbullying, fake news, privacy settings, verification of sources.

7. Wider impact

Employment: automation displaces roles but creates IT jobs. Environment: e-waste, energy use vs paperless efficiency. Monitoring: workplace tracking, CCTV — balance with privacy laws (GDPR-style).

Exam tips: name the threat precisely (pharming ≠ phishing), then the matched defence; ethics answers need principle + application, not opinion.

title: Exam technique: Measures of Variation
content:
### What earns the marks

Five values are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. The mean is 25 / 5 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1 and 16, which sum to 28. The variance is 28 / 5 = 5.6, and the standard deviation is the square root, about 2.37. Show the squared deviations line on the paper, since the method mark depends on it.

title: Exam technique: Transformations and Vectors
content:
### What earns the marks
For translations and vector arithmetic, each component computed separately earns credit: show x and y lines. For magnitude, the root-of-sum-of-squares line earns the method mark before evaluation. For reflections and rotations, the coordinate rule stated ((y; -x) for 90 degrees clockwise) earns the method mark. For describing transformations, all three of type, centre or line, and size or angle are needed for full marks.
### Traps
Error: writing column vectors as bracket rows that lose a row. Correction: use (x; y) form and keep both components. Error: (100) or 14 for the magnitude of (6; 8). Correction: square, add, then root. Error: (-y; x) for a clockwise rotation. Correction: clockwise is (y; -x). Error: negating both coordinates for a single-axis reflection. Correction: one axis changes, the other stays.
### Worked example
Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). Write each coordinate step on its own line.

Point A(1; 2) is translated by the vector (3; -1), giving A'(4; 1). Reflecting A' in the x-axis gives (4; -1). Rotating the point (3; -1) 90 degrees clockwise about the origin gives (-1; -3), using the rule (x; y) to (y; -x). Scaling (1; 2) by a factor of 2 from the origin gives (2; 4). title: Exam technique: Sampling
content:
### What earns the marks
For method choice, random vs stratified vs systematic justified earns the mark. For stratified allocation, the proportion of each stratum applied earns the method mark. For bias discussion, the named source of bias with its effect earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: sample claimed unbiased with no method. Correction: name and justify the method. Error: equal numbers per stratum. Correction: allocate proportionally. Error: population confused with frame. Correction: frame is the list used.
### Worked example
A school has 600 students: 120 in Year 11 and 480 in Year 10. A stratified sample of 50 is needed with proportional allocation. Year 11 gets 120/600 x 50 = 10 students, and Year 10 gets 480/600 x 50 = 40 students. The two numbers add to 50, which confirms the allocation. Random selection then happens inside each group.

title: Proof — Study Notes
content:
Proof

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 2 (WMA12), sat at AS.

Proof is a logical argument that shows a statement is true in every case in its domain. At AS level you must know the four proof techniques, choose the right one for a given statement, and produce or critique a short algebraic argument.

Direct proof

Start from known facts and deduce the result by valid steps. Most algebraic identities are proved this way: expand, factorise or substitute until the required form appears.

  • To prove "the sum of two even numbers is even": write the numbers as 2a and 2b, so their sum is 2(a + b), which is even by definition.
  • To prove "the sum of two consecutive integers is odd": write them as n and n + 1, so the sum is 2n + 1, which is odd.

Proof by exhaustion

Check every case one by one. Only valid when the number of cases is finite and small, for example proving a statement about the factors of 12 by listing 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.

Disproof by counter-example

A single case where the statement fails disproves a universal claim. This is the fastest way to kill a false statement: for "n^2 + n + 17 is prime for all n", the case n = 16 gives 289 = 17 x 17, so the claim is false.

Proof by contradiction

Assume the statement is false, then deduce something impossible. The classic is proving that the square root of 2 is irrational: assume sqrt(2) = p/q in lowest terms, derive that both p and q must be even, contradicting the lowest-terms assumption.

Common algebraic forms

  • Even: 2n. Odd: 2n + 1. Consecutive integers: n, n + 1, n + 2.
  • Consecutive even numbers: 2n, 2n + 2, 2n + 4.
  • A square number is n^2; the difference of two squares is (a - b)(a + b).
  • Divisibility: show the expression can be written as the required factor times an integer.

title: Acid-base Equilibria Quick Revision
content:
Quick revision: Acid-base Equilibria

Chemistry — A2 Level. Edexcel IAL Chemistry Topic 14 covers Brønsted-Lowry proton transfer, pH scales, strong and weak acids and bases, ionic product of water, buffers, and titration curves.

  • Brønsted-Lowry acids are proton donors and bases are proton acceptors, forming conjugate acid-base pairs linked by proton transfer.
  • pH is defined as −log[H+] and hydrogen ion concentration is calculated using [H+] = 10^(−pH).
  • Strong acids dissociate completely, whereas weak acids dissociate partially, quantified by the acid dissociation constant Ka and pKa = −log(Ka).
  • The ionic product of water, Kw = [H+][OH−], allows calculation of strong base pH using pKw = −log(Kw).
  • Experimental analysis includes measuring pH after dilution, finding Ka from weak acid pH and mass, and interpreting monoprotic and diprotic titration curves to select suitable indicators.
  • Buffer solutions resist pH changes upon addition of small amounts of acid or alkali, and their pH is calculated using Ka and component concentrations.
  • Biological and food systems rely heavily on buffers such as H2CO3 / HCO3− to maintain stable environments.

Worked example

Calculate the pH of a 0.100 mol dm−3 solution of ethanoic acid, given that Ka = 1.70 × 10^(−5) mol dm−3. Step 1: Set up the expression Ka = [H+][CH3COO−] / [CH3COOH]. Step 2: Assume [H+] equals [CH3COO−] and un-dissociated [CH3COOH] equals the initial concentration 0.100 mol dm−3. Step 3: Rearrange to [H+] = √(Ka × [CH3COOH]) = √(1.70 × 10^(−5) × 0.100) = 1.304 × 10^(−3) mol dm−3. Step 4: Calculate pH = −log(1.304 × 10^(−3)) = 2.89.

Key points to remember

Students often forget that the approximation [H+] = [CH3OOH-equilibrium] only holds true for weak acids with small Ka values where dissociation is less than 5 percent. When diluting a weak acid 10 times, the pH increases by less than 1 unit, whereas a strong acid pH increases by exactly 1 unit. Remember that diprotic acids donate two protons per molecule, requiring stoichiometric adjustments in neutralisation calculations and titration curves with two distinct equivalence points. When preparing buffers, the weak acid must be in excess or partially neutralised by a strong base to ensure both the acid and its salt are present in significant quantities. For core practical 11, measuring the pH at the half-neutralisation point directly gives pKa because [HA] equals [A−], meaning Ka equals [H+].

title: Exam technique: Data Handling
content:
### What earns the marks

Four values are 2, 3, 3, 5, 8, 9 (six values in total). The median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values: (3 + 5) / 2 = 4. For a mean of 9 from four values, the total must be 36: write the sum first, then divide by 4. Both steps earn their own marks.

### Compare distributions in context
When asked to compare two sets of data, give one comparison of an average and one comparison of spread, and state both in terms of the data. A correct statement with no link to the context earns only part of the mark.

title: Chemical Equilibria Quick Revision
content:
Chemical Equilibria Quick Revision

Chemistry — A2. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13, covers chemical equilibria, including equilibrium constants and the effects of changes in concentration, pressure, and temperature. The equilibrium constant tells you the position of that equilibrium at a given temperature.

  • The equilibrium constant Kc is expressed as [products]/[reactants] for homogeneous systems and Kp is expressed as partial pressures of products/partial pressures of reactants in atm.
  • Changes in temperature, pressure, or the presence of a catalyst affect the equilibrium composition, but the value of the equilibrium constant is not affected by changes in concentration or pressure or by the addition of a catalyst.
  • The effect of temperature on the equilibrium constant is explained using a change in the value of the equilibrium constant, with an increase in temperature increasing Kc for endothermic reactions and decreasing Kc for exothermic reactions.

Worked example

For the reaction N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, Kc = [NH3]^2 / ([N2] * [H2]^3). If the equilibrium concentrations are [NH3] = 0.5 mol dm^-3, [N2] = 0.2 mol dm^-3, and [H2] = 0.3 mol dm^-3, then Kc = (0.5)^2 / (0.2 * (0.3)^3) = 0.5^2 / (0.2 * 0.027) = 0.25 / 0.0054 = 46.3.

Key points to remember

Students often forget that the equilibrium constant is not affected by changes in concentration or pressure, but is affected by changes in temperature. The value of the equilibrium constant can be used to predict the extent to which a reaction takes place.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Heterogeneous Systems and Partial Pressures

When writing expressions for Kc or Kp for heterogeneous systems, pure solids and pure liquids are omitted because their concentrations remain essentially constant throughout the reaction. For example, in the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO3(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2(g), the expression simplifies to Kp = p(CO2), where p(CO2) represents the equilibrium partial pressure of carbon dioxide measured in atmospheres.

Calculating Kp from Experimental Data

To calculate Kp, you must first determine the mole fraction of each gas present at equilibrium. The mole fraction is calculated by dividing the number of moles of a specific gas by the total number of moles of all gases in the mixture. The partial pressure of an individual gas is then found by multiplying its mole fraction by the total pressure of the system in atm. For instance, if a gas has a mole fraction of 0.25 and the total pressure is 4.0 atm, its partial pressure is 1.0 atm.

Thermodynamics and Equilibrium Constants

The link between entropy and the equilibrium constant is established through the equation Stotal = R ln(K), where R is the universal gas constant and ln(K) is the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant. For an endothermic reaction, increasing the temperature causes Stotal to become more positive, leading to an increase in the value of the equilibrium constant. Conversely, for an exothermic reaction, increasing the temperature decreases the value of the equilibrium constant as total entropy change falls.

Advanced Worked Example

Consider the equilibrium reaction 2SO2(g) + O2(g) ⇌ 2SO3(g). In a 5.0 dm³ container, 2.0 moles of SO2 and 1.0 mole of O2 are allowed to reach equilibrium. At equilibrium, 1.6 moles of SO3 are present. Calculate Kc. First, find equilibrium moles: SO3 = 1.6, so moles of SO2 reacted = 1.6, leaving 2.0 − 1.6 = 0.4 moles of SO2. Moles of O2 reacted = 1.6 ÷ 2 = 0.8, leaving 1.0 − 0.8 = 0.2 moles of O2. Convert to concentrations by dividing by 5.0 dm³: [SO3] = 0.32 mol dm⁻³, [SO2] = 0.08 mol dm⁻³, [O2] = 0.04 mol dm⁻³. Substitute into Kc = [SO3]² / ([SO2]² * [O2]) = (0.32)² / ((0.08)² * 0.04) = 0.1024 / (0.0064 * 0.04) = 0.1024 / 0.000256 = 400 dm³ mol⁻¹.

Additional Examination Tips

Examiners frequently penalize students for omitting units or using incorrect units for equilibrium constants. Always derive the units by substituting mol dm⁻³ for concentrations and atm for partial pressures into the rearranged equilibrium expression. Furthermore, remember that a very large value of Kc or Kp (greater than 10¹⁰) indicates that the position of equilibrium lies heavily to the right, meaning the reaction goes almost to completion, whereas a very small value indicates that hardly any reaction takes place.

title: Acids, Bases and Salts
content:
Acids, Bases and Salts

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 7 (statements 7.1–7.3). Acid and base properties, strong versus weak acids, oxide classification, and the preparation of soluble and insoluble salts with full practical detail.

7.1 Acids and bases

  • An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a base is a proton acceptor. An alkali is a soluble base. Neutralisation is H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
  • Acid reactions: with metals to give a salt and hydrogen; with bases to give a salt and water; with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
  • Strong acids (hydrochloric, sulfuric, nitric) are fully dissociated in water; weak acids (ethanoic, carbonic) are only partly dissociated. Both can be dilute or concentrated — strength and concentration are different ideas.

7.2 Oxides

  • Basic oxides are metal oxides such as CuO; acidic oxides are non-metal oxides such as SO₂; amphoteric oxides react with both acids and bases — Al₂O₃ and ZnO are the syllabus examples.

7.3 Preparation of salts

  • Soluble salts by titration: dissolve the acid, use a pipette and burette with an indicator, add alkali until neutralised, then evaporate to crystallise.
  • Soluble salts from an excess insoluble reactant: add excess metal or insoluble base or carbonate to the acid, filter off the excess, evaporate the filtrate.
  • Insoluble salts by precipitation: mix two solutions whose ions combine to form an insoluble salt; filter, wash and dry. Silver chloride and barium sulfate are the standard examples.
  • Hydrated salts contain water of crystallisation (CuSO₄·5H₂O); heating drives it off to give the anhydrous salt, which turns blue again with water.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Method choice, applied to making pure copper sulfate crystals from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid: copper oxide is insoluble, so add it in excess to the acid, filter, then crystallise. You cannot titrate here — there is no soluble base to measure. Justify the choice of method in one sentence; that justification is the mark.
  • Purity reasoning, applied to crystals dried too quickly: crystals coated with impure surface moisture give a melting point below the pure value and a broad range. A pure substance melts sharply at a single temperature — quote the sharp range as the evidence.
  • Strong versus weak, applied to equal concentrations of hydrochloric and ethanoic acid: hydrochloric acid has a lower pH and a greater temperature rise when reacting with the same mass of magnesium, because it is fully dissociated and supplies more H⁺ per mole. Name dissociation as the reason.

Common errors

  • Confusing strong (fully dissociated) with concentrated (lots of solute per dm³).
  • Forgetting to filter off the excess solid when preparing a salt from an insoluble reactant.
  • Choosing titration for a preparation where one reactant is insoluble.

title: Exam technique: Probability
content:
### What earns the marks
For combined events, each branch probability with the changed denominator earns a mark: write 3/5 then 2/4 for no-replacement draws. For expectation, probability times trials stated earns the mark even with arithmetic slips. For conditional probability, restricting the denominator to the given condition earns the method mark: write 12/20 before simplifying. For P(A or B), the overlap subtracted earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: unchanged denominator after a no-replacement draw. Correction: both numerator and denominator drop. Error: dividing by 50 for a given-glasses probability. Correction: condition first, population second. Error: adding P(A) + P(B) without subtracting the overlap. Correction: both-occurring counted twice. Error: adding single-coin probabilities for two coins. Correction: multiply along branches.
### Worked example
A bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters. Two are drawn without replacement. P(both red) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 3/10. Write each branch fraction with its changed denominator before multiplying. P(at least one red) is quicker as 1 − P(both blue) = 1 − (2/5 × 1/4) = 9/10.

title: Tenses in Context — Study Notes
content:
Why tenses are harder than they look

Tense choice depends on time, but time is only the start. Two sentences about the same event can use different tenses and mean different things. A student who picks the right tense for a single gap usually gets the harder questions wrong because they have learned the form, not the use. These notes build from the form to the use, and then to the situations where examiners ask you to choose.

The tense families

It is easier to think in families than in a list of twelve forms. Each family groups tenses that share one central idea. Learn the idea first; the exact form comes from the time you are talking about.

Present family

The present family covers what is true now, what happens regularly, and what is happening at this moment.

  • Present simple: facts, general truths, routines, states. Water boils at 100 C. The bus leaves at seven. She works in a bank.
  • Present continuous: actions happening now, temporary situations, fixed future arrangements. I am studying for my exams this week. They are meeting the principal tomorrow.
  • Present perfect: a past action connected to now, with since, for, ever, never, just, already, yet. I have lived here since 2019. Have you ever been to Paris?

The common mistake is using the present perfect with a finished time word. Write "I have lived here since 2019", not "I have lived here in 2019". "Ago" forces the past simple: "I lived here two years ago".

Past family

The past family covers finished actions and states, whether the time is stated or simply understood.

  • Past simple: a completed action at a definite past time. She went to the cinema yesterday. We moved to Leeds in 2015.
  • Past continuous: an action in progress at a past moment, often as background to a shorter action. When the phone rang, I was taking a shower.
  • Past perfect: an action completed before another past time. By the time we arrived, the film had started. She had already left when I called.

Students often use the past simple where the past perfect is needed because both refer to the past. The difference is order: the past perfect happened first. If two past events appear, the earlier one takes the past perfect.

Future family

English has several future forms, and the choice depends on how certain the future event is and how it is viewed.

  • Will: spontaneous decisions, predictions without present evidence, offers, promises. I will help you with that. It will rain tomorrow.
  • Going to: predictions with present evidence, plans and intentions. Look at those clouds - it is going to rain. She is going to study medicine.
  • Present continuous for future: fixed arrangements with a time and place. I am meeting her at six. We are flying to Madrid next week.
  • Future continuous: an action in progress at a future time. This time next week, we will be lying on the beach.
  • Future perfect: an action completed before a future time. By next year, she will have graduated. By the time you arrive, they will have finished.

The most common error is using "will" when present evidence is clear. "Look at those clouds - it will rain" is weaker than "it is going to rain" because the evidence is present now.

Perfect family

The perfect forms connect two times. The auxiliaries have/has/had + past participle always carry that connection.

  • Present perfect: past to now. I have lost my keys (and I still cannot get in).
  • Past perfect: earlier past to later past. When I got home, she had cooked dinner.
  • Future perfect: now to a future point. By 2030, the bridge will have been built.

The perfect is not about the action itself but about the link it makes. "I lost my keys" tells you the action; "I have lost my keys" tells you the action and its present result.

Continuous family

The continuous forms carry the idea of duration or interruption rather than completion.

  • Past continuous: background action interrupted by a shorter past action.
  • Present continuous: action around now, or a temporary state.
  • Future continuous: action in progress at a future point.

A continuous form is right when the focus is on the activity in progress, not on the fact that it is finished.

Passive voice

The passive puts the receiver first: the subject receives the action. It is common in formal and scientific writing, and in exam questions where the actor is unknown or unimportant.

  • The report was written by the team.
  • The bridge is being built this year.
  • The results have been published.

Form: be + past participle. Keep the tense of "be" correct - the passive of the present simple is "is/are + past participle", the passive of the past simple is "was/were + past participle", the passive of the present perfect is "has/have been + past participle".

Do not overuse the passive. Use it when the receiver matters more than the actor, or when the actor is unknown.

Conditionals

Conditionals describe what happens if a condition is met. The four main types are:

  • Zero conditional: general truth. If you heat ice, it melts. Present simple in both parts.
  • First conditional: real future possibility. If it rains, I will stay home. If + present simple, will + infinitive.
  • Second conditional: unreal present. If I had more time, I would learn the piano. If + past simple, would + infinitive.
  • Third conditional: unreal past. If I had studied harder, I would have passed. If + past perfect, would have + past participle.

The most common errors are mixing the types (e.g. "If I would have known, I would tell you") and using "was" instead of "were" in the second conditional ("If I were you"). After verbs of suggestion (suggest, recommend, insist), the base form is standard: "She suggested that he leave early".

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the past simple with since/for: "I lived here since 2019" should be "I have lived here since 2019".
  • Using "will" where present evidence makes "going to" better: "Look at those clouds - it will rain" should be "it is going to rain".
  • Using "ago" in the present perfect: "I have seen him ago" should be "I saw him a week ago".
  • Using the past perfect without a later past event to compare with.
  • Confusing "used to" (past habit, no longer true) with "would" (repeated past action): "When I was young, I used to swim every day" and "When I was young, I would swim every day" are both correct, but "used to" emphasises that the habit has ended.
  • Writing "I am knowing" - stative verbs such as know, believe, want, like, belong usually do not take the continuous form.

How to choose in an exam question

When a gap-fill or multiple-choice question asks for a tense, work through these checks in order:

  1. Is there a time word? "Yesterday", "in 2015", "ago" leads to past simple. "Since", "for", "ever", "never" leads to present perfect. "By the time", "before" with another past event leads to past perfect.
  2. Is the action finished or still connected to now? Finished and no present link leads to past simple. Finished but with a present result leads to present perfect.
  3. Is one action in progress when another happens? The longer action leads to continuous. The shorter, interrupting action leads to simple.
  4. Is the future event a fixed arrangement, a plan, or a spontaneous decision? Fixed arrangement leads to present continuous. Plan or intention with evidence leads to going to. Spontaneous decision leads to will.
  5. Is there a condition? Identify the type (real future, unreal present, unreal past) and match the form.

Most exam tense questions can be solved by finding the time word or the relationship between the events, then matching the family.

Examples that teach the rule

A tense is easier to remember when you see the contrast. These pairs show how the meaning changes with the tense:

  • Present simple vs present continuous: "She teaches maths" (permanent job) vs "She is teaching maths this term" (temporary).
  • Past simple vs present perfect: "I lived in London in 2019" (finished) vs "I have lived in London since 2019" (continues now).
  • Past simple vs past perfect: "When I arrived, she cooked dinner" (she cooked after I arrived, or at about the same time) vs "When I arrived, she had cooked dinner" (the dinner was ready when I arrived).
  • Will vs going to: "I think it will rain tomorrow" (prediction) vs "Look at those clouds - it is going to rain" (present evidence).
  • First vs second conditional: "If I have time, I will help" (possible) vs "If I had time, I would help" (impossible now).
  • Active vs passive: "The team wrote the report" (actor important) vs "The report was written by the team" (receiver important) vs "The report was written" (actor unknown or unimportant).

Quick reference

Present simple: facts, routines, states. Present continuous: happening now, temporary, fixed future arrangement. Present perfect: past action connected to now, with since, for, ever, never, just, already, yet. Past simple: finished past action, with yesterday, last week, in 2015, ago. Past continuous: action in progress at a past moment, often as background. Past perfect: action before another past event, with by the time, before, after a past reference. Future will: prediction, decision, offer, promise. Future going to: plan, intention, prediction with present evidence. Future continuous: action in progress at a future time. Future perfect: action completed before a future point, with by next year, by 2030, by the time. Passive: receiver first, actor unknown or unimportant. First conditional: real future possibility. Second conditional: unreal present. Third conditional: unreal past.

Use this as a check, not as a substitute for understanding the families. If you can explain why a tense fits a situation, you can choose correctly in any exam question.

title: Exam technique: Simplifying and Expanding
content:
### What earns the marks
For expansion, calculate earns a mark for every correct pair of products shown before collecting terms. For factorisation, the HCF stated earns the first mark and the fully divided bracket earns the second: partial factorisation scores at most half. For algebraic fractions, factorise first earns the method mark even when cancellation follows.
### Traps
Error: (x + 5)(x - 2) = x squared + 10. Correction: four products, then collect. Error: 3(2x squared - 3x) called fully factorised. Correction: extract x as well. Error: cancelling terms instead of factors in a fraction. Correction: factorise numerator and denominator first.
### Worked example
Expand (2x − 3)(x + 4). The four products are 2x², 8x, −3x and −12. Collecting terms gives 2x² + 5x − 12. For factorisation, 6x² − 9x has HCF 3x, so 6x² − 9x = 3x(2x − 3). Check by expanding the answer back to the original expression.
### Expand in order
Multiply each term in one bracket by each term in the other, then collect like terms. Write the expanded line before you simplify, since the examiner awards marks for each correct expansion.
### Factorise by taking out the common factor first
Take out the highest common factor of all terms before you try any other method. A question asking for a fully factorised answer is incomplete if a common factor is still left in a bracket.
### Index laws
Multiply powers by adding indices, divide by subtracting indices, and raise a power to a power by multiplying indices. Check a simplified expression by substituting a simple number such as 2 for the letter.

title: Exam technique: Representation via Numerical Measures
content:
### What earns the marks
For skewness direction, mean vs median comparison stated earns the mark. For box plots, all five values labelled earn one mark and the skew comment earns the second. For outlier checks, the fence calculation shown earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: skew direction flipped. Correction: tail side names the skew. Error: quartiles mislabeled on plots. Correction: order min, Q1, median, Q3, max. Error: max value called an outlier by eye. Correction: test against the fence.
### Worked example
Data: 2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 20. The mean is 49 / 7 = 7 and the median is 5, so the mean is larger and the skew is positive. The lower half {2, 4, 5} has median 4 (Q1). The upper half {6, 7, 20} has median 7 (Q3). IQR = 3, so the upper fence is 7 + 1.5 × 3 = 11.5, and 20 is an outlier.
### Use the statistics mode carefully
Enter the data with the correct frequencies, and check the calculator's output for the mean and standard deviation. Decide whether the question wants the population or sample standard deviation before you read the answer.

### Show the formulae you used
Write the formula for the mean, or for the variance as E(X²) − [E(X)]², before substituting. Method marks are awarded for a correct formula even when the calculator result is wrong.

### Interpret the measure
Say what the mean or median tells you about the data in the context of the question, and comment on the spread when it is asked for.

title: Algorithms & Programming — Study Notes
content:
Algorithms & Programming

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): pseudocode, flowcharts, standard algorithms (linear/bubble), trace tables, validation & verification.

1. Pseudocode

OUTPUT "Enter n"
INPUT n
IF n MOD 2 = 0 THEN
  OUTPUT "even"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "odd"
ENDIF

FOR i ← 1 TO 10
  total ← total + i
NEXT i

WHILE total < 100
  total ← total + n
ENDWHILE

FUNCTION square(x : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
  RETURN x * x
ENDFUNCTION

Assignment ←, comparison =, MOD/DIV for remainders/quotients.

2. Flowchart symbols

Terminator (oval), process (rectangle), decision (diamond), input/output (parallelogram), flow lines with arrows.

3. Standard algorithms

  • Linear search: check each item until found/end — works unsorted.
  • Bubble sort: repeated adjacent swaps; largest bubbles to the end each pass; n−1 passes max; early exit when no swaps.
  • Counting/totaling patterns; max/min with a running best value.

4. Trace tables

One column per variable; log every assignment in order; watch loop counters and reassignments.

x ← 1; total ← 0
WHILE x <= 4
  total ← total + x * 2
  x ← x + 1
ENDWHILE  // total = 20

5. Validation vs verification

  • Validation: automatic checks on data — range (exam mark 0–100), length (password ≥ 8), type, format (postcode pattern), presence (field not empty), check digit (barcode).
  • Verification: data matches the source — double entry, visual/proof reading.

6. Testing

Normal (typical), abnormal (rejects invalid), boundary (extremes just inside/outside). Test data tables list input → expected output.

Exam tips: write pseudocode with ENDIF/NEXT/ENDWHILE terminators; in trace tables record the condition result too; boundary choices need "just above/below/at" values.

Algorithm design in practice

A good algorithm is correct, efficient and easy to follow. Designers begin by breaking the problem into smaller parts, a method called decomposition. Each part is then written as a step, and the steps are tested with sample data, including data at the limits of the input range.

Pseudocode is a way of writing an algorithm in plain structured English before it is coded in a specific language. It makes the logic clear, so it can be checked and changed without worrying about syntax. Flowcharts show the same logic with symbols for input, process, decision and output.

Exam tip: trace the algorithm step by step with a table of values to show that it produces the expected output.

Worked example: tracing a linear search

Take the list 14, 7, 22, 9, 31 and search for 22. Start at index 0 and compare: 14 is not 22, so move on. Index 1 holds 7, not a match. Index 2 holds 22, which matches, so the algorithm returns index 2 and stops. If the target were 40, every element would be compared and the algorithm would report that the value is absent after checking all five. A trace table with columns for index, value compared and result makes this easy to show in an exam answer.

Common mistakes in algorithm questions

  • Stopping a loop one element too early or too late. Check the start value, the end condition and whether the upper bound is inclusive.
  • Confusing a counter with the value being tested. Trace both variables separately.
  • Writing pseudocode without a clear output. Always state what the algorithm returns or prints.

title: Transformations and Vectors — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Transformations and Vectors

Mathematics — OL. reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

  • 1. Transformations — full descriptions
  • 2. Combined transformations
  • 3. Vectors
  • 4. Vector geometry

Core facts to recall

  • Reflection: state the mirror line. Under y = x the coordinates swap, so (a, b) maps to (b, a).
  • Rotation: state the centre, the angle and the direction. A 90° anticlockwise rotation about the origin maps (x, y) to (−y, x).
  • Translation: give a column vector (x; y). Every point moves by the same amount.
  • Enlargement: state the scale factor and the centre. A negative scale factor rotates the image 180° about the centre as well as scaling it.
  • Vectors: the magnitude of (x; y) is √(x² + y²). A resultant is found by adding the component vectors head to tail.

title: Reproduction
content:
Reproduction

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 16 (statements 16.1–16.6). Asexual and sexual reproduction, plant reproduction from flower to seed, human reproduction, sex hormones and sexually transmitted infections.

16.1 to 16.2 Asexual and sexual reproduction

  • Asexual reproduction involves one parent and mitosis, producing genetically identical offspring — binary fission in bacteria, budding in yeast, plant propagation by runners or cuttings. There is no variation.
  • Sexual reproduction involves two parents and the fusion of gametes, producing genetically varied offspring, which gives an advantage in changing environments.

16.3 Plant reproduction

  • Flower structure: anthers produce pollen, ovaries contain ovules. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from anther to stigma — self-pollination or cross-pollination (by insects or wind). Fertilisation is the fusion of male and female nuclei; the ovule develops into the seed and the ovary wall into the fruit.
  • Seed germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature; the seed coat breaks, the radicle emerges first, and the seedling first uses stored food until it can photosynthesise.

16.4 to 16.6 Human reproduction

  • Testes produce sperm and testosterone; ovaries produce eggs and oestrogen and progesterone. Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube; the blastocyst implants in the uterus lining, and the placenta allows exchange of glucose, amino acids, oxygen, antibodies and wastes between mother and foetus, with the umbilical cord carrying blood.
  • Sexually transmitted infections including HIV are spread by unprotected sexual contact, shared needles or mother to child; prevention uses condoms, screening and education.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Comparison reasoning, applied to why sexual reproduction produces variation: meiosis creates new combinations of alleles through crossing over and independent assortment, and fertilisation combines two different parents' genes. Name the two mechanisms of meiosis — each is its own mark.
  • Placenta exchange reasoning, applied to why antibodies cross but large cells do not: antibodies are small proteins that diffuse across the placental barrier, protecting the foetus; pathogens generally do not cross, which is why some immunity is transferred rather than infection. Explain with size and diffusion, not just "they pass through".
  • Germination evaluation, applied to a seed experiment at different temperatures: the independent variable is temperature, and water and oxygen must be controlled in excess so temperature is the limiting factor. Name which factor would be limiting if water were scarce — that shows you understand limiting factors, not just procedure.

Common errors

  • Confusing pollination (pollen transfer) with fertilisation (nuclei fusion).
  • Saying the placenta is part of the foetus. It forms from uterine tissue and both mother and foetus contribute to it.
  • Claiming seeds need light to germinate. The required factors are water, oxygen and the right temperature.

title: Web Technologies and Security — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Web Technologies and Security

Computer Science — A2. Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

Key areas to revise

  • The Three Layers
  • SQL Injection
  • Encryption
  • Hashing vs Encryption

Core facts to recall

  • Client-side code runs in the browser; server-side code, such as PHP, runs on the server and returns HTML.
  • Parameterised queries keep user input separate from SQL, which prevents SQL injection.
  • Hashing is one-way: a stored hash is compared with a hash of the input, so the original password is not recoverable.
  • Symmetric encryption uses one shared key; asymmetric encryption uses a public and a private key.
  • Name the threat, then the countermeasure: SQL injection needs parameterised queries, and interception needs encryption.

title: Circular Motion and SHM — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Circular Motion and SHM

Physics — A2. Angular speed ω = 2π/T; v = ωr; a = ω²r = v²/r; F = mv²/r toward the centre.

Key areas to revise

  • Circular Motion Recap
  • Simple Harmonic Motion
  • Energy in SHM
  • Damping and Resonance

Core facts to recall

  • Angular speed: ω = 2π / T. Linear speed v = ωr, and the centripetal acceleration is a = ω²r = v² / r.
  • SHM displacement: x = A cos ωt for a body released from maximum displacement. The maximum speed is v = ωA.
  • Acceleration is always directed to the equilibrium position: a = −ω²x.
  • Spring-mass period: T = 2π√(m / k). Simple pendulum period: T = 2π√(l / g) for small angles.
  • Energy: kinetic and potential energy trade places, while total energy stays constant when there is no damping.

title: Continuous Random Variables — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Continuous Random Variables

Mathematics — A2. A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

Key areas to revise

  • Probability Density Functions
  • Finding Unknown Constants
  • Expectation and Variance
  • The Median and Mode
  • Uniform Distribution

Core facts to recall

  • Density function: f(x) ≥ 0 everywhere, and the total area under it is 1.
  • Probability: P(a < X < b) = ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx. A single point has zero probability.
  • Mean: E(X) = ∫ x f(x) dx. Variance: Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
  • Median m: the area to its left is 0.5, so ∫ from the lower limit to m of f(x) dx = 0.5. Mode: the x-value where f(x) is greatest.
  • Uniform distribution on [a, b]: f(x) = 1 / (b − a), mean (a + b) / 2, variance (b − a)² / 12.

title:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 3 Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development. It covers the cell as the unit of life, eukaryotic and prokaryotic ultrastructure, microscopy and measurement, the cell cycle and mitosis, meiosis and genetic variation, gametes and fertilisation in mammals and flowering plants, stem cells, and the genetic control of development through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance. Every statement below the topic owns is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Cells as the units of life and the levels of organisation

All living organisms are made of cells, and all cells share some common features: a plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) enclosing the cell, cytoplasm in which most chemical reactions occur, and ribosomes for protein synthesis. Differences between cell types are explained from these common features — for example the presence or absence of a cell wall, a nucleus, or membrane-bound organelles decides what a cell can do. In multicellular organisms, cells are organised into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into organ systems, each level carrying out a particular function. A tissue is a group of similar cells working together; an organ is made of several tissues with a combined function; an organ system is a group of organs whose functions are linked, such as the digestive system. Understanding this hierarchy matters because a structure at one level is shaped by the level below it — the properties of a tissue follow from the cells it contains.

2. Eukaryotic cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles

Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus that contains the chromosomes, and a range of membrane-bound organelles, each with a distinct function. The plasma membrane (cell surface membrane) is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it, controlling what enters and leaves the cell. The nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear envelope with nuclear pores, and contains the cell's DNA; the nucleolus inside the nucleus is the site of ribosome assembly. Ribosomes, made of a large and a small subunit, are the sites of protein synthesis and occur free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The rough endoplasmic reticulum (rER) is a stack of membrane-bound sacs studded with ribosomes; it synthesises proteins and passes them on in vesicles. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum (sER) lacks ribosomes and synthesises lipids and carbohydrates. Mitochondria have a double membrane, the inner one folded into cristae to increase surface area, and a matrix that contains the enzymes for aerobic respiration; they supply ATP. Centrioles are paired microtubule cylinders that organise the spindle fibres during nuclear division. Lysosomes are membrane-bound sacs containing hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out cell components and pathogens. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles for secretion or for delivery to other parts of the cell; it is also involved in the formation of extracellular enzymes. The cytoskeleton of microtubules and microfilaments maintains cell shape, holds organelles in place and enables movement within the cell.

3. Prokaryotic cell ultrastructure and how to tell the two apart

Prokaryotic cells are much smaller than eukaryotic cells and lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Their genetic material is a single, circular DNA molecule that lies free in the cytoplasm, not associated with histones. The cell wall is made of peptidoglycan and gives rigidity and shape. Many prokaryotes have a protective capsule outside the cell wall. Plasmids are small circles of DNA separate from the main chromosome; they can be transferred between cells and often carry genes for antibiotic resistance. Flagella — rigid helical tails that rotate — give motility in some prokaryotes, and pili help cells attach to surfaces and to each other and mediate conjugation. Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, smaller than the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotes. A bacterium therefore shows, in EM images: cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, plasmids, and, where present, flagella and pili — and none of the membrane-bound organelles found in a eukaryotic cell.

4. Seeing the ultrastructure: light and electron microscopy

A light microscope uses visible light passed through a specimen; its maximum useful magnification is around ×1500 and its resolution is about 0.2 µm, limited by the wavelength of light. An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, giving far higher resolution and magnification; transmission electron microscopes (TEM) show the internal ultrastructure of thin sections, and scanning electron microscopes (SEM) show the surface detail of a specimen. Staining is essential in light microscopy because most cells are transparent — stains such as methylene blue for animal cells or iodine solution for starch make structures visible and show up nuclei, starch grains and cell walls. The electron microscope can show the organelles listed in 3.3 — nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rER, sER, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, Golgi apparatus — and, in prokaryotes, the cell wall, capsule, plasma membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, flagella and pili, so that students can recognise the organelles from electron micrographs. In a light microscope the total magnification equals eyepiece magnification × objective magnification; a graticule (eye-piece graticule) fitted with a stage micrometer lets you calibrate it so real sizes can be measured, and specimens can be drawn to scale from the microscope.

5. Core Practical 5 — observing and drawing animal cells

Use a light microscope to make observations and labelled drawings of suitable animal cells, for example cheek epithelial cells. The steps are: sterilise by wiping the mouth, smear a thin layer of cells onto a slide, stain with methylene blue, lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, and observe under the microscope. Draw what you see with the correct relative sizes of nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane, label the parts, and add a title and magnification. Core Practical 5 also develops the skill of using a graticule with a microscope to make measurements and understand the concept of scale — the graticule is calibrated against a stage micrometer at each objective, so the real size of a cell or organelle can be calculated from the number of graticule divisions it spans.

6. Cell division: mitosis, the cell cycle and genetic variation by meiosis

Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for growth and asexual reproduction and is one part of the cell cycle, which is the regular sequence of events in a dividing cell: interphase (during which the cell grows, and DNA is replicated — G1, S and G2), mitosis and cytokinesis. Mitosis itself has stages — prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase — in which the copied chromosomes line up on the equator, separate and move to opposite poles, and new nuclei form, followed by division of the cytoplasm. A useful calculation is the mitotic index, the proportion of cells in a sample that are dividing: mitotic index = number of cells undergoing mitosis ÷ total number of cells in the field of view. This is used in Core Practical 6, the root tip squash, to see and count the stages of mitosis. Meiosis, by contrast, produces genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation: in metaphase I the homologous chromosomes line up as pairs and assort independently (independent assortment), and in prophase I crossing over exchanges alleles between the chromatids of a homologous pair, so that gametes carry new combinations of alleles. A locus is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome; genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together, so linked genes do not assort independently.

7. Gametes, fertilisation in mammals and fertilisation in flowering plants

Mammalian gametes are specialised for their function. Sperm are small and motile, with a haploid nucleus, a lot of mitochondria to power the flagellum, and an acrosome at the head containing enzymes that digest a path through the egg's outer layers. Egg cells are larger, with cytoplasm containing food reserves; the zona pellucida is a glycoprotein layer around the egg that sperm must penetrate. Fertilisation in mammals begins when the acrosome reaction releases enzymes that digest the zona pellucida, then the cortical reaction releases cortical granules into the space around the egg, hardening the zona pellucida and preventing more than one sperm from entering; finally the sperm and egg nuclei fuse, restoring the diploid number. In flowering plants, fertilisation begins with pollination and the growth of a pollen tube from the pollen grain down through the style to the embryo sac; two male nuclei travel down the tube, one fertilising the egg to form the zygote (which develops into the embryo) and one fusing with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm that will feed the developing seed — double fertilisation, unique to flowering plants.

8. Stem cells and what society does with them

A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell that can divide to produce more stem cells and differentiated cells. Totipotent stem cells can develop into any cell type and form a complete organism; the zygote and the cells of the early embryo up to the 16-cell morula are totipotent. Pluripotent stem cells can give rise to many, but not all, cell types; cells of the blastocyst are pluripotent, and in plants many meristem cells are totipotent, which is why a whole plant can be grown from a single cell or tissue. Stem cells are used medically — for example in bone marrow transplants for leukaemia — and their use raises ethical and social questions: the source of embryonic stem cells, the balance of benefit against risk, and decisions made by individuals, committees and governments all draw on scientific knowledge but also on values. Students should be able to discuss these issues from a range of ethical viewpoints.

9. Gene expression: how one gene makes more than one protein and how proteins control cells

Cells become specialised through differential gene expression — different genes are switched on or off in different cells, producing active mRNA and then proteins that control cell processes or determine cell structure. One gene can give rise to more than one protein through post-transcriptional changes to messenger RNA (mRNA) such as alternative splicing, in which the same primary transcript is spliced in different ways to make different mRNAs and therefore different polypeptides. Transcription factors switch genes on or off by binding to DNA and promoting or blocking transcription, so they control which proteins a cell makes. Epigenetic modification — including DNA methylation and histone modification — alters the activation of certain genes without changing the DNA sequence itself, and these modifications can be passed on following cell division, so that a cell's gene activity can be inherited by its daughter cells and, in some cases, across generations.

10. Inheritance: alleles, genotypes, phenotypes and how they vary

A gene is a sequence of bases on a DNA molecule that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide. The allele is one of the different forms of a gene; the genotype is the alleles an organism has; the phenotype is the observable feature that results from the genotype and the environment. Recessive alleles only show in the phenotype when homozygous; dominant alleles show even in the heterozygous state; codominance is when both alleles in the heterozygote contribute to the phenotype. Sex linkage is the inheritance of a gene carried on the X chromosome, such as red-green colour blindness in humans, which appears more often in males because they have only one X chromosome and so express a recessive allele on it. Some phenotypes are affected by multiple alleles for the same gene, and others by polygenic inheritance, where many genes each contribute a small effect, giving rise to continuous variation in the phenotype — height in humans is a classic example. The environment can also affect phenotype, so that a feature is the result of an interaction between genotype and environment rather than genotype alone.

11. Mutations: how they arise and what they can do

Errors in DNA replication can give rise to mutations — changes to the base sequence of DNA. A substitution replaces one base with another and may change one amino acid or none (because the code is degenerate); an insertion adds one or more bases, and a deletion removes one or more, and these can cause a frameshift that changes every amino acid after the mutation and often produces a non-functional protein. Mutations are the source of new alleles, and some mutations give rise to cancer or genetic disorders, while many have no observable effect. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder caused by a recessive allele; the faulty allele affects chloride ion channels, so the functioning of the gaseous exchange, digestive and reproductive systems is impaired — thick mucus blocks the airways, the pancreas duct is blocked so digestion is affected, and fertility in males is reduced because the vas deferens is absent or blocked.

12. Genetic screening and the questions it raises

Genetic screening can identify carriers of a recessive allele, and prenatal testing — including amniocentesis (sampling the fluid around the embryo) and chorionic villus sampling (taking a sample of placental tissue) — can check an embryo or fetus for genetic disorders. Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) is used during IVF to test embryos before implantation so that only unaffected embryos are used. These techniques raise ethical and social questions: the reliability and risk of the test, the right to know or not to know, who decides what is a disorder worth preventing, the cost and access to treatment, and the risk of starting down a path toward selecting traits rather than preventing disease. Students should be able to identify and discuss these issues from religious, moral and social viewpoints.

13. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working section by section through the topic, checking that you can name every organelle, state its function, and recognise it in an electron micrograph. Practise the calculations — magnification, real size from image size and magnification, mitotic index, and the index of diversity and the calculations that appear in the genetics sections. Revise by drawing and labelling an animal cell and a plant cell from memory, annotating each organelle with its function, then testing yourself on meiosis and on how variation arises. After this topic, revise Topic 4 Plant structure, biodiversity and conservation, and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because the genetics here underpins inheritance in those later topics.

  • Magnification, applied to a mitochondrion measuring 4.2 cm on a micrograph at ×20 000: actual size = image size ÷ magnification. 4.2 cm = 42 000 µm, so the real length is 42 000 ÷ 20 000 = 2.1 µm. Convert every unit to µm before you divide, and write the magnification formula out.

title: States of Matter
content:
States of Matter

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 1 (statements 1.1–1.2). Everything a top-grade answer needs on solids, liquids and gases, kinetic theory, heating and cooling curves, and diffusion — plus the reasoning examiners reserve the last marks for.

1.1 Solids, liquids and gases

  • Solids: particles packed in a regular lattice, touching, vibrating about fixed positions. Liquids: close together but randomly arranged, moving past each other. Gases: far apart, random rapid motion, mostly empty space.
  • Melting and boiling are endothermic; freezing and condensing are exothermic. During a change of state the temperature stays constant while the energy is used to overcome the forces between particles — this is why heating curves have flat sections.
  • Heating a gas: its particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. Cooling it: they lose kinetic energy. Increasing the pressure of a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature pushes the particles closer together, so the volume decreases.

1.2 Diffusion

  • Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, due to random motion. It happens in gases and in liquids, and is faster at higher temperatures.
  • A light gas diffuses faster than a heavy one at the same temperature, because the average speed of the particles is higher for the lower relative molecular mass (Mr). So ammonia (Mr 17) diffuses faster than hydrogen chloride (Mr 36.5).

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Heating curve reasoning, applied to a solid being heated to a gas: the two flat sections are melting and boiling. Say that energy is being used to overcome the forces of attraction between particles, NOT that bonds in the particles are breaking — the particles themselves are unchanged in a physical change.
  • Diffusion calculation, applied to a cotton wool plug experiment: two plugs are soaked in concentrated ammonia and concentrated hydrochloric acid at opposite ends of a tube. NH₃ (Mr 17) travels faster than HCl (Mr 36.5), so the white ring of NH₄Cl forms closer to the HCl end. The ratio of distances travelled equals the ratio of speeds, which is roughly the inverse ratio of the square roots of Mr: √36.5 ÷ √17 = 6.04 ÷ 4.12 = 1.47, so the ring is about 1.47 times further from the ammonia end.
  • Explain-type mark scheme: when asked why gases mix, the three marks are random particle motion, particles moving down a concentration gradient, and the system becoming more spread out. Give all three.

Common errors

  • Saying gas particles expand when heated — the particles gain speed, the spaces between them grow.
  • Attributing the flat part of a heating curve to bonds inside molecules breaking. In 0620 it is the forces between particles being overcome.
  • Claiming diffusion needs stirring. It does not — random motion does the work.

title: Exam technique: Materials and Deformation
content:
### What earns the marks
For stress and strain, each definition quoted with units or unitless noted earns a mark. For Young modulus, stress over strain earns the method mark with a steel-scale answer. For graphs, area read as stored energy earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: strain given units. Correction: strain is a pure ratio. Error: force-extension gradient called energy. Correction: gradient is stiffness; area is energy. Error: plastic region called elastic. Correction: only the straight line obeys Hooke.
### Worked example
Under a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin, the point (3, 1) maps to (−1, 3). Each point's x and y change places with one sign reversed. Under a reflection in the line y = x, the same point maps to (1, 3), so the coordinates swap. For a translation by vector (2; −3), the point (3, 1) maps to (5, −2).
### Calculate stress and strain separately
Stress = F / A, using the cross-sectional area in m². Strain = extension / original length, which has no unit. Write both before you divide to find the Young modulus.

### Use the force-extension graph properly
Within the limit of proportionality the graph is a straight line through the origin, and the gradient gives k in F = kx. The area under the graph gives the energy stored, which is ½Fx for a linear region.

### Describe what happens beyond the elastic limit
Explain that the material no longer returns to its original length, and that the graph curves, so the stress is no longer proportional to strain.

title: Ethics and AI — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Ethics and AI

Computer Science — AS. This summary condenses the Ethics and AI topic. Use it to check which ideas you can state from memory before you open the full notes.

Key areas to revise

  • Professional Bodies
  • Ethical Scenarios
  • AI Characteristics
  • Machine Learning
  • Ethics of AI

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Worked check

A school wants to use an AI tool to grade written homework. Name one benefit, one ethical risk, and one safeguard. A strong answer might say: benefit, faster feedback for students; risk, a model trained on biased data may grade some writing styles unfairly; safeguard, a teacher reviews a sample of the grades and students can appeal. Naming a specific safeguard for a specific risk earns the mark, because general statements such as "AI is bad" do not.

Common mistakes

  • Describing a professional body without saying what it requires of its members.
  • Treating machine learning as a set of hand-written rules. The system learns its behaviour from data, so the quality of that data sets the limits of the output.

title: Exam technique: Programming and Algorithms
content:
### What earns the marks
For validation, the rejected range stated plus the rejection loop earns both marks. For structure, single entry and exit modules using only sequence, selection and iteration earn the design marks. For traces, each variable tracked per line earns method credit. For testing, the stage named with its setting (isolated module vs live users) earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: fixed FOR loops for unknown-attempt validation. Correction: WHILE-until-valid loops. Error: binary search on unsorted data. Correction: sort first or use linear search. Error: unit and acceptance settings swapped. Correction: unit is isolated with test data; acceptance is live with real users.
### Worked example
A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. For a linear search, the program checks each item in turn and can take up to n comparisons. A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.

A binary search on a sorted list halves the search space each time, so 16 sorted items need at most about log₂16 = 4 comparisons. Binary search only works if the list is sorted.

title: Exam technique: Quadratics
content:
### What earns the marks
For solving, the factorised form shown earns the first mark and each root earns credit after. For discriminants, the substitution with signs tracked earns the method mark and the root-count conclusion earns the second. For completing the square, the subtracted square earns the method mark and the turning point stated as a pair earns the final one.
### Traps
Error: negated root pairs from sign slips. Correction: expand-check each bracket. Error: one-sided k ranges. Correction: negative branch included. Error: negative length roots kept. Correction: reject with a reason stated.
### Choose the method
Factorise if the roots are simple, complete the square when the question asks for a turning point or a form such as a(x + p)^2 + q, and use the formula when the roots are not whole numbers. Name the method you have chosen in one line.
### The discriminant
For ax^2 + bx + c, the discriminant b^2 - 4ac tells you the number of real roots: positive gives two distinct roots, zero gives one repeated root and negative gives no real roots. Quote the value before you state the conclusion.
### Sketch the curve
Mark the y intercept at c, the roots where the curve crosses the x axis and the turning point. Label each point with its coordinates when the question asks for a sketch.
### Common slips
Sign errors when substituting a negative b into the formula, and forgetting to divide by 2a at the end.

title: Human Nutrition
content:
Human Nutrition

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 7 (statements 7.1–7.5). Balanced diets and nutrient functions, the digestive system, physical and chemical digestion, and absorption in the small intestine.

7.1 Diet

  • A balanced diet contains the right proportions of carbohydrate, protein, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Carbohydrates and lipids provide energy; protein builds and repairs tissues; vitamins and minerals regulate body processes; fibre adds bulk; water is a solvent and coolant.
  • Deficiency diseases: scurvy (vitamin C), rickets (vitamin D), anaemia (iron), kwashiorkor (protein).

7.2 to 7.4 Digestion

  • The alimentary canal runs mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum. The liver produces bile, the pancreas produces pancreatic juice, and both empty into the small intestine.
  • Physical digestion: chewing breaks food into smaller pieces; bile emulsifies fats into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for enzymes. Bile is alkaline, neutralising stomach acid so enzymes work at their optimum.
  • Chemical digestion by enzymes: amylase (salivary, pancreatic) breaks starch to maltose; pepsin (stomach, acidic) breaks proteins to smaller polypeptides; trypsin (pancreatic, alkaline) continues protein digestion; lipase (pancreatic) breaks emulsified fats to fatty acids and glycerol. Each enzyme works best at the pH of its site.

7.5 Absorption

  • Absorption happens in the small intestine: villi have a large surface area, a one-cell-thick wall, a rich blood supply to carry products away, and lacteals for fatty acids and glycerol. Glucose and amino acids pass into the blood capillaries.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Enzyme site reasoning, applied to why pepsin works in the stomach but trypsin in the small intestine: pepsin's optimum is pH 2 (gastric acid) and trypsin's is about pH 8 (bile neutralises the acid). State the pH of each site and the enzyme's optimum — the matching is the explanation.
  • Adaptation chains, applied to villus features: large surface area increases the rate of absorption; thin wall shortens the diffusion path; the blood supply maintains the concentration gradient by carrying products away. One structure, one function, one mark — write them as separate sentences.
  • Fat absorption reasoning, applied to fatty acids and glycerol: they are lipid-soluble, so they pass into the lacteal rather than the blood capillary, and are then carried in the lymphatic system before entering the bloodstream. Naming the lacteal and the route both earn marks.

Common errors

  • Calling bile an enzyme. It is not — it is a salt emulsion that prepares fats for lipase.
  • Saying absorption happens in the large intestine. Water is absorbed there; nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
  • Confusing digestion (breaking down) with absorption (moving into blood).

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies and Security
content:
### What earns the marks
For trust, the CA signature chain described earns both marks: CA binds key to identity, browsers check against roots. For bulk data, symmetric speed plus asymmetric key exchange earns the hybrid pair. For verification, re-hash and compare stated earns the integrity mark with mismatch meaning change.
### Traps
Error: encryption claimed to stop phishing. Correction: valid TLS carries fake sites too; check identity. Error: hashes claimed to prove authorship. Correction: hashes prove integrity, signatures prove authorship. Error: self-claims accepted as trust. Correction: only CA signatures establish it.
### Client and server
State which side does the work. A client sends requests and displays results, and a server processes requests and stores data. Name the technology on each side when asked.
### Security on the web
Name the threat and the control together. SQL injection is countered by parameterised queries and input validation, and cross-site scripting is countered by escaping output. A control stated without the threat it stops earns only half the mark.
### HTTPS
Explain that HTTPS encrypts data in transit with TLS, so a third party on the network cannot read it, and that the certificate lets the browser check the server's identity.

title: Further Trigonometry — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Further Trigonometry

Mathematics — A2 (9709). Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Key areas to revise

  • Compound Angles
  • Double Angles
  • The R-Form
  • Reciprocal Functions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

The expression a cos θ + b sin θ can be written as R cos(θ − α), where R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a. The same method gives R sin(θ ± α) or R cos(θ ± α) with the matching sign. Writing the expression in this form gives its maximum value R and its minimum value −R, and shows where they occur.

Secant, cosecant and cotangent are the reciprocals of cos, sin and tan. Use the identities 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ to simplify expressions and solve equations. Find all solutions within the given interval, using the quadrants in which the ratio is positive or negative.

title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency — Study Notes
content:
Central Tendency: Mean, Median and Mode

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 1 (WST01), sat at AS.

The Mean

For data x₁, ..., xₙ the mean is

  • x̄ = Σx/n

For a frequency table with midpoints x and frequencies f: x̄ = Σfx/Σf. The mean uses every value, so a single extreme value drags it — that is its main weakness.

The Median

The median is the middle value: position (n + 1)/2 for ordered raw data. With n even, average the two middle values. The median ignores the size of extreme values, so it describes skewed data more honestly. For grouped data, estimate the median by linear interpolation within the median class.

The Mode

The most frequent value. A dataset may have no mode or several. For grouped data the modal class is the one with the highest frequency density (frequency ÷ class width), not the highest frequency.

Effects of Data Changes

Adding a constant a to every value adds a to the mean and median (the mode too) but leaves the spread untouched. Multiplying every value by b multiplies mean and median by b.

Coding

Subtract a constant and divide by a convenient width: y = (x − a)/b. Then x̄ = b·ȳ + a. Coding simplifies arithmetic and always preserves the relationship — the coded mean decodes exactly.

Example: data 2, 4, 4, 10: mean = 5, median = 4, mode = 4. Change 10 to 100: mean = 27.5, median and mode unchanged — the mean chased the outlier.

Exam tips: always state which average you used and why. When asked to compare two distributions, pair a central measure with a spread measure; a mean without a spread is only half an answer.

Exam method: mean, median and mode

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values. The median is the middle value of the ordered list, at position (n + 1)/2, and the mode is the value that occurs most often. Always order the data before finding the median.

For grouped data, the mean is Σfx/Σf using the class midpoints. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and the median class is the one containing the (n + 1)/2 th value.

Each average suits different data. The mean uses every value, so an outlier pulls it away from the centre, while the median is unaffected by extreme values. Say which average is more representative when the question asks you to comment.

Changing one value changes the mean but may not change the median, which is useful to check a calculation.

Exam cue: When the question gives a mean and asks for a missing value, form the equation Σx = n × mean and solve for the unknown.

Worked example: the mean of grouped data

A frequency table gives class intervals, not individual values, so each class is represented by its midpoint. For the classes 0 to 10 with frequency 4, 10 to 20 with frequency 9 and 20 to 30 with frequency 7, the midpoints are 5, 15 and 25. The estimated total is 4 × 5 + 9 × 15 + 7 × 25 = 20 + 135 + 175 = 330, and the total frequency is 20, so the estimated mean is 330 ÷ 20 = 16.5. Because the midpoints replace the true values, this is an estimate, and the answer should be stated as approximately 16.5.

Worked example: the median from a cumulative frequency table

With n = 20 the median is the value of the 10.5th item. Read the cumulative frequency up to the class that contains the 10.5th item, which is the class 10 to 20 here, and interpolate within that class using the proportion of its frequency that lies before the median. The median is the lower boundary of the class plus the class width multiplied by (10.5 − 4) ÷ 9. Here that is 10 + 10 × 6.5 ÷ 9, which gives a median of approximately 17.2.

Choosing a measure

The mean uses every value, so one extreme value moves it. The median is unaffected by extreme values and is the better choice for skewed data such as house prices. The mode is the most common value and is the only measure that can be used for categorical data. A question that asks which average is most representative should be answered by giving a reason tied to the shape of the data.

title: Exam technique: Ethics and AI
content:
### What earns the marks
For bias scenarios, the mechanism stated (training data encodes past discrimination) earns the first mark and a concrete mitigation (balanced data plus outcome audits) earns the second. For legislation, the act named plus the offence matched earns both marks: access offences belong to Computer Misuse, copying to Copyright, personal data to Data Protection.
### Traps
Error: data called neutral. Correction: models inherit their training distribution. Error: every offence labelled hacking. Correction: match offence to act. Error: benefits claimed to excuse rights violations. Correction: consent and licensing still required.
### Balance both sides
Ethics questions reward a structured answer: name the stakeholder, state the benefit, then state the risk. A one-sided answer that only praises or only criticises a technology loses the evaluation mark.
### Use a concrete example
Anchor the point in a real use such as facial recognition, automated exam marking or a recommendation system. Explain who is affected and how, and say what safeguard would reduce the harm.
### Bias and data
When the question concerns bias, trace it to the data: a training set that under-represents a group will produce a model that performs worse for that group. Say this in one clear sentence rather than using the word bias without a cause.

title: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes

English as a Second Language (Oxford) — IGCSE. Many English words are built from a root with prefixes (added to the front) and suffixes (added to the end). Knowing common parts lets you understand new words and spell them correctly.

Key areas to revise

  • Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Normal Distribution
content:
### What earns the marks
For standardising, Z = (X-mu)/sigma written earns the method mark. For areas, the symmetry or complement step shown earns the second mark. For inverse problems, the z-value from tables stated earns the first mark before unstandardising.
### Traps
Error: variance used as sd in Z. Correction: root the variance first. Error: P(X>a) read directly as the lower tail. Correction: subtract from 1. Error: two unknowns solved from one statement. Correction: need two area statements.
