title: Alkenes Revision Notes Edexcel IAL AS Chemistry
content:
Alkenes AS Level Chemistry

These revision notes cover Topic 5 Alkenes from the Edexcel International AS Level Chemistry specification, detailing hydrocarbon unsaturation, geometric isomerism, electrophilic addition mechanisms, addition polymerisation, and polymer waste management.

Structure and bonding in alkenes

Alkenes and cycloalkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons containing a carbon-carbon double bond, which consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond. The general formula for non-cyclic alkenes is CnH2n. A sigma bond is formed by the direct head-on overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis, providing restricted rotation. A pi bond is formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals above and below the plane of the carbon atoms. The carbon atoms of a C=C double bond are planar, with bond angles of approximately 120 degrees due to three regions of electron density repelling each other.

  • General formula for alkenes: CnH2n
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons possess a carbon-carbon double bond consisting of one sigma bond and one pi bond
  • Cycloalkenes also contain a C=C double bond and are unsaturated hydrocarbons
  • The pi bond electron cloud is susceptible to attack by electrophiles
  • Carbon atoms of the C=C double bond are trigonal planar with 120° bond angles

Geometric isomerism and E-Z naming

Geometric isomerism arises due to the restricted rotation around the C=C double bond caused by the presence of the pi bond. For geometric isomers to exist, each carbon atom of the C=C double bond must be attached to two different groups. When the traditional cis- and trans- naming system breaks down because the groups attached to the double-bonded carbons are not identical or simple, the E-Z naming system must be used. Priorities are assigned to the groups on each carbon using the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules based on atomic number. The E isomer has the highest priority groups on opposite sides of the double bond, while the Z isomer has the highest priority groups on the same side.

  • Restricted rotation around the C=C double bond prevents free rotation of substituents
  • Each carbon in the double bond must have two different groups attached for geometric isomerism
  • E-Z system is necessary when cis- and trans- terms become ambiguous or break down
  • Priority is determined by higher atomic number attached directly to the double-bonded carbon
  • E means entgegen (opposite sides); Z means zusammen (same side)

Reactions of alkenes

Alkenes undergo addition reactions where the pi bond breaks and two new single bonds form. Hydrogen addition occurs at 150 degrees Celsius using a nickel catalyst to form an alkane through catalytic hydrogenation. Halogens add rapidly at room temperature to produce a di-substituted halogenoalkane. Hydrogen halides add across the double bond to produce mono-substituted halogenoalkanes. Steam addition requires a phosphoric acid catalyst or sulfuric acid catalyst under high temperature and pressure to produce alcohols. Acidified potassium manganate(VII) oxidises the double bond in a cold solution to produce a diol, causing a colour change from purple to colourless.

  • Hydrogenation: Alkene + H2 in the presence of a Ni catalyst forms an alkane
  • Halogenation: Alkene + X2 produces a di-substituted halogenoalkane
  • Hydrohalogenation: Alkene + HX produces a mono-substituted halogenoalkane
  • Hydration: Alkene + H2O(g) with an acid catalyst (H3PO4) produces an alcohol
    • Oxidation: Alkene + acidified KMnO4 produces a diol with a purple to colourless transition

Testing for unsaturation

The qualitative test for the presence of a C=C double bond uses bromine or bromine water. When an orange-brown bromine solution is shaken with an alkene, the bromine adds across the double bond in an electrophilic addition reaction, causing the solution to decolourise from orange-brown to colourless. Alkanes do not react with bromine water in the dark and the solution remains orange-brown.

  • Reagent: Bromine water or liquid bromine
    • Observation with an alkene: Colour changes from orange-brown to colourless
  • Observation with an alkane: No reaction, solution remains orange-brown
  • Test confirms the presence of an unsaturated carbon-carbon double bond

Mechanisms of electrophilic addition

Electrophilic addition is the characteristic reaction mechanism of alkenes. An electrophile is an electron pair acceptor. The high electron density of the pi bond induces a dipole in non-polar halogen molecules. Curly arrows start from a bond or a lone pair of electrons and point to the electron-deficient site. In the electrophilic addition of bromine to ethene, the pi bond electrons attack the bromine molecule, heterolytically breaking the Br-Br bond and forming a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate or carbocation, followed by attack from the bromide ion. In hydrogen bromide addition, HBr is polar. The hydrogen ion acts as an electrophile, and addition to unsymmetrical alkenes such as propene can yield two possible carbocation intermediates. The major product is formed via the more stable carbocation intermediate. Carbocation stability follows the order: tertiary greater than secondary greater than primary, due to the positive inductive effect of alkyl groups which push electron density towards the positively charged carbon atom.

  • Electrophile definition: An electron pair acceptor
  • Curly arrows must start precisely from a bond or a lone pair
    • Carbocation stability order: tertiary > secondary > primary
  • Primary carbocation has one alkyl group attached to the positively charged carbon
  • Secondary carbocation has two alkyl groups attached
  • Tertiary carbocation has three alkyl groups attached, making it the most stable due to maximum positive inductive effect
  • Major product prediction follows Markovnikov rule: the hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogens already attached

Addition polymerisation

Addition polymerisation involves many small unsaturated alkene molecules, called monomers, joining together to form a long saturated chain called a polymer. The double bond of each monomer opens up to form single covalent bonds with adjacent monomers. To draw the repeat unit given the monomer, change the C=C double bond into a single C-C bond, extend the bonds outside square brackets, and place a letter n outside. To find the monomer from a repeat unit, identify the two-carbon repeat backbone and convert the single bond back into a double bond.

    Polymerisation type: Addition polymerisation of alkenes
  • Monomers contain a carbon-carbon double bond; polymers contain a saturated carbon backbone
  • Repeat unit formula is enclosed in brackets with bonds extending through the brackets
  • Do not leave dangling double bonds inside the repeat unit structure
  • Poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) are standard examples of addition polymers

Polymer disposal and environmental management

Chemists limit environmental problems caused by polymer disposal through innovative chemical engineering. Non-biodegradable polymers persist in landfill sites. Biodegradable polymers, such as those made from poly(lactic acid) derived from plant starch, are broken down by microorganisms into natural substances. Incineration of halogen-containing polymers like poly(chloroethene) produces toxic acidic waste gases such as hydrogen chloride. Chemists remove these toxic waste gases by flue gas desulfurisation or base neutralisation, passing the waste gases through alkaline scrubbers containing calcium carbonate or calcium oxide to neutralise the acidic gases before they escape into the atmosphere.

  • Biodegradable polymers degrade naturally via microorganisms
  • Incineration of polymers releases thermal energy but can produce toxic waste gases
  • Poly(chloroethene) combustion produces toxic hydrogen chloride gas
  • Acidic waste gases are removed using alkaline scrubbers or neutralisation towers
  • Calcium carbonate or calcium oxide reacts with HCl to form neutral salts and water

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Drawing curly arrows starting from empty space rather than from a bond or lone pair. Correction: Always start curly arrows precisely on a covalent bond line or a pair of non-bonding electrons.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that carbocation stability dictates the major product. Correction: Remember that tertiary carbocations are more stable than secondary, which are more stable than primary, because alkyl groups donate electron density.
  • Mistake: Leaving a double bond inside the repeat unit of an addition polymer. Correction: Convert the double bond into a single bond and ensure the bonds extend outside the square brackets.
  • Mistake: Confusing the E and Z labels by not applying priority rules correctly. Correction: Assign priorities using atomic numbers to the groups on each carbon of the double bond separately.

Exam-style questions

    1. State the general formula for alkenes and define the term unsaturated hydrocarbon. Answer: The general formula is CnH2n. An unsaturated hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms with at least one carbon-carbon double bond consisting of a sigma and a pi bond. (1 mark for general formula, 1 mark for definition).
    2. Explain why geometric isomerism can occur in pent-2-ene but not in pent-1-ene. Answer: Pent-2-ene has restricted rotation about the C=C double bond and each carbon of the double bond is attached to two different groups (a methyl group and a hydrogen atom on one, an ethyl group and a hydrogen atom on the other). Pent-1-ene has one carbon of the double bond attached to two identical hydrogen atoms, so geometric isomers cannot form. (2 marks).
    3. Outline the mechanism for the electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide to propene, naming the major product and explaining why it forms in greater yield. Answer: Draw the curly arrow from the C=C pi bond to the hydrogen of HBr, and another arrow from the H-Br bond to the bromine atom. Show two possible carbocation intermediates: a secondary carbocation and a primary carbocation. The major product is 2-bromopropane, which forms via the secondary carbocation because secondary carbocations are more stable than primary carbocations due to the electron-donating inductive effect of two alkyl groups. (4 marks).
    4. Describe the qualitative test to distinguish between hexane and hexene. Answer: Add bromine water to both liquids and shake. Hexene decolourises the orange-brown bromine water to colourless due to electrophilic addition across the double bond. Hexane shows no reaction, and the orange-brown colour remains. (2 marks).
    5. Explain how chemists minimise environmental hazards caused by the disposal of poly(chloroethene). Answer: Poly(chloroethene) is non-biodegradable and produces toxic hydrogen chloride gas upon incineration. Chemists pass the waste gases through alkaline scrubbers or neutralisation towers containing calcium carbonate to react with and neutralise the acidic hydrogen chloride before release. (3 marks).

Use these notes alongside active recall and past paper question practice. Ensure you can draw mechanisms step by step with correct curly arrow origins. Proceed next to review Halogenoalkanes and Reaction Mechanisms.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • E/Z naming, applied to CHBr=CHCl: on each carbon, the group with the higher atomic number takes priority. Br beats H and Cl beats H, so if the two higher-priority groups are on opposite sides, the isomer is E. Compare atomic numbers on the atom attached to the double bond, not the whole group.
  • Markovnikov addition, applied to propene with HBr: the electrophile H⁺ adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, so the carbocation forms on the more substituted carbon. The major product is 2-bromopropane. The stability order is tertiary > secondary > primary carbocation, and that order explains the major product.
  • Mechanism marks: show a curly arrow from the C=C π bond to the H of HBr, then a second curly arrow from the Br⁻ lone pair to the positive carbon. The first arrow is the step that earns the mark, so draw it from the bond, not from a carbon.
  • Bromine water test: decolourisation of orange bromine water shows unsaturation. An alkane does not decolourise it, so an alkene and an alkane are distinguished by this test alone.

title: Exam technique: Differentiation II
content:
### What earns the marks
For chain rule, outer derivative times inner derivative stated earns both marks. For products and quotients, the full rule quoted earns the method mark before substitution. For parametric and implicit work, dy/dt over dx/dt (or -Fx/Fy structure) earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: inner derivative forgotten. Correction: multiply by it always. Error: product rule halved. Correction: both halves required. Error: dy/dx inverted for parametrics. Correction: y-derivative over x-derivative.
### Choose the right rule
Identify whether the function is a product, a quotient or a composite before you differentiate. Writing the outer and inner functions down first prevents the common error of differentiating only the outside.

### Keep the working tidy
Differentiate, substitute the point, and then simplify. Leave the answer in exact form if the question asks for it, and only use decimals when they are requested.

### Justify the nature of a stationary point
Give the sign of the second derivative, or the signs of the gradient either side of the point, and then state whether the point is a maximum or a minimum.

title: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic — Study Notes
content:
Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): six gates, truth tables, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

1. The six gates

ABANDORNANDNORXOR
0000110
0101101
1001101
1111000

NOT inverts. NAND = AND + invert; NOR = OR + invert; XOR = 1 when inputs differ.

2. Truth tables

2 inputs → 4 rows; 3 inputs → 8 rows. Work gate by gate, adding intermediate columns for sub-circuit outputs.

3. Logic expressions

A Boolean expression describes a circuit in logic: X = A AND NOT B, or X = (A OR B) AND C. Brackets fix the order — work out bracketed parts first, then AND, then OR.

  • Circuit → expression: label the output of every gate (P, Q, …), write one expression per gate in order, then combine them at the final gate.
  • Truth table → expression: mark the rows where the output is 1; for each such row write a term that is true only in that row (write NOT for an input that is 0, AND between the inputs); join the terms with OR. For XOR: X = (NOT A AND B) OR (A AND NOT B).
  • Expression → truth table: add an intermediate column for each sub-expression before the output column.
  • Rules used to simplify: A AND 1 = A; A AND 0 = 0; A OR 1 = 1; A OR 0 = A; A AND A = A; A AND NOT A = 0; A OR NOT A = 1; NOT(NOT A) = A; X OR (X AND Y) = X. (AS extension, 9618: De Morgan's laws — NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B and NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.)

Example: a light X is on only when switch A is on and switch B is off → X = A AND NOT B, so X = 1 in exactly one row of its truth table (A = 1, B = 0).

4. Problem → logic

Define inputs/outputs first. Alarm rings (X=1) if sensor P triggered AND (door D OR window W): X = P AND (D OR W). Then draw the circuit: OR first, then AND.

5. Describing circuits

Write the expression from a diagram gate by gate; annotate output of each gate (X, Y) before combining.

Exam tips: check your truth table row count before writing; in problem questions, state "input P = 1 means sensor triggered" — definitions earn marks.

Worked example: building an expression from a circuit

A circuit gives Q = (A AND B) OR NOT C. Build it in stages: first the AND gate on A and B, then a NOT gate on C, then an OR gate combining the two outputs. A truth table with columns A, B, C, then the intermediate AND output, NOT C and finally Q, has eight rows for three inputs. Set out every row in order so that no combination is missed.

Simplifying with Boolean laws

Laws such as De Morgan's theorem let you rewrite NOT (A AND B) as NOT A OR NOT B. Use them to reduce a gate count before drawing a circuit. Always check a simplified expression against the original truth table, because a single misapplied law changes the output for some inputs.

title: Integration II — Study Notes
content:
Integration II

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 4 (WMA14), sat at A2.

Standard Integrals

  • ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c
  • ∫ cos x dx = sin x + c
  • ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c
  • ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c
  • ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + c

With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Substitution

Reverse of the chain rule. For ∫ 2x e^(x²) dx, let u = x²: du = 2x dx, so the integral is ∫ e^u du = e^(x²) + c.

Integration by Parts

∫ u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫ v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that simplifies when differentiated (LIATE: logs, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential).

Example: ∫ x e^x dx = x e^x − ∫ e^x dx = x e^x − e^x + c.

Partial Fractions

Break rational functions into pieces like ∫ 1/(x+1) dx = ln|x + 1| + c.

Example: ∫ 4x/(x² − 1) dx = ∫ [2/(x − 1) + 2/(x + 1)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| + 2 ln|x + 1| + c.

Exam tips: definite integrals: substitute limits into the transformed variable directly; for by-parts integrals like ∫ ln x dx, take u = ln x, dv/dx = 1.

Exam method: exponential and reciprocal integrals

The integral of e^(kx) is (1/k) e^(kx) + c, and the integral of e^x is e^x + c. The integral of 1/(ax + b) is (1/a) ln|ax + b| + c. Dividing by the coefficient of x is the step most often missed, so check it by differentiating your answer.

For a definite integral, evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit, subtract its value at the lower limit, and write the bracket with its limits, such as [e^(2x)/2] from 0 to 1.

When the integrand is a product, integration by parts gives ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Choose u to be the part that becomes simpler when differentiated, such as x in x eˣ.

Substitution changes the limits as well as the variable. Either change the limits to the new variable or substitute back before using the original limits; do not mix the two.

Exam cue: Give the answer as an exact value, such as (e² − 1)/2, unless the question asks for a decimal.

Worked example: integration by parts

Find the integral of x e^x with respect to x. Let u = x and dv/dx = e^x, so du/dx = 1 and v = e^x. Then the integral equals x e^x minus the integral of e^x, which is x e^x − e^x + c = (x − 1) e^x + c. Differentiate the answer to check that it returns the integrand.

Definite integrals and area

For a region above the x-axis, the definite integral between the limits gives its area. If part of the curve lies below the axis, that part contributes a negative value to the integral, so the total area is the sum of the absolute values of each part. Sketch the curve first. Integrating across a point where the curve crosses the axis gives the signed net value, not the area.

Checking your answer

  • After integrating, differentiate the answer and confirm that it reproduces the original function.
  • Include the constant of integration on indefinite integrals, and never write it on a definite integral.
  • When a substitution changes the variable, change the limits too, or convert back to x before substituting the original limits.

The integration topic of the Cambridge AS and A Level Mathematics 9709 syllabus expects these methods to be applied to standard forms and to exam-style problems, with the method stated clearly at each step.

title: Transition Metals and their Chemistry Quick Revision
content:
Quick revision: Transition Metals and their Chemistry

Chemistry — A2. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15, Topic 17. Transition metals form coloured complex ions, show variable oxidation states and act as catalysts. These properties come from partly filled d orbitals.

Key areas to revise

  • Complex ions and ligands
  • Colour
  • Ligand substitution and isomerism
  • Catalysis

Worked example

Deduce the electronic configuration of the Fe2+ ion given atomic number Z = 26. Step 1: Write the neutral atom configuration, which is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d6. Step 2: Remove electrons from the outermost principal quantum shell first, meaning the two 4s electrons are removed. Answer: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6.

Key points to remember

Transition metals are d-block elements forming one or more stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals. Scandium and zinc are d-block elements but not transition metals because Sc3+ has an empty d-orbital (3d0) and Zn2+ has a full d-orbital (3d10). Variable oxidation numbers occur because the 4s and 3d sub-shells are very close in energy, requiring similar amounts of energy for successive ionization. A ligand is a species with a lone pair of electrons that can form a dative coordinate bond with a central metal ion to form a complex ion, which consists of a central metal ion surrounded by ligands. Aqueous transition metal ions are coloured due to d-orbital splitting caused by the electrostatic field of surrounding ligands, where light is absorbed promoting an electron between split d-orbitals. Lack of colour in ions like Sc3+ (3d0) or Zn2+ (3d10) arises because d-orbitals are empty or completely full, so no d-to-d electron transitions can occur. Coordination number is the total number of coordinate bonds formed between ligands and the central metal ion.

Colour changes in transition metal ions arise from changes in the oxidation number of the ion, changes in the ligand, or changes in the coordination number of the complex. Water (H2O), hydroxide (OH−) and ammonia (NH3) act as monodentate ligands forming six-coordinate octahedral complexes. Chloride ions (Cl−) are relatively large, so fewer can fit around a central metal ion, forming four-coordinate tetrahedral complexes. Square planar complexes are formed by certain metal ions such as Pt(II); cis-platin is a square planar platinum(II) complex used as an anticancer drug, supplied as a single cis isomer because the trans isomer is inactive. Bidentate ligands like ethane-1,2-diamine (NH2CH2CH2NH2) donate two lone pairs, and hexadentate ligands like EDTA4− donate six lone pairs. Haemoglobin is an iron(II) complex containing a polydentate macrocyclic ligand, where oxygen bound to haemoglobin undergoes ligand exchange and is replaced by carbon monoxide due to stronger binding affinity.

Vanadium exhibits four oxidation states in aqueous solution with distinct colours: +5 is yellow (VO2+), +4 is blue (VO2+), +3 is green (V3+), and +2 is violet (V2+). These can be interconverted using zinc in acidic conditions, where Eo values dictate the reduction steps. Dichromate(VI) ions (Cr2O7 2−) can be reduced to Cr3+ and Cr2+ using zinc in acidic conditions, or produced from Cr3+ by oxidation with hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions followed by acidification. Dichromate(VI) ions exist in equilibrium with chromate(VI) ions: Cr2O7 2− + H2O = 2CrO4 2− + 2H+. Transition metal ions like Cr3+, Mn2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Co2+, Ni2+, Cu2+, and Zn2+ react with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia to form characteristic precipitates, some of which dissolve in excess alkali or ammonia due to amphoteric behaviour, deprotonation, or ligand exchange. Notable ligand exchanges include forming [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ via Cu(OH)2(H2O)4, forming [CuCl4]2− from [Cu(H2O)6]2+, and forming [CoCl4]2− from [Co(H2O)6]2+. Substituting monodentate ligands with bidentate or hexadentate ligands increases entropy (positive ΔSsystem), driving the chelate effect and yielding a more stable complex ion.

Catalysis by transition metals is split into heterogeneous and homogeneous types. Heterogeneous catalysts are in a different phase from reactants, with reactions occurring on the active sites of the catalyst surface, as seen with V2O5 acting via oxidation state changes in the contact process (SO2 to SO3), and catalytic converters adsorbing CO and NO, weakening bonds, reacting to form CO2 and N2, and desorbing the products. Homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase as reactants and proceed via intermediate species, such as Fe2+ ions catalysing the reaction between I− and S2O8 2− ions, and Mn2+ ions autocatalysing the reaction between MnO4− and C2O4 2− ions. Core Practical 14 involves the laboratory preparation of a transition metal complex such as copper(II) sulfate crystals or potassium tris(oxalato)ferrate(III).

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Summary Writing — Study Notes
content:
A summary task tests whether you can select the relevant information and express it concisely in your own words. Accuracy and economy matter more than style.

Reading the task first

Read the question before the text. It tells you which points to select, and it sets the word limit. Mark the text lightly as you read, looking for the points the question asks for and ignoring examples and illustrations unless they are needed.

Selecting points

  • Include main points that answer the question directly.
  • Leave out anecdotes, examples and repeated ideas.
  • Keep the order logical, usually following the text's order unless the question asks otherwise.

Paraphrasing

Paraphrasing means rewriting an idea in your own words and sentence structure. Changing one or two words is not enough.

Techniques

  • Replace phrases with equivalent expressions, for example "in the not-too-distant future" becomes "soon".
  • Combine two sentences into one where the ideas are connected.
  • Use a general word for a list of specific examples where the question allows it.

Staying concise

Cut filler such as "in my opinion" or "it is important to note that". Each sentence should carry a required point. Count your words and stay within the limit.

Checking your summary

Read your summary alone. Does it answer the question? Could a reader understand it without the original text? Is every sentence necessary?

title: Exam technique: Measurement and Units
content:
### What earns the marks
For instrument choice, the micrometer for small diameters earns the mark with its 0.01 mm precision. For density, mass over volume with correct units earns both marks. For readings, meniscus bottom at eye level earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: parallax ignored in cylinders. Correction: eye level with the meniscus. Error: newton expanded wrongly. Correction: kg m/s squared from F = ma. Error: volume of a box miscalculated. Correction: multiply all three sides.
### Method marks
Convert units before calculating. 1 cm³ = 1 mL, and 1 m³ = 10^6 cm³. Density is in g/cm³ or kg/m³, so check which one the question wants. Write each conversion on its own line so the examiner can award method marks.
### Reading instruments
For a single reading, the uncertainty is half the smallest division. For repeated readings, use the spread of the readings. Quote the uncertainty with the same number of decimal places as the reading.
### Common slips
Reading a measuring cylinder from the top of the water surface. Read at eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Study Notes
content:
`# Programming and Algorithms

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: sections 9, 11 and 12 (Algorithm design; Programming; Software development), examined in AS Paper 2.

Design Approaches

  • Top-down (stepwise refinement): decompose into modules — planned structure
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulating state + behaviour — reusability
  • WAD (write all down): rapid prototyping — evolves during coding

Pseudocode Conventions

DECLARE x : INTEGER
IF x > 10 THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF
WHILE ... ENDWHILE
FOR i ← 1 TO n ... NEXT i
FUNCTION f(a) RETURNS INTEGER

Searching

  • Linear: check each item, O(n), works unsorted
  • Binary: halve a sorted list each step, O(log n)

Example: 1,000,000 items: binary search needs ≤ 20 comparisons.

Sorting

AlgorithmBestAverageIdea
BubbleO(n)O(n²)swap neighbours
InsertionO(n)O(n²)insert into sorted prefix
MergeO(n log n)O(n log n)divide and merge

Merge sort example: [5,2,9,1] → [5,2][9,1] → [2,5][1,9] → [1,2,5,9].

Recursion

A function calling itself with a base case. Factorial: f(0)=1, f(n)=n·f(n−1). Stack frames handle state.

Exam tips: state the Big-O and justify it; for traces, tabulate variable changes per iteration.

Testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data

Normal test data is typical valid input that the program should accept and process correctly. Boundary (extreme) test data sits at the edges of the valid range, such as the lowest and highest permitted values, because errors often occur there. Erroneous test data is invalid input that the program should reject, such as text entered where a number is required.

A trace table records the value of each variable at each step of an algorithm. Tracing a algorithm by hand with test data shows where it departs from the intended result, and it is a common exam task.

Exam tip: a complete test plan includes all three kinds of data, with the expected output written beside each test value.

Worked example: tracing a binary search

Search for 23 in the sorted list 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91. The first middle position is (0 + 9) ÷ 2 = 4 (rounded down), which holds 16. Since 23 is greater than 16, the lower bound becomes 5. The next middle is (5 + 9) ÷ 2 = 7, which holds 56. Since 23 is less than 56, the upper bound becomes 6. The next middle is (5 + 6) ÷ 2 = 5, which holds 23, so the item is found after 3 comparisons. A linear search of the same list would need 6 comparisons.

Worked example: bubble sort passes

Sort 5, 1, 4, 2, 8 into ascending order. In the first pass the algorithm compares adjacent pairs and swaps them when they are out of order, giving 1, 4, 2, 5, 8. The second pass gives 1, 2, 4, 5, 8. A third pass makes no swaps, which shows the list is sorted. Stopping early when a pass has no swaps is a common improvement and is worth stating in an answer.

Worked example: recursion

The factorial function is defined as factorial(n) = n × factorial(n − 1), with the base case factorial(0) = 1. Then factorial(4) = 4 × factorial(3) = 4 × 3 × factorial(2) and so on until the base case is reached, giving 24. A recursive routine must always have a base case, otherwise it never stops and the stack overflows.

Exam point: a trace table with one column per variable is the clearest way to show an algorithm's steps, and it earns method marks even when the final answer is wrong.

title: Binomial Distribution — Quick Revision Summary

Quick revision: Binomial Distribution

Mathematics — A2. X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

Key areas to revise

  • When Binomial Applies

  • Cumulative Probabilities
  • Expectation and Variance
  • Modelling Decisions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example For X ~ B(n, p), P(X = r) = nCr pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ, with mean np and variance np(1 − p). For n = 5 and p = 0.2, P(X = 2) = 10 × 0.2² × 0.8³ = 10 × 0.04 × 0.512 = 0.2048. The mean is 5 × 0.2 = 1.

Key points to remember

If X ~ B(n, p), then P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 − p). Check the conditions first: a fixed number of independent trials, two outcomes, and a constant probability of success.

Use cumulative probabilities for P(X ≤ r) or P(X ≥ r). For P(X ≥ r), subtract P(X ≤ r − 1) from 1, and watch whether the wording says more than or at least, because that changes the boundary value. A normal approximation needs both np and n(1 − p) to be large (usually above 5), and then a continuity correction must be applied.

title: Hypothesis Testing — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Hypothesis Testing

Mathematics — A2. The null hypothesis H₀ is the default claim (no change, p = p₀). The alternative H₁ is what a suspicious observation suggests (p > p₀, p < p₀, or p ≠ p₀). The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true H₀ — the false-alarm rate, usually 5% or 1%.

Key areas to revise

  • The Framework
  • Test for a Binomial Proportion
  • One-Tailed vs Two-Tailed
  • Critical Regions
  • Conclusions in Context

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails. ### Worked example A test of a claimed mean has a null hypothesis H₀ and an alternative H₁. Choose a significance level such as 5%, calculate the test statistic and its p-value, then reject H₀ if p < α. A two-tailed test looks for a change in either direction, so the 5% is split between the two tails.

title:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This short revision note is the companion to the longer respiration, muscles and internal environment notes and is written to be used when you want a focused summary of the topic rather than a full working-through of every specification statement. It is built around the same specification points, so each section corresponds to one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note stays at exam depth, but more compactly: it gives the reasoning, the key contrasts and the common mistakes that lose marks, without re-covering every detail of the longer note. Use it to check the core of the topic and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards when time is short.

1. What the topic is for and how the three parts connect

Respiration is the set of reactions that releases energy from nutrient molecules and links that energy to the ATP the cell uses for work. Muscles are where a large share of that ATP is used in movement, and they cannot work unless the supply of ATP, oxygen and fuel keeps up with demand. The internal environment is the fluid and conditions around the body’s cells, and it has to stay within limits while respiration and muscle activity push it around with heat, carbon dioxide, water and changes in solute balance. The topic is therefore a connected system: respiration powers the cell, the muscle is a big ATP user, and the internal environment has to cope with what the muscle and the respiration produce. If you see the topic as one connected system, the links between the parts become easier to answer, and that is where many of the better marks sit.

2. Aerobic respiration as a sequence of stages

Aerobic respiration is a sequence of stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Glycolysis breaks glucose down to pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and reduced NAD. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle produce the reduced coenzymes and carbon dioxide. Oxidative phosphorylation uses the reduced coenzymes to make most of the ATP and reduces oxygen to water. The important idea is that respiration is staged and aerobic, and that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation, which is what allows the bulk of ATP to be made.

A good answer says that respiration is a sequence of stages, states the four stages and where they happen, and says that oxygen is used in oxidative phosphorylation as the final electron acceptor. It does not say that respiration is one reaction that turns glucose straight into ATP, because it is not, and it does not say that the Krebs cycle is where oxygen is used, because it is not. If you can give the stages in order and say where each happens, you have the respiration idea in a form that scores marks.

3. Glycolysis and the link reaction and the Krebs cycle: what each contributes

Glycolysis phosphorylates glucose and splits it, then oxidises the triose phosphate, producing pyruvate, a small ATP yield by substrate-level phosphorylation and reduced NAD. The link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A, releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD. The Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group, releasing more carbon dioxide, making a small amount of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, and producing reduced NAD and reduced FAD. The main conceptual point is that the stages after glycolysis exist largely to supply the reduced coenzymes and to release carbon dioxide, and that the ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation in the cycle is small compared with the ATP from oxidative phosphorylation.

A good answer says that glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD; that the link reaction produces acetyl coenzyme A, CO2 and reduced NAD; and that the Krebs cycle produces reduced coenzymes, a little ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and CO2. It does not say that the Krebs cycle makes most of the ATP, because it does not, and it does not say that the cycle happens in the cytoplasm, because it happens in the mitochondrial matrix. If you can say what each stage contributes, you have the pathway in a form that scores marks.

4. Oxidative phosphorylation and the role of the inner membrane and oxygen

Oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane. The reduced coenzymes deliver hydrogen and the energy from the electrons is used to pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient. As protons flow back through ATP synthase, ATP is made. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with protons to form water. The important point is that ATP is made by chemiosmosis using the proton gradient, not by the electron transport chain directly handing a phosphate to ADP, and that oxygen is essential because it keeps the chain working as the final acceptor.

A good answer says that the inner membrane is folded into cristae to provide surface area, that the energy from the electrons pumps protons, that the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase, and that oxygen is the final electron acceptor forming water. It does not say that ATP is made directly by the chain itself; that is one of the most common mark-losers on this topic. If you can keep the chain and ATP synthase in their separate roles, you have the oxidative phosphorylation idea in a form that scores marks.

5. ATP as the energy currency and why respiration is staged

ATP is the immediate energy currency that respiration supplies to the cell. The energy for most cellular processes does not come directly from glucose; it comes from the hydrolysis of ATP. Respiration exists to regenerate ATP from ADP using the energy in food, and then the ATP is used for active transport, movement, biosynthesis and other endergonic processes. Respiration is staged so that the energy from food is released in manageable amounts that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP, and so that the rate can be controlled according to the cell’s needs. A good answer says that respiration is staged so the energy can be captured in ATP and that ATP is the energy currency used by the cell. It does not say that the cell could simply burn glucose in one step for the same practical result, because the control and capture are the point.

6. Muscle contraction: sliding filaments, ATP and calcium

Muscle contraction works by the sliding filament mechanism. The actin and myosin filaments slide past one another, so the sarcomere shortens, but the filaments themselves do not shorten. Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and pull, then detach and re-cock, pulling the thin filament past the thick one in a cycle powered by ATP. Calcium exposes the actin binding sites so the myosin heads can bind, and relaxation happens when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again. A good answer says that the filaments slide, that ATP is used for detachment and re-cocking and for the cycle, and that calcium is needed for the binding. It does not say that the filaments shorten during contraction; that is one of the most common mistakes on this topic. If you can say that the filaments slide and that ATP and calcium are both needed, you have the contraction idea in a form that scores marks.

7. The response to exercise: heart rate, breathing rate and breathing volume

During exercise, heart rate, breathing rate and the volume of air breathed per breath all increase. The heart pumps faster and often harder to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat. Breathing increases in frequency and depth so that more oxygen is brought in and more carbon dioxide is removed. The point is that the body responds on several fronts at once, because exercise raises the ATP demand and therefore the oxygen demand and the waste production. A good answer says that both rate and depth of breathing increase, and that heart rate increases, and that these raise the supply of oxygen and the removal of carbon dioxide and heat. It does not say that breathing rate alone is the response, because depth matters too, and it does not say the heart only beats faster without considering the increased delivery overall. If you can say that the response is multi-system and that it serves the supply and removal needs, you have the exercise response in a form that scores marks.

8. Thermoregulation and the control of heat loss and heat production

Thermoregulation is the control of body temperature, which is part of homeostasis. When the body needs to lose heat, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, increasing blood flow near the surface and heat loss; this is vasodilation. When the body needs to conserve heat, those vessels constrict, reducing blood flow near the surface and heat loss; this is vasoconstriction. The body can also produce more heat by shivering, which uses ATP and therefore links back to respiration, and it can make behavioural changes such as putting on clothing. A good answer says that vasodilation increases heat loss and vasoconstriction reduces it, that shivering produces heat, and that these are part of homeostasis. It does not invert the relationship, so vasodilation is not linked to cold and vasoconstriction to heat. If you keep the direction correct, you avoid one of the most common mistakes on this part of the topic.

9. Homeostasis, negative feedback and the internal environment

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the main control principle: a change from the set point is detected, and the response reduces the change and returns the variable toward the set point. The internal environment matters because cells can only work properly within a limited range of conditions, so water balance, temperature, pH and solute concentrations have to be controlled. Respiration and exercise put demands on all of these, because they produce heat, carbon dioxide and water and change the balance of solutes. A good answer says that homeostasis is stability within limits, that negative feedback opposes the change, and that the body keeps variables within a normal range rather than making them absolutely constant all the time. It does not say that the internal environment never changes, because it does; it says that it is kept within limits. If you can say that, you have the homeostasis idea in a form that scores marks.

10. Water and solute balance and the role of the kidneys

The body has to manage water and solute balance because cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment. If it becomes too concentrated, water leaves cells by osmosis; if too dilute, water enters. Either change can disrupt cell function. Water is also lost through breathing, sweating and urine, so the balance is dynamic. The kidneys help by removing waste from the blood and by adjusting the water and solute content of the urine, so they are part of the internal environment control system. A good answer says that water and solute balance are part of homeostasis, that cells depend on the water potential around them, and that the kidneys remove waste and help control water and solute balance. It does not say that water balance is only about drinking, because breathing and sweating also matter. If you can say that, you have the water-balance idea in a form that scores marks.

11. How the topic fits together: supply, work and control

The topic is really about a chain. Respiration makes ATP from glucose, muscles use ATP to do work, and the work changes the internal environment so the supply and control systems have to respond. The heart and lungs respond to the oxygen demand and the carbon dioxide production. Thermoregulation responds to the heat. Water and solute balance are affected by sweating and by the increased rate of exchange. Homeostasis keeps the whole thing within limits while the muscles demand more and the metabolism produces more waste. If you can trace that chain, you can answer the questions that span the parts, which are often the best-marked ones. If you treat respiration, muscles and internal environment as three unrelated topics, you lose the reasoning that makes them connected.

12. Typical mistakes

  • Saying respiration is one reaction that turns glucose straight into ATP, instead of a sequence of stages.
  • Saying the filaments shorten during contraction, instead of sliding past each other.
  • Saying ATP alone starts contraction, without mentioning calcium exposing the binding sites.
  • Saying the Krebs cycle happens in the cytoplasm or is where oxygen is used.
  • Saying ATP is made directly by the electron transport chain, instead of by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.
  • Forgetting that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation.
  • Saying breathing rate alone is the response to exercise, forgetting breathing depth and heart rate.
  • Inverting vasodilation and vasoconstriction so vasodilation goes with cold and vasoconstriction with heat.
  • Treating homeostasis as meaning the internal environment never changes, rather than staying within limits by negative feedback.
  • Forgetting that sweating and breathing both affect water balance, not just drinking and urine.
  • Saying positive feedback is the main homeostatic mechanism, when negative feedback is.
  • Saying glycolysis makes most of the ATP from respiration; it does not.
  • Describing thermoregulation responses without saying whether they conserve or produce heat.
  • Missing the link that exercise stresses the internal environment so the control systems have to cope.

13. Exam-style questions

  1. Describe aerobic respiration and state the role of oxygen in the process. Answer: Aerobic respiration is a sequence of stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD; the link reaction and Krebs cycle produce reduced NAD and reduced FAD and release CO2; oxidative phosphorylation uses the reduced coenzymes to make ATP and uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor, forming water. (5 marks)
  2. Explain why respiration is an energy-releasing process but still needs to be staged. Answer: Respiration releases energy from glucose, but a single reaction releasing all the energy at once would mostly waste it as heat. The stages release energy in manageable amounts that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, the energy currency for cell work, and the staging also allows the rate to be controlled to match the cell’s needs. (4 marks)
  3. Describe the sliding filament model of muscle contraction and state the role of ATP. Answer: During contraction the actin and myosin filaments slide past each other rather than shortening themselves, so the sarcomere shortens. Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and pull the thin filament, then detach and re-cock. ATP is required for detachment and re-cocking of the myosin head and for the energy of the cycle, so contraction is powered by ATP hydrolysis. (4 marks)
  4. Explain the roles of calcium and ATP in contraction and relaxation. Answer: When a muscle is stimulated, calcium is released and exposes the binding sites on actin so myosin heads can bind. ATP powers the cross-bridge cycle and the detachment of myosin heads. Relaxation occurs when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again; ATP is still needed for detachment, which is why a muscle without ATP stays contracted, as in rigor mortis. (5 marks)
  5. Describe the body’s response during exercise in terms of heart rate and breathing, and explain why each increases. Answer: During exercise heart rate increases to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat, and breathing rate and depth increase to bring in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide. Both increase because the muscles’ ATP demand rises and the supply and waste-removal systems have to keep up with the increased metabolism. (5 marks)
  6. Describe how the skin blood vessels help control body temperature and state the direction of the response. Answer: In heat, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, increasing blood flow near the surface and increasing heat loss. In cold, they constrict, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss. This is part of thermoregulation and homeostasis, along with other responses such as sweating or shivering and behavioural changes. (4 marks)
  7. Define homeostasis and explain the principle of negative feedback, with one example. Answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the control principle in which a change from the set point is detected and the response reduces the change, returning the variable toward normal. Example: in temperature control, if body temperature rises, sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, returning temperature toward the set point; if it falls, shivering and vasoconstriction reduce heat loss or increase heat production. (5 marks)
  8. Explain why water and solute balance are part of homeostasis and what happens if the internal environment becomes too concentrated or too dilute. Answer: Cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment. If it becomes too concentrated, water moves out of cells by osmosis; if too dilute, water moves into cells. Either can disrupt cell function, so the concentrations of water and solutes must be controlled. The body loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, so water balance is dynamic and has to be regulated. (4 marks)
  9. State what the kidneys do to help maintain the internal environment. Answer: The kidneys remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance by adjusting the composition of the urine, so they are important for maintaining the internal environment and for disposing of waste products of metabolism. (3 marks)
  10. Describe the link between respiration and muscle activity during exercise. Answer: Muscle activity uses ATP, so respiration must increase to supply ATP. Aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable if oxygen supply is sufficient, but during vigorous exercise oxygen delivery may not keep up with demand, so the muscle relies relatively more on pathways that do not need oxygen and produces different products, which is why breathing and heart rate rise and the body shifts its metabolism. (4 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one mechanism, one location and one reason. Practise the respiration stages and their products, the sliding filament idea with ATP and calcium, the exercise responses and the thermoregulation responses, and the homeostasis and negative feedback principle with examples. Check that you can say where each process happens and why, not just what happens. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

  1. Describe aerobic respiration and state the role of oxygen in the process. Answer: Aerobic respiration is a sequence of stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD; the link reaction and Krebs cycle produce reduced NAD and reduced FAD and release CO2; oxidative phosphorylation uses the reduced coenzymes to make ATP and uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor, forming water. (5 marks)
  2. Explain why respiration is an energy-releasing process but still needs to be staged. Answer: Respiration releases energy from glucose, but a single reaction releasing all the energy at once would mostly waste it as heat. The stages release energy in manageable amounts that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP to ATP, the energy currency for cell work, and the staging also allows the rate to be controlled to match the cell’s needs. (4 marks)
  3. Describe the sliding filament model of muscle contraction and state the role of ATP. Answer: During contraction the actin and myosin filaments slide past each other rather than shortening themselves, so the sarcomere shortens. Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot and pull the thin filament, then detach and re-cock. ATP is required for detachment and re-cocking of the myosin head and for the energy of the cycle, so contraction is powered by ATP hydrolysis. (4 marks)
  4. Explain the roles of calcium and ATP in contraction and relaxation. Answer: When a muscle is stimulated, calcium is released and exposes the binding sites on actin so myosin heads can bind. ATP powers the cross-bridge cycle and the detachment of myosin heads. Relaxation occurs when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again; ATP is still needed for detachment, which is why a muscle without ATP stays contracted, as in rigor mortis. (5 marks)
  5. Describe the body’s response during exercise in terms of heart rate and breathing, and explain why each increases. Answer: During exercise heart rate increases to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat, and breathing rate and depth increase to bring in more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide. Both increase because the muscles’ ATP demand rises and the supply and waste-removal systems have to keep up with the increased metabolism. (5 marks)
  6. Describe how the skin blood vessels help control body temperature and state the direction of the response. Answer: In heat, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, increasing blood flow near the surface and increasing heat loss. In cold, they constrict, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss. This is part of thermoregulation and homeostasis, along with other responses such as sweating or shivering and behavioural changes. (4 marks)
  7. Define homeostasis and explain the principle of negative feedback, with one example. Answer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within limits. Negative feedback is the control principle in which a change from the set point is detected and the response reduces the change, returning the variable toward normal. Example: in temperature control, if body temperature rises, sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, returning temperature toward the set point; if it falls, shivering and vasoconstriction reduce heat loss or increase heat production. (5 marks)
  8. Explain why water and solute balance are part of homeostasis and what happens if the internal environment becomes too concentrated or too dilute. Answer: Cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment. If it becomes too concentrated, water moves out of cells by osmosis; if too dilute, water moves into cells. Either can disrupt cell function, so the concentrations of water and solutes must be controlled. The body loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, so water balance is dynamic and has to be regulated. (4 marks)
  9. State what the kidneys do to help maintain the internal environment. Answer: The kidneys remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance by adjusting the composition of the urine, so they are important for maintaining the internal environment and for disposing of waste products of metabolism. (3 marks)
  10. Describe the link between respiration and muscle activity during exercise. Answer: Muscle activity uses ATP, so respiration must increase to supply ATP. Aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable if oxygen supply is sufficient, but during vigorous exercise oxygen delivery may not keep up with demand, so the muscle relies relatively more on pathways that do not need oxygen and produces different products, which is why breathing and heart rate rise and the body shifts its metabolism. (4 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one mechanism, one location and one reason. Practise the respiration stages and their products, the sliding filament idea with ATP and calcium, the exercise responses and the thermoregulation responses, and the homeostasis and negative feedback principle with examples. Check that you can say where each process happens and why, not just what happens. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

title: A2 Level Chemistry: Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality
content:
Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality

Edexcel International A Level Chemistry — Unit 4 (WCH14), Topic 15, covers the concepts of carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and chirality. This topic includes the reactions and tests of aldehydes and ketones, the properties and reactions of carboxylic acids, and the concept of optical isomerism and chirality.

Introduction to Carbonyl Compounds

Carbonyl compounds contain the carbonyl group, C=O. Aldehydes have the C=O group at the end of a chain (RCHO), while ketones have it inside the chain (RCOR). The carbon of C=O is slightly positive, making it susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

  • Aldehydes: RCHO
  • Ketones: RCOR

Reactions of Carbonyl Compounds

Carbonyl compounds undergo nucleophilic addition reactions. The products of these reactions can be carboxylic acids, alcohols, or molecules with a chiral centre.

  • Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O: RCHO + HCN → RCN
  • Sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) (NaBH4) reduces aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols
  • 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) gives an orange or yellow precipitate with any carbonyl compound
  • Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with aldehydes but not with ketones
  • The iodoform test gives a yellow precipitate of triiodomethane with compounds containing CH3CO– or CH3CH(OH)– groups

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain –COOH and are weak acids. They are more acidic than alcohols because the carboxylate ion is stabilised by delocalisation.

  • Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to form esters
  • Primary alcohols are oxidised to carboxylic acids by heating with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux

Chirality and Optical Isomerism

A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached. Molecules with a chiral centre exist as a pair of enantiomers. Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light.

  • A chiral carbon atom has four different groups attached
  • Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their effect on plane-polarised light
  • An equimolar mixture of the two enantiomers is a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive

Optical Activity

Optical activity is the ability of a single optical isomer to rotate the plane of polarisation of plane-polarised monochromatic light.

  • Optical activity is measured using a polarimeter
  • The specific rotation of a compound is a characteristic property

Nomenclature of Aldehydes and Ketones

Aldehydes and ketones are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the carbonyl group.

  • Aldehydes: RCHO
  • Ketones: RCOR

Nomenclature of Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the carboxyl group.

  • Carboxylic acids: RCOOH

Nomenclature of Acyl Chlorides and Esters

Acyl chlorides and esters are named based on the longest continuous chain containing the acyl group.

  • Acyl chlorides: RCOCl
  • Esters: RCOOR

Reactions of Acyl Chlorides

Acyl chlorides undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions.

  • Acyl chlorides react with water to form carboxylic acids
  • Acyl chlorides react with alcohols to form esters
  • Acyl chlorides react with concentrated ammonia to form amides
  • Acyl chlorides react with amines to form amides

Hydrolysis of Esters

Esters undergo hydrolysis reactions in acidic and alkaline solutions.

  • Esters react with water in the presence of an acid catalyst to form carboxylic acids and alcohols
  • Esters react with water in the presence of a base to form carboxylic acids and alcohols

Condensation Polymerisation

Polyesters are formed by condensation polymerisation reactions.

  • Polyesters are formed by the reaction of carboxylic acids and alcohols

Mass Spectra

Mass spectra provide information about the molecular mass of a compound.

  • The molecular ion is the ion with the highest mass-to-charge ratio
  • The base peak is the ion with the highest intensity

13C NMR Spectroscopy

13C NMR spectroscopy provides information about the environments of carbon atoms in a molecule.

  • The chemical shift of a carbon atom is a characteristic property
  • The number of peaks in a 13C NMR spectrum is equal to the number of different environments of carbon atoms

Proton NMR Spectroscopy

Proton NMR spectroscopy provides information about the environments of hydrogen atoms in a molecule.

  • The chemical shift of a hydrogen atom is a characteristic property
  • The number of peaks in a proton NMR spectrum is equal to the number of different environments of hydrogen atoms
  • The intensity of a peak is proportional to the number of hydrogen atoms in that environment

Chromatography

Chromatography is a technique used to separate the components of a mixture.

  • Chromatography separates components based on their affinity for a stationary phase and a mobile phase
  • The Rf value is a measure of the distance traveled by a component relative to the distance traveled by the solvent front

Typical Mistakes

  • Confusing the reactions of aldehydes and ketones
  • Forgetting to show the nucleophile attacking the carbon of C=O in nucleophilic addition reactions
  • Not understanding the concept of optical isomerism and chirality

Exam-Style Questions

  1. What is the difference between an aldehyde and a ketone? Answer: An aldehyde has the C=O group at the end of a chain, while a ketone has it inside the chain.
  2. What is the reaction of hydrogen cyanide with an aldehyde? Answer: Hydrogen cyanide adds across C=O to form a cyanohydrin.
  3. What is the specific rotation of a compound? Answer: The specific rotation of a compound is a characteristic property that is measured using a polarimeter.

To revise this topic, make sure to understand the reactions and tests of aldehydes and ketones, the properties and reactions of carboxylic acids, and the concept of optical isomerism and chirality. Practice drawing the structures of aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids, and practice solving problems involving the reactions of these compounds. Also, make sure to understand the concepts of 13C NMR spectroscopy, proton NMR spectroscopy, and chromatography, and practice solving problems involving these techniques. Finally, practice answering exam-style questions to test your understanding of the topic.

Detailed Mechanisms of Nucleophilic Addition: HCN and KCN

The addition of hydrogen cyanide to carbonyl compounds is a classic Edexcel A2 mechanism. Because HCN is a weak acid and provides a very low concentration of cyanide ions, potassium cyanide (KCN) is added to provide a higher concentration of the active nucleophile, CN−. The mechanism proceeds via nucleophilic addition:

  • Step 1: The lone pair on the carbon atom of the cyanide ion (CN−) attacks the slightly positive carbon atom of the carbonyl group (C=O). A curly arrow goes from the lone pair on carbon to the carbonyl carbon.
  • Step 2: Simultaneously, the pi bond of the carbonyl group breaks, with both electrons moving entirely to the oxygen atom. This forms a negatively charged intermediate (an alkoxide ion) and shows a curly arrow from the C=O bond to the oxygen.
  • Step 3: The intermediate accepts a proton (H+) from HCN or from the acidic aqueous environment to form a hydroxy-nitrile (cyanohydrin).

Stereochemical Evidence from Carbonyl Addition to Unsymmetrical Ketones

When an unsymmetrical aldehyde or ketone reacts with hydrogen cyanide, the planar nature of the carbonyl group allows the nucleophile (CN−) to attack from either above or below the plane with equal probability. If the product molecule contains a single chiral centre (i.e., four different groups attached to the central carbon), a racemic mixture of two optical isomers (enantiomers) is formed in equal amounts. This proves that the intermediate is planar around the original carbonyl carbon and provides crucial mechanistic evidence for the reaction pathway.

Physical Properties of Carbonyl Compounds and Carboxylic Acids

Understanding intermolecular forces explains the differing boiling temperatures and water solubilities:

  • Aldehydes and ketones cannot form hydrogen bonds with themselves because they lack a hydrogen atom bonded directly to a strongly electronegative oxygen or nitrogen atom. Their molecules are held together by permanent dipole-dipole attractions and London forces, resulting in lower boiling temperatures than corresponding alcohols or carboxylic acids of similar relative molecular mass.
  • Aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules through their lone pairs on the carbonyl or hydroxyl oxygens, which explains why smaller members of these homologous series are completely soluble in water.
  • Carboxylic acids can form stable hydrogen-bonded dimers with each other in the liquid and vapour phases. This effectively doubles their relative molecular mass during vaporisation, leading to significantly higher boiling temperatures than alcohols of comparable molecular mass.

Comprehensive Analysis of Spectroscopic Data

Examiners frequently test the ability to combine mass spectrometry, carbon-13 NMR, and proton NMR data to deduce molecular structures:

  • Mass Spectrometry: High-resolution mass spectrometry provides accurate relative molecular masses to four decimal places, allowing chemists to distinguish between molecules with the same nominal integer mass (e.g., CO, N2, and C2H4 all have a nominal mass of 28, but accurate masses separate them precisely). Fragmentation patterns reveal structural fragments, such as the loss of 15 (CH3), 17 (OH), or 45 (COOH).
  • Carbon-13 NMR: Each peak in a 13C NMR spectrum corresponds to a carbon atom in a distinct chemical environment. The chemical shift value (measured in ppm) gives information about the types of adjacent atoms or functional groups (e.g., carbon in a C=O group appears around 160 to 220 ppm, while aliphatic sp3 carbons appear between 0 and 50 ppm).
  • Proton (1H) NMR: The number of distinct peaks indicates the number of different hydrogen environments. The relative peak areas (integration traces) show the ratio of hydrogen atoms in each environment. The splitting pattern of each peak is determined by the number of adjacent non-equivalent protons using the (n + 1) rule, where n is the number of protons on adjacent carbon atoms. TMS (tetramethylsilane) is used as an internal reference standard because it produces a single sharp peak at 0 ppm, is inert, volatile, and non-toxic.

Advanced Chromatography Techniques

In addition to basic thin-layer chromatography (TLC) and paper chromatography where Rf values are calculated as the distance travelled by the solute divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front, modern analytical separation relies on column-based methods:

  • High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC): Uses a liquid mobile phase pumped under high pressure through a tightly packed column containing a solid stationary phase. Components separate based on their differing partition coefficients between the two phases.
  • Gas Chromatography (GC): Uses an inert carrier gas (such as helium or neon) as the mobile phase passing through a column containing a high-boiling liquid stationary phase coated on a solid support. Retention time is the time taken for a component to pass through the column from injection to detection.
  • Coupled Techniques: Both HPLC and GC can be directly coupled with mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS or GC-MS). This allows the chromatographic separation of complex mixtures followed immediately by mass spectral identification of each separated component, widely applied in forensic science, drug testing in sport, and environmental monitoring.

Worked Examples

  1. Worked Example: Calculating Rf Values
    Question: In a TLC experiment, the solvent front travels 8.4 cm from the baseline. A specific organic component travels 3.5 cm from the baseline. Calculate the Rf value for this component.
    Method: Use the formula Rf = (distance travelled by spot) ÷ (distance travelled by solvent front).
    Answer: Rf = 3.5 ÷ 8.4 = 0.42 (no units).
  2. Worked Example: Predicting 1H NMR Splitting
    Question: Predict the splitting pattern for the protons in the CH2 group of ethanol (CH3CH2OH), assuming standard high-resolution conditions.
    Method: Identify the number of non-equivalent protons (n) on the adjacent carbon atom. The adjacent carbon is the CH3 group, which has 3 protons. Apply the (n + 1) rule: 3 + 1 = 4.
    Answer: A quartet.

Common Student Mistakes and Corrections

  • Mistake: Confusing the action of Tollens reagent with Fehling solution on aliphatic aldehydes and aromatic aldehydes.
    Correction: Both Tollens reagent and Fehling solution give positive tests with aliphatic aldehydes (silver mirror and red precipitate respectively). However, aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde reduce Tollens reagent to form a silver mirror, but they do NOT reduce Fehling solution.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that carboxylic acids react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide gas, whereas alcohols do not.
    Correction: Always use sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate solution to distinguish carboxylic acids from alcohols or phenols, as only carboxylic acids are strong enough acids to liberate carbon dioxide gas with effervescence.
  • Mistake: Misinterpreting peak splitting in proton NMR by counting protons on both sides indiscriminately.
    Correction: The (n + 1) rule only applies to protons on directly adjacent, non-equivalent carbon atoms. Protons separated by oxygen atoms or multiple bonds do not couple.

Exam-Style Questions and Answers

  1. Question: State why 1,1-dichloroethane and 1,2-dichloroethane have different numbers of peaks in their carbon-13 NMR spectra.
    Answer: 1,1-dichloroethane has two carbon environments (the CH3 carbon and the CHCl2 carbon), so it shows 2 peaks in its 13C NMR spectrum. 1,2-dichloroethane has only one carbon environment due to molecular symmetry (both carbons are bonded to a chlorine and a hydrogen and feel the same electronic environment), so it shows only 1 peak.
    Credit Point: Awarded for correctly identifying the carbon environments and linking them directly to the number of observed peaks.
  2. Question: Write an equation for the reaction of propanoyl chloride with concentrated ammonia, and name the organic product.
    Answer: CH3CH2COCl + 2NH3 → CH3CH2CONH2 + NH4Cl. The organic product is propanamide.
    Credit Point: Awarded for correct balanced stoichiometry (including the 2 moles of ammonia to react with the formed HCl) and correct naming of the amide.
  3. Question: Explain why a racemic mixture shows no optical activity when analysed in a polarimeter.
    Answer: A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of two enantiomers. Each enantiomer rotates the plane of plane-polarised light by an equal angle in opposite directions, resulting in the rotations cancelling each other out entirely.
    Credit Point: Awarded for mentioning equal amounts of enantiomers and the equal and opposite rotation of plane-polarised light.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Nucleophilic addition, applied to propanone with HCN and KCN: the cyanide ion attacks the δ+ carbon of the C=O, forming an alkoxide that picks up H⁺. The product is 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile. Show the curly arrow from the C=O π bond to the oxygen.
  • Racemic product: the carbonyl carbon is planar, so the cyanide can attack from either face with equal likelihood. Propanal gives a racemic mixture of two enantiomers, and the product has no net optical activity. A chiral centre is one with four different groups attached.
  • Chirality, applied to 2-bromobutane: the second carbon carries H, Br, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, four different groups, so the molecule is chiral and has two enantiomers that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.
  • Tests: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine gives an orange precipitate with any carbonyl. Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror only with aldehydes, and acidified dichromate turns from orange to green with aldehydes. Name the test and the observation together.

title: Exam technique: Circular Motion and SHM
content:
### What earns the marks
For SHM acceleration, minus omega squared x with direction stated earns both marks. For periods, the correct root form quoted earns the method mark. For energy, equilibrium named for max KE earns the mark; resonance at natural frequency earns the explanation.
### Traps
Error: sign dropped in a = -omega squared x. Correction: acceleration points to equilibrium. Error: pendulum and spring formulae swapped. Correction: root(L/g) versus root(m/k). Error: resonance blamed on damping alone. Correction: matching frequencies drive it.
### Use the defining equation of SHM
Show that the acceleration is proportional to the negative of the displacement, a = −ω²x, before you use the equations of SHM. This is the standard justification mark for these questions.

### Choose the correct displacement or velocity form
Use x = A cos ωt when the object is at maximum displacement at time zero, and x = A sin ωt when it starts at the centre. Check the starting condition in the question before you write the equation.

### Relate energy to amplitude
The total energy is ½mω²A², and it is shared between kinetic and potential energy. At the centre all of the energy is kinetic, and at the extremes all of it is potential.

title: Exam technique: Thermal Physics (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For gases, pV = nRT quoted earns the method mark with kelvin used. For theory, KE proportional to T stated earns the explanation mark. For heating, mcT and mL chosen by phase versus temperature change earn one mark each; first-law signs tracked earn the final mark.
### Traps
Error: Celsius used in gas laws. Correction: convert to kelvin. Error: latent heat applied to temperature change. Correction: latent is isothermal; mcT is for change. Error: work signs flipped in delta U. Correction: work done by the gas subtracts.
### Use the ideal gas equation with consistent units
Write pV = nRT, and convert the temperature to kelvin and the volume to m³ before you substitute. Give pressure in pascals, and state the value of R you used.

### Link the kinetic theory to temperature
For a fixed amount of gas, pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩, and the mean kinetic energy of a molecule depends only on temperature. Use this to explain why the pressure rises when the temperature rises at constant volume.

### Calculate heating and phase change separately
Use Q = mcΔθ for a change in temperature and Q = mL for a change of state. During a change of state the temperature stays constant, and the energy goes into breaking bonds.

title: Exam technique: Simulation, Sensors and Real Data
content:
### What earns the marks
For control systems, sensor plus actuator plus loop type each earn a mark: feedback reads back every cycle. For conversions, the direction named (ADC into the controller) earns the mark with resolution tied to bit depth. For regimes, the hazard speed matched to sampling earns the design mark.
### Traps
Error: DAC into the controller. Correction: sensors are analog, controllers digital: ADC. Error: batch uploads for flood alerts. Correction: fast hazards need real-time sensing. Error: tripling identical sensors for redundancy. Correction: diversify physics so failures stay independent.
### Sensors and data
A sensor converts a physical quantity into a signal, and an ADC turns that signal into digital values. When asked why a reading is inaccurate, name the cause, such as a poorly calibrated sensor or too low a sampling rate.
### Simulation
Explain that a simulation models a real system with a set of rules and variables, which lets it test situations that would be dangerous or expensive in reality. State one limitation, such as the model being only as accurate as the assumptions behind it.
### Real data
Give the stage of processing in order: collect, validate, clean, then analyse. Name a check such as a range check or a presence check when asked how to validate input.

title: Exam technique: Probability Distributions
content:
### What earns the marks
For distribution tables, probabilities summing to 1 checked earns the first mark. For expectation, each x times p(x) summed earns the method mark. For variance, E(X squared) computed separately then subtracted earns the second mark.
### Traps
Error: sigma used as variance. Correction: sigma is sd; square it. Error: E(X squared) computed as E(X) squared. Correction: square the x values first. Error: function-of-X expectation via E(X) substituted. Correction: sum g(x)p(x) directly.
### Build the full distribution table
List every value of X and its probability, and check that the probabilities add to 1. An error in the table usually causes an error in every later part of the question.

### Calculate E(X²) before the variance
Square each value of X, multiply by its probability, and sum. Then subtract the square of the mean. Do not substitute the mean squared for E(X²), because that is a different quantity.

### Apply the linear rules correctly
Use E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). The constant b changes the mean but not the variance.

title: Waves & Sound — Study Notes
content:
Waves & Sound

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): general wave properties; reflection/refraction/diffraction; sound.

1. Wave basics

v = fλ. Transverse (oscillation ⊥ travel — light, water, S-waves) vs longitudinal (parallel — sound, P-waves). Amplitude, wavelength, frequency f = 1/T; wavefront diagrams.

2. Ripple tank behaviours
