  • Reflection: angle in = angle out; speed/frequency unchanged, direction changes.
  • Refraction: speed change at boundary bends wavefronts (shallow water slows ripples).
  • Diffraction: spreading through gaps ≈ λ wide; around edges.

3. Electromagnetic spectrum (order)

Radio → micro → IR → visible (red 700 nm – violet 400 nm) → UV → X → gamma. All travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum; transverse; uses and dangers (IR heating; UV skin; X/gamma ionising).

4. Sound

  • Longitudinal; needs a medium (bell in vacuum demo). Speed ~340 m/s air, faster in liquids/solids.
  • Range 20 Hz–20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz (sonar, prenatal scans, cleaning).
  • Pitch ↔ frequency; loudness ↔ amplitude.

5. Echo problems

Distance = (v × t)/2 (there and back).

Example: echo after 0.6 s, v = 340 → cliff 102 m away.

Exam tips: in diagrams always label wavelength as crest-to-crest; for refraction, state "changes speed" first, then direction; quote EM uses with the hazard.

Wave equation and sound

The wave equation is v = fλ, where v is the wave speed, f the frequency and λ the wavelength. Sound is a longitudinal wave that needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum. All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s. In reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. For an echo, the sound travels to the reflecting surface and back, so the distance to the surface is half the total distance travelled.

Worked example: wave equation

A sound wave has frequency 500 Hz and travels at 340 m s⁻¹ in air. Using v = fλ, the wavelength is λ = 340/500 = 0.68 m. Doubling the frequency to 1000 Hz halves the wavelength to 0.34 m. The speed is fixed by the medium, not by the frequency, so the product fλ stays constant.

Echo calculations

A reflected sound returns after a time t. The distance to the reflecting surface is d = vt/2, because the sound travels to the surface and back. Forgetting the factor of one half doubles the answer, which is the most common error in echo questions.

Reflection, refraction and diffraction

  • Reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal, not from the surface.
  • Refraction: a wave changes speed and direction at a boundary between media, but its frequency stays the same.
  • Diffraction: spreading is greatest when the gap or obstacle is comparable to the wavelength. Low-pitched sound, with its longer wavelength, bends around a doorway more than high-pitched speech does.

These are the wave properties examined in the wave topic of the Cambridge IGCSE 0625 and AS 9702 syllabi. Name each property precisely and apply it to a labelled diagram.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and Series

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 2 (WMA12), sat at AS.

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

Formulae and exam method

Arithmetic progression: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is known.

Geometric progression: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r).

To find the number of terms, substitute the known sum or term and solve for n. When n sits in an exponent, take logarithms. Check that n is a positive integer.

Sigma notation: Σ from r = 1 to n of (ar + b) is evaluated with the standard sums, but write out the first few terms when the pattern is unclear.

Exam cue: Identify whether the question is AP or GP before choosing a formula, and state the value of r when using the sum to infinity.

Exam method: arithmetic and geometric sums

For an arithmetic sequence with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is a + (n − 1)d and the sum of the first n terms is S_n = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d). For a geometric sequence with ratio r, the nth term is ar^(n − 1) and S_n = a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.

The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, say so explicitly rather than applying the formula.

Exam cue: Identify whether the sequence is arithmetic or geometric from the common difference or ratio before choosing a formula. Check the number of terms n carefully when you set up the equation.

Worked example: arithmetic progression

The sequence 3, 7, 11, … has first term a = 3 and common difference d = 4. The 20th term is a + 19d = 3 + 76 = 79. The sum of the first 20 terms is Sₙ = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d) = 10 × (6 + 76) = 820.

Check with the average method: the first and last terms average (3 + 79)/2 = 41, and 41 × 20 = 820.

Worked example: geometric progression

The sequence 5, 10, 20, … has r = 2. The 8th term is 5 × 2⁷ = 640. The sum of the first six terms is 5(2⁶ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 315. Adding them directly gives 5 + 10 + 20 + 40 + 80 + 160 = 315, which confirms the formula.

Sum to infinity

A geometric series has a sum to infinity only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). For 81, 27, 9, … the ratio is 1/3, so S∞ = 81/(2/3) = 121.5. If |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and the sum does not converge, so say so rather than quoting a formula.

Binomial expansion

For (1 + 2x)⁵, the first terms are 1 + 5(2x) + 10(2x)² + … The coefficient of x² is C(5, 2) × 2² = 10 × 4 = 40. The expansion is valid for |2x| < 1, so the range of x must be stated when the question asks for it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using n instead of n − 1 in the n-th term formula, which shifts every term.
  • Confusing the nth term with the sum of the first n terms, a very common error on exam questions that ask for both.
  • Dividing a/(1 − r) when the series starts at a term other than the first, so check the index on the first term before using the formula.
  • Forgetting that the binomial expansion of (a + b)ⁿ has a coefficient C(n, r) on each term, and that the powers of a and b add to n.

title: Exam technique: Computational Thinking
content:
### What earns the marks
For recursion, the base case quoted plus the shrinking argument earns both marks. For dry runs, each call tracked with its print earns method credit. For strategy choice, the signature named (splitting for divide-and-conquer, retreating for backtracking) earns the mark with a fitting example.
### Traps
Error: base case omitted. Correction: every recursion needs a reachable stop. Error: greedy claimed to backtrack. Correction: greedy never retreats. Error: linear search called divide-and-conquer. Correction: it never divides.
### Decompose the problem
Computational thinking questions often ask for a decomposition. Break the task into smaller sub-problems, then say which can be solved independently and which depends on another result.
### Abstraction and algorithms
Abstraction removes the detail that is not needed for a task. When asked to write an algorithm, give the steps in order and name the input and output; a bullet list of ideas without an order does not earn the algorithm mark.
### Show the trace
Where a question gives a short algorithm, trace it with a table of variable values, one row per iteration.

title: Databases and Data Definition — Study Notes
content:
Databases and Data Definition

Syllabus note: in 9618, databases is AS content (section 8, AS Paper 1). This is the condensed companion to the full AS Databases note, not separate A2 content.

Relational Concepts

A table (relation) stores rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). The primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key references a primary key in another table, creating the relationship. A composite key uses two or more columns together.

Normalisation

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF plus every non-key attribute depends on the whole key (kills partial dependency in composite keys).
  • 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependency — non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.

Normalisation reduces redundancy and prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.

DDL and DML

DDL defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP. DML manipulates data: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE. Joins combine related tables: FROM Student s JOIN Enrolment e ON s.id = e.StudentID. Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING.

Transactions and Concurrency

A transaction is a unit of work obeying ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Record locking blocks conflicting simultaneous edits; a deadlock occurs when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs.

Exam tips: normalise a small table through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF naming the dependency removed at each step; write a two-table SELECT with JOIN; state which ACID property a scenario breaks.

DDL and DML

Data Definition Language (DDL) creates and changes the structure of a database: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. Data Manipulation Language (DML) works with the data inside the structure: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.

Example: CREATE TABLE Student (ID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(30)); is DDL; INSERT INTO Student VALUES (1, 'Ana'); is DML.

Exam tip: classify each statement by whether it changes structure or changes data.

Worked example: a SELECT query

To list the names of students in Year 11 who study Physics, sorted by surname, a query joins two tables and filters the result: SELECT Name FROM Student INNER JOIN Enrolment ON Student.StudentID = Enrolment.StudentID WHERE Year = 11 AND Subject = 'Physics' ORDER BY Name. Read the question word by word and map each condition onto a clause.

Keys and integrity

  • A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table and cannot be null.
  • A foreign key holds the primary key of another table, which links the two tables together.
  • A candidate key is any field, or combination of fields, that could serve as the primary key.

Entity-relationship modelling

A one-to-many relationship, such as one teacher and many classes, is shown by placing the primary key of the "one" side in the "many" table. A many-to-many relationship, such as students and courses, needs a third, linking table that holds a foreign key for each side. Without it the database would repeat data or store several values in one field, which breaks normalisation.

Exam point: CREATE TABLE statements declare the data types, the primary key and each foreign key. DROP and ALTER change the structure; INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and SELECT work with the records.

title: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Mathematics — OL. congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

  • 1. Congruence
  • 2. Similarity
  • 3. Length, area, volume factors
  • 4. Area/volume calculations from similarity
  • 5. Symmetry

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Two shapes are congruent when they have the same shape and size, so one matches the other exactly after a translation, reflection or rotation. Similar shapes have the same shape but different sizes, with all lengths in the same ratio, and their corresponding angles are equal. The scale factor links the lengths of the two shapes.

For a pair of similar shapes, find the scale factor from one pair of matching sides, then multiply or divide the other lengths by it. For areas, the ratio of areas is the square of the scale factor, which is a common exam trap.

title: Bonding and Structure — Study Notes
content:
Bonding and Structure

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 3. Every statement 3.1 to 3.22 is covered below, with its code in the heading so you can check your own gaps against the specification. The big idea: the type of bonding and the shape of a molecule explain almost every physical property a question can ask about, including melting point, conductivity, solubility and polarity.

3.1 to 3.2: Evidence for ions, and how they form

  • Evidence for ions: ionic compounds conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved, because the ions are then free to move. In electrolysis, a coloured ion such as manganate(VII), MnO₄⁻, migrates to the positive electrode (the anode), which is direct evidence that it carries a negative charge.
  • Electron density maps for ionic compounds show near-spherical regions of electron density around each ion, with a clear drop in density between them.
  • Formation by loss or gain of electrons: sodium loses one electron to form Na⁺ (2,8,1 becomes 2,8), while chlorine gains one to form Cl⁻ (2,8,7 becomes 2,8,8). A metal loses electrons to form a positive ion; a non-metal gains electrons to form a negative ion.

3.3: Dot-and-cross diagrams for ions

  • Show the outer electrons of each atom as dots or crosses. For a cation such as Mg²⁺, the outer shell is empty, so the symbol is written with square brackets and the charge: [Mg]²⁺.
  • For an anion such as O²⁻, the transferred electrons are added to the outer shell, which then holds eight electrons: [O]²⁻ with eight dots and crosses inside the brackets.
  • Always put the charge outside the brackets, and check that the total number of electrons transferred matches the charges.

3.4 to 3.5: Giant ionic lattices and the ionic bond

  • An ionic crystal is a giant lattice of alternating positive and negative ions, repeating in three dimensions. There are no discrete molecules, so the formula, such as NaCl, is only the simplest ratio of ions. In sodium chloride each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by six Na⁺ ions (6:6 coordination).
  • An ionic bond is the strong net electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. "Net" matters: the attraction between a cation and an anion is partly cancelled by repulsion between like ions, but the attraction wins at the equilibrium distance.

3.6: Effect of ionic radius and ionic charge on bond strength

  • The electrostatic attraction grows with the charge on the ions and falls as the ions get larger, because the centres of charge are further apart.
  • Compare MgO (melting point about 2850 °C) with NaCl (about 800 °C). Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double charges and are small, so their attraction is much stronger than that between the singly charged, larger Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

3.7: Trends in ionic radius

  • Down a group, ionic radius increases, because each ion has an additional electron shell. Li⁺ is smaller than Na⁺, which is smaller than K⁺.
  • Across a set of isoelectronic ions, all the species have the same number of electrons (ten, in the series N³⁻, O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺). The nuclear charge rises from 7 to 13 across the series, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly and the radius falls. N³⁻ is the largest and Al³⁺ the smallest.

3.8 to 3.9: Polarisation of ions

  • Polarisation is the distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation. The cation pulls the anion's electron density towards itself, so the bonding stops being purely ionic and gains covalent character.
  • The polarising power of a cation is greatest when it is small and highly charged. Al³⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Na⁺.
  • The polarisability of an anion is greatest when it is large and highly charged, because its outer electrons are held loosely. I⁻ is more polarisable than Br⁻, which is more polarisable than Cl⁻, which is more polarisable than F⁻.
  • Example: aluminium chloride has a low melting point and sublimes, far below what a purely ionic lattice would need. The small, highly charged Al³⁺ polarises the chloride ions strongly, so the bonding is largely covalent.

3.10: Covalent bonding and the evidence for it

  • A covalent bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between two nuclei (both positive) and the shared pair of electrons between them.
  • Evidence: giant atomic structures such as diamond and silicon(IV) oxide have very high melting points, which only strong covalent bonds can explain. Electron density maps for simple molecules such as hydrogen show a build-up of electron density between the two nuclei.

3.11: Dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent substances

  • Multiple bonds: in carbon dioxide, O=C=O, each double bond is two shared pairs. In nitrogen, N≡N, there are three shared pairs.
  • Dative (coordinate) bonds: both electrons in the shared pair come from one atom, the donor, which has a lone pair. The arrow points from donor to acceptor. In the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, the nitrogen in NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺.
  • Aluminium chloride dimer, Al₂Cl₆: each aluminium has four chlorines. Two of the chlorines bridge the two aluminium atoms, and each bridging chlorine forms a dative bond from a chlorine lone pair into the empty orbital of the other aluminium.

3.12: Giant carbon structures: diamond, graphite and graphene

  • Diamond: each carbon forms four single covalent bonds in a tetrahedral giant lattice. It is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct, because there are no free electrons. It is used in cutting and drilling tools.
  • Graphite: each carbon forms three bonds in flat hexagonal sheets. The fourth outer electron on each carbon is delocalised, so graphite conducts along the sheets. The sheets are held by weak forces and slide over each other, so graphite is soft and is used as a lubricant and as electrodes.
  • Graphene: a single sheet of graphite, one atom thick. It is very strong, conducts well and is light and flexible. Applications include electronics, sensors and composite materials.

3.13 to 3.14: Electronegativity and the bonding continuum

  • Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding pair of electrons in a covalent bond. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (4.0 on the Pauling scale).
  • The bonding continuum: the bigger the electronegativity difference between two atoms, the more polar the bond. A very small difference gives a non-polar covalent bond, a moderate difference gives a polar covalent bond (as in HCl), and a very large difference gives essentially ionic bonding (as in NaCl). Ionic and covalent bonding are the two ends of this continuum, not separate categories.

3.15: Polar bonds and polar molecules

  • A polar bond has a permanent dipole. A molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel, so polar bonds do not automatically make a polar molecule.
  • Carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄: the C–Cl bonds are polar, but the tetrahedral arrangement cancels them, so the molecule is non-polar.
  • Water, H₂O, is bent, so its dipoles add up and the molecule is polar. Carbon dioxide is linear, so its two C=O dipoles cancel and it is non-polar.

3.16 to 3.19: Electron-pair repulsion and molecular shapes

  • Electron-pair repulsion theory: bonding pairs and lone pairs around a central atom repel each other and arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.
  • Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so lone pairs compress bond angles. The order of repulsion is lone pair to lone pair, then lone pair to bonding pair, then bonding pair to bonding pair.
  • 3.17, bond length and bond angle: bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Bond angle is the angle between two bonds at the central atom. Triple bonds are shorter than double bonds, which are shorter than single bonds (C≡C shorter than C=C shorter than C–C).

3.18, the shapes and bond angles of the named species:

SpeciesElectron pairs on central atomShapeBond angle
BeCl₂2 bondingLinear180°
BCl₃3 bondingTrigonal planar120°
CH₄4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
NH₃3 bonding, 1 loneTrigonal pyramidalabout 107°
NH₄⁺4 bondingTetrahedral109.5°
H₂O2 bonding, 2 loneBentabout 104.5°
CO₂2 bonding (double bonds)Linear180°
PCl₅ (gas)5 bondingTrigonal bipyramidal90° and 120°
SF₆6 bondingOctahedral90°
C₂H₄3 regions around each carbonPlanar around each carbonabout 120°

Applying the same rules to analogous species (3.19): SiH₄ is tetrahedral (109.5°), BF₃ is trigonal planar (120°), PH₃ is pyramidal (about 93°), H₂S is bent (about 92°), XeF₄ is square planar (90°, with two lone pairs), and ClF₃ is T-shaped. Count the electron pairs first, then decide how many are lone pairs.

3.20 to 3.22: Metallic bonding and the properties of metals

  • A metal is a giant lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons, the outer electrons that are free to move through the whole structure.
  • 3.21, metallic bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the metal cations and the delocalised electrons. It is not a bond between two particular atoms.
  • Electrical conduction: the delocalised electrons carry charge through the metal when a voltage is applied.
  • High melting temperature: the attraction is strong and is non-directional, so a lot of energy is needed to overcome it. Magnesium melts at about 650 °C, far above sodium at about 98 °C, because Mg²⁺ carries a double charge and provides two delocalised electrons per atom.
  • Malleability: the layers of ions can slide over each other, and the delocalised electrons keep the ions attracted to each other as they move, so the metal does not shatter.

A* extension: worked reasoning for the hardest bonding questions

  • Bond angles, 3.18 applied: CH₄ is 109.5°, NH₃ about 107°, and H₂O about 104.5°. Each lone pair pushes the bonding pairs closer together, because lone pair to bonding pair repulsion is stronger than bonding pair to bonding pair. So the angle falls by roughly 2.5° per lone pair. An A* answer states the reason in these terms, not just the number.
  • Polarity, 3.15 applied: CH₃Cl is polar, because the C–Cl dipole is not cancelled by the C–H bonds, which point in roughly symmetrical directions but carry much smaller dipoles. CCl₄ is non-polar, because four identical C–Cl dipoles point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel exactly. Always say which dipoles cancel and why.
  • Electronegativity and bonding continuum, 3.14 applied: aluminium chloride has an electronegativity difference of about 1.5 between Al and Cl. That is not large enough to make it purely ionic, so it is a polar covalent bond, which is consistent with its low melting point and the polarisation argument in 3.8 to 3.9.
  • Lattice and bond strength, 3.6 applied: when asked to compare two ionic compounds, name both the charge and the radius, and say which one dominates. Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ beat Na⁺ and Cl⁻ on both counts, so MgO has the much higher melting point.
  • Mark-scheme phrasing for metallic bonding (3.21): "giant lattice of positive ions", "sea of delocalised electrons", "strong electrostatic attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons". Each phrase earns its own mark, so use all three.
  • Graphite versus graphene, 3.12 applied: an electrode question expects you to name the delocalised electron, and a lubricant question expects you to name the weak forces between layers. Give both mechanisms when the question says "explain".

Common errors that lose marks

  • Saying covalent or metallic bonds are "between molecules" (they are within the structure; the forces between molecules are intermolecular forces).
  • Calling a polar bond a polar molecule. Always check the shape before you decide the molecule's polarity.
  • Saying ions "move" in solid ionic compounds. They vibrate in place; only molten or dissolved compounds conduct through ion movement.

title: Complex Numbers — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Complex Numbers

Mathematics — A2 (9709). i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Key areas to revise

  • Basics
  • Conjugates
  • Argand Diagram
  • Modulus–Argument Form
  • de Moivre and Roots

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Use i² = −1. The sum (2 + 3i) + (1 − 4i) = 3 − i. The product (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 2 + i + 3 = 5 + i. The modulus of 3 + 4i is √(9 + 16) = 5. The conjugate of 2 + 3i is 2 − 3i, and z multiplied by its conjugate gives |z|² = 13.

Key points to remember

A complex number z = x + iy has real part x and imaginary part y, where i² = −1. To divide, multiply the numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate x − iy of the denominator. The modulus |z| = √(x² + y²) is the distance from the origin on an Argand diagram, and the argument is the angle from the positive real axis.

For a polynomial equation with real coefficients, complex roots occur in conjugate pairs: if 2 + 3i is a root then 2 − 3i is also a root. Use this to factorise a quadratic with no real roots. Sketch the Argand diagram when a question asks about a locus or region, and check that your answer agrees with the picture.

title: Binomial Expansion — Study Notes
content:
Binomial expansion

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 4 (WMA14), sat at A2.

The binomial theorem expands (1 + x)^n in ascending powers of x. For positive integer n the series terminates; for negative or fractional n it is an infinite series valid only inside a restricted range.

The expansion

(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + [n(n - 1)/2!] x^2 + [n(n - 1)(n - 2)/3!] x^3 + ...

The coefficient of x^r is n(n - 1)...(n - r + 1) / r!. Note this is NOT C(n, r) unless n is a positive integer.

Non-integer n

When n is negative or fractional the expansion is an infinite series, and it is valid only for |x| < 1. If the bracket is (1 + kx), validity becomes |kx| < 1, i.e. |x| < 1/|k|.

Rewriting awkward brackets

  • Factor out the constant: (3 + 2x)^n = 3^n (1 + 2x/3)^n, then expand the bracket.
  • Negative powers and reciprocals: (1 - 2x)^(-2), 1/sqrt(1 + x) = (1 + x)^(-1/2).

Approximations

To estimate a surd, force the (1 + x) form with a small x:

  • sqrt(1.04) = (1 + 0.04)^(1/2) approx 1 + 0.02 - 0.0002 = 1.0198.
  • Use three terms for 3 s.f. accuracy, and state the range of validity.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to halve (or divide by r!) the product in the coefficient.
  • Losing the minus signs when n is negative or x is negative.
  • Ignoring the validity condition when asked for the range of x.

title: Sequences and Series — Study Notes
content:
Sequences and series

Level note: progressions and sigma notation are Pure 2 (WMA12) in Edexcel, sat at AS; this note is the deeper revision treatment of the same material.

An arithmetic progression (AP) adds a constant difference d each term; a geometric progression (GP) multiplies by a constant ratio r. You must master both closed forms, their sums, and the conditions for an infinite sum.

Arithmetic progression

  • nth term: a_n = a + (n - 1)d.
  • Sum: S_n = n/2 [2a + (n - 1)d] = n/2 (first + last).
  • The difference between consecutive terms is constant: a_{n+1} - a_n = d.

Geometric progression

  • nth term: a_n = a r^(n - 1).
  • Sum: S_n = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1) = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r).
  • Sum to infinity: S_inf = a/(1 - r), valid ONLY when |r| < 1.

Sigma notation

  • sum of r from 1 to n = n(n + 1)/2; sum of r^2 = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; sum of r^3 = [n(n + 1)/2]^2.
  • sum of a constant c over n terms is cn.
  • Split sums: sum (3r + 1) = 3 sum r + sum 1.

Modelling

  • Arithmetic: hire charges, stacked rows, simple interest.
  • Geometric: depreciation, compound interest, population growth, drug decay.
  • For repeated percentage change, multiplier = (1 + percentage/100) per period.

Exam technique

  • Write the first few terms before committing to a formula.
  • Check the sum formula by substituting n = 1 and n = 2.
  • For 'sum exceeds X' questions solve the inequality and take the first integer.

title: Algebra — Equations — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Equations

Mathematics — OL. linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

  • 1. Linear equations
  • 2. Forming equations
  • 3. Simultaneous equations
  • 4. Quadratics by formula
  • 5. Completing the square

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Solve 3(x − 2) = 2x + 5. Expand to 3x − 6 = 2x + 5, then subtract 2x and add 6 to get x = 11. Check by substitution: 3(11 − 2) = 27 and 2(11) + 5 = 27. For rearranging, make t the subject of v = u + at by subtracting u and dividing by a, giving t = (v − u)/a.

Key points to remember

Solve a linear equation by doing the same operation to both sides until the unknown stands alone. Do the inverse operations in reverse order of BIDMAS, so undo addition or subtraction before multiplication or division. For an equation with the unknown on both sides, collect the terms with the unknown on one side first.

Check every answer by substituting it back into the original equation. When an equation has brackets or fractions, expand or clear the fractions before you start rearranging, and show each line of working so that a method mark can be awarded even if the final answer is wrong.

title: Variation and Selection
content:
Variation and Selection

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 18 (statements 18.1–18.3). Types of variation, adaptive features, and natural selection including antibiotic resistance as the standard application.

18.1 Variation

  • Continuous variation shows a range of values (height, mass); discontinuous variation falls into distinct categories (blood group, tongue rolling). Variation has genetic causes (alleles) and environmental causes (diet, climate); most characteristics show both.

18.2 Adaptive features

  • Adaptive features are structural (shape, camouflage), behavioural (migration, nocturnal activity) or physiological ( venom production, heat generation) and they improve survival and reproduction in a specific environment.

18.3 Selection

  • Natural selection: organisms vary, those best adapted survive and reproduce, and they pass their advantageous alleles to offspring. Over generations the population changes. Darwin's theory, supported by evidence including selective breeding, fossils and antibiotic resistance.
  • Selective breeding (artificial selection) chooses parents with desired traits — higher crop yield, docile behaviour in livestock — over many generations.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Selection chain, applied to bacteria and antibiotics: the population already contains a few resistant individuals by random mutation; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant, so the survivors reproduce without competition and the resistant alleles increase in frequency. Name random mutation first — the ordering of the chain is what earns the marks.
  • Variation classification, applied to a data set of leaf lengths: continuous, and likely controlled by many genes plus environment. If the question gives discrete categories, it is discontinuous with a simpler genetic control. Justify from the data, not from a memorised list.
  • Evaluation reasoning, applied to whether evolution is "progress": argue that selection favours fit in the current environment, not perfection, and that a change in environment can reverse which variant is favoured. That nuance is what separates top-band answers.

Common errors

  • Saying organisms "try to adapt" or "develop resistance". Variation is random; selection is not.
  • Claiming acquired characteristics are inherited (Lamarck's error).
  • Confusing selective breeding with genetic modification — selective breeding uses existing variation.

title: Thermal Physics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Thermal Physics

Physics — OL. kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

  • 1. Kinetic model
  • 2. Gas pressure and temperature
  • 3. Thermal expansion
  • 4. Specific heat capacity
  • 5. State changes
  • 6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Thermal energy moves by conduction in solids, convection in fluids, and radiation, which can pass through a vacuum.
  • Dark, matt surfaces are good absorbers and good emitters of infrared radiation.
  • Energy for a temperature change: Q = m c Δθ. Energy for a change of state: Q = m L.
  • The temperature stays constant during a change of state because the energy is used to break bonds between particles.

Common errors

Convection needs a fluid to flow, so it cannot occur in a solid. Do not say that heat is stored in a substance; it is thermal energy that is transferred.

title: Magnetism & Electromagnetism — Study Notes
content:
Magnetism & Electromagnetism

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): magnets & fields; magnetic effect of a current; force on a current-carrying conductor; motor effect; electromagnetic induction (Extended); transformers (Extended).

1. Magnets and fields

Iron/steel/cobalt/nickel; like poles repel. Field lines exit N, enter S; compass plotting; plotting compass aligns with field. Induced magnetism: iron (temporary) vs steel (permanent).

2. Electromagnets

Solenoid field like a bar magnet; strength ↑ with current, turns, iron core. Uses: relays, scrapyard crane, electric bell, speaker. Hard/soft magnetic materials choose permanent vs core use.

3. Force on a current-carrying conductor

F = BIL, direction by Fleming's left hand (fIeld, current, force). Reversing current or field reverses force. D.C. motor: coil, commutator reverses current each half-turn for continuous rotation; speed/torque ↑ with current, field strength, turns/area.

4. Electromagnetic induction (Extended)

Induced e.m.f. when a conductor cuts field lines or flux changes. Fleming's right hand (generator). Factors: speed, field strength, turns. A.C. generator: slip rings; dynamo effect; Lenz's law opposes change (direction of induced current).

5. Transformers (Extended)

Vp/Vs = Np/Ns; Pin ≈ Pout (100% assumed): IpVp = IsVs. Step-up raises V, lowers I → lower I²R transmission losses; a.c. required (changing flux).

Magnetic fields and electromagnets

Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract. Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole. A solenoid is a coil of wire; its field is strengthened by increasing the current, increasing the number of turns, or placing a soft iron core inside it. An electromagnet can be switched on and off by the current, unlike a permanent magnet.

A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force, which is the basis of the motor effect used in electric motors.

Exam tip: when asked how to make an electromagnet stronger, give two changes, such as more turns and a larger current.

Worked example: force on a current-carrying conductor

A wire of length 0.5 m carries a current of 3 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.2 T. The force is F = B × I × L = 0.2 × 3 × 0.5 = 0.3 N. The force is at right angles to both the field and the current, and the direction can be found with Fleming's left-hand rule: the first finger is the field, the second finger is the current and the thumb is the motion.

Worked example: a transformer

An ideal step-down transformer has 1000 turns on the primary and 100 turns on the secondary. A primary voltage of 230 V gives a secondary voltage of Vs = Vp × Ns ÷ Np = 230 × 100 ÷ 1000 = 23 V. If the primary current is 0.5 A, the secondary current is Is = Ip × Vp ÷ Vs = 0.5 × 230 ÷ 23 = 5 A. The input power is 230 × 0.5 = 115 W and the output power is 23 × 5 = 115 W, so the ideal transformer loses no power. A step-down transformer lowers the voltage and raises the current.

Why a transformer needs alternating current

A transformer works by electromagnetic induction. The changing flux in the iron core induces a voltage in the secondary coil only while the flux is changing. A steady direct current produces a steady flux, so no voltage is induced and the transformer does not work with direct current.

Exam point: quote the transformer equation in the form Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns, and check whether the question assumes an ideal transformer, where input and output power are equal.

title: Exam technique: Mensuration
content:
### What earns the marks
For circles, sectors and arcs, the fraction of 360 stated earns the method mark: write 60/360 before multiplying. For cylinders, cones and spheres, the formula quoted earns a mark on its own, so write Volume = (1/3) pi r squared h even when confident. For compound shapes, split earns marks: compute each part separately, then add or subtract with a clear statement.
### Traps
Error: 2 pi r used for area. Correction: circumference versus area check first. Error: omitting 1/3 for cones and pyramids. Correction: quote the formula every time. Error: using diameter as radius in a semicircle cut-out. Correction: halve the diameter before any pi work. Error: forgetting the square root in a Pythagoras step. Correction: label squared lines as squared.
### Worked example
A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Its volume is πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. A sector of angle 60° in a circle of radius 6 cm has arc length (60/360) × 2π × 6 = 2π cm.
### Worked example
A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. Its perimeter is 2(8 + 5) = 26 cm and its area is 40 cm². A triangular prism with triangular cross-section area 12 cm² and length 7 cm has volume 12 × 7 = 84 cm³.

title: Chemical Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes
content:
Chemical Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry Revision Notes

This revision note belongs to Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 13 Chemical Equilibria, covering homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, equilibrium constants Kc and Kp, the factors affecting equilibrium composition and constant values, total entropy links, and reaction extent predictions.

Expressions for Kc in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Systems

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system, it eventually reaches a dynamic equilibrium where the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, and the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. The equilibrium constant Kc allows you to deduce the position of equilibrium quantitatively.

  • Be able to deduce an expression for Kc, for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium concentrations.
  • For a general homogeneous system where all species are in the same phase, such as aA + bB reversible cC + dD, the expression is Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b), where square brackets denote equilibrium concentrations in mol dm⁻³.
  • For heterogeneous systems containing species in different phases, pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from the Kc expression because their concentrations remain essentially constant throughout the reaction. For example, for the decomposition of calcium carbonate, CaCO3(s) reversible CaO(s) + CO2(g), the expression is simply Kc = [CO2].

Expressions for Kp in Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Systems

For systems involving gases, it is often more convenient to use partial pressures rather than concentrations to define the equilibrium position.

  • Be able to deduce an expression for Kp for homogeneous and heterogeneous systems, in terms of equilibrium partial pressures in atm.
  • The mole fraction of a gas in a mixture is calculated as the number of moles of that individual gas divided by the total number of moles of all gases present in the mixture.
  • The partial pressure of an individual gas is its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure of the gas system, measured in units of atmospheres or atm.
  • For a homogeneous gas phase reaction such as N2O4(g) reversible 2NO2(g), the partial pressure expression is Kp = p(NO2)² / p(N2O4).
  • For a heterogeneous gas-solid equilibrium such as C(s) + CO2(g) reversible 2CO(g), pure solid carbon is omitted from the expression, giving Kp = p(CO)² / p(CO2).

Calculating Equilibrium Constants from Experimental Data

Calculations involving Kc and Kp require systematic tracking of initial moles, change in moles, and equilibrium moles, converting them to concentrations or partial pressures.

  • Be able to calculate a value, with units where appropriate, for the equilibrium constants Kc and Kp for homogeneous and heterogeneous reactions, from experimental data.
  • For Kc calculations, divide equilibrium moles by the total volume in dm³ to find equilibrium concentrations, substitute into the Kc formula, and cancel out units or combine them using indices such as mol⁻² dm⁶.
  • For Kp calculations, find total moles at equilibrium, determine mole fractions for each gas, multiply by total pressure to find partial pressures in atm, substitute into Kp, and derive units like atm or atm².

Worked Example for Kc Calculation

For H2 + I2 reversible 2HI, suppose 1.00 mol of hydrogen and 1.00 mol of iodine are heated in a 2.00 dm³ flask. At equilibrium, 1.60 mol of hydrogen iodide has formed.

  • Step 1: Set up an ICE table. Initial moles: H2 = 1.00, I2 = 1.00, HI = 0.00.
  • Step 2: Equilibrium moles: HI = 1.60. Since stoichiometry shows 2 mol of HI form, 0.80 mol of H2 and 0.80 mol of I2 must have reacted.
  • Step 3: Calculate remaining equilibrium moles: H2 = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 mol; I2 = 1.00 − 0.80 = 0.20 mol.
  • Step 4: Convert to concentrations by dividing by the volume of 2.00 dm³: [HI] = 1.60 ÷ 2.00 = 0.80 mol dm⁻³, [H2] = 0.20 ÷ 2.00 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, [I2] = 0.20 ÷ 2.00 = 0.10 mol dm⁻³.
  • Step 5: Substitute into Kc expression: Kc = [HI]² / ([H2] × [I2]) = 0.80² / (0.10 × 0.10) = 0.64 / 0.01 = 64. The units cancel out entirely because the number of moles of reactants equals the number of moles of products.

Effects of Changes on Equilibrium Composition

Le Chatelier's principle helps predict how a system responds to external stresses, altering equilibrium composition without changing the constant itself unless temperature changes.

  • Understand how, if at all, a change in temperature, pressure or the presence of a catalyst affects the equilibrium composition in a homogeneous or heterogeneous system.
  • Adding reactant or removing product shifts the position towards the products. Adding product shifts it towards the reactants.
  • Increasing pressure or decreasing volume favours the side of the reaction with fewer gas molecules. Changing the volume has the same effect as changing pressure.
  • Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction. Lowering the temperature shifts it in the exothermic direction.
  • A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, but it has no effect on the equilibrium position or composition.

Independence of Equilibrium Constants from Concentration and Pressure

While altering conditions shifts the position of equilibrium, the underlying constant remains strictly invariant under specific conditions.

  • Understand that the value of the equilibrium constant is not affected by changes in concentration or pressure or by the addition of a catalyst.
  • A change in concentration or pressure shifts the equilibrium composition to counteract the change, but the ratio of products to reactants at the new equilibrium exactly equals the original Kc or Kp value.
  • A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse rates equally, leaving the equilibrium constant completely unchanged.

Effect of Temperature on Equilibrium Constants

Temperature is unique because it alters the actual value of the equilibrium constant Kc and Kp, reflecting a change in the position of equilibrium.

  • Know the effect of changing the temperature on the equilibrium constant Kc and Kp for both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
  • Understand that the effect of temperature on the position of equilibrium is explained using a change in the value of the equilibrium constant.
  • For an exothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature decreases the value of Kc and Kp, as the equilibrium shifts to the left. Lowering the temperature increases Kc and Kp.
  • For an endothermic forward reaction, raising the temperature increases the value of Kc and Kp, as the equilibrium shifts to the right. Lowering the temperature decreases Kc and Kp.

Entropy, Total Entropy, and Equilibrium Constants

Thermodynamics links the position of equilibrium to total entropy change and the magnitude of the equilibrium constant.

  • Understand the effect of a change in temperature on the value of Stotal and the magnitude of the equilibrium constant, since Stotal = R ln K.
  • The equation Stotal = R ln K bridges kinetics, equilibrium, and thermodynamics, where R is the universal gas constant and ln K is the natural logarithm of the equilibrium constant.
  • When temperature changes, it alters Stotal, which in turn directly alters the magnitude of K. A larger positive Stotal corresponds to a much larger equilibrium constant, meaning the reaction goes virtually to completion.

Predicting the Extent of Reaction

The numerical value of an equilibrium constant gives immediate insight into whether a reaction proceeds far towards products or stays mostly as reactants.

  • Be able to apply knowledge of the value of equilibrium constants to predict the extent to which a reaction takes place.
  • When an equilibrium constant value is very large, greater than 10 to the power of 10, the numerator is vastly larger than the denominator, indicating that the reaction goes essentially to completion with very few reactants remaining.
  • When an equilibrium constant value is very small, less than 10 to the power of minus 10, the denominator dominates, indicating that virtually no reaction takes place and the system remains almost entirely as reactants.
  • When an equilibrium constant is around 1, significant amounts of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Including pure solids or pure liquids in Kc or Kp expressions. Correction: Omit pure solids and pure liquids because their active masses do not change.
  • Mistake: Forgetting to divide equilibrium moles by volume when calculating Kc. Correction: Always divide moles by the volume in dm³ to obtain concentration values before substituting into Kc.
  • Mistake: Believing that increasing pressure changes the value of Kc. Correction: Pressure changes the position of equilibrium and shifts concentrations, but Kc remains constant at a fixed temperature.
  • Mistake: Using mass in grams instead of mole fractions or partial pressures for Kp calculations. Correction: Always convert mass to moles, find mole fractions, and multiply by total pressure in atm.

Exam-style questions

  1. Write the expression for Kc for the heterogeneous reaction C(s) + H2O(g) reversible CO(g) + H2(g).

    Answer: Kc = [CO] [H2] / [H2O]. Solid carbon is omitted.

  2. State and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the value of Kc for an endothermic forward reaction.

    Answer: Kc increases. Raising temperature favours the endothermic direction, increasing product concentrations and decreasing reactant concentrations, raising the numerator of Kc.

  3. Calculate the units of Kp for the equilibrium N2(g) + 3H2(g) reversible 2NH3(g) when pressure is measured in atm.

    Answer: Kp = p(NH3)² / (p(N2) × p(H2)³). Units are atm² / (atm × atm³) = atm⁻².

  4. Explain why a catalyst has no effect on the numerical value of Kc.

    Answer: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse rates equally by lowering the activation energy, leaving the equilibrium constant ratio unchanged.

  5. Explain what a Kc value of 10 to the power of 15 indicates about the extent of a reaction.

    Answer: The reaction goes almost entirely to completion, with the equilibrium position lying far to the right.

Use these revision notes to test your understanding of equilibrium expressions, unit derivations, and thermodynamic links via Stotal. Next, revise reaction kinetics and acid-base equilibria.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Kc expression, applied to H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g): Kc = [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]). The units depend on the equation, here none, because the moles cancel. Write the units only when they do not cancel, and state the units explicitly when you give Kc.
  • Kp, applied to N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: partial pressure of a gas = mole fraction × total pressure. Kp = p(NH₃)² ÷ (p(N₂) × p(H₂)³), and its units are Pa⁻² here. Give the units with Kp, because the pressures do not cancel.
  • Le Chatelier and Kc, applied to an exothermic reaction: raising the temperature moves the equilibrium to the left and decreases Kc. Adding a catalyst does not change Kc, because it speeds up the forward and backward reactions equally. Adding more reactant changes the position but not Kc.
  • Pressure effects: for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, four gas molecules become two, so higher pressure favours the product. The equilibrium moves to the side with fewer gas molecules, and Kp stays the same at a fixed temperature.

title: Data Structures — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Data Structures

Computer Science — AS. A data structure organises data so that it can be accessed and changed efficiently. The choice depends on which operations a program needs most often.

Key areas to revise

  • Arrays and lists: fixed-size arrays give fast access by index, while lists can grow and shrink.
  • Stack: last in, first out (LIFO). The main operations are push and pop, and a stack is used for function calls and undo.
  • Queue: first in, first out (FIFO). The main operations are enqueue and dequeue, and a queue is used for scheduling and buffers. A circular queue reuses the space at the start of the array.
  • Linked list: each node stores data and a pointer to the next node. Insertion and deletion need only the pointers to change, but finding an item means checking nodes one at a time.
  • Hash table: a hashing function turns a key into an index. Collisions happen when two keys produce the same index, and they must be handled.
  • Complexity: describe how the time for an operation grows with the number of items, for example constant, linear or logarithmic.

Core facts to recall

  • A stack reverses the order of items; a queue keeps their order.
  • A linked list is useful when items are added and removed often in the middle of the structure.
  • Explain a structure by naming an operation it does well and one it does badly.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Drugs
content:
Drugs

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 15 (statement 15.1). What drugs are, medicinal versus recreational drugs, antibiotic use and resistance, and the effects of alcohol and heroin.

15.1 Drugs

  • A drug is any substance that changes the way the body or mind works. Medicinal drugs treat or prevent disease; recreational drugs are taken for their psychological effects and can be addictive.
  • Antibiotics kill bacteria (bactericidal) or stop them multiplying (bacteriostatic). They do not work against viruses, because viruses use the host cell's own machinery and have no processes for antibiotics to block.
  • Antibiotic resistance arises by random mutation in a bacterial population; antibiotic use selects for resistant bacteria because the non-resistant ones die and the resistant ones reproduce unchecked. Misuse — not finishing a course, unnecessary prescriptions — accelerates resistance.
  • Alcohol is a depressant that slows reaction times and damages liver cells; heroin is an addictive opiate that depresses the central nervous system and carries overdose and infection risks from shared needles.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Selection reasoning, applied to a course of antibiotics stopped early: the most susceptible bacteria die first, leaving behind those with partial resistance, which multiply in the absence of competition. Explain with variation and selection — not "the antibiotics teach bacteria to resist". That misconception loses the mark outright.
  • Stewardship evaluation, applied to proposals to restrict antibiotic use in farming: argue both sides — reduced selection pressure slows resistance, but animal health and welfare may suffer. A top answer weighs both and reaches a justified judgement.
  • Drug classification reasoning, applied to why a vaccine is not an antibiotic: a vaccine stimulates the immune system to make its own antibodies against a virus, while an antibiotic acts directly on bacterial structures. Match the agent to the pathogen type in every case.

Common errors

  • Saying bacteria "become resistant because of antibiotics". Resistance is a random pre-existing mutation that antibiotics select.
  • Claiming antibiotics treat colds. Colds are viral.
  • Describing an overdose risk of heroin without naming respiratory depression as the cause.

title: Poisson Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Poisson Distribution

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 2 (WST02), sat at A2.

The Model

X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

The Formula

P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, ...

Example: X ~ Po(2). P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. P(X = 1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.2707.

Mean and Variance

The defining signature of the Poisson:

  • E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ — the mean and variance are equal.

If a question gives a mean m, then λ = m; the variance is also m.

Scaling the Interval

If X ~ Po(λ) per hour, then 3 hours gives Y ~ Po(3λ). Rates must be adjusted to the same interval before computing anything. Halving an interval halves λ.

Adding Poissons

If X ~ Po(λ₁) and Y ~ Po(λ₂) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ₁ + λ₂). Two independent queues merging into one server produce a Poisson with summed rate.

Exam tips: check independence and constant rate before modelling — if events cluster (rush hours), Poisson fails. Convert the interval first: a rate of 8 per 20 minutes becomes 24 per hour. In "at least" questions use the complement exactly as with the binomial.

Exam method: Poisson probabilities

If X ~ Po(λ), then P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r! for r = 0, 1, 2, … The mean and the variance are both equal to λ, so the parameter is found directly from either quantity given in the question.

Use the calculator's Poisson function or the formula with the exact value of e^(−λ). When a question asks for P(X ≤ r) or P(X ≥ r), add the separate probabilities, or subtract the complement from 1.

The rate must match the interval. If events occur at 4 per hour and the question asks about a 30-minute period, the new mean is 2. Always rescale λ to the period in the question.

A Poisson model is appropriate for counts of events that occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate.

Exam cue: Check the rescaling of λ first; it is the most common error in Poisson questions, and it costs the whole question.

Worked example: a Poisson probability

The number of emails received per hour, X, follows a Poisson distribution with mean λ = 3, written X ~ Po(3). Then P(X = 2) = e⁻³ × 3² ÷ 2! = 0.04979 × 9 ÷ 2 = 0.2240 (to 4 decimal places). Use the calculator's Poisson function when the examination permits it, or the tables in the formula booklet.

Scaling the interval

If emails arrive at a mean rate of 3 per hour, the mean for 20 minutes is 3 × 20/60 = 1. Always multiply λ by the length of the new interval so that the rate and the time use the same unit.

Adding independent Poisson variables

If X ~ Po(2) and Y ~ Po(5) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(7). The means add, and so do the variances, because for a Poisson distribution the mean and the variance are both λ.

Exam method

  • State the distribution and its parameter in the form X ~ Po(λ) before calculating.
  • For P(X at least 1), use 1 − P(X = 0), which is usually quicker.
  • Give probabilities to 3 significant figures unless the question asks for a different accuracy.

title: The Normal Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Normal Distribution

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 1 (WST01), sat at AS. The normal-approximation section continues in Statistics 2 (WST02) at A2.

The Model

A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Standardising

Convert any normal variable to the standard normal Z ~ N(0, 1) with

  • Z = (X − μ)/σ

Then read probabilities from the normal table. For X ~ N(50, 4²): P(X > 56) = P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668.

Backwards Problems

Given a probability, find μ or σ. Convert the target percentile to a z-value from the table, then solve (x − μ)/σ = z.

Example: P(X < 30) = 0.15 with unknown σ. From tables z = −1.036, so (30 − μ)/σ = −1.036 — one equation per unknown; use a second condition if both are missing.

Symmetry Shortcuts

P(X > μ) = 0.5. P(X < a) for a above the mean uses the complement. Tables usually give Φ(z) for z ≥ 0 only; use Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z).

Normal Approximation to the Binomial

For large n with p near ½, X ~ B(n, p) ≈ N(np, np(1 − p)). The condition usually quoted at this level is np > 5 and n(1 − p) > 5. Apply a continuity correction: to approximate P(X ≥ 12) for a binomial, compute P(Y > 11.5) for the normal Y.

Example: B(100, 0.5) ≈ N(50, 25). P(X ≥ 55) ≈ P(Y > 54.5) = P(Z > 0.9) = 0.1841.

Exam tips: always sketch and shade — the picture prevents complement errors. State the standardisation step explicitly; marks sit in the working. Check whether a question says "mean and standard deviation" (σ) or "variance" (σ²) before standardising.

Exam method: standardising and symmetry

For X ~ N(μ, σ²) the standard score is z = (x − μ)/σ, and Z ~ N(0, 1). Note that the second parameter is the variance, so take the square root to get σ before standardising. Many errors come from using 25 instead of 5 when the variance is 25.

Probabilities are found from the standard normal table or calculator using Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z). Because the curve is symmetric about 0, Φ(−z) = 1 − Φ(z), and P(Z > z) = 1 − Φ(z).

For a probability between two values, P(a < X < b) = Φ(z_b) − Φ(z_a). Standardise each limit separately and subtract.

To find a value from a probability, read the z-value from the table with the required area, and then rearrange z = (x − μ)/σ to find x.

Exam cue: Sketch the curve and shade the area asked for, then match it to the table value, since the sketch catches sign errors.

Standardising a normal variable

If X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ, then Z = (X − μ) ÷ σ follows the standard normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Standardising allows any normal probability to be read from the standard normal table. For example, if X is normal with mean 50 and standard deviation 4, then P(X > 54) = P(Z > 1), which the table gives as about 0.1587.

Worked example: finding a value from a probability

Suppose P(X < k) = 0.9 for a normal variable with mean 20 and standard deviation 3. The table gives the z-value 1.2816 for a probability of 0.9, so k = 20 + 1.2816 × 3 = 23.85. When the probability is less than 0.5, the z-value is negative, so take care with the sign. Sketch the normal curve and shade the area you need before you use the table, because the sketch shows whether the answer should be above or below the mean.

Symmetry and the 68-95-99 rule

The normal curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(Z < −a) = P(Z > a). Roughly 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two and 99.7% within three. These approximate figures are useful for checking whether a calculated probability is reasonable.

title:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note covers the A2 biology topic that links microorganisms, the immune response and the forensic use of biology. It is written around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more statements the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the comparisons and worked ideas that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards, not just to re-read facts.

1. The point of the topic and what “microbiology” means here

In this topic, microbiology is the study of the small living things that are too small to see individually without magnification: bacteria, viruses and the other agents of infection, and some of the fungi and other microorganisms that are important as pathogens, as tools and as part of the normal biosphere. The focus of this topic is not a general survey of all microbes, but the ones that matter for disease, immunity and the forensic use of biological evidence. That means the biology here has three strands: what the pathogens are, how the body defends itself against them, and how biological evidence is used in the service of identification and interpretation. If you can keep those three strands in view, the topic is easier to remember, because you are not memorising three unrelated lists.

A good answer sees the topic as one connected system: a pathogen is a microorganism with the ability to cause disease; the body has barriers and specific defences; and the forensic use of biology depends on the same kind of reasoning that the rest of biology uses, namely that evidence is interpreted rather than just collected. If you treat the topic as a bag of facts, you lose the logic that makes it answerable in an exam. If you treat it as a set of connected ideas, you can answer questions that cross the strands, which is where many of the marks sit.

2. Bacteria as living cells and as pathogens

Bacteria are living cells with a cell wall, cytoplasm, ribosomes and genetic material, but they are much smaller and simpler than plant or animal cells, and they may have extra features such as a capsule, flagella or plasmids. Some are harmless or even useful; some are pathogens that cause disease by damaging tissues directly, by producing toxins, or by triggering responses that themselves cause harm. A good answer says that bacteria are cells with cell walls, cytoplasm and ribosomes, that they may have capsules, flagella or plasmids, that they reproduce by binary fission, and that pathogenic bacteria cause disease because they damage tissues, release toxins or provoke harmful responses. It does not say that all bacteria are pathogens, because they are not, and it does not say that bacteria cause disease only by one route, because there is more than one way a bacterium can harm the host.

The distinction between infection and disease is also worth keeping clear. Infection means the microorganism is present and multiplying; disease is the harm that results. A person can be infected without being obviously diseased, and a person can be diseased without the term “infection” meaning the same thing in every context. If you can make that distinction, you avoid the sloppy language that loses marks when the question is precise. The capsule, flagella and plasmids are also useful ideas because they are examples of bacterial features that affect how pathogenic a bacterium can be, how it spreads and how it can be identified. If you can name them and say what they do, you are answering at the right level.

3. Viruses as non-cellular agents and why they are not “alive” in the same sense

Viruses are not cells. They have genetic material, DNA or RNA, inside a protein coat, and some have an outer envelope, but they have no cytoplasm, no ribosomes and no independent metabolism. Because of that, they cannot reproduce by themselves; they must get inside a host cell and use the host’s machinery to make new virus particles. That is why viruses are often described as non-living in the usual biological sense, even though they are a major cause of disease and a major part of this topic. A good answer says that a virus is a small particle with genetic material surrounded by a protein coat, that some have an envelope, that viruses lack the machinery to reproduce independently and must use a host cell, and that this is why they are not treated as living cells in the normal sense. It does not say that a virus is a very small bacterium, because it is not, and it does not say that viruses can reproduce on their own outside a host, because they cannot.

The host-cell dependence is the central idea, because it explains both why viruses cause disease and why some antiviral strategies work by targeting the interaction with the host cell rather than the virus as if it were a cell itself. A good answer says that viruses depend on host cells to replicate, and that the damage they cause is often a consequence of how they use or damage host cells. It does not need to describe every step of every viral life cycle to answer at the right level, but it should say that the virus is not a cell and that it cannot replicate independently. If you keep that distinction clear, you can answer the questions without confusing bacteria and viruses, which is one of the most common mark-losers in this topic.

4. Culturing microorganisms safely and why aseptic technique matters

Microorganisms can be cultured under controlled conditions, but culturing carries a risk of contamination and of growing unwanted or harmful microbes, so aseptic technique matters. Aseptic technique means working in a way that minimises the chance of unwanted microbes entering the culture or the workspace, and of the culture leaving the workspace where it could cause harm. A good answer says that microorganisms are cultured on media such as agar, that aseptic technique is used to prevent contamination of the culture and to prevent the cultured microbes from contaminating the environment and people, and that the aim is to keep the culture pure and to keep the process safe. It does not say that aseptic technique is only about being tidy, because it is specifically about controlling the movement of microbes.

The safety point is important because microbiology is done with living organisms that can multiply quickly. A good answer therefore includes the idea that cultures are handled with care, that equipment is sterilised where needed, that the culture is contained, and that waste is disposed of safely. If the question asks for safety precautions, these are the kinds of idea to include: sterilisation of equipment, containment of the culture, and safe disposal. If the question asks why aseptic technique is used, say both that it protects the culture from contamination and that it protects the environment and people from the culture. If you can say that, you have the safety and purity point both correct.

5. Growth curves and the idea that a culture changes over time

A microbial culture does not stay static; it goes through phases as the organisms grow, use resources and respond to the environment. A typical growth curve includes a lag phase, an exponential or log phase, a stationary phase and a decline or death phase. The pattern exists because growth depends on resources, waste accumulation, space and the conditions in the medium. A good answer says that microbial growth is not constant, that the culture passes through phases including lag, exponential, stationary and decline, and that the phases reflect the conditions in the culture and the limits on growth. It does not say that growth is a steady increase forever, because it is not, and it does not say that the phases are the same in every culture without qualification, because the shape depends on the organism and the conditions. If you can say that, you have the growth idea in a form that scores marks.

The exponential phase is the one where the population is increasing as fast as the conditions allow, and it is often the phase of interest in practicals and in questions about growth rate. The lag phase is where the organisms are adapting to the new conditions; the stationary phase is where growth is balanced by death; and the decline phase is where death exceeds growth. A good answer can describe those in general terms without needing to give exact timings, because the point is the pattern and the reasons for it. If you can describe the pattern and say why it occurs, you have the answer the examiners are after.

6. Factors that affect microbial growth

Microbial growth depends on environmental factors such as temperature, pH, water availability, oxygen, nutrients and inhibitory substances. Which factors matter most depends on the organism, so a thermophile and a mesophile have different temperature ranges, and an aerobe and an anaerobe have different oxygen requirements. A good answer says that growth depends on factors such as temperature, pH, water, oxygen, nutrients and inhibitors, and that the optimum and range depend on the organism. It does not say that all microbes have the same requirements, because they do not, and it does not say that only one factor matters at a time, because in practice several factors interact. If you can say that, you have the microbial growth idea in a form that scores marks.

The conceptual point is that growth rate is controlled by the environment, and that the environment includes more than just the presence of food. If a question asks why a culture grows faster or slower, the answer should consider the relevant factors and why they change the outcome, rather than just saying “the conditions were better” without explanation. That is the kind of reasoning the specification expects. If you can give the factors and the direction of their effect, you have a better answer than a vague label.

7. The first line of defence: barriers and non-specific responses

The body’s first defence against pathogens is a set of barriers and non-specific responses. The skin is a physical barrier; mucous membranes, tears, saliva and stomach acid help block or destroy microbes; inflammation is a non-specific response that brings blood and immune cells to the site of infection or damage; and phagocytosis is a non-specific process in which cells such as phagocytes engulf and destroy pathogens. A good answer says that the first defences include physical and chemical barriers, inflammation and phagocytosis, and that these are non-specific because they act against a broad range of pathogens rather than one particular type. It does not say that the first line of defence is always enough, because it is not, and it does not treat non-specific defence as the same thing as specific immunity, because it is not. If you can say that, you have the first-line idea in a form that scores marks.

Phagocytosis is worth describing with a little structure: the phagocyte engulfs the pathogen into a phagosome, which fuses with a lysosome where enzymes and other chemicals destroy the pathogen. A good answer says that the pathogen is engulfed, enclosed in a vesicle, and destroyed by enzymes and other contents of the lysosome. It does not say that phagocytosis is a specific response, because it is not; it is non-specific, although it is part of the broader immune response. If you can describe the process and the role of the lysosome, you have the answer at the right level.

Inflammation is also part of the immediate response. It is the local reaction to injury or infection, bringing more blood, phagocytes and other responses to the area, and producing the classic signs such as redness, heat and swelling. A good answer says that inflammation is a non-specific response that increases blood flow and brings phagocytes and other defences to the site, and that it helps contain and clear the problem. It does not say that inflammation is the same thing as infection, or that it only happens when bacteria are present, because it can happen after injury as well. If you can say that, you have the inflammation idea in a form that scores marks.

8. Antigens, antibodies and the idea of specific recognition

Specific immunity depends on the recognition of antigens, which are substances, usually proteins or other molecules on the surface of pathogens or on other cells, that the immune system can recognise and respond to. In response to an antigen, the body produces antibodies, proteins that bind to that antigen and help neutralise, mark or remove the pathogen. The important point is that the response is specific: an antibody is made for a particular antigen, and this is what makes the adaptive immune system different from the non-specific first lines of defence. A good answer says that antigens are molecules that the immune system recognises, that antibodies are proteins produced in response to a specific antigen, and that the response is specific because it targets a particular antigen rather than all pathogens. It does not say that antibodies kill pathogens directly in every case, because they work in different ways, and it does not say that antigens are only on pathogens, because they can be on other cells too. If you can say that, you have the antigen-antibody idea in a form that scores marks.

The structure of an antibody matters because it explains why it can be specific. An antibody has a constant region and variable regions that form the antigen-binding site, and the shape of the binding site is what makes the antibody specific to one antigen. A good answer says that an antibody has a constant region and variable binding regions, and that the binding site is specific to one antigen. It does not say that the antibody is a generic killer regardless of shape, because its specificity is the point. If you can describe the structure in terms of constant and variable regions and say why that matters for specificity, you have the answer at the right level.

9. B cells, T cells and the difference between the two kinds of specific response

Specific immunity involves lymphocytes, especially B cells and T cells, which respond to antigens but in different ways. B cells are involved in the humoral response, producing antibodies that act in body fluids and help mark or neutralise pathogens. T cells are involved in the cell-mediated response and in helping coordinate the response, and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells. A good answer says that B cells are associated with antibody production and the humoral response, that T cells are associated with cell-mediated responses and with helping and controlling the immune response, and that both are lymphocytes but with different roles. It does not say that B cells and T cells do exactly the same thing, because they do not, and it does not say that the two systems are unrelated, because they work together. If you can say that, you have the B-cell and T-cell idea in a form that scores marks.

The distinction is important because it is a standard exam point. B cells are the antibody-making arm; T cells are the cell-mediated and helper arm. A good answer can also say that the response includes memory cells, which allow a faster response on later exposure. If you can separate the roles and still see that the response is integrated, you have the immune system in a form that scores marks. If you blur B and T cells into a single “immune cell” idea, you lose the marks that depend on the distinction.

10. Primary and secondary immune responses and why memory matters

On first exposure to an antigen, the primary immune response is slower to develop, because the specific B and T cells have to be activated and expanded. On later exposure, the secondary immune response is faster and stronger, because memory cells from the first exposure are already present and ready. This is the basis of immunological memory and of vaccination. A good answer says that the primary response is slower to develop, that the secondary response is faster and stronger, that memory cells are responsible for the difference, and that this is why vaccination works by exposing the immune system to an antigen without causing the disease. It does not say that the immune system “remembers” in a vague sense without saying what the memory cells do, because the memory cell is the point. If you can say that, you have the primary and secondary response idea in a form that scores marks.

The comparison is worth making explicitly: primary response is slower and smaller, secondary response is faster and larger. A good answer can say that and then explain that the memory cells from the first exposure allow a quicker and larger response the next time. If the question asks about vaccination, the answer should link the idea to exposure to the antigen without disease, so that the immune system is primed without the person having to suffer the infection first. If you can make that link, you have answered the question at the right level.

11. The lymphatic system and why it matters in immunity

The lymphatic system helps the immune system work by draining fluid from tissues, returning it to the blood, and providing sites where immune cells can meet antigens and where immune responses can be organised, such as the lymph nodes. A good answer says that the lymphatic system returns tissue fluid to the blood and provides sites for immune responses, including the lymph nodes where immune cells can encounter antigens. It does not say that the lymphatic system is the same as the blood circulation, because it is not; it is a related but distinct system that returns fluid and is involved in immunity. If you can say that, you have the lymphatic system idea in a form that scores marks.

The immune cell trafficking point is also useful: lymphocytes and other immune cells move through lymph and blood and meet antigens in lymph nodes and other tissues. A good answer can say that the lymph nodes are places where antigens are encountered and immune responses are started. It does not need to describe every detail of lymphatic anatomy to answer at the right level, but it should recognise the role of the lymphatic system in returning fluid and in providing immune sites. If you can do that, you have the answer at the right level.
