12. Vaccination, herd immunity and the reasoning behind it

Vaccination works by priming the immune system against a pathogen without causing the disease, so that memory cells are produced and the body can respond faster and more strongly on real exposure. Herd immunity happens when enough people are immune that the pathogen has difficulty spreading through the population, so that even people who are not immune are less likely to be exposed. A good answer says that vaccination exposes the immune system to an antigen without causing disease, producing memory cells, and that herd immunity arises when a high enough proportion of the population is immune to reduce transmission. It does not say that vaccination makes everyone completely invulnerable, because it does not, and it does not say that herd immunity works by making every individual immune, because it does not; it works by reducing the spread through the population. If you can say that, you have the vaccination and herd immunity idea in a form that scores marks.

The practical and ethical reasoning around vaccination is often part of the topic. A good answer can say that vaccination protects the individual and, at high enough coverage, the population, but that there are issues around coverage, exemptions, side effects and public acceptance, and that the balance matters. If the question asks for evaluation, mention both the benefits and the issues, and say that the importance of coverage is why public health programmes focus on it. If you can do that, you have the evaluation in the right form rather than a one-sided answer.

13. Monoclonal antibodies and how they are made and used

Monoclonal antibodies are antibodies that are identical and specific to one antigen, made from clones of a single antibody-producing cell. They are useful because they can be produced in quantity and directed against a specific antigen, so they can be used in diagnosis, research and therapy. A good answer says that monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies specific to one antigen, that they are produced from clones of a single cell, and that they are useful in diagnosis, research and therapy because they can be directed against a specific antigen and produced in quantity. It does not say that monoclonal antibodies are produced by the natural immune response of one person in the usual sense, because they are cloned from a single hybridoma or equivalent line, and it does not say that they are always therapeutic, because they are also diagnostic and research tools. If you can say that, you have the monoclonal antibody idea in a form that scores marks.

The usefulness comes from specificity and scale. A good answer can say that because each monoclonal antibody is specific to one antigen, it can be used to detect that antigen or target cells carrying it, and because it can be made in large amounts, it can be used practically. If the question asks for uses, mention diagnosis, research and therapy, and give a little detail for each rather than just listing the words. If you can do that, you have the monoclonal antibody answer at the right level.

14. Epidemiology and the study of disease patterns

Epidemiology is the study of the patterns, causes and control of disease in populations. It is the way we move from individual cases to understanding how a disease spreads, who is at risk and what can be done about it. A good answer says that epidemiology studies the occurrence and patterns of disease in populations, that it is used to identify causes and risk factors, and that it informs control measures. It does not say that epidemiology is only about counting cases, because it also looks at causes and control, and it does not say that epidemiology proves causation in every case by itself, because it often points to associations that then need explanation. If you can say that, you have the epidemiology idea in a form that scores marks.

The population view is the important one, because epidemiology is not the same as the clinical study of one patient. A good answer can say that epidemiology looks at groups and patterns, such as who is affected, where, when and at what rate, and that this helps identify risk factors and guide public-health action. If you can make that population-level reasoning clear, you can answer epidemiology questions better than by just saying “it is the study of disease in populations” without saying what that actually involves.

15. Forensic biology: what it is and what it depends on

Forensic biology is the use of biological evidence in the service of investigation and identification. It includes things such as DNA profiling, the analysis of blood and other bodily fluids, and the use of biological material to link people to places, objects or other people. A good answer says that forensic biology uses biological evidence such as DNA to help identify individuals and to link evidence to people or scenes, and that the evidence is interpreted rather than taken as a simple yes/no answer on its own. It does not say that biological evidence is proof in a magic sense, because it is evidence to be interpreted in context, and it does not confuse the collection of evidence with its interpretation. If you can say that, you have the forensic biology idea in a form that scores marks.

The forensic use of biology depends on the same scientific reasoning as the rest of biology: the evidence has to be collected, preserved and interpreted in a way that is reliable and relevant to the question being asked. A good answer can say that contamination, chain of custody and context matter, because those are things that can affect the meaning of the evidence. If you can mention those without overclaiming, you have the forensic reasoning at the right level.

16. DNA profiling and the logic behind it

DNA profiling, also called DNA fingerprinting, is a technique that uses the variation in certain regions of DNA to distinguish individuals. The basic idea is that samples from a person, a crime scene or a paternity case can be compared and matched or excluded based on the pattern of DNA variants. A good answer says that DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA from different samples and can be used to identify individuals, exclude suspects, or establish biological relationships, and that the result depends on the match between the patterns. It does not say that DNA profiling identifies someone with absolute certainty in every sense without context, because the interpretation depends on the quality of the sample and the comparison, and it does not say that DNA profiling is the same thing as sequencing the whole genome for every purpose, because profiling is about the informative regions and the pattern they give. If you can say that, you have the DNA profiling idea in a form that scores marks.

The technical basis is also worth a little detail: profiling is possible because there is variation between individuals in certain DNA regions, and those differences can be detected and compared. If the question asks about the principle, say that the method compares DNA patterns and that the differences between individuals are what make identification possible. If the question asks about uses, mention identification, exclusion and paternity or relationship testing. If you can do both, you have a stronger answer than one that just says “DNA fingerprinting identifies people”.

17. Blood and other bodily-fluids evidence, and the need for care

Blood and other bodily fluids can be evidence, but they are also a source of contamination and a source of interpretation problems if they are not handled properly. A good answer says that evidence such as blood, saliva, hair with follicles and other biological material can be used in forensic biology, but that it has to be collected and preserved properly, and that contamination must be avoided. It does not say that any trace of blood is automatically proof of guilt or innocence, because it is evidence to be interpreted, and it does not say that the mere presence of a substance is the same as a meaningful match, because it is not. If you can say that, you have the bodily-fluid evidence idea in a form that scores marks.

The practical point is that forensic biology is as much about reliability as about possibility. A good answer can say that the value of the evidence depends on how it was collected, whether it was contaminated, and whether the interpretation matches the question. If you can mention those points, you have the forensic reasoning rather than a simple list of evidence types. That is the kind of answer examiners like, because it shows understanding of the limits of the evidence, not just the fact that it exists.

18. How the three strands fit together: microbes, immunity and forensics

The topic is really about three related ways of thinking about small-scale biology. Microbiology gives you the pathogens and the way they grow and spread. Immunity gives you the defence system that fights them, from barriers and phagocytosis through antibodies and memory. Forensics gives you the use of biological evidence, especially DNA, to identify and link. If you see the topic as one connected picture, you can answer the questions that ask for the links, such as why memory matters, why aseptic technique matters, why herd immunity matters, or why DNA profiling is both powerful and limited. If you treat the three strands as separate lists, you lose the reasoning that makes them answerable.

A good answer can move between the strands when needed: the same idea of recognition that explains antibodies also explains why DNA profiling can compare patterns, and the same idea of contamination that matters in microbiology culturing also matters in forensic evidence. The ability to move between the strands is what the higher marks are often about. If you can do that, you are working at the level the specification is aiming for, rather than just recalling a list of facts.

19. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use this note by working through each section and checking that you can describe bacteria and viruses and explain how they differ; describe aseptic technique and why it is used; describe microbial growth and the factors that affect it; describe the first line of defence including barriers, inflammation and phagocytosis; describe antigens, antibodies and the specificity of the antibody response; describe B cells and T cells and the difference between them; describe the primary and secondary immune responses and the role of memory cells; describe vaccination and herd immunity; describe monoclonal antibodies and their uses; describe epidemiology and what it studies; and describe forensic biology, DNA profiling and the care needed with biological evidence. After this topic, revise the related systems and the practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

The note is long because the topic is broad and the specification asks for the biology of microbes, the biology of defence and the biology of forensic evidence in enough detail to be useful. A revision note has to cover the pathogens, the immune system and the forensic application in enough detail, and it has to link them, because the exam questions do. Study it section by section, check yourself against the specification statements, and practise the kinds of answer that explain rather than list. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying all bacteria are pathogens, or saying bacteria and viruses are the same kind of thing.
  • Saying viruses are cells or that they can reproduce independently outside a host.
  • Saying aseptic technique is only about tidiness, rather than about preventing contamination of the culture and protecting people and the environment.
  • Saying microbial growth is a steady increase forever, instead of passing through phases.
  • Saying the first line of defence is always enough, or treating non-specific defence as if it were specific immunity.
  • Saying antibodies kill pathogens in exactly the same way in every case, without recognising that they mark, neutralise and help remove them in different ways.
  • Saying antigens are only on pathogens, instead of being molecules that can be recognised on pathogens and other cells.
  • Blurring B cells and T cells into “immune cells” without distinguishing the antibody-producing and cell-mediated roles.
  • Saying the immune system “remembers” without mentioning memory cells, or saying the secondary response is identical to the primary response.
  • Saying herd immunity means every individual is immune, rather than meaning the spread through the population is reduced.
  • Saying monoclonal antibodies are just any antibodies from one person, rather than identical antibodies from a single cloned line specific to one antigen.
  • Saying epidemiology is only counting cases, without mentioning patterns, causes and control.
  • Saying DNA profiling is proof in a magic sense, without recognising interpretation, sample quality and context.
  • Saying that the mere presence of blood or another fluid is automatically proof of guilt or innocence.
  • Confusing the collection of forensic evidence with its interpretation or reliability.
  • Forgetting that contamination matters in both microbiology and forensic biology, for different but related reasons.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe two differences between bacteria and viruses in structure and one difference in the way they reproduce. Answer: Bacteria are cells with a cell wall, cytoplasm and ribosomes and may have capsules, flagella and plasmids; viruses are not cells and have genetic material inside a protein coat, with some having an envelope. Difference in reproduction: bacteria reproduce independently by binary fission, whereas viruses cannot reproduce on their own and must use a host cell to replicate. (3 marks)
  2. Explain why aseptic technique is used when culturing microorganisms and name two precautions that would be part of it. Answer: Aseptic technique is used to prevent contamination of the culture by unwanted microbes and to prevent the cultured microbes from contaminating the environment and people. Precautions include sterilising equipment, working near a flame or in a sterile field, sealing or covering the culture and disposing of it safely. (4 marks)
  3. Describe the phases of a typical microbial growth curve and explain why the curve is not a steady increase. Answer: A typical growth curve includes a lag phase, an exponential phase, a stationary phase and a decline phase. Growth is not a steady increase forever because it depends on factors such as nutrients, space, waste accumulation and the conditions in the culture; as resources become limited and waste builds up, growth slows, stops and may decline. (4 marks)
  4. Describe the non-specific first line of defence against pathogens and give one example of such a defence. Answer: The first line of defence includes physical and chemical barriers such as skin, mucous membranes, tears, saliva and stomach acid, together with non-specific responses such as inflammation and phagocytosis. Example: phagocytes engulf pathogens into a phagosome, which fuses with a lysosome where enzymes and other chemicals destroy the pathogen. (4 marks)
  5. Explain the difference between antigens and antibodies and why the antibody response is described as specific. Answer: Antigens are molecules, often on the surface of pathogens or other cells, that the immune system recognises and responds to. Antibodies are proteins produced in response to a specific antigen. The response is specific because each antibody has a binding site that fits one antigen, so it targets that antigen rather than all pathogens. (4 marks)
  6. Describe the different roles of B cells and T cells in the specific immune response. Answer: B cells are involved in the humoral response and produce antibodies that act in body fluids to mark or neutralise pathogens. T cells are involved in the cell-mediated response and help control and coordinate the immune response, and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells. Both are lymphocytes but with different roles. (4 marks)
  7. Explain the difference between the primary and secondary immune responses and link this to the role of memory cells. Answer: The primary response is slower to develop after first exposure because the specific lymphocytes must be activated and expanded. The secondary response is faster and stronger after later exposure, because memory cells from the first exposure are already present and can respond quickly. (4 marks)
  8. Describe how vaccination works and explain the idea of herd immunity. Answer: Vaccination exposes the immune system to an antigen without causing the disease, so that memory cells are produced and the body can respond faster on real exposure. Herd immunity occurs when a high enough proportion of the population is immune, reducing the spread of the pathogen so that even people who are not immune are less likely to be exposed. (4 marks)
  9. Describe monoclonal antibodies and give two uses of them. Answer: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies specific to one antigen, produced from clones of a single antibody-producing cell. Uses include diagnosis, such as detecting a specific antigen; research, such as tracking or isolating a molecule; and therapy, such as targeting cells that carry a particular antigen. (4 marks)
  10. Explain what epidemiology is and why it is useful in the study of infectious disease. Answer: Epidemiology is the study of the patterns, causes and control of disease in populations. It is useful because it looks at who is affected, where, when and at what rate, helps identify risk factors and causes, and informs control measures such as vaccination or public-health interventions. (4 marks)
  11. Describe forensic biology and explain how DNA profiling can be used in an investigation. Answer: Forensic biology uses biological evidence such as DNA to help identify individuals and to link evidence to people, objects or scenes. DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA from different samples; a match can identify a person or link a sample to a scene, while a mismatch can exclude a person, and the result is interpreted in context rather than taken as a simple yes/no answer on its own. (5 marks)
  12. Explain two reasons why biological evidence such as blood must be handled carefully in a forensic context. Answer: Biological evidence must be handled carefully because of the risk of contamination, which can compromise the reliability of the result, and because the interpretation of the evidence depends on the context, the quality of the sample and the way it was collected and preserved, so that a result is meaningful only if the process has been reliable and the evidence is relevant to the question being asked. (4 marks)
  13. Describe how phagocytosis works and state whether it is a specific or non-specific defence. Answer: Phagocytosis is a non-specific defence in which a phagocyte engulfs a pathogen into a phagosome, which then fuses with a lysosome containing enzymes and other chemicals that destroy the pathogen. It is non-specific because it acts against a broad range of pathogens rather than targeting one particular antigen. (4 marks)
  14. Explain the role of the lymphatic system in immunity. Answer: The lymphatic system returns tissue fluid to the blood and provides sites for immune responses, such as the lymph nodes, where immune cells can encounter antigens and where immune responses can be started and organised. (3 marks)
  15. Describe what is meant by immunological memory and why it is important. Answer: Immunological memory is the ability of the immune system to respond faster and more strongly to an antigen it has met before, because memory cells from the first exposure are already present. It is important because it makes the secondary response quicker and stronger than the primary response, which is the basis of vaccination and long-term protection. (4 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one example, one mechanism and one reason. Practise the bacteria-versus-virus distinction, the aseptic technique and growth-curve ideas, the first-line defences and phagocytosis, the antigen-antibody and B-cell and T-cell distinctions, the primary and secondary responses and memory cells, the vaccination and herd immunity reasoning, the monoclonal antibody uses, and the forensic biology and DNA profiling reasoning with its care and limits. Check that you can say what each thing is, how it works and why it matters, not just what it is called. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.
content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note covers the A2 biology topic that links microorganisms, the immune response and the forensic use of biology. It is written around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more statements the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the comparisons and worked ideas that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards, not just to re-read facts.

1. The point of the topic and what “microbiology” means here

In this topic, microbiology is the study of the small living things that are too small to see individually without magnification: bacteria, viruses and the other agents of infection, and some of the fungi and other microorganisms that are important as pathogens, as tools and as part of the normal biosphere. The focus of this topic is not a general survey of all microbes, but the ones that matter for disease, immunity and the forensic use of biological evidence. That means the biology here has three strands: what the pathogens are, how the body defends itself against them, and how biological evidence is used in the service of identification and interpretation. If you can keep those three strands in view, the topic is easier to remember, because you are not memorising three unrelated lists.

A good answer sees the topic as one connected system: a pathogen is a microorganism with the ability to cause disease; the body has barriers and specific defences; and the forensic use of biology depends on the same kind of reasoning that the rest of biology uses, namely that evidence is interpreted rather than just collected. If you treat the topic as a bag of facts, you lose the logic that makes it answerable in an exam. If you treat it as a set of connected ideas, you can answer questions that cross the strands, which is where many of the marks sit.

2. Bacteria as living cells and as pathogens

Bacteria are living cells with a cell wall, cytoplasm, ribosomes and genetic material, but they are much smaller and simpler than plant or animal cells, and they may have extra features such as a capsule, flagella or plasmids. Some are harmless or even useful; some are pathogens that cause disease by damaging tissues directly, by producing toxins, or by triggering responses that themselves cause harm. A good answer says that bacteria are cells with cell walls, cytoplasm and ribosomes, that they may have capsules, flagella or plasmids, that they reproduce by binary fission, and that pathogenic bacteria cause disease because they damage tissues, release toxins or provoke harmful responses. It does not say that all bacteria are pathogens, because they are not, and it does not say that bacteria cause disease only by one route, because there is more than one way a bacterium can harm the host.

The distinction between infection and disease is also worth keeping clear. Infection means the microorganism is present and multiplying; disease is the harm that results. A person can be infected without being obviously diseased, and a person can be diseased without the term “infection” meaning the same thing in every context. If you can make that distinction, you avoid the sloppy language that loses marks when the question is precise. The capsule, flagella and plasmids are also useful ideas because they are examples of bacterial features that affect how pathogenic a bacterium can be, how it spreads and how it can be identified. If you can name them and say what they do, you are answering at the right level.

3. Viruses as non-cellular agents and why they are not “alive” in the same sense

Viruses are not cells. They have genetic material, DNA or RNA, inside a protein coat, and some have an outer envelope, but they have no cytoplasm, no ribosomes and no independent metabolism. Because of that, they cannot reproduce by themselves; they must get inside a host cell and use the host’s machinery to make new virus particles. That is why viruses are often described as non-living in the usual biological sense, even though they are a major cause of disease and a major part of this topic. A good answer says that a virus is a small particle with genetic material surrounded by a protein coat, that some have an envelope, that viruses lack the machinery to reproduce independently and must use a host cell, and that this is why they are not treated as living cells in the normal sense. It does not say that a virus is a very small bacterium, because it is not, and it does not say that viruses can reproduce on their own outside a host, because they cannot.

The host-cell dependence is the central idea, because it explains both why viruses cause disease and why some antiviral strategies work by targeting the interaction with the host cell rather than the virus as if it were a cell itself. A good answer says that viruses depend on host cells to replicate, and that the damage they cause is often a consequence of how they use or damage host cells. It does not need to describe every step of every viral life cycle to answer at the right level, but it should say that the virus is not a cell and that it cannot replicate independently. If you keep that distinction clear, you can answer the questions without confusing bacteria and viruses, which is one of the most common mark-losers in this topic.

4. Culturing microorganisms safely and why aseptic technique matters

Microorganisms can be cultured under controlled conditions, but culturing carries a risk of contamination and of growing unwanted or harmful microbes, so aseptic technique matters. Aseptic technique means working in a way that minimises the chance of unwanted microbes entering the culture or the workspace, and of the culture leaving the workspace where it could cause harm. A good answer says that microorganisms are cultured on media such as agar, that aseptic technique is used to prevent contamination of the culture and to prevent the cultured microbes from contaminating the environment and people, and that the aim is to keep the culture pure and to keep the process safe. It does not say that aseptic technique is only about being tidy, because it is specifically about controlling the movement of microbes.

The safety point is important because microbiology is done with living organisms that can multiply quickly. A good answer therefore includes the idea that cultures are handled with care, that equipment is sterilised where needed, that the culture is contained, and that waste is disposed of safely. If the question asks for safety precautions, these are the kinds of idea to include: sterilisation of equipment, containment of the culture, and safe disposal. If the question asks why aseptic technique is used, say both that it protects the culture from contamination and that it protects the environment and people from the culture. If you can say that, you have the safety and purity point both correct.

5. Growth curves and the idea that a culture changes over time

A microbial culture does not stay static; it goes through phases as the organisms grow, use resources and respond to the environment. A typical growth curve includes a lag phase, an exponential or log phase, a stationary phase and a decline or death phase. The pattern exists because growth depends on resources, waste accumulation, space and the conditions in the medium. A good answer says that microbial growth is not constant, that the culture passes through phases including lag, exponential, stationary and decline, and that the phases reflect the conditions in the culture and the limits on growth. It does not say that growth is a steady increase forever, because it is not, and it does not say that the phases are the same in every culture without qualification, because the shape depends on the organism and the conditions. If you can say that, you have the growth idea in a form that scores marks.

The exponential phase is the one where the population is increasing as fast as the conditions allow, and it is often the phase of interest in practicals and in questions about growth rate. The lag phase is where the organisms are adapting to the new conditions; the stationary phase is where growth is balanced by death; and the decline phase is where death exceeds growth. A good answer can describe those in general terms without needing to give exact timings, because the point is the pattern and the reasons for it. If you can describe the pattern and say why it occurs, you have the answer the examiners are after.

6. Factors that affect microbial growth

Microbial growth depends on environmental factors such as temperature, pH, water availability, oxygen, nutrients and inhibitory substances. Which factors matter most depends on the organism, so a thermophile and a mesophile have different temperature ranges, and an aerobe and an anaerobe have different oxygen requirements. A good answer says that growth depends on factors such as temperature, pH, water, oxygen, nutrients and inhibitors, and that the optimum and range depend on the organism. It does not say that all microbes have the same requirements, because they do not, and it does not say that only one factor matters at a time, because in practice several factors interact. If you can say that, you have the microbial growth idea in a form that scores marks.

The conceptual point is that growth rate is controlled by the environment, and that the environment includes more than just the presence of food. If a question asks why a culture grows faster or slower, the answer should consider the relevant factors and why they change the outcome, rather than just saying “the conditions were better” without explanation. That is the kind of reasoning the specification expects. If you can give the factors and the direction of their effect, you have a better answer than a vague label.

7. The first line of defence: barriers and non-specific responses

The body’s first defence against pathogens is a set of barriers and non-specific responses. The skin is a physical barrier; mucous membranes, tears, saliva and stomach acid help block or destroy microbes; inflammation is a non-specific response that brings blood and immune cells to the site of infection or damage; and phagocytosis is a non-specific process in which cells such as phagocytes engulf and destroy pathogens. A good answer says that the first defences include physical and chemical barriers, inflammation and phagocytosis, and that these are non-specific because they act against a broad range of pathogens rather than one particular type. It does not say that the first line of defence is always enough, because it is not, and it does not treat non-specific defence as the same thing as specific immunity, because it is not. If you can say that, you have the first-line idea in a form that scores marks.

Phagocytosis is worth describing with a little structure: the phagocyte engulfs the pathogen into a phagosome, which fuses with a lysosome where enzymes and other chemicals destroy the pathogen. A good answer says that the pathogen is engulfed, enclosed in a vesicle, and destroyed by enzymes and other contents of the lysosome. It does not say that phagocytosis is a specific response, because it is not; it is non-specific, although it is part of the broader immune response. If you can describe the process and the role of the lysosome, you have the answer at the right level.

Inflammation is also part of the immediate response. It is the local reaction to injury or infection, bringing more blood, phagocytes and other responses to the area, and producing the classic signs such as redness, heat and swelling. A good answer says that inflammation is a non-specific response that increases blood flow and brings phagocytes and other defences to the site, and that it helps contain and clear the problem. It does not say that inflammation is the same thing as infection, or that it only happens when bacteria are present, because it can happen after injury as well. If you can say that, you have the inflammation idea in a form that scores marks.

8. Antigens, antibodies and the idea of specific recognition

Specific immunity depends on the recognition of antigens, which are substances, usually proteins or other molecules on the surface of pathogens or on other cells, that the immune system can recognise and respond to. In response to an antigen, the body produces antibodies, proteins that bind to that antigen and help neutralise, mark or remove the pathogen. The important point is that the response is specific: an antibody is made for a particular antigen, and this is what makes the adaptive immune system different from the non-specific first lines of defence. A good answer says that antigens are molecules that the immune system recognises, that antibodies are proteins produced in response to a specific antigen, and that the response is specific because it targets a particular antigen rather than all pathogens. It does not say that antibodies kill pathogens directly in every case, because they work in different ways, and it does not say that antigens are only on pathogens, because they can be on other cells too. If you can say that, you have the antigen-antibody idea in a form that scores marks.

The structure of an antibody matters because it explains why it can be specific. An antibody has a constant region and variable regions that form the antigen-binding site, and the shape of the binding site is what makes the antibody specific to one antigen. A good answer says that an antibody has a constant region and variable binding regions, and that the binding site is specific to one antigen. It does not say that the antibody is a generic killer regardless of shape, because its specificity is the point. If you can describe the structure in terms of constant and variable regions and say why that matters for specificity, you have the answer at the right level.

9. B cells, T cells and the difference between the two kinds of specific response

Specific immunity involves lymphocytes, especially B cells and T cells, which respond to antigens but in different ways. B cells are involved in the humoral response, producing antibodies that act in body fluids and help mark or neutralise pathogens. T cells are involved in the cell-mediated response and in helping coordinate the response, and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells. A good answer says that B cells are associated with antibody production and the humoral response, that T cells are associated with cell-mediated responses and with helping and controlling the immune response, and that both are lymphocytes but with different roles. It does not say that B cells and T cells do exactly the same thing, because they do not, and it does not say that the two systems are unrelated, because they work together. If you can say that, you have the B-cell and T-cell idea in a form that scores marks.

The distinction is important because it is a standard exam point. B cells are the antibody-making arm; T cells are the cell-mediated and helper arm. A good answer can also say that the response includes memory cells, which allow a faster response on later exposure. If you can separate the roles and still see that the response is integrated, you have the immune system in a form that scores marks. If you blur B and T cells into a single “immune cell” idea, you lose the marks that depend on the distinction.

10. Primary and secondary immune responses and why memory matters

On first exposure to an antigen, the primary immune response is slower to develop, because the specific B and T cells have to be activated and expanded. On later exposure, the secondary immune response is faster and stronger, because memory cells from the first exposure are already present and ready. This is the basis of immunological memory and of vaccination. A good answer says that the primary response is slower to develop, that the secondary response is faster and stronger, that memory cells are responsible for the difference, and that this is why vaccination works by exposing the immune system to an antigen without causing the disease. It does not say that the immune system “remembers” in a vague sense without saying what the memory cells do, because the memory cell is the point. If you can say that, you have the primary and secondary response idea in a form that scores marks.

The comparison is worth making explicitly: primary response is slower and smaller, secondary response is faster and larger. A good answer can say that and then explain that the memory cells from the first exposure allow a quicker and larger response the next time. If the question asks about vaccination, the answer should link the idea to exposure to the antigen without disease, so that the immune system is primed without the person having to suffer the infection first. If you can make that link, you have answered the question at the right level.

11. The lymphatic system and why it matters in immunity

The lymphatic system helps the immune system work by draining fluid from tissues, returning it to the blood, and providing sites where immune cells can meet antigens and where immune responses can be organised, such as the lymph nodes. A good answer says that the lymphatic system returns tissue fluid to the blood and provides sites for immune responses, including the lymph nodes where immune cells can encounter antigens. It does not say that the lymphatic system is the same as the blood circulation, because it is not; it is a related but distinct system that returns fluid and is involved in immunity. If you can say that, you have the lymphatic system idea in a form that scores marks.

The immune cell trafficking point is also useful: lymphocytes and other immune cells move through lymph and blood and meet antigens in lymph nodes and other tissues. A good answer can say that the lymph nodes are places where antigens are encountered and immune responses are started. It does not need to describe every detail of lymphatic anatomy to answer at the right level, but it should recognise the role of the lymphatic system in returning fluid and in providing immune sites. If you can do that, you have the answer at the right level.

12. Vaccination, herd immunity and the reasoning behind it

Vaccination works by priming the immune system against a pathogen without causing the disease, so that memory cells are produced and the body can respond faster and more strongly on real exposure. Herd immunity happens when enough people are immune that the pathogen has difficulty spreading through the population, so that even people who are not immune are less likely to be exposed. A good answer says that vaccination exposes the immune system to an antigen without causing disease, producing memory cells, and that herd immunity arises when a high enough proportion of the population is immune to reduce transmission. It does not say that vaccination makes everyone completely invulnerable, because it does not, and it does not say that herd immunity works by making every individual immune, because it does not; it works by reducing the spread through the population. If you can say that, you have the vaccination and herd immunity idea in a form that scores marks.

The practical and ethical reasoning around vaccination is often part of the topic. A good answer can say that vaccination protects the individual and, at high enough coverage, the population, but that there are issues around coverage, exemptions, side effects and public acceptance, and that the balance matters. If the question asks for evaluation, mention both the benefits and the issues, and say that the importance of coverage is why public health programmes focus on it. If you can do that, you have the evaluation in the right form rather than a one-sided answer.

13. Monoclonal antibodies and how they are made and used

Monoclonal antibodies are antibodies that are identical and specific to one antigen, made from clones of a single antibody-producing cell. They are useful because they can be produced in quantity and directed against a specific antigen, so they can be used in diagnosis, research and therapy. A good answer says that monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies specific to one antigen, that they are produced from clones of a single cell, and that they are useful in diagnosis, research and therapy because they can be directed against a specific antigen and produced in quantity. It does not say that monoclonal antibodies are produced by the natural immune response of one person in the usual sense, because they are cloned from a single hybridoma or equivalent line, and it does not say that they are always therapeutic, because they are also diagnostic and research tools. If you can say that, you have the monoclonal antibody idea in a form that scores marks.

The usefulness comes from specificity and scale. A good answer can say that because each monoclonal antibody is specific to one antigen, it can be used to detect that antigen or target cells carrying it, and because it can be made in large amounts, it can be used practically. If the question asks for uses, mention diagnosis, research and therapy, and give a little detail for each rather than just listing the words. If you can do that, you have the monoclonal antibody answer at the right level.

14. Epidemiology and the study of disease patterns

Epidemiology is the study of the patterns, causes and control of disease in populations. It is the way we move from individual cases to understanding how a disease spreads, who is at risk and what can be done about it. A good answer says that epidemiology studies the occurrence and patterns of disease in populations, that it is used to identify causes and risk factors, and that it informs control measures. It does not say that epidemiology is only about counting cases, because it also looks at causes and control, and it does not say that epidemiology proves causation in every case by itself, because it often points to associations that then need explanation. If you can say that, you have the epidemiology idea in a form that scores marks.

The population view is the important one, because epidemiology is not the same as the clinical study of one patient. A good answer can say that epidemiology looks at groups and patterns, such as who is affected, where, when and at what rate, and that this helps identify risk factors and guide public-health action. If you can make that population-level reasoning clear, you can answer epidemiology questions better than by just saying “it is the study of disease in populations” without saying what that actually involves.

15. Forensic biology: what it is and what it depends on

Forensic biology is the use of biological evidence in the service of investigation and identification. It includes things such as DNA profiling, the analysis of blood and other bodily fluids, and the use of biological material to link people to places, objects or other people. A good answer says that forensic biology uses biological evidence such as DNA to help identify individuals and to link evidence to people or scenes, and that the evidence is interpreted rather than taken as a simple yes/no answer on its own. It does not say that biological evidence is proof in a magic sense, because it is evidence to be interpreted in context, and it does not confuse the collection of evidence with its interpretation. If you can say that, you have the forensic biology idea in a form that scores marks.

The forensic use of biology depends on the same scientific reasoning as the rest of biology: the evidence has to be collected, preserved and interpreted in a way that is reliable and relevant to the question being asked. A good answer can say that contamination, chain of custody and context matter, because those are things that can affect the meaning of the evidence. If you can mention those without overclaiming, you have the forensic reasoning at the right level.

16. DNA profiling and the logic behind it

DNA profiling, also called DNA fingerprinting, is a technique that uses the variation in certain regions of DNA to distinguish individuals. The basic idea is that samples from a person, a crime scene or a paternity case can be compared and matched or excluded based on the pattern of DNA variants. A good answer says that DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA from different samples and can be used to identify individuals, exclude suspects, or establish biological relationships, and that the result depends on the match between the patterns. It does not say that DNA profiling identifies someone with absolute certainty in every sense without context, because the interpretation depends on the quality of the sample and the comparison, and it does not say that DNA profiling is the same thing as sequencing the whole genome for every purpose, because profiling is about the informative regions and the pattern they give. If you can say that, you have the DNA profiling idea in a form that scores marks.

The technical basis is also worth a little detail: profiling is possible because there is variation between individuals in certain DNA regions, and those differences can be detected and compared. If the question asks about the principle, say that the method compares DNA patterns and that the differences between individuals are what make identification possible. If the question asks about uses, mention identification, exclusion and paternity or relationship testing. If you can do both, you have a stronger answer than one that just says “DNA fingerprinting identifies people”.

17. Blood and other bodily-fluids evidence, and the need for care

Blood and other bodily fluids can be evidence, but they are also a source of contamination and a source of interpretation problems if they are not handled properly. A good answer says that evidence such as blood, saliva, hair with follicles and other biological material can be used in forensic biology, but that it has to be collected and preserved properly, and that contamination must be avoided. It does not say that any trace of blood is automatically proof of guilt or innocence, because it is evidence to be interpreted, and it does not say that the mere presence of a substance is the same as a meaningful match, because it is not. If you can say that, you have the bodily-fluid evidence idea in a form that scores marks.

The practical point is that forensic biology is as much about reliability as about possibility. A good answer can say that the value of the evidence depends on how it was collected, whether it was contaminated, and whether the interpretation matches the question. If you can mention those points, you have the forensic reasoning rather than a simple list of evidence types. That is the kind of answer examiners like, because it shows understanding of the limits of the evidence, not just the fact that it exists.

18. How the three strands fit together: microbes, immunity and forensics

The topic is really about three related ways of thinking about small-scale biology. Microbiology gives you the pathogens and the way they grow and spread. Immunity gives you the defence system that fights them, from barriers and phagocytosis through antibodies and memory. Forensics gives you the use of biological evidence, especially DNA, to identify and link. If you see the topic as one connected picture, you can answer the questions that ask for the links, such as why memory matters, why aseptic technique matters, why herd immunity matters, or why DNA profiling is both powerful and limited. If you treat the three strands as separate lists, you lose the reasoning that makes them answerable.

A good answer can move between the strands when needed: the same idea of recognition that explains antibodies also explains why DNA profiling can compare patterns, and the same idea of contamination that matters in microbiology culturing also matters in forensic evidence. The ability to move between the strands is what the higher marks are often about. If you can do that, you are working at the level the specification is aiming for, rather than just recalling a list of facts.

19. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use this note by working through each section and checking that you can describe bacteria and viruses and explain how they differ; describe aseptic technique and why it is used; describe microbial growth and the factors that affect it; describe the first line of defence including barriers, inflammation and phagocytosis; describe antigens, antibodies and the specificity of the antibody response; describe B cells and T cells and the difference between them; describe the primary and secondary immune responses and the role of memory cells; describe vaccination and herd immunity; describe monoclonal antibodies and their uses; describe epidemiology and what it studies; and describe forensic biology, DNA profiling and the care needed with biological evidence. After this topic, revise the related systems and the practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

The note is long because the topic is broad and the specification asks for the biology of microbes, the biology of defence and the biology of forensic evidence in enough detail to be useful. A revision note has to cover the pathogens, the immune system and the forensic application in enough detail, and it has to link them, because the exam questions do. Study it section by section, check yourself against the specification statements, and practise the kinds of answer that explain rather than list. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying all bacteria are pathogens, or saying bacteria and viruses are the same kind of thing.
  • Saying viruses are cells or that they can reproduce independently outside a host.
  • Saying aseptic technique is only about tidiness, rather than about preventing contamination of the culture and protecting people and the environment.
  • Saying microbial growth is a steady increase forever, instead of passing through phases.
  • Saying the first line of defence is always enough, or treating non-specific defence as if it were specific immunity.
  • Saying antibodies kill pathogens in exactly the same way in every case, without recognising that they mark, neutralise and help remove them in different ways.
  • Saying antigens are only on pathogens, instead of being molecules that can be recognised on pathogens and other cells.
  • Blurring B cells and T cells into “immune cells” without distinguishing the antibody-producing and cell-mediated roles.
  • Saying the immune system “remembers” without mentioning memory cells, or saying the secondary response is identical to the primary response.
  • Saying herd immunity means every individual is immune, rather than meaning the spread through the population is reduced.
  • Saying monoclonal antibodies are just any antibodies from one person, rather than identical antibodies from a single cloned line specific to one antigen.
  • Saying epidemiology is only counting cases, without mentioning patterns, causes and control.
  • Saying DNA profiling is proof in a magic sense, without recognising interpretation, sample quality and context.
  • Saying that the mere presence of blood or another fluid is automatically proof of guilt or innocence.
  • Confusing the collection of forensic evidence with its interpretation or reliability.
  • Forgetting that contamination matters in both microbiology and forensic biology, for different but related reasons.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe two differences between bacteria and viruses in structure and one difference in the way they reproduce. Answer: Bacteria are cells with a cell wall, cytoplasm and ribosomes and may have capsules, flagella and plasmids; viruses are not cells and have genetic material inside a protein coat, with some having an envelope. Difference in reproduction: bacteria reproduce independently by binary fission, whereas viruses cannot reproduce on their own and must use a host cell to replicate. (3 marks)
  2. Explain why aseptic technique is used when culturing microorganisms and name two precautions that would be part of it. Answer: Aseptic technique is used to prevent contamination of the culture by unwanted microbes and to prevent the cultured microbes from contaminating the environment and people. Precautions include sterilising equipment, working near a flame or in a sterile field, sealing or covering the culture and disposing of it safely. (4 marks)
  3. Describe the phases of a typical microbial growth curve and explain why the curve is not a steady increase. Answer: A typical growth curve includes a lag phase, an exponential phase, a stationary phase and a decline phase. Growth is not a steady increase forever because it depends on factors such as nutrients, space, waste accumulation and the conditions in the culture; as resources become limited and waste builds up, growth slows, stops and may decline. (4 marks)
  4. Describe the non-specific first line of defence against pathogens and give one example of such a defence. Answer: The first line of defence includes physical and chemical barriers such as skin, mucous membranes, tears, saliva and stomach acid, together with non-specific responses such as inflammation and phagocytosis. Example: phagocytes engulf pathogens into a phagosome, which fuses with a lysosome where enzymes and other chemicals destroy the pathogen. (4 marks)
  5. Explain the difference between antigens and antibodies and why the antibody response is described as specific. Answer: Antigens are molecules, often on the surface of pathogens or other cells, that the immune system recognises and responds to. Antibodies are proteins produced in response to a specific antigen. The response is specific because each antibody has a binding site that fits one antigen, so it targets that antigen rather than all pathogens. (4 marks)
  6. Describe the different roles of B cells and T cells in the specific immune response. Answer: B cells are involved in the humoral response and produce antibodies that act in body fluids to mark or neutralise pathogens. T cells are involved in the cell-mediated response and help control and coordinate the immune response, and some T cells are important in dealing with infected cells. Both are lymphocytes but with different roles. (4 marks)
  7. Explain the difference between the primary and secondary immune responses and link this to the role of memory cells. Answer: The primary response is slower to develop after first exposure because the specific lymphocytes must be activated and expanded. The secondary response is faster and stronger after later exposure, because memory cells from the first exposure are already present and can respond quickly. (4 marks)
  8. Describe how vaccination works and explain the idea of herd immunity. Answer: Vaccination exposes the immune system to an antigen without causing the disease, so that memory cells are produced and the body can respond faster on real exposure. Herd immunity occurs when a high enough proportion of the population is immune, reducing the spread of the pathogen so that even people who are not immune are less likely to be exposed. (4 marks)
  9. Describe monoclonal antibodies and give two uses of them. Answer: Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies specific to one antigen, produced from clones of a single antibody-producing cell. Uses include diagnosis, such as detecting a specific antigen; research, such as tracking or isolating a molecule; and therapy, such as targeting cells that carry a particular antigen. (4 marks)
  10. Explain what epidemiology is and why it is useful in the study of infectious disease. Answer: Epidemiology is the study of the patterns, causes and control of disease in populations. It is useful because it looks at who is affected, where, when and at what rate, helps identify risk factors and causes, and informs control measures such as vaccination or public-health interventions. (4 marks)
  11. Describe forensic biology and explain how DNA profiling can be used in an investigation. Answer: Forensic biology uses biological evidence such as DNA to help identify individuals and to link evidence to people, objects or scenes. DNA profiling compares patterns of variation in DNA from different samples; a match can identify a person or link a sample to a scene, while a mismatch can exclude a person, and the result is interpreted in context rather than taken as a simple yes/no answer on its own. (5 marks)
  12. Explain two reasons why biological evidence such as blood must be handled carefully in a forensic context. Answer: Biological evidence must be handled carefully because of the risk of contamination, which can compromise the reliability of the result, and because the interpretation of the evidence depends on the context, the quality of the sample and the way it was collected and preserved, so that a result is meaningful only if the process has been reliable and the evidence is relevant to the question being asked. (4 marks)
  13. Describe how phagocytosis works and state whether it is a specific or non-specific defence. Answer: Phagocytosis is a non-specific defence in which a phagocyte engulfs a pathogen into a phagosome, which then fuses with a lysosome containing enzymes and other chemicals that destroy the pathogen. It is non-specific because it acts against a broad range of pathogens rather than targeting one particular antigen. (4 marks)
  14. Explain the role of the lymphatic system in immunity. Answer: The lymphatic system returns tissue fluid to the blood and provides sites for immune responses, such as the lymph nodes, where immune cells can encounter antigens and where immune responses can be started and organised. (3 marks)
  15. Describe what is meant by immunological memory and why it is important. Answer: Immunological memory is the ability of the immune system to respond faster and more strongly to an antigen it has met before, because memory cells from the first exposure are already present. It is important because it makes the secondary response quicker and stronger than the primary response, which is the basis of vaccination and long-term protection. (4 marks)

Revise this topic by matching each numbered specification point to one example, one mechanism and one reason. Practise the bacteria-versus-virus distinction, the aseptic technique and growth-curve ideas, the first-line defences and phagocytosis, the antigen-antibody and B-cell and T-cell distinctions, the primary and secondary responses and memory cells, the vaccination and herd immunity reasoning, the monoclonal antibody uses, and the forensic biology and DNA profiling reasoning with its care and limits. Check that you can say what each thing is, how it works and why it matters, not just what it is called. Then move on to the next topic and the related practicals, because the practicals are the way the specification ties the ideas to hands-on work.

title: Exam technique: Ratio, Rate and Proportion
content:
### What earns the marks
For sharing in a ratio, total parts and value of one part each earn a mark: write 5 parts = 600 before splitting. For scales and maps, the real-distance multiplication shown earns the method mark, with each unit conversion (cm to m to km) credited. For proportion with powers, the constant k found first earns the mark: write y = k x squared and solve for k.
### Traps
Error: dividing by 2 and 3 directly for a 2:3 split. Correction: parts first, always. Error: 1.40 hours for 1 h 40 min in speed questions. Correction: 40 min = 2/3 h. Error: linear scaling for an x-squared relation. Correction: square the ratio. Error: inverted map scale (dividing by 50000). Correction: real is bigger than map.
### Worked example
Share £120 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. The total parts are 12, so one part is £10 and the shares are £20, £30 and £70. Check: 20 + 30 + 70 = 120. For speed, 150 km in 2.5 hours gives 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h. Direct proportion means y = kx, so doubling x doubles y.
### Worked example
Share £120 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. The total parts are 12, so one part is £10 and the shares are £20, £30 and £70. Check: 20 + 30 + 70 = 120. For speed, 150 km in 2.5 hours gives 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h. Direct proportion means y = kx, so doubling x doubles y.

title: Statistics (S1) — Study Notes
content:
Statistics 1: data, sampling and correlation

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 1 (WST01), sat at AS.

S1 is about collecting, summarising and relating data. You must choose sensible models, compute summary statistics quickly, code data, spot outliers and fit a regression line.

Sampling

  • Random sample: every member of the population has equal chance of selection.
  • Systematic: every kth member. Stratified: split population into strata, sample each in proportion.
  • Bias must be avoided: random numbers, representative strata, no convenience sampling.

Averages

  • Mean: x-bar = (sum of x) / n. Sensitive to outliers.
  • Median: the middle value; for n values ordered, position (n + 1)/2. Robust to outliers.
  • Mode: the most frequent value.

Measuring spread

  • Range = largest - smallest.
  • Quartiles: Q1 is the median of the lower half, Q3 the median of the upper half; IQR = Q3 - Q1.
  • Variance = (sum of x^2)/n - (x-bar)^2, and SD = sqrt(variance).
  • The variance uses squared units; the SD returns to the original units.

Coding

For x = a + by: mean of x = a + b x-bar, SD of x = |b| SD of y. Coding never changes the correlation coefficient.

Outliers and box plots

An outlier lies below Q1 - 1.5 x IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR. Box plots show min, Q1, median, Q3, max (whiskers to the furthest non-outlier).

Correlation and regression

  • The product moment correlation coefficient r measures linear strength: -1 <= r <= 1.
  • r close to +1: strong positive linear; close to -1: strong negative; close to 0: no linear correlation. Correlation is not causation.
  • Regression line of y on x: y = a + bx with b = Sxy / Sxx and a = y-bar - b x-bar. Use it to interpolate, never extrapolate.

title: Exam technique: Sets
content:
### What earns the marks
For Venn problems, the union formula n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersect B) quoted earns the method mark; subtracting the intersection corrects the double count explicitly. For neither, the subtraction from the universal set shown earns the final mark. For notation, the complement symbol with the correct parent set earns precision marks.
### Traps
Error: adding all three Venn counts including the intersection. Correction: the overlap was counted twice, subtract once. Error: element confused with subset (2 vs {2}). Correction: only a set can be a subset. Error: empty set equated with {0}. Correction: {0} has one element; the empty set has none. Error: modal-style single numbers for grouped answers. Correction: classes are intervals.
### Worked example
In a group of 30 students, 18 play football, 12 play hockey and 5 play both. The number who play at least one sport is n(F ∪ H) = 18 + 12 − 5 = 25. The number who play neither is 30 − 25 = 5. Subtracting the overlap avoids counting those 5 students twice.

title: Plant Nutrition
content:
Plant Nutrition

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 6 (statements 6.1–6.2). The photosynthesis equation, limiting factors, uses of glucose, mineral requirements and leaf structure as adaptations.

6.1 Photosynthesis

  • Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, in the presence of light and chlorophyll. Balanced: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
  • Glucose is used for: respiration, making cellulose for cell walls, making starch for storage, making amino acids when combined with mineral ions, and making oils. Mineral ions needed include nitrate (for amino acids and proteins), magnesium (for chlorophyll) and phosphate.
  • A limiting factor is the variable in shortest supply — light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature — which caps the rate. Raising a limiting factor raises the rate until another factor becomes limiting.

6.2 Leaf structure

  • Upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll (packed with chloroplasts, at the top for maximum light), spongy mesophyll (large air spaces for gas exchange), lower epidermis with stomata (guard cells control opening), and veins carrying water in and sugars out.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Limiting factor analysis, applied to a graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity at two CO₂ levels: the curve rises then plateaus; the plateau is set by CO₂ concentration or temperature. When asked which factor limits at a point, name the variable that, if increased, would raise the rate — that is the operational definition examiners want.
  • Mineral deficiency reasoning, applied to a plant with yellowing young leaves in magnesium-deficient soil: magnesium is the central ion in chlorophyll, so without it chlorophyll cannot be made and chlorosis appears. Nitrate deficiency gives poor growth overall because amino acids, and therefore proteins, cannot be synthesised.
  • Adaptation reasoning, applied to why palisade cells are column-shaped and stacked: the shape packs the maximum chloroplasts near the light, and vertical orientation lets light penetrate. Tie each structural feature to its function explicitly — each pairing is its own mark.
  • Equation writing, applied to a word-symbol answer: include the balanced symbol equation with the condition above the arrow, light and chlorophyll. An unbalanced equation loses the mark even when the chemistry is right.

Common errors

  • Writing water as a product instead of a reactant in the photosynthesis equation.
  • Saying stomata open "to let carbon dioxide in" as a complete answer — guard cell turgor caused by potassium ion movement is the mechanism.
  • Confusing magnesium (chlorophyll) with nitrate (amino acids) when explaining deficiencies.

title: Reading for Information and Inference — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Reading for Information and Inference

English First Language (Cambridge) — IGCSE. Reading questions reward two different skills: finding information that is stated, and working out what is implied. Keep them apart when you plan an answer.

Key areas to revise

  • Scanning for key words
  • Building a strong inference
  • Common mistakes

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Narrative Writing — Study Notes
content:
A narrative needs a character who wants something, obstacles that stand in the way, and a sequence of events that builds to a change. Writing well is about controlling what the reader knows and when.

Structure

A common shape is: opening hook, rising tension, a turning point, a climax, and a resolution. You do not need every stage to be long, but each should be clear.

The opening

  • Begin in the middle of action or with a striking detail.
  • Establish the character and a hint of the problem early.
  • Avoid long backstory before anything happens.

Tension

Tension comes from withholding information and controlling pace. Delay the answer to a question, slow the moment before a discovery, and let small threats build.

Techniques

  • End a section on a question or a small reveal.
  • Use short sentences at moments of danger.
  • Let the character misjudge a situation, so the reader worries.

Dialogue

Dialogue should reveal character and move the plot forward. Each speaker should sound distinct, and the reader should learn something from each exchange. Use punctuation correctly and begin a new line for each speaker.

Point of view

First person gives direct access to one mind, using I. Third person can be close to one character or wider in view. Choose one viewpoint and keep it consistent.

Ending

A satisfying ending resolves or meaningfully changes the central conflict. It can be open, but it should feel earned, not abandoned.

title: Exam technique: Algebra — Equations
content:
### What earns the marks
For linear equations, clearing fractions first earns the method mark. For quadratics, the factorised pair checked by substitution earns both marks. For word problems, the defined unknown plus the formed equation earn one mark each.
### Traps
Error: dividing through by x in quadratics. Correction: factorise, or lose the zero root. Error: unsimplified surds left hanging. Correction: simplify fully for the accuracy mark. Error: negative roots kept for lengths. Correction: reject what the context forbids.
### Keep the equation balanced
Whatever you do to one side of an equation you must do to the other. Write each step on its own line with the operation named in words, such as "subtract 3 from both sides", because the method mark depends on showing the balancing.
### Fractions and brackets
Clear fractions first by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator, and expand brackets before you collect like terms. Leaving a fraction in the equation is the most common cause of a lost mark.
### Check by substitution
Put your answer back into the original equation. If the two sides do not agree, find the slip before you write the final answer.

title: Exam technique: Further Trigonometry
content:
### What earns the marks
For multiple solutions, the full period family (180-2x style use of all quadrants) earns both marks. For R-formulae, completing Rcos(x-a) earns the method mark and R and alpha earn one each. For trig proofs, each identity substitution earns stepwise credit.
### Traps
Error: one solution pair only. Correction: list all in the range. Error: degrees with radian-range answers. Correction: match the stated range. Error: sin(x+y) expanded as sin x + sin y. Correction: use the formula.
### Write the form before you solve
Express a cos θ + b sin θ as R cos(θ − α) or R sin(θ ± α) first. Then solve the simpler equation, which avoids the many-solution errors that come from squaring both sides.

### Find every solution in the interval
Use the principal value from the calculator, then use the symmetry of the graph to find the others. Check which quadrants the ratio is positive or negative in, and list every value in the given range.

### Use the identities deliberately
Replace sec, cosec and cot with their reciprocals, or use the Pythagorean identities to change the form of an equation so it can be solved.

title: Permutations and Combinations — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Permutations and Combinations

Mathematics — A2. If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Key areas to revise

  • The Multiplication Principle
  • Permutations — Order Matters
  • Combinations — Order Irrelevant
  • Restricted Permutations
  • Combinations with Constraints

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A permutation is an ordered arrangement, so nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!. A combination ignores order, so nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!). Five people in a line can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people gives 8C3 = 56, while choosing a ranked top 2 from 5 gives 5P2 = 20. ### Worked example A permutation is an ordered arrangement, so nPr = n! ÷ (n − r)!. A combination ignores order, so nCr = n! ÷ (r!(n − r)!). Five people in a line can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people gives 8C3 = 56, while choosing a ranked top 2 from 5 gives 5P2 = 20.

title: Exam technique: Work Energy and Power
content:
### What earns the marks
For work, force times distance along the force earns both marks. For energy, mgh and half m v squared quoted earn one mark each. For efficiency, useful over total earns the method mark with waste named.
### Traps
Error: g taken as 10 without comment at AS. Correction: use 9.81 for energy work. Error: efficiency above 100 percent. Correction: impossible; check the ratio. Error: power and energy units swapped. Correction: watts are joules per second.
### Calculate work from the component of the force
Work done = F s cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. Draw the angle on the diagram, because many marks are lost by using the wrong angle.

### Track the energy transfers
Write the energy before and after as kinetic, gravitational potential or elastic potential, and include the wasted energy. The total energy in must equal the total energy out.

### Use efficiency with the correct ratio
Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, and it is always less than 1. Give your answer as a fraction or a percentage, and state the unit you used.

title: Poisson Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Poisson Distribution

Mathematics — A2. X ~ Po(λ) counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently, at a constant average rate λ, and never twice at the same instant. Classic settings: calls per hour at a helpdesk, typos per page, cars per minute at a quiet junction.

Key areas to revise

  • The Model
  • The Formula
  • Mean and Variance
  • Scaling the Interval
  • Adding Poissons

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

If X ~ Po(λ), then P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ / r!. The mean and the variance are both equal to λ. A Poisson model needs events that occur singly, at a constant average rate, independently of one another in a fixed interval.

If X ~ Po(λ) and Y ~ Po(μ) are independent, then X + Y ~ Po(λ + μ). When the time or length interval changes, scale λ to match: a rate of 3 per minute gives λ = 15 for five minutes. Use cumulative tables for P(X ≤ r), and remember that P(X ≥ r) = 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1).

title: Vectors — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Vectors

Mathematics — A2 (9709). A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Key areas to revise

  • Components and Arithmetic
  • Position and Direction
  • Scalar (Dot) Product
  • Angle Between Vectors
  • Lines and Points

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

The scalar product of two vectors is a · b = |a||b| cos θ, and in component form a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃. Use it to find the angle between two vectors, and note that two vectors are perpendicular when their scalar product is zero.

A line can be written in the vector form r = a + λb, where a is a point on the line and b is its direction. To find where two lines meet, equate the components and solve the resulting simultaneous equations for the two parameters. Check that the lines are not parallel before you conclude that they intersect.

title: Motion in a Circle and Gravity — Study Notes
content:
Motion in a circle and gravity

Edexcel International A Level Physics, A2: circular motion in Unit 4 (WPH14) and gravitational fields in Unit 5 (WPH15).

Circular motion

  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed has a centripetal acceleration of v²/r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = mω²r, and it is provided by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity. It does no work on the body, because it is always perpendicular to the velocity.

Gravitational field

The gravitational field strength at a point is the force per unit mass placed at that point: g = F/m. Unit: N kg⁻¹. Field lines point towards the mass that creates the field.

Newton's law of gravitation

F = GMm/r², where r is measured from the centre of each point mass. Doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter.

Gravitational field of a point mass

g = GM/r². Outside a uniform sphere, its field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

Gravitational potential

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative, is zero at infinity, and becomes more negative closer to the mass: V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m is Ep = mV.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object moves in a circle of radius 0.50 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹. The centripetal force is F = mv²/r = (2.0 × 3.0²) ÷ 0.50 = 36 N.

Exam tips: use r as the distance from the centre, not the surface. State that gravitational potential is negative and rises to zero at infinity. Field strength and potential are different quantities: do not mix their units.

Gravitational potential and escape velocity

Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point, so φ = -GM/r. Potential is negative because work must be done against gravity to remove a mass to infinity. The change in gravitational potential energy between two radii is GMm(1/r1 - 1/r2). A body escapes a planet when its kinetic energy equals the potential energy needed to reach infinity, which gives the escape speed v = √(2GM/r).

Exam tip: use the zero of potential at infinity, and keep the sign of the potential negative in every calculation.

Worked example: orbital speed and period

A satellite of mass m orbits a planet of mass M at radius r. Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r). The orbital period follows from T = 2πr/v, which gives T² = (4π²/GM) r³. This is Kepler's third law in the form used at AS level.

Example: a satellite at radius 7.0 × 10⁶ m around a planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. The speed is v = √((6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.0 × 10²⁴)/(7.0 × 10⁶)) = √(5.7 × 10⁷) ≈ 7.6 × 10³ m s⁻¹. The period is T = 2π × 7.0 × 10⁶ / 7.6 × 10³ ≈ 5.8 × 10³ s, about 97 minutes.

Geostationary orbit

A geostationary satellite has a period of exactly 24 hours and orbits in the equatorial plane.
