Its radius is fixed by the period, so every geostationary satellite has the same radius and speed, regardless of its mass. Its orbit must lie above the equator, which is why communication satellites sit over one point on the ground.

Why orbiting bodies are weightless

Astronauts in orbit are not outside the pull of gravity; gravity supplies their centripetal acceleration. The spacecraft and its occupants fall freely together, so there is no contact force, and the apparent weightlessness follows from that free fall.

Circular motion: banked roads and conical pendulums

On a banked road with no friction, the horizontal component of the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force: N sin θ = mv²/r, while the vertical component balances weight: N cos θ = mg. Dividing gives tan θ = v²/(rg). The design speed depends only on the angle, the radius and g, not on the mass of the vehicle.

  • For a conical pendulum, tension has a vertical component that balances weight and a horizontal component that supplies the centripetal force.
  • Always draw a free-body diagram and resolve forces into components along the radius and the vertical before writing equations.
  • The centripetal force is not an extra force on the diagram; name the real forces that supply it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Including centripetal force as a separate force in the free-body diagram, which double-counts the force.
  • Using the planet's surface radius where the question gives the distance from the centre, or the reverse.
  • Stating that the satellite is stationary in orbit. It is moving at constant speed, so its velocity changes direction continuously and it is accelerating.

title: Transformations and Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Transformations and Vectors

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): reflection, rotation, translation, enlargement (incl. negative SF); vector notation, resultant, magnitude, vector geometry.

1. Transformations — full descriptions

  • Reflection: mirror line (x = 0, y = x, y = −x…).
  • Rotation: centre, angle, direction (anticlockwise positive).
  • Translation: column vector.
  • Enlargement: centre + scale factor; negative SF inverts through the centre.

"Enlargement, SF 2, centre (0, 3)" — every word earns a mark.

2. Combined transformations

Apply right-to-left: "reflect in y = x, then rotate 90°" — rotate the reflected image.

3. Vectors

  • Column vector (x; y); magnitude = √(x² + y²).
  • Resultant by component addition; parallel vectors are scalar multiples.
  • Position vectors: AB = OB − OA.

Example: A(1, 2), B(4, 6): AB = (3; 4), |AB| = 5.

4. Vector geometry

Midpoint of AB = ½(a + b). Prove collinearity: show AB = k·BC (shared point). Prove parallelogram: AB = DC. Use route paths: AC = AB + BC.

Exam tips: tracing paper is allowed for transformations; in proofs, end with a conclusion sentence ("hence A, B, C are collinear").

Translations

A translation moves every point the same distance in the same direction, described by a column vector (x; y): x units across (positive to the right) and y units up (positive upwards). The shape and orientation do not change.

Reflections, rotations and enlargements

A reflection is described by its mirror line, such as x = 2 or y = x. A rotation needs its centre, angle and direction. An enlargement needs its centre and scale factor; a negative scale factor inverts the image. Check the image by measuring its distance from the centre.

Vectors and magnitude

Write a column vector as (x; y). Its magnitude is √(x² + y²). Adding vectors adds the corresponding components, and multiplying by a scalar multiplies each component. The vector from A to B is found as the position vector of B minus the position vector of A.

Worked example: enlargement

Point P(3, 1) is enlarged by scale factor 2 with centre O(0, 0). Each coordinate is multiplied by 2, so P' = (6, 2). If the centre is (1, 1) instead, the vector from the centre to P is (2; 0), which becomes (4; 0) after the enlargement, so P' = (5, 1). Measure the distance from the centre to check the image.

Vectors as column vectors

  • Addition: (2; 1) + (−3; 5) = (−1; 6). Add the components in the same position.
  • Scalar multiple: 3 × (2; −1) = (6; −3). Multiply each component by the number.
  • Magnitude: |(3; 4)| = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.

Translation of a point

Translating A(1, 2) by the vector (4; −2) gives A' = (1 + 4, 2 − 2) = (5, 0). A translation has no centre and does not change the size or orientation of a shape.

Exam point: a transformation needs a full description. For a reflection give the mirror line; for a rotation give the centre, the angle and the direction; for an enlargement give the centre and the scale factor.

title: Pressure & Density — Study Notes
content:
Pressure & Density

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

1. Pressure basics

p = F/A (Pa = N/m²). Increase F or decrease A to raise pressure; explain applications (snowshoes, knives, hydraulic press).

2. Liquids

  • Pressure increases with depth: p = ρgh (Extended).
  • Same level, same liquid ⇒ same pressure (hydrostatic paradox).
  • Hydraulic systems transmit pressure — force multiplier: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.

3. Atmospheric pressure

~10⁵ Pa at sea level; demonstrated by collapsing can, mercury barometer 760 mmHg; decreases with altitude.

4. Density revisited

ρ = m/V; floating condition; upthrust = weight of displaced fluid (qualitative).

5. Gas pressure (particle model)

Particles collide with walls → force per area. Volume ↓ at same T ⇒ pressure ↑ (more frequent collisions). Temperature ↑ ⇒ faster particles ⇒ more frequent, harder impacts.

Density in more depth

Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg/m³, and 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. An object of a given density will float in a fluid only if the fluid has a higher density. To find the density of an irregular solid, measure its mass on a balance and its volume by displacement of water in a measuring cylinder.

Pressure and depth

Pressure is force per unit area, p = F/A, with unit the pascal (Pa = N/m²). In a liquid, the pressure increases with depth, p = hρg, and acts equally in all directions at a given depth. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

Exam tip: convert the area to m² before you calculate pressure, and use the density in kg/m³ in p = hρg.

Worked method for pressure questions

Step 1: write down the force in newtons and the area in m². Step 2: divide, p = F/A. Step 3: if the question is about a liquid, use p = hρg with h in metres, ρ in kg/m³ and g = 10 N/kg, and remember that the pressure is the same at equal depths in the same liquid. Atmospheric pressure is added to the liquid pressure when a question asks for total pressure at depth.

Worked example: pressure from a force

A force of 600 N acts on an area of 0.04 m². The pressure is p = F ÷ A = 600 ÷ 0.04 = 15 000 Pa, which is 15 kPa. Check the units first: the area must be in m² for the answer to be in pascals.

Pressure in a liquid

The pressure at depth in a liquid is p = h × ρ × g, where h is the depth in metres, ρ the density in kg/m³ and g the gravitational field strength (about 10 N/kg). For water of depth 2.5 m, p = 2.5 × 1000 × 10 = 25 000 Pa. The pressure depends on depth and density only, not on the shape of the container or the area of the base.

Density

Density is mass divided by volume, ρ = m ÷ V. A block of mass 540 g and volume 200 cm³ has density 540 ÷ 200 = 2.7 g/cm³. Convert to kg/m³ by multiplying by 1000, giving 2700 kg/m³, because 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Objects with a density greater than the fluid sink, and objects with a lower density float.

Exam point: state the formula, substitute the values with their units, and give the answer with the correct unit.

title: Numerical Methods — Study Notes
content:
Numerical methods

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 3 (WMA13), sat at A2.

When an equation cannot be solved algebraically, numerical methods locate roots to required accuracy. You must know three families: change of sign, fixed-point iteration and Newton-Raphson.

Change of sign (decimal search)

If f is continuous and f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, there is a root in (a, b). Bisection repeatedly halves the interval; a decimal search tests x = 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, ... until the sign changes. The method fails for repeated roots (the graph touches the axis without crossing).

Fixed-point iteration

Rearrange f(x) = 0 into x = g(x), then iterate x_(n+1) = g(x_n). Near the root the iteration converges when |g'(x)| < 1 at the root; if |g'(x)| > 1 it diverges. The iteration staircase/cobweb diagrams show this.

Newton-Raphson

x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n) / f'(x_n).

It uses the tangent at the current estimate and converges quadratically (fast), but it can fail: if f'(x_n) = 0 the tangent is vertical, and a poor starting point can send the sequence to a different root or into a loop.

Accuracy and error bounds

  • A sign change over an interval of width w brackets the root to within w; quoting the midpoint gives error at most w/2.
  • Iterate until successive values agree to the required accuracy (e.g. 3 s.f.).
  • Always substitute the final value back into f to confirm f(root) is close to 0.

Choosing a method

  • Bisection: guaranteed on a bracketed interval but slow.
  • Newton-Raphson: fast, needs f' and a good starting value.
  • Iteration: simple, but convergence depends on the rearrangement.

title: Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms
content:
Characteristics and Classification of Living Organisms

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 1 (statements 1.1–1.3). The seven life processes, classification systems and keys, and the features of the major groups of organisms.

1.1 Characteristics of living organisms

  • The seven life processes are often remembered as MRS GREN: Movement, Respiration, Sensitivity, Growth, Reproduction, Excretion, Nutrition. Every living organism performs all seven.
  • Each process has a precise definition worth memorising word for word: respiration is the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrients and release energy; sensitivity is the detection of, and response to, changes in the internal or external environment; excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism.

1.2 Classification systems

  • Organisms are classified into groups (taxa) using shared features. A classification key works by offering paired contrasting statements; each choice narrows the group until one name remains.
  • A species is a group of similar organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring. The binomial system names each species with a genus name and a specific epithet in italics, genus capitalised, for example Homo sapiens.

1.3 Features of organisms

  • Animals and plants are multicellular eukaryotes; animals digest internally and store glycogen, plants photosynthesise and have cellulose cell walls. Fungi are multicellular eukaryotes (yeast excepted) that absorb digested food externally and have chitin cell walls.
  • Prokaryotes (bacteria) are single-celled with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Protoctists are single-celled eukaryotes such as Amoeba and Chlorella. Viruses are not cells at all: a nucleic acid core inside a protein coat, which can only replicate inside a living host cell.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Living or not, applied to a virus: it shows none of the seven life processes on its own — no respiration, no movement, no growth outside a host. It can only be described as living when it has invaded a cell. Exam answers must state that viruses are acellular and obligate parasites, not "very small living things".
  • Classification reasoning, applied to an unfamiliar organism that is single-celled, has a nucleus, engulfs its food and has no cell wall: it is a protoctist. Give the reasoning chain — eukaryotic, so not a bacterium; unicellular, so not an animal or plant; ingestive nutrition and no cell wall, so not a fungus.
  • Key construction, applied to writing your own key: choose the feature that splits the remaining organisms into two equal groups first, usually cell arrangement or nutrition mode, then work down. A good key never offers more than two choices at a step.

Common errors

  • Saying plants do not respire. All living cells respire.
  • Calling viruses single-celled. They have no cell structure at all.
  • Confusing the specific epithet with the genus: in Panthera leo, Panthera is the genus.

title: Exam technique: Forces and Equilibrium
content:
### What earns the marks
For resultants, the vector triangle or Pythagoras with angle earns both marks. For moments, force times perpendicular distance earns each mark. For equilibrium, both zero force and zero moment stated earns the full explanation.
### Traps
Error: one equilibrium condition given alone. Correction: both are required. Error: couple torque taken as force only. Correction: multiply by the separation. Error: upthrust equated to object weight. Correction: it equals displaced fluid weight.
### Resolve before you sum
Split every force into components along two perpendicular directions, and write the equations ΣF_x = 0 and ΣF_y = 0 separately. Keep the sign convention you chose on the diagram.

### Take moments about a sensible point
Choose a pivot where an unknown force acts, so that its moment is zero. Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot, and the clockwise and anticlockwise sums must be equal for equilibrium.

### Use the triangle of forces when three forces meet at a point
Draw the forces head to tail to form a closed triangle. Use the sine rule or cosine rule to find an unknown force or angle, and label the triangle clearly.

title: Web Technologies — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Web Technologies

Computer Science — OL. HTML structure/tags, CSS styling, JS interactivity, the DOM, microprocessors/controllers in web context.

  • 1. HTML
  • 2. CSS
  • 3. JavaScript and the DOM
  • 4. How pages load

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

A web page is written in HTML, which defines the structure and content, and styled with CSS, which controls how it looks. A web browser acts as the client and sends requests to a web server, which returns the requested files. This exchange uses HTTP, and a URL identifies the page being requested.

A website can be static, with the same content for every visitor, or dynamic, where the server builds the page from data for each request. Forms send user input to the server, so validation of that input is important for security. Use the correct term from the syllabus, and link each technology to the job it does.

title: Prepositions and Collocations — Study Notes
content:
Prepositions (in, on, at, for, of) and collocations (words that naturally go together) are not always logical, so they are best learned in phrases rather than one word at a time.

Time prepositions

  • At: a clock time or a specific moment (at 10 a.m., at night).
  • On: a day or a date (on Monday, on 5 May).
  • In: a month, a year or a longer period (in June, in 2020).

Example: The meeting is on Monday at 10 a.m.

Prepositions after adjectives and verbs

Many adjectives and verbs take a fixed preposition:

  • interested in
  • good at
  • depend on
  • listen to
  • belong to

Learn these as complete phrases.

Collocations

Collocations are common word pairings. Learn the verb that goes with the noun:

  • make a decision, make an effort, make a mistake
  • do homework, do the washing, do research
  • take a break, take a photo, take part

Using make where do is needed, or the reverse, is one of the most common errors for learners.

Strategy

  • Keep a notebook of phrases, not single words.
  • Record the preposition or verb with each noun or adjective.
  • Read widely and notice which words appear together in good writing.

title: Superposition — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Superposition

Physics — AS. When waves meet, displacements add. In phase → constructive (big amplitude); antiphase → destructive (cancellation).

Key areas to revise

  • The Principle of Superposition
  • Coherence and Path Difference
  • Double-Slit (Young)
  • Diffraction Grating
  • Stationary Waves

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Superposition: at any point, the resultant displacement is the sum of the displacements from the separate waves.
  • Constructive interference occurs when the path difference is n λ; destructive interference occurs when it is (n + ½) λ.
  • In a stationary wave, adjacent nodes are λ / 2 apart, and the phase is the same on both sides of a node.
  • Diffraction grating: n λ = d sin θ, where d is the grating spacing.

Common errors

In a double-slit fringe spacing calculation, use the slit separation s in w = λ D / s, not the grating spacing. Check that the angle in the grating equation is measured from the normal.

title: Ethics and Ownership
content:
Ethics and Ownership

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 7 (Ethics and ownership), examined in AS Paper 1.

Professional Bodies

ACM/IEEE-CS and BCS codes: public interest, competence, integrity, avoid harm, respect privacy. Violations cost trust and employment.

Ethical Scenarios

  • Collecting more personal data than needed (privacy)
  • Releasing software with known bugs that risks safety (competence/honesty)
  • Automated decisions without human review (accountability)

Laws: data protection (GDPR-style), computer misuse (unauthorised access is a crime regardless of intent).

Exam tips: structure ethics answers as: identify the principle → apply to the scenario → give consequences for stakeholders.

Ownership and licensing

Copyright gives the creator legal protection over how their software and other original work is copied, distributed and changed. Copying software without permission is a breach of copyright and can be illegal. Open source software is released under licences that allow others to use, study and modify it, often on the condition that changes are shared in the same way.

Exam tip: link each ethical point to a consequence for a real user, such as a person losing a job or a loan being refused unfairly.

Ownership and licensing questions

  • Software written by an employee in the course of their job is normally owned by the employer, while software written by a freelancer is usually owned by the freelancer unless a contract says otherwise.
  • An open-source licence sets the conditions for using, changing and sharing code. Using open-source code in a commercial product still requires following its licence terms.

title: Exam technique: Database Systems
content:
### What earns the marks
For keys, primary identified as unique plus foreign as the link earns one mark each. For SQL, SELECT plus FROM plus WHERE in order earns each mark. For flat versus relational, one concrete drawback of duplication earns the discussion mark.
### Traps
Error: SELECT * claimed as precise. Correction: name the fields asked for. Error: primary key assigned to a non-unique field. Correction: keys must be unique. Error: flat file praised for large data. Correction: duplication corrupts it.### Worked example
For the names of students in class 10A, write SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Class = '10A'. Each clause earns credit on its own, so a correct WHERE with a wrong SELECT still scores. Use field names exactly as the table defines them and quote text values. A foreign key is only a foreign key when it links to a primary key in another table.
### Recall check
Explain the difference between a primary key and a foreign key in one sentence each. Explain why repeating the same data in several tables causes an update anomaly when one copy is changed and the others are not.

title: Word Formation: Prefixes and Suffixes — Study Notes
content:
Many English words are built from a root with prefixes (added to the front) and suffixes (added to the end). Knowing common parts lets you understand new words and spell them correctly.

Prefixes

A prefix changes the meaning of the root.

  • un- means not: unbelievable, unclear
  • im-, in-, il-, ir- also mean not: impossible, incorrect, illegal, irregular
  • dis- means not or the reverse: disagree, dishonest
  • re- means again: rewrite, replay
  • pre- means before: preview, pre-war

Suffixes that change word class

Suffixes often change a word from one class to another.

  • Noun suffixes: -ness (happiness), -tion (decision), -ment (development), -ity (possibility)
  • Adjective suffixes: -ful (helpful), -less (careless), -able (readable), -ous (dangerous)
  • Adverb suffix: -ly (quickly)

Changing the form

Changing happy to happiness, or imagine to imagination, needs care with spelling. Some words change the final letter or drop an e before a suffix.

The suffix -less

-less means without: hopeless means without hope, careless means without care.

Practice strategy

Learn words in families. Write the noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms together, for example: decide, decision, decisive, decisively. This builds range and helps your writing.

title: System Software and Security — Study Notes
content:
`# System Software and Security

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: sections 5 and 6 (System software; Security, privacy and data integrity), examined in AS Paper 1.

Operating System Roles

  • Manage memory (paging/segmentation, virtual memory to disk)
  • Schedule processes (round robin, priorities)
  • Handle I/O via device drivers and spooling
  • Provide the UI, file systems, and security (users, permissions)

Translators

  • Assembler: assembly → machine code (1:1)
  • Compiler: whole source → machine code, reports all errors, produces standalone executables
  • Interpreter: line-by-line execution, stops at first error, needs the interpreter present

Bytecode + VM (e.g. Java) combines both: compile once, run anywhere the VM exists.

Linkers and Loaders

Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking binds at runtime (smaller files, shared libraries). The loader places the program in memory, relocating addresses.

IDEs

Editors with syntax highlighting, autocompletion, debugger (breakpoints, stepping, variable watch), and integrated compilation.

Malware and Defences

Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, phishing. Defences: antivirus (signature + heuristic scanning), firewalls (packet filtering by port/IP), sandboxing, user education, patches.

Exam tips: compare compiler vs interpreter with concrete error-handling differences; explain firewall rules using ports and addresses.

Malware types and prevention

A virus attaches itself to a file or program and needs a host to spread. A worm spreads across a network without a host file. A trojan looks like useful software but carries a hidden harmful payload. Phishing uses fake emails or websites to trick a user into revealing login details or other personal data.

A firewall monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks traffic that does not meet its rules. Anti-malware software scans for and removes known threats. Regular software updates close security weaknesses, and regular backups allow data to be restored after an attack.

Exam tip: match each threat to how it spreads, and each prevention method to the threat it stops. Do not confuse a virus with a worm.

Worked example: tracing a program through the toolchain

A programmer writes the source code for a calculator in a high-level language. A compiler translates the whole program into machine code before it runs, and reports syntax errors as a list. A linker then joins this object code with the library routines it calls, producing one executable file. A loader copies that executable into main memory and starts it. If the same program were run by an interpreter, each statement would be translated and executed in turn, so an error in line 40 would only appear when the program reached line 40.

Comparing translators

  • Compiler: translates everything first, produces a fast executable and a separate file for the output, and is harder to debug while running.
  • Interpreter: translates line by line, starts quickly and eases debugging, but runs more slowly because it translates again each time.
  • Assembler: converts assembly language, which uses mnemonics such as ADD and MOV, into machine code, with a one-to-one correspondence between each instruction and its binary form.

Why the operating system loads the program

The loader is part of the operating system's work of managing memory. It reserves space, places the instructions and data in that space and sets the starting address. Without this step the processor would not know where the program begins or which memory it may use.

Exam point: name the translator for each stage in the question, and state one advantage and one disadvantage of the translator the question describes.

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Mathematics — OL. substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

  • 1. Substitution
  • 2. Collecting like terms
  • 3. Expanding
  • 4. Factorising
  • 5. Algebraic fractions

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Expand (x + 3)(x − 5) to get x² − 2x − 15. Check at x = 1: the left side is 4 × (−4) = −16, and the right side is 1 − 2 − 15 = −16. Simplify 3a²b × 4ab³ = 12a³b⁴ by multiplying coefficients and adding the powers of each letter. Factorise 6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3).

Key points to remember

To expand a single bracket, multiply every term inside by the term outside, keeping the signs. To expand two brackets, multiply each term of the first by each term of the second, then collect like terms. Factorising reverses this: take out the highest common factor first, then check whether the remaining bracket can be factorised again.

A common error is to drop a sign when the outside term is negative, for example writing -2(x - 3) as -2x - 6 instead of -2x + 6. Substitute a simple value such as x = 1 into both the original and the answer to check your expansion or factorisation.

title: AS Pure Mathematics — Full Revision Booklet
content:
Algebra — Equations

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): linear equations, simultaneous equations, quadratic formula, completing the square, forming equations from words.

1. Linear equations

3(x − 2) = x + 4 → 3x − 6 = x + 4 → 2x = 10 → x = 5. With fractions, multiply through by the LCD first.

2. Forming equations

Translate shapes/situations: "rectangle length 3 cm more than width, perimeter 34" → 2w + 2(w + 3) = 34 → w = 7.

3. Simultaneous equations

  • Elimination: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 → add → 3x = 9 → x = 3, y = 1.
  • Substitution for linear–quadratic: substitute y = 2x into x² + y² = 20 → 5x² = 20 → x = ±2.

4. Quadratics by formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.

Example: 2x² − 4x − 3 = 0 → x = (4 ± √(16 + 24))/4 = 2.58 or −0.58 (2 d.p.).

5. Completing the square

x² + bx + c = (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c. x² − 6x + 5 = (x − 3)² − 4 → minimum at (3, −4). Use for turning points and for solving when factorising fails.

Exam tips: substitute answers back to verify; in word problems define the unknown clearly ("let w = width in cm"); give quadratic solutions to the accuracy demanded.

Solving linear equations step by step

Collect the unknown on one side and the numbers on the other, undoing operations in the reverse order to BODMAS. Whatever you do to one side you must do to the other. When brackets are present, expand first, then collect like terms. Fractions are cleared by multiplying every term by the lowest common denominator.

Simultaneous equations

Two linear equations in x and y can be solved by elimination (make the coefficient of one unknown equal and opposite, then add or subtract) or by substitution (rearrange one equation for one unknown and put it into the other). Check the answer in both original equations. Examiners award method marks for a correct, clearly shown elimination even when arithmetic slips later.

Rearranging formulae

Treat the subject letter as the unknown and apply inverse operations. Where the subject appears twice, gather every term containing it, factorise, then divide. Square roots or squares are undone with a square and a root, applied to both sides.

Worked example: equations with fractions

Solve 3(x − 2)/4 = x + 1. Multiply both sides by 4 to clear the denominator: 3(x − 2) = 4(x + 1), so 3x − 6 = 4x + 4, which gives −10 = x. Check by substitution: left side 3(−12)/4 = −9 and right side −10 + 1 = −9. Both agree, so x = −10.

Examiners award the method mark for clearing the fraction correctly, so write the line where every term is multiplied by the denominator before you expand.

Unknowns on both sides

Solve 5x + 3 = 2x − 9. Subtract 2x from both sides to get 3x + 3 = −9, then subtract 3 to get 3x = −12, so x = −4. Keeping the unknowns on the side where the coefficient stays positive avoids negative-sign slips.

Quadratics and the discriminant

For ax² + bx + c = 0, the discriminant b² − 4ac decides how many real roots there are. If it is positive there are two distinct real roots, if it is zero there is one repeated root, and if it is negative there are no real roots.

Example: 2x² + 3x − 5 = 0 has discriminant 9 + 40 = 49. The formula gives x = (−3 ± 7)/4, so x = 1 or x = −2.5. Check x = 1: 2 + 3 − 5 = 0.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Dividing both sides of an equation by a variable, which can lose a solution (for example x² = 4x has solutions 0 and 4).
  • Applying the quadratic formula with the wrong sign on b, for example writing −3 when b = +3 in the formula.
  • Stopping at a rearranged formula without isolating the subject, or leaving a square root unsimplified when the question asks for an exact answer.

Algebra — Graphs

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): straight lines (gradient, intercept), key curves (quadratic, cubic, reciprocal, exponential), tangents, kinematic reading.

1. Straight lines

  • Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
  • y = mx + c; parallel ⇒ equal m; perpendicular ⇒ m₁m₂ = −1.

Example: through (2, −1) parallel to y = 3x + 1: y + 1 = 3(x − 2) ⇒ y = 3x − 7.

2. Drawing curves

Table of values, plot, smooth curve. Parabola symmetry axis x = −b/2a. Recognise reciprocal y = 1/x (two branches) and exponential y = aˣ (through (0,1)).

3. Interpreting

  • Roots = x-intercepts; y-intercept from x = 0.
  • Turning points of quadratics by completing the square.

4. Tangents and rates

Gradient of tangent at a point = instantaneous rate: draw a large triangle, rise/run. Area under a speed–time graph = distance (trapezium estimate).

5. Graphical solutions

Simultaneous: intersection points. Quadratic = line: intersections give roots. Read off carefully to the accuracy allowed.

Exam tips: quote gradients as fractions where exact; when estimating a tangent gradient, use a triangle spanning at least 4 grid squares.

Plotting and reading straight-line graphs

A table of values is set up from the equation, points are plotted and joined with a ruler. For y = mx + c, m is the gradient and c the y-intercept. The gradient is the change in y divided by the change in x, measured on a large triangle drawn on the line, not between two points read from a table.

Quadratic and cubic curves

Curves are drawn freehand as smooth curves through plotted points. Turning points, roots (where the curve cuts the x-axis) and the y-intercept are read directly from the graph. A quadratic has one turning point; a cubic can have up to two.

Using graphs to solve equations

To solve f(x) = k, draw the line y = k and read the x-coordinates where it meets the curve. Intersections of two graphs give simultaneous solutions. Always state the solutions to the accuracy the question asks for.

Worked example: gradient and equation of a line

A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, −3). The gradient is (−3 − 3)/(4 − 1) = −6/3 = −2. Substituting into y = mx + c with the point (1, 3) gives 3 = −2 + c, so c = 5 and the equation is y = −2x + 5.

A parallel line has the same gradient, so a line through (0, 1) parallel to this one is y = −2x + 1. A perpendicular line has gradient 1/2.

Turning points of a quadratic

For y = x² − 6x + 5, complete the square: y = (x − 3)² − 4. The minimum turning point is (3, −4), and the curve crosses the x-axis where (x − 3)² = 4, that is at x = 1 and x = 5. Sketch the curve through these points and label the turning point.

Gradient of a curve at a point

Between two points on a curve, the average rate of change is the gradient of the chord. To estimate the gradient at a point, draw a tangent by eye and find its gradient from two clearly read points on the tangent, using a large triangle. The answer will only be as accurate as your tangent.

Reading a graph in context

A distance–time graph has gradient equal to speed, so a horizontal section means the object is stationary. A speed–time graph has gradient equal to acceleration, and the area under it equals the distance travelled. Always state the units of the gradient, for example m/s or m/s².

  • Plot points carefully and join curves with a smooth line, not straight segments.
  • When a question asks you to use a graph to solve an equation, draw the line y = (the right-hand side) and read off the x-values where the curve crosses it.

Algebra — Inequalities

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): solving linear inequalities, integer solution sets, shading regions on graphs (linear programming context).

1. Solving

Like equations, but reverse the sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative: −2x ≥ 6 ⇒ x ≤ −3.

Example: 3x − 5 < 2x + 1 ⇒ x < 6.

2. Integer solutions

−1 ≤ x < 4 ⇒ x ∈ {−1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Closed endpoint for ≤/≥, open for </>.

3. Double inequalities

Handle both sides: −3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 7 → −4 < 2x ≤ 6 → −2 < x ≤ 3.

4. Shading regions

  • Draw the boundary line: dashed for </>, solid for ≤/≥.
  • Test a point (usually (0,0)) to pick the wanted side; shade the unwanted side or label the wanted region.
  • Feasible region satisfies all constraints simultaneously.

Example: y ≤ 2x + 1: solid line, test (0,0): 0 ≤ 1 ✓ → region containing origin.

Exam tips: never divide by an unknown sign — move x terms first; list integer solutions inside curly brackets; state which region you shade.

Solving linear inequalities

Inequalities are solved like equations, with one crucial exception: multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Answers are written as a single inequality such as x > 3, or as a set such as -2 < x ≤ 5 when two bounds are given.

Representing inequalities on a number line

An open circle marks a strict bound (< or >) that is not included; a filled circle marks an inclusive bound (≤ or ≥). Shade the region that satisfies the statement.

Regions on a coordinate grid

Draw each boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥ and a dashed line for < or >. Test a point such as (0, 0) if it is not on the line; shade the side that makes the inequality true. Where several regions are required, the wanted region is the overlap of all the shaded areas. Integer points inside a region are counted when a question asks for them.

Worked example: solving a linear inequality

Solve 3x − 7 < 2x + 4. Subtract 2x from both sides to get x − 7 < 4, then add 7 to get x < 11. The solution set is every number less than 11, which has no lower bound.

Double inequalities and integer solutions

Solve −3 ≤ 2x + 1 < 7. Subtract 1 from each part: −4 ≤ 2x < 6. Divide each part by 2: −2 ≤ x < 3. The integer solutions are −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2. Remember that the ≤ sign includes −2 and the < sign excludes 3.

Multiplying or dividing by a negative number

Solve 8 − 3x > 2. Subtract 8: −3x > −6. Divide by −3 and reverse the sign: x < 2. Forgetting to reverse the sign is the most common lost mark in this topic.

Quadratic inequalities

Solve x² − x − 6 ≤ 0. Factorise to (x − 3)(x + 2) ≤ 0. The expression is zero at x = 3 and x = −2, and it is negative between them. The solution is −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. Sketch the parabola to see which region is below the axis.

Shading regions on a grid

  • Draw a boundary line as a solid line for ≤ or ≥, and as a dashed line for < or >.
  • Test a point that is not on the line, usually (0, 0) if the line does not pass through it, to decide which side to shade.
  • If the question asks for a region bounded by several inequalities, shade each one lightly and leave the overlap clear.

Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

Finding the nth term of a linear sequence

For a sequence with a constant difference d, the nth term is dn + (a − d), where a is the first term. Check the rule by substituting n = 1, 2 and 3 before using it. Given a term value, set the nth term equal to it and solve for n to test whether it belongs to the sequence.

Functions as machines

A function takes an input and gives exactly one output. Composite functions are applied right to left: fg(x) means apply g first, then f. The inverse f⁻¹ reverses each step, found by writing y = f(x), swapping x and y, and rearranging for y.

Domain and range

The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs produced. Restrictions usually come from division by zero or from taking square roots of negative numbers. State both when asked to describe a function fully.

Worked examples: sequences

Linear. The sequence 5, 9, 13, 17 has a common difference of 4. The nth term is 4n + 1, since the nth term of a linear sequence is dn + (first term − d). Check the 10th term: 4 × 10 + 1 = 41.

Quadratic. For 2, 6, 12, 20, the first differences are 4, 6, 8 and the second difference is 2. The coefficient of n² is half the second difference, so it is 1. Subtract n² from each term: 1, 2, 3, 4, which is linear with nth term n. So the nth term is n² + n. Check n = 3: 9 + 3 = 12 ✓.

Function notation with composites

Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x − 1. Then fg(x) means f(g(x)) = f(x − 1) = 2(x − 1) + 3 = 2x + 1. Note that gf(x) = g(2x + 3) = 2x + 2, which is different. Composition is not commutative, and questions often ask for both to test whether you apply the inner function first.

Inverse functions

To find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = 2x + 3: write y = 2x + 3, swap to x = 2y + 3 and solve, giving y = (x − 3)/2. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 2(x − 3)/2 + 3 = x ✓. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in the line y = x.

Domain and range

For f(x) = √(x − 2), the expression under the root must be non-negative, so the domain is x ≥ 2. The output of a square root is never negative, so the range is f(x) ≥ 0. For a rational function such as 1/(x − 4), the domain excludes x = 4, and the range excludes y = 0, since the value 0 is never reached.

Common errors

  • Taking the nth term of a quadratic sequence from the first term alone; the second difference must be used.
  • Reversing the order of composition: fg(x) and gf(x) are not the same.
  • Writing the domain as x > 2 when the question allows equality, or stating the range with an inequality in the wrong direction.
  • Forgetting to swap x and y before solving for the inverse.

Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

Expanding brackets

Each term outside a bracket multiplies every term inside it. For a double bracket, multiply each term in the first by each term in the second, then collect like terms. Expanding (x + 3)(x − 5) gives x² − 2x − 15. Keep track of signs carefully, since most lost marks come from negative terms.

Factorising

Take out the highest common factor first, then look for a pair of brackets. For a quadratic x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. For the difference of two squares, a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). Check by expanding your answer.

Algebraic fractions

Simplify by factorising the numerator and denominator and cancelling common factors. Add or subtract fractions by writing them over a common denominator. Never cancel terms that are added, only factors that multiply.

Worked example: expanding and collecting terms

Expand (2x + 3)(x − 4). Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second: 2x × x = 2x², 2x × (−4) = −8x, 3 × x = 3x, 3 × (−4) = −12. Collect the like terms: 2x² − 5x − 12.

A quick check is to substitute x = 1: (5)(−3) = −15, and 2 − 5 − 12 = −15. The two agree.

Factorising quadratics and the difference of two squares

Factorise x² + x − 12. Find two numbers that multiply to −12 and add to +1: +4 and −3. So x² + x − 12 = (x + 4)(x − 3).

The difference of two squares gives 4x² − 9 = (2x − 3)(2x + 3). Recognise it whenever there is no middle term and both terms are squares with a minus sign between them.

Simplifying algebraic fractions

Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6). Factorise the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3) and the denominator as (x + 3)(x − 2). Cancel the common factor (x + 3) to get (x − 3)/(x − 2), with the restriction x ≠ −3 stated because the original expression is undefined there.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Writing (a + b)² = a² + b², which drops the middle term 2ab.
  • Cancelling a term rather than a factor, for example simplifying (x + 3)/(x + 2) to 3/2.
  • Expanding a negative bracket without changing the signs inside it: −(x − 4) = −x + 4.

Functions

This note builds the functions work used throughout the Cambridge AS & A Level Mathematics 9709 course. A function maps each input in its domain to exactly one output in its range. Notation such as f(x) = 2x + 1 names the rule, and the examiner expects you to state domain, range and inverse clearly.

Domain, range and notation

The domain is the set of inputs the function accepts. Restrictions usually come from denominators (which cannot be zero), square roots (which need a non-negative argument) and logarithms (which need a positive argument). The range is the set of outputs the function actually produces over that domain. For f(x) = x² on all real numbers, the range is f(x) ≥ 0. Writing the domain as x ≥ 0 gives the same range but changes whether an inverse exists.

A many-to-one function, such as x² on all reals, sends two inputs to the same output. A one-to-one function never does. Only one-to-one functions have inverses.

Composite functions

The composite function fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f to the result. Order matters, so in general fg(x) and gf(x) are different functions.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x².

  • fg(x) = f(x²) = 2x² + 1
  • gf(x) = g(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1

When a restriction is involved, check the range of the inner function against the domain of the outer one. If g(x) = x − 3 with domain x ≥ 0 is followed by f(x) = √x, the range of g is x ≥ −3, which is wider than the domain of f, so the composite fg(x) = √(x − 3) needs x ≥ 3 to be defined. The exam often asks for this domain explicitly.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ reverses the action of f, so f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2. Write y = 3x − 2, swap to x = 3y − 2, then y = (x + 2)/3. So f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 3 × (x + 2)/3 − 2 = x.

An inverse exists only if f is one-to-one on its domain. If it is not, restrict the domain to make it so. For f(x) = x² with domain x ≥ 0, the inverse is f⁻¹(x) = √x with domain x ≥ 0. Without the restriction, x² would have no single inverse, because both 3 and −3 square to 9.

The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f. The graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, so a point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹. Use this to check an answer: if (2, 5) is on the graph of f, then (5, 2) must be on the graph of f⁻¹.

Transformations of graphs

Each change to the rule moves or stretches the graph in a predictable way. Learn these as a table:

Transformed graphEffect on the graph of y = f(x)
y = f(x) + atranslation by a units up (a < 0: down)
y = f(x + a)translation by a units left (a < 0: right)
y = a f(x)vertical stretch, scale factor a
y = f(ax)horizontal stretch, scale factor 1/a
y = −f(x)reflection in the x-axis
y = f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

The horizontal translation runs against the sign: y = (x − 3)² is the graph of x² moved 3 units to the right. A common error is to move it left. For a sequence of transformations, apply them in the order the question gives, tracking a few key points such as the vertex or the intercepts.

Method for exam questions

  • For a composite function, write out fg(x) and gf(x) separately whenever the question names two functions, and simplify each.
  • For an inverse, state both the rule and its domain. A correct rule with the domain missing loses marks.
  • To show a function has an inverse, argue that it is one-to-one on the stated domain, usually because it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing there.
  • When sketching y = f⁻¹(x), reflect the graph of f in y = x and mark where the line crosses it, since that point lies on both graphs.

Exam cue: whenever a question says "hence" or "using your answer to part", the composite or inverse from the earlier part is usually the route to the answer, so keep it in simplified form.

Quadratics

A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Completing the Square

Rewrite x² + bx + c as (x + b/2)² − (b/2)² + c.

Example: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, so the vertex is at (−3, −4).

For a > 1, factor out a first: 2x² + 12x + 19 = 2(x² + 6x) + 19 = 2(x + 3)² − 18 + 19 = 2(x + 3)² + 1.

Vertex form a(x − h)² + k gives the minimum/maximum value k at x = h — this is how you find a maximum area or minimum cost.

The Discriminant

Δ = b² − 4ac decides how the curve meets the x-axis:

ΔRootsGraph
Δ > 0two distinct real rootscrosses x-axis twice
Δ = 0repeated roottouches (tangent)
Δ < 0no real rootsnever meets x-axis

Example: kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 has equal roots when 16 − 4k = 0, so k = 4.

Quadratic Inequalities

Solve by sketching. For x² − 5x + 4 < 0, factorise: (x − 1)(x − 4) < 0, and the curve is below the axis between the roots, so 1 < x < 4.

Tip: flip the inequality when dividing by a negative number, and always sketch to check which interval you need.

Curve and Line Intersections

Set the equations equal; the resulting quadratic's discriminant tells you if the line is a secant (Δ > 0), tangent (Δ = 0) or misses (Δ < 0).

Exam tips: complete the square before reading off turning points; state the discriminant condition explicitly before solving for an unknown coefficient.

Discriminant and inequalities: exam method

For ax² + bx + c = 0 the discriminant is b² − 4ac. Positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots. Use this without solving the equation when the question asks about the nature of the roots.

To find the values of k for which a quadratic has no real roots, require b² − 4ac < 0 and solve the resulting inequality in k.

To solve a quadratic inequality, find the roots, sketch the U-shaped (a > 0) or inverted-U (a < 0) curve, and read off the region above or below the axis. For x² − 5x + 6 < 0 the roots are 2 and 3, and the solution is 2 < x < 3.

Exam cue: Completing the square gives the turning point (p, q) and shows the minimum or maximum value directly.

Worked example: completing the square with a coefficient

Write 2x² + 8x + 3 in the form a(x + p)² + q. Factor the 2 from the first two terms: 2(x² + 4x) + 3. Complete the square inside the bracket: x² + 4x = (x + 2)² − 4. So the expression is 2((x + 2)² − 4) + 3 = 2(x + 2)² − 5.

The minimum value is −5, reached when x = −2, so the minimum point is (−2, −5). Always factor the leading coefficient out first, otherwise the constant term comes out wrong.

Discriminant and the range of a parameter

The equation x² + kx + 4 = 0 has no real roots when the discriminant is negative: k² − 16 < 0. Solve as a quadratic in k to get −4 < k < 4. Stating the range is the mark-earning step, so write the inequality in full.

If the discriminant equals zero, the line is a tangent to the curve; if it is positive the line cuts the curve at two points.

Tangent to a curve

Find where y = x² − 2x + 3 meets the line y = 2x + k. Substitute to get x² − 4x + (3 − k) = 0. For a tangent the discriminant is zero: 16 − 4(3 − k) = 0, so k = −1. The tangent is y = 2x − 1, touching the curve at x = 2, where y = 3 on both.

Solving a quadratic inequality with a sketch

Solve 2x² − 5x − 3 > 0. Factor as (2x + 1)(x − 3) and find the roots x = −½ and x = 3. The parabola has a positive leading coefficient, so it is above the axis outside the roots. The solution is x < −½ or x > 3. Note the word or: this is two separate intervals, not one.

  • Positive leading coefficient: the expression is positive outside the roots and negative between them.
  • Negative leading coefficient: the reverse is true.
  • If the quadratic has no real roots, the sign never changes, so test one value to decide whether the inequality holds for all x.

Circular Measure

Cambridge International AS & A Level Mathematics 9709, Paper 1: radian measure, arc length, and the areas and perimeters of sectors and segments. Every formula here takes its angle in radians — that is the single fact most marks hinge on.

Radians

One radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius. The full circumference is 2πr, so a full turn is 2π radians and π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Example: 150° = 150π/180 = 5π/6 ≈ 2.618 rad.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π. Example: 1.5 rad = 1.5 × 180/π ≈ 85.9°.

Learn the common values: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π. Leave answers in terms of π unless the question asks for a decimal — and when it does, give three significant figures.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 6 × π/3 = 2π.

A chord splits the circumference into a minor arc and a major arc, and their lengths add to 2πr. If a question gives the major angle, use θ_major = 2π − θ_minor before substituting.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Minor and major sector areas add to πr². The perimeter of a sector is P = 2r + s = 2r + rθ — the two straight edges count, so an arc length alone is not a perimeter.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

The segment is the sector minus the triangle ½r²sin θ — that subtraction is where the formula comes from, and writing it down earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips. Its perimeter is the arc plus the chord, with chord length 2r sin(θ/2).

Putting It Together

Worked example: a sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.1 rad. Arc length s = 8 × 1.1 = 8.8 cm. Area A = ½ × 64 × 1.1 = 35.2 cm². Perimeter P = 2 × 8 + 8.8 = 24.8 cm.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²
  • r = s/θ, and r = √(2A/θ) — isolate the squared term first, then take the positive root only, since a radius is a length.

Exam traps: never mix degrees into s = rθ or A = ½r²θ — convert first, and check the calculator is in radian mode. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing. Read whether the question asks for the major or the minor arc, sector, or segment, and confirm area answers carry squared units while arcs and perimeters are plain lengths.

Worked example: arc length and sector area

A sector has radius 5 cm and angle 0.8 radians. The arc length is rθ = 5 × 0.8 = 4 cm. The sector area is ½r²θ = ½ × 25 × 0.8 = 10 cm².

Both formulas need the angle in radians. If the question gives degrees, convert first: 60° = π/3 radians, and 1 radian is about 57.3°. Writing a degree value into rθ is one of the most common lost marks in this topic.

Exact answers with π

For radius 6 cm and angle π/3, the arc length is 6 × π/3 = 2π cm, and the sector area is ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π cm². Leave answers in terms of π when the question asks for an exact value, and give a decimal only if it asks for one.

Segment area

A segment is the region between a chord and an arc. Its area is the sector area minus the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord, so segment = ½r²(θ − sin θ).

Example: with r = 5 and θ = 0.8, sin 0.8 is about 0.7174, so the segment area is ½ × 25 × (0.8 − 0.7174) = 1.03 cm² to 2 decimal places. Keep sin θ in your calculator, not rounded, until the final line.

Finding an angle or radius from a perimeter or arc

If an arc has length 12 cm on a circle of radius 4 cm, the angle is θ = 12/4 = 3 radians. If the perimeter of a sector is given, the perimeter is 2r + rθ, so set that expression equal to the known value and solve for the unknown.

  • Check that the answer is reasonable: an angle of 3 radians is less than π, so the sector must be less than a half-disc.
  • Sketch the sector and label the radii and the angle before you substitute.
  • When a question combines two sectors or a sector with a triangle, find each area separately and then add or subtract, stating which operation you used.

Trigonometry

Exact Values

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/2√3/3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3

Key Identities

  • sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
  • tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
  • sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ

Solving Equations

Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

For cos x = 0.5 in 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°: x = 60° and 360° − 60° = 300°.

Always check the required interval and give every solution.

Graphs and Transformations

y = a sin(bx) + c has amplitude a, period 2π/b, and vertical shift c.

Example: y = 3 sin(2x) has amplitude 3 and period π.

Using Identities

If sin x = 0.6 with x acute, then cos x = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 (positive in the first quadrant).

Exam tips: write the general second solution using graph symmetry rather than memorising CAST blindly; square both sides only with care, as it can add false solutions.

Exact values and exam method

Use CAST to find the quadrant signs: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third, cosine in the fourth. Find the acute angle first, then the other solutions in the range the question specifies.

For sin x = k, the solutions in 0° to 360° are α and 180° − α, where α is the acute angle with sin α = |k|. For cos x = k they are α and 360° − α. Always check the range; an answer outside it earns no mark.

Write a sin x + b cos x as R sin(x + α) or R cos(x − α). Expanding gives R = √(a² + b²), and for the sine form tan α = b/a. The maximum value is R, which gives the turning points that exam questions often ask for.

Reciprocal functions: sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x, cot x = 1/tan x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 and 1 + tan²x = sec²x to simplify.

Exam cue: Show the working that gives the acute angle before stating the answers in the required range.

Worked example: exact values and a quadrant rule

Use the exact values sin 30° = ½, cos 45° = 1/√2 and tan 60° = √3. For an angle such as 150°, sin 150° = sin(180° − 30°) = sin 30° = ½, because sine is positive in the second quadrant. For 225°, tan 225° = tan 45° = 1, because tangent is positive in the third quadrant.

Draw a quick CAST diagram to decide the sign: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third and cosine in the fourth.

Solving a trigonometric equation

Solve 2cos x = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. Then cos x = ½, so x = π/3 or x = 2π − π/3 = 5π/3. Always find the principal value first, then use the symmetry of the graph to find the other solutions in the range.

Solve 2sin²x − sin x − 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°. Factor as (2 sin x + 1)(sin x − 1) = 0. Then sin x = 1, giving x = 90°, or sin x = −½, giving x = 210° and 330°.

Proving an identity

Show that (sin x + cos x)² = 1 + sin 2x. Expand the left side: sin²x + 2 sin x cos x + cos²x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 to get 1 + 2 sin x cos x, and recall sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, so the left side equals 1 + sin 2x.

Graphs and transformations

  • y = 3 sin 2x + 1 has amplitude 3, period 180° (or π radians), and the maximum value 4 occurs at x = 45°.
  • The range of y = 3 sin 2x + 1 is −2 ≤ y ≤ 4.
  • A horizontal stretch by factor ½ halves the period; a vertical shift of +1 moves the whole graph up by one unit.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Working in degrees when the question uses radians, or the reverse. Check the units in the question before you start.
  • Giving only the principal value and missing the other solutions in the range. Always check the quadrant signs.
  • Squaring both sides of an equation to remove a root, which can add extra solutions. Check each answer in the original equation.

Differentiation

Basic Rules

  • d/dx (xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹
  • d/dx (k) = 0, d/dx (kx) = k

Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3.

Chain Rule

dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

Example: y = (3x − 1)⁵: dy/dx = 5(3x − 1)⁴ × 3 = 15(3x − 1)⁴.

Tangents and Normals

The tangent gradient at a point is dy/dx there; the normal gradient is −1/(dy/dx).

Example: y = x² at (2, 4): tangent y = 4x − 4; normal has gradient −1/4.

Stationary Points

Set dy/dx = 0, then classify with the second derivative:

  • d²y/dx² > 0 → minimum
  • d²y/dx² < 0 → maximum
  • d²y/dx² = 0 → test either side

Example: y = x³ − 3x: dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0 at x = ±1; d²y/dx² = 6x, so a maximum at x = −1 and a minimum at x = 1.

Rates of Change

dy/dx is a rate: if V = 4/3 πr³, then dV/dr = 4πr² links volume change to radius change.

Exam tips: always restart gradients from the derivative at the exact point, and answer rate questions with units.

Rules and exam method

For y = axⁿ, dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹. Differentiate each term of a polynomial separately; a constant term differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: √x = x^(1/2) and 1/x² = x⁻².

Product rule: d/dx(uv) = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Quotient rule: d/dx(u/v) = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Chain rule: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. For (ax + b)ⁿ the result is na(ax + b)ⁿ⁻¹.

Stationary points occur where dy/dx = 0. Classify them by the sign of dy/dx either side of the point, or with d²y/dx²: positive gives a minimum, negative a maximum, and zero means use the sign change. The gradient at a point gives the tangent; the normal has the negative reciprocal gradient.

Exam cue: Give the tangent or normal as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), or simplified to y = mx + c, as the question asks. Check it by substituting the point back into the line.

Worked example: a full stationary-point analysis

Let y = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5. Then dy/dx = 3x² − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1). Stationary points occur when dy/dx = 0, so x = 3 or x = −1. The second derivative is d²y/dx² = 6x − 6. At x = −1 it is −12, which is negative, so there is a maximum; at x = 3 it is +12, so there is a minimum. Substitute back into the original equation for the y-coordinates: (−1, 10) is a maximum and (3, −22) is a minimum. Always state both coordinates.

Tangent and normal at a point

At x = 2, y = 8 − 12 − 18 + 5 = −17 and dy/dx = 12 − 12 − 9 = −9. The tangent has gradient −9 through (2, −17), so y + 17 = −9(x − 2). The normal is perpendicular, with gradient 1/9, so y + 17 = (1/9)(x − 2). Keep the equations in the form the question asks for, and do not mix the gradient of the normal with the tangent.

Rates of change: a chain rule example

The volume of a sphere is V = (4/3)πr³. If the radius increases at 0.5 cm/s, find the rate of change of volume when r = 3. dV/dr = 4πr², so dV/dt = dV/dr × dr/dt = 4π(9)(0.5) = 18π cm³/s ≈ 56.5 cm³/s. Linking the rates through the chain rule is the method being tested, so write the link explicitly.

Increasing and decreasing

The sign of dy/dx tells you whether the function is increasing (dy/dx > 0) or decreasing (dy/dx < 0). For y = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5, the curve increases for x < −1, decreases between −1 and 3, and increases again for x > 3. State these intervals with the correct inequalities; an answer that says "x > −1" for the decreasing part loses the mark.

Common errors

  • Concluding a maximum or minimum from dy/dx = 0 alone without a sign test or second derivative.
  • Substituting the x-value into dy/dx to give the y-coordinate of the stationary point.
  • Using the gradient of the tangent in the normal equation, instead of its negative reciprocal.
  • Forgetting the chain-rule factor when the rate of change question involves two variables.

Integration

Indefinite Integrals

Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1).

Examples: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + c; ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + c; ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + c; ∫ e^x dx = e^x + c.

Definite Integrals

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). Constants of integration cancel.

Example: ∫₀¹ 6x² dx = [2x³]₀¹ = 2.

Areas Under Curves

Area between a curve and the x-axis = ∫ₐᵇ y dx, where y ≥ 0. If the curve dips below the axis, split the integral at the roots and add the absolute values.

Example: area between y = x² − 4 and the x-axis: roots ±2, and the area is |∫₋₂² (x² − 4) dx| = 32/3.

Trapezium Rule

A ≈ h/2 [y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁) + yₙ], h = (b − a)/n. More strips → better estimate; always an over-estimate for convex curves.

Exam tips: never forget +c on indefinite integrals; for areas with negative regions, sketch first and split.

Rules and exam method

For xⁿ with n ≠ −1, ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + c. Integrate term by term. The special case is ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + c. An indefinite integral needs + c; a definite integral does not.

For a definite integral, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative. Write the limits as [F(x)] between a and b, and substitute carefully: a negative limit raised to a power needs brackets.

The area between a curve and the x-axis is ∫ y dx when y ≥ 0 over the interval. If the curve lies below the axis the integral is negative, so take the modulus. If the curve crosses the axis, find the root and integrate each part separately, adding the moduli of the parts.

The area between two curves is the integral of (upper − lower) between their intersection points, found by solving the equations simultaneously.

Exam cue: Show the expanded antiderivative before substituting limits; method marks are given for a correct integration even when the arithmetic later slips.

Worked examples: indefinite and definite integrals

Example 1. Find ∫(3x² + 2x − 5) dx. Integrate term by term and add a constant: x³ + x² − 5x + c. Always include + c for an indefinite integral; examiners remove the mark when it is missing.

Example 2. Evaluate ∫13 x² dx = [x³/3] from 1 to 3 = (27/3) − (1/3) = 9 − 1/3 = 26/3. Substitute the upper limit, then subtract the value at the lower limit; the constant of integration cancels and is not written.

Reverse chain rule

∫(2x + 1)⁵ dx = (2x + 1)⁶ / (6 × 2) + c = (2x + 1)⁶/12 + c. Check by differentiating: the chain rule gives 6(2x + 1)⁵ × 2 / 12 = (2x + 1)⁵. The divisor is the new power multiplied by the coefficient of x inside the bracket.

Area between a curve and the x-axis

A definite integral gives a signed area. If the curve crosses the x-axis between the limits, the integral from a to b can be smaller than the true area, because the part below the axis counts negatively. Split the integral at each crossing and take the modulus of each part: area = |∫ from a to c| + |∫ from c to b|. Sketch the curve before integrating; it is the quickest way to see where the crossings are.

Area between two curves

For y = f(x) above y = g(x) between x = a and x = b, the area is ∫ab [f(x) − g(x)] dx. Find the intersection points by solving f(x) = g(x), since they give the limits. A common error is subtracting in the wrong order, which gives a negative answer; the area is always positive.

Trapezium rule

With n strips of equal width h, the trapezium rule gives ∫ab y dx ≈ (h/2)[y₀ + 2(y₁ + … + yn−1) + yn]. Where the curve is concave down the estimate is an underestimate, and where it is concave up it is an overestimate. Give the answer to the accuracy the question asks for and show the y-values in a table to earn the method marks.

Common errors

  • Forgetting + c on an indefinite integral, or writing + c on a definite one.
  • Dividing by the power before the coefficient in a reverse chain rule question.
  • Reporting a negative area from a definite integral without splitting at the x-axis crossings.
  • Using the trapezium rule with the wrong number of ordinates: n strips need n + 1 y-values.

Sequences and Series

Arithmetic Progressions (AP)

Terms increase by a common difference d.

  • nth term: uₙ = a + (n − 1)d
  • Sum: Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d]

Example: AP 5, 8, 11: the 20th term is 5 + 19 × 3 = 62.

Geometric Progressions (GP)

Terms multiply by a common ratio r.

  • nth term: uₙ = arⁿ⁻¹
  • Sum: Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
  • Sum to infinity (|r| < 1 only): S∞ = a/(1 − r)

Example: a = 8, r = 1/2 gives S∞ = 8/(1/2) = 16.

Binomial Expansion

(1 + x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n − 1)/2! x² + n(n − 1)(n − 2)/3! x³ + …, valid for |x| < 1.

For positive integer n, coefficients come from Pascal's triangle: (1 + 2x)⁴ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + 32x³ + 16x⁴.

Exam tips: identify a, d or r first; for "sum to infinity" questions check |r| < 1 explicitly, and for binomial expansions give terms up to the power asked (usually x² or x³).

Formulae and exam method

Arithmetic progression: the nth term is Tₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference. The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sₙ = n/2 (a + l) when the last term l is known.

Geometric progression: Tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹, and Sₙ = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r).

To find the number of terms, substitute the known sum or term and solve for n. When n sits in an exponent, take logarithms. Check that n is a positive integer.

Sigma notation: Σ from r = 1 to n of (ar + b) is evaluated with the standard sums, but write out the first few terms when the pattern is unclear.

Exam cue: Identify whether the question is AP or GP before choosing a formula, and state the value of r when using the sum to infinity.

Exam method: arithmetic and geometric sums

For an arithmetic sequence with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is a + (n − 1)d and the sum of the first n terms is S_n = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d). For a geometric sequence with ratio r, the nth term is ar^(n − 1) and S_n = a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1.

The sum to infinity exists only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1, say so explicitly rather than applying the formula.

Exam cue: Identify whether the sequence is arithmetic or geometric from the common difference or ratio before choosing a formula. Check the number of terms n carefully when you set up the equation.

Worked example: arithmetic progression

The sequence 3, 7, 11, … has first term a = 3 and common difference d = 4. The 20th term is a + 19d = 3 + 76 = 79. The sum of the first 20 terms is Sₙ = n/2 (2a + (n − 1)d) = 10 × (6 + 76) = 820.

Check with the average method: the first and last terms average (3 + 79)/2 = 41, and 41 × 20 = 820.

Worked example: geometric progression

The sequence 5, 10, 20, … has r = 2. The 8th term is 5 × 2⁷ = 640. The sum of the first six terms is 5(2⁶ − 1)/(2 − 1) = 315. Adding them directly gives 5 + 10 + 20 + 40 + 80 + 160 = 315, which confirms the formula.

Sum to infinity

A geometric series has a sum to infinity only when |r| < 1, and then S∞ = a/(1 − r). For 81, 27, 9, … the ratio is 1/3, so S∞ = 81/(2/3) = 121.5. If |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and the sum does not converge, so say so rather than quoting a formula.

Binomial expansion

For (1 + 2x)⁵, the first terms are 1 + 5(2x) + 10(2x)² + … The coefficient of x² is C(5, 2) × 2² = 10 × 4 = 40. The expansion is valid for |2x| < 1, so the range of x must be stated when the question asks for it.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using n instead of n − 1 in the n-th term formula, which shifts every term.
  • Confusing the nth term with the sum of the first n terms, a very common error on exam questions that ask for both.
  • Dividing a/(1 − r) when the series starts at a term other than the first, so check the index on the first term before using the formula.
  • Forgetting that the binomial expansion of (a + b)ⁿ has a coefficient C(n, r) on each term, and that the powers of a and b add to n.

Coordinate Geometry

Distance and midpoint

For A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂): length AB = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Midpoint M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).

Gradients

Gradient m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), where x₂ ≠ x₁. A horizontal line has m = 0; a vertical line has no gradient.

Parallel lines have equal gradients. Perpendicular lines (neither vertical nor horizontal) satisfy m₁ × m₂ = −1.

Equations of a straight line

  • Gradient–intercept form: y = mx + c, where c is the y-intercept.
  • Point–gradient form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
  • General form: ax + by + c = 0, with gradient −a/b.

Example: Find the line through P(2, −1) perpendicular to y = 3x − 4. The perpendicular gradient is −1/3, so y + 1 = −1/3 (x − 2). Multiply by 3: 3y + 3 = −x + 2, giving x + 3y + 1 = 0.

Intersection of two lines

Solve the two equations simultaneously, by substitution or elimination. Lines with equal gradients and no common point are parallel.

Example: y = 2x + 1 and x + y = 7. Substituting gives x + 2x + 1 = 7, so 3x = 6, x = 2 and y = 5. The lines meet at (2, 5).

Circles

A circle with centre (a, b) and radius r has equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r².

The expanded form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c). Complete the square in x and y to convert between the forms.

Example: x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 3 = 0 has g = −3, f = 2, c = −3. Centre (3, −2), radius √(9 + 4 + 3) = 4.

Tangents

A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. Find the radius gradient from the centre to the point, then take the negative reciprocal for the tangent.

Exam technique

  • Sketch the figure first, and check whether the question asks about a line, a circle or both.
  • Keep exact values (fractions and surds) until the final step unless decimals are requested.
  • Check that a line passes through a given point by substituting its coordinates.

title: Exam technique: Networks and the Internet
content:
### What earns the marks
For protocol choice, the requirement matched earns each mark: delay-sensitive goes UDP, accuracy-critical goes TCP. For devices, the layer and key stated (MAC for bridges, IP for routers) earn the pair. For topologies, the failure scope described earns the resilience mark.
### Traps
Error: one protocol for both voice and files. Correction: optimise per requirement. Error: hubs credited with MAC forwarding. Correction: hubs broadcast; switches target. Error: star failure claimed total. Correction: only the spoke drops.
### Layers and protocols
When a question names a protocol, state the layer it belongs to and its job. TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery and IP handles addressing and routing. Quoting the name alone is not enough.
### Packet switching
Explain that a message is split into packets, each packet can take a different route, and the packets are reassembled at the destination. Link the idea to resilience: a failed link is bypassed.
### DNS and HTTP
Describe a process as a sequence. A DNS lookup turns a domain name into an IP address, and then the browser sends an HTTP request to that address.

title: Alkenes Quick Revision
content:
Alkenes

Edexcel International AS Level Chemistry revision notes covering the structure, bonding, isomerism, addition reactions, mechanisms, and polymer disposal of alkenes.

  • Alkenes and cycloalkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with a general formula CnH2n containing a carbon-carbon double bond consisting of one sigma bond and one pi bond.
  • Geometric isomerism arises due to restricted rotation around the C=C double bond and different substituents on each carbon atom of the double bond.
  • The E-Z naming system uses Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority rules, becoming necessary when the cis- and trans- naming system breaks down due to non-identical groups on the carbon atoms.
  • Alkenes undergo addition reactions including hydrogenation with a nickel catalyst, halogenation to di-halogenoalkanes, addition of hydrogen halides to mono-halogenoalkanes, hydration with steam and an acid catalyst to form alcohols, and oxidation with acidified potassium manganate(VII) to diols.
  • Bromine or bromine water acts as a qualitative test for a C=C double bond, turning from orange/brown to colourless.
  • Electrophilic addition mechanisms for bromine and hydrogen bromide with ethene, and hydrogen bromide with propene, involve curly arrows starting from bonds or lone pairs and proceed via carbocation intermediates whose stability increases in the order primary < secondary < tertiary.
  • Addition polymerisation produces long-chain polymers from alkene monomers, requiring the ability to draw repeat units from monomers and vice versa.
  • Polymer disposal problems are mitigated by developing biodegradable polymers and removing toxic waste gases produced by incineration.

Worked example

Deduce the E-Z isomer designation for (E)-1-bromo-1,2-dichloroethene. Step 1: Assign priorities to the groups attached to each carbon of the C=C double bond using atomic numbers. On carbon 1, bromine (atomic number 35) outranks chlorine (atomic number 17). On carbon 2, chlorine outranks hydrogen (atomic number 1). Step 2: Locate the highest priority groups on each carbon. Since the bromine on carbon 1 and the chlorine on carbon 2 are on opposite sides of the double bond, the isomer is designated as (E).

Key points to remember

Students often forget that a pi bond is formed by the sideways overlap of p-orbitals, which restricts rotation and causes geometric isomerism. When drawing curly arrows for electrophilic addition, ensure the arrow starts precisely from the electron source, either a bond or a lone pair, and points to the electron-deficient species. In addition of hydrogen bromide to propene, remember that the major product is formed via the more stable secondary carbocation intermediate rather than the less stable primary carbocation. When naming geometrical isomers, always apply the E-Z priority rules systematically rather than relying on cis and trans prefixes when more than two different groups are attached to the double-bonded carbons.

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Bubble sort compares adjacent pairs and swaps them when they are out of order. Sorting 3, 1, 2 in one pass: compare 3 and 1 to get 1, 3, 2, then compare 3 and 2 to get 1, 2, 3. A second pass with no swaps shows the list is finished. Linear search checks each item in turn, while binary search needs a sorted list.

Key points to remember

An algorithm is a finite, precise set of steps that solves a problem. Linear search checks each item in turn and works on unsorted data; binary search repeatedly halves a sorted list and is much faster on large data. Bubble sort compares adjacent pairs and swaps them, repeating passes until no swaps are needed. In exam answers, name the algorithm, state the condition it needs (for example, a sorted list for binary search), and trace it step by step when asked.

Pseudocode questions reward precise control structures: use IF...THEN...ENDIF, WHILE...ENDWHILE and FOR...NEXT as the syllabus shows them, and declare every variable you use.

title: Integration — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Integration

Mathematics — AS (9709). Reverse the power rule and add a constant: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + c (n ≠ −1).

Key areas to revise

  • Indefinite Integrals
  • Definite Integrals
  • Areas Under Curves
  • Trapezium Rule

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Integration reverses differentiation. For a term ax^n, ∫ax^n dx = a x^(n+1)/(n+1) + c, provided n is not −1. Add the constant of integration c for an indefinite integral, and use a given point on the curve to find it. For a definite integral, evaluate the upper limit minus the lower limit.

The area between a curve and the x-axis from x = a to x = b is ∫y dx. If part of the area lies below the axis, that part gives a negative value, so split the integral at the crossing points, take the absolute value of each part and then add them. Check whether the question asks for an exact value or a decimal to the required accuracy.
