title: Quadratics — Study Notes
content:
Quadratics

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11), sat at AS. Quadratic questions ask for a turning point, the roots, or a condition on a parameter. Most multi-part questions use all three, so decide the job of each part before you calculate.

Start from a question

The function is f(x) = 2x² − 8x + 11.

  1. Find the minimum value of f(x) and the value of x at which it occurs.
  2. Find the values of k for which f(x) = k has real roots.
  3. Find the value of m for which the line y = x + m is a tangent to y = f(x).

Part 1. Complete the square: f(x) = 2(x − 2)² + 3. The minimum value is 3, at x = 2.

Part 2. f(x) = k gives 2x² − 8x + (11 − k) = 0. The discriminant is 64 − 8(11 − k) = 8k − 24. Real roots need 8k − 24 ≥ 0, so k ≥ 3, which agrees with Part 1.

Part 3. Substituting y = x + m gives 2x² − 9x + (11 − m) = 0. A tangent needs equal roots, so 81 − 8(11 − m) = 0. That gives 8m − 7 = 0, so m = 7/8.

Turning points and the square

For ax² + bx + c, the turning point is at x = −b/2a. The sign of a decides the type: a > 0 gives a minimum and a < 0 gives a maximum. Example: for 2x² − 12x + 7, the turning point is at x = 3, and the value there is 18 − 36 + 7 = −11.

Solving

Try factorising first. If that fails, use x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a and simplify the surd. Example: 3x² + 5x − 4 = 0 has discriminant 25 + 48 = 73, so x = (−5 ± √73)/6.

The discriminant counts roots

D = b² − 4ac gives the number of real roots: D > 0 gives two distinct roots, D = 0 gives one repeated root, and D < 0 gives none. Example: 4x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots when k² = 4 × 4 × 9 = 144, so k = ±12. With k = 12 the equation is (2x + 3)² = 0.

A parameter inside the discriminant

When D contains an unknown, form the inequality and solve it. Example: x² + (k − 1)x + 4 = 0 has real roots when (k − 1)² − 16 ≥ 0. So |k − 1| ≥ 4, which gives k ≤ −3 or k ≥ 5.

Sketch, then read the region

For a positive a, the curve is below the x-axis between its roots and above it outside them. Example: 2x² − x − 6 < 0 factorises as (2x + 3)(x − 2) < 0, so −3/2 < x < 2.

Example: 5 − 3x − 2x² ≥ 0. Multiplying by −1 gives 2x² + 3x − 5 ≤ 0, and the inequality reverses. (2x + 5)(x − 1) ≤ 0 gives −5/2 ≤ x ≤ 1.

A line and a curve

Set the two equations equal and rearrange into one quadratic. Example: y = x + 3 and y = 2x² − x meet where 2x² − 2x − 3 = 0. Here D = 28 > 0, so the line cuts the curve at two points.

Traps that cost marks

  • Multiplying an inequality by a negative number and forgetting to reverse it.
  • Using D = 0 for a "no real roots" condition, when it should be D < 0.
  • Giving a single value when the question allows a range of values.
  • Dropping the ± when taking the square root of both sides.

title: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

Mathematics — OL. scatter diagrams, types of correlation, line of best fit, interpolation vs extrapolation.

  • 1. Correlation types
  • 2. Line of best fit
  • 3. Using the line
  • 4. Correlation ≠ causation
  • 5. Outliers

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

A scatter diagram plots two variables against each other, and the pattern shows the type of correlation. Positive correlation means that y tends to rise as x rises, and negative correlation means that y falls. No correlation shows no clear pattern.

A line of best fit is a straight line drawn close to the points so that about the same number lie on each side of it. Use it to estimate a value inside the data range, which is interpolation, but be cautious about extending it beyond the data, because that is extrapolation and it may not be reliable. Correlation does not prove that one variable causes the other.

title: Formal Writing: Register and Linking Words — Study Notes
content:
Formal writing uses a measured register: full forms instead of contractions, precise vocabulary, and connectives that show how ideas relate. Using the right register is as important as using correct grammar.

Formal and informal register

Informal writing uses slang, contractions and abbreviations. Formal writing avoids them.

  • Informal: Hey, we can't go tomorrow.
  • Formal: We are unable to attend the meeting tomorrow.

Linking words

Linking words show the relationship between ideas.

  • Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition
  • Contrast: however, nevertheless, although
  • Result: consequently, therefore, as a result
  • Sequence: first, then, meanwhile
  • Similarity: similarly, likewise

Choosing a connective

Ask what the relationship is. If the second idea contradicts the first, use a contrast word. If it follows from the first, use a result word. Avoid starting every sentence with the same word.

Opening and closing formal letters

  • Use Dear Sir or Madam when you do not know the name.
  • Use Dear followed by a name when you do.
  • End with Yours faithfully for Dear Sir or Madam, and Yours sincerely for a named person.

Checking an essay

Remove contractions. Replace casual words with precise ones. Check that each connective matches the logic between the sentences.

  • 2. Quadratic sequences

  • 6. Inverse functions

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example For the sequence 4, 7, 10, 13, the common difference is 3, so the nth term is 3n + 1. Check n = 4: 3(4) + 1 = 13. For f(x) = 2x + 3, the inverse is f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2, so f⁻¹(11) = 4. For composition, g(x) = x² and f(x) = 2x + 3 give fg(3) = f(9) = 21.

Key points to remember

A sequence is a list of terms that follow a rule. Find the term-to-term rule by checking the difference or ratio between consecutive terms. A linear sequence has a constant difference, so its nth term has the form an + b, where a is the common difference.

A function takes an input and gives exactly one output. Use function notation such as f(x) = 2x + 3, and find f(4) by substituting 4 for x. For an inverse function, swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject, and check by composing the two functions.

title: Exam technique: Waves (AS)
content:
### What earns the marks
For phase, one lambda equated to 360 degrees earns the mark. For refraction, n = c/v quoted earns the method mark. For TIR, both conditions stated earn one mark each with sin c = 1/n earning the calculation mark.
### Traps
Error: TIR claimed with one condition only. Correction: denser medium plus beyond critical angle. Error: spectrum order flipped. Correction: radio longest, gamma shortest. Error: phase from amplitude guessed. Correction: phase comes from path or time difference.
### Use the wave equation with care
Apply v = fλ, and convert the frequency and wavelength to SI units first. Check that the answer is a reasonable speed for the medium before you give it.

### Distinguish transverse from longitudinal waves
A transverse wave oscillates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, as with light. A longitudinal wave oscillates parallel to it, as with sound. Use the correct term in your explanation.

### Describe the phase difference clearly
Two points are in phase if they are a whole number of wavelengths apart, and in antiphase if they are an odd number of half-wavelengths apart. Give the phase difference in radians or degrees if asked.

title: Further Algebra — Study Notes
content:
Further Algebra

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics: partial fractions are Pure Mathematics 4 (WMA14, A2); the polynomial-division and modulus sections recap Pure 2 (WMA12, AS).

Polynomial Division and the Remainder Theorem

Divide to rewrite p(x) = (x − a)q(x) + r. The remainder when dividing by (x − a) equals p(a).

Example: p(x) = x³ − 2x² + 5. p(2) = 8 − 8 + 5 = 5, so dividing by (x − 2) leaves remainder 5.

If p(a) = 0, then (x − a) is a factor — that is the factor theorem. Divide out fully to reduce a cubic to a quadratic and factorise completely.

The Modulus Function

|x| measures distance from zero: |x| = x for x ≥ 0, −x for x < 0. Its graph is V-shaped.

Solving |2x − 1| = 5: split into 2x − 1 = 5 or 2x − 1 = −5, giving x = 3 or −2.

Inequalities: |2x − 1| < 5 becomes −5 < 2x − 1 < 5, so −2 < x < 3.

Partial Fractions

Reverse of combining fractions — needed before binomial expansion of rational functions.

  • Repeated linear: (4x + 1)/(x + 1)² = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 1)²
  • Distinct linear: (7x + 4)/(x + 1)(x + 2) = A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 2)

Example: cover the (x + 1) factor with x = −1: B = 3; then compare coefficients for A = 4.

Exam tips: for |ax + b| > c, remember two separate regions; check factor-theorem roots by substitution before long division.

Exam method: partial fractions

Partial fractions split a rational function into simpler fractions whose sum equals the original. Before splitting, check the degrees: if the numerator has degree at least that of the denominator, divide first to get a polynomial plus a proper fraction.

For distinct linear factors (x − p)(x − q), write the expression as A/(x − p) + B/(x − q). Multiply through by the denominator and compare coefficients, or substitute x = p and x = q to find A and B directly. This substitution is the cover-up method and is the fastest route when the factors are linear and distinct.

A repeated factor (x − p)² needs two terms, A/(x − p) + B/(x − p)². An irreducible quadratic factor such as x² + 1 needs a linear numerator over it, (Ax + B)/(x² + 1).

Partial fractions are used to integrate rational functions, so the split is often followed by a logarithmic integral. Check the answer by recombining the fractions at one simple value of x.

Exam cue: State the form of the partial fractions before finding the constants, because the form is credited separately from the values.

Worked example: remainder theorem

Find the remainder when f(x) = x³ − 2x² + 3x − 4 is divided by (x − 2). By the remainder theorem, the remainder equals f(2) = 8 − 8 + 6 − 4 = 2. The same test checks for a factor: if the remainder is zero, then (x − 2) is a factor. Here f(1) = −2 ≠ 0, so (x − 1) is not a factor of f(x).

Exam method: long division with a missing term

When a polynomial is missing a term, write that term with a coefficient of zero before dividing, for example x⁴ + 3x² − 1 becomes x⁴ + 0x³ + 3x² + 0x − 1. Leaving out the placeholder is the usual cause of an incorrect quotient. Check the answer by multiplying the quotient by the divisor and adding the remainder; the result should give back the original polynomial.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Introductory Organic Chemistry and Alkanes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 4 introduces organic chemistry: how carbon compounds are named and drawn, how reactions are classified, how bonds break, and how alkanes are obtained and used. It also carries the safety material on hazard and risk, which is examined in a short-answer question nearly every year. The topic is the vocabulary and grammar of everything that follows, so the mechanisms and IUPAC rules must be exact rather than approximate.

Hazard and risk

A hazard is something with the potential to cause harm: a corrosive acid, a flammable solvent, a toxic gas. Risk is the chance that harm will actually occur when the hazard is used, and it depends on exposure as well as on the hazard itself. A concentrated acid sealed in a bottle is hazardous but carries little risk; the same acid being poured in a busy laboratory carries a real risk.

That distinction is why a risk assessment is made before practical work. It identifies the hazards, decides who might be harmed and how, evaluates the likelihood and severity, and records the controls.

Organic compounds are often hazardous because many are volatile and flammable, and because some are toxic or irritant. Ways to reduce risk include:

  • Working on a smaller scale, which reduces the amount of vapour released and the consequences of a spill.
  • Taking precautions specific to the hazard: a fume cupboard for a volatile toxic liquid, a water bath instead of a naked flame for a flammable solvent, gloves for a corrosive, eye protection at all times.
  • Using an alternative method with less hazardous substances, for example a lower-risk solvent or a reaction that avoids a toxic reagent.
  • Following safe practice for heating: never heat a closed system, and use anti-bump granules or a stirrer to avoid violent boiling.

The question usually asks you to suggest controls for a named procedure, so link each control to the specific hazard rather than listing generic safety advice.

Homologous series and functional groups

A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same general formula, the same functional group and similar chemical properties, in which each member differs from the next by a CH₂ unit. Because the formula changes by CH₂, the molar mass changes by 14, and the physical properties change gradually along the series while the chemical properties stay similar.

A functional group is the group of atoms responsible for the characteristic reactions of a compound. The functional groups examined at AS level are:

FamilyFunctional groupGeneral formula
AlkaneC–C and C–H single bonds onlyCₙH₂ₙ₊₂
Cycloalkanering of C–C single bondsCₙH₂ₙ
AlkeneC=C double bondCₙH₂ₙ
HalogenoalkaneC–X (X = Cl, Br, I)CₙH₂ₙ₊₁X
Alcohol–OHCₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH
Aldehyde–CHOCₙH₂ₙO
KetoneC=O between two carbon atomsCₙH₂ₙO
Carboxylic acid–COOHCₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH

Naming and drawing organic compounds

IUPAC nomenclature follows a fixed sequence of steps. Work through them in order every time.

  1. Find the longest carbon chain containing the functional group; that gives the stem (meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex...).
  2. Number the chain so that the functional group gets the lowest possible number.
  3. Name and number the substituents, and list them alphabetically (ethyl before methyl), with a multiplier for repeats (di-, tri-).
  4. Add the functional group suffix, with its number: -an- for an alkane, -en- for an alkene, -ol for an alcohol, -al for an aldehyde, -one for a ketone, -oic acid for a carboxylic acid.
  5. Use hyphens between numbers and letters, and commas between numbers.

Worked example. The compound CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂OH has a four-carbon chain containing the –OH group, numbered from the end nearer the alcohol so that the OH is on carbon 1. There is a methyl group on carbon 3, so the name is 3-methylbutan-1-ol. Numbering from the other end would give 2-methylbutan-4-ol, which is wrong because the principal group must have the lowest number.

Three ways of drawing a compound are examined and you must be able to convert between them:

  • Structural formula: shows how the atoms are grouped, for example CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.
  • Displayed formula: shows every atom and every bond, including the O–H bond, drawn out in full. Required for mechanisms.
  • Skeletal formula: shows the carbon skeleton as a line, with carbon atoms at the ends and vertices and hydrogen atoms attached to carbon implied. Functional groups and the hydrogens on heteroatoms are drawn explicitly.

Where a compound has a double bond, the position is numbered and geometric isomerism may exist; cis and trans (or E and Z) describe the arrangement around the C=C bond and is covered with the alkenes.

Classifying reactions

Every organic reaction can be placed in one of five categories, and the classification is often the first mark of a question.

  • Addition: two molecules join to form one, with no atom lost. Ethene plus bromine gives 1,2-dibromoethane.
  • Substitution: one atom or group is replaced by another. Methane plus chlorine gives chloromethane plus hydrogen chloride.
  • Oxidation: an increase in the oxygen content or a loss of hydrogen, such as a primary alcohol becoming a carboxylic acid.
  • Reduction: a gain of hydrogen or a loss of oxygen, such as an alkene becoming an alkane.
  • Polymerisation: small molecules (monomers) join to form a large molecule (a polymer), as in the addition polymerisation of ethene.

Bond breaking can be classified in the same way. In homolytic fission the shared pair is split equally, one electron going to each atom, producing two free radicals. In heterolytic fission the shared pair goes entirely to one atom, producing a positive and a negative ion. A free radical is a species with an unpaired electron, shown with a single dot, such as Cl·. An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor, such as HBr or Br₂ in an addition reaction; a nucleophile is an electron-pair donor, such as OH⁻ or NH₃.

Which fission happens depends on the conditions. Ultraviolet light supplies enough energy to break a Cl–Cl bond homolytically, which is why the chlorination of alkanes is a radical reaction; in a polar solvent, heterolytic fission is favoured and produces ions, which is why halogenoalkane hydrolysis is a nucleophilic substitution.

Alkanes and structural isomerism

Alkanes are hydrocarbons: compounds of carbon and hydrogen only. They are saturated, containing single bonds only, and their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; cycloalkanes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ because the ring uses two hydrogens to close.

Structural isomers are molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. Isomerism arises because the carbon skeleton can be arranged differently, and the number of isomers grows quickly with chain length. The alkanes with up to six carbon atoms are examined directly.

FormulaNumber of structural isomersNames
C4H102butane; 2-methylpropane
C5H123pentane; 2-methylbutane; 2,2-dimethylpropane
C6H145hexane; 2-methylpentane; 3-methylpentane; 2,2-dimethylbutane; 2,3-dimethylbutane

A systematic way to find them all is to take the longest chain first, then shorten the main chain by one carbon and place the removed carbon as a methyl substituent in every distinct position, then shorten again. Never place a methyl group on the end of a chain, because that only lengthens the chain and produces a duplicate.

Obtaining alkanes from crude oil

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons. It is separated by fractional distillation, which works because the fractions have different boiling temperatures: the larger the molecule, the stronger the London forces and the higher the boiling temperature. The column is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top, so smaller molecules rise further before condensing.

Demand is for short-chain molecules, especially fuels, so longer chains are broken down by cracking. Thermal cracking uses high temperature and pressure; catalytic cracking uses a zeolite catalyst at a lower temperature and pressure. In both cases a long alkane becomes a shorter alkane and an alkene:

C10H22 → C8H18 + C2H4

Reforming rearranges straight-chain alkanes into branched alkanes and cycloalkanes, or converts them into aromatic compounds, without changing the number of carbon atoms. Branched isomers are preferred in petrol because they burn more smoothly and resist premature ignition (knocking). A typical reforming equation shows a straight chain becoming a branched isomer with the same formula, or a cycloalkane plus hydrogen:

C6H14 → cyclo-C6H12 + H2

Combustion and pollution

Alkanes burn in a plentiful supply of oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water:

C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O

With insufficient oxygen, combustion is incomplete and produces carbon monoxide, carbon particulates (soot) and unburned hydrocarbons. Combustion in air at high temperature also produces oxides of nitrogen, because nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine in the hot engine.

PollutantSourceProblem
Carbon monoxideIncomplete combustionToxic: it binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, forming carboxyhaemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen and the body is starved of it
Oxides of nitrogen, NO and NO₂Nitrogen and oxygen combining at high temperature in enginesDissolve in rainwater to form nitric acid, contributing to acid rain, which damages buildings, soils and trees and acidifies lakes; also contribute to photochemical smog and respiratory irritation
Sulfur dioxideSulfur impurities in fossil fuelsDissolves to form sulfurous and sulfuric acid, contributing to acid rain
Carbon particulatesIncomplete combustion, especially dieselRespiratory damage; contributes to smog and deposits on buildings
Unburned hydrocarbonsIncomplete combustion and evaporationReact with nitrogen oxides in sunlight to form photochemical smog, and some are carcinogenic
Carbon dioxideComplete combustion of any carbon fuelA greenhouse gas, contributing to climate change

Catalytic converters reduce these emissions by converting carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen into carbon dioxide and nitrogen, and oxidising unburned hydrocarbons:

2CO + 2NO → 2CO2 + N2

The catalyst is a ceramic honeycomb coated with platinum, palladium and rhodium. It works best when hot, which is why a cold engine emits more pollution, and it requires unleaded petrol because lead poisons the catalyst.

Alternative fuels and carbon neutrality

Fossil fuels are finite and their combustion adds carbon dioxide that was locked away for millions of years, so alternatives are developed to improve sustainability and reduce emissions. Sustainability means meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

  • Bioethanol is produced by fermentation of sugars from crops. It is renewable, but growing the crops uses land, water and fertiliser, and the carbon dioxide released when it burns was recently absorbed by the plants.
  • Hydrogen releases only water when burned or used in a fuel cell, so it produces no carbon dioxide at the point of use. Whether it is low-carbon depends on how it was made: from renewable electricity by electrolysis it is clean, but from methane by steam reforming it is not.
  • Biodiesel from vegetable oils is renewable and can be used in existing diesel engines, but it competes for agricultural land.

Carbon neutrality means that the amount of carbon dioxide released when a fuel is used is balanced by the amount removed from the atmosphere when the fuel was produced. Petrol is not carbon neutral: the carbon in it was stored underground for millions of years and is added to the atmosphere when burned. Bioethanol is often described as carbon neutral because the crops absorbed carbon dioxide as they grew, but it is only truly neutral if the farming, harvesting, transport and distillation are also carbon neutral, and those processes usually burn fossil fuel. Hydrogen made by electrolysis using renewable electricity can be carbon neutral; hydrogen from steam reforming is not.

Reactions of alkanes

Alkanes are relatively unreactive because their C–C and C–H bonds are strong and non-polar. Two reactions are examined.

Combustion. As above: complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water, incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide and soot. Alkanes are good fuels because they release a large amount of energy per gram.

Halogenation. In the dark there is no reaction. In the presence of ultraviolet light, a halogen such as chlorine reacts with an alkane in a substitution reaction:

CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl

The reaction is a free radical substitution. It proceeds in three stages, and each must be shown with the correct species and the correct curly half-arrows.

Initiation. Ultraviolet light supplies the energy to break the Cl–Cl bond homolytically, producing two chlorine radicals:

Cl2 → 2Cl·

One half-arrow starts at the middle of the Cl–Cl bond and curves to one chlorine atom, and a second half-arrow curves from the bond to the other chlorine atom, showing one electron going each way.

Propagation. A chlorine radical collides with a methane molecule and removes a hydrogen atom, forming hydrogen chloride and a methyl radical; the methyl radical then reacts with a chlorine molecule to form chloromethane and a new chlorine radical:

Cl· + CH4 → CH3· + HCl
CH3· + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl·

Because a chlorine radical is regenerated in the second step, the reaction is a chain reaction. In each propagation step one radical is used and one is produced, so the number of radicals stays constant.

Termination. Two radicals combine and the chain ends:

Cl· + Cl· → Cl2
CH3· + Cl· → CH3Cl
CH3· + CH3· → C2H6

The last termination step explains why ethane is found among the products of the chlorination of methane, even though it is not part of the desired reaction.

Free radical substitution has limited use in synthesis because the reaction does not stop at the first substitution. Chloromethane can react again to give dichloromethane, trichloromethane and tetrachloromethane, and the propagation steps also produce hydrogen chloride and small amounts of ethane, so the product is a mixture that must be separated. To obtain a single product in good yield, a different route such as nucleophilic substitution of an alcohol is preferred.

Typical mistakes

  • Confusing hazard with risk: a hazard is the potential for harm, risk is the chance of it happening.
  • Numbering a chain from the end that gives the substituent the lowest number while ignoring the principal functional group.
  • Writing a radical with a full negative charge instead of a single dot, or forgetting the dot entirely.
  • Showing initiation with a heterolytic split, which would produce ions rather than radicals.
  • Giving the general formula of an alkene (CₙH₂ₙ) for an alkane, or forgetting that cycloalkanes share the alkene's general formula.
  • Missing a structural isomer by placing a methyl group at the end of a chain, which is the same molecule renamed.
  • Describing cracking as the addition of hydrogen, which is hydrogenation, or reforming as breaking molecules into smaller ones.
  • Claiming that a biofuel is automatically carbon neutral without accounting for its production.
  • Leaving ultraviolet light out of the conditions for halogenation, or writing the equation as an addition reaction.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the terms hazard and risk, and explain why a risk assessment is needed before heating ethanol over a Bunsen burner. Answer: a hazard is something with the potential to cause harm; risk is the chance that harm occurs. Ethanol is volatile and highly flammable, so heating it directly risks a flash fire; a risk assessment identifies that hazard and specifies the control, such as heating in a water bath and keeping the apparatus away from naked flames.
  2. Name the compound CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂OH. Answer: the longest chain containing the OH group has four carbons and is numbered from the right so that the OH is on carbon 1; the methyl group is on carbon 3, so the name is 3-methylbutan-1-ol.
  3. Draw and name all the structural isomers of C₅H₁₂. Answer: pentane (a straight chain of five carbons), 2-methylbutane (a four-carbon chain with a methyl on carbon 2), and 2,2-dimethylpropane (a three-carbon chain with two methyls on carbon 2).
  4. Explain why the reaction between methane and chlorine needs ultraviolet light. Answer: the C–H and Cl–Cl bonds are strong and the molecules are non-polar, so collisions at room temperature do not have enough energy to break them. Ultraviolet light provides the energy for homolytic fission of the Cl–Cl bond, which produces chlorine radicals and starts the chain reaction.
  5. Outline the mechanism for the monochlorination of ethane, naming each type of step. Answer: initiation: Cl2 → 2Cl· under UV light. Propagation: Cl· + C2H6 → C2H5· + HCl, then C2H5· + Cl2 → C2H5Cl + Cl·. Termination: Cl· + Cl· → Cl2, C2H5· + Cl· → C2H5Cl, C2H5· + C2H5· → C4H10.

Practise naming and drawing as one skill: take a name, draw the skeletal formula, then the displayed formula, then write the molecular formula, and reverse the process. That fluency is assumed in every later organic topic, especially halogenoalkanes, alcohols and spectra.

title: Exam technique: Operating Systems
content:
### What earns the marks
For OS functions, each of processor, memory, device and file management stated earns credit. For interrupts, the cause plus the handler action earns both marks. For utilities, the named tool matched to its job earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: operating system confused with utility software. Correction: the OS manages hardware; utilities do jobs. Error: buffer and spooling swapped. Correction: buffers smooth speed gaps, spooling queues print jobs. Error: one function listed for describe questions. Correction: give the full set.### Worked example
Asked why an operating system uses interrupts, the strong answer covers four steps: a device signals the processor that it needs attention, the current task is paused and its state saved, the interrupt service routine handles the event, then the saved task resumes. Naming the trigger and the saved state earns the marks the words alone do not.
### Recall check
Name four functions of an operating system and give one example for each. Explain why a defragmenter is a utility and not the operating system itself, by comparing what each one is responsible for.

title: Exam technique: Programming Concepts
content:
### What earns the marks
For loops, the counted loop for known repeats versus conditional for unknown earns the choice mark. For procedures versus functions, parameters in plus value returned out earns each mark. For arrays, the index range declared earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: WHILE used for fixed repeats. Correction: FOR loops count known iterations. Error: function with no return described. Correction: functions return a value; procedures do not. Error: array indices started at 0 in pseudocode. Correction: pseudocode arrays usually start at 1.### Worked example
A FOR loop counting from 1 to 10 has a fixed start and end, so the number of passes is known before the loop begins. A REPEAT UNTIL loop runs at least once and stops when its condition becomes true, which suits input validation. Write the loop type and the reason for choosing it together; naming the construct alone rarely earns the explanation mark.
### Recall check
Write a function that takes two integers and returns the larger one, then state why it is a function rather than a procedure. Declare an array of ten integers and say which index holds the first value under the pseudocode convention the paper uses.

title: Reading for Information and Inference — Study Notes
content:
Reading questions reward two different skills: finding information that is stated, and working out what is implied. Keep them apart when you plan an answer.

Information: what the text says

Information questions ask for facts the writer states directly. Locate the key words in the question, scan the text for matching ideas, and copy only the words you need. Do not add personal comment unless the question asks for it.

Scanning for key words

  • Underline the nouns and verbs in the question.
  • Look for synonyms, because the text rarely repeats the question's exact words.
  • Check the line reference if one is given, then read a sentence either side to confirm the context.

Inference: what the text suggests

An inference is a conclusion supported by evidence. The writer does not state it, so you must show how the evidence points to it.

Building a strong inference

  • Choose a precise quotation or a short phrase.
  • Explain what the word or phrase suggests, using a verb such as suggests, implies or hints.
  • Link the suggestion back to the character, mood or idea the question asks about.

Common mistakes

  • Retelling the plot instead of explaining the evidence.
  • Quoting a long passage with no comment.
  • Stating a fact when the question asks for a feeling or an opinion.

Exam approach

Answer the information questions quickly and accurately, because they are worth marks for precision. Spend the most time on inference questions: one well-explained quotation usually earns more than three vague ones.
