title: Differentiation II — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Differentiation II

Mathematics — A2 (9709). Example: y = x² e^x gives dy/dx = 2x e^x + x² e^x = e^x(2x + x²).

Key areas to revise

  • Product and Quotient Rules
  • Standard Derivatives
  • Chain Rule Everywhere
  • Implicit Differentiation
  • Parametric Curves

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Use the chain rule for composite functions. For y = (x² + 1)³, dy/dx = 3(x² + 1)² × 2x = 6x(x² + 1)². At x = 1 this is 6 × 1 × 4 = 24. Check using the derivative of the outer function at the inner value: 3 × 2² × 2 = 24. The product rule gives d/dx(x sin x) = sin x + x cos x.

Key points to remember

The chain rule differentiates a function of a function: if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x)) × g′(x). The product rule for y = uv gives dy/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx. The quotient rule for y = u/v gives dy/dx = (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v². Identify the outer and inner functions before you differentiate.

For implicit differentiation, differentiate each term with respect to x, remembering that a term in y gives a dy/dx factor, then rearrange for dy/dx. To classify a stationary point, find the second derivative and check its sign there, or check the gradient either side of the point.

title: Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins
content:
Quick revision: Organic Nitrogen Compounds: Amines, Amides, Amino Acids and Proteins

Chemistry A2 level revision notes covering Edexcel IAL Topic 19, focusing on the synthesis, reactions, nomenclature, and properties of amines, amides, amino acids, and polymers.

  • Amines: nomenclature, basicity, hydrogen bonding with water, reactions of primary aliphatic and aromatic amines, and preparation methods.
  • Amides: nomenclature, structural representations, and preparation from acyl chlorides.
  • Polymers: condensation polymerisation for polyamides, proteins, and addition polymers like poly(propenamide) and poly(ethenol), along with physical property analysis.
  • Amino acids and proteins: zwitterions, optical activity, peptide bond formation, acidity and basicity behaviour, and core practical analysis.

Key areas to revise

  • 19.1 Nomenclature, structural, displayed and skeletal formulae for amides, amines and amino acids.
  • 19.2 Reactions of primary aliphatic (butylamine) and aromatic (phenylamine) amines with water, acids, halogenoalkanes, ethanoyl chloride and copper(II) ions.
  • 19.3 Miscibility of amines with water via hydrogen bonding and basicity differences between ammonia, primary aliphatic amines and primary aromatic amines.
  • 19.4 Preparation of primary aliphatic amines from halogenoalkanes and by reduction of nitriles.
  • 19.5 Preparation of aromatic amines from aromatic nitro-compounds using tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid.
  • 19.6 Reaction of aromatic amines with nitrous acid to form benzenediazonium ions and coupling with phenol to form a dye.
  • 19.7 Preparation of amides from acyl chlorides.
  • 19.8 Condensation polymerisation for polyamides and proteins, and addition polymerisation for poly(propenamide) and poly(ethenol).
  • 19.9 Structural formulae of repeat units for nylon, proteins, poly(propenamide) and poly(ethenol).
  • 19.10 Physical properties of polyamides and aqueous solubility of poly(ethenol) via hydrogen bonding for laundry bags and liquid-detergent capsules.
  • 19.11 Amino acid behaviour including acidity, basicity, zwitterions, optical activity on plane-polarised monochromatic light, and peptide bond condensation.
  • 19.12 Core Practical 15 analysis of inorganic and organic unknowns.

Worked example

Describe the preparation of phenylamine from nitrobenzene. Step 1: Heat nitrobenzene under reflux with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid to form a phenylammonium salt mixed with excess acid. Step 2: Add excess sodium hydroxide solution to neutralise the acid and release the free phenylamine base. The final product is separated by steam distillation.

Key points to remember

Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia because alkyl groups push electron density towards the nitrogen atom via the positive inductive effect, increasing the availability of the lone pair for protons. Aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia because the lone pair on the nitrogen delocalises into the benzene ring electron system, reducing proton affinity. Phenylamine reacts with nitrous acid below 5 °C to form a benzenediazonium ion, which reacts with alkaline phenol in a coupling reaction to yield a brightly coloured azo dye. Polyamides like nylon-6,6 are formed by condensation polymerisation releasing small molecules such as water, resulting in hydrogen bonding between polymer chains that imparts high strength and melting points. Poly(ethenol) dissolves in water due to extensive hydrogen bonding between its hydroxyl groups and water molecules, making it ideal for soluble laundry capsules.

How to use this: skim the key areas above, read the full study notes for any weak sections, and finish with the topic quiz to check your understanding.

title: Exam technique: Nuclear Physics
content:
### What earns the marks
For radiations, alpha-beta-gamma ordered by penetration earns one mark with absorbers earns the second. For half-life, each halving step shown earns stepwise credit. For deflection, mass difference used to explain earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: paper claimed to stop beta. Correction: paper stops alpha only. Error: half-life mass subtracted linearly. Correction: halve each period. Error: closer source assumed lower rate. Correction: closer means higher count rate.
### Method marks
For alpha, beta and gamma decay, write the nuclear equation with mass number and atomic number balanced on both sides. Alpha decreases the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2. Beta-minus increases the atomic number by 1 with the mass number unchanged.
### Explain, do not just name
Half-life is the time for half the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay. A question about random decay needs "each nucleus decays independently, so temperature and pressure cannot change the rate".
### Traps
Confusing half-life with the total time for a sample to decay away, and using the count when the question asks for activity. Activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei.

title: Quantum Physics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Quantum Physics

Physics — A2. Light and matter show particle behaviour as well as wave behaviour. The photon model explains the photoelectric effect, and energy levels explain line spectra. Example: a photon of wavelength 500 nm has E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, which is about 2.5 eV.

Key areas to revise

  • Photons: light arrives in packets of energy E = hf. Higher frequency means more energy per photon, and higher intensity means more photons per second.
  • The photoelectric effect: a surface emits electrons only when the frequency is above the threshold frequency f₀. Einstein's equation is hf = φ + KE(max), where φ = hf₀ is the work function.
  • Wave–particle duality: electron diffraction shows waves, and the de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p.
  • Energy levels and line spectra: an electron that falls between levels emits a photon with ΔE = hf, and that gives a line spectrum. Absorption at the same energies gives dark lines.

Core facts to recall

  • Increasing the intensity of light above the threshold frequency increases the number of electrons emitted but not their maximum kinetic energy.
  • Stopping potential V gives the maximum kinetic energy: eV = KE(max).
  • In a calculation, convert nanometres to metres and electronvolts to joules before substituting.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Intermolecular Forces

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7 explains the forces that hold molecules to one another, as distinct from the covalent bonds inside them. These forces are far weaker than covalent bonds, yet they decide boiling temperature, volatility, solubility and the anomalous behaviour of water, and they are the reason a molecule with polar bonds is not necessarily a polar molecule. Examiners test the explanation rather than the label, so every answer should name the force, say what causes it, and relate it to the property asked about.

Three types of intermolecular force

All intermolecular forces are electrostatic: they arise from the attraction between regions of opposite charge. They differ in what creates those regions.

ForceOriginTypical strength
London forces (instantaneous dipole–induced dipole)Fluctuating electron density in one molecule induces a dipole in a neighbourVery weak, but increases with the number of electrons
Permanent dipole–permanent dipolePermanently polar bonds and an asymmetric shape leave one end of the molecule slightly positive and the other slightly negativeWeak, roughly 5–20 kJ mol⁻¹
Hydrogen bondingA hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F in another moleculeStrongest of the three, up to about 40 kJ mol⁻¹

London forces

Electrons are in constant motion, so at any instant the electron distribution in a molecule may be uneven. That creates an instantaneous dipole, which in turn distorts the electron cloud of a neighbouring molecule and induces a dipole in it. The two dipoles then attract. The effect is present in every substance, including the noble gases and non-polar molecules such as methane, and it is the only intermolecular force in a non-polar substance.

The strength of London forces depends on how easily the electron cloud can be distorted, which is called polarisability. Two factors control it:

  • Number of electrons: more electrons means a larger, more polarisable cloud. Iodine (I₂) is a solid and chlorine (Cl₂) a gas at room temperature for this reason.
  • Surface area and shape: a long unbranched chain has more surface contact between neighbouring molecules than a compact branched isomer with the same formula, so it has stronger London forces.

London forces are also the reason why a noble gas such as argon can be liquefied at low temperature, even though its atoms have no permanent dipole and no bonds to break.

Permanent dipole–dipole interactions

A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar: the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge, δ−, and the less electronegative atom carries δ+. If the molecule is not symmetrical, the individual bond dipoles do not cancel, and the molecule as a whole has a permanent dipole. Neighbouring molecules then line up with opposite ends together, and the attraction is a permanent dipole–permanent dipole interaction.

Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is polar and its molecules attract this way. Carbon dioxide has two polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is linear and symmetrical, so the dipoles cancel exactly and CO₂ has no permanent dipole; its molecules are held only by London forces. Tetrachloromethane, CCl₄, is also symmetrical and non-polar for the same reason, while trichloromethane, CHCl₃, is polar because the fourth substituent is hydrogen rather than chlorine and the symmetry is broken. Whether a molecule is polar therefore needs two checks: are the bonds polar, and is the shape symmetrical?

Hydrogen bonding

Hydrogen bonding is a particularly strong form of permanent dipole attraction. It occurs only when two conditions are satisfied:

  • A hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom, limited to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine.
  • A lone pair is available on an N, O or F atom in a neighbouring molecule, which the δ+ hydrogen can approach.

The result is a strong attraction between the δ+ hydrogen and the lone pair, often drawn as a dotted line: O–H···O. The bond is directional, which is why hydrogen bonding produces specific structures rather than a random arrangement.

Water, ammonia and hydrogen fluoride all hydrogen bond:

SubstanceHydrogen-bonding unitNumber of hydrogen bonds per molecule in the liquid
H₂OO–H···OTwo hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs allow an extensive network
NH₃N–H···NThree hydrogen atoms but only one lone pair, so fewer bonds than water
HFF–H···FOne hydrogen atom and three lone pairs; chains of HF molecules

Hydrogen bonding is not the same as a covalent bond to hydrogen. It is an intermolecular attraction, so it is broken when a substance melts or boils, while the O–H covalent bond stays intact. That distinction is worth stating explicitly in an answer.

The anomalous properties of water

Water's properties do not follow the pattern of similar molecules, and hydrogen bonding is the explanation.

High melting and boiling temperatures. Compared with hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, which has a similar formula, water boils about 160 °C higher. The molecules of H₂S are held only by London forces and weak dipole–dipole attractions, whereas each water molecule can hydrogen bond to several neighbours. Breaking those attractions needs far more energy, so the melting and boiling temperatures are unusually high, and water is a liquid at room temperature while H₂S is a gas.

Ice is less dense than liquid water. In ice, each water molecule hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a regular tetrahedral arrangement, which holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid and leaves open hexagonal spaces. When ice melts, much of that open framework collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so liquid water is denser than ice. This is why ice floats, and why a lake freezes from the top, insulating the water beneath and allowing aquatic life to survive.

Hydrogen bonding also gives water a high surface tension, a high specific heat capacity and a high enthalpy of vaporisation, all of which follow from the energy needed to overcome the network of hydrogen bonds.

Predicting hydrogen bonding

To decide whether a molecule can hydrogen bond, look for an O–H, N–H or F–H group and for a lone pair on O, N or F. Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, can hydrogen bond because of its O–H group; ethanal, CH₃CHO, has a C=O bond with lone pairs but no hydrogen attached to an electronegative atom, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond, although its oxygen can accept one. A molecule such as CH₃F has no H–F bond, so it does not hydrogen bond. Methanol and water mix in all proportions because both can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, whereas methane, with only C–H bonds, cannot.

Intermolecular forces and physical properties

Boiling temperature is a measure of the energy needed to separate molecules, so it reports the strength of the intermolecular forces, not the strength of the covalent bonds. Four trends are examined.

Boiling temperature of alkanes increases with chain length. Each additional CH₂ group adds electrons and surface area, so the London forces between the molecules become stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. Methane boils at −162 °C, ethane at −89 °C and decane at 174 °C.

Branching lowers the boiling temperature. Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane have the same molecular formula, but the branched molecule is more compact. Its molecules have less surface contact, so its London forces are weaker and it boils at 9.5 °C compared with 36 °C for pentane. The same reasoning explains why branched isomers have lower boiling temperatures throughout the alkanes.

Alcohols have higher boiling temperatures than alkanes of similar electron count. Ethanol (46 electrons) boils at 78 °C while propane (26 electrons) boils at −42 °C. The comparison is not quite like for like, but the key point is that ethanol molecules hydrogen bond through the O–H group, while propane molecules have only London forces. The hydrogen bonding more than compensates for the smaller number of electrons.

Boiling temperatures of the hydrogen halides are not a simple trend. HF is the highest because of hydrogen bonding. From HCl to HBr to HI, London forces grow as the number of electrons increases, so the boiling temperatures rise in that order: HCl −85 °C, HBr −67 °C, HI −35 °C. HF, at 20 °C, sits far above the smooth trend, and that outlier is the evidence for hydrogen bonding.

Choosing a solvent

Dissolving depends on the solute particles being separated and surrounded by solvent particles, so the solute–solvent attractions must be comparable to the forces they replace. In practice, like dissolves like.

  • Water dissolves ionic compounds because the polar water molecules attract the ions: the partially negative oxygen surrounds a cation and the partially positive hydrogens surround an anion. This is hydration, and it releases hydration enthalpy that helps to compensate for the lattice enthalpy that must be overcome.
  • Water dissolves simple alcohols such as methanol and ethanol, because the alcohol's O–H group can both donate a hydrogen bond to water and accept one from it. As the hydrocarbon chain grows, the non-polar part becomes a larger fraction of the molecule and solubility falls: ethanol mixes with water in all proportions, but hexan-1-ol is only slightly soluble.
  • Water is a poor solvent for halogenoalkanes and other polar organic molecules such as chloroethane. The molecule has a dipole, so it is attracted to water to some extent, but it has no O–H group and cannot hydrogen bond with water, and its hydrocarbon part cannot interact favourably with the water network. The solute–solvent attractions are too weak to overcome the hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
  • Non-aqueous solvents are used when the solute's intermolecular forces resemble the solvent's. Iodine, a non-polar molecule held by London forces, dissolves in hexane, which is also non-polar; bromine dissolves in cyclohexane for the same reason. Propanone is a useful intermediate case, dissolving both polar and many non-polar substances because it has a polar C=O group and a hydrocarbon part.

A good answer states the force between solvent molecules, the force between solute and solvent, and whether the second is strong enough to replace the first.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying a substance has hydrogen bonds when the hydrogen is bonded to carbon; only N–H, O–H and F–H count.
  • Describing hydrogen bonding as a covalent bond, or claiming that boiling water breaks O–H bonds.
  • Assuming that a molecule with polar bonds must be polar, without checking whether the shape cancels the dipoles.
  • Attributing the trend in alkane boiling temperatures to stronger covalent bonds rather than to stronger London forces.
  • Explaining branching by saying the molecule has fewer electrons; the number of electrons is the same, the surface contact is not.
  • Explaining the lower density of ice as an expansion on freezing without mentioning the open hydrogen-bonded lattice.
  • Describing London forces as "weak covalent forces" or as attractions between permanent dipoles.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why the boiling temperature of iodine is higher than that of chlorine. Answer: iodine has more electrons and a larger, more polarisable electron cloud, so the London forces between its molecules are stronger; more energy is needed to separate the molecules.
  2. Explain why 2-methylbutane has a lower boiling temperature than pentane. Answer: both have the molecular formula C5H12 and the same number of electrons. 2-methylbutane is more branched and more compact, so its molecules have less surface area in contact, the London forces between them are weaker, and less energy is needed to separate them.
  3. Explain, in terms of intermolecular forces, why ethanol is soluble in water but chloroethane is not. Answer: ethanol has an O–H group and can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds with water, so the solute–solvent attractions are strong enough to replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Chloroethane is polar but has no O–H group, so it cannot hydrogen bond with water; its attractions to water are too weak to compensate for breaking the water–water hydrogen bonds.
  4. Explain why ice is less dense than liquid water. Answer: in ice each water molecule forms hydrogen bonds to four neighbours in a tetrahedral arrangement, producing an open lattice with spaces between the molecules. When ice melts the lattice collapses and the molecules pack more closely, so the liquid is denser.
  5. Identify the strongest intermolecular force in each of the following and justify your answer: (a) HCl, (b) CH₃OH, (c) CCl₄. Answer: (a) permanent dipole–permanent dipole, because the molecule is polar and has no O–H, N–H or F–H group; (b) hydrogen bonding, because of the O–H group; (c) London forces, because the molecule is symmetrical and the bond dipoles cancel, so it is non-polar.

When revising, practise the three-part answer: name the force, explain what causes it in these molecules, then link it to the property in the question. Move on to Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria next, where the same molecular picture explains why reactions need collisions with sufficient energy.

title: Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages — Study Notes
content:
Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): conversions between fractions, decimals and percentages; percentage change; reverse percentages; compound change.

1. Conversions

Fraction → decimal by division; decimal → percentage ×100. Recurring decimals: let x = 0.7̄, then 10x − x = 7 ⇒ x = 7/9.

Compare fractions by common denominator or by converting to decimals.

2. Operating on fractions

  • Add/subtract: common denominator. 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.
  • Multiply: top×top, bottom×bottom. Divide: flip and multiply — 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 5/6.
  • Of: 3/5 of 45 = 27.

3. Percentage change

change ÷ original × 100. Increase $80 by 15%: 80 × 1.15 = $92.

4. Reverse percentages

Original = new ÷ multiplier. "After a 20% increase a coat is $72" → 72 ÷ 1.2 = $60. "After 12% discount a phone is $440" → 440 ÷ 0.88 = $500.

5. Compound change

Multiplierⁿ. Simple interest I = Prt/100 vs compound P(1 + r/100)ⁿ.

Example: $800 at 3% for 4 years → 800 × 1.03⁴ = $900.41. Successive +10% then −10% ⇒ ×0.99 (net 1% decrease).

Exam tips: identify "increase TO" vs "increase BY"; for reverse questions divide, never subtract the percentage; quote money to 2 d.p.

Equivalent fractions and simplifying

Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number. Simplify by dividing both by their highest common factor. Mixed numbers are converted to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing.

Adding and subtracting fractions

Find the lowest common denominator, rewrite each fraction over it, then add or subtract the numerators only. Multiplying fractions multiplies the numerators and the denominators; dividing multiplies by the reciprocal of the second fraction.

Percentages

To find a percentage of a quantity, multiply by the decimal equivalent: 15% of 240 is 0.15 × 240 = 36. Percentage change is the change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100. Repeated percentage change multiplies by one plus the multiplier each time, so 5% increase twice is × 1.05 × 1.05.

Worked example: reverse percentage

After a 15% increase, a price is 230. The original price is the amount that equals 115% of itself, so divide by 1.15: 230 ÷ 1.15 = 200. Finding 15% of 230 and subtracting it gives 195.50, which is wrong, because 15% is taken of the original price, not the new one.

Compound change

1000 is invested at 4% per year for 3 years. Each year multiplies the value by 1.04, so the final value is 1000 × 1.04 × 1.04 × 1.04 = 1000 × 1.04³ = 1124.86 (to 2 decimal places). Simple interest would give only 1120, so the difference shows why compound growth is treated separately in the examination.

Choosing a method

  • To find a fraction of an amount, divide by the denominator and multiply by the numerator: 3/4 of 80 = 80 ÷ 4 × 3 = 60.
  • To add or subtract fractions, write both over a common denominator first.
  • Write a percentage change as a multiplier: a 20% decrease is multiplier 0.8, and a 5% increase is 1.05.

Exam point: give the final answer in the form the question asks for, such as a fraction in its simplest form or a percentage to 1 decimal place.

title: Operating Systems — Study Notes
content:
Operating Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): OS roles, memory/process management, hardware–software layer, interrupts, buffers, utility software.

1. What an OS does

Manages memory, processes/files, I/O via drivers, security (users, permissions), and provides the UI (CLI/GUI) between user, applications and hardware.

2. Memory and process management

  • Paging/segmentation move programs in/out; virtual memory extends RAM to disk when RAM is full.
  • Multitasking: scheduler gives each process time slices; context switching saves/restores state.

3. Interrupts and buffers

Interrupts signal events (I/O complete, timer); CPU saves context, services via ISR, resumes. Buffers hold data in transit (printing) so slow devices don't block the CPU; spooling queues jobs.

4. Utility software

Disk formatter, defragmenter (reduces head movement on HDDs; unnecessary for SSD), backup scheduler, compression, antivirus, file compression.

5. UI and drivers

CLI: precise, scriptable, low overhead. GUI: icons/windows, discoverable, more resources. Device drivers translate OS calls to hardware specifics — each device needs its own.

Exam tips: "manage" verbs earn marks: manages memory, manages processes, manages peripherals; explain virtual memory by RAM-full scenario, not definition alone.

Interrupts and scheduling

An interrupt is a signal that tells the processor to stop its current task and deal with an event, such as a key press, a timer ending or an error. The processor saves the state of the current task, runs the interrupt service routine, and then resumes the task it was doing. Interrupts let the processor respond to devices without checking them constantly.

The operating system manages several programs at once through scheduling. Each program receives processor time in turn, which gives the impression that they run at the same time. Memory management keeps each program's data separate, and the operating system provides a user interface and manages files and devices.

Exam tip: describe the steps of an interrupt in order: save state, run the routine, restore state.

Worked example: round-robin scheduling

Three processes arrive together at time 0: A needs 5 ms, B needs 3 ms and C needs 1 ms. The time quantum is 2 ms. The timeline is A (0 to 2), B (2 to 4), C (4 to 5, finished), A (5 to 7), B (7 to 8, finished), A (8 to 9, finished). The completion times are A = 9 ms, B = 8 ms and C = 5 ms. The processor is shared fairly, but a short job such as C still waits for the earlier turns of the others.

Virtual memory and paging

The operating system divides a program into fixed-size pages and keeps only the pages in use in main memory. When a page that is needed is not in RAM, a page fault occurs and the operating system loads it from secondary storage. This allows programs larger than the physical memory to run, at the cost of slower access when faults are frequent.

Batch processing and multiprogramming

  • Batch processing runs a set of jobs one after another with no user interaction, which suits payroll runs.
  • Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory at once and switches between them, so the processor is not idle while one job waits for input or output.
  • Real-time systems guarantee a response within a fixed deadline, which matters in control systems such as a car's braking system.

Exam point: when a question asks why an operating system is needed, link each function to the hardware problem it solves, for example scheduling because there is one processor and many processes.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Halogenoalkanes, Alcohols and Spectra

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 10 is the largest organic topic in the AS year. It covers how to classify reactions and mechanisms, the chemistry of halogenoalkanes and alcohols with their characteristic substitution, elimination and oxidation reactions, the practical techniques used to prepare and purify a liquid organic compound, and the two spectroscopic methods, mass spectrometry and infrared, that identify what a compound is. The mechanisms are examined with curly arrows, so the drawing and the explanation must both be right.

Classifying reactions and the idea of a mechanism

Every organic reaction belongs to one of these categories, and the classification is often the first mark of a question:

  • Addition: two species combine into one, with nothing lost, as when an alkene adds hydrogen bromide.
  • Elimination: a small molecule is removed from a larger one, leaving a double bond, as when a halogenoalkane forms an alkene.
  • Substitution: one atom or group is replaced by another, as when a halogenoalkane becomes an alcohol.
  • Oxidation: gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen, as when an alcohol becomes an aldehyde or a carboxylic acid.
  • Reduction: gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen.
  • Hydrolysis: breaking a bond by reaction with water or aqueous alkali, as in the hydrolysis of a halogenoalkane.
  • Polymerisation: monomers join into a polymer.

A reaction mechanism is a step-by-step description of how the electrons move during a reaction. It shows which bonds break, in what order, and which species are formed on the way. Mechanisms are drawn with curly arrows: a full arrow shows the movement of a pair of electrons, and a half-arrow shows the movement of one electron in a radical reaction. A curly arrow always starts at a bond or at a lone pair and points to where the electrons go.

The type of mechanism depends on bond polarity. When a bond is polar, the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge and the other a partial positive charge, so the molecule has an electron-rich site and an electron-poor site. That is an invitation to attack by a species with the opposite character:

  • A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor: it has a lone pair and is attracted to an electron-poor (δ+) carbon. Examples are OH⁻, NH₃, CN⁻ and water.
  • An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor: it is attracted to an electron-rich site such as a C=C double bond. Examples are HBr, Br₂ and the nitrosonium ion in nitration.

So a polar C–X bond, with δ+ on the carbon, is attacked by nucleophiles and undergoes nucleophilic substitution. A C=C double bond with its exposed π electrons is attacked by electrophiles and undergoes electrophilic addition. Heterolytic fission produces these ions and charged species; homolytic fission produces radicals and leads to radical substitution.

Halogenoalkanes: naming and classification

A halogenoalkane has a halogen atom in place of a hydrogen on an alkane chain. The halogen is named as a prefix (fluoro-, chloro-, bromo-, iodo-) with its position number, and the chain is numbered to give the substituent the lowest number: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl is 1-chloropropane, and CH₃CHClCH₃ is 2-chloropropane.

Halogenoalkanes are classified by how many carbon atoms are bonded directly to the carbon that carries the halogen:

ClassDefinitionExample
Primary (1°)The C–X carbon is bonded to one other carbonCH₃CH₂Cl, chloroethane
Secondary (2°)The C–X carbon is bonded to two other carbonsCH₃CHClCH₃, 2-chloropropane
Tertiary (3°)The C–X carbon is bonded to three other carbons(CH₃)₃CCl, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane

Reactions of halogenoalkanes

The reagent and the solvent decide whether substitution or elimination happens. Learn the table as a set of conditions, not as separate facts.

Reagent and conditionsProductTypeEquation (with 1-bromopropane)
Aqueous potassium hydroxide, heatAlcoholNucleophilic substitutionC3H7Br + OH⁻ → C3H7OH + Br⁻
Ethanolic potassium hydroxide, heatAlkeneEliminationC3H7Br + OH⁻ → C3H6 + H2O + Br⁻
Aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol, warmAlcohol, with a silver halide precipitateHydrolysisC3H7Br + H2O → C3H7OH + HBr, then Ag+ + Br⁻ → AgBr(s)
Alcoholic ammonia, heated under pressureAmineNucleophilic substitutionC3H7Br + 2NH3 → C3H7NH2 + NH4Br
Alcoholic potassium cyanide, heatNitrileNucleophilic substitutionC3H7Br + CN⁻ → C3H7CN + Br⁻

In the first reaction the hydroxide ion acts as a nucleophile: its lone pair attacks the δ+ carbon and the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically, with the bromide ion leaving. In the second the same ion acts as a base instead, removing a hydrogen from an adjacent carbon and pushing the electrons into a new C=C bond, so the molecule loses HBr and becomes an alkene. The solvent is the switch: water favours substitution, ethanol favours elimination.

Ammonia is used in excess because the first substitution gives an amine, which can itself act as a nucleophile and react again with the halogenoalkane to give a secondary and then a tertiary amine. The cyanide reaction is useful because it lengthens the carbon chain by one carbon: the nitrile can be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid.

The nucleophilic substitution mechanisms

For a primary halogenoalkane, the mechanism is a one-step bimolecular process. In the exam you draw the displayed formula of the halogenoalkane, place the nucleophile beside it, and use curly arrows.

With aqueous potassium hydroxide. The arrow from the lone pair on the oxygen of OH⁻ points to the δ+ carbon of the C–Br bond. A second arrow starts at the middle of the C–Br bond and points to the bromine, showing the pair leaving with the bromine as Br⁻. The product is the alcohol and the leaving group.

With ammonia. The arrow from the lone pair on the nitrogen of NH₃ points to the δ+ carbon, and a second arrow from the C–Br bond points to the bromine. The initial product is an alkylammonium ion, which loses a proton to give the amine, so the overall equation is a substitution of Br by NH₂. Drawing the ammonium ion is the detail that separates a full-mark answer from a partial one.

The carbon being attacked is electron-poor because bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so the bond is polarised Cδ+–Brδ−. The nucleophile is electron-rich and is attracted to that δ+ carbon, which is why the mechanism is described as nucleophilic substitution rather than electrophilic addition. A secondary or tertiary halogenoalkane may instead react by an ionisation-then-attack route, with a carbocation intermediate; that distinction, SN1 versus SN2, is examined in Unit 4, not here.

Comparing the rates of hydrolysis

The rate of hydrolysis can be followed by warming the halogenoalkane with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol and timing how long it takes for a precipitate of silver halide to appear. Water is the nucleophile, and the silver ion removes the halide as it is released, which keeps the reaction moving and makes the halide visible.

R-X + H2O → R-OH + HX          then          Ag+(aq) + X-(aq) → AgX(s)
HalidePrecipitate colourRelative rate
Chloro-WhiteSlowest
Bromo-CreamIntermediate
Iodo-Pale yellowFastest

Two comparisons are made. Structurally, tertiary halogenoalkanes hydrolyse faster than secondary, which are faster than primary, because the intermediate carbocation is more stable when more alkyl groups can donate electron density, and because the crowded carbon is more easily approached. Across the halogens, the rate increases from chloro- to bromo- to iodo- because the C–X bond enthalpy decreases down the group: C–Cl is the strongest bond, so it is the hardest to break, and C–I the weakest, so it breaks most readily.

Core Practical 5 carries out exactly this investigation. A measured volume of the halogenoalkane is added to silver nitrate in ethanol at a fixed temperature, and the time to the first appearance of the precipitate is recorded; rate is taken as 1/time. Water baths keep the temperature constant, and the same volumes and concentrations must be used so that the comparison is fair. The evaluation should note that the precipitate appearance is a subjective endpoint, that temperature control is critical because rate is very sensitive to it, and that different halogenoalkanes have different solubilities in ethanol.

Core Practical 6 prepares 2-chloro-2-methylpropane by shaking 2-methylpropan-2-ol with concentrated hydrochloric acid. The tertiary alcohol reacts readily by substitution, and the product separates as an organic layer, which is washed with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution to remove excess acid, dried, and distilled. The boiling temperature of the distillate is checked against the data book value as a test of purity.

Alcohols: naming and classification

An alcohol contains the –OH group. The suffix is -ol with the position number: CH₃CH₂OH is ethanol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH is propan-1-ol, and CH₃CHOHCH₃ is propan-2-ol.

Alcohols are classified in the same way as halogenoalkanes, by the number of carbons attached to the carbon carrying the –OH group: primary (one), secondary (two), tertiary (three). This classification predicts how each alcohol behaves on oxidation, so it is examined directly.

ClassExampleOxidation product
Primarypropan-1-olPropanal with distillation, propanoic acid under reflux
Secondarypropan-2-olPropanone; no further oxidation under normal conditions
Tertiary2-methylpropan-2-olNo reaction with acidified dichromate at AS level

Reactions of alcohols

Reagent and conditionsProductNotes
Oxygen in air, ignitionCarbon dioxide and waterCombustion; alcohols are fuels
Phosphorus(V) chloride, PCl5, room temperatureChloroalkaneAlso gives misty fumes of HCl and is used as a qualitative test for an –OH group
Concentrated sulfuric acid with potassium bromideBromoalkaneThe HBr generated in situ substitutes the OH
Red phosphorus with iodineIodoalkaneRed phosphorus and iodine generate phosphorus(III) iodide in situ
Concentrated phosphoric acid, heatAlkeneElimination of water (dehydration)
Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heatAldehyde or carboxylic acid (primary), ketone (secondary)The orange dichromate turns green as it is reduced

For the halogenating agents, the mechanisms are not required, but the equations and the observation are. With PCl₅ the test is the white fumes or misty vapour of hydrogen chloride, which turns damp blue litmus paper red. For the sulfuric acid and potassium bromide route, the acid and the bromide produce hydrogen bromide, which then reacts with the alcohol:

KBr + H2SO4 → KHSO4 + HBr
C2H5OH + HBr → C2H5Br + H2O

Concentrated phosphoric acid dehydrates an alcohol to an alkene, and the alkene can be identified by decolourising bromine water.

Oxidation of alcohols

The oxidising agent is acidified potassium dichromate(VI), written as [O] in equations. The colour change from orange to green is the visual evidence that oxidation has occurred.

Primary alcohols. The product depends on the apparatus. If the aldehyde is distilled off as it forms, it escapes before it can be oxidised further:

C2H5OH + [O] → CH3CHO + H2O

If the mixture is heated under reflux, the aldehyde stays in contact with the oxidising agent and is oxidised again to the carboxylic acid:

C2H5OH + 2[O] → CH3COOH + H2O

Secondary alcohols. Oxidation gives a ketone, which resists further oxidation because the carbonyl carbon has no hydrogen attached:

CH3CHOHCH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O

Tertiary alcohols. No reaction with acidified dichromate, because the carbon carrying the OH has no hydrogen to remove and cannot form a C=O bond.

The products are distinguished by tests:

  • Aldehydes reduce Fehling's solution to a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, and Benedict's solution similarly, on warming. Ketones do not react.
  • Carboxylic acids react with sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate to give effervescence of carbon dioxide; aldehydes and ketones do not.
  • Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with an aldehyde and no change with a ketone.

Preparing and purifying a liquid organic compound

Five techniques are examined together, because a preparation uses several of them in sequence.

  • Heating under reflux: a vertical condenser returns vapour to the flask, so the mixture can be heated for a long time without losing solvent or volatile product. It is used when the reaction is slow or needs prolonged heating, such as the oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid.
  • Extraction with a solvent using a separating funnel: the product is shaken with a solvent in which it is more soluble than in the reaction mixture, the two layers are allowed to separate, and the layer containing the product is run off. The stopper must be vented during shaking to release pressure.
  • Distillation: separates a volatile product from involatile impurities or from a solvent with a different boiling temperature. The fraction boiling over the expected range is collected.
  • Drying with an anhydrous salt: anhydrous magnesium sulfate or calcium chloride is added to remove traces of water; it clumps and can be filtered off once it stops clumping.
  • Boiling temperature determination: a pure compound boils at a sharp, known temperature. A range that is wide or different from the data book value indicates impurities.

Core Practical 7 oxidises propan-1-ol to propanal and to propanoic acid. For the aldehyde, the oxidising agent is added slowly to the alcohol and the product is distilled off as it forms, collecting the fraction that boils near 48 °C. For the acid, the mixture is heated under reflux, then the acid is separated and purified. The questions on this practical usually ask why the aldehyde must be removed as it forms, and what the observation of the dichromate colour shows.

Mass spectrometry

In a mass spectrometer a molecule is ionised, usually by electron impact, and the ions are separated by mass-to-charge ratio. The most intense peak of the molecular ion, M⁺, gives the relative molecular mass. Fragmentation produces smaller ions, and the pattern of peaks is a fingerprint of the structure.

  • The molecular ion peak is the peak with the highest m/z value (ignoring small isotope peaks), and its m/z equals Mᵣ.
  • A peak at M−15 often indicates the loss of a methyl group, CH₃.
  • A peak at M−29 indicates the loss of an ethyl group, C₂H₅.
  • Peaks at 15, 29, 43 correspond to CH₃⁺, C₂H₅⁺ and C₃H₇⁺, and are common in alkanes and alkyl chains.
  • A peak at m/z 31 is characteristic of CH₂OH⁺ from a primary alcohol.
  • For a chloro- or bromo-compound, the isotope pattern is decisive: chlorine gives peaks two units apart in roughly 3:1 ratio, and bromine gives peaks two units apart in roughly 1:1 ratio, because of the ³⁵Cl/³⁷Cl and ⁷⁹Br/⁸¹Br isotopes.

Worked example. A compound has a molecular ion peak at m/z 74 and major fragments at 43 and 31. Mᵣ = 74 is consistent with C₄H₁₀O (4 × 12 + 10 + 16 = 74). A fragment at 43 corresponds to C₃H₇⁺ (loss of CH₂OH), and a fragment at 31 corresponds to CH₂OH⁺, so the compound is butan-1-ol, a primary alcohol. A secondary alcohol such as butan-2-ol would not give the 31 peak, because it cannot lose a CH₂OH group.

Infrared spectroscopy

Infrared radiation is absorbed by bonds that vibrate with a change in dipole. Different functional groups absorb at different wavenumbers, so an infrared spectrum identifies which groups are present.

BondWavenumber / cm⁻¹Appearance and group
O–H2500–3300, broadBroad absorption, carboxylic acid (with C=O)
O–H3230–3550, broadBroad absorption, alcohol
N–H3300–3500Sharp, amines
C–H2850–3300Stretching in alkanes, alkenes and aldehydes
C=O1680–1750, strongStrong sharp absorption: aldehyde, ketone or carboxylic acid
C=C1620–1680Weak to moderate, alkenes
C–O1000–1300Alcohols, ethers, esters
C–X500–800Halogenoalkanes

Two practical points are examined. First, an absorption at about 1700 cm⁻¹ alone does not distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone from a carboxylic acid: look for the broad O–H absorption of the acid as well, or the aldehyde C–H absorptions near 2700 and 2800 cm⁻¹. Second, the region below about 1500 cm⁻¹ is the fingerprint region, with many overlapping absorptions; it is used to identify a compound by matching its whole spectrum to a known one, not to identify individual groups.

The O–H absorption of an alcohol is broad because hydrogen bonding varies the O–H bond strength across the sample; the carboxylic acid O–H is even broader and extends over a wider range because of strong hydrogen bonding. This is why the shape and position of the broad absorption, not just its presence, carries information.

Core Practical 8: analysis of unknowns

An unknown inorganic or organic substance is identified by a sequence of tests, each chosen to eliminate possibilities. For an organic unknown, the sequence is usually: test for unsaturation with bromine water; test for an alcohol with PCl₅ or by oxidation with acidified dichromate; test for an aldehyde with Fehling's or Tollens' reagent; test for a carboxylic acid with sodium carbonate; then use infrared and mass spectra to confirm the functional groups and the molecular mass. Each positive result should be recorded with its observation, because the observation is the evidence.

Typical mistakes

  • Using aqueous KOH for elimination, or ethanolic KOH for substitution: the solvent decides the reaction.
  • Forgetting that the hydroxide ion is a nucleophile in substitution but a base in elimination.
  • Drawing a curly arrow from the wrong place, or drawing arrows that point to an atom rather than to a bond or lone pair.
  • Thinking a tertiary alcohol oxidises to a ketone; it does not react under these conditions.
  • Distilling a primary alcohol oxidation and expecting the carboxylic acid, or refluxing and expecting the aldehyde.
  • Calling the dichromate colour change a test for an aldehyde; it shows that oxidation has occurred, and Fehling's or Tollens' distinguishes the aldehyde.
  • Confusing the broad O–H absorption of an alcohol with the sharper C=O absorption, or ignoring the fingerprint region.
  • Quoting the base peak as the molecular ion peak; the base peak is the most intense, not necessarily the highest m/z.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain why 1-iodobutane hydrolyses faster than 1-chlorobutane with aqueous silver nitrate. Answer: the C–I bond has a lower bond enthalpy than the C–Cl bond because the halogen atom is larger and the overlap with the carbon orbital is poorer, so the C–I bond breaks more easily and the iodide is released faster, giving a precipitate sooner.
  2. State the reagent and conditions needed to convert 1-bromopropane into propan-1-ol, and name the mechanism. Answer: aqueous potassium hydroxide, heated; nucleophilic substitution.
  3. Describe how you would obtain propanal from propan-1-ol, including the apparatus and the observation. Answer: warm propan-1-ol with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and distill the product as it forms, collecting the fraction boiling near 48 °C. The orange dichromate turns green. Distilling the aldehyde off prevents it being oxidised further to propanoic acid.
  4. A compound with the molecular formula C₃H₇Br gives a precipitate with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol, and on heating with ethanolic potassium hydroxide gives a gas that decolourises bromine water. Identify the type of reaction and explain the observation. Answer: the first is hydrolysis, releasing bromide ions that give a cream precipitate of silver bromide. The second is elimination, producing propene, which decolourises bromine water by electrophilic addition.
  5. A compound shows a strong absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹, a broad absorption at 3000 cm⁻¹ and no absorption at 2500–3300 cm⁻¹. Its mass spectrum has a molecular ion at m/z 58. Identify the compound. Answer: Mᵣ = 58 is consistent with C₃H₆O. The strong 1715 cm⁻¹ absorption is C=O, and the absence of a very broad acid O–H absorption means it is not a carboxylic acid, so it is propanone (or propanal, which would also show aldehyde C–H absorptions near 2700–2800 cm⁻¹).

Revise this topic by working from the functional group outwards: reagent, conditions, product, mechanism, then the observation that proves it. That single chain of reasoning answers most of the questions on halogenoalkanes, alcohols and spectra.

title: Dynamics — Study Notes
content:
Dynamics

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 1 (WPH11), sat at AS.

Momentum

  • Momentum p = mv. It is a vector, with unit kg m s⁻¹, and it has the same direction as the velocity.
  • Momentum and kinetic energy are different. Momentum is a vector and changes sign with direction. Kinetic energy is a scalar.

Newton's laws of motion

  • First law: a body stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity unless a resultant (net) force acts on it.
  • Second law: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = ma for constant mass. The acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force.
  • Third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The two forces are the same type and act on different bodies, so they never cancel.

Weight and mass

Mass is the amount of matter (scalar, kg). Weight is the gravitational force on it, W = mg (vector, N). Mass is the same everywhere; weight changes with the value of g.

Impulse

Impulse = FΔt = Δp = m(v − u). The area under a force–time graph equals the impulse. A longer contact time for the same change in momentum means a smaller average force, which is why airbags and crumple zones work.

Conservation of linear momentum

For a system with no resultant external force, the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after. In an elastic collision momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved. In an inelastic collision only momentum is conserved. In a collision where the bodies stick together, the kinetic energy lost is greatest.

Worked example: a 0.5 kg trolley moving at 4 m s⁻¹ hits a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. Total momentum before = 0.5 × 4 = 2.0 kg m s⁻¹. Common velocity = 2.0 / 1.5 ≈ 1.3 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: choose a positive direction and keep signs consistent in every momentum term. State that the system is isolated before applying conservation. For a recoil question, the two momenta are equal and opposite.

Worked example: explosion and recoil

A 2.0 kg gun at rest fires a 0.020 kg bullet at 300 m s⁻¹. Before the shot, total momentum is zero. After it, the bullet has momentum 0.020 × 300 = 6.0 kg m s⁻¹ forwards, so the gun must recoil with momentum 6.0 kg m s⁻¹ backwards. Its recoil velocity is 6.0/2.0 = 3.0 m s⁻¹. The same reasoning holds for any explosion from rest: the fragments' momenta sum to zero.

Two-dimensional collisions

Momentum is a vector, so it is conserved separately in each perpendicular direction. In a collision where a 2.0 kg ball moving east at 4.0 m s⁻¹ strikes a stationary ball of equal mass at an angle, resolve the momentum of each ball along the original direction and perpendicular to it. Apply conservation in both directions, then combine the components to find the resultant speed or angle.

Kinetic energy in collisions

Kinetic energy is lost in any inelastic collision. For the trolley example above, the initial kinetic energy is ½ × 0.5 × 4² = 4.0 J, and the final kinetic energy is ½ × 1.5 × (1.33)² ≈ 1.33 J. About 2.7 J has been transferred to sound, heat and deformation. Calculate the energies to show that the collision is inelastic, rather than just saying it is.

Impulse and the force–time graph

If a force of 40 N acts for 0.25 s, the impulse is 10 N s. Where the force varies, find the area under the force–time graph: count the squares, or split the area into triangles and rectangles. A large area means a large change in momentum, even if the peak force is modest.

  • Use Δp = m(v − u) with the sign of each velocity included. A ball that bounces back has a negative final velocity relative to its initial motion.
  • For a bounce, the change in momentum is larger than for a ball that stops, because the ball reverses direction.
  • When a question asks for the average force on a ball, use the impulse and the contact time, and state the direction of the force.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Adding the speeds of two bodies moving in opposite directions instead of subtracting, because direction was not included.
  • Treating a non-isolated system as isolated, for example ignoring friction or a gravitational force that acts on the system from outside.
  • Confusing the impulse with the force, or failing to convert the time into seconds.

title: Earth & Space — Study Notes
content:
Earth & Space

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): Earth & Solar System; stars & the Universe (Extended).

1. Earth, Moon, Sun

Earth rotates 24 h (day/night), orbits 365¼ d (year + leap). Moon orbits Earth ~27.3 d; phases from viewing angle; lunar/solar eclipses when aligned. Seasons from axial tilt (23.5°), not distance.

2. Solar system

Planets (Mercury → Neptune), dwarf planets (Pluto), moons, asteroids, comets (eccentric orbits, tails away from Sun), natural satellites. Gravity keeps orbits; orbital speed & radius relate to the central mass.

3. Orbital motion

Orbital speed v = 2πr/T. T grows with r (Kepler trend). Comets speed up near the Sun (ellipse, Sun at focus).

4. Stars (Extended)

Star formation: nebula → protostar (gravity, KE→thermal) → main sequence (hydrogen fusion: H→He, radiation pressure balances gravity) → red giant → white dwarf (Sun-mass) or supergiant → supernova → neutron star/black hole (massive stars). Elements heavier than iron form in supernovae.

5. Universe (Extended)

The Sun is one star in the Milky Way; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. Redshift: receding galaxies show stretched wavelengths → the Universe is expanding → Big Bang model; CMB is the afterglow. Hubble: farther ⇒ faster recession.

6. Scales

light-year = distance light travels in a year (9.5 × 10¹⁵ m); astronomical unit = Earth–Sun distance (1.5 × 10¹¹ m).

Orbits and the Solar System in more depth

The planets orbit the Sun because the Sun's gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps them on their paths. A moon is a natural satellite that orbits a planet, and an artificial satellite is launched by people. The Earth rotates once on its axis in one day, and it orbits the Sun once in one year. The phases of the Moon are caused by the changing proportion of its sunlit side that we see as it orbits the Earth.

Exam tip: state the object that provides the gravitational force when you describe why an orbit is stable.

Worked example: orbital speed of the Earth

The Earth orbits the Sun at a mean distance of about 1.5 × 10¹¹ m and takes one year, about 3.15 × 10⁷ s. Its average speed is v = 2πr/T = 2π × 1.5 × 10¹¹ / 3.15 × 10⁷ ≈ 3.0 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹, about 30 km per second.

Why the seasons happen

The seasons come from the tilt of the Earth's axis, about 23.5°, not from changes in distance to the Sun. When the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, sunlight arrives more directly and is spread over a smaller area, so the surface receives more energy per unit area and the days are longer.

Day, month and year

  • A solar day, noon to noon, is about 24 hours. The sidereal day, measured against the stars, is about 23 hours 56 minutes.
  • The Moon takes about 27.3 days to orbit the Earth relative to the stars, but about 29.5 days to return to the same phase, because the Earth moves along its own orbit in the meantime.
  • The phase of the Moon depends on how much of its sunlit half faces the Earth. The Earth's shadow causes an eclipse only when the three bodies are almost in line.

title: Algebra — Sequences and Functions — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Sequences and Functions

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): nth term (linear & quadratic), special sequences, function notation, composites, inverses.

1. Linear sequences

nth term = a + (n − 1)d. 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2. Check n = 1, 2, 3.

2. Quadratic sequences

Second difference = 2a → an² + bn + c. 3, 8, 15, 24 … has second difference 2 → n² + bn + c; subtract n² → 2, 4, 6, 8 → 2n; so nth term = n² + 2n.

3. Special sequences

Even/odd, triangular (½n(n+1)), squares, cubes, Fibonacci-type (each term = sum of previous two), geometric (×r).

4. Function notation

f(x) = 2x − 5: f(3) = 1. Solve f(x) = 11 → x = 8.

5. Composite functions

fg(x) = f(g(x)) — g first. f(x) = 2x − 5, g(x) = x²: gf(2) = g(1) = 1; fg(3) = f(9) = 13.

6. Inverse functions

Swap x and y, rearrange. f(x) = 2x − 5 ⇒ f⁻¹(x) = (x + 5)/2. Domain of inverse = range of original. Verify: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x.

Exam tips: write the bracket order explicitly in composites; show the "swap and rearrange" line for inverses — answer-only scores little.

Finding the nth term of a linear sequence

For a sequence with a constant difference d, the nth term is dn + (a − d), where a is the first term. Check the rule by substituting n = 1, 2 and 3 before using it. Given a term value, set the nth term equal to it and solve for n to test whether it belongs to the sequence.

Functions as machines

A function takes an input and gives exactly one output. Composite functions are applied right to left: fg(x) means apply g first, then f. The inverse f⁻¹ reverses each step, found by writing y = f(x), swapping x and y, and rearranging for y.

Domain and range

The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the range is the set of outputs produced. Restrictions usually come from division by zero or from taking square roots of negative numbers. State both when asked to describe a function fully.

Worked examples: sequences

Linear. The sequence 5, 9, 13, 17 has a common difference of 4. The nth term is 4n + 1, since the nth term of a linear sequence is dn + (first term − d). Check the 10th term: 4 × 10 + 1 = 41.

Quadratic. For 2, 6, 12, 20, the first differences are 4, 6, 8 and the second difference is 2. The coefficient of n² is half the second difference, so it is 1. Subtract n² from each term: 1, 2, 3, 4, which is linear with nth term n. So the nth term is n² + n. Check n = 3: 9 + 3 = 12 ✓.

Function notation with composites

Let f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x − 1. Then fg(x) means f(g(x)) = f(x − 1) = 2(x − 1) + 3 = 2x + 1. Note that gf(x) = g(2x + 3) = 2x + 2, which is different. Composition is not commutative, and questions often ask for both to test whether you apply the inner function first.

Inverse functions

To find f⁻¹(x) for f(x) = 2x + 3: write y = 2x + 3, swap to x = 2y + 3 and solve, giving y = (x − 3)/2. So f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 2(x − 3)/2 + 3 = x ✓. The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in the line y = x.

Domain and range

For f(x) = √(x − 2), the expression under the root must be non-negative, so the domain is x ≥ 2. The output of a square root is never negative, so the range is f(x) ≥ 0. For a rational function such as 1/(x − 4), the domain excludes x = 4, and the range excludes y = 0, since the value 0 is never reached.

Common errors

  • Taking the nth term of a quadratic sequence from the first term alone; the second difference must be used.
  • Reversing the order of composition: fg(x) and gf(x) are not the same.
  • Writing the domain as x > 2 when the question allows equality, or stating the range with an inequality in the wrong direction.
  • Forgetting to swap x and y before solving for the inverse.

title:
Membranes, Proteins, DNA and Gene Expression — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 2. Membrane structure and the fluid mosaic model, Core Practical 3 on membrane permeability, osmosis and water potential and the different kinds of transport, protein structure from amino acid to tertiary and quaternary, DNA structure and the evidence for semi-conservative replication from Meselson and Stahl, the genetic code and how genes work, transcription and translation and alternative splicing, mutation types and their effects, patterns of inheritance including sex linkage, cystic fibrosis as a gene-mutation disorder, and genetic screening and its ethical and social issues.

  • 2.2 Membrane structure (fluid mosaic model): a phospholipid bilayer with hydrophilic heads out and hydrophobic tails in, proteins (channel, carrier, receptor, recognition) embedded or attached, cholesterol moderating fluidity in animal cells; the membrane is fluid and mosaic, an interpretation of the evidence.
  • 2.3 Core Practical 3: beetroot cylinders in water at different temperatures or in different alcohol concentrations; colourimeter measures the pigment leaked as membranes are damaged — permeability rises with temperature and alcohol as proteins denature and the bilayer is disrupted.
  • 2.4 Osmosis and water potential: osmosis is the net movement of free water through a partially permeable membrane down a water potential gradient; solute lowers water potential; pure water has the highest (zero) water potential; animal cells swell and may haemolyse or crenate; plant cells become turgid (supported) or plasmolysed.
  • 2.5 Passive and active transport: diffusion of small non-polar molecules through the bilayer; facilitated diffusion of ions and large polar molecules through channel and carrier proteins down their gradient; active transport against the gradient using ATP; endocytosis and exocytosis for bulk materials in vesicles.
  • 2.9 Mononucleotides and DNA/RNA structure: a mononucleotide is deoxyribose (or ribose) + phosphate + base (A, C, G, T in DNA; A, C, G, U in RNA); nucleotides join by phosphodiester bonds; two complementary strands hydrogen-bond A–T (two bonds) and C–G (three bonds) in an antiparallel double helix.
  • 2.10 DNA replication (semi-conservative): double helix unzips, each strand is a template, DNA polymerase joins free nucleotides; Meselson and Stahl's 15N/14N experiment gave a single hybrid band in generation 1 and hybrid + light bands later — exactly what semi-conservative replication predicts and ruling out the conservative and dispersive alternatives.
  • 2.11 Genetic code: triplet, non-overlapping and degenerate — three bases code for one amino acid and several codons can code for the same amino acid; a stop codon signals the end.
  • 2.12 Gene: a sequence of bases on DNA that codes for a sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
  • 2.13 Protein synthesis: transcription by RNA polymerase makes mRNA from the template (antisense) strand; mRNA goes to ribosomes; tRNA brings amino acids with anticodons that pair with mRNA codons, building the polypeptide in the order of the codons until a stop codon.
  • 2.14 Mutations: substitution may change one amino acid or none; insertion/deletion (not in threes) causes a frameshift, changing all later amino acids and usually destroying function; some mutations cause cancer or genetic disorders, many do nothing.
  • 2.15 Inheritance: gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, dominant, recessive, codominance, homozygote, heterozygote; monohybrid crosses with ratios; sex linkage on the X chromosome (red-green colour blindness, haemophilia — more common in males); pedigree diagram interpretation.
  • 2.16 Cystic fibrosis: a mutation in a chloride-channel gene (often a three-base deletion removing one amino acid) — chloride and water transport fails, mucus is thick; affects gaseous exchange (blocked airways, infections), digestion (blocked pancreatic duct, poor digestion, malnutrition) and reproduction (absent or blocked vas deferens, male infertility).
  • 2.17 Genetic screening: identifies carriers; prenatal testing (amniocentesis at 15–17 wks, CVS at 8–12 wks); PGD used with IVF to test embryos before implantation — testing for genetic disorders before pregnancy.
  • 2.18 Ethical and social issues: safety and reliability of the test, miscarriage risk with invasive tests, right to know or not to know, what counts as a disorder, choice to terminate, anxiety, access and cost, and the risk of moving from preventing disease to selecting non-medical traits.

Worked example

Monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa): Punnett gives AA (¼), Aa (½), aa (¼); phenotype ratio 3 : 1 if A is completely dominant; genotype ratio 1 : 2 : 1. Sex linkage: a carrier female (XᴮXᵇ) and a normal male (XᴮY): sons ½ colour-blind (XᵇY) and ½ normal (XᴮY); daughters ½ carriers (XᴮXᵇ) and ½ normal (XᴮXᴮ), none colour-blind (unless the father is colour-blind). Heterozygosity index: in a population of 20 individuals at one locus, 8 are heterozygotes → H = 8/20 = 0.40.

Key points to remember

Membranes: temperature and alcohol disrupt proteins and the bilayer — permeability rises. Osmosis: water moves from high to low water potential; the direction and whether a cell bursts, crenates, becomes turgid or plasmolysed depends on the water potential of the solution compared with the cell. Transport: diffusion and facilitated diffusion are passive; active transport uses ATP and goes against the gradient; endocytosis and exocytosis use vesicles and ATP. Protein structure: peptide bond from condensation; primary = sequence; secondary = alpha-helix and beta-sheet (hydrogen bonds); tertiary = overall 3D folding with hydrogen, ionic, disulfide and hydrophobic bonds; quaternary = several polypeptides together (haemoglobin). DNA: antiparallel, A–T (2 H-bonds), C–G (3 H-bonds); semi-conservative replication shown by Meselson and Stahl. Protein synthesis: transcription → mRNA; translation on ribosomes with tRNA anticodons; alternative splicing means one gene can make more than one protein. Mutation types: substitution, insertion, deletion (frameshift). Cystic fibrosis: faulty chloride channel → thick mucus → lung, digestion, reproduction problems. Screening: carriers, PGD, amniocentesis, CVS; weigh benefits against ethical and social issues.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing a cell membrane and labelling the bilayer, proteins and cholesterol; carrying out the beetroot permeability practical and explaining the trend and control variables; drawing DNA, showing base pairing and antiparallel strands, and explaining semi-conservative replication and the Meselson and Stahl evidence; drawing protein synthesis (transcription and translation) with mRNA, tRNA and the ribosome; and working through a monohybrid cross, a sex-linked cross and a pedigree to explain each ratio.

title: Circular Measure — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Circular Measure

Mathematics — AS (9709). One radian is the angle subtending an arc equal in length to the radius. π radians = 180°.

Key areas to revise

  • Radians
  • Arc Length
  • Sector Area
  • Segment Area
  • Rearranging

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example An arc of a circle of radius r and angle θ in radians has length s = rθ. The sector area is ½r²θ. With r = 5 cm and θ = 0.6 rad, s = 3 cm and the area is 0.5 × 25 × 0.6 = 7.5 cm². To convert, 180° = π radians, so 60° = π/3 ≈ 1.047 radians.

Key points to remember

Angles in radians: π radians is 180°, so 1 radian is about 57.3°. Arc length s = rθ and sector area A = ½r²θ, where θ must be in radians. Convert before you use these formulae, because a calculator left in degree mode is the most common reason for a wrong answer.

For a segment, subtract the triangle from the sector: area = ½r²(θ − sin θ). Check that the segment is smaller than the sector. In perimeter questions, add the two radii to the arc length, and give units in your final answer.

title: Exponentials and Logarithms — Study Notes
content:
Exponentials and logarithms

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 2 (WMA12), sat at AS.

The exponential function e^x and the natural logarithm ln x are inverse functions. They model growth and decay (populations, radioactive decay, cooling) and appear in almost every AS/A2 paper.

The functions

  • e is Euler's number, e = 2.71828... to 4 s.f.
  • y = e^x is always positive, passes through (0, 1), and grows rapidly for large x.
  • y = ln x is defined for x > 0, passes through (1, 0), and is the inverse of e^x: ln(e^x) = x and e^(ln x) = x.
  • The graph of ln x is the reflection of e^x in the line y = x.

Logarithm laws

  • ln(ab) = ln a + ln b
  • ln(a/b) = ln a - ln b
  • ln(a^n) = n ln a
  • The same laws hold for logs to any base; log base a of x = ln x / ln a.

Solving equations

  • To solve e^(kx + c) = d: take ln of both sides, kx + c = ln d, then rearrange.
  • To solve ln(ax + b) = c: exponentiate, ax + b = e^c.
  • To solve a^x = b where a is not e: take logs, x = ln b / ln a.

Modelling

  • Growth/decay: N = N0 e^(kt), k > 0 for growth, k < 0 for decay.
  • Half-life: the time for a quantity to halve, found from ln(0.5) = k t_half.
  • Compound interest and continuously compounded growth use the same form.

Key results

  • The derivative of e^x is e^x; the derivative of ln x is 1/x (know these for later calculus).
  • e^0 = 1, ln 1 = 0, ln e = 1.
  • The curve y = e^x has gradient 1 at x = 0.

title: Exam technique: Kinematics
content:
### What earns the marks
For graphs, gradient read as acceleration and area as displacement earns one mark each. For SUVAT, the correct equation chosen with substitution earns both marks. For projectiles, horizontal constancy stated earns the explanation mark.
### Traps
Error: area and gradient roles swapped. Correction: area is displacement, gradient is acceleration. Error: wrong SUVAT picked. Correction: list knowns first, then choose. Error: horizontal motion given gravity. Correction: no horizontal force means constant velocity.
### Pick the equation that matches the given quantities
List the values you know for displacement s, initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a and time t. Choose the suvat equation that contains only the unknown you want and the quantities you know.

### Use the graph to check the answer
The gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity and the area under a velocity-time graph is displacement. If your algebra gives a displacement that does not match the area, recheck the sign and the values.

### Watch the direction of vectors
Take one direction as positive and keep to it. A ball thrown upwards has a negative acceleration of about 9.8 m s⁻² if upwards is positive, so a negative answer for velocity can still be correct.

title: Programming Paradigms and Low-Level — Study Notes
content:
Programming Paradigms and Low-Level

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 20 (Further programming), examined in Paper 3. Assembly language also appears at AS section 4.2.

Paradigms

  • Procedural: programs as sequences of instructions in procedures — good for straightforward algorithms.
  • Object-oriented: classes encapsulate state (attributes) and behaviour (methods); supports encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
  • Declarative: state what is required, not how (SQL queries, logic programming).
  • Low-level: assembly maps closely to machine code; used where hardware control or timing precision is needed.

Assembly Essentials

The opcode names the operation (LDM load, STR store, ADD, CMP compare, JMP branch, IN/OUT for I/O). The operand names the data. The assembler translates mnemonics to machine code one-to-one; two-pass assemblers resolve forward references via the symbol table.

Addressing Modes

  • Immediate: operand is the constant itself, ADD #5.
  • Direct: operand is the memory address of the data.
  • Indirect: operand is the address OF the address; one extra memory read.
  • Indexed: effective address = base + index register; ideal for arrays.
  • Relative: address given as an offset from the program counter; enables position-independent code.

Fetch-Execute

Fetch: PC gives address, instruction loads into the CIR, PC increments. Decode: control unit interprets the opcode. Execute: the operation runs, possibly updating registers or memory. Interrupts are checked at cycle boundaries.

Exam tips: trace short assembly programs register by register; compute effective addresses for each addressing mode; state one advantage of OOP for large systems.

Programming paradigms

An imperative paradigm describes how to do a task as a sequence of statements that change state. An object-oriented paradigm groups data and the methods that act on it into classes. A declarative paradigm states the result wanted and leaves the method to the system, as in SQL.

Exception handling

An exception is a run-time error such as a missing file or a division by zero. A try block runs the risky code, and a catch (or except) block handles the exception so the program can recover rather than crash.

Exam tip: name the paradigm and give one feature that shows it, such as classes for object-oriented programming.

Worked example: tracing a short assembly fragment

Memory location 10 holds 5 and location 11 holds 7. The program LDA 10, ADD 11, STA 12 is traced as follows. LDA 10 (direct addressing) copies the contents of location 10 into the accumulator, so ACC = 5. ADD 11 adds the contents of location 11 to the accumulator, so ACC = 12. STA 12 stores the accumulator into location 12, which now holds 12. With immediate addressing, LDA #5 would load the number 5 itself rather than the contents of location 5, and that difference is a common exam trap.

Exam method: naming a paradigm and justifying it

When asked to describe a paradigm, give one defining feature and one consequence of it. Imperative or procedural programming describes a sequence of statements that change state, object-oriented programming groups data and the methods that act on it into classes, and declarative or functional programming describes what the result should be rather than the step-by-step method. Answers that name a feature without linking it to the question scenario usually earn only part of the mark.

title: Abstract Data Types — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Abstract Data Types

Computer Science — A2. An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Key areas to revise

  • What is an ADT?
  • Linked Lists
  • Stacks and Queues
  • Binary Search Trees
  • Hash Tables

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example An abstract data type defines the data and operations without fixing the implementation. A stack is last-in-first-out: push adds an item to the top and pop removes the top item. If you push 3, then 7, then pop twice, the first pop returns 7 and the second returns 3. A queue is first-in-first-out, so enqueue and dequeue return 3 then 7 in the same sequence. ### Worked example An abstract data type defines the data and operations without fixing the implementation.
