title: Exam technique: Thermal Physics
content:
### What earns the marks
For conduction, free electrons named earn the explanation mark. For convection, rise of hot less-dense fluid earns the mark. For radiation, matt black as best emitter and absorber earns the mark; Q = mcT quoted earns the calculation marks.
### Traps
Error: convection claimed in solids. Correction: conduction only in solids. Error: shiny surfaces called best emitters. Correction: matt black emits and absorbs best. Error: evaporation cooling unexplained. Correction: fastest molecules escape.
### Method marks
For heating, use Q = mcΔθ, where c is the specific heat capacity. For a change of state, use Q = mL, where there is no temperature change while melting or boiling.
### Explain, do not just name
Conduction in metals depends on free electrons, and in non-metals on vibrating particles passing energy along. Convection needs a fluid that can move, so it cannot happen in a solid. Radiation needs no medium at all.
### Traps
Reading the melting point as the boiling point on a heating graph. A flat section is the latent heat stage, not a sign that the substance has stopped absorbing energy.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Study Notes
content:
Electric Fields and Capacitance

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 4 (WPH14), sat at A2.

Coulomb's law

The force between two point charges is F = kQ₁Q₂/r², with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. The force acts along the line joining the charges.

Example: +2.0 μC and −3.0 μC, 0.30 m apart, attract with F = 0.60 N.

Electric field strength

Field strength E is the force per unit positive charge: E = F/Q, in N C⁻¹ (or V m⁻¹). For a point charge E = kQ/r², radially outward for positive charge.

Uniform field: between parallel plates, E = V/d, with the field constant in magnitude and direction. A charge q in it feels F = qE.

Example: plates 4.0 cm apart with p.d. 600 V have E = 1.5 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹.

Electric potential and potential energy

Electric potential V at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small charge from infinity to that point: V = kQ/r for a point charge. Potential is a scalar. Field strength is the negative potential gradient, E = −dV/dr, so a steep potential-distance graph means a strong field. The field points from high to low potential.

Capacitance

Capacitance C = Q/V, measured in farads (C V⁻¹). The energy stored is W = ½QV = ½CV² = ½Q²/C. The area under a graph of V against Q equals the stored energy.

Example: a 10 μF capacitor charged to 200 V stores 0.20 J.

Capacitors in series and parallel

  • In parallel the capacitances add: C = C₁ + C₂.
  • In series the reciprocals add: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. The total is smaller than the smallest.

Discharge: through a resistor R, the charge falls exponentially, Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC). The time constant RC is the time for the charge or p.d. to fall to 37% of its initial value.

Exam tips: convert μF and cm to SI units before calculating. Check whether a question asks for field strength (vector) or potential (scalar). Series capacitors share the charge; parallel capacitors share the p.d.

Worked example: field between parallel plates

Two parallel plates are 0.040 m apart with a potential difference of 2.0 kV. The uniform field strength is E = V/d = 2000/0.040 = 5.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. A proton placed at rest between the plates feels a force F = eE = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)(5.0 × 10⁴) = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ N, directed from the positive plate towards the negative plate.

Radial fields and potential

For a point charge, E = Q/(4πε₀r²), so field strength falls with the square of distance. The potential is V = Q/(4πε₀r), which falls only with the first power of distance. Students often mix these two; the field depends on r², the potential on r.

Energy and the electronvolt

The work done in moving a charge Q through a potential difference V is W = QV. A charge accelerated from rest through 500 V gains 500 eV of kinetic energy, which is 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J for an electron. Expressing energies in electronvolts makes many A-level questions faster to work through.

  • Field lines point away from positive charge and towards negative charge, and they never cross.
  • Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines.
  • Energy stored in a capacitor is ½CV² = ½QV = ½Q²/C. Choose the form that matches the data given.

title: Exam technique: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic
content:
### What earns the marks
For truth tables, every row completed correctly earns stepwise credit. For circuits, each gate output labelled earns one mark before the final column. For expressions, brackets showing the gate order earn the method mark.
### Traps
Error: NAND confused with AND plus NOT placed wrongly. Correction: NAND inverts the AND output. Error: half-filled tables guessed. Correction: list all input combinations. Error: XOR read as OR. Correction: XOR excludes both-1.### Worked example
For Q = (A AND B) OR NOT C, evaluate the brackets first: write the AND column, then the NOT C column, then the OR of those two. Three inputs give eight rows, so write the input pattern in binary order from 000 to 111 before filling any output. Each gate column is worth checking on its own, so an error in the final column does not cost the intermediate marks.
### Recall check
Complete the output of NOT (A OR B) for all four input rows, then check it against De Morgan's law: it equals NOT A AND NOT B. Explain why an XOR gate outputs 0 when both inputs are 1, using the phrase exactly one input.

title: Coordinate Geometry — Study Notes
content:
Coordinate Geometry

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11), sat at AS. Coordinate questions fall into four types: a shape test, a line from two facts, a meeting point, and a circle. Identify the type from the wording before you touch a formula, because each type has its own first step.

Match the wording to the method

  • "Show that the shape is a rhombus, square or parallelogram": find side lengths and gradients, then compare them. Lengths decide equal sides; gradients decide right angles and parallel sides.
  • "Find the line through … parallel or perpendicular to …": take the gradient from the given line, change it if needed, then build the line from one point.
  • "Find where the line meets the curve or the other line": substitute one equation into the other, then solve the single equation that results.
  • "Find the circle … tangent at …": find the centre and radius first. Tangents are always perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.

Shape test: lengths first, then gradients

Take P(0, 1), Q(4, 4), R(8, 1) and S(4, −2). Side PQ has change (4, 3), so its length is √(16 + 9) = 5. QR has change (4, −3), length 5. RS has change (−4, −3), length 5, and SP has change (−4, 3), length 5. All four sides are equal.

Equal sides alone do not prove a rhombus when the shape could fold. Check one diagonal: PR has gradient (1 − 1)/(8 − 0) = 0, so it is horizontal. QS is vertical, since Q and S both have x = 4. The diagonals are perpendicular, so PQRS is a rhombus. The midpoints of both diagonals are (4, 1), which confirms the two diagonals bisect each other.

A line from two facts

Find the line through (3, −1) perpendicular to 2x − 5y + 1 = 0. Rearranging gives y = (2/5)x + 1/5, so the given gradient is 2/5. The perpendicular gradient is −5/2. Then y + 1 = −(5/2)(x − 3), which becomes 5x + 2y − 13 = 0.

Check the point: 5(3) + 2(−1) − 13 = 0. Always substitute the point you started from, because it catches sign errors in the gradient step.

Where two lines meet

For 3x + y = 7 and x − 2y = −4, rearrange the first to y = 7 − 3x and substitute into the second: x − 2(7 − 3x) = −4, so 7x = 10 and x = 10/7. Then y = 7 − 30/7 = 19/7. Check in the second equation: 10/7 − 38/7 = −4. The point is (10/7, 19/7).

Two lines with the same gradient and different intercepts never meet, so the substitution leaves a false statement such as 0 = 5. Report that as "no intersection", not as an error in your algebra.

Circles

A circle with centre (2, −3) through (5, 1) has r² = (5 − 2)² + (1 + 3)² = 25. Its equation is (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25, which expands to x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 = 0.

The tangent at (5, 1) is perpendicular to the radius. The radius has gradient 4/3, so the tangent has gradient −3/4. Then y − 1 = −(3/4)(x − 5), which gives 3x + 4y − 19 = 0.

To find where the line y = 2x − 1 meets this circle, substitute: (x − 2)² + (2x + 2)² = 25. Expanding gives 5x² + 4x − 17 = 0. The discriminant is 16 + 340 = 356, which is positive, so the line cuts the circle at two points.

Converting between forms

Gradient form y = mx + c is easiest for comparing gradients. Form ax + by + c = 0 is what many final answers need. Going from the centre-radius form to the expanded form means multiplying out both brackets, then collecting the x, y and constant terms.

Traps that cost marks

  • Taking the gradient of the given line as its y-coefficient, rather than −(a/b) in ax + by + c = 0.
  • Forgetting to negate the gradient when the question asks for a perpendicular line.
  • Using the radius value r instead of r² in the circle equation.
  • Leaving a meeting point as one coordinate, when the question asks for both.

title: Thermal Physics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Thermal Physics

Physics — A2. Sum of random kinetic + potential energies of molecules. Temperature rise → KE up; phase change → PE up (bonds stretch) at constant temperature.

Key areas to revise

  • Internal Energy
  • Specific Heat and Latent Heat
  • Gas Laws
  • Kinetic Theory

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Ideal gas equation: p V = n R T, where T is in kelvin.
  • Number of molecules N = n N_A, and the Boltzmann constant k = R / N_A.
  • Kinetic theory: p V = ⅓ N m ⟨c²⟩, and the mean kinetic energy of molecules is proportional to the absolute temperature.
  • First law of thermodynamics: ΔU = Q + W, where W is the work done on the gas.

Common errors

Use the sign convention carefully: heat taken in by a gas is positive, and work done on the gas is positive. Converting degrees Celsius to kelvin is always required before using pV = nRT or the mean kinetic energy relation.

title:
Cell Structure, Reproduction and Development — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 3. The cell as the unit of life, eukaryotic and prokaryotic ultrastructure, light and electron microscopy and measurement, mitosis and the cell cycle, meiosis and variation, gametes and fertilisation in mammals and flowering plants, stem cells and their uses, and genetic control through gene expression, epigenetics and inheritance patterns.

  • 3.1 Common features of all cells: a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes are shared by every cell; differences such as a nucleus, cell wall and organelles explain cell function.
  • 3.2 Levels of organisation: cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems; each level carries out a particular function and shapes the level above it.
  • 3.3 Eukaryotic ultrastructure: nucleus with nuclear envelope and nucleolus, ribosomes (80S) on rER and free, rER (protein synthesis and transport), sER (lipid synthesis), mitochondria (double membrane, cristae, matrix, aerobic respiration), centrioles (spindle organisation), lysosomes (digestive enzymes), Golgi (modifies, sorts and packages proteins, forms extracellular enzymes).
  • 3.4 rER and Golgi: the rER makes proteins and passes them to the Golgi in vesicles; the Golgi modifies, sorts and packages them, and is involved in forming extracellular enzymes.
  • 3.5 Prokaryotic ultrastructure: no membrane-bound nucleus — a single circular DNA free in the cytoplasm; cell wall of peptidoglycan; capsule; plasmids (small rings of DNA, often carrying resistance genes); flagella (rotate for motility); pili (attachment and conjugation); 70S ribosomes — smaller than eukaryotic 80S.
  • 3.6 EM recognition: in EM images, recognise nucleus, nucleolus, ribosomes, rER, sER, mitochondria, centrioles, lysosomes, Golgi and — in prokaryotes — the cell wall, capsule, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, flagella and pili.
  • 3.7 Microscopy and staining: light microscopes use visible light and have low resolution (~0.2 µm, ~×1500 max); electron microscopes (TEM for internal ultrastructure, SEM for surface detail) give far higher resolution and magnification. Staining with methylene blue (animal cells) or iodine (starch, cell walls) makes transparent structures visible; a graticule calibrated with a stage micrometer lets you measure real sizes.

Worked example

Calibrate a graticule: one eyepiece division at ×400 equals 2.5 µm (calibrated against a stage micrometer). A cell spans 20 divisions, so its real length = 20 × 2.5 µm = 50 µm. To find real size from image size, real size = image size ÷ magnification, so a cell drawn 50 mm long at ×2000 is 50 mm ÷ 2000 = 0.025 mm = 25 µm.

Key points to remember

  • Magnification ≠ resolution; resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points and sets the useful limit of detail.
  • In a light microscope total magnification = eyepiece × objective; always calibrate the graticule at each objective before measuring.
  • A stain makes transparent structures visible — methylene blue shows nuclei in animal cells, iodine shows starch grains and cell walls.
  • Staining matters in electron microscopy too: heavy-metal stains increase contrast in TEM and SEM images.
  • The plasma membrane is an active, protein-studded barrier; without it the cell cannot control what enters and leaves.
  • The nucleus holds the DNA and nucleolus; the nucleolus makes ribosomes, which then leave the nucleus.
  • Ribosomes are the same fundamental structure in all living things (though smaller in prokaryotes: 70S), and that is part of the evidence for common ancestry.
  • Mitochondria have a double membrane and cristae that increase surface area for aerobic respiration — the energy for cell activities.
  • The Golgi modifies and packages proteins; extracellular enzymes (such as digestive enzymes) are secreted by exocytosis after Golgi packaging.
  • Endocytosis and exocytosis move materials in vesicles, and both need ATP — another place ATP is used beyond respiration.

Key points to remember

Know the cell cycle: interphase (G1, S, G2 — growth and DNA replication) then mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) then cytokinesis; mitosis makes genetically identical cells for growth and asexual reproduction. Meiosis makes genetically non-identical gametes and is the source of variation, through independent assortment in metaphase I and crossing over in prophase I. A locus is the position of a gene on a chromosome; linked genes do not assort independently. Sperm are specialised: small, motile, with an acrosome of digestive enzymes, mitochondria for energy and a haploid nucleus; eggs are large with food reserves and the zona pellucida. Fertilisation in mammals: acrosome reaction digests the zona pellucida, cortical reaction blocks further sperm, nuclei fuse to form the zygote. In flowering plants: pollen tube grows to the embryo sac, double fertilisation — one male nucleus fertilises the egg (zygote → embryo), one fuses with the two polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. Mitotic index = number of cells dividing ÷ total cells; used in Core Practical 6 root tip squash to count mitotic stages. Totipotent cells (zygote, early embryo, plant meristems) can form a whole organism; pluripotent cells (blastocyst cells) can form many but not all cell types. Stem cells are used in bone marrow transplants, and their use raises ethical and social questions.

Key points to remember

Cells become specialised by differential gene expression — different genes switched on or off produce different proteins; one gene can give several proteins through alternative splicing of mRNA. Transcription factors switch genes on or off. Epigenetic modification — DNA methylation and histone modification — changes gene activity without changing the DNA sequence, and the modification can be passed on after cell division. Phenotype is genotype plus environment: multiple alleles (ABO blood groups), polygenic inheritance (height — continuous variation) and environment all contribute. Mutations are changes in DNA base sequence: substitution may change one amino acid or none, insertion/deletion may cause a frameshift. Mutations are the source of new alleles and can cause cancer or genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis (faulty chloride channel — lung, gut and reproductive problems). Pedigree diagrams show inheritance patterns; sex linkage (red-green colour blindness, haemophilia) is carried on the X and is more common in males. Genetic screening can identify carriers and test embryos (PGD) or a fetus (amniocentesis, CVS); this raises ethical and social questions — consent, the right to know, what counts as a disorder, the choice to terminate, access and cost, and the risk of selecting for non-medical traits.

How to use this

Read the summary list first, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing and labelling a plant cell and an animal cell from memory with each organelle's function; carrying out the graticule calibration and mitotic index calculations; and working through a monohybrid cross, a sex-linked cross and a pedigree to explain the ratios and the logic for each.

title: Analysing Language Choices — Study Notes
content:
Language analysis asks how a writer uses words to create an effect. A device is only worth naming if you explain what it does and why the writer chose it.

Identifying devices

Name the device precisely, then move straight to its effect.

Common devices

  • Simile: a comparison using like or as, for example "like a black curtain drawn across the sky".
  • Metaphor: a direct comparison with no like or as.
  • Personification: giving human qualities to something non-human, for example "the city devoured the last of the daylight".
  • Onomatopoeia: a word that imitates a sound, such as buzz or crack.
  • Hyperbole: deliberate exaggeration for effect.

Explaining the effect

A strong comment has three parts: the word or phrase, what it suggests, and the reader's likely response.

Word-level analysis

  • Consider connotations: the feelings a word carries beyond its literal meaning.
  • Compare a chosen word with a plausible alternative to show why this one works better.
  • Notice verbs and adjectives, since they often carry the emotional weight of a description.

Sentence-level analysis

  • A short sentence after several long ones creates emphasis or sudden impact.
  • A list of three can build rhythm or momentum.
  • A rhetorical question makes the reader pause and consider the point.

Structuring your answer

Choose two or three clear examples rather than listing everything. Each paragraph should name the device, quote the words, and explain the effect in full sentences.

title: Vectors — Study Notes
content:
Vectors

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 4 (WMA14), sat at A2.

Components and Arithmetic

A vector a = 3i + 4j has magnitude |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5. Parallel vectors are scalar multiples; unit vector = a/|a|.

Position and Direction

The line through point A with direction d: r = a + t d. Two lines are parallel if their directions are multiples.

Example: r = (1, 2) + t(3, −1).

Scalar (Dot) Product

a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂.

Perpendicular ⇔ a · b = 0. Parallel ⇔ cross-multiplied components are equal (in 2D: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0).

Example: (2, 3) · (−6, 4) = −12 + 12 = 0, so they are perpendicular.

Angle Between Vectors

cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|).

Example: between (1, 0) and (1, 1): cos θ = 1/(1 × √2), θ = 45°.

Lines and Points

Foot of perpendicular from P to a line, intersection of two lines, and shortest distances all come from dot products and parameter t.

Exam tips: write column vectors cleanly; check answers by substituting the found t back into both position vectors; keep exact surd magnitudes rather than decimals.

Exam method: components, magnitude and scalar product

A vector in two dimensions is written as a column (x; y), and in three dimensions as (x; y; z) or in unit vector form xi + yj + zk. The magnitude is |a| = √(x² + y² + z²), which is Pythagoras applied in each direction.

The scalar product a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ is a number, not a vector. It also equals |a||b| cos θ, where θ is the angle between the vectors. Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero.

Use the scalar product to find the angle between two vectors: cos θ = (a · b)/(|a||b|). Give the angle in degrees or radians as the question asks.

A unit vector has magnitude 1. Divide a vector by its magnitude to find the unit vector in the same direction.

Exam cue: Write each component with its sign before adding, because a sign slip in the scalar product changes the answer without changing the method.

Worked example: angle between two vectors

Find the angle between a = (3; 4) and b = (5; −2). The scalar product is a·b = 15 − 8 = 7. The magnitudes are |a| = √(9 + 16) = 5 and |b| = √(25 + 4) = √29 ≈ 5.385. So cos θ = 7/(5 × 5.385) ≈ 0.260, giving θ ≈ 74.9°.

Perpendicular vectors

Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is zero. Use this to find an unknown component: if (2; k) is perpendicular to (4; −3), then 8 − 3k = 0, so k = 8/3.

Vector equation of a line

  • The line r = a + λd passes through the point with position vector a and has direction d; λ is the parameter.
  • To test whether a point lies on the line, find λ from one component and check that it satisfies the other components.
  • Two lines are parallel when their direction vectors are scalar multiples of each other. They are skew when they neither meet nor are parallel.

title: Programming and Algorithms — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Programming and Algorithms

Computer Science — AS. An algorithm is a clear sequence of steps that solves a problem. Good programs are designed in stages, written in clear pseudocode, and checked against the purpose they were written for.

Key areas to revise

  • Design approaches: top-down design breaks a problem into smaller parts, and stepwise refinement adds detail one level at a time.
  • Pseudocode conventions: use clear keywords such as IF, WHILE and FOR, indent blocks, and name variables so that their purpose is obvious.
  • Searching: a linear search checks each item in turn and works on any list, while a binary search halves a sorted list at each step.
  • Sorting: bubble sort and insertion sort repeatedly compare and swap or move items until the list is in order.
  • Recursion: a recursive function calls itself. It must have a base case that stops the calls and a recursive case that moves towards it.

Core facts to recall

  • A binary search needs a sorted list; on a list of 1024 items it needs at most 10 comparisons.
  • Linear search takes up to n comparisons for n items, so the work grows in step with the list.
  • When you trace an algorithm, write a table with one column per variable and one row per step.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Further Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Further Trigonometry

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 3 (WMA13), sat at A2.

Compound Angles

  • sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
  • cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Example: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = (√2/2)(√3/2) + (√2/2)(1/2) = (√6 + √2)/4.

Double Angles

  • sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A
  • cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A = 2cos²A − 1 = 1 − 2sin²A

Example: express 4 sin x cos x in one term: 2 sin 2x.

The R-Form

a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x + α) with R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b/a.

Example: 3 sin x + 4 cos x = 5 sin(x + 0.927). This instantly gives the maximum 5 and minimum −5.

Reciprocal Functions

sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ. Key identity: 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ.

Exam tips: choose the cos 2A form that eliminates the unwanted function; when solving with R-form, divide by R before using inverse trig, and translate intervals carefully.

Exam method: reciprocal functions and identities

The reciprocal functions are sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x and cot x = 1/tan x. Rewrite them in terms of sine and cosine when a question mixes functions, because this usually shows which identity to use.

The Pythagorean identities are sin² x + cos² x = 1, 1 + tan² x = sec² x and 1 + cot² x = cosec² x. Divide the first identity by cos² x or sin² x to obtain the second or third.

To solve an equation such as sec x = 2, first rewrite it as cos x = 1/2, then find the acute angle and the other solutions in the required range. For cos x = k the solutions in 0 to 2π are α and 2π − α, where α is the acute angle.

To prove an identity, work on the more complicated side only, and keep rewriting until it matches the other side.

Exam cue: Give each solution in the range asked for, using exact values such as π/3 when the angle is standard.

Exam method: R-form

To write a sinθ + b cosθ as R sin(θ + α), expand R sin(θ + α) = R sinθ cosα + R cosθ sinα and compare coefficients. This gives R = √(a² + b²) and tan α = b / a, with α in the quadrant where cos α and sin α have the signs of a and b.

Exam cue: Find the maximum and minimum from R, then solve for θ over the stated interval. Give α in the correct quadrant before writing the final angles.

Worked example: solving sin 2x = cos x

Solve sin 2x = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. Using the double angle formula, 2 sin x cos x = cos x. Move everything to one side and factorise: cos x (2 sin x − 1) = 0. So cos x = 0, giving x = π/2 or 3π/2, or sin x = ½, giving x = π/6 or 5π/6. The four solutions are π/6, π/2, 5π/6 and 3π/2. Dividing both sides by cos x at the start would lose the two solutions where cos x = 0, and that is the most common way to drop marks on this type of question.

Exam method: choosing an identity

Before you start, look at which angles appear. If the question mixes x and 2x, rewrite the double angle first so that everything is in one angle. Always state the range of solutions in the form the question asks for, in radians or degrees, and check that each answer lies inside the range. Substituting each answer back into the original equation is a quick way to catch a sign error.

title: Exam technique: Functions
content:
### What earns the marks
For range, the domain endpoints evaluated earn the first mark with monotonicity justifying the interval. For composites, the inner value written down earns a mark before the outer application. For inverses, the swap-and-solve shown earns the method mark; domain restriction discussed earns the reasoning mark.
### Traps
Error: gf computed as fg. Correction: start from the rightmost letter. Error: inverse claimed on many-one functions. Correction: restrict the domain first. Error: full reals claimed despite a bounded domain. Correction: map the endpoints.
### Domain and range
State the domain as the set of inputs the function accepts and the range as the set of outputs it produces. Restrictions often come from a square root needing a non-negative value or a denominator that cannot be zero.
### Composite functions
For fg(x), apply g first and then f to the result. Write the expression for each step so the order is visible in your working.
### Inverse functions
To find the inverse, write y = f(x), swap x and y, and rearrange for y. State the domain of the inverse when the question asks for it, because it is the range of the original function.
### Check
Apply the inverse to a value and then the original function to confirm you return the starting value.

title: Exam technique: Complex Numbers
content:
### What earns the marks
For modulus and argument, root(x squared + y squared) and tan inverse (y/x) each earn a mark with the quadrant checked. For quadratics, the negative discriminant shown earns the method mark and the a+bi pair earns the second. For loci, the geometric name (circle, line, half-line) earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: modulus squared reported as modulus. Correction: root last. Error: stopping at no real roots. Correction: continue into complex pair. Error: i squared treated as 1 in products. Correction: it equals -1.
### Plan the algebra before you start
Multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator when you divide complex numbers. Write each step on its own line, so a sign error is easier to spot.

### Check your answer on the Argand diagram
Sketch the points or the locus. The argument should lie in the quadrant you expect, and the modulus should match the distance from the origin you estimate from the sketch.

### Use the conjugate root theorem
For a polynomial with real coefficients, the complex roots come in conjugate pairs. Use this to find a missing root immediately instead of solving the whole equation again.

title: Organisation of the Organism
content:
Organisation of the Organism

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 2 (statements 2.1–2.2). Cell structure across the major groups, specialised cells, levels of organisation, and the magnification calculations examiners build questions around.

2.1 Cell structure

  • Eukaryotic cells share a nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and mitochondria; plant cells add a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole. Bacterial cells have a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, a circular DNA loop and often plasmids — no nucleus.
  • Functions worth stating precisely: nucleus controls the cell's activities and contains DNA; mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration; ribosomes build proteins; the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves; the cell wall gives support; chloroplasts contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis; the vacuole holds cell sap and keeps the cell turgid.
  • Specialised cells are adapted by structure: root hair cells have a long extension for water absorption; palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts; red blood cells are biconcave and lack a nucleus to carry more haemoglobin; ciliated cells move mucus; nerve cells have long axons to carry impulses.
  • Levels of organisation: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism. Each level must be defined by its members, not just listed.

2.2 Size of specimens

  • Magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object. Rearrange as needed: real size = image size ÷ magnification. 1 mm = 1000 µm, 1 cm = 10 mm.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Magnification, applied to a cell 50 µm long drawn as 8 cm: 8 cm = 80 mm = 80 000 µm, so magnification = 80 000 ÷ 50 = ×1600. Convert every unit to µm before dividing; unit errors are the single largest source of lost marks in this topic.
  • Organelle reasoning, applied to why a liver cell has many mitochondria: liver cells carry out many energy-requiring reactions such as detoxification and active transport, so they need many mitochondria. Link structure to the specific function of THAT cell, not to a generic "it needs energy".
  • Identification from a micrograph, applied to a drawing showing a large vacuole, chloroplasts and a rigid rectangular shape: it is a plant cell. State the two features that rule out an animal cell — the cell wall and chloroplasts — as separate marks.

Common errors

  • Saying the cell wall is the same as the cell membrane. They are different structures with different functions.
  • Calling the nucleus the "brain of the cell" as a full answer. It controls activities because it contains genetic material — give the mechanism.
  • Confusing magnification with the power of a microscope in objective × eyepiece terms when the question gives image and real sizes.

title: Probability Distributions — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Probability Distributions

Mathematics — A2. A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Key areas to revise

  • Probability Distributions
  • Expectation
  • Variance
  • Linear Transforms
  • Independent Variables

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

For a discrete random variable X, the probabilities in the distribution table must add to 1. The expected value is E(X) = Σx P(X = x), and the variance is Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]². Calculate E(X²) by squaring each value of x before you multiply by its probability.

For a linear transformation, E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). The constant b shifts the mean but does not change the variance. Check your answer for the variance is never negative, which catches a sign error in the formula.

title: Differentiation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Differentiation

Mathematics — AS (9709). Differentiation finds the gradient of a curve at any point. Example: y = 5x² − 3x gives dy/dx = 10x − 3, so at x = 2 the gradient is 17.

Key areas to revise

  • Basic rules: for y = xⁿ, dy/dx = nxⁿ⁻¹. Multiply by the power and reduce the power by one; a constant term differentiates to zero.
  • Chain rule: dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) for y as a function of u, where u is a function of x.
  • Product and quotient rules: for y = uv, dy/dx = u(dv/dx) + v(du/dx); for y = u/v, use (v du/dx − u dv/dx)/v².
  • Tangents and normals: the tangent has the gradient dy/dx at the point, and the normal is perpendicular to it, with gradient −1/m.
  • Stationary points: where dy/dx = 0. The sign of the gradient on each side, or the second derivative, shows whether it is a maximum or a minimum.
  • Rates of change: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt), which links a rate for one variable to another.

Core facts to recall

  • Check each stationary point by finding the y-value and the sign of the gradient either side.
  • State the equation of the tangent in the form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), and simplify only when asked.
  • Keep the answer exact, such as a fraction, unless the question asks for a decimal.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Web Technologies
content:
### What earns the marks
For web roles, HTML for structure plus CSS for presentation plus JavaScript for behaviour earns each mark. For threats, phishing versus pharming versus smishing distinguished earns one mark each. For cookies, session versus persistent with a use earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: HTML claimed to style pages. Correction: CSS styles, HTML structures. Error: every scam called phishing. Correction: pharming redirects sites, smishing uses texts. Error: HTTPS said to block all attacks. Correction: it encrypts transit only.### Worked example
A question asking how a website keeps a user logged in: a session cookie holds a token for the browsing session, so the server recognises the user on each page request. A persistent cookie stores data across sessions, for example a language preference. Give the use together with the type to earn both marks, as the traps above show.
### Recall check
Describe how phishing differs from pharming and give one measure a user can take against each. Explain what HTTPS protects and what it does not, in one sentence each.

title: Entropy and Energetics Quick Revision
content:
Entropy and Energetics Quick Revision

Chemistry — A2. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 12, covering entropy, energetics, and feasibility of reactions. Entropy and enthalpy changes are crucial in determining the spontaneity of a reaction.

  • Entropy measures disorder and randomness, increasing with temperature and phase changes.
  • Gibbs free energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict reaction feasibility.
  • Total entropy change is the sum of system and surroundings entropy changes.
  • Temperature affects reaction feasibility, with higher temperatures decreasing the magnitude of surroundings entropy change.
  • Worked examples illustrate how to calculate entropy changes and Gibbs free energy.

Worked example

Calculate the total entropy change for a reaction with ΔS_system = 100 J/K and ΔH = -50000 J, at 298 K, using S_surroundings = -ΔH / T, then S_total = ΔS_system + S_surroundings.

Key points to remember

Remember that entropy increases with temperature and phase changes, and that the total entropy change determines reaction spontaneity. Also, recall that the Gibbs free energy equation, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS, is used to predict reaction feasibility.

How to use this: skim the key points, read the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Born-Haber Cycles and Lattice Energy

A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's Law to construct an energy level diagram for the formation of an ionic solid from its elements in their standard states. The standard enthalpy change of atomisation, delta_at H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element under standard conditions. Electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one electron is added to each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1- ions. Lattice energy is defined as the exothermic process for the formation of one mole of an ionic solid from its gaseous ions.

Discrepancies between experimental lattice energy values obtained from Born-Haber cycles and theoretical values calculated from pure electrostatic point-charge models indicate the presence of covalent character. When cations polarise large or highly charged anions, electron density is drawn into the region between the nuclei, leading to partial covalent bonding which releases more energy than predicted by pure ionic models.

Enthalpy of Solution and Hydration

The enthalpy change of solution, delta_sol H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute is dissolved in enough solvent to form an infinitely dilute solution. The enthalpy change of hydration, delta_hyd H, is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions is dissolved in water to form an infinitely dilute solution. You can use energy cycles combining lattice energy and hydration enthalpies to calculate the enthalpy change of solution.

Ionic charge and radius significantly affect these energetic values. High charge density, resulting from small ionic radius and high ionic charge, leads to more exothermic hydration and lattice energies because of stronger electrostatic attractions between the ions and water molecules or oppositely charged ions.

Thermodynamic Stability versus Kinetic Stability

Thermodynamic stability indicates whether a substance or reaction is feasible based on total entropy change and free energy, showing if a reaction is spontaneous. Kinetic stability refers to the rate of a reaction; a system can be thermodynamically unstable yet kinetically stable if the activation energy barrier is too high for the reaction to proceed at a measurable rate at room temperature.

Additional Worked Example

Calculate the enthalpy change of solution for sodium chloride, given that its lattice energy is +790 kJ / mol and the hydration enthalpies of sodium and chloride ions are −406 kJ / mol and −364 kJ / mol respectively. Using the energy cycle, delta_sol H = lattice energy + sum(delta_hyd H). Therefore, delta_sol H = +790 + (−406 + (−364)) = +790 − 770 = +20 kJ / mol.

More Key Points to Remember

Remember that the total entropy change, delta_S total = delta_S system + delta_S surroundings, must be positive for any spontaneous process. The term delta_S surroundings is calculated using − delta_H / T. Solubility trends down group 2 depend on the relative sizes of the decrease in lattice energy compared to the decrease in hydration enthalpy as cation size increases. Polarisation increases down the group for anions or with smaller cations, driving deviations from theoretical lattice energy calculations.
