content:
Microbiology, Immunity and Forensics

Edexcel International A Level Biology — Unit 4 (WBI14), Topic 6. Every statement 6.1 to 6.20 is covered below, with its code in the heading. The topic links three big ideas: how microorganisms are grown and measured, how the body defends itself and why pathogens keep finding ways around those defences, and how DNA techniques are used to identify organisms and people.

6.1: Culturing microorganisms with aseptic technique

  • Aseptic technique keeps a culture pure: only the wanted microorganism grows. Sterilise media and equipment first, usually in an autoclave at 121 °C under pressure for about 15 minutes.
  • Work close to a Bunsen flame, flame the inoculating loop until red-hot before and after use, keep Petri dish lids mostly closed, and never pipette by mouth.
  • Incubate cultures inverted at a safe temperature, usually 25 °C for school work, so condensation does not drip onto the agar.

6.2: Measuring the growth of microorganisms

  • Direct cell counts: use a haemocytometer (counting chamber) under a microscope, counting cells in a known volume to get the number per cm³.
  • Viable counts by dilution plating: make a serial dilution, spread known volumes on agar, incubate, and count colonies on plates with about 30 to 300 colonies. Each colony is assumed to grow from one viable cell, so the count shows living cells only.
  • Mass methods: measure the dry mass of cells collected by centrifuging or filtering a known volume of culture.
  • Optical methods (turbidity): a colorimeter or spectrophotometer measures how much light the cloudy culture absorbs. Absorbance rises with cell density, so a calibration curve converts it to cell numbers.

6.3: The bacterial growth curve and the growth rate constant

  • Lag phase: cells adapt to the medium and synthesise enzymes; there is little or no division.
  • Exponential (log) phase: cells divide at a constant rate, so the population doubles each generation. N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings.
  • Stationary phase: births equal deaths, because nutrients run short and waste builds up.
  • Death phase: deaths exceed births and the population falls.
  • Growth rate constant: in exponential growth N = N₀eᵏᵗ. So k = (ln N₂ − ln N₁) ÷ (t₂ − t₁). Plotting ln N against time gives a straight line whose gradient is k.

6.4: Core practical 13: growth of microorganisms in liquid culture

  • Inoculate a sterile liquid medium, take samples at regular intervals, and measure turbidity or cell count each time.
  • Plot the results to show the four phases of the curve, then calculate the exponential growth rate constant from the straight-line part.
  • Safe and ethical use: use only non-pathogenic strains, keep the culture closed, disinfect the bench, and autoclave all used material before disposal.

6.5: Structure of bacteria and viruses

  • Bacteria are cells with a cell wall (peptidoglycan), cell membrane, cytoplasm with ribosomes, and a circular DNA loop, often with plasmids. They have no nucleus.
  • Viruses are not cells. They have a nucleic acid core, either DNA or RNA, surrounded by a protein capsid. Some also have a lipid envelope taken from the host.
  • Comparisons: Ebola virus has single-stranded RNA and an envelope. Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) has single-stranded RNA in a helical capsid, with no envelope. HIV has two RNA strands, reverse transcriptase and an envelope. Lambda phage, a virus of bacteria, has double-stranded DNA in a head with a tail and no envelope.
  • Lytic cycle: the virus takes over the host cell, makes new viruses, and the cell bursts (lyses) to release them.
  • Latency: the viral genome stays in the host cell without producing new viruses, and can become active later.

6.6: How Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV infect human cells

  • Tuberculosis: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled into the alveoli. Macrophages engulf it, but the bacterium survives inside them and multiplies. The body forms granulomas (tubercles) around the infection, and the lung tissue is destroyed. Symptoms include a persistent cough, fever, night sweats and weight loss. If untreated it can be fatal.
  • HIV: the virus binds to CD4 receptors and a co-receptor on helper T cells. Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from its RNA, which is inserted into the host genome. New viruses bud from the cell. The helper T cell population falls, so the immune system fails and opportunistic infections and cancers take hold (AIDS).

6.7: Routes of entry and barriers

  • Routes: inhalation (airborne droplets), ingestion (contaminated food and water), contact through broken skin or wounds, sexual contact, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Barriers: intact skin (keratin, dryness, and the skin flora that competes with pathogens), stomach acid (pH about 2, which kills many ingested microbes), and gut flora that competes for space and nutrients. Mucus and cilia in the airways trap and move pathogens out.

6.8: Non-specific responses to infection

  • Inflammation: damaged cells release chemicals such as histamine, which dilate blood vessels and make them leaky. The area becomes red, hot and swollen, and white blood cells are recruited to the site.
  • Lysozyme: an enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus that breaks the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls.
  • Interferon: proteins released by virus-infected cells that warn neighbouring cells, which then resist viral replication. Interferon is antiviral, not a direct killer of the virus.
  • Phagocytosis: neutrophils and macrophages engulf a pathogen into a phagosome. Lysosomes fuse with it and enzymes digest the contents.

6.9: Antigens, antibodies, plasma cells, macrophages and antigen-presenting cells

  • An antigen is a foreign molecule, usually a protein or glycoprotein on a pathogen's surface, that triggers an immune response.
  • An antibody is a Y-shaped glycoprotein whose binding sites are complementary to one specific antigen. Antibodies mark pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins.
  • Plasma cells are B cells that have been activated and that secrete antibodies in large amounts.
  • Macrophages and antigen-presenting cells engulf the pathogen, break it down, and display its antigens on their surface (on MHC proteins). This shows helper T cells what to respond to.

6.10: B cells and T cells

  • B effector (plasma) cells secrete antibodies. B memory cells survive for years and give a faster, larger response on the next exposure to the same antigen.
  • T helper cells (CD4) recognise the antigen on an antigen-presenting cell and release cytokines that activate B cells and T killer cells.
  • T killer (cytotoxic, CD8) cells bind to infected or abnormal cells and kill them, for example by releasing perforin.
  • T memory cells persist after the infection and respond quickly if the same pathogen returns.

6.11: Types of immunity

  • Natural active: the person is infected and makes their own antibodies and memory cells.
  • Natural passive: antibodies pass from mother to baby across the placenta or in breast milk. Protection is immediate but short-lived, and no memory cells are formed.
  • Artificial active: vaccination with an antigen, a weakened or dead pathogen, or a toxoid. The person makes antibodies and memory cells without becoming ill.
  • Artificial passive: injected antibodies, such as antivenom or antitoxin. Protection is immediate and short-lived, and the person's own immune system does not learn.

6.12: The evolutionary race between pathogens and hosts

  • Pathogens evolve evasion mechanisms. Antigenic variation changes the surface antigens: influenza and HIV mutate rapidly, so antibodies no longer fit.
  • Other evasion: hiding inside host cells (tuberculosis in macrophages, HIV in T cells), entering latency, and suppressing the immune response.
  • The host responds with new antibodies and T cells, so pathogens and hosts keep evolving against each other. This is the evolutionary race.

6.13: Bacteriostatic and bactericidal antibiotics

  • Bacteriostatic antibiotics stop bacteria growing and dividing, for example by blocking protein synthesis. The immune system then clears the infection.
  • Bactericidal antibiotics kill bacteria, for example penicillin, which stops cell wall synthesis so the cell bursts.
  • Antibiotics do not act on viruses, which use the host cell's machinery.

6.14: Core practical 14: the effect of antibiotics on bacteria

  • Spread a lawn of bacteria on agar, place antibiotic discs on it, and include a control disc with no antibiotic.
  • Incubate, then measure the diameter of each clear zone of inhibition. A larger zone means the bacteria are more sensitive.
  • Use aseptic technique and non-pathogenic strains, and autoclave the plates before disposal.

6.15: Hospital-acquired infections and codes of practice

  • Contributory causes include overuse of broad-spectrum antibiotics, which selects for resistant strains such as MRSA, poor hand hygiene, indwelling catheters, surgical wounds, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Codes of practice respond to these causes: prescribe antibiotics only when needed and according to guidelines, enforce hand hygiene, isolate infected patients, and clean equipment and wards.

6.16: Decomposition and the carbon cycle

  • Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They secrete extracellular enzymes that digest complex organic matter such as cellulose and proteins, then absorb the simpler products.
  • Respiration by decomposers releases carbon dioxide, which returns carbon to the atmosphere for producers. Ammonium released from proteins feeds the nitrogen cycle.

6.17: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

  • Each cycle has three steps: denaturation at about 95 °C separates the strands, annealing at about 50 to 65 °C lets primers bind, and extension at about 72 °C is when Taq polymerase builds the new strands.
  • Taq polymerase comes from the heat-tolerant bacterium Thermus aquaticus, so it survives the high temperatures. Around 30 cycles give an exponential increase in the number of copies.

6.18: Gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments

  • DNA carries a negative charge from its phosphate groups, so it moves towards the positive electrode (anode) through a gel.
  • Smaller fragments move faster and further, so fragments separate by length. A DNA ladder of known sizes is run alongside for comparison, and the bands are stained to make them visible.

6.19: DNA profiling for identification and relatedness

  • DNA profiling compares short tandem repeats (STRs) or variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). These regions vary in length between individuals, so each person gives a distinctive band pattern.
  • Uses include identifying suspects, establishing paternity, and comparing the banding patterns of plants or animals to show how closely related they are.

6.20: Estimating the time of death from forensic evidence

  • Body temperature: the body cools towards the surroundings, so the rate of cooling gives an estimate of time since death.
  • Muscle contraction: rigor mortis sets in over hours, peaks, then fades over about a day or two.
  • Decomposition and succession: bacterial decomposition gives a predictable sequence of changes. Forensic entomology uses the stage of blowfly larvae and the succession of insect species to estimate how long the body has been exposed.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Growth rate, 6.3 applied: a culture grows from 2.0 × 10⁴ cells cm⁻³ at 2 hours to 1.6 × 10⁵ at 5 hours. N₂ ÷ N₁ = 8 = 2³, so three doublings in three hours. k = (ln 1.6 × 10⁵ − ln 2.0 × 10⁴) ÷ 3 = ln 8 ÷ 3 = 0.69 per hour. The doubling time is ln 2 ÷ k = 1.0 hour. Check the answer against the doubling count before you write it down.
  • Viable count, 6.2 applied: 150 colonies grow from 0.1 cm³ of a 10⁻⁵ dilution. That is 150 ÷ 0.1 = 1500 colonies per cm³ in the diluted sample, and multiplying by the dilution factor gives 1.5 × 10⁸ viable cells per cm³. A haemocytometer count would include dead cells, so the two methods can give different numbers from the same culture. Name which one you are using.
  • Log phase, 6.3 applied: plotting ln N against time gives a straight line only during exponential growth. A curve that bends is a sign that the lag, stationary or death phase has been included by mistake. Use only the straight section to find k.
  • Primary and secondary immune response, 6.10 and 6.12 applied: the first exposure has a lag of several days before antibodies peak at a lower level. A second exposure gives a faster, larger and longer-lasting response, because memory cells are already present. Use all three words, faster, larger and longer, to earn the full mark.
  • Antigen presentation, 6.9 applied: helper T cells (CD4) recognise antigen presented on MHC class II proteins, and killer T cells (CD8) recognise it on MHC class I, as on infected body cells. Naming the MHC class shows you understand which cell carries the antigen.
  • Antibiotic action, 6.13 applied: penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan in the cell wall, so a growing cell bursts. An antibiotic that targets a process human cells do not use, such as the bacterial ribosome, is more selective. Resistance arises by chance mutation and is selected for by the antibiotic, so the explanation must say the mutation was already present and survived.
  • PCR, 6.17 applied: after n cycles one DNA molecule has become 2ⁿ molecules. After 30 cycles that is 2³⁰, about 1.07 × 10⁹ copies. This is why a very small sample is enough, and why contamination with foreign DNA is a serious error.
  • Gel electrophoresis, 6.18 applied: the distance moved is roughly linear with the logarithm of the fragment length. Use a DNA ladder to plot log size against distance, then read the unknown band from that graph rather than from the ladder bands by eye.
  • Forensic estimates, 6.20 applied: a time-of-death answer is always a range. Temperature cooling assumes a stable environment, and a hot or wet site or a body wrapped in clothing changes the rate. Say which factor is most uncertain and why.

Exam tip: time-of-death questions are estimates. Name the method, say what it measures, and state the limitation, for example that temperature depends on the environment.

title: The Normal Distribution — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: The Normal Distribution

Mathematics — A2. A continuous distribution with the familiar bell shape, symmetric about the mean, described by two parameters: X ~ N(μ, σ²). The curve is fully determined by μ (centre) and σ (width). Total probability is 1, and because X is continuous, P(X = a) = 0 for any single point — inequalities do not need strictness.

Key areas to revise

  • The Model
  • Standardising
  • Backwards Problems
  • Symmetry Shortcuts
  • Normal Approximation to the Binomial

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ². Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ and read the probability from tables. For Z < 1.5, the table gives 0.9332. The curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(X < μ) = 0.5, and about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two. ### Worked example X follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ². Standardise with Z = (X − μ)/σ and read the probability from tables. For Z < 1.5, the table gives 0.9332. The curve is symmetric about the mean, so P(X < μ) = 0.5, and about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two.

title: Chemical Energetics
content:
Chemical Energetics

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 5 (statement 5.1). Energy changes, exothermic and endothermic reactions, reaction pathway diagrams, activation energy and bond energy calculations.

5.1 Exothermic and endothermic reactions

  • Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings; the temperature of the surroundings rises. Combustion and neutralisation are exothermic. Endothermic reactions take in energy; the temperature falls. Thermal decomposition and photosynthesis are endothermic.
  • Enthalpy change, ΔH, is the energy change for a reaction. Exothermic: ΔH is negative. Endothermic: ΔH is positive.
  • Bond breaking is endothermic (energy is put in); bond making is exothermic (energy is released).
  • A reaction pathway (energy profile) diagram plots energy against progress: the reactants sit at one level, the products at another, and the difference is ΔH. The hump between them is the activation energy, Ea.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Bond energy calculation, applied to H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl: bonds broken are H–H (436 kJ/mol) and Cl–Cl (242 kJ/mol), total in = 678 kJ/mol. Bonds made are two H–Cl bonds (431 kJ/mol each), total out = 862 kJ/mol. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol. The reaction is exothermic, and the negative sign must be written.
  • Sign convention, applied to an endothermic decomposition: energy in is greater than energy out, so ΔH is positive. When the question asks "is the reaction exothermic or endothermic?", the sign of ΔH is your evidence — quote it.
  • Activation energy reasoning, applied to why a catalyst does not change ΔH: a catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful and the rate rises. The energy of reactants and products is unchanged, so ΔH is the same. State both halves of that argument.
  • Experimental enthalpy change, applied to an acid–alkali neutralisation measured in a polystyrene cup: q = mcΔT, with m the mass of the solution (use the volumes added, 1 cm³ ≈ 1 g), c = 4.2 J/g°C. If 50.0 cm³ rises by 6.8 °C, q = 50.0 × 4.2 × 6.8 = 1428 J. Divide by the moles of water formed to get ΔH per mole; the sign is negative because the solution warmed.

Common errors

  • Getting the ΔH sign backwards — energy out means negative.
  • Adding bond energies that are broken and made together instead of subtracting.
  • Calling the activation energy "the energy of the reaction". It is the minimum energy needed to start the reaction.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Processor Fundamentals

Computer Science — AS. The processor repeatedly fetches, decodes and executes instructions. Every instruction passes through the same cycle, and the registers and buses are the parts that carry it.

Key areas to revise

  • The fetch-decode-execute cycle: the address in the program counter is copied to the memory address register, the instruction is fetched into the memory data register and then the current instruction register, the instruction is decoded, and it is executed.
  • Registers: the program counter (PC), memory address register (MAR), memory data register (MDR), current instruction register (CIR) and accumulator (ACC), each with one job.
  • Buses: the address bus carries addresses one way from the processor, the data bus carries data both ways, and the control bus carries signals such as read and write.
  • Interrupts: a signal that stops the current task so that a higher-priority event can be handled, after which the saved state is restored.
  • Assembly and addressing: immediate addressing uses the value itself, direct addressing uses a memory address, indirect addressing uses an address stored at that address, and indexed addressing adds an index register to a base address.

Core facts to recall

  • The processor clock speed sets how many cycles happen each second, but more cycles do not always mean faster programs.
  • Pipelining lets the next instruction be fetched while the current one is executed.
  • In an exam, trace the registers one step at a time and write each value down.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Trigonometry (AS)
content:
### What earns the marks
For equations, the principal value earns one mark and each symmetry-derived solution earns the rest: sine mirrors at 180, tangent repeats every 180, squared roots split sign first. For identities, the Pythagorean substitution shown earns the method mark. For graphs, amplitude and period changes each earn a mark with the direction correct.
### Traps
Error: single solutions for full-range equations. Correction: map all quadrants. Error: negative cosine roots dropped. Correction: split plus-or-minus first. Error: 2x read as doubling the period. Correction: it halves it.
### Exact values
Learn the exact values of sine, cosine and tangent at 30, 45 and 60 degrees, because many questions ask for an answer in surd form. Use a diagram of the triangle to check a value rather than relying on memory alone.
### Use the quadrant rule
When you solve sin x = k, find the acute angle first, then use the sign of the function and the CAST diagram to find the second solution in the required range.
### List every solution
Give all solutions in the interval the question asks for and reject any that lie outside it. A question on a range of 0 to 360 degrees usually has two solutions for sine and cosine equations.
### Identities
Use sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1 and tan x = sin x / cos x to rewrite an equation in a single trigonometric ratio before you solve it.

title: Experimental Techniques and Chemical Analysis
content:
Experimental Techniques and Chemical Analysis

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 12 (statements 12.1–12.5). Apparatus and measurement, titration, chromatography and Rf, separation and purification, and the tests for ions and gases. Practical skills are examined directly in Paper 5 or 6.

12.1 to 12.2 Apparatus and titration

  • Measure time with a stopwatch, temperature with a thermometer, mass with a balance, volume of liquids with a burette, pipette or measuring cylinder. A volumetric pipette delivers one exact volume; a burette delivers a variable, measured volume.
  • Titration setup: rinse the burette with the solution it will hold, fill above zero, run out to remove the air bubble in the tip, record the initial reading at eye level with the meniscus. Swirl throughout and wash down near the endpoint.

12.3 Chromatography

  • Separation happens because components differ in solubility in the solvent and attraction to the paper. Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by the solvent. Colourless substances are located with a locating agent such as ninhydrin.

12.4 Separation and purification

  • Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; crystallisation obtains a dissolved solid; simple distillation obtains a solvent; fractional distillation separates miscible liquids with close boiling points. Purity is assessed by a sharp melting or boiling point.

12.5 Ion and gas tests

  • Carbonate + dilute acid → carbon dioxide (turns limewater milky). Halides with acidified silver nitrate: white (Cl⁻), cream (Br⁻), yellow (I⁻). Sulfate with acidified barium chloride → white precipitate. Nitrate + sodium hydroxide + aluminium foil → ammonia. Flame tests: lithium/calcium red, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, copper(II) green-blue, barium light green.
  • Aqueous cations with aqueous sodium hydroxide: copper(II) gives a blue precipitate soluble in excess only in ammonia; iron(II) pale green, iron(III) red-brown, aluminium white soluble in excess, zinc white soluble in excess. Ammonia: copper(II) deep blue solution, zinc white precipitate soluble in excess.
  • Gases: hydrogen relights a glowing splint with a squeaky pop; oxygen relights a glowing splint; carbon dioxide turns limewater milky; ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue; chlorine bleaches damp litmus.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Rf calculation, applied to a spot moving 3.6 cm while the solvent moves 9.0 cm: Rf = 3.6 ÷ 9.0 = 0.40. Rf has no unit and is always less than 1. Two spots with the same Rf on the same chromatogram are likely the same substance — say "on the same chromatogram", because Rf values are not comparable between different runs.
  • Evaluation reasoning, applied to a titration with titres of 22.35, 22.40 and 24.10 cm³: the 24.10 cm³ titre is a concordant outlier — discard it, because the first two agree within 0.10 cm³ and the third does not. Average the concordant titres: (22.35 + 22.40) ÷ 2 = 22.375 cm³, reported as 22.38 cm³.
  • Plan-a-method questions: name the independent variable (what you change), the dependent variable (what you measure) and the control variables (what you keep the same). Then give the safety point and one improvement. Structure answers in that order and every part of the question gets its mark.
  • Ion identification, applied to a white solid giving a yellow precipitate with silver nitrate that dissolves in excess ammonia: the halide is iodide. Write the full test, observation and conclusion as a chain — Cambridge marks each link separately, and skipping the observation loses the middle marks.

Common errors

  • Calling the milky limewater precipitate "a white precipitate in the test tube". The observation is that limewater turns milky.
  • Forgetting to state that the burette reading is taken at eye level to avoid parallax error.
  • Reporting Rf to the wrong precision or without showing the division.

title: Biological Molecules
content:
Biological Molecules

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 4 (statement 4.1). The building blocks and roles of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, plus the four food tests and their expected results.

4.1 Biological molecules

  • Carbohydrates are built from monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) joined by condensation into disaccharides (maltose, sucrose, lactose) and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose). Starch stores energy in plants; glycogen in animals; cellulose builds plant cell walls.
  • Proteins are built from about 20 amino acids joined by peptide bonds in condensation reactions. The sequence of amino acids determines the protein's shape and function; denaturation by heat or extreme pH changes that shape permanently.
  • Lipids (fats and oils) are glycerol plus three fatty acids joined into ester bonds. Fats store more energy per gram than carbohydrates, provide insulation and protection; oils are liquid because of unsaturated fatty acid chains.
  • Food tests: starch + iodine solution → blue-black. Reducing sugar + Benedict's solution, heat → brick-red precipitate. Protein + biuret reagent → purple. Lipid + ethanol then water → white emulsion.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Bond reasoning, applied to forming one triglyceride: three ester bonds form, and three molecules of water are released — one per bond. Condensation joins and releases water; hydrolysis breaks and requires water. State the numbers, not just the names.
  • Test interpretation, applied to a food sample that gives a brick-red precipitate with Benedict's but no colour change with biuret: it contains a reducing sugar and no protein. Write the conclusion as "contains X and not Y" — half-credit answers that identify the positive result only.
  • Structure-to-function reasoning, applied to why haemoglobin is a protein not a carbohydrate: its function of carrying oxygen requires a specific three-dimensional shape with haem groups, which only the amino acid sequence of a protein can provide. Function drives the answer — always name the specific function.
  • Denaturation reasoning, applied to enzyme protein denatured at high temperature: the bonds maintaining the tertiary structure break, so the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits. Reversible versus irreversible should be stated: at very high temperatures the change is permanent.

Common errors

  • Forgetting to heat the Benedict's test — no heat, no reaction.
  • Saying starch is a protein because it is "organic". Name the monomer and the test.
  • Confusing the emulsion test order: ethanol first to dissolve the lipid, then water to make the emulsion visible.

title: Quantum Physics — Study Notes
content:
Quantum Physics

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 2 (WPH12), sat at AS: photons, the photoelectric effect and wave–particle duality.

Photons and photon energy

Electromagnetic radiation travels as photons, each with energy E = hf, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is the Planck constant. Since c = fλ, the energy is also E = hc/λ. Shorter wavelength means higher energy.

Example: a photon of wavelength 500 nm has E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.0 × 10⁸)/(5.0 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 2.5 eV.

The photoelectric effect

When light shines on a metal surface, electrons are emitted only if the frequency of the light is at or above the threshold frequency f₀. Each photon transfers its whole energy to a single electron. Increasing the intensity increases the number of photons per second, so more electrons are emitted, but it does not increase the energy of each electron. The emission is instantaneous, with no time delay.

Wave theory cannot explain the threshold frequency or the lack of a time delay. The photon model explains both.

Einstein's photoelectric equation

hf = φ + E_k(max), where φ is the work function of the metal, the minimum energy needed to free an electron. The threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h. The stopping potential V_s satisfies eV_s = E_k(max).

Example: a work function of 2.0 eV gives f₀ = (2.0 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹)/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) ≈ 4.8 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

Wave-particle duality

Particles also have wave properties. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle with momentum p is λ = h/p. Electrons diffract through crystal lattices, showing wave behaviour, while photons show particle behaviour in the photoelectric effect. Both are needed to describe the same entities.

Energy levels and line spectra

Electrons in an atom occupy discrete energy levels. When an electron falls from a higher level E₁ to a lower level E₂, it emits a single photon with hf = E₁ − E₂. Absorption happens when a photon with exactly this energy is taken in. Because only specific energies are allowed, the spectrum is a set of sharp lines rather than a continuous band.

Example: a transition from −3.4 eV to −13.6 eV releases 10.2 eV, a wavelength of about 122 nm.

Exam tips: convert eV to joules (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) before using E = hf. Say which quantity the intensity changes and which it does not. Quote hf = φ + E_k(max) in photoelectric questions.

Worked example: threshold frequency and stopping voltage

Zinc has a work function of 4.3 eV. Converted to joules, that is 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so the threshold frequency is f₀ = φ/h = 6.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ ≈ 1.04 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Light of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz gives photons of energy 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.5 × 10¹⁵ ≈ 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or about 6.2 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the ejected electrons is 6.2 − 4.3 ≈ 1.9 eV, so the stopping voltage is about 1.9 V. Quote values with their units, and keep eV and joules consistent within each step.

Exam method: photon energy and wavelength

Combine E = hf with c = fλ to give E = hc/λ. Convert wavelengths to metres before you substitute into hc, because a wavelength given in nanometres must be multiplied by 10⁻⁹ first. A wrong power of ten is the most common way to lose the final mark, so estimate the answer before you calculate it precisely.

title: Dynamics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Dynamics

Physics — AS. Dynamics links forces to the motion they cause. Example: a 2 kg mass with a 10 N resultant force accelerates at a = F/m = 10/2 = 5 m s⁻².

Key areas to revise

  • Newton's laws: a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless a resultant force acts; F = ma gives the acceleration; every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
  • Weight and mass: weight is W = mg, a force measured in newtons, while mass is the amount of matter, measured in kilograms.
  • Momentum: p = mv. The impulse of a force equals the change in momentum, Ft = Δp.
  • Friction and connected bodies: friction F = μR opposes motion, and in connected bodies the tension is the same throughout a light string over a smooth pulley.

Core facts to recall

  • Draw a free-body diagram first, and show every force with its direction.
  • Resolve forces into components along and perpendicular to a slope before you apply F = ma.
  • Check units at each step: newtons, kilograms and metres per second squared must agree.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Communication and Networking
content:
### What earns the marks
For switching and protocols, describe earns marks for the mechanism plus its consequence: packets carry addresses and sequence numbers so routers forward independently and the receiver reassembles. For TCP vs UDP, justify earns marks for matching reliability to the use case, not for declaring one better. For security, name earns the control plus what it inspects: packet-filtering checks headers against rules.
### Traps
Error: circuit-switching features credited to packet switching. Correction: dedicated path and guaranteed bandwidth are circuit properties. Error: TCP recommended for live video. Correction: delay hurts more than loss there, so UDP. Error: claiming wireless uses collision detection. Correction: senders cannot listen while sending, so avoidance (RTS/CTS).
### Worked example
A local area network of computers in one room connects to the internet through a router. The router uses the IP address to send packets to the correct network. Each computer's network card has a MAC address that is fixed at manufacture, and a switch uses it to deliver frames within the local network.

title:
Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 4. Plant cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles and cell wall components (cell wall, chloroplasts, amyloplasts, vacuole and tonoplast, plasmodesmata, pits, middle lamella); starch and cellulose and why their structure fits storage and strength; how cellulose microfibril arrangement and secondary thickening give physical properties to xylem and sclerenchyma; the similarities and differences in structure, position and function of sclerenchyma fibres (support, dead, lignified), xylem vessels (support and water/mineral transport, dead, lignified, open tube) and phloem (translocation of organic solutes, living sieve tubes with companion cells, perforated walls); Core Practical 7 transverse sections; the uses of plant fibres and starch in sustainability as replacements for oil-based plastics; water and mineral ions to plants and Core Practical 8 the tensile strength of plant fibres; the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical on antimicrobial plant substances and zones of inhibition; drug testing from Withering's digitalis to modern double-blind placebo-controlled trials; classification and the species concept and the three-domain system from molecular evidence; biodiversity and endemism and how they are threatened by human activity; biodiversity measurements (species richness, heterozygosity index = heterozygotes/total, and the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1)) and comparing habitats; and the niche and behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations.

  • 4.1 Plant cell ultrastructure: cell wall (cellulose microfibrils in a gel matrix — shape, support, prevents bursting when turgid), chloroplast (double membrane, chlorophyll, thylakoid/grana for light reactions, stroma for light-independent reactions), amyloplast (colourless plastid, stores starch), vacuole + tonoplast (large central vacuole with cell sap, turgor and rigidity), plasmodesmata (channels through walls connecting adjacent cells' cytoplasm), pits (thin regions allowing water/solutes between cells), middle lamella (cements adjacent walls). Ribosomes, nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria and golgi are present as in animal cells; higher plants lack centrioles.
  • 4.2 EM recognition: recognise plasma membrane, nucleus and nucleolus, chloroplasts (with stacked grana), mitochondria, rER with ribosomes, golgi (dictyosomes), large central vacuole with tonoplast, cell wall and middle lamella, and plasmodesmata; distinguish plant from animal cells (plant has cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole, plasmodesmata, generally no centrioles).
  • 4.3 Starch and cellulose: starch = alpha-glucose polymer (amylose helical, amylopectin branched — compact, insoluble, osmotically inert, good for storage); cellulose = beta-glucose polymer (straight chains, hydrogen bonds between chains make strong microfibrils — structural); both from glucose but different bonds and shape give different roles.
  • 4.4 Microfibrils and secondary thickening: in growing cells microfibrils laid down at right angles to growth direction so the cell expands in length; when growth stops, secondary thickening deposits more cellulose and (in some cells) lignin on the inside, making the wall rigid and waterproof; in sclerenchyma fibres the walls are heavily lignified and the cells die at maturity — strong, flexible, tough — for support and human use; in xylem vessels the walls are lignified with rings, spirals or nets, and the cells are dead with end walls broken down — a continuous tube that resists collapse under transpiration tension.
  • 4.5 Fibres, xylem and phloem: sclerenchyma fibres — long, narrow, thick lignified walls, small lumen, dead, bundles — support and human use; xylem vessels — long open lignified tubes, dead, pits in walls — water and mineral transport plus support; phloem — living sieve tube elements end to end with sieve plates (perforated end walls), little cytoplasm, no nucleus at maturity, each with a companion cell connected by plasmodesmata that keeps it alive and supplies ATP — translocation of sucrose in solution from source (leaves/storage) to sink (growing points, roots, fruits).
  • 4.6 Core Practical 7: cut a thin transverse section with a razor blade, float on water, stain (toluidine blue or iodine) to distinguish lignified xylem, sclerenchyma and phloem, draw a plan diagram of the whole section showing tissue arrangement (not cells), label, title and magnification; then observe and label the cells — thick lignified xylem and sclerenchyma walls, sieve plates and companion cells of phloem, thin-walled cortex and pith cells.
  • 4.7 Plant fibres and starch for sustainability: plant fibres (from sclerenchyma or phloem) are strong, renewable, biodegradable — used in textiles, paper, building materials, composites, replacing oil-based plastics; starch can be processed into bioplastics for packaging, plates and disposable items — renewable and biodegradable, but land, water, energy and food competition must be weighed.
  • 4.8 Water and ions to plants: water for photosynthesis (reactant, medium), transport (solvent), support (turgor) and cooling (transpiration) — enters roots by osmosis, moves up the xylem; nitrate (NO₃⁻) for amino acids, proteins, DNA, chlorophyll — deficiency causes stunted growth and chlorosis of older leaves; calcium for middle lamella and membranes — deficiency gives stunted growth and necrosis of growing points and young leaves; magnesium for chlorophyll — deficiency causes chlorosis of older leaves; Core Practical: grow plants in complete solution and in solutions missing one ion, observe and measure effects over weeks.
  • 4.9 Core Practical 8: tensile strength of a plant fibre — clamp one end, hang weights from the other, add until it breaks, record the weight (force = mass × g) at breaking; repeat for several fibres; compare fibres from different plants or parts; safety: sharp blades, falling weights.
  • 4.10 Bacterial growth conditions: nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals, and for some organic factors), water, suitable temperature (many pathogenic bacteria ~37 °C, many environmental ~25 °C, but ranges vary), oxygen (aerobic, anaerobic, or facultative), suitable pH, time to multiply; cultured in nutrient broth or on agar, at a set temperature, with or without oxygen, in sterile conditions; aseptic technique: sterilise equipment (flame/autoclave), work near a flame for upward air current, cover plates, dispose of cultures by sterilising first.
  • 4.11 Antimicrobial plant substances: substances from plants (e.g. garlic) can inhibit bacteria or fungi; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies); modern drugs include many from plants; Core Practical: agar plates, sterile discs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate, measure the zone of inhibition (clear diameter where bacteria did not grow), compare extracts and concentrations; aseptic technique: sterilise discs and loops, work near a flame, spread bacteria in a controlled way, seal plates with tape (not all the way — keep them aerated), incubate at a safe temperature.

Worked example

Index of diversity: in habitat A species counts are 12, 8, 4 (N = 24). Σn(n−1) = (12×11) + (8×7) + (4×3) = 132 + 56 + 12 = 200; N(N−1) = 24×23 = 552; D = 552/200 = 2.76. In habitat B species counts are 20, 1, 1, 1, 1 (N = 24). Σn(n−1) = (20×19) + 4×(1×0) = 380 + 0 = 380; N(N−1) = 552; D = 552/380 = 1.45. So habitat A is more diverse than habitat B — even though both have four species and the same total — because in B one species dominates and the others are rare.

Key points to remember

The structure that makes a plant cell rigid is the cell wall, the large central vacuole and turgor, and the arrangement of cellulose microfibrils; the organelle with stacked membranes for photosynthesis is the chloroplast (grana in the thylakoids, stroma around them); starch stores glucose compactly and insoluble so no osmotic effect; cellulose's straight beta-glucose chains form hydrogen-bonded microfibrils, strong and supportive; secondary thickening and lignification stiffen walls for support and for the xylem to resist tension; xylem transports water and minerals and supports, phloem translocates sucrose from source to sink; water is essential for photosynthesis, transport, support (turgor) and cooling; nitrate, calcium and magnesium each have a specific role and deficiency gives characteristic symptoms; antibiotic plant substances and the aseptic practical involve zones of inhibition; drug testing progressed from uncontrolled historic trials to double-blind, placebo-controlled, phased, large multi-centre trials; classification is based on relationships using phenotypic and (increasingly) genotypic data, the species concept is a group that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, and the three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) came from molecular evidence (ribosomal RNA); biodiversity is the variety of life, endemism is being restricted to one place, human activity threatens it; biodiversity is measured by species richness, heterozygosity (heterozygotes/total) and the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1); the niche is the organism's role and its adaptations can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological.

Key points to remember

In the heterozygosity index, if a population of 20 individuals at a locus has 8 heterozygotes, H = 8/20 = 0.40, so the higher the number the greater the genetic diversity; in the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1), the larger D the more diverse, and the comparison between habitats means you calculate D for each and compare the values, explaining which is more diverse and what that suggests. Distinguish species richness (the number of species) from the index of diversity (which also reflects how even the individuals are among species). In drug testing, the placebo controls for the placebo effect, double-blind avoids bias from patient and clinician expectations, and the phases test safety (Phase 1), efficacy and side effects (Phase 2), and the drug against current treatment or placebo in a large group (Phase 3). The bacteriophage does not belong here — the antimicrobials come from plants, not from viruses; keep plant antimicrobial substances separate from the unrelated concept. The distinction between the habitat (the place) and the niche (the role and resources) is often asked — an organism's niche is more than where it lives.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: identifying plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an EM image and stating each organelle's function; drawing starch and cellulose and explaining the structure–function link; comparing sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in a table (structure, position, function); carrying out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explaining the variables and safety; describing the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical; describing the development of drug testing from Withering's digitalis to modern trials and evaluating the designs; defining classification and the species concept, describing the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it; defining biodiversity and endemism and listing the threats; carrying out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations including the worked comparison between habitats; and defining niche and giving behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations.
content:
Plant Structure and Function, Biodiversity and Conservation — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 4. Plant cell ultrastructure and the functions of the organelles and cell wall components (cell wall, chloroplasts, amyloplasts, vacuole and tonoplast, plasmodesmata, pits, middle lamella); starch and cellulose and why their structure fits storage and strength; how cellulose microfibril arrangement and secondary thickening give physical properties to xylem and sclerenchyma; the similarities and differences in structure, position and function of sclerenchyma fibres (support, dead, lignified), xylem vessels (support and water/mineral transport, dead, lignified, open tube) and phloem (translocation of organic solutes, living sieve tubes with companion cells, perforated walls); Core Practical 7 transverse sections; the uses of plant fibres and starch in sustainability as replacements for oil-based plastics; water and mineral ions to plants and Core Practical 8 the tensile strength of plant fibres; the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical on antimicrobial plant substances and zones of inhibition; drug testing from Withering''s digitalis to modern double-blind placebo-controlled trials; classification and the species concept and the three-domain system from molecular evidence; biodiversity and endemism and how they are threatened by human activity; biodiversity measurements (species richness, heterozygosity index = heterozygotes/total, and the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1)) and comparing habitats; and the niche and behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations.

  • 4.1 Plant cell ultrastructure: cell wall (cellulose microfibrils in a gel matrix — shape, support, prevents bursting when turgid), chloroplast (double membrane, chlorophyll, thylakoid/grana for light reactions, stroma for light-independent reactions), amyloplast (colourless plastid, stores starch), vacuole + tonoplast (large central vacuole with cell sap, turgor and rigidity), plasmodesmata (channels through walls connecting adjacent cells'' cytoplasm), pits (thin regions allowing water/solutes between cells), middle lamella (cements adjacent walls). Ribosomes, nucleus, nucleolus, mitochondria and golgi are present as in animal cells; higher plants lack centrioles.
  • 4.2 EM recognition: recognise plasma membrane, nucleus and nucleolus, chloroplasts (with stacked grana), mitochondria, rER with ribosomes, golgi (dictyosomes), large central vacuole with tonoplast, cell wall and middle lamella, and plasmodesmata; distinguish plant from animal cells (plant has cell wall, chloroplasts, large central vacuole, plasmodesmata, generally no centrioles).
  • 4.3 Starch and cellulose: starch = alpha-glucose polymer (amylose helical, amylopectin branched — compact, insoluble, osmotically inert, good for storage); cellulose = beta-glucose polymer (straight chains, hydrogen bonds between chains make strong microfibrils — structural); both from glucose but different bonds and shape give different roles.
  • 4.4 Microfibrils and secondary thickening: in growing cells microfibrils laid down at right angles to growth direction so the cell expands in length; when growth stops, secondary thickening deposits more cellulose and (in some cells) lignin on the inside, making the wall rigid and waterproof; in sclerenchyma fibres the walls are heavily lignified and the cells die at maturity — strong, flexible, tough — for support and human use; in xylem vessels the walls are lignified with rings, spirals or nets, and the cells are dead with end walls broken down — a continuous tube that resists collapse under transpiration tension.
  • 4.5 Fibres, xylem and phloem: sclerenchyma fibres — long, narrow, thick lignified walls, small lumen, dead, bundles — support and human use; xylem vessels — long open lignified tubes, dead, pits in walls — water and mineral transport plus support; phloem — living sieve tube elements end to end with sieve plates (perforated end walls), little cytoplasm, no nucleus at maturity, each with a companion cell connected by plasmodesmata that keeps it alive and supplies ATP — translocation of sucrose in solution from source (leaves/storage) to sink (growing points, roots, fruits).
  • 4.6 Core Practical 7: cut a thin transverse section with a razor blade, float on water, stain (toluidine blue or iodine) to distinguish lignified xylem, sclerenchyma and phloem, draw a plan diagram of the whole section showing tissue arrangement (not cells), label, title and magnification; then observe and label the cells — thick lignified xylem and sclerenchyma walls, sieve plates and companion cells of phloem, thin-walled cortex and pith cells.
  • 4.7 Plant fibres and starch for sustainability: plant fibres (from sclerenchyma or phloem) are strong, renewable, biodegradable — used in textiles, paper, building materials, composites, replacing oil-based plastics; starch can be processed into bioplastics for packaging, plates and disposable items — renewable and biodegradable, but land, water, energy and food competition must be weighed.
  • 4.8 Water and ions to plants: water for photosynthesis (reactant, medium), transport (solvent), support (turgor) and cooling (transpiration) — enters roots by osmosis, moves up the xylem; nitrate (NO₃⁻) for amino acids, proteins, DNA, chlorophyll — deficiency causes stunted growth and chlorosis of older leaves; calcium for middle lamella and membranes — deficiency gives stunted growth and necrosis of growing points and young leaves; magnesium for chlorophyll — deficiency causes chlorosis of older leaves; Core Practical: grow plants in complete solution and in solutions missing one ion, observe and measure effects over weeks.
  • 4.9 Core Practical 8: tensile strength of a plant fibre — clamp one end, hang weights from the other, add until it breaks, record the weight (force = mass × g) at breaking; repeat for several fibres; compare fibres from different plants or parts; safety: sharp blades, falling weights.
  • 4.10 Bacterial growth conditions: nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals, and for some organic factors), water, suitable temperature (many pathogenic bacteria ~37 °C, many environmental ~25 °C, but ranges vary), oxygen (aerobic, anaerobic, or facultative), suitable pH, time to multiply; cultured in nutrient broth or on agar, at a set temperature, with or without oxygen, in sterile conditions; aseptic technique: sterilise equipment (flame/autoclave), work near a flame for upward air current, cover plates, dispose of cultures by sterilising first.
  • 4.11 Antimicrobial plant substances: substances from plants (e.g. garlic) can inhibit bacteria or fungi; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies); modern drugs include many from plants; Core Practical: agar plates, sterile discs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate, measure the zone of inhibition (clear diameter where bacteria did not grow), compare extracts and concentrations; aseptic technique: sterilise discs and loops, work near a flame, spread bacteria in a controlled way, seal plates with tape (not all the way — keep them aerated), incubate at a safe temperature.

Worked example

Index of diversity: in habitat A species counts are 12, 8, 4 (N = 24). Σn(n−1) = (12×11) + (8×7) + (4×3) = 132 + 56 + 12 = 200; N(N−1) = 24×23 = 552; D = 552/200 = 2.76. In habitat B species counts are 20, 1, 1, 1, 1 (N = 24). Σn(n−1) = (20×19) + 4×(1×0) = 380 + 0 = 380; N(N−1) = 552; D = 552/380 = 1.45. So habitat A is more diverse than habitat B — even though both have four species and the same total — because in B one species dominates and the others are rare.

Key points to remember

The structure that makes a plant cell rigid is the cell wall, the large central vacuole and turgor, and the arrangement of cellulose microfibrils; the organelle with stacked membranes for photosynthesis is the chloroplast (grana in the thylakoids, stroma around them); starch stores glucose compactly and insoluble so no osmotic effect; cellulose''s straight beta-glucose chains form hydrogen-bonded microfibrils, strong and supportive; secondary thickening and lignification stiffen walls for support and for the xylem to resist tension; xylem transports water and minerals and supports, phloem translocates sucrose from source to sink; water is essential for photosynthesis, transport, support (turgor) and cooling; nitrate, calcium and magnesium each have a specific role and deficiency gives characteristic symptoms; antibiotic plant substances and the aseptic practical involve zones of inhibition; drug testing progressed from uncontrolled historic trials to double-blind, placebo-controlled, phased, large multi-centre trials; classification is based on relationships using phenotypic and (increasingly) genotypic data, the species concept is a group that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, and the three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) came from molecular evidence (ribosomal RNA); biodiversity is the variety of life, endemism is being restricted to one place, human activity threatens it; biodiversity is measured by species richness, heterozygosity (heterozygotes/total) and the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1); the niche is the organism''s role and its adaptations can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological.

Key points to remember

In the heterozygosity index, if a population of 20 individuals at a locus has 8 heterozygotes, H = 8/20 = 0.40, so the higher the number the greater the genetic diversity; in the index of diversity D = N(N−1)/Σ n(n−1), the larger D the more diverse, and the comparison between habitats means you calculate D for each and compare the values, explaining which is more diverse and what that suggests. Distinguish species richness (the number of species) from the index of diversity (which also reflects how even the individuals are among species). In drug testing, the placebo controls for the placebo effect, double-blind avoids bias from patient and clinician expectations, and the phases test safety (Phase 1), efficacy and side effects (Phase 2), and the drug against current treatment or placebo in a large group (Phase 3). The bacteriophage does not belong here — the antimicrobials come from plants, not from viruses; keep plant antimicrobial substances separate from the unrelated concept. The distinction between the habitat (the place) and the niche (the role and resources) is often asked — an organism''s niche is more than where it lives.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: identifying plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an EM image and stating each organelle''s function; drawing starch and cellulose and explaining the structure–function link; comparing sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in a table (structure, position, function); carrying out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explaining the variables and safety; describing the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical; describing the development of drug testing from Withering''s digitalis to modern trials and evaluating the designs; defining classification and the species concept, describing the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it; defining biodiversity and endemism and listing the threats; carrying out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations including the worked comparison between habitats; and defining niche and giving behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations.

title: Circular Measure — Study Notes
content:
Circular Measure

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11), sat at AS: radian measure, arc length, and the areas and perimeters of sectors and segments. Every formula here takes its angle in radians — that is the single fact most marks hinge on.

Radians

One radian is the angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius. The full circumference is 2πr, so a full turn is 2π radians and π radians = 180°.

  • Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Example: 150° = 150π/180 = 5π/6 ≈ 2.618 rad.
  • Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π. Example: 1.5 rad = 1.5 × 180/π ≈ 85.9°.

Learn the common values: 30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2, 180° = π, 360° = 2π. Leave answers in terms of π unless the question asks for a decimal — and when it does, give three significant figures.

Arc Length

s = rθ (θ in radians).

Example: r = 6, θ = π/3 gives s = 6 × π/3 = 2π.

A chord splits the circumference into a minor arc and a major arc, and their lengths add to 2πr. If a question gives the major angle, use θ_major = 2π − θ_minor before substituting.

Sector Area

A = ½r²θ.

Example: r = 5, θ = 1.2 gives A = ½ × 25 × 1.2 = 15.

Minor and major sector areas add to πr². The perimeter of a sector is P = 2r + s = 2r + rθ — the two straight edges count, so an arc length alone is not a perimeter.

Segment Area

A = ½r²(θ − sin θ). For r = 2, θ = π/2: A = 2(π/2 − 1) = π − 2.

The segment is the sector minus the triangle ½r²sin θ — that subtraction is where the formula comes from, and writing it down earns method marks even if the arithmetic slips. Its perimeter is the arc plus the chord, with chord length 2r sin(θ/2).

Putting It Together

Worked example: a sector has radius 8 cm and angle 1.1 rad. Arc length s = 8 × 1.1 = 8.8 cm. Area A = ½ × 64 × 1.1 = 35.2 cm². Perimeter P = 2 × 8 + 8.8 = 24.8 cm.

Rearranging

  • θ = s/r (must be radians)
  • θ = 2A/r²
  • r = s/θ, and r = √(2A/θ) — isolate the squared term first, then take the positive root only, since a radius is a length.

Exam traps: never mix degrees into s = rθ or A = ½r²θ — convert first, and check the calculator is in radian mode. Sketch the sector and mark r and θ before computing. Read whether the question asks for the major or the minor arc, sector, or segment, and confirm area answers carry squared units while arcs and perimeters are plain lengths.

Worked example: arc length and sector area

A sector has radius 5 cm and angle 0.8 radians. The arc length is rθ = 5 × 0.8 = 4 cm. The sector area is ½r²θ = ½ × 25 × 0.8 = 10 cm².

Both formulas need the angle in radians. If the question gives degrees, convert first: 60° = π/3 radians, and 1 radian is about 57.3°. Writing a degree value into rθ is one of the most common lost marks in this topic.

Exact answers with π

For radius 6 cm and angle π/3, the arc length is 6 × π/3 = 2π cm, and the sector area is ½ × 36 × π/3 = 6π cm². Leave answers in terms of π when the question asks for an exact value, and give a decimal only if it asks for one.

Segment area

A segment is the region between a chord and an arc. Its area is the sector area minus the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord, so segment = ½r²(θ − sin θ).

Example: with r = 5 and θ = 0.8, sin 0.8 is about 0.7174, so the segment area is ½ × 25 × (0.8 − 0.7174) = 1.03 cm² to 2 decimal places. Keep sin θ in your calculator, not rounded, until the final line.

Finding an angle or radius from a perimeter or arc

If an arc has length 12 cm on a circle of radius 4 cm, the angle is θ = 12/4 = 3 radians. If the perimeter of a sector is given, the perimeter is 2r + rθ, so set that expression equal to the known value and solve for the unknown.

  • Check that the answer is reasonable: an angle of 3 radians is less than π, so the sector must be less than a half-disc.
  • Sketch the sector and label the radii and the angle before you substitute.
  • When a question combines two sectors or a sector with a triangle, find each area separately and then add or subtract, stating which operation you used.
