Key relationships

  • Speed = distance / time, and an object with a constant velocity has zero resultant force.
  • Newton's second law: resultant force = mass × acceleration.
  • Weight W = mg, where g is about 9.8 N/kg on Earth.
  • Momentum = mass × velocity, and a falling object reaches terminal velocity when drag equals its weight.

Common errors

Mass and weight are different: mass is measured in kilograms and is the same everywhere, while weight is a force in newtons. Do not say a moving object needs a force to keep it moving.

title: Inheritance
content:
Inheritance

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 17 (statements 17.1–17.4). DNA, genes and chromosomes, mitosis and meiosis, and monohybrid inheritance with genetic diagrams and probability.

17.1 Chromosomes, genes and proteins

  • DNA is a double helix of two strands made of nucleotides; genes are sections of DNA that code for proteins. Chromosomes carry many genes. An allele is a version of a gene; genotype is the allele combination; phenotype is the expressed characteristic.

17.2 Mitosis

  • Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells for growth, repair and asexual reproduction. It follows DNA replication, then one division.

17.3 Meiosis

  • Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid gametes. Two divisions follow replication; crossing over and independent assortment create variation. Fertilisation restores the diploid number.

17.4 Monohybrid inheritance

  • A genetic diagram shows parents' genotypes, the gametes, the Punnett square, then offspring genotypes and phenotypes with ratios. For two heterozygotes Bb × Bb, offspring are 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, phenotypic ratio 3 : 1.
  • Sex determination: females XX, males XY. A father's gamete decides the sex of the offspring — 50% chance of a girl, 50% of a boy.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Genetic diagram, applied to albinism (recessive a): two heterozygous parents Aa × Aa have offspring in the ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so 1 in 4 is albino. If the question asks for the chance from several children, each conception is independent — multiply the probabilities, and state that assumption.
  • Crossing over reasoning, applied to why meiosis increases variation: non-sister chromatids exchange sections during prophase I, so alleles that were on the same chromosome appear on different ones. That recombination, with independent assortment of chromosome pairs, produces new combinations.
  • Sex-linked reasoning, applied to haemophilia (Xᴴ normal, Xʰ affected): a carrier mother XᴴXʰ and a normal father XᴴY have a 25% overall chance of an affected son — 1 in 4 of all children, or 1 in 2 of their sons. State which denominator you are using; the ambiguity loses marks otherwise.

Common errors

  • Writing gametes with paired alleles. Gametes carry one allele of each gene.
  • Saying meiosis makes identical cells. Genetic variation is the point of meiosis.
  • Confusing the phenotypic ratio (3:1) with the genotypic ratio (1:2:1).

title: Measurement & Units — Study Notes
content:
Measurement & Units

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): 1.1 lengths & volumes; 1.2 density; 1.3 forces & motion context (measurements) — plus measurement techniques, SI units, scalars/vectors.

1. Measuring

  • Length: ruler (mm), vernier calipers (0.1 mm / 0.01 cm), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm).
  • Volume: measuring cylinder read at the meniscus bottom; regular solids by calculation; irregular by displacement (eureka can).
  • Time: stopwatch — human reaction time ±0.2 s; measure many oscillations and divide (e.g. 20 T).
  • Pendulum: T = time/oscillations; f = 1/T.

2. SI units and prefixes

QuantityUnitSymbol
lengthmetrem
masskilogramkg
timeseconds
currentampereA
temperaturekelvin (°C used)K

kilo 10³; centi 10⁻²; milli 10⁻³; micro 10⁻⁶; nano 10⁻⁹.

3. Scalars and vectors

Scalars: distance, speed, mass, energy, time. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum. Vector addition by scale diagram (tip-to-tail) or by components.

4. Density

ρ = m/V (kg/m³ or g/cm³; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³). Determining: mass on balance; volume by displacement. Floating: ρobject < ρfluid.

5. Accuracy and improvements

Avoid parallax (eye level with reading), zero errors (subtract the zero reading), measure multiple laps for small times. Suggest improvements by naming the error and the fix.

Making accurate measurements

The SI base unit of length is the metre (m), and common multiples and submultiples are given in kilometres, centimetres and millimetres. A micrometer screw gauge measures small lengths to about 0.01 mm. A zero error is a reading that is not zero when it should be, and every reading must be corrected by it. Parallax error occurs when the eye is not directly in line with the scale, and it is avoided by reading the scale straight on.

Repeating a measurement and calculating the mean reduces random error. Time many oscillations of a pendulum and divide by the number, to reduce the effect of reaction time on a stopwatch.

Exam tip: give a reading to the same precision as the instrument, and state the unit.

Significant figures and decimal places

Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit. The number 0.00304 has three significant figures, and 4500 to two significant figures is written as 4.5 × 10³. Decimal places count digits after the point. When rounding a measurement, give the answer to the precision of the least precise measurement used in the calculation, and do not show more digits than the data justify.

Worked example: converting between units

To convert 2.5 km into metres, multiply by 1000 to get 2500 m. To convert 450 cm² into m², divide by 10 000, because one square metre is 100 cm × 100 cm, which gives 0.045 m². A common error is to convert a length by 100 when an area or a volume is required. For volume, one cubic metre is 1 000 000 cm³, so 3 m³ is 3 000 000 cm³.

Reading scales and measuring accurately

To read an analogue scale, identify the value of the smallest division, then estimate the reading to a tenth of that division. Record every reading with the same number of decimal places as the scale. A measurement of the thickness of a sheet of paper is made more accurate by measuring many sheets together and dividing by their number, which reduces the effect of the reading error on a single sheet.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): kinetic particle model; thermal expansion; specific heat capacity; melting/boiling; conduction, convection, radiation.

1. Kinetic model

Solid: fixed positions, vibrate — fixed shape/volume. Liquid: move around, touching — fixed volume, flows. Gas: far apart, fast random motion — fills container. Brownian motion evidences random molecular motion.

2. Gas pressure and temperature

Pressure from wall collisions. Heating at fixed volume → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions → higher pressure.

3. Thermal expansion

Heating → particles vibrate more → solids expand slightly (gases expand most). Applications: bimetallic strip (fire alarm/thermostat), gaps in bridges/rails; the liquid-in-glass thermometer.

4. Specific heat capacity

c = ΔE/(mΔθ). Heating: ΔE = mcΔθ.

Example: 2 kg water (c = 4200), 20→80 °C: ΔE = 2×4200×60 = 504 kJ.

High c of water → coolant; temperature rise measured with known heater power P in time t: c = Pt/(mΔθ).

5. State changes

Melting/boiling at fixed temperature despite heating (energy breaks bonds, not temperature). Condensation/ freezing release energy. Impurities raise melting point of mixtures/lower freezing; boiling needs nucleation.

6. Transfer: conduction, convection, radiation

  • Conduction: mainly metals (delocalised electrons + lattice vibration); non-metals poor; insulators trap air.
  • Convection: hot fluid expands, density falls, rises; denser cool fluid sinks — currents.
  • Radiation: infrared EM waves; no medium; matte black best absorber/emitter, shiny silver worst.

Applications: vacuum flask, house insulation, car radiators, solar heating panels.

Heat transfer and heat capacity

Energy transfer by conduction happens through a solid when particles vibrate and pass energy to their neighbours, with free electrons carrying energy in metals. Convection in fluids occurs because hotter, less dense fluid rises and is replaced by cooler, denser fluid. Black, matt surfaces are good absorbers and emitters of infrared radiation.

The energy needed to change the temperature of a substance is Q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity. Latent heat is the energy absorbed or released during a change of state with no change in temperature.

Worked example: heating a substance

A 2 kg block of aluminium with specific heat capacity 900 J/(kg °C) is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. The energy supplied is Q = mcΔθ = 2 × 900 × 50 = 90 000 J, which is 90 kJ. The specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C, so the same calculation with a different material gives a different energy for the same mass and temperature rise.

Worked example: melting ice

The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is the energy needed to change 1 kg of ice at 0 °C into water at 0 °C without any change in temperature. For 0.5 kg of ice with latent heat 334 000 J/kg, the energy needed is Q = mL = 0.5 × 334 000 = 167 000 J. During melting the temperature stays constant, so the energy goes into breaking the bonds between molecules rather than raising the temperature.

Conduction, convection and radiation

Conduction transfers thermal energy through a solid by particles passing on kinetic energy to their neighbours, and metals conduct well because of their free electrons. Convection transfers energy through a fluid, because warmer, less dense fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks. Radiation transfers energy as infrared waves, which need no medium, and a dark matt surface is both the best absorber and the best emitter of radiation. Name the process in the question and link it to the property of the material that controls it.

title: Exam technique: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages
content:
### What earns the marks
For percentages of amounts, the 10-percent building blocks shown earn method marks without a calculator. For reverse percentages, state what the given amount represents (64 dollars = 80 percent) before dividing: that line earns the mark. For compound interest, each year on its own line earns credit. For Steel-type growth and decay, the multiplier (1/2 cubed) stated earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: adding 20 percent to the sale price for the original. Correction: the sale price is the base of nothing; divide by 0.8. Error: simple interest applied twice for compound growth. Correction: grow each year from the new total. Error: decimal-point slips in 3/8 to percent. Correction: decimal first (0.375), then times 100.
### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.
### Worked example
Find 35% of 240: 0.35 × 240 = 84. A value increases by 20% to reach 180. The original is 180 ÷ 1.2 = 150, because you divide by the multiplier rather than taking 20% of 180. Check: 150 × 1.2 = 180. For fractions, 3/4 + 2/5 = 15/20 + 8/20 = 23/20 = 1 3/20.

title: Databases — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Databases

Computer Science — AS. A database stores related data in tables so that it can be searched, updated and shared safely. Good design keeps each fact in one place, so that an update does not leave conflicting copies behind.

Key areas to revise

  • Relational basics: tables (entities), records (rows), fields (columns), a primary key that identifies each record uniquely, and a foreign key that links one table to another.
  • Normalisation: first normal form removes repeating groups and keeps values atomic; second normal form removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key; third normal form removes fields that depend on a non-key field.
  • SQL: SELECT with FROM and WHERE to query, ORDER BY to sort, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE to change data, and JOIN to combine tables through matching keys.
  • Transactions: a group of changes that must all succeed or all fail. ACID means atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.

Core facts to recall

  • Data redundancy wastes space and causes update anomalies; normalisation reduces both.
  • A referential integrity rule stops a foreign key from pointing at a record that does not exist.
  • Explain a normal form by naming the dependency it removes, and give a field from your own example.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Pressure & Density — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Pressure & Density

Physics — OL. pressure & pressure differences in fluids, density review (Extended pressure-depth).

  • 1. Pressure basics
  • 2. Liquids
  • 3. Atmospheric pressure
  • 4. Density revisited
  • 5. Gas pressure (particle model)

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Pressure p = force / area, measured in pascals.
  • Pressure in a liquid is p = h ρ g, where h is the depth, ρ is the density and g is the gravitational field strength.
  • Density ρ = mass / volume.
  • An object floats when its density is less than the density of the fluid, and atmospheric pressure falls as altitude increases.

Common errors

Liquid pressure depends on depth and density, not on the total volume or shape of the container. Use depth measured vertically below the surface, not the length of the slope.

title: Scatter Diagrams and Correlation — Study Notes
content:
Scatter Diagrams and Correlation

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): scatter diagrams, types of correlation, line of best fit, interpolation vs extrapolation.

1. Correlation types

  • Positive: both increase (revision time vs score).
  • Negative: one increases, other decreases (price vs demand).
  • No correlation: random scatter.
  • Strength: strong (tight to a line) vs weak (loose).

2. Line of best fit

Balance points either side of the line; it need not pass through the origin. Use two well-separated points on your line (not necessarily data points) to estimate its gradient and equation.

Example: line through (10, 24) and (50, 60): m = 36/40 = 0.9 → y = 0.9x + 15.

3. Using the line

Interpolation (inside the data range) is reliable; extrapolation (outside) is a risk — say so if asked.

4. Correlation ≠ causation

A third factor may drive both variables (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise with temperature). Describe relationships, don't over-claim.

5. Outliers

Points far from the trend: identify, and comment on their effect on the line; ignore them when drawing the best fit if instructed.

Exam tips: describe correlation in full ("strong positive linear correlation"); quote the equation only from two points on the drawn line, not raw data.

Reading a scatter diagram

Each point plots one pair of values. Positive correlation means y tends to rise as x rises; negative correlation means it falls. The strength of correlation depends on how closely the points cluster around a line. Correlation does not prove causation.

Lines of best fit

Draw a straight line through the middle of the points, with roughly equal numbers of points on each side, and use it to estimate values. Interpolation (inside the data range) is generally reliable; extrapolation (beyond the data) is less so and should be stated as an estimate.

Outliers

A point far from the general pattern is an outlier. Mention it in your answer and state whether it affects the conclusion, rather than ignoring it silently.

Worked example: using a line of best fit

A line of best fit for the data is y = 2x + 1. To predict y when x = 6, substitute to get y = 2 × 6 + 1 = 13. The value x = 6 lies inside the range of the data, so this is interpolation and is usually reliable. If the data only covered x from 0 to 10, predicting y when x = 30 would be extrapolation, which assumes the trend continues beyond the data and is unreliable.

Strength of the relationship

  • Strong positive correlation: the points lie close to a rising line, so the line of best fit is a good model.
  • Weak correlation: the points are scattered widely, so any prediction from the line is of little value.
  • No correlation: the points show no pattern, and a line of best fit should not be used for prediction.

Interpreting the gradient

In a question about height and arm span, the gradient of the line shows how much the second quantity changes for each unit increase in the first. Always include units in the interpretation, for example "each extra centimetre of height is associated with about 1.1 cm of arm span", and avoid saying that height causes arm span.

Exam point: a line of best fit should pass through the mean point (x̄, ȳ) and should have about as many points above it as below it. Reading the value from a graph should be done with a dotted line drawn from the axis to the line and then to the other axis.

title: Exam technique: Databases
content:
### What earns the marks
For DBMS benefits, justify earns marks per benefit tied to the scenario: integrity plus concurrency for multi-user systems. For keys, the composite identified earns one mark and the foreign-key link earns the second. For SQL, the clause order SELECT-FROM-WHERE-ORDER BY correct earns marks stepwise; text literals in quotes earn precision.
### Traps
Error: single repeating field claimed as primary key. Correction: test uniqueness across all rows. Error: SELECT * accepted for named fields. Correction: list only asked fields. Error: ASC/DESC swapped. Correction: DESC runs high to low.
### Write SQL in clauses
For a SELECT question, build the statement clause by clause: SELECT the fields, FROM the tables, JOIN on the matching key, WHERE to filter rows, then GROUP BY and ORDER BY where asked. Check that every field in SELECT is either aggregated or in GROUP BY.
### Keys and normalisation
A primary key uniquely identifies each record and a foreign key links to another table's primary key. When asked why data is normalised, say that it removes repeated data, so an update changes one row and cannot leave inconsistent copies.
### Common slips
Using WHERE where HAVING is needed after an aggregate, and forgetting that a join without the correct key produces every combination of rows.

title: Transition Metals and their Chemistry - A2 Chemistry
content:
Transition Metals and their Chemistry - A2 Level

This topic belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Level (IAL) Chemistry specification, Unit 5 (WCH15), and covers the electronic configurations, variable oxidation states, complex ion formation, ligand exchange, colour changes, standard electrode potentials of vanadium and chromium systems, catalysis, and practical preparations associated with d-block transition elements of Period 4 from scandium to zinc.

Definition and Electronic Configurations of Transition Metals

Transition metals are defined as d-block elements that form one or more stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals. Scandium and zinc are in the d-block but are not true transition metals because Sc3+ has an empty d-orbital (3d0) and Zn2+ has a completely filled d-orbital (3d10). To deduce electronic configurations of Period 4 atoms and ions from Sc to Zn, remember that the 4s orbital fills before 3d, but when positive ions are formed, electrons are always removed from the 4s orbital before the 3d orbitals.

  • Transition metals are d-block elements forming stable ions with incompletely-filled d-orbitals (17.1).
  • Electronic configuration rules: fill 4s then 3d, empty 4s before 3d when forming ions (17.2).
  • Example atom Ti (atomic number 22): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d2 (17.2).
  • Example ion Fe2+ (atomic number 26): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6, with the two 4s electrons removed (17.2).
  • Example ion Cu+ (atomic number 29): 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 (17.2).
  • Variable oxidation numbers occur because the 4s and 3d sub-shells have very similar energies, allowing different numbers of electrons to be lost or involved in bonding with minimal energy penalty (17.3).

Complex Ions, Ligands, and Coordination Numbers

A complex ion consists of a central metal ion surrounded by species called ligands. A ligand is a species containing at least one lone pair of electrons that forms a dative covalent (coordinate) bond to the central metal ion. The coordination number is the total number of coordinate bonds formed to the central metal ion. The nature and size of ligands determine the spatial arrangement and geometry of the resulting complex ion.

  • Ligand definition: a species with a lone pair that forms a dative covalent bond to a metal ion (17.4, 17.5).
  • Complex ion definition: a central metal ion surrounded by ligands (17.6).
  • Coordination number: the number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion (17.10).
  • Monodentate ligands donate one pair of electrons; H2O, OH− and NH3 act as monodentate ligands (17.12).
  • Six-fold coordination complexes have an octahedral shape, such as [M(H2O)6]n+, [M(OH)6]n−, and [M(NH3)6]n+ (17.13).
  • Tetrahedral complexes form with relatively large ligands such as Cl−, for example [CuCl4]2− and [CoCl4]2−, due to steric hindrance preventing six chloride ions from packing around the small metal centre (17.14).
  • Square planar complexes are also formed by transition metal ions; cis-platin, [Pt(NH3)2Cl2], is a square planar complex used in cancer treatment supplied as a single active cis isomer rather than a mixture with the inactive trans form (17.15).
  • Bidentate ligands have two donor atoms donating two lone pairs, such as ethane-1,2-diamine (NH2CH2CH2NH2). Hexadentate ligands have six donor atoms, such as EDTA4− (17.16).
  • Haemoglobin is an iron(II) complex containing a polydentate porphyrin ring ligand; ligand exchange occurs when an oxygen molecule bound to haemoglobin in the lungs is replaced by a carbon monoxide molecule in the body tissues (17.17).

Colour and d-Orbital Splitting

Aqueous solutions of transition metal ions are usually coloured because the presence of surrounding ligands causes the five degenerate d-orbitals to split into two different energy levels. When white light passes through the solution, electrons absorb specific frequencies of visible light to jump from the lower d-orbitals to the higher d-orbitals. The colour observed is due to the remaining unabsorbed wavelengths transmitted or reflected. A lack of colour in some aqueous ions or complex ions, such as Sc3+ (3d0) or Zn2+ (3d10), occurs because their d-orbitals are either completely empty or completely full, so d-d electronic transitions are impossible.

  • Aqueous solutions of transition metal ions are usually coloured (17.7).
  • Colour arises from the splitting of the energy levels of d-orbitals by the electrostatic field of surrounding ligands (17.8).
  • Lack of colour in ions like Sc3+ (3d0) and Zn2+ (3d10) is due to empty or full d-orbitals preventing d-d electron transitions (17.9).
  • Colour changes in transition metal ions arise from changes in oxidation number, changes in ligand, or changes in the coordination number of the complex (17.11).

Vanadium and Chromium Redox Chemistry

Vanadium exhibits four stable oxidation states in aqueous solution, each with a characteristic colour: +5 (yellow, VO2+), +4 (blue, VO2+), +3 (green, V3+), and +2 (violet, V2+). These oxidation states can be interconverted via redox reactions using zinc metal in acidic conditions as a reducing agent, driven by standard electrode potential (Eo) values. Similarly, chromium chemistry involves the interconversion of Cr3+ and dichromate(VI) ions, Cr2O7 2−. Dichromate(VI) ions can be reduced using zinc in acid and produced by oxidising Cr3+ with hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions followed by acidification. In aqueous solution, dichromate(VI) ions exist in a pH-dependent equilibrium with chromate(VI) ions.

  • Vanadium oxidation states and colours: +5 is yellow (VO2+), +4 is blue (VO2+), +3 is green (V3+), and +2 is violet (V2+) (17.18).
  • Redox interconversion of vanadium oxidation states is achieved using zinc in acidic solution, evaluated through relevant Eo values where Zn/Zn2+ is sufficiently negative to reduce V5+ down to V2+ (17.19).
  • Dchromate(VI) ions (Cr2O7 2−) can be reduced to Cr3+ and further to Cr2+ using zinc in acidic conditions (17.20i).
  • Dichromate(VI) ions can be produced by the oxidation of Cr3+ ions using hydrogen peroxide in alkaline conditions, followed by subsequent acidification (17.20ii).
  • Dichromate(VI) ion equilibrium with chromate(VI): Cr2O7 2− + H2O <-> 2CrO4 2− + 2H+ (17.21). Adding acid shifts this equilibrium left towards orange dichromate; adding alkali shifts it right towards yellow chromate.

Reactions of Aqueous Transition Metal Ions with Hydroxide and Ammonia

Aqueous metal ions react with sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia to produce precipitates, which may show amphoteric behaviour or dissolve in excess reagent due to ligand exchange. You must know the exact observations and write balanced ionic equations for Cr3+(aq), Mn2+(aq), Fe2+(aq), Fe3+(aq), Co2+(aq), Ni2+(aq), Cu2+(aq), and Zn2+(aq).

  • Cr3+(aq) + 3OH−(aq) -> Cr(OH)3(H2O)3(s) (grey-green precipitate). Excess OH− gives [Cr(OH)6]3− (dark green solution) demonstrating amphoteric behaviour (17.22, 17.23).
  • Cr3+(aq) with NH3(aq): grey-green precipitate of Cr(OH)3(H2O)3, insoluble in excess ammonia (17.22).
  • Mn2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Mn(OH)2(s) (off-white precipitate, turns brown on standing in air due to oxidation). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Fe2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Fe(OH)2(s) (green precipitate, turns brown on surface in air). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Fe3+(aq) + 3OH−(aq) -> Fe(OH)3(s) (rusty-brown precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH− and excess NH3 (17.22).
  • Co2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Co(OH)2(s) (blue precipitate, turns pink on standing). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, forms [Co(NH3)6]2+ (pale yellow solution turning brown) via ligand exchange (17.22, 17.23, 17.24).
  • Ni2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Ni(OH)2(s) (green precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, dissolves to form [Ni(NH3)6]2+ (blue solution) (17.22, 17.23).
  • Cu2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Cu(OH)2(s) (pale blue precipitate). Insoluble in excess OH−. With excess NH3, dissolves to form [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (deep blue solution) (17.22, 17.23, 17.24).
  • Zn2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Zn(OH)2(s) (white precipitate). Dissolves in excess OH− to form [Zn(OH)4]2− (colourless solution) demonstrating amphoteric behaviour (17.22, 17.23).
  • Zn2+(aq) with excess NH3(aq): white precipitate dissolves to form [Zn(NH3)4]2+ (colourless solution) (17.22, 17.23).
  • Deprotonation reactions involve aqueous metal ions losing protons from coordinated water molecules to form neutral hydroxide precipitates (17.23).

Specific Ligand Exchange Reactions and Entropy

Ligand exchange occurs when one ligand in a complex is replaced by another, accompanied by a distinct colour change and often a change in coordination number. The thermodynamic stability of complex ions is significantly enhanced when monodentate ligands are replaced by bidentate or hexadentate ligands, known as the chelate effect. This can be understood in terms of the positive increase in entropy (Ssystem) because there are more free moles of product species than reactant species in solution.

  • Formation of [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ (deep blue) from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (pale blue) proceeds via an intermediate Cu(OH)2(H2O)4 precipitate upon adding ammonia, which then redissolves in excess ammonia (17.24i).
  • Formation of [CuCl4]2− (yellow-green) from [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (blue) occurs upon adding concentrated hydrochloric acid, resulting in a change in coordination number from 6 to 4 and a shape change from octahedral to tetrahedral (17.24ii).
  • Formation of [CoCl4]2− (blue) from [Co(H2O)6]2+ (pink) occurs on adding concentrated hydrochloric acid, changing coordination number from 6 to 4 and shape from octahedral to tetrahedral (17.24iii).
  • Substitution of monodentate ligands by bidentate or hexadentate ligands leads to a more stable complex ion due to a positive increase in system entropy (Ssystem), as the number of independent particles in solution increases (17.25).

Catalysis by Transition Metals

Transition metals and their compounds are exceptionally effective catalysts, operating as either heterogeneous catalysts (in a different phase from reactants, with reactions occurring on the catalyst surface) or homogeneous catalysts (in the same phase as reactants, proceeding via intermediate species). V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process for manufacturing sulfur trioxide. Catalytic converters in vehicles use solid platinum/rhodium heterogeneous catalysts to remove carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide emissions via adsorption, bond weakening, reaction, and desorption. Homogeneous catalysis is exemplified by Fe2+ catalysing the reaction between iodide and peroxydisulfate ions, and Mn2+ autocatalysing the reaction between manganate(VII) and ethanedioate ions.

  • Heterogeneous catalyst: in a different phase from reactants; reaction occurs at the active sites on the surface of the catalyst (17.26, 17.27).
  • V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process by being reduced from V(V) to V(IV) by SO2, then reoxidised back to V(V) by O2: SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + V2O4, followed by V2O4 + 0.5O2 -> V2O5 (17.28).
  • Catalytic converter mechanism: 1. Adsorption of CO and NO molecules onto the metal surface, weakening covalent bonds. 2. Chemical reaction between adsorbed species to form CO2 and N2. 3. Desorption of product molecules from the surface (17.29).
  • Homogeneous catalyst: in the same phase as reactants, proceeding through distinct intermediate species (17.30).
  • Role of Fe2+ in catalysing reaction between I− and S2O8 2−: Fe2+ reduces S2O8 2− to SO4 2− forming Fe3+ intermediate (S2O8 2− + 2Fe2+ -> 2SO4 2− + 2Fe3+), then Fe3+ oxidises I− back to I2 regenerating Fe2+ (2Fe3+ + 2I− -> 2Fe2+ + I2) (17.31).
  • Role of Mn2+ in autocatalysing reaction between MnO4 − and C2O4 2−: reaction starts very slowly, but the Mn2+ product acts as a catalyst, speeding up the reaction as its concentration increases (autocatalysis) (17.32).
  • Core Practical 14: The preparation of a transition metal complex, such as potassium tris(oxalato)ferrate(III) trihydrate, involving ligand substitution, precipitation, recrystallisation, and percentage yield calculation (17.33).

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Removing electrons from 3d orbitals before 4s orbitals when writing ion configurations. Correction: Always fill 4s before 3d, but remove electrons from the 4s orbital first when forming positive ions.
  • Mistake: Stating that Sc3+ or Zn2+ solutions are coloured. Correction: They are colourless because they do not have incompletely-filled d-orbitals to permit d-d electron transitions.
  • Mistake: Confusing coordination number with the number of ligands. Correction: Coordination number is the total number of coordinate bonds, which equals the number of monodentate ligands, but is double the number of bidentate ligands.
  • Mistake: Omitting phase or charge when writing complex ion formulas. Correction: Always enclose the complex in square brackets with the overall charge outside, e.g., [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that cis-platin must be supplied as a single isomer. Correction: Cis-platin is supplied specifically as the cis isomer because only this form binds to DNA to inhibit cancer cell replication.

Exam-style questions

  1. Deduce the ground state electronic configuration of a cobalt(II) atom (atomic number 27) and a cobalt(III) ion. (2 marks)

    Answer: Co atom is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d7 (1 mark). Co3+ ion is 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d6, with electrons removed from 4s first (1 mark).

  2. Explain why aqueous copper(II) sulfate is blue, whereas aqueous scandium(III) chloride is colourless. (3 marks)

    Answer: Cu2+ has an incompletely-filled 3d9 configuration; d-orbitals split in the ligand field, allowing d-d electron transitions which absorb specific frequencies of visible light (2 marks). Sc3+ has a 3d0 configuration with no d-electrons, so no d-d transitions are possible, making it colourless (1 mark).

  3. Describe what you would observe when excess aqueous ammonia is added dropwise to an aqueous solution containing copper(II) ions. Write ionic equations for the reactions that occur. (4 marks)

    Answer: Observations: pale blue solution forms a pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)2, which then dissolves in excess ammonia to form a deep blue solution (2 marks). Equations: Cu2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) -> Cu(OH)2(s) followed by Cu(OH)2(s) + 4NH3(aq) + 2H2O(l) -> [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+(aq) + 2OH−(aq) (2 marks).

  4. Explain why the substitution of six monodentate water ligands by three bidentate ethane-1,2-diamine ligands in a complex ion is thermodynamically favoured by entropy. (2 marks)

    Answer: There is an increase in the total number of independent particles/molecules in solution from 4 reactants to 7 products (1 mark), leading to a positive entropy change (Ssystem > 0) making the complex more stable (1 mark).

  5. Outline how V2O5 acts as a heterogeneous catalyst in the Contact process, including chemical equations. (3 marks)

    Answer: V2O5 is in a different phase (solid) from the gaseous reactants (1 mark). It oxidises SO2 to SO3, being reduced itself: SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + V2O4 (1 mark). The V2O4 is then reoxidised by oxygen back to V2O5: V2O4 + 0.5O2 -> V2O5 (1 mark).

Use these revision notes alongside active recall of colour changes, precipitation reactions, and equation writing. Practise balancing redox equations for vanadium and chromium, and ensure you can explain the chelate effect using entropy arguments before moving on to past paper practice.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Colour, applied to [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺: the d-orbitals split into two energy levels in an octahedral complex. The complex absorbs light that promotes an electron across that gap, and the colour seen is the complementary colour. A change in ligand changes the splitting, and so changes the colour.
  • Ligand exchange with entropy, applied to [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ with excess NH₃: [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ + 4NH₃ → [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺ + 4H₂O. The number of particles is unchanged, so ΔS is about zero. Compare this with EDTA, where the chelate gives an increase in the number of particles and a positive ΔS.
  • Vanadium oxidation states: V²⁺ is lilac, V³⁺ green, VO²⁺ blue and VO₂⁺ yellow. A reduction from VO₂⁺ to VO²⁺ and then to V³⁺ can be followed by the colour change, which is why it is used in redox titrations.
  • Catalysis: the contact process uses V₂O₅ in SO₂ + ½O₂ → SO₃, where the vanadium changes oxidation state in the cycle, V(V) to V(IV) and back. Haber uses iron. Name the oxidation state change in the cycle, because mark schemes award it separately.

title: Exam technique: Permutations and Combinations
content:
### What earns the marks
For counting, the permutation vs combination choice justified earns the method mark. For restricted arrangements, fixing the block first then permuting earns both marks. For probability of selections, the hypergeometric fraction built stepwise earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: P used where order is irrelevant. Correction: C for choose. Error: double counting symmetric selections. Correction: divide by the internal permutations. Error: identical items permuted fully. Correction: divide by repeats factorial.
### Decide whether order matters
If the order of selection matters, use permutations. If it does not, use combinations. Many questions combine the two, so read the wording carefully before you start.

### Handle restrictions in a fixed order
Place the items with the most restrictions first, such as a particular person who must sit at one end, then fill in the remaining places. Writing each step as a product of counts keeps the working transparent.

### Watch for identical items and repeated selection
Divide by the factorial of any repeated items, and check whether the question allows the same item to be chosen more than once before you multiply.

title: Thermal Physics — Study Notes
content:
Thermal Physics

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 5 (WPH15), sat at A2.

Temperature and scales

Thermodynamic temperature is measured in kelvin. The kelvin and Celsius scales have the same size of degree, with T/K = θ/°C + 273. Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles of an ideal gas have minimum kinetic energy.

Example: 25 °C = 298 K.

Specific heat capacity and latent heat

Specific heat capacity c is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔθ. Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without a change in temperature: Q = mL. Melting and boiling absorb energy without a temperature rise, because the energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, not into kinetic energy.

Example: warming 2.0 kg of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹) by 10 K needs 84 kJ. Melting 0.20 kg of ice (L = 334 kJ kg⁻¹) needs 67 kJ.

The mole and Avogadro constant

One mole contains N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ particles. The number of particles is N = nN_A, where n is the amount in moles. Molar mass is the mass of one mole, in kg mol⁻¹ in SI units.

Equation of state for an ideal gas

pV = nRT, where R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and T must be absolute. Equivalently pV = NkT, with k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.

Example: 0.10 mol at 300 K in 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ has p = nRT/V ≈ 1.2 × 10⁵ Pa.

Kinetic theory

The pressure of an ideal gas comes from molecules colliding with the container walls. The mean kinetic energy of a molecule is ⟨Ek⟩ = 3kT/2, so it depends only on the absolute temperature. At 300 K it is about 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J.

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy of an ideal gas is the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy depends only on temperature. The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = Q + W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done on the system. Heat lost by a system is therefore negative.

Example: a gas has 500 J of work done on it and loses 200 J of heat. ΔU = −200 + 500 = +300 J.

Exam tips: convert to kelvin before using pV = nRT or the kinetic-energy formula. Check the sign convention for W in the question. Use latent heat only when the temperature is constant.

Worked example: pressure of a fixed amount of gas

A sample of 0.50 mol of ideal gas is at 300 K in a container of volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Using pV = nRT with R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, the pressure is p = (0.50 × 8.31 × 300) ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻³) ≈ 6.2 × 10⁵ Pa. If the same gas is heated to 600 K in a rigid container, the pressure doubles, because for a fixed amount of gas at constant volume p is proportional to T in kelvin. Converting temperatures to kelvin before multiplying is the step examiners check first.

Exam method: units and conversions

Convert cm³ to m³ by dividing by 1 000 000, and convert °C to K by adding 273 (or 273.15). Mass in grams must be turned into kilograms for kinetic energy calculations, and into moles using the molar mass. A quick unit check helps: pressure in pascals multiplied by volume in cubic metres gives joules, the unit of energy.

title: Trigonometry — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11), sat at AS.

Exact Values

Anglesincostan
30°1/2√3/2√3/3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3

Key Identities

  • sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
  • tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
  • sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ

Solving Equations

Use the symmetry of the graphs. For sin x = 1/2 in 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: the acute answer is π/6, and the second solution is π − π/6 = 5π/6.

For cos x = 0.5 in 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°: x = 60° and 360° − 60° = 300°.

Always check the required interval and give every solution.

Graphs and Transformations

y = a sin(bx) + c has amplitude a, period 2π/b, and vertical shift c.

Example: y = 3 sin(2x) has amplitude 3 and period π.

Using Identities

If sin x = 0.6 with x acute, then cos x = √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 (positive in the first quadrant).

Exam tips: write the general second solution using graph symmetry rather than memorising CAST blindly; square both sides only with care, as it can add false solutions.

Exact values and exam method

Use CAST to find the quadrant signs: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third, cosine in the fourth. Find the acute angle first, then the other solutions in the range the question specifies.

For sin x = k, the solutions in 0° to 360° are α and 180° − α, where α is the acute angle with sin α = |k|. For cos x = k they are α and 360° − α. Always check the range; an answer outside it earns no mark.

Write a sin x + b cos x as R sin(x + α) or R cos(x − α). Expanding gives R = √(a² + b²), and for the sine form tan α = b/a. The maximum value is R, which gives the turning points that exam questions often ask for.

Reciprocal functions: sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x, cot x = 1/tan x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 and 1 + tan²x = sec²x to simplify.

Exam cue: Show the working that gives the acute angle before stating the answers in the required range.

Worked example: exact values and a quadrant rule

Use the exact values sin 30° = ½, cos 45° = 1/√2 and tan 60° = √3. For an angle such as 150°, sin 150° = sin(180° − 30°) = sin 30° = ½, because sine is positive in the second quadrant. For 225°, tan 225° = tan 45° = 1, because tangent is positive in the third quadrant.

Draw a quick CAST diagram to decide the sign: all positive in the first quadrant, sine in the second, tangent in the third and cosine in the fourth.

Solving a trigonometric equation

Solve 2cos x = 1 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. Then cos x = ½, so x = π/3 or x = 2π − π/3 = 5π/3. Always find the principal value first, then use the symmetry of the graph to find the other solutions in the range.

Solve 2sin²x − sin x − 1 = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°. Factor as (2 sin x + 1)(sin x − 1) = 0. Then sin x = 1, giving x = 90°, or sin x = −½, giving x = 210° and 330°.

Proving an identity

Show that (sin x + cos x)² = 1 + sin 2x. Expand the left side: sin²x + 2 sin x cos x + cos²x. Use sin²x + cos²x = 1 to get 1 + 2 sin x cos x, and recall sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, so the left side equals 1 + sin 2x.

Graphs and transformations

  • y = 3 sin 2x + 1 has amplitude 3, period 180° (or π radians), and the maximum value 4 occurs at x = 45°.
  • The range of y = 3 sin 2x + 1 is −2 ≤ y ≤ 4.
  • A horizontal stretch by factor ½ halves the period; a vertical shift of +1 moves the whole graph up by one unit.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Working in degrees when the question uses radians, or the reverse. Check the units in the question before you start.
  • Giving only the principal value and missing the other solutions in the range. Always check the quadrant signs.
  • Squaring both sides of an equation to remove a root, which can add extra solutions. Check each answer in the original equation.

title: Intermolecular Forces — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Intermolecular Forces

Chemistry — AS. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 7. Intermolecular forces are the attractions between molecules, not the bonds inside them. They determine boiling points, solubility and how molecules pack together.

Key areas to revise

  • Types of intermolecular force

title: Probability Distributions — Study Notes
content:
Discrete Random Variables

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 1 (WST01), sat at AS.

Probability Distributions

A discrete random variable X takes values xᵢ with probabilities pᵢ where each pᵢ ≥ 0 and Σpᵢ = 1. A probability distribution can be given as a table, a formula, or a function. Any missing probability is found by subtraction.

Example: X = number of heads in 2 fair tosses: P(0) = 1/4, P(1) = 1/2, P(2) = 1/4.

Expectation

The mean of X is

  • E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ

It is a weighted average — the long-run average value over many repetitions. E(X) need not equal any value X can actually take.

Variance

  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

where E(X²) = Σxᵢ²pᵢ — square the values before multiplying by probabilities. The standard deviation is √Var(X).

Linear Transforms

For constants a and b:

  • E(aX + b) = a·E(X) + b and Var(aX + b) = a²·Var(X)

Adding a constant shifts but does not spread; multiplying scales the spread by |a|.

Independent Variables

If X and Y are independent: E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) and Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). The addition rule for expectation always holds; the variance addition needs independence. The same applies to differences: Var(X − Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) — the subtraction does not cancel spread.

Exam tips: first verify Σp = 1 in any given table. Write E(X²) and (E(X))² separately; merging them is the most common exam error. In games of chance, set the expected profit to zero to find a fair entry fee.

Exam method: discrete distributions

A discrete probability distribution gives P(X = x) for each value x. Each probability lies between 0 and 1, and the probabilities sum to 1. Use the sum to find an unknown constant before calculating any other probability.

The expected value is E(X) = Σ x P(X = x), and E(X²) = Σ x² P(X = x). The variance is Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]². Set out the values, probabilities and products in a table to keep the working clear.

For a function of X, such as Y = 2X + 3, the expected value is E(Y) = 2E(X) + 3. The variance changes as Var(2X + 3) = 4 Var(X), because adding a constant does not change the spread.

When a question asks for P(X ≤ x) or P(X ≥ x), add the probabilities for the values in the range.

Exam cue: Check that the probabilities sum to 1 before reporting any expected value, because a missing or wrong probability makes the rest of the answer wrong.

Worked example: expectation and variance of a discrete variable

Let X take the values 0, 1, 2 and 3 with probabilities 0.1, 0.4, 0.3 and 0.2. The expectation is E(X) = 0(0.1) + 1(0.4) + 2(0.3) + 3(0.2) = 0 + 0.4 + 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.6. To find the variance, first find E(X²) = 0 + 0.4 + 1.2 + 1.8 = 3.4, then Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² = 3.4 − 2.56 = 0.84. Calculating E(X²) directly and subtracting the square of the mean is quicker than summing squared deviations, and it is the method to use when the probabilities are given as a table.

Checking a probability distribution

Every probability must lie between 0 and 1 inclusive, and the probabilities must sum to 1. If a question gives an unknown probability, use the sum to find it before calculating any expectation. Writing the check on the page shows the examiner that the distribution is valid, and it protects you from losing the later method marks when a slip appears in the first line.

The binomial distribution

If X is the number of successes in n independent trials, each with success probability p, then X follows a binomial distribution. Its mean is np and its variance is np(1 − p). The probability of exactly r successes is the binomial coefficient multiplied by p to the power r and by (1 − p) to the power n − r. State the conditions of independence and constant probability when you use this model.

Key points to remember

The index laws let you combine powers: multiply by adding indices, divide by subtracting them, and raise a power to another power by multiplying. A zero index gives 1, and a negative index means the reciprocal. A fractional index such as one half means the square root.

Standard form writes a number as A times 10 to the power n, where A is at least 1 and less than 10. A large number has a positive power and a small number a negative one. Count how far the decimal point moves to find n, and check that A lies between 1 and 10 before you finish.

title: Articles and Determiners — Study Notes
content:
Articles (a, an, the) and determiners (some, many, much, each) tell the reader whether a noun is specific, general, countable or uncountable. Small words like these are often where accuracy is lost in writing.

Indefinite article: a and an

Use a or an with a singular countable noun when it is first mentioned or not specific.

  • I bought a bag.
  • He arrived after an hour.

Choose the form by sound, not spelling. Use an before a vowel sound, even when the spelling begins with a consonant: an hour. Use a before a consonant sound, even when the spelling begins with a vowel: a university, a European.

Definite article: the

Use the when both speaker and listener know which thing is meant.

  • The café we visited last week was closed.
  • The sun rises in the east.

No article

Use no article for general plural or uncountable nouns.

  • I like coffee in the morning.
  • Children need sleep.

Determiners with countable and uncountable nouns

  • Many and few go with countable nouns: many books, few students.
  • Much and little go with uncountable nouns: much water, little time.
  • Some and any work with both.

Checking your writing

Ask two questions: is this noun specific to the reader? Is it countable? Those two answers decide the article and the determiner.

title: Redox Equilibria Revision Notes
content:
Redox Equilibria Revision Notes

These revision notes cover Edexcel International A2 Level Chemistry Topic 16, exploring electron transfer, standard electrode potentials, cell diagrams, thermodynamic feasibility, fuel cells, and quantitative redox titrations.

  • Oxidation is loss of electrons and increase in oxidation number, while reduction is gain of electrons and decrease in oxidation number, applied across s-, p- and d-block elements.
  • Standard electrode potentials, Eo, are measured under standard conditions of 298 K temperature, 100 kPa pressure, and 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration of ions using a reference standard hydrogen electrode.
  • Different half-cell arrangements measure potentials for metals in contact with their ions, non-metals with their ions, or inert platinum electrodes for ions of the same element with different oxidation numbers.
  • Core Practical 12 involves investigating electrochemical cells to measure cell potentials and understand how half-cells combine.
  • Standard cell emf, Eo cell, is calculated by combining two standard electrode potentials using Eo cell = Eo right − Eo left, and can be represented using conventional cell diagrams.
  • Electrode potentials vary when conditions depart from standard values, and Eo cell is directly proportional to total entropy change and to lnK for a reaction.
  • Standard electrode potentials predict thermodynamic feasibility and disproportionation reactions, though kinetic stability and non-standard conditions can limit these predictions.
  • Standard electrode potentials are also known as standard reduction potentials and form an electrochemical series.
  • Core Practicals 13a and 13b involve carrying out structured and unstructured redox titrations using iron(II) with potassium manganate(VII), and sodium thiosulfate with iodine, while analysing measurement uncertainties.
  • Hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells generate voltage from the reaction of a fuel with oxygen using either acidic or alkaline electrolytes, with methanol and other hydrogen-rich fuels also utilised.

Worked example

Calculate the standard cell emf for a cell made of Zn(2+) / Zn (Eo = −0.76 V) and Cu(2+) / Cu (Eo = +0.34 V) half-cells. Write the conventional cell diagram and determine feasibility. The more positive half-cell undergoes reduction on the right, so Eo cell = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. The positive emf indicates the reaction is thermodynamically feasible. The cell diagram is written as Zn(s) | Zn(2+)(aq) || Cu(2+)(aq) | Cu(s).

Key points to remember

Students frequently forget that conventional cell diagrams place the oxidized species next to the salt bridge or phase boundary, using a single vertical line for phase boundaries and a double vertical line for salt bridges. Remember that inert platinum electrodes must be included in cell diagrams and half-cell setups when all species in the half-cell are in aqueous solution and no solid metal conductor is present.

When calculating titration results, always ensure balanced ion-electron half-equations are combined correctly to establish stoichiometric ratios, particularly for manganate titrations where 1 mole of MnO4(−) reacts with 5 moles of Fe(2+), and thiosulfate titrations where 2 moles of S2O3(2−) react with 1 mole of I2. Discussing measurement uncertainties requires distinguishing between percentage errors in volumetric glassware and reading uncertainties on burettes.

title:
Respiration, Muscles and the Internal Environment — Edexcel International A2 Level Biology

This revision note covers the biology topics that sit behind the energy use of cells and animals and behind the maintenance of the internal environment. It is built around the specification statements rather than around a loose theme, so each numbered section reflects one or more things the specification expects a candidate to be able to do. The note is deliberately at exam depth: it explains the reasoning, gives the worked examples and comparisons that examiners look for, and lists the common mistakes that lose marks in this topic. Use it to check what you actually know and to practise the kinds of answer the specification rewards.

1. Why respiration matters and what the topic is for

Respiration is the set of reactions that release energy from nutrient molecules and couple that energy to the work cells do. The main nutrient in most questions is glucose, and the main energy currency that respiration produces is ATP. The practical point is that cells do not get energy directly from glucose; they get it from ATP, and respiration is the process that links the fuel to the currency. Understanding respiration therefore means understanding where the energy comes from, how the cell captures it, and how that energy is used in muscles and in the rest of the body.

The topic also connects to the internal environment, because muscles and tissues can only work properly if the internal conditions stay within limits, and because the energy demand of the body changes when muscles work. The link between respiration, muscles and the internal environment is that exercise changes the demand for ATP, which changes the demand for oxygen and fuel and the production of waste, and the internal environment has to respond. If you see the topic as one connected question about supply, demand and control, the parts will fit together rather than staying as separate facts.

2. Aerobic respiration as a sequence of stages, not a single reaction

Aerobic respiration is not one enzyme-controlled reaction but a sequence of stages: the stages are glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP and reduced NAD. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle happen in the mitochondrial matrix and produce reduced coenzymes and carbon dioxide. Oxidative phosphorylation happens in the inner mitochondrial membrane and uses the reduced coenzymes to make the bulk of the ATP and to reduce oxygen to water.

The important idea is that respiration is staged: each stage does a specific job and the stages are connected. Glycolysis starts the breakdown of glucose. The link reaction converts pyruvate and removes carbon dioxide. The Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group and harvests hydrogen. Oxidative phosphorylation harvests the energy from the hydrogen and passes it to ATP. A good answer says that respiration is staged, gives the four stages in order, and says where each occurs. It does not say that respiration is a single reaction that turns glucose into ATP in one step, because that is not what happens and it loses marks.

A good answer also says that oxygen is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation and that this is why the process is aerobic: without oxygen the chain stops and ATP production from oxidative phosphorylation stops. The link between oxygen and ATP is one of the reasons aerobic respiration yields more ATP than anaerobic alternatives, because the full oxidation is completed and the hydrogen carriers can be re-oxidised at the end of the chain. If you can say that, you have the aerobic idea in a form that scores marks.

3. Glycolysis: the investment and payoff phases and the net yield

Glycolysis is the first stage of respiration and it happens in the cytoplasm. It phosphorylates glucose, splits the phosphorylated intermediate, and then oxidises triose phosphate, producing pyruvate, a small net yield of ATP and reduced NAD. The investment phase uses ATP to phosphorylate glucose and its intermediates; the payoff phase produces the ATP and reduced NAD that make glycolysis worth doing.

The classic net yield for the overall equation taught in this specification is often stated as producing a small amount of ATP per glucose, with the rest coming later from the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. The important point is not to memorise only the number but to understand that glycolysis produces pyruvate, ATP and reduced NAD, and that the ATP comes from substrate-level phosphorylation, while the reduced NAD is a carrier of hydrogen that will feed into oxidative phosphorylation if oxygen is available. A good answer says that glycolysis phosphorylates glucose, splits it, oxidises triose phosphate, produces pyruvate and a small amount of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and produces reduced NAD. It does not say that glycolysis makes the most ATP, because it does not; that comes later.

The intermediate phosphorylation is the reason glycolysis is not just a simple split. Glucose has to be primed with phosphate so that it can be split and so that the triose phosphate can be oxidised. The ATP investment at the start pays off later, which is why the net yield is what it is. If you can say that, you have the logic of glycolysis rather than just a list of steps.

4. The link reaction and the Krebs cycle: decarboxylation and hydrogen harvesting

The link reaction converts pyruvate into acetyl coenzyme A, releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD. The Krebs cycle then oxidises the acetyl group, releasing more carbon dioxide, producing ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and generating reduced NAD and reduced FAD. The carbon dioxide released in these stages is the CO2 that the cell, and the organism, must dispose of, and the hydrogen carried by the reduced coenzymes is what feeds oxidative phosphorylation.

The link reaction is the bridge between glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion, is oxidised and decarboxylated to form the acetyl group, which is attached to coenzyme A. The Krebs cycle then uses the acetyl group to regenerate oxaloacetate and to produce the reduced coenzymes and substrate-level phosphorylation that are the point of the cycle. A good answer says that the link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl coenzyme A with release of CO2 and reduced NAD, and that the Krebs cycle oxidises the acetyl group with release of CO2, production of ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation and production of reduced NAD and reduced FAD. It does not say that the Krebs cycle happens in the cytosol, because it happens in the mitochondrial matrix. It also does not say that the Krebs cycle is the stage that uses oxygen, because oxygen is used in oxidative phosphorylation, not in the cycle itself.

The main conceptual point of the Krebs cycle is that it is a cycle that oxidises a two-carbon acetyl group and harvests hydrogen, releasing carbon dioxide along the way. The ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation in the cycle is small compared with the ATP from oxidative phosphorylation, but the cycle’s real job is to supply the reduced coenzymes. If you can say that, you have the role of the Krebs cycle rather than just a sequence of intermediates.

5. Oxidative phosphorylation and the role of the inner membrane and oxygen

Oxidative phosphorylation is the stage that makes the most ATP and the stage where oxygen is used. It happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where the reduced coenzymes deliver hydrogen and the energy from the electrons is used to pump protons, creating a proton gradient that drives ATP synthesis as protons flow back through ATP synthase. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain, and water is formed.

The key point is that ATP is made by chemiosmosis, not by a single enzyme directly handing a phosphate to ADP. Energy from the electron transport chain is used to pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, and the resulting proton gradient is what drives ATP synthesis when protons flow back through ATP synthase. Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with protons to form water, so without oxygen the chain stops and the gradient cannot be maintained. A good answer says that oxidative phosphorylation happens on the inner mitochondrial membrane, that the energy from the electrons pumps protons, that the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase, and that oxygen is the final electron acceptor forming water. It does not say that ATP is made directly by the electron transport chain itself; it is made by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.

The distinction between the electron transport chain and ATP synthase is important because it is one of the places where a lack of precision loses marks. The chain creates the gradient; ATP synthase uses it. If you keep that distinction clear, you can explain why a poison that blocks the chain, or a lack of oxygen, stops ATP production. The model is also the reason that the inner membrane is folded into cristae: it increases the surface area for the proteins of the chain and for ATP synthase. If you can say that, you have connected the structure to the function.

6. ATP as the energy currency and why respiration is staged

ATP is the immediate energy currency that respiration supplies to the cell. The energy for most cellular processes does not come directly from glucose or food; it comes from the hydrolysis of ATP. Respiration exists so that the energy in food can be used to regenerate ATP, and then the ATP can be used for endergonic processes, active transport, movement and biosynthesis. The role of ATP is to act as a small, reusable and immediately available packet of energy that can be used where and when it is needed.

The reason respiration is staged rather than a single big burn is that staged release is more controllable and more efficient in the biological sense. The energy is not released all at once as heat, but in a way that the cell can use to phosphorylate ADP; the carrier molecules handle the hydrogen and the energy between stages; and the stages can be regulated according to the cell’s needs. A good answer says that respiration is staged so that the energy is released in manageable amounts that the cell can use to make ATP, and that ATP is the energy currency used by the cell. It does not say that the stages are only for historical reasons or that the cell could simply burn glucose in one step for the same practical result, because the control and capture are the point.

The link between ATP and work is that ATP hydrolysis is endergonic to reverse but exergonic in the cell’s direction, so it provides energy for processes that would not otherwise occur. The cell uses ATP to drive active transport, to drive movement including muscle contraction, and to drive biosynthesis, and respiration is what keeps the ATP supply up. If you can say that, you have the currency idea in a form that scores marks.

7. Contraction as sliding filaments, not shortening of the filaments themselves

Muscle contraction works by the sliding filament model, not by the filaments shortening. The actin and myosin filaments slide past one another, so the sarcomere shortens even though the filaments themselves do not get shorter. The thick filaments are myosin, the thin filaments are actin, and the contraction happens when myosin heads bind to actin, pivot, release and re-bind further along, pulling the thin filament past the thick one.

The important point is that contraction is sliding, and that the length of the filaments does not change. A good answer says that during contraction the filaments slide past each other so the sarcomere shortens, that the filaments themselves do not shorten, and that myosin heads bind to actin and pivot to pull the thin filament past the thick one. It does not say that the filaments shorten; it says that they slide. That is one of the most common mistakes in this topic, because it is easy to think that contraction means the filaments get shorter when it actually means they get closer together and the overlap increases.

The energy for the sliding is provided by ATP. ATP is used both to power the power stroke and to detach the myosin head so the cycle can repeat. The calcium ions that are released into the sarcoplasm when the muscle is stimulated allow the myosin head to bind to actin in the first place. The full story is therefore ATP plus calcium plus the filament arrangement, but the most important exam point is the sliding filament idea itself. If you can say that, you have the contraction idea in a form that scores marks.

8. The role of ATP and calcium in the contraction cycle

The contraction cycle uses ATP and calcium. Calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum when the muscle is stimulated, and the calcium allows the myosin head to bind to actin by exposing the binding sites. ATP then is used to break the myosin-actin link and re-cock the myosin head, and another ATP is hydrolysed to position the head for the next stroke. When calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered again, the muscle relaxes.

A good answer says that calcium exposes the actin binding sites so myosin can bind, that ATP is used to break the cross-bridge and re-cock the head, and that the cycle is powered by ATP hydrolysis. It also says that relaxation happens when calcium is removed and the binding sites are covered. It does not say that relaxation uses no ATP, because it does not; the detachment and repositioning of myosin need ATP, and that is one reason rigor mortis happens, because ATP is no longer available and the myosin stays bound. If you can say that, you have the energy story of contraction in a form that scores marks.

The calcium role is essential, not optional. Without calcium, the myosin heads cannot bind to actin and the muscle cannot contract, even if ATP is present. ATP alone is not enough; you need calcium to start the cycle and ATP to keep it going. If you can keep that distinction clear, you can answer the question correctly and avoid the common mistake of saying that ATP alone is what starts contraction.

9. ATP supply during exercise and the limits of aerobic capacity

During exercise the demand for ATP rises, and the rate of respiration must rise to match it. Aerobic respiration can supply ATP for sustained moderate exercise, but when the rate of demand exceeds the rate at which oxygen can be supplied, the muscle shifts toward anaerobic pathways and the balance of products changes. The point is that exercise is a test of the energy supply system and of the system that supports it, including breathing and circulation.

Aerobic respiration is efficient and sustainable, but it depends on oxygen delivery. If oxygen delivery cannot keep up, the cell relies more on pathways that do not need as much oxygen, and this changes the products. A good answer says that aerobic respiration supplies ATP efficiently but needs oxygen, that during strenuous exercise the demand may outstrip oxygen supply, and that this forces a shift in the balance of ATP production. It does not say that the muscle simply switches off aerobic respiration and does nothing else; it says that the balance shifts. The energy story is continuous, not a simple on-off switch.

The practical point is that sustained exercise depends on the ability to deliver oxygen and remove waste, which is why breathing and heart rate rise. The biology here ties respiration, muscle and the internal environment together, because the muscle cannot work unless the supply system keeps up and the internal conditions stay tolerable. If you can see that, you can answer the questions that link the parts, which are often where the higher marks are.

10. The response to exercise: heart rate, breathing rate and breathing volume

During exercise, heart rate, breathing rate and the volume of air breathed per breath all increase. The heart pumps faster and harder to deliver more oxygenated blood to the muscles and to remove more carbon dioxide and heat. Breathing increases in frequency and depth to bring in more oxygen and to remove more carbon dioxide. The point is that the body responds to the higher demand on several fronts at once.

The increase in breathing is not just faster breathing; it is also deeper breathing, so the volume of air exchanged per minute rises more than the rate alone would suggest. The increase in heart rate rises the rate of blood delivery, and a stronger heartbeat can also increase the stroke volume, so the cardiac output rises. A good answer says that during exercise breathing rate and depth increase, that heart rate increases, and that these changes raise the supply of oxygen and the removal of carbon dioxide and heat. It does not say that only breathing rate changes, because depth matters too. It does not say that the heart only beats faster, because the strength of the beat can change as well.

A common mistake is to describe the response to exercise only in terms of breathing, or only in terms of heart rate, when the question asks for both. A good answer gives both and links them, because they are part of the same supply system. The internal environment is what both systems are serving: without the increased supply, the muscles cannot work and the internal conditions would drift out of limits. If you can say that, you have the response in a form that scores marks.

11. Thermoregulation, vasodilation and vasoconstriction, and the control of heat loss

Thermoregulation is the control of body temperature, which is part of homeostasis. The body controls heat loss and heat production to keep temperature within limits. When the body needs to lose heat, blood vessels near the skin surface dilate, allowing more blood flow near the surface so heat is lost to the environment; this is vasodilation. When the body needs to conserve heat, those vessels constrict, reducing blood flow near the surface and reducing heat loss; this is vasoconstriction.

A good answer says that vasodilation increases blood flow near the skin surface and increases heat loss, and that vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the surface and reduces heat loss. It does not say that vasodilation happens only when it is hot and vasoconstriction only when it is cold, as absolute rules, though that is the typical pattern, because the system is about control, not just a fixed setting. The deeper point is that the skin blood flow is one of the ways the body moves heat around and loses it, and that the control is part of homeostasis.

Other responses to overheating may include sweating, which cools by evaporation, and behavioural changes. Responses to cold include shivering and reducing heat loss by vasoconstriction. The important idea is that the body has both heat-loss and heat-production responses, and that homeothermy is maintained by balancing them. A good answer says that the body controls temperature by adjusting heat loss and heat production, names vasodilation and vasoconstriction as examples of changing heat loss, and mentions that the responses are part of homeostasis. If you can say that, you have the thermoregulation idea in a form that scores marks.

12. The concept of the internal environment and why homeostasis matters

The internal environment is the fluid environment around the cells, and homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite changes outside and inside. The idea is important because cells can only work properly within a limited range of conditions, so the internal environment has to be kept within those limits: water balance, temperature, pH and the concentrations of substances have to be controlled, and respiration and exercise put demands on all of them.

Homeostasis is not a single process but a collection of control systems. Negative feedback is the main control principle, in which a change from the set point is detected and the system acts to bring it back. A good answer says that homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment, that cells can only function within narrow limits, and that negative feedback is the main control mechanism. It does not say that the internal environment never changes, because it does change; it says that it is kept within limits. That is the difference between a mark-scoring answer and one that treats homeostasis as meaning no change at all.

The link to respiration and muscles is that exercise stresses the internal environment: it produces heat, carbon dioxide and water, changes pH in the tissues and the blood, and demands more fuel and oxygen. Homeostasis has to cope with all of that, and that is why the topic brings together respiration, muscles and internal environment control. If you can say that, you have the unifying idea that makes the topic more than three separate lists.

13. Negative feedback and the way control systems work

Negative feedback is the main control principle in homeostasis. A change away from the set point is detected by a receptor, the information is passed to a control centre, and effectors act to reduce the change and bring the variable back toward the set point. The effect opposes the change, which is why it is called negative feedback. This is the principle behind temperature control, blood glucose control and the control of many other variables.

A good answer describes the components of a negative feedback system: receptor, coordination or control centre and effector, and says that the response reduces the original change. It does not describe positive feedback as the main homeostatic mechanism, because positive feedback amplifies the change and is used in a small number of cases such as childbirth, not as the general principle. The general principle is negative feedback, and the exam questions on this topic usually test that principle. If you can say that, you have the control idea in a form that scores marks.

The point of negative feedback is that it reduces the error from the set point. It does not have to eliminate the change entirely; real systems have a normal range. A good answer therefore does not say that homeostasis keeps every variable exactly constant at all times; it says that it keeps the variable within a normal range by opposing deviations. If you can say that, you have the principle and its limitations both correct.

14. Water and solute balance, and why the internal environment has to manage them

The internal environment has to manage water and solute balance because cells depend on the water potential of their surroundings. If the internal environment is too concentrated, water leaves cells by osmosis; if it is too dilute, water enters cells. Either can disrupt cell function. The control of water and solute balance is therefore part of homeostasis, and it connects to respiration and muscles because the body gains and loses water through breathing, sweating and urine, and because the balance matters for the tissues that are doing the work.

A good answer says that water and solute balance are part of homeostasis, that cells depend on the water potential of the internal environment, and that changes in water potential can move water by osmosis and affect cell function. It does not say that water balance is only about drinking, because the body also loses water in breathing, sweating and urine, and gains it in food and drink. The point is that the balance is dynamic and has to be controlled. If you can say that, you have the water-balance idea in a form that scores marks.

The link to respiration is that breathing loses water vapour, so respiration and breathing are part of the water balance as well as part of the gas exchange. The link to exercise is that sweating loses both water and heat, so the same response that cools can also disturb water balance. If you can see those links, you can answer questions that cross the parts, which are common at this level.

15. The role of the kidneys in the internal environment, briefly and at the right level

The kidneys are central to the internal environment because they control the composition of the urine and so the balance of water, ions and waste products in the blood. They remove waste from the blood and adjust the water and solute content of the body. In this topic the kidneys matter because they are one of the systems that keeps the internal environment within limits, and because the products of respiration have to be dealt with by the body as a whole.

A good answer describes the kidneys as organs that remove waste from the blood and help control water and solute balance, and links them to homeostasis and to the disposal of waste from respiration. It does not overreach by describing every nephron detail if the question does not ask for it; the key point is the role in the internal environment. The kidneys are part of the disposal and balance system that allows respiration and exercise to happen without wrecking the internal conditions. If you can say that, you have the right level.

The important idea is that the body is an integrated system: respiration makes ATP and produces waste, muscles use ATP and produce heat and waste, and the internal environment systems, including the kidneys, breathing and thermoregulation, keep the whole thing within limits. If you can see the integration, you can answer the questions that ask for the links, which are often the best-marked ones.

16. CPIR and the iodide concentration problem; the direction of control

The basics of thermoregulation include the idea that blood vessel diameter in the skin changes to control heat loss, and that the control is part of homeostasis. The anatomy point that is often tested is which vessels are involved and how they control the flow near the surface. In the skin, arteriole vasodilation and vasoconstriction change the flow to superficial vessels, and the presence of a rich superficial vessel bed lets the skin lose more heat when it is hot and conserve more when it is cold.

A good answer says that vasodilation near the skin surface increases heat loss and vasoconstriction near the skin surface reduces it, and that this is part of the way the body controls temperature. It does not say that the skin is the only place where this happens, or that the control is the only thermoregulatory response, because sweating, shivering and behaviour also matter.
