How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind and is simplified by dividing each part by the highest common factor. To share a quantity in a given ratio, add the parts of the ratio to find the total, divide the quantity by that total to find one part, then multiply.

A rate compares quantities of different kinds, such as speed in metres per second. Direct proportion means that one quantity doubles when the other doubles, and it is written y = kx. Inverse proportion means that one quantity halves when the other doubles, and it is written y = k/x. Identify which kind of proportion the question describes before you calculate.

title: Reading for Main Ideas and Detail — Study Notes
content:
Reading in English means knowing which reading method fits the task. Skimming, scanning and close reading are three different tools, and using the right one saves time and improves understanding.

Skimming

Skimming means reading quickly to get the general idea. Read the title, the first sentence of each paragraph, and any headings. Ask: what is this text about, and who is it for?

Scanning

Scanning means searching for a specific piece of information, such as a date, a name or a number. Move your eyes quickly over the text looking for the key word, and ignore everything else.

Main ideas

The main idea of a paragraph is the point the paragraph makes. It is often in the topic sentence, which is frequently near the start, but it is not always there. Ask: what do the other sentences support?

Supporting details

Supporting details are examples, facts, reasons and explanations that develop the main idea.

  • Main idea: The city is a centre of innovation.
  • Supporting detail: The city hosts three major universities and many technology firms.

Unknown words

When you meet an unfamiliar word:

  • Look at the words around it for clues.
  • Check whether the word is a familiar root with a prefix or suffix.
  • Decide whether you need its exact meaning to answer the question.

Do not stop reading to look up every word. Often the meaning is clear from context.

title: Processor Fundamentals — Study Notes
content:
`# Processor Fundamentals

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 4 (Processor fundamentals), examined in AS Paper 1.

The FDE Cycle

  • Fetch: PC → MAR; read memory → MDR; instruction → CIR; PC increments
  • Decode: control unit interprets the opcode
  • Execute: ALU/registers act; results stored; PC may be overwritten (jumps)

Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being accessed
MDRdata in transit
CIRcurrent instruction
ACCaccumulator results

Buses

  • Address bus: one-way, CPU → memory (width sets addressable space)
  • Data bus: two-way, carries instructions/data
  • Control bus: timing and command signals

Interrupts

Signals that pause the current program (I/O complete, timer, errors). The CPU saves context, runs the ISR, then resumes — enabling multitasking.

Assembly and Addressing

Immediate (#5), direct (address holds value), indirect (address points to address), indexed (base + offset — arrays), relative (PC + offset — jumps).

Example: LDD 100 loads from 100 (direct); LDI 100 loads from the address stored at 100 (indirect).

Exam tips: trace register contents step by step in trace tables; explain the stored program concept — instructions as data in memory.

The fetch-decode-execute cycle and registers

The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction. During fetch, that address is copied to the memory address register (MAR), the instruction is read into the memory data register (MDR) and then into the current instruction register (CIR), and the PC is incremented. During decode the control unit works out what the instruction means, and during execute the ALU or another part of the CPU carries it out.

The accumulator is a register that holds the results of arithmetic and logic operations. Registers are very fast storage inside the CPU, and the CPU uses them so that it does not have to wait for main memory on every step.

Exam tip: learn the purpose of each register in one sentence. Examiners often ask which register holds the address, and which holds the instruction.

Exam method: tracing the fetch-decode-execute cycle

Write the register contents after each stage. In the fetch stage the address in the program counter is copied to the memory address register, the instruction at that address is copied to the memory data register and then to the current instruction register, and the program counter is incremented so that it points to the next instruction. In the decode stage the control unit works out what the instruction means. In the execute stage the instruction is carried out, which may change the accumulator or write a value back to memory.

The program counter is incremented before execution. A jump instruction then overwrites it, which is why a jump changes the order of execution without any special fetch step.

Common errors

  • Saying the program counter holds the instruction. It holds the address of the next instruction, while the current instruction register holds the instruction itself.
  • Describing the buses as storing data. Buses only carry data, addresses and control signals between components.

title: Exam technique: Indices and Standard Form
content:
### What earns the marks
For index laws, each law applied on its own line earns credit: subtract for division, multiply for powers of powers. For fractional powers, the root-first order (cube root, then square) stated earns the method mark. For standard form, the coefficient between 1 and 10 with the power justified by the point shift earns both marks. For surds, the split into square factor times prime remainder earns the method mark, and rationalising must finish simplified.
### Traps
Error: (x to the 5th / x squared) cubed answered x to the 6th. Correction: inner subtraction first, then multiply powers. Error: 27 x 2/3 for 27 to the 2/3. Correction: root, then power. Error: unsimplified 6 root 3 / 3 accepted as final. Correction: always cancel to 2 root 3. Error: non-standard-form coefficients (45 x 10 to the -5). Correction: one non-zero digit, then fix the power.
### Worked example
Write 0.00042 in standard form. Move the decimal point until one non-zero digit is in front: 4.2. The point moved 4 places to the right, so the power is −4, giving 4.2 × 10⁻⁴. Now work out (3 × 10⁵)(2 × 10⁴). Multiply the numbers to get 6 and add the powers to get 10⁹, so the answer is 6 × 10⁹.

title: Permutations and Combinations — Study Notes
content:
Permutations and Combinations

Board note: permutations and combinations are not examined in the Edexcel International A Level main specification; Cambridge examines them at A2 (9709). This note serves both boards.

The Multiplication Principle

If a task is done in successive stages with m, n, ... choices at each stage, the total is the product of the choices. This underpins every counting problem: a menu with 4 starters and 6 mains gives 24 meals.

Permutations — Order Matters

The number of ways of arranging r objects from n distinct objects is

  • ⁿPᵣ = n!/(n − r)!

The number of arrangements of n distinct objects is n!. Five books on a shelf: 5! = 120 ways.

Combinations — Order Irrelevant

The number of ways of choosing r objects from n is

  • ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!)

Choosing a committee of 3 from 8 people: ⁸C₃ = 56. Choosing is not arranging — a committee has no internal order, so we divide by r!.

Restricted Permutations

  • No two specified people adjacent: arrange everyone else, then slot the restricted people into gaps. For n people with 2 who must be separated: arrange the other n − 2 (ways), then place 2 people in distinct gaps between them.
  • Specified people together: bundle them as one item, arrange the bundle, then multiply by the internal arrangements of the bundle.
  • Words with repeated letters: divide by the factorials of each repeat count. ARRANGE has 7 letters with A appearing twice and R twice, so 7!/(2!·2!) = 1260.

Combinations with Constraints

  • At least / at most: split into cases and add. A team of 5 from 6 boys and 5 girls with at least 3 girls is ⁵C₃⁶C₂ + ⁵C₄⁶C₁ + ⁵C₅⁶C₀.
  • "Must include" pairs: choose the required items first, then choose freely from the remainder.

Exam tips: state whether a scenario is a permutation or combination before computing anything. Most lost marks come from counting an arrangement where order does not actually matter. Check every answer against a small case you can enumerate by hand.

Exam method: arrangements and selections

The number of arrangements of r objects from n distinct objects is nPr = n!/(n − r)!. The number of ways to select r objects from n, where order does not matter, is nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!). Ask first whether order matters, because that decides which formula to use.

Arrangements with restrictions are solved by treating a block as one object or by placing the restricted items first. For example, if two people must sit together, treat them as one unit and multiply by 2 for their internal order.

Use the identity nCr = nC(n − r) to check answers, and remember that nC0 = nCn = 1. Pascal's identity nCr = (n−1)C(r−1) + (n−1)Cr links the two formulae.

When a question has several groups with separate conditions, count each part on its own and multiply the results, provided the parts are independent.

Exam cue: Write the formula with the numbers substituted before simplifying, since method marks are given for the correct expression.

title: Further Mechanics — Study Notes
content:
Further mechanics: momentum, impulse and circular motion

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 4 (WPH14), sat at A2.

This unit unifies two big ideas: momentum (with its conservation law) and circular motion (with its centripetal requirement). Both are favourite sources of longer exam questions.

Momentum and impulse

  • Momentum p = mv, a vector measured in kg m/s.
  • Impulse = force x time = change of momentum: F t = m(v - u). Units N s (equivalently kg m/s).
  • Newton's second law in momentum form: F = rate of change of momentum = m(v - u)/t.
  • A force-time graph has area = impulse.

Conservation of momentum

  • In a closed system (no external resultant force) total momentum before = total after. This is a vector law: in two dimensions, resolve along two perpendicular axes.
  • It holds for all collisions, explosions and separations.

Collisions

  • Elastic: total kinetic energy is conserved as well as momentum (e.g. perfectly hard spheres).
  • Inelastic: kinetic energy is not conserved — it transforms into heat, sound and deformation.
  • Perfectly inelastic: the bodies stick together; this gives the maximum kinetic energy loss.
  • In one dimension use simultaneous momentum (and, if elastic, energy) equations.

Circular motion

  • Angular speed: omega = 2 pi / T = 2 pi f = v / r.
  • A body moving in a circle at constant speed still accelerates: centripetal acceleration a = v^2 / r = omega^2 r, directed towards the centre.
  • The centripetal force is the resultant force towards the centre: F = m v^2 / r = m omega^2 r. It is not a new type of force — tension, weight, friction or normal reaction can supply it.

Vertical circles and pendulums

  • For a body on a string in a vertical circle, the string stays taut at the top only if v >= sqrt(g r).
  • Conical pendulum: a mass on a string sweeps a horizontal circle; with string length L at angle theta to the vertical, tan(theta) = v^2/(r g) and the period is T = 2 pi sqrt(L cos(theta)/g).
  • Banked track with no friction: tan(theta) = v^2/(r g); the normal reaction supplies the centripetal force.

Exam technique

  • Momentum is a vector: fix a positive direction and keep signs consistent.
  • Energy is scalar and never negative; check whether the collision is elastic before conserving energy.
  • For circles, draw the force diagram at the point of interest first, then resolve towards the centre.

title: Databases — Study Notes
content:
Databases

This note covers the Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618 content on databases: the structure of a relational database, keys and relationships, normalisation to third normal form, SQL for querying and changing data, and the transaction properties that keep data reliable. Each section ends with the points examiners reward.

Relational basics

A relational database stores data in tables (also called relations). Each table describes one type of entity. The columns are fields, each recording one attribute of the entity, and each row is a record holding one instance of the entity. A school might use a Students table (StudentID, Name, DateOfBirth), a Courses table (CourseID, Title, Fee) and an Enrolments table that links them.

Keys control how records are identified and linked:

  • Primary key: a field, or combination of fields, that uniquely identifies each record. It cannot be empty and it cannot repeat.
  • Candidate key: any field or combination that could serve as the primary key. A table can have several candidate keys; one is chosen as the primary key.
  • Composite key: a primary key made of two or more fields. In Enrolments, the pair (StudentID, CourseID) is a natural composite key because a student enrols on a course once.
  • Foreign key: a field in one table that holds the primary key of a record in another table. It creates the relationship and lets the database enforce referential integrity, so an enrolment cannot refer to a student who does not exist.

Relationships are described by how many records on each side can be linked. In a one-to-many relationship, one customer can place many orders but each order belongs to one customer, so the foreign key sits on the many side (Orders.CustomerID). A many-to-many relationship, such as students and courses, cannot be stored directly; it needs a junction table such as Enrolments, which holds two foreign keys.

Data redundancy and why it matters

Data redundancy means the same fact is stored more than once. It wastes storage, but the greater danger is inconsistency: a customer's address is changed in one copy and left unchanged in another, and the database then holds two different answers to the same question. Good design stores each fact in one place and links to it with keys. Normalisation is the systematic method for removing redundancy.

Normalisation

  • First normal form (1NF): every field holds a single atomic value and there are no repeating groups. A cell listing "Maths; Physics" breaks 1NF.
  • Second normal form (2NF): the table is in 1NF and every non-key field depends on the whole primary key. This matters only when the key is composite; a partial dependency is a non-key field that depends on just part of it.
  • Third normal form (3NF): the table is in 2NF and no non-key field depends on another non-key field (no transitive dependency).

Worked example. Consider one table, Enrolments(StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, CourseFee). The key is the composite (StudentID, CourseID). StudentName depends only on StudentID, which is a partial dependency and breaks 2NF. CourseFee depends only on CourseID, another partial dependency. Moving StudentName to a Students table and CourseFee to a Courses table gives three tables whose non-key fields depend on the whole of their own keys. Check 3NF on the Courses table as well: if it held a DepartmentName that depended on DepartmentID rather than CourseID, that would be a transitive dependency, and the department would need its own table.

Normalising too far creates many small tables and more joins. The exam expects you to normalise to 3NF unless the question says otherwise.

Querying with SQL

SQL is the language used to create, read, change and delete data. The core statements are:

SELECT Name, DateOfBirth
  FROM Students
  WHERE DateOfBirth >= '2008-01-01'
  ORDER BY Name ASC;

INSERT INTO Students (StudentID, Name, DateOfBirth)
  VALUES (105, 'Amina Hassan', '2008-03-14');

UPDATE Students
  SET Name = 'Amina Ali'
  WHERE StudentID = 105;

DELETE FROM Students
  WHERE StudentID = 105;

Two points are easy to lose marks on. First, an UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause changes or removes every row in the table. Second, WHERE compares against field values, so text values are written in quotes and numbers are not.

Joins combine rows from two tables where a key matches. An inner join returns only the matching pairs:

SELECT Students.Name, Courses.Title
  FROM Enrolments
  INNER JOIN Students ON Enrolments.StudentID = Students.StudentID
  INNER JOIN Courses ON Enrolments.CourseID = Courses.CourseID
  WHERE Courses.Title = 'Physics';

The join condition must compare a primary key with the foreign key that refers to it. Joining on unrelated fields returns meaningless pairs.

Transactions and integrity

A transaction is a group of database operations that must succeed or fail together, such as debiting one account and crediting another. Transactions have the ACID properties:

  • Atomicity: all operations happen, or none do. A failed step triggers a rollback.
  • Consistency: the database moves from one valid state to another, and rules such as keys and constraints still hold afterwards.
  • Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work. Record locking stops two users changing the same record at once and losing one of the changes.
  • Durability: once committed, a change survives a power failure or crash.

Referential integrity and validation rules are further protections. A foreign key constraint refuses an enrolment that points at a missing student, and a range check refuses a mark of 150 out of 100.

Exam tips

  • When asked to normalise, name the normal form you are reaching, state the dependency you have removed, and show the resulting tables with their keys.
  • When asked about a foreign key, say which table it sits in and which primary key it refers to.
  • Write SQL with the exact field and table names from the question, and always check the WHERE clause on UPDATE and DELETE.
  • For transactions, describe the all-or-nothing outcome and name the property being demonstrated.

title: Exam technique: Quantum Physics
content:
### What earns the marks
For photons, hf quoted with substitution earns both marks. For photoelectricity, threshold frequency reasoning earns the explanation mark regardless of intensity. For matter waves, h/p quoted earns the method mark; diffraction named as wave proof earns the conclusion.
### Traps
Error: brighter light assumed to beat threshold. Correction: frequency decides, intensity only sets rate. Error: line spectra blamed on heat alone. Correction: discrete levels give lines. Error: electron mass used in photon formula. Correction: photons use hf, electrons use h/p.
### Apply the photoelectric equation
Use hf = φ + KE_max, where φ is the work function. Convert the frequency or wavelength into SI units first, and convert electronvolts to joules when needed.

### Use the threshold frequency correctly
The threshold frequency is f₀ = φ / h. Below it, no electrons are emitted whatever the intensity, and explain this with the particle model of light.

### Use de Broglie and energy-level relations
The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p. For an electron transition between levels, hf = E₁ − E₂, so calculate the energy difference first and then the frequency or wavelength of the photon.

title: A2 Level Chemistry: Entropy and Energetics
content:
A2 Level Chemistry: Entropy and Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 12 covers the concept of entropy and energetics, including the relationship between enthalpy, entropy, and the feasibility of reactions. This topic explains that enthalpy alone does not decide whether a reaction happens, and that entropy measures how energy and matter are spread out. The Gibbs energy combines enthalpy and entropy to predict feasibility.

Entropy

Entropy S measures the disorder or the number of ways energy can be dispersed. Its standard unit is J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Entropy increases when a solid melts or dissolves, when a liquid evaporates, and when the number of gas molecules increases. Entropy decreases when gas molecules condense or when a crystal forms from solution.

  • Entropy increases with temperature.
  • Entropy increases as solid, liquid, gas.
  • Perfect crystals at zero kelvin have zero entropy.
  • Standard entropy values are given in data books.
  • The entropy change for a reaction is ΔS = Σ S(products) − Σ S(reactants).

Entropy Changes

Entropy changes occur during changes of state, dissolving of a solid ionic lattice, and reactions in which there is a change in the number of moles from reactants to products.

  • ΔS = +ve for endothermic processes.
  • ΔS = -ve for exothermic processes.
  • ΔS = +ve for increase in moles of gas.
  • ΔS = -ve for decrease in moles of gas.

Total Entropy Change

The total entropy change is ΔS total = ΔS system + ΔS surroundings. For the surroundings, ΔS surroundings = −ΔH / T.

  • ΔS total = ΔS system + ΔS surroundings.
  • ΔS surroundings = −ΔH / T.

Gibbs Free Energy

The Gibbs energy change is ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where T is in kelvin. ΔH is in J mol⁻¹ and ΔS in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, so convert ΔH from kJ to J before calculating.

  • ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
  • A reaction is feasible when ΔG is negative.
  • When ΔG = 0 the system is at equilibrium.

Temperature and Feasibility

For a reaction with positive ΔH and positive ΔS, ΔG becomes negative above the temperature T = ΔH / ΔS. High temperature therefore makes the reaction feasible.

  • For a reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS positive, ΔG becomes negative above T = ΔH / ΔS.
  • For a reaction with ΔH positive and ΔS negative, ΔG is always positive, so the reaction is never feasible.

Worked Example

For CaCO3 → CaO + CO2, ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The temperature at which ΔG = 0 is T = 178 000 / 161 = 1106 K, so the decomposition becomes feasible above about 1100 K.

Thermodynamic Stability and Kinetic Stability

Thermodynamic stability refers to the feasibility of a reaction, while kinetic stability refers to the rate of the reaction.

  • Thermodynamic stability: ΔG negative.
  • Kinetic stability: slow reaction rate.

Standard Enthalpy Change of Atomisation

The standard enthalpy change of atomisation is the energy required to break one mole of a substance into its constituent atoms.

  • ΔH atomisation = energy required to break one mole of a substance into its constituent atoms.

Electron Affinity

Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to an atom.

  • Electron affinity = energy released when an electron is added to an atom.

Lattice Energy

Lattice energy is the energy released when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions.

  • Lattice energy = energy released when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions.

Born-Haber Cycle

A Born-Haber cycle is a diagram that shows the energy changes involved in the formation of an ionic solid from its constituent elements.

  • Born-Haber cycle: diagram showing energy changes involved in the formation of an ionic solid.

Covalent Bonding

Covalent bonding refers to the sharing of electrons between atoms.

  • Covalent bonding: sharing of electrons between atoms.

Polarisation of Anions

Polarisation of anions refers to the distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation.

  • Polarisation of anions: distortion of electron cloud of an anion by a nearby cation.

Enthalpy Change of Solution

Enthalpy change of solution is the energy change involved in the dissolution of a substance.

  • Enthalpy change of solution = energy change involved in the dissolution of a substance.

Enthalpy Change of Hydration

Enthalpy change of hydration is the energy change involved in the hydration of an ion.

  • Enthalpy change of hydration = energy change involved in the hydration of an ion.

Typical Mistakes

  • Forgetting to convert ΔH from kJ to J before calculating ΔG.
  • Not using the correct units for ΔS and ΔH.
  • Not considering the sign of ΔS and ΔH when determining the feasibility of a reaction.

Exam-Style Questions

  1. What is the entropy change for the reaction CaCO3 → CaO + CO2? Answer: ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
  2. What is the temperature at which the reaction CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 becomes feasible? Answer: T = 1106 K.
  3. What is the lattice energy of an ionic solid? Answer: Lattice energy = energy released when one mole of an ionic solid is formed from its gaseous ions.

To revise this topic, make sure to understand the concepts of entropy, Gibbs free energy, and thermodynamic stability. Practice calculating ΔG and determining the feasibility of reactions. Also, make sure to remember the typical mistakes and how to avoid them. After revising this topic, move on to the next topic, which covers the kinetics of chemical reactions.

Detailed Born-Haber Cycle Calculations

Constructing a Born-Haber cycle requires applying Hess's Law to equate the enthalpy change of formation of an ionic compound to the sum of its stepwise enthalpy changes: atomisation of the metal, first (and subsequent) ionisation energies of the metal, atomisation of the non-metal, electron affinities of the non-metal, and lattice energy. For magnesium chloride, MgCl2, the cycle starts with Mg(s) + Cl2(g) going to MgCl2(s). The steps are: enthalpy of atomisation of Mg, first and second ionisation energies of Mg, twice the enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine (or bond enthalpy of Cl2), twice the first electron affinity of chlorine, and lattice energy. Rearranging the energy level loop allows any single unknown enthalpy term to be calculated.

  • Write the thermochemical equation for formation at the bottom level.
  • Draw upward arrows for endothermic processes: atomisation, ionisation energies, and bond dissociation.
  • Draw downward arrows for exothermic processes: electron affinities and lattice energy.
  • Set the sum of energy changes along the direct route equal to the alternative pathway route.

Worked Example: Born-Haber Cycle for Sodium Chloride

Calculate the lattice energy of sodium chloride, NaCl, using the following standard enthalpy changes: enthalpy of formation of NaCl = −411 kJ mol⁻¹, enthalpy of atomisation of Na = +107 kJ mol⁻¹, first ionisation energy of Na = +496 kJ mol⁻¹, enthalpy of atomisation of Cl2 = +121 kJ mol⁻¹, and first electron affinity of Cl = −364 kJ mol⁻¹. The equation linking these is: ΔHf = ΔHat(Na) + IE1(Na) + 1/2 ΔHdiss(Cl2) + EA1(Cl) + Lattice Energy. Substituting the values: −411 = 107 + 496 + 121 + (−364) + Lattice Energy. Solving gives: −411 = 360 + Lattice Energy, so Lattice Energy = −411 − 360 = −771 kJ mol⁻¹.

Experimental Versus Theoretical Lattice Energies

Perfect ionic model assumes spherical point charges with 100 percent electrostatic attraction. When experimental lattice energies obtained from Born-Haber cycles are more exothermic than theoretical values calculated from electrostatic theory, it indicates that additional bonding character is present. This extra stability arises from partial covalent character caused by the polarisation of the anion.

  • Larger difference between experimental and theoretical values signifies greater covalent character.
  • Polarisation is promoted by small, highly charged cations (high charge density) and large, easily polarisable anions.
  • Fajans' rules help rationalize these trends across different halides and oxides.

Hydration Enthalpies and Enthalpy of Solution

Enthalpy change of solution is the enthalpy change when one mole of a solute dissolves in water to form an infinitely dilute solution. This is related to lattice energy and hydration enthalpies by the equation: ΔHsol = Lattice Energy + Σ ΔHhyd(ions). Because lattice energy is endothermic when viewed as breaking the lattice (positive value) and hydration is exothermic (negative value), the overall enthalpy of solution can be slightly positive, zero, or negative. For sparingly soluble salts, ΔHsol is strongly positive.

  • Hydration enthalpy is always exothermic (negative) due to ion-dipole attractions between the gaseous ions and water molecules.
  • Magnitude of hydration enthalpy increases with increasing ionic charge and decreasing ionic radius.
  • Magnitude of lattice energy also increases with high charge and small radius, meaning lattice energy and hydration enthalpy tend to counteract each other across periodic trends.

Solubility Trends in Group 1 and Group 2 Compounds

The solubility of ionic compounds depends on the balance between lattice energy and hydration enthalpies, alongside the entropy change of the system and surroundings. Down Group 2, both lattice energy and hydration enthalpies decrease in magnitude as the cation radius increases, but hydration enthalpy decreases faster for smaller anions (like sulfates) compared to larger anions (like hydroxides).

  • Group 2 sulfates become less soluble down the group because the hydration enthalpy drops faster than the lattice energy, making ΔHsol increasingly endothermic.
  • Group 2 hydroxides become more soluble down the group because lattice energy decreases more rapidly than hydration enthalpy, making ΔHsol less endothermic or more exothermic.
  • Overall feasibility of dissolving requires calculating ΔStotal using ΔHsol and the entropy change of the solution process.

Typical Mistakes in Energetics and Born-Haber Cycles

  • Omitting the stoichiometric multipliers when using bond enthalpies or atomisation energies for diatomic gases like chlorine or oxygen.
  • Confusing first and second electron affinities, where second electron affinities are endothermic due to repulsion with the incoming electron.
  • Forgetting that lattice energy in standard definitions is exothermic, but must be treated with the correct sign when substituting into energy cycle equations depending on the cycle direction used.

Exam-Style Questions and Worked Solutions

  1. Define the standard enthalpy change of atomisation. Answer: The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state under standard conditions. Credit is earned by mentioning 'one mole of gaseous atoms' and 'element in its standard state'.
  2. Explain why the experimental lattice energy of silver iodide is significantly more exothermic than the theoretical value. Answer: Silver ions have a d-block configuration that polarises the large iodide ion effectively, introducing covalent character which releases extra energy. Credit is earned by linking cation polarisation of the anion to increased stability.
  3. Calculate the enthalpy of solution of potassium chloride given that its lattice energy is −701 kJ mol⁻¹ and the sum of the hydration enthalpies of its ions is −684 kJ mol⁻¹. Answer: ΔHsol = Lattice Energy + Σ ΔHhyd = 701 (if defined as formation) or using standard sign conventions, ΔHsol = −684 − (−701) = +17 kJ mol⁻¹ (or using the exact cycle definition, −701 + 684 = −17 kJ mol⁻¹ depending on data book sign convention for lattice energy release vs absorption). Step for credit: showing ΔHsol = Lattice Energy + Hydration Enthalpies with proper sign substitution.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Feasibility temperature, applied to CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) with ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +161 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹: at ΔG = 0, T = ΔH ÷ ΔS = 178 000 ÷ 161 = 1106 K. Above this temperature ΔG is negative and the reaction is feasible. Convert the entropy to kJ before you divide, or the answer is wrong by a factor of 1000.
  • Total entropy, applied to a reaction at 298 K: ΔS(total) = ΔS(system) + ΔS(surroundings), where ΔS(surroundings) = −ΔH ÷ T. A reaction is spontaneous when the total change is positive. Using ΔS(system) alone is a common error that loses the mark.
  • Born-Haber sign convention: lattice energy is the energy released when gaseous ions form one mole of solid lattice. Written as an enthalpy of formation, it is negative. Cycles give the lattice energy as a negative number, so check the sign of each arrow before you add.
  • Stability wording: thermodynamic stability depends on ΔG, while kinetic stability depends on activation energy. A reaction can be feasible but slow, so answers about why a substance does not react must name the activation energy.

title: Electricity: D.C. Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity: D.C. circuits

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 2 (WPH12), sat at AS.

Current and charge

  • Current I = charge Q ÷ time t, so Q = It. Unit: ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹.
  • Electron drift velocity is very small, but the electric field propagates through the circuit almost at the speed of light.

Potential difference and power

  • Potential difference V = energy transferred ÷ charge. Unit: volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
  • Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Unit: watt (W).

Resistance and resistivity

R = V/I (Ohm's law for an ohmic conductor, at constant temperature). For a wire of length L and cross-sectional area A, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity in Ω m. Resistance rises with length and falls with area.

Practical circuits

An ammeter is connected in series with the component it measures. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component. An ideal ammeter has zero resistance; an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance.

Kirchhoff's laws

  • First law: at a junction, the total current entering equals the total current leaving (conservation of charge).
  • Second law: around any closed loop, the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential differences (conservation of energy).

Potential dividers

For two resistors R1 and R2 in series across a supply V, the potential difference across R2 is V × R2/(R1 + R2).

Worked example: a 100 Ω and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across 12 V. The current is 12/400 = 0.030 A, and the voltage across the 300 Ω resistor is 0.030 × 300 = 9.0 V.

Exam tips: draw the meter in the correct place, in series or in parallel. Apply Kirchhoff's first law to currents and the second law to loops, with consistent signs. Check that units are converted (e.g. mm² to m²) before using ρL/A.

Resistivity and temperature

For a metallic conductor at constant temperature, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. Resistivity, ρ = RA/L, is a property of the material. As temperature rises, the ions in a metal vibrate more and impede the flow of electrons, so resistivity increases. A thermistor behaves differently: its resistance falls as temperature rises, because more charge carriers are released.

Exam tip: when asked to explain a resistance change, relate it to charge carriers and collisions, not just to the formula.

Worked example: resistors in series and in parallel

Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series have a combined resistance of 10 Ω, and the same current flows through each. In parallel, the same two resistors have a combined resistance found from 1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12, so R = 2.4 Ω. The combined resistance in parallel is always less than the smallest individual resistance, and adding a branch to a parallel circuit always reduces the total resistance.

Worked example: EMF and internal resistance

A cell with EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω supplies a current of 2 A. The terminal potential difference is V = E − Ir = 1.5 − (2 × 0.5) = 0.5 V. Writing V = E − Ir before substituting shows that the energy lost inside the cell is the difference between the EMF and the terminal voltage. A cell with a larger current supplied has a smaller terminal voltage.

The potential divider

Two resistors in series across a supply give an output voltage across one of them that depends on the ratio of the resistances. For a supply of 12 V with resistors of 2 kΩ and 4 kΩ in series, the voltage across the 4 kΩ resistor is 12 × 4 ÷ 6 = 8 V. A thermistor or light-dependent resistor in place of one of the resistors makes this arrangement a sensor, because the output voltage changes with temperature or light level.

title: Programming Paradigms and Low-Level — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Programming Paradigms and Low-Level

Computer Science — A2. The opcode names the operation (LDM load, STR store, ADD, CMP compare, JMP branch, IN/OUT for I/O). The operand names the data. The assembler translates mnemonics to machine code one-to-one; two-pass assemblers resolve forward references via the symbol table.

Key areas to revise

  • Paradigms
  • Assembly Essentials
  • Addressing Modes
  • Fetch-Execute

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

A programming paradigm is a style of programming. Procedural programming organises code into procedures that run in sequence. Object-oriented programming groups data and the methods that act on it into objects, and uses classes as templates for objects. Low-level programming, such as assembly language, works closely with the registers and memory of the processor.

An assembly instruction usually names an operation and an operand, for example moving a value into a register. Explain a paradigm by naming its key features and giving one situation where it suits the task, since the examiner looks for a reason, not only a description.

title: Metals
content:
Metals

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 9 (statements 9.1–9.6). Metal properties and uses, alloys, the reactivity series, rusting and its prevention, and extraction of metals including the blast furnace and electrolysis of aluminium ore.

9.1 to 9.4 Properties, uses, alloys and reactivity

  • Metals are good conductors, malleable, ductile, lustrous and usually solid with high melting points. Aluminium: low density and a protective oxide layer, so it is used in aircraft and drink cans. Copper: excellent conductivity and ductility, so it is used in wiring.
  • An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements. Brass (copper and zinc) and stainless steel (iron, chromium, nickel) are the syllabus examples. Different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide — the alloy is harder than the pure metal.
  • Reactivity series: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold. More reactive metals react more vigorously with water or steam and dilute acids, and displace less reactive metals from their compounds.

9.5 Corrosion

  • Rusting needs both oxygen and water. Barriers (paint, grease, plastic) exclude them. Galvanising coats iron with zinc; sacrificial protection uses a more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium that corrodes instead of the iron.

9.6 Extraction of metals

  • Iron: in the blast furnace, carbon monoxide (from coke and hot air) reduces iron(III) oxide: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Limestone removes sandy impurities as slag.
  • Aluminium: extracted by electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide in cryolite, which lowers the melting point and saves energy. The carbon anodes burn away and must be replaced, and oxygen at the anode reacts with the carbon.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Extraction choice, applied to a metal found as the pure element in the ground: gold is extracted by physical methods because it is below hydrogen and does not react with acids or oxygen. Zinc and iron need chemical reduction; aluminium needs electrolysis because it is more reactive than carbon. Link the method to the position in the reactivity series in one sentence.
  • Reactivity deduction, applied to experimental results where metal X displaces metal Y from its salt: X is more reactive than Y. If metal Y does not react with dilute acid but X does, X is above hydrogen and Y below it. Build the order from the evidence, then justify each step.
  • Blast furnace chemistry, applied to the role of coke: coke burns in a blast of hot air to make carbon dioxide (exothermic, providing heat), then carbon dioxide reacts with more coke to make carbon monoxide, the actual reducing agent. Distinguish the two roles — heat provider and reducing agent.
  • Rusting protection reasoning, applied to an iron pipe under a ship: a block of magnesium attached to it corrodes instead, because magnesium is more reactive than iron and loses electrons in preference. That is sacrificial protection; name the electron transfer.

Common errors

  • Saying alloys are harder because "they are stronger". The mark is for disrupted layers that cannot slide.
  • Claiming the carbon anode in aluminium extraction is inert. It burns away.
  • Confusing galvanising (a coating) with sacrificial protection (a more reactive metal doing the corroding).

title: Electrochemistry
content:
Electrochemistry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 4 (statements 4.1–4.2). Electrolysis of molten and aqueous electrolytes, electrode products, half-equations, electroplating and fuel cells.

4.1 Electrolysis

  • Electrolysis is the breakdown of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by the passage of electricity. Cations (positive ions) move to the cathode (negative electrode) and are reduced; anions (negative ions) move to the anode (positive electrode) and are oxidised.
  • Molten lead(II) bromide: Pb²⁺ → Pb at the cathode (grey lead forms), 2Br⁻ → Br₂ at the anode (brown bromine vapour). Only the ions of the compound are present, so the products are unambiguous.
  • Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride: hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, sodium hydroxide left in solution. Dilute sulfuric acid: hydrogen at the cathode, oxygen at the anode (water is preferentially discharged over the sulfate ion).
  • Aqueous copper(II) sulfate with inert electrodes: copper at the cathode, oxygen at the anode. With copper electrodes the anode dissolves instead, so the concentration stays constant — this is electroplating and industrial copper refining.
  • Half-equations (Extended): 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂; 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Include electrons on the correct side and balance charge as well as atoms.

4.2 Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells

  • A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell uses hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity, with water as the only product. Advantages: no carbon dioxide at the point of use, high efficiency. Disadvantages: hydrogen is hard to store and transport, and producing it may itself burn fossil fuels.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Product prediction, applied to molten aluminium oxide: Al³⁺ → Al at the cathode, O²⁻ → O₂ at the anode. The Extended rule is that in aqueous solutions the hydrogen ion discharges in preference to a metal low in the reactivity series, and the hydroxide ion in preference to most anions. State the rule you are applying.
  • Electroplating, applied to plating a key with silver: the key is the cathode (it must be negative so Ag⁺ ions deposit on it), the silver object is the anode (it dissolves to replace the Ag⁺ used up), and the electrolyte is a soluble silver salt such as silver nitrate. Name all three — a three-mark question.
  • Mass deposited calculation, applied to a current plating with copper for a given time: moles of copper = mass ÷ 64. From Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, two moles of electrons are needed per mole of copper. The reasoning marks come from linking the mass to the half-equation, not from the arithmetic alone.

Common errors

  • Swapping anode and cathode. The anode is positive and oxidation happens there; the cathode is negative and reduction happens there.
  • Writing half-equations with unbalanced charge.
  • Saying the anode "loses mass" for inert electrodes in dilute sulfuric acid — it is the water that is oxidised, and oxygen gas forms.

title: Organic Chemistry
content:
Organic Chemistry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 11 (statements 11.1–11.8). Formulae and functional groups, naming, fuels and fractional distillation, alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic acids and polymers.

11.1 to 11.2 Formulae and naming

  • A homologous series shares a general formula and functional group, with similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties. Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (saturated), alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (unsaturated, C=C), alcohols CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH, carboxylic acids CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH.
  • Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae — butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are a syllabus example.

11.3 to 11.5 Fuels, alkanes and alkenes

  • Petroleum is a mixture of hydrocarbons separated by fractional distillation. Fractions with shorter chains have lower boiling points, are more volatile, less viscous and burn more easily. From the top: refinery gas, gasoline, naphtha, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen.
  • Alkanes are saturated and burn; complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water, incomplete combustion gives carbon monoxide and soot. Substitution with chlorine in ultraviolet light: methane + chlorine → chloromethane + hydrogen chloride.
  • Alkenes have a carbon–carbon double bond and decolourise orange bromine water — the test for unsaturation. Cracking breaks long-chain alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes, using a hot catalyst of silica or alumina.

11.6 to 11.8 Alcohols, acids and polymers

  • Ethanol by fermentation (yeast, 25–35 °C, no air) or by hydration of ethene (300 °C, 60 atm, phosphoric acid catalyst). Fermentation uses a renewable feedstock but is slow and gives dilute ethanol; hydration is fast and pure but uses a finite feedstock.
  • Ethanoic acid forms from ethanol oxidation; it reacts with metals (salt + hydrogen), bases (salt + water) and carbonates (salt + water + carbon dioxide). Carboxylic acid + alcohol gives an ester (the syllabus example is ethyl ethanoate).
  • Addition polymerisation: many ethene monomers join to make poly(ethene); the repeat unit keeps all atoms. Condensation polymerisation releases a small molecule (water or HCl) per link — nylon and PET are the syllabus examples, and proteins are natural condensation polymers of amino acids.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Repeat unit reasoning, applied to a polymer shown with a backbone: find the two carbons of the monomer double bond, keep the other groups attached, and redraw as a repeat unit with single bonds and extension bonds on each side. Deduce the monomer from the repeat unit by restoring the double bond — the exam habit that prevents lost marks.
  • Cracking equations, applied to C₁₀H₂₂ cracking to octane: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄. Atoms must balance on both sides, so the second product must be an alkene. Check carbon and hydrogen counts before writing the final answer.
  • Fermentation yield calculation, applied to 100 g of glucose (Mr 180) giving ethanol: moles = 100 ÷ 180 = 0.556 mol. From C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂, ethanol = 1.11 mol, mass = 1.11 × 46 = 51.1 g. Percentage yield compares this theoretical mass with the actual mass obtained.
  • Homologous series trends, applied to naming and properties: as chain length increases in alkanes, boiling point rises (stronger intermolecular forces), viscosity rises and flammability falls. Use intermolecular forces as the reason, not "molecules get bigger".

Common errors

  • Breaking the polymer chain when drawing a repeat unit. The extension bonds must remain.
  • Forgetting the ultraviolet light in the alkane substitution conditions, or the catalyst and conditions in cracking.
  • Saying alkenes "react with bromine water by substitution". It is addition, and the decolourisation is the test.

title: Atoms, Elements and Compounds
content:
Atoms, Elements and Compounds

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 2 (statements 2.1–2.7). Atomic structure, isotopes, ionic and covalent bonding, giant covalent and metallic structures, with the structure-to-property reasoning top grades are built on.

2.2 Atomic structure and the Periodic Table

  • Protons: charge +1, relative mass 1. Neutrons: charge 0, mass 1. Electrons: charge −1, negligible mass. Atoms are neutral because the numbers of protons and electrons are equal; ions form when electrons are lost or gained.
  • Proton (atomic) number counts protons; mass (nucleon) number counts protons plus neutrons. Neutrons = mass number − proton number.
  • Electron arrangement for proton numbers 1–20: shells fill in order 2, 8, 8, 2. Sodium (11): 2,8,1. Calcium (20): 2,8,8,2. The outer-shell electron count gives the group number; the number of occupied shells gives the period number.

2.3 Isotopes

  • Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same proton number) with different numbers of neutrons. They have identical chemical properties because chemistry depends on the electron arrangement, which is unchanged.

2.4 to 2.7 Bonding and structure

  • Ionic bonding: metal atoms lose electrons, non-metal atoms gain them, and the strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions is the bond. Sodium chloride forms a giant lattice with 6:6 coordination; it conducts only when molten or dissolved.
  • Covalent bonding: a shared pair of electrons attracted to two nuclei. Simple molecules (H₂, H₂O, CH₄, NH₃, CO₂, N₂) have weak forces between molecules, so low melting and boiling points, and no conductivity.
  • Giant covalent: diamond has each carbon bonded to four others in a tetrahedral lattice — very hard, very high melting point, no conduction. Graphite has layers of hexagonal rings with one delocalised electron per carbon — conducts, soft, used as lubricant and electrodes. Silicon(IV) oxide has the same giant structure as diamond but with Si and O alternating.
  • Metallic bonding: a giant lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons. Metals conduct (delocalised electrons carry charge), are malleable (layers slide, the electrons keep the attraction), and have high melting points.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Relative atomic mass, applied to lithium: 90% ⁷Li and 10% ⁶Li gives Ar = (7 × 90 + 6 × 10) ÷ 100 = 6.9. Show the abundances as percentages in the formula and give the answer to one decimal place.
  • Dot-and-cross reasoning, applied to magnesium oxide: Mg (2,8,2) loses two electrons, O (2,8,6) gains two, giving Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ with full outer shells and a 1:1 ratio. The formula is MgO, not Mg₂O₂ — the simplest ratio is written.
  • Property explanations, applied to why graphite conducts but diamond does not: each carbon in graphite forms three bonds, leaving one delocalised electron that is free to move between layers. In diamond all four outer electrons are used in bonds, so no electrons are free. Name the delocalised electron — it is what earns the mark.
  • Structure comparison, applied to silicon(IV) oxide versus silicon(IV) chloride: SiO₂ is giant covalent with very high melting point; SiCl₄ is simple molecular with a low melting point. The difference is structure, not the elements involved.

Common errors

  • Calling the attraction in NaCl a bond between one Na and one Cl. It is a lattice-wide electrostatic attraction.
  • Forgetting to put the charge outside square brackets in dot-and-cross diagrams.
  • Saying graphite conducts because it is a metal. It conducts because of its delocalised electrons.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Formulae, Equations and Amount of Substance

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH11, Topic 1 is the quantitative foundation of the whole course: every later topic, from titrations to equilibria to organic mechanisms, is marked using the ideas here. This topic covers the vocabulary of formulae, relative masses and the mole, balanced and ionic equations with state symbols, concentration in mol dm⁻³ and ppm, empirical and molecular formulae from experimental data, reacting masses, gas volumes including pV = nRT, percentage yield and atom economy, and the two core practicals that turn these ideas into measurements.

The language of formulae

Chemistry names substances at three levels: the particle, the formula and the amount. The vocabulary is examined directly, so learn the definitions precisely.

  • Atom: the smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction.
  • Element: a substance containing only one type of atom; it cannot be broken down chemically into anything simpler.
  • Ion: a particle with a charge produced when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.
  • Molecule: two or more atoms joined by covalent bonds; it is the smallest particle of a covalent substance that can exist independently.
  • Compound: a substance containing two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
  • Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
  • Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound.

A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula. Hydrogen peroxide has the empirical formula HO and the molecular formula H₂O₂; ethanoic acid has the empirical formula CH₂O and the molecular formula C₂H₄O₂. Compounds with giant structures, such as sodium chloride or silicon dioxide, have no molecules, so they are described by their empirical formula alone.

Relative masses and the mole

Relative atomic mass, Aᵣ, is the weighted mean mass of the atoms of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Because it is a mean, it takes account of the natural abundances of the isotopes, which is why chlorine has Aᵣ = 35.5 rather than a whole number.

Relative molecular mass, Mᵣ, is the sum of the relative atomic masses in a molecule. For compounds with giant structures, use the term relative formula mass instead: NaCl has a relative formula mass of 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5. Molar mass, M, is the mass per mole of a substance in g mol⁻¹, and it is numerically equal to Mᵣ or the relative formula mass.

The mole is the unit for amount of substance. One mole contains the Avogadro number of particles, L = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Three relationships do nearly all the work in this topic:

RelationshipUse it for
n = m / Mconverting a mass in grams to moles, and back
N = n × Lconverting moles to a number of particles
n = c × V / 1000moles from concentration in mol dm⁻³ and volume in cm³

Worked example. How many molecules are in 4.40 g of carbon dioxide? M(CO₂) = 12.0 + 2(16.0) = 44.0 g mol⁻¹, so n = 4.40 / 44.0 = 0.100 mol. Then N = 0.100 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²² molecules. The number of oxygen atoms is twice that, 1.20 × 10²³, because each molecule holds two oxygen atoms.

Balanced equations, state symbols and ionic equations

A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, and the total charge must balance too. State symbols (s), (l), (g) and (aq) are part of the answer, not decoration: they are how you show that, for example, a reaction produces hydrogen gas rather than hydrogen atoms. Never change a formula to balance an equation; change only the coefficients. Balance the elements that appear once first, leave hydrogen and oxygen until the end, and check by counting a polyatomic ion such as sulfate or nitrate as one unit.

Ionic equations show only the species that change. To construct one, write the full equation, split every soluble ionic compound into its ions, then cancel the ions that appear unchanged on both sides. Those unchanged ions are spectator ions.

Worked example. Silver nitrate solution added to sodium chloride solution:

AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq)
Ag+(aq) + NO3−(aq) + Na+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s) + Na+(aq) + NO3−(aq)
Ag+(aq) + Cl−(aq) → AgCl(s)

Sodium and nitrate ions appear on both sides unchanged, so they are spectators. The ionic equation shows the actual change: hydrated silver ions meeting chloride ions to form a white precipitate.

You must be able to link equations to test-tube observations. Displacement reactions, typical acid reactions and precipitation reactions all follow this pattern: the observation is a change in appearance, and the equation explains it.

ObservationIonic equation
Magnesium added to dilute hydrochloric acid: fizzing, metal dissolves, gas pops with a lighted splintMg(s) + 2H+(aq) → Mg2+(aq) + H2(g)
Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution: blue colour fades, red-brown solid formsZn(s) + Cu2+(aq) → Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)
Barium chloride solution added to sodium sulfate solution: white precipitateBa2+(aq) + SO42−(aq) → BaSO4(s)
Calcium carbonate added to nitric acid: fizzing, solid dissolves, gas turns limewater milkyCaCO3(s) + 2H+(aq) → Ca2+(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)

Concentration, dilution and ppm

Concentration is the amount of solute per unit volume of solution. Two units are used and both are examinable:

  • mol dm⁻³ (molarity): moles of solute per cubic decimetre of solution. 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³.
  • g dm⁻³: mass of solute per cubic decimetre of solution.

The bridge between them is molar mass: g dm⁻³ = mol dm⁻³ × M. So 0.250 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide contains 0.250 × 40.0 = 10.0 g dm⁻³.

Worked example. 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide is diluted to 250 cm³. The moles of solute do not change: n = 0.100 × 25.0 / 1000 = 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol. The new concentration is 2.50 × 10⁻³ / 0.250 = 0.0100 mol dm⁻³. Diluting tenfold divides the concentration by ten.

Parts per million, ppm, expresses very small proportions and is used for trace gases in the atmosphere and impurities in water. One ppm means one part in a million by mass or by volume, depending on the context:

ppm = (mass of component / mass of sample) × 10^6

If the atmosphere contains 410 ppm of carbon dioxide and the total pressure is 100 kPa, the partial pressure of carbon dioxide is 410 / 10⁶ × 100 kPa = 0.0410 kPa. The same number treated as a volume fraction gives 0.041 % by volume.

Empirical and molecular formulae from experiment

Experimental data is converted into a formula in four steps: mass, moles, simplify, then scale using the molar mass.

Worked example. A compound contains 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen by mass, and its molar mass is 180 g mol⁻¹.

ElementMass in 100 gDivide by AᵣDivide by smallest
C40.040.0 / 12.0 = 3.331
H6.76.7 / 1.0 = 6.672
O53.353.3 / 16.0 = 3.331

The empirical formula is CH₂O, with empirical formula mass 30.0. The molecular formula is (CH₂O)n where n = 180 / 30.0 = 6, so the molecular formula is C6H12O6. Always check that a ratio such as 1 : 1.5 is multiplied through to 2 : 3 before writing a formula.

Two related experiments are examined. In a magnesium oxide determination, a known mass of magnesium is burned in a crucible, the lid is lifted periodically to let air in, and the mass of the white powder is found; the increase in mass is the mass of oxygen that combined. In a water-of-crystallisation determination, a hydrated salt is heated to constant mass and the loss in mass is the water driven off, giving the value of x in a formula such as CuSO4·xH2O. In both cases heating to constant mass is essential, and in both the evaluation should name the errors: some magnesium oxide may escape as smoke, magnesium may react with nitrogen in the air to form a nitride, or the heating may not have removed all the water.

Reacting masses

A reacting-mass calculation follows the same route every time: balance the equation, convert the known mass to moles, use the mole ratio, convert back to a mass.

Worked example. What mass of iron is produced when 8.00 g of iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide?

Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2

M(Fe₂O₃) = 2(55.8) + 3(16.0) = 159.6 g mol⁻¹, so n(Fe₂O₃) = 8.00 / 159.6 = 0.0501 mol. The ratio is 1 : 2, so n(Fe) = 0.100 mol and m(Fe) = 0.100 × 55.8 = 5.59 g. Notice that the mass of the solid fell: the oxygen was removed as carbon dioxide, and mass is conserved because the carbon dioxide carries it away.

Where two reactant amounts are given, one will be limiting. Calculate the moles of each, divide by the coefficient in the balanced equation, and the smaller quotient is the limiting reactant. The other is in excess and does not take part fully. All product calculations use the limiting reactant.

Gas volumes, molar volume and pV = nRT

One mole of any gas occupies the same volume at the same temperature and pressure. At room temperature and pressure, this molar volume is approximately 24 dm³ mol⁻¹, so 0.0500 mol of any gas occupies 1.20 dm³. Use this only when the conditions are stated as room temperature and pressure.

When conditions differ, use the ideal gas equation:

pV = nRT

In this equation p is in pascals, V in m³, n in moles, T in kelvin and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Unit conversion causes most lost marks: 1 kPa = 1000 Pa, 1 dm³ = 1 × 10⁻³ m³, and T = θ + 273.

Worked example. A 0.250 g sample of a volatile liquid is vaporised in a syringe at 100 °C and 100 kPa, and occupies 97 cm³. Find its molar mass.

p = 100 000 Pa, V = 97 × 10⁻⁶ m³, T = 373 K. Then n = pV / RT = (100000 × 97 × 10⁻⁶) / (8.31 × 373) = 9.7 / 3099 = 3.13 × 10⁻³ mol. M = m / n = 0.250 / 3.13 × 10⁻³ = 79.9 g mol⁻¹, so the liquid is likely a small molecule such as benzene (Mᵣ = 78).

Percentage yield and atom economy

Percentage yield compares what you actually obtained with the maximum the equation allows:

percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100

Reasons for a yield below 100 % include incomplete reaction, reversible reactions, loss during transfer or filtration, side reactions producing other products, and impurities in the reactants.

Atom economy asks a different question: how much of the mass of all the reactants ends up in the product you want?

atom economy = (molar mass of desired product / sum of molar masses of all products) × 100

Worked example. Ethene is hydrated to ethanol: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH. The only product is ethanol, so the atom economy is 100 %, even though the yield may be well below that because the reaction is reversible. Compare the synthesis of bromoethane from ethene and hydrogen bromide: C2H4 + HBr → C2H5Br also has 100 % atom economy. In a reaction such as CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl, the desired product has Mᵣ = 50.5 and the products total 50.5 + 36.5 = 87.0, so the atom economy is 58.0 %. The HCl is a co-product with little value, which is why industry prefers addition reactions to substitutions.

Core Practical 1: measurement of the molar volume of a gas

A known mass of magnesium ribbon reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid and the hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe. The apparatus is assembled and checked for leaks, the acid is added, and the final syringe reading is taken once the reaction has finished and the apparatus has cooled to room temperature.

Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)

Calculation. If 0.024 g of magnesium gives 24.0 cm³ of hydrogen, n(Mg) = 0.024 / 24.3 = 9.88 × 10⁻⁴ mol, and the ratio is 1 : 1, so n(H₂) is the same. The molar volume is 24.0 / 9.88 × 10⁻⁴ = 24 300 cm³ mol⁻¹ = 24.3 dm³ mol⁻¹, close to the accepted 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹ at room temperature and pressure.

Evaluation. The main sources of error are gas escaping before the bung is replaced, a syringe that sticks or leaks, the temperature not being room temperature when the reading is taken, and the small mass of magnesium producing a large percentage uncertainty in mass. Using a larger mass of magnesium reduces the percentage uncertainty but needs a larger syringe.

Typical mistakes

  • Using the mass of a solution rather than the mass of solute, or forgetting to divide by 1000 when converting cm³ to dm³.
  • Rounding an empirical formula ratio such as 1 : 2.5 to 1 : 3 instead of doubling it to 2 : 5.
  • Changing a subscript to balance an equation instead of the coefficient in front of the formula.
  • Leaving state symbols out of an equation when the question asks for a full equation, or including spectator ions in an ionic equation.
  • Forgetting to convert temperature to kelvin, or pressure to pascals, in pV = nRT.
  • Using the actual yield as the theoretical yield in a percentage-yield calculation.
  • Calculating atom economy from the reactants rather than from the products.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the terms empirical formula and molecular formula, using a compound of your choice to show the difference. Answer: the empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element; the molecular formula is the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule. Ethanoic acid has the empirical formula CH2O and the molecular formula C2H4O2.
  2. 0.500 g of a hydrated salt, MgSO4·xH2O, is heated to constant mass and 0.244 g of anhydrous magnesium sulfate remains. Find x. Answer: mass of water lost = 0.500 − 0.244 = 0.256 g. n(MgSO4) = 0.244 / 120.4 = 2.03 × 10⁻³ mol; n(H2O) = 0.256 / 18.0 = 1.42 × 10⁻² mol. The ratio is 1.42 × 10⁻² / 2.03 × 10⁻³ = 7.0, so x = 7 and the formula is MgSO4·7H2O.
  3. Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between aqueous sodium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid, and state one observation. Answer: CO32−(aq) + 2H+(aq) → CO2(g) + H2O(l); effervescence, and the gas turns limewater milky.
  4. 25.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 0.100 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. Calculate the volume of alkali required. Answer: n(HCl) = 0.150 × 25.0 / 1000 = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O, so n(NaOH) = 3.75 × 10⁻³ mol and V = n / c = 3.75 × 10⁻³ / 0.100 = 0.0375 dm³ = 37.5 cm³.
  5. Explain why the percentage yield of a reaction can be less than 100 %, and why a reaction with a high percentage yield can still have a low atom economy. Answer: the yield is reduced by incomplete reaction, side reactions, losses in transfer and purification, or by the reaction being reversible. Atom economy depends only on the balanced equation, so a reaction can convert nearly all the limiting reactant into products while most of the product mass is an unwanted co-product.

Revise this topic by practising calculations with the units written at every step, because each mark scheme rewards the mole ratio and the correct final unit as much as the numerical answer. Next, move to Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table, where the mole is used again for relative atomic mass and mass spectra.

title: Exam technique: Pressure and Density
content:
### What earns the marks
For solids, p = F/A with substitution earns both marks. For liquids, proportionality with depth stated earns the explanation mark. For hydraulics, pressure equated across pistons earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: force and pressure interchanged. Correction: pressure divides by area. Error: depth effect inverted. Correction: deeper means greater pressure. Error: atmospheric pressure guessed at 10 Pa. Correction: about 100 kPa at sea level.
### Method marks
Pressure = force ÷ area, and the area must be in m² for the answer in pascals. Density = mass ÷ volume. For an irregular solid, find the volume from the displacement of water.
### Explain, do not just name
Pressure in a liquid increases with depth because the weight of the column above increases. Write p = hρg and name each symbol in the explanation.
### Traps
Using cm² without converting: 1 cm² = 10^-4 m². Forgetting that the pressure in a fluid at a given depth acts equally in all directions.

### Convert units before you calculate
Density questions often give mass in grams and volume in cm³. Convert to kg and m³ if the answer needs SI units, and show the conversion because examiners award it as a mark.

### Use p = hρg for liquids
For pressure at a depth, write p = hρg, state which density you used, and remember that the pressure depends only on depth in the liquid, not on the shape of the container.

### Explain floating and sinking with a comparison
A body floats when its weight equals the upthrust, which equals the weight of displaced fluid. Compare densities of the object and the fluid in your explanation.

content:
Quick revision: Logic Gates & Boolean Logic

Computer Science — OL. six gates, truth tables, logic expressions, building/describing circuits, problem-to-logic mapping.

  • 1. The six gates
  • 2. Truth tables
  • 3. Logic expressions
  • 4. Problem → logic
  • 5. Describing circuits

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Logic gates process binary inputs to give one output. AND gives 1 only when all inputs are 1. OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1. NOT inverts its single input. NAND and NOR are the NOT of AND and OR respectively, and XOR gives 1 when its inputs differ.

Complete a truth table by listing every combination of inputs in binary order, then work through the logic one gate at a time. For a logic diagram, draw each gate with the correct symbol and label every connection, because the examiner checks the output of each gate separately.

title: Organisms and their Environment
content:
Organisms and their Environment

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 19 (statements 19.1–19.4). Energy flow, food chains and webs, nutrient cycles, and populations with sampling.

19.1 to 19.3 Energy and nutrient cycles

  • Energy flows one way through an ecosystem: from the Sun to producers, then consumers, with about 10% passed on at each transfer; most is lost in respiration and as heat. Nutrients, by contrast, are recycled.
  • Trophic levels: producers (plants), primary consumers (herbivores), secondary consumers (carnivores), decomposers (bacteria and fungi) which break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil.
  • The carbon cycle: photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide, respiration and combustion return it, and decomposition releases carbon from dead organisms. The nitrogen cycle involves nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules, nitrifying bacteria, and denitrifying bacteria returning nitrogen to the air.

19.4 Populations

  • A population is all the organisms of one species in an area; a community is all the populations; an ecosystem includes the abiotic factors too. Sampling uses quadrats for plants and random selection for mobile animals.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Energy calculation, applied to 3000 kJ reaching producers: 300 kJ reach primary consumers and 30 kJ reach secondary consumers. Explain the 10% rule with the losses — respiration, uneaten parts, faeces, heat. State the losses explicitly; quoting the percentage alone is not the explanation.
  • Cycle reasoning, applied to why adding fertiliser can cause eutrophication: nitrates wash into the water, algae bloom, light is blocked, plants die, and decomposer bacteria multiply and use up dissolved oxygen, killing fish. Give the full chain — each step is a separate mark.
  • Sampling evaluation, applied to a quadrat survey: randomise positions by throwing a marker or using random coordinates, take a large number of quadrats, and state that this reduces bias and improves reliability. Name both randomisation and sample size as improvements.

Common errors

  • Saying energy is recycled in an ecosystem. Only nutrients cycle; energy flows out as heat.
  • Forgetting decomposers when describing a nutrient cycle.
  • Placing quadrats in a line "to be systematic" without justifying; systematic sampling suits gradient studies, random sampling suits population estimates.

title: Exam technique: Hypothesis Testing
content:
### What earns the marks
For hypotheses, H0 and H1 in words or symbols earn the first mark. For the test statistic, its value compared against the critical value earns the method mark. For conclusions, contextual wording (evidence of change, not proof) earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: significant claimed equals proven. Correction: evidence only. Error: wrong tail direction. Correction: H1 fixes the tail. Error: H0 restated in the conclusion without context. Correction: answer about the situation.
### Write the hypotheses in words and symbols
State H₀ and H₁ clearly, using the parameter of the population, such as the mean or the proportion. Use a one-tailed test when the question states a direction, and a two-tailed test otherwise.

### Compare the test statistic with the critical value
Find the critical region at the given significance level, decide whether the test statistic falls inside it, and then state the conclusion as a decision about H₀.

### Finish in context
Conclude in words that refer to the situation in the question, for example that there is or is not sufficient evidence that the proportion has changed.
