How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

An operating system manages the hardware and gives the user and programs a controlled way to use it. Its main tasks are managing processes, memory, files, input and output devices, and user accounts. Multitasking lets the processor switch between processes so that several appear to run at once.

Interrupts signal the processor that an event needs attention, such as a key press or the end of a disk read. Virtual memory uses secondary storage to extend the memory available to running programs. When an answer asks why an OS is needed, link each function to the problem it solves for the user.

title: Web Technologies and Security — Study Notes
content:
Web Technologies and Security

Syllabus note: the encryption content follows section 17 (Security, Paper 3); the HTML/CSS/JavaScript sections are supporting background and are not separately examined in 9618.

The Three Layers

  • HTML gives structure and content: elements, attributes, forms for user input.
  • CSS gives presentation: selectors, properties, responsive layout.
  • JavaScript gives client-side behaviour: validation before submission, DOM updates without reload.

Server-side scripting (PHP) runs on the server: reads form fields ($_POST), queries the database, outputs HTML. The client never sees PHP source.

SQL Injection

An attack where crafted input changes the meaning of a query. If a login query concatenates the username directly, entering X OR 1=1 can match every row. Defences: parameterised queries (prepared statements) that separate code from data, validation, and least-privilege database accounts.

Encryption

  • Symmetric: one shared key (AES). Fast, but key distribution is the weak point.
  • Asymmetric: public/private key pair (RSA). Anyone encrypts with the public key; only the holder decrypts with the private key. Slower, so used to exchange a symmetric session key.
  • SSL/TLS combines both: certificates verify the server, asymmetric key exchange establishes a symmetric session key, then traffic is encrypted. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS on port 443.

Hashing vs Encryption

Hashing (e.g. SHA-256) is one-way: passwords should be stored hashed with a unique salt, never encrypted reversibly.

Exam tips: explain why parameterised queries stop injection; describe the TLS handshake in three steps; distinguish hashing from encryption with password storage as the example.

Symmetric and asymmetric encryption

Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast, but the key must be shared securely. Asymmetric encryption uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt. TLS uses asymmetric encryption to agree a shared symmetric key at the start of a session.

A digital certificate binds a public key to an organisation. A trusted certificate authority signs it so that a browser can check the site's identity.

Exam tip: explain the hybrid approach: asymmetric for the key exchange, symmetric for the bulk data.

Exam method: choosing a defence

Match each threat to the control that stops it. Parameterised queries stop SQL injection because user input is passed as data and never run as part of the command. Input validation rejects unexpected characters before they reach the database. HTTPS uses encryption to protect data in transit, so an eavesdropper on the network sees only ciphertext. Passwords should be stored as salted hashes, so a stolen database does not reveal the original passwords.

Answer the question that is asked. If the question is about protecting data sent over a network, encryption is the answer. If it is about checking a password without storing it, a hash is the answer. Giving the wrong defence for the threat loses the marks even when the explanation is accurate.

Common errors

  • Describing a hash as reversible. A hash is one-way, so the original value cannot be recovered from it.
  • Calling a web page secure simply because it uses a padlock. The padlock shows encryption, not that the site is free of flaws.

title: Exam technique: Hardware and Logic Gates
content:
### What earns the marks
For device choice, sense-process-store-output each matched earns credit: sensors for capture, processor for decisions, storage for logs, transmitter for remote output. For logic, the gate-by-gate evaluation shown earns method marks; the law named (absorption, De Morgan) earns the final mark. For architecture, each register with its single role earns precision.
### Traps
Error: office peripherals for sensing tasks. Correction: sensing needs sensors. Error: MAR/MDR roles swapped. Correction: address out via MAR, instruction back via MDR. Error: B claimed for A AND (A OR B). Correction: absorption gives A.
### Truth tables in full
Build a truth table with one column per input and one per intermediate gate output, so every row can be checked. For n inputs there are 2^n rows. Working the intermediate columns is where method marks are awarded.
### Simplify with Boolean laws
Apply De Morgan's laws and the absorption and identity laws to reduce an expression. Show each law you use on a separate line; a simplified answer with no working cannot earn the method marks.
### Drawing circuits
Read the expression from the inside out and draw one gate per operator. Check the output against a row of the truth table before you finish.

title: Exponentials and Logarithms — Study Notes
content:
Exponentials and logarithms in calculus and modelling

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 3 (WMA13), sat at A2.

The A2 work on e^x and ln x adds calculus and rates of change to the AS algebraic toolkit.

Differentiation and integration

  • d/dx (e^(kx)) = k e^(kx); so d/dx (e^x) = e^x.
  • d/dx (ln x) = 1/x; by the chain rule d/dx (ln(ax + b)) = a/(ax + b).
  • d/dx (ln(kx)) = 1/x for any constant k > 0.
  • The integral of e^(kx) is (1/k) e^(kx) + c; the integral of 1/x is ln x + c (x > 0).
  • Product rule with logs: d/dx (x ln x) = ln x + 1.

Solving equations

  • ln(x^2) = 4 gives x^2 = e^4, so x = e^2 or x = -e^2 (check the domain).
  • Log equations combine: ln a + ln b = ln(ab); always reject solutions outside the domain.
  • ln(x) = 1 + ln(3) gives ln x = ln(3e), so x = 3e.

Exponential growth and decay

  • If dN/dt = kN then N = N0 e^(kt): the rate of change is proportional to the quantity itself.
  • Examples: population growth, radioactive decay, cooling, compound interest.
  • Doubling time = ln 2 / k; half-life = ln(0.5) / k.

Graphs and limits

  • e^x grows without bound; e^(-x) tends to 0 as x increases (asymptote y = 0).
  • The gradient of e^x at x = 0 is 1.
  • ln x grows slowly; its graph crosses the x-axis at (1, 0).

title: Kinetics
content:
Kinetics Revision Notes

Edexcel IAL Chemistry A2 Unit 4 Topic 11. This topic covers the quantitative study of reaction rates, rate equations, reaction mechanisms, catalysis, and the Arrhenius equation.

  • Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, while rate equation is expressed as rate = k[A]m[B]n where m and n are orders 0, 1 or 2.
  • Order with respect to a substance is the power to which its concentration term is raised in the rate equation, and overall order is the sum of all individual orders.
  • Rate constant k is constant for a given temperature, half-life t1/2 is the time taken for the concentration of a reactant to halve, and rate-determining step is the slowest step in a multi-step mechanism.
  • Activation energy Ea is the minimum energy colliding particles must possess to react, heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from reactants, and homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase.
  • First-order reactions have a constant half-life independent of concentration, calculated from concentration-time graphs.
  • Experimental techniques to monitor rates include titration, colorimetry, mass change, volume of gas evolved, and other methods such as conductivity or pH measurement.
  • Initial-rate methods use separate experiments with different initial concentrations, and continuous monitoring tracks a single reaction over time to plot concentration-time or volume-time graphs.
  • Orders 0, 1 or 2 can be deduced from concentration-time graphs, rate-concentration graphs, or initial-rate method data.
  • Acid-catalysed iodination of propanone uses titrimetric methods to find orders with respect to propanone, iodine, and hydrogen ions to deduce the rate-determining step and mechanism.
  • Rate-determining step dictates the rate equation, and a reaction mechanism must agree with the stoichiometric equation and the rate equation.
  • Hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes provides evidence for SN1 (unimolecular, tertiary) and SN2 (bimolecular, primary) mechanisms based on rate equations involving hydroxide ions.
  • Activation energy can be calculated using graphical methods from experimental rate constant data at various temperatures using the Arrhenius equation.
  • Solid heterogeneous catalysts provide an active surface for gas-phase industrial reactions by adsorbing reactants, weakening bonds, and desorbing products.
  • Core Practical 9a and 9b involve following the rate of the iodine-propanone reaction by titrimetry and investigating clock reactions like the Harcourt-Esson or iodine clock.
  • Core Practical 10 involves finding the activation energy of a reaction using titrimetric or colorimetric methods at different temperatures.

Worked example

For a reaction with rate equation rate = k[A][B]2, if the initial concentration of A is doubled and B is halved, the new rate becomes rate = k(2[A])(0.5[B])2 = k × 2[A] × 0.25[B]2 = 0.5 × k[A][B]2, meaning the rate halves.

Key points to remember

Students often forget that rate equations must be determined experimentally, never from the stoichiometric balancing numbers in the overall equation unless the step is elementary. When calculating activation energy from the Arrhenius equation, remember to convert temperatures from Celsius to Kelvin and ensure units of k match the overall order of the reaction. For heterogeneous catalysts, always mention adsorption onto the active surface, reaction, and desorption of products.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Right-Angled Trigonometry
content:
### What earns the marks
For finding sides or angles, the correct ratio chosen (sin, cos, tan) with sides labelled earns the method mark: write sin(angle) = opposite / hypotenuse before substituting. For Pythagoras, the squared equation earns the mark before the root. For exact values, the surd form (root 3 / 2) earns the exactness mark; decimals lose it. For angles of elevation and depression, the diagram with the equality stated earns credit.
### Traps
Error: sine used where cosine belongs (adjacent involved). Correction: label O, A, H on the diagram first. Error: 225 given as the hypotenuse. Correction: root last. Error: 0.866 accepted for sin 60. Correction: exact means surd. Error: sin used for a tan situation in height problems. Correction: opposite over adjacent when the hypotenuse is absent.
### Worked example
In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is 10 cm and one angle is 30°. The side opposite the 30° angle is 10 sin 30° = 5 cm. Given the sides 3 and 4 with a right angle between them, the angle θ opposite the side 3 satisfies tan θ = 3/4, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 36.9°.

title: Exam technique: System Software and Security
content:
### What earns the marks
For OS roles, each role tied to the scenario earns a mark: paging for oversized workloads, scheduling for shared CPUs. For malware, the propagation method contrasted (self-spreading worms vs host-bound viruses) earns both marks. For hashing, one-way verification plus salt against rainbow tables earns the pair.
### Traps
Error: single-driver answers for whole-OS management. Correction: name memory, processor, devices, security. Error: worms and viruses reversed. Correction: worms roam alone; viruses ride hosts. Error: encryption claimed where hashing belongs. Correction: password checks verify hashes, never decrypt.
### Name the threat, then the control
Security questions score when the threat and the matching control are both given. For example, phishing is countered by user awareness and email filtering, and brute force attacks are countered by account lockout and longer passwords.
### Operating system functions
When asked about the operating system, list its functions by name, such as memory management, process scheduling, file management and user interface, and give one sentence for each.
### Utility and system software
Distinguish system software from application software. Compilers, linkers and loaders are system software; a word processor is not.

title:
Molecules, Transport and Health — Quick Revision Summary

Biology — AS Edexcel IAL, WBI12 Unit 1 Topic 1. Water as a polar solvent and its role in transport, carbohydrates (monosaccharides, disaccharides, polysaccharides including starch, glycogen and cellulose) and their structure and role in energy storage and structure, lipids (triglycerides, saturated and unsaturated) and their roles, proteins and their structure from amino acid to tertiary and quaternary, gas exchange surfaces and Fick's law and the mammalian lung adaptations, the mammalian heart and circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve and the Bohr effect and fetal haemoglobin, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, risk factors for CVD (diet, blood pressure, smoking, age, gender, inactivity, cholesterol, obesity) and how each acts, diet and antioxidants and cholesterol and the evidence, people using scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments (antihypertensives, statins, anticoagulants, platelet inhibitors), and the data analysis skills of distinguishing correlation from causation and evaluating study design and sample size — plus the two core practicals (Benedict's and iodine semi-quantitative tests, DCPIP vitamin C, biuret protein, enzyme factors).

  • 1.1 Water: a dipole — oxygen slightly negative, hydrogen slightly positive — so it forms hydrogen bonds, has high specific heat capacity and high latent heat of vaporisation, is cohesive, and is an excellent solvent for ions and polar molecules (because the partial charges surround and dissolve them); in transport it carries dissolved substances.
  • 1.2 Carbohydrates: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose — hexoses, C₆H₁₂O₆); disaccharides by condensation forming glycosidic bonds (maltose = glucose+glucose, sucrose = glucose+fructose, lactose = glucose+galactose); polysaccharides: starch (amylose helical and amylopectin branched — glucose storage in plants, compact and insoluble), glycogen (more branched storage in animals, mainly liver and muscle), cellulose (beta-glucose straight chains, hydrogen-bonded into microfibrils — structural).
  • 1.3 Core Practical 1: Benedict's reagent turns blue → green → yellow → orange → brick-red as reducing sugar concentration increases (heat with the sample, compare with a colour standard chart to estimate); iodine solution turns blue-black with starch — compare intensity with a colour standard to estimate.
  • 1.4 Glycosidic bonds: monosaccharides join by condensation (losing water, forming a glycosidic bond) to make disaccharides and polysaccharides; hydrolysis (adding water) breaks the bond — starch → maltose → glucose; sucrose → glucose + fructose; lactose → glucose + galactose.
  • 1.5 Triglycerides: one glycerol + three fatty acids, joined by ester bonds; saturated fatty acids have no double bonds (straight, pack tight — solid fats), unsaturated have double bonds (kinks, loose packing — liquid oils); roles: energy storage (more energy per gram than carbohydrate), phospholipid bilayer, myelin sheath, waterproof skin layer (subcutaneous fat), steroid hormones.
  • 1.6 Why animals need a heart and circulation: as organisms grow, diffusion alone becomes too slow to supply cells deep inside the body — surface area to volume ratio falls with size, so a mass transport system (heart, blood vessels, blood) moves materials fast.
  • 1.7 Blood vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure — thick muscular, elastic walls, narrow lumen, no valves; veins carry blood to the heart at low pressure — thinner walls, wide lumen, valves to prevent backflow; capillaries are one cell thick with the smallest lumen — thin walls and large total surface area for exchange.
  • 1.8 Cardiac cycle: atrial systole (atria contract, blood into ventricles), ventricular systole (ventricles contract, blood into aorta and pulmonary artery, AV valves close → first heart sound), diastole (heart relaxes, ventricles fill, semilunar valves close → second heart sound); valves ensure one-way flow; left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it pumps to the whole body at higher pressure; the heart is myogenic.
  • 1.9 Haemoglobin and oxygen transport: haemoglobin has four polypeptide chains each with a haem group carrying one O₂ molecule, so one haemoglobin carries four O₂; the oxygen dissociation curve shows saturation rising steeply then levelling; the Bohr effect: higher CO₂ and lower pH lower haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, so it unloads more O₂ in respiring tissues; fetal haemoglobin has a higher oxygen affinity than adult haemoglobin, so it can take oxygen from adult haemoglobin across the placenta.
  • 1.10 Atherosclerosis: endothelial dysfunction (damage from high blood pressure, smoking chemicals or immune responses) → inflammatory response, white blood cells enter the wall, LDL oxidised and taken up, smooth muscle and fibrous tissue build up → plaque (fibrous cap over a lipid core); the plaque narrows the artery, raises pressure, and can rupture → clot (thrombus) → blocked artery → myocardial infarction (heart attack) or stroke.
  • 1.11 Blood clotting: vessel damage exposes collagen, platelets activate and release thromboplastin, thromboplastin + Ca²⁺ converts prothrombin → thrombin, thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen → insoluble fibrin threads that form a mesh trapping platelets and red blood cells → a clot; clotting prevents blood loss and pathogen entry, but a clot on a ruptured plaque can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction or a cerebral artery and cause a stroke.

Worked example

Risk calculation from data: a study finds that smokers have a 15% chance of a heart attack by age 70, and non-smokers 4% — the relative risk for smokers = 15/4 = 3.75, so smokers are about 3.75 times as likely to have a heart attack by 70; but this is a correlation — part of the risk is caused by smoking itself (mechanistically, the chemicals damage the endothelium, raise blood pressure and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin), and it may also be that smokers differ in other ways (diet, exercise); still, smoking is a causal risk factor, so the relative risk is used as evidence, not proof, and decisions use the whole body of evidence. To evaluate the study, check the sample (is it representative, and large enough, and free from bias in selection or loss of participants) and the method (were the groups comparable, and were confounding factors such as diet and exercise accounted for).

Key points to remember

Risk factors for CVD and how they act: high blood pressure damages endothelium and raises heart strain and atherosclerosis risk; high saturated fat and cholesterol raise LDL and contribute to plaques; smoking introduces chemicals that damage endothelium, raise blood pressure and heart rate and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin (carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin); age increases risk as damage accumulates and repair is less efficient; males are at higher risk than females at younger ages; inactivity contributes to blood pressure, obesity and cholesterol; genetics/family history affects baseline risk; obesity (BMI = mass (kg)/height (m)², and waist-to-hip ratio) is a risk factor; high cholesterol (total and LDL) is linked to CVD and HDL is protective. Diet and antioxidants: vitamin C and E (from fruit and vegetables) may reduce risk by preventing oxidation of LDL; evidence for cholesterol causing CVD comes from the biology and from the results of statin trials, which lower cholesterol and reduce events. People use this knowledge — BMI, waist-to-hip ratio, exercise, smoking, diet — to reduce their risk. Benefits and risks of treatments: antihypertensives lower blood pressure (dizziness, fatigue, kidney effects, over-lowering); statins lower cholesterol (muscle pain, digestive upset, rarely liver effects); anticoagulants (warfarin) and platelet inhibitors (aspirin) reduce clotting (bleeding risk, gut bleeding, not for everyone). Distinguish correlation from causation and evaluate study design — sample selection (representative or biased), sample size (small samples less reliable, more chance variation), and whether confounding factors were controlled.

How to use this

Read the summary list, then open the full revision notes for any point that feels weak, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself. Revise next by: drawing a triglyceride and distinguishing saturated and unsaturated; drawing a cholesterol molecule and stating how saturated and unsaturated fats differ; carrying out the Benedict's, iodine and DCPIP practicals and explaining the variables, the colour standards and the control variables; describing the cardiac cycle and drawing the pressure/volume changes through a heartbeat; sketching the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin, showing the Bohr effect and the fetal haemoglobin curve to the left; describing the stages of atherosclerosis and blood clotting and the enzymes and factors in clotting; listing the risk factors for CVD and stating how each acts; and working through a risk calculation from study data and evaluating the study design.

title: Biotechnology and Genetic Modification
content:
Biotechnology and Genetic Modification

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 21 (statements 21.1–21.3). Biotechnology and microorganisms, industrial fermentation with aseptic technique, and genetic modification with its applications and risks.

21.1 to 21.2 Biotechnology

  • Biotechnology uses living organisms or their products industrially. Microorganisms ferment sugars to make bread, beer, yoghurt and cheese, and are used to produce insulin and antibiotics.
  • Industrial fermentation controls temperature, pH, nutrient supply and oxygen, with aseptic technique preventing contamination by unwanted microbes. Sterilise equipment before, work near a flame, and autoclave waste after.

21.3 Genetic modification

  • Genetic modification transfers a gene for a desired characteristic into another organism: extract the gene, insert it into a vector (plasmid or virus), introduce the vector into host cells, and select the modified cells. Examples include insulin-producing bacteria, GM crops with pest resistance, and Golden Rice enriched with beta-carotene.
  • Benefits include higher yields and improved nutrition; risks include genes spreading to wild populations, effects on biodiversity, and consumer concerns.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Process chain, applied to producing human insulin in bacteria: the human insulin gene is cut with a restriction enzyme, joined to a plasmid with DNA ligase, and the recombinant plasmid is put into bacteria which then produce the insulin as they multiply. Name restriction enzyme and DNA ligase — both appear as separate marks every year.
  • Evaluation reasoning, applied to GM crops in a developing country: weigh higher yield and lower pesticide use against seed costs, gene flow to wild relatives, and farmer dependency. Reach a justified judgement; both sides must appear for the top band.
  • Aseptic technique reasoning, applied to why a fermenter must be sterilised first: unwanted microbes would compete for nutrients and could produce toxic or unwanted products, ruining the batch. Link each technique step to the reason it exists.

Common errors

  • Saying GM "changes the animal's own genes by breeding". GM transfers a gene directly across species boundaries.
  • Confusing restriction enzymes (cut) with DNA ligase (join).
  • Forgetting aseptic technique is needed AFTER as well as before fermentation, for safe disposal.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Energy, Work & Power

Physics — OL. stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

  • 1. Energy stores & transfers
  • 2. Formulas
  • 3. Energy sources
  • 4. Efficiency
  • 5. Energy-chain problems

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Work done W = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.
  • Power P = energy transferred / time, and efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input × 100%.
  • Kinetic energy = ½mv² and gravitational potential energy = mgh.
  • Energy is conserved, so the total energy after a transfer equals the total before it.

Common errors

Do not confuse work with power, or energy with power. Efficiency can never be more than 100%, so a larger answer means an error in the calculation.

Quick revision: Data Representation

  • 1. Number systems
  • 2. Two's complement (signed)
  • 3. Text
  • 4. Images and sound
  • 5. Compression

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example Convert 157 to binary by using place values 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 157, which gives 10011101. Grouping the bits in fours gives 1001 1101, which is 9D in hexadecimal, and 9 × 16 + 13 = 157 confirms it. An 8-bit unsigned number can represent 0 to 255.

Key points to remember

Computers store all data as binary. Convert denary to binary by repeatedly dividing by two or by subtracting place values from 128 down to 1. Hexadecimal groups four bits per digit, so 1111 1010 is FA in hex. Two's complement represents negative integers: invert the bits of the positive value and add one, and the leftmost bit is the sign.

Text is stored using character sets such as ASCII, where each character has a fixed numeric code. Images are stored as pixels, each holding a colour value, and sound as samples of amplitude taken at a sample rate. Show your working for every conversion, because a single wrong bit loses the whole mark.

title: Geometry — Congruence and Similarity — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Congruence and Similarity

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): congruence criteria, similar shapes, scale factors for length/area/volume, symmetry.

1. Congruence

Criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA (AAS), RHS. State the criterion used when proving triangles congruent, then transfer matching sides/angles.

2. Similarity

Equal angles + sides in proportion. Scale factor k = corresponding new ÷ old.

Example: triangles with sides 4, 6, 8 and 6, 9, 12: k = 1.5.

3. Length, area, volume factors

Length ×k; area ×k²; volume ×k³ — including reverse problems.

Example: volumes 250 cm³ and 2000 cm³: k³ = 8 ⇒ k = 2 ⇒ areas ×4.

4. Area/volume calculations from similarity

Find k from a matching length pair, then apply the right power. Watch hidden pairs (radii, heights, slants).

5. Symmetry

Line symmetry (reflect) and rotational symmetry order — for 2-D shapes and 3-D solids (prisms, cubes, pyramids).

Exam tips: write the matching-vertex order in similarity statements (△ABC ~ △DEF); choose which k-power applies before calculating.

Congruent triangles

Two triangles are congruent when they match on one of four conditions: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the included angle), ASA or AAS (two angles and a side), or RHS (right angle, hypotenuse and a side) for right-angled triangles. SSA is not a condition. Name the congruence test in every proof.

Similar shapes and scale factors

Similar shapes have equal angles and proportional sides. The linear scale factor k multiplies lengths, k² multiplies areas and k³ multiplies volumes. To find a missing side, set up the ratio of corresponding sides and cross-multiply.

Transformations in geometry questions

A translation is described by a column vector, a rotation by its centre, angle and direction, a reflection by its mirror line and an enlargement by its centre and scale factor. Image points are checked by measuring the same distance from the centre or the mirror line.

Worked example: proving congruence

Triangles ABC and PQR have AB = PQ, angle B = angle Q and BC = QR. These are two sides and the included angle, so the triangles are congruent by SAS. A correct proof names the criterion and lists the equal parts in the same order as the letters.

The four congruence conditions

  • SSS: three pairs of equal sides.
  • SAS: two pairs of equal sides with the angle between them equal.
  • ASA or AAS: two pairs of equal angles and one pair of equal sides.
  • RHS: a right angle, the hypotenuse and one other side equal, for right-angled triangles only.

SSA is not a valid condition, because the angle may not be the one between the sides, and two different triangles can share those measurements.

Similar shapes and scale factors

If two shapes are similar with scale factor k, every length multiplies by k, every area by k², and every volume by k³. Example: two similar solids have a height ratio 2 : 3. The area ratio is 4 : 9 and the volume ratio is 8 : 27.

To find a missing length, set up the ratio from a known pair: if a side of 6 cm on the small shape matches 9 cm on the large one, the scale factor is 1.5 and an 8 cm side becomes 12 cm.

Symmetry

  • A shape has rotational symmetry of order n if it looks the same after rotations of 360°/n about its centre.
  • A regular hexagon has six lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 6.
  • Count lines of symmetry on the diagram itself, and check each one with a tracing or a mirror image.

title: Abstract Data Types — Study Notes
content:
Abstract Data Types

Syllabus note: 9618 introduces abstract data types at AS (section 10.4, AS Paper 2); this note is the extended treatment — trees and hash tables go beyond the AS introduction.

What is an ADT?

An abstract data type is a logical description of a collection of data plus the operations on it, independent of implementation. Stacks, queues, linked lists, binary trees and hash tables are all ADTs; in A Level you must show how they are built from arrays or records with pointers.

Linked Lists

Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; a start pointer marks the head and a null marks the end. Insertion rewires two pointers — no shifting — giving O(1) insertion at a known position, but access requires walking the list, O(n).

Stacks and Queues

A stack is LIFO (push and pop at the top); a queue is FIFO (enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front). Both can be arrays with index pointers or linked lists. Stack uses include call stacks and expression evaluation; queue uses include print buffers and breadth-first search.

Binary Search Trees

Each node has up to two children; left subtree keys are smaller, right subtree keys larger. Search, insert and (average-case) delete are O(log n). An in-order traversal outputs keys in ascending order. A degenerate (linear) tree from sorted input degrades to O(n).

Hash Tables

Covered in file organisation, but as an ADT a hash table pairs a hash function with bucket storage for O(1) average access.

Exam tips: be able to draw a tree after a sequence of insertions and write its three traversals; state the pointer changes for a linked-list insertion; compare ADT operations with Big-O.

Abstract data types in practice

An abstract data type is defined by the operations it supports and their behaviour, not by how it is stored. A stack is defined by push, pop and isEmpty; the programmer using it does not need to know whether it is built from an array or a linked list.

Separating the interface from the implementation lets the implementation change without breaking the code that uses it, and makes each part easier to test.

Exam tip: when asked to define an ADT, name the operations and say what each does, not how it is stored.

Worked example: building a binary search tree

Insert 8, 3, 10, 1 and 6 in that order. The first value, 8, becomes the root. Since 3 is less than 8, it goes to the left; 10 goes to the right. The value 1 is less than 8 and less than 3, so it sits to the left of 3. The value 6 is less than 8 and greater than 3, so it sits to the right of 3. An in-order traversal (left, node, right) then lists the values in sorted order: 1, 3, 6, 8, 10.

Complexity of the main operations

  • Search, insert and delete in a balanced tree take O(log n) time, because each comparison discards about half the remaining nodes.
  • If the values are inserted in sorted order, the tree becomes a chain and the same operations degrade to O(n).
  • Hash table lookup takes O(1) on average but gives no ordering, so a hash table cannot list the data in sorted order.

Choosing between the structures

A stack, a queue and a linked list each store a collection, but they differ in how items are added and removed. A stack is last in, first out. A queue is first in, first out. A linked list allows insertion and deletion at a known position without shifting other items. The exam question usually asks you to justify the choice, so state the access pattern the data needs.

Exam method: tracing a stack and a queue

Write the contents after every operation. Start with an empty stack. Push 5, push 9, pop, then push 2. After the pop the stack holds 5 only, so the final push leaves 5 at the bottom and 2 at the top. The value returned by the pop is 9, because a stack returns the most recently added item.

A queue works in the opposite order. Enqueue 5, enqueue 9, then dequeue. The dequeue returns 5, the item that entered first, and 9 remains at the front. Marks are given for the returned value and for the final state, so show both.

Common errors

  • Describing a stack as first in, first out. That describes a queue; a stack is last in, first out.
  • Forgetting to check for an empty structure before a pop or dequeue. Good answers say what the program should do when the structure is empty.
  • Saying an array-based queue never needs wrapping. A fixed-size array queue can waste space at the front unless its pointers wrap round to the start.

title: Exam technique: Data Types and File Organisation
content:
### What earns the marks
For records, the mixed-type justification earns the mark: arrays hold one type only. For file access, the task matched to the method earns each mark: full runs suit sequential scans, single lookups suit indexed jumps. For floating point, the bias arithmetic shown earns the exponent mark.
### Traps
Error: plain arrays for heterogeneous records. Correction: composite types exist for exactly this. Error: sequential scan for one lookup. Correction: jump via the index. Error: bias forgotten in exponent. Correction: add the bias every time.
### Data types
Choose the data type with the reason: an integer for whole-number counts, a real for measured values, a Boolean for a yes-or-no state and a string for text. A question asking for the most suitable type needs the reason as well as the name.
### File organisation
Sequential files are read in order and suit batch processing, random files give direct access by a key and suit fast look-up, and serial access reads from start to finish. Name the access method and a use for each.
### Common slips
Confusing the bit pattern of a value with its denary value. Always convert both ways and check the result against the range that the number of bits allows.

title: The Periodic Table
content:
The Periodic Table

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 8 (statements 8.1–8.5). Periodic trends, Group I and Group VII properties and displacement reactions, transition elements, and the noble gases.

8.1 Arrangement

  • Elements are arranged in order of increasing proton number, in periods (rows) and groups (columns). Metallic character decreases across a period from left to right and increases down a group.

8.2 Group I

  • Alkali metals: soft, low density, low melting point. Reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily. Products with water: a metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

8.3 Group VII

  • Halogens: reactivity decreases down the group because the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so an atom gains an electron less easily. Denser and darker down the group: fluorine pale yellow gas, chlorine green-yellow gas, bromine red-brown liquid, iodine grey solid.

8.4 to 8.5 Transition elements and noble gases

  • Transition elements: high density, high melting point, form coloured compounds, act as catalysts, and show variable oxidation states (iron(II) and iron(III) are the syllabus examples).
  • Noble gases: full outer shells, so they are monatomic and unreactive.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Displacement reasoning, applied to chlorine added to potassium bromide: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂. Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces the bromide ions. The chlorine is reduced (0 to −1) and the bromide is oxidised (−1 to 0). Name both half-changes for full marks.
  • Prediction, applied to astatine: it sits below iodine, so it is a solid, less reactive than iodine, and would be displaced from its salts by chlorine, bromine and iodine. Predictions must be justified from the group trend, not asserted.
  • Trend explanation, applied to why potassium reacts more violently with water than lithium: the outer electron in potassium is in shell 4 versus shell 2 in lithium, so it is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, so it is lost more easily. Use the words shielding and nuclear attraction.

Common errors

  • Saying reactivity of Group VII increases down the group. It decreases.
  • Explaining Group I trends by "atoms get bigger" without the electron-loss link.
  • Calling transition metal catalysts "changing the product". They change the rate, not the products.

title: Communication and Networking — Study Notes
content:
`# Communication and Networking

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 2 (Communication), examined in AS Paper 1.

Transmission

  • Serial: one bit at a time — cheaper, reliable over distance
  • Parallel: multiple bits simultaneously — fast but suffers skew and crosstalk over long runs
  • Direction: simplex (one way), half-duplex (alternating), full-duplex (both ways)

Packets and Protocols

Data splits into packets with header (addresses, sequence) and trailer (checksum). A protocol is an agreed rule set — without one, devices cannot interpret signals.

  • TCP/IP stack: application → transport → network → link
  • HTTP/HTTPS: web transfer; HTTPS encrypts with TLS
  • FTP: file transfer; SMTP/POP3/IMAP: email

Network Types

  • LAN: small site, privately owned; WAN: large geographic scale (the internet)
  • Topologies: bus, star, mesh (star is most common — central switch)

Hardware

Routers join networks by IP; switches forward frames by MAC within a LAN; gateways translate protocols.

Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

Client-server: central services, easy administration, single point of failure. P2P: every node shares files directly — cheap, hard to manage (torrents, blockchain).

Exam tips: explain packet switching with header/trailer details; justify protocol choice per application (email vs streaming).

Network topologies and hardware

In a star topology every device connects to a central switch. If one cable or device fails, the others keep working, but if the central switch fails the whole network stops. In a bus topology all devices share one cable, which is cheap but means a break in the cable disables the network.

A switch connects devices within a local area network (LAN) and sends each frame only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses. A router connects separate networks together and forwards packets using IP addresses. A wireless access point lets wireless devices join a wired LAN.

Exam tip: when comparing topologies, state what happens when one device fails and when the central device fails. Those two cases are the usual differentiators.

Worked example: transfer time and latency

A 2 Mbit file sent over a link of 1 Mbit per second takes 2 seconds to transfer, ignoring overheads. Latency is the delay before the first bit arrives, and it adds to the total time. If the latency is 0.2 seconds, the complete delivery takes about 2.2 seconds. Stating which quantity you are calculating, and the units, earns method marks even when the final figure is slightly off.

Bandwidth and the shared medium

  • Bandwidth is the maximum data rate of a link. Actual throughput is lower when many devices share the medium, because they take turns or collide.
  • Wired connections such as Ethernet usually give more stable speeds than wireless, which is affected by distance, walls and interference.

title: Exam technique: DC Circuits
content:
### What earns the marks
For junctions, Kirchhoff current sums stated earn the mark. For combinations, the parallel reciprocal form quoted earns the method mark. For terminal p.d., E minus Ir earns both marks with the lost volts identified.
### Traps
Error: series rules applied to parallel branches. Correction: voltage is the shared quantity in parallel. Error: emf quoted as terminal voltage. Correction: subtract the Ir drop. Error: resistivity factors muddled. Correction: R scales with L over A.
### Apply Ohm's law and the circuit rules
Use V = IR for each component, then state whether the circuit is in series, where the current is the same everywhere, or in parallel, where the voltage is the same across each branch.

### Combine resistors step by step
For resistors in series, add the resistances. For resistors in parallel, use 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ and invert at the end. Redraw the circuit after each combination so you can see what is left.

### Use the potential divider only when it is clear
State the ratio V_out / V_in, identify which resistor the output is across, and explain how the output changes when a resistor changes value.

title: Exam technique: Robotics & AI
content:
### What earns the marks
For expert systems, knowledge base plus inference engine plus explanation system earns each mark. For machine learning, training on data stated earns the method mark. For robotics, the named sensor matched to its reading earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: AI claimed to understand like a human. Correction: it matches patterns from training. Error: inference engine confused with interface. Correction: inference reasons, interface talks to users. Error: automation effects one-sided. Correction: weigh jobs lost against jobs created.### Worked example
For an expert system that helps diagnose illness: the knowledge base holds rules from doctors, the inference engine applies those rules to the patient's symptoms, and the explanation facility tells the user why a conclusion was reached. Naming the three parts with their roles earns full marks. The trap is describing the system as having human understanding, when it only applies stored rules.
### Recall check
Give one advantage and one disadvantage of automation in a factory, then state a reasoned conclusion. Describe how a machine learning system is trained, naming the data it needs.

title: Stoichiometry
content:
Stoichiometry

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 3 (statements 3.1–3.3). Formulae, equations, the mole, reacting masses, gas volumes, concentration and titration calculations — the highest-weight calculation topic on the paper.

3.1 to 3.2 Formulae and masses

  • An empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; a molecular formula is the actual number of each atom. Mr of a substance is the sum of the Ar values in its formula.
  • Equations must be balanced and carry state symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq). Conservation of mass means the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides.

3.3 The mole

  • One mole of any substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant). Moles = mass ÷ Mr. At room temperature and pressure, one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³.
  • Concentration can be given in g/dm³ or mol/dm³. Moles in solution = concentration (mol/dm³) × volume (dm³), with cm³ ÷ 1000 = dm³.
  • Titration data gives moles of one reagent; the balanced equation gives the ratio; the other reagent's moles and concentration follow. Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Reacting masses, applied to 12 g of magnesium burning in oxygen: moles of Mg = 12 ÷ 24 = 0.5 mol. From 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, 0.5 mol Mg gives 0.5 mol MgO, so mass = 0.5 × 40 = 20 g. Oxygen used = 20 − 12 = 8 g. Always convert to moles first, then use the ratio.
  • Gas volume, applied to 5.6 g of calcium carbonate decomposing: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Moles of CaCO₃ = 5.6 ÷ 100 = 0.056 mol, so 0.056 mol CO₂ forms. Volume = 0.056 × 24 = 1.34 dm³ (1340 cm³, to 3 significant figures).
  • Titration chain, applied to 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ NaOH needing 22.0 cm³ of HCl: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O, ratio 1:1. Moles NaOH = 0.100 × 0.0250 = 2.50 × 10⁻³, so moles HCl = 2.50 × 10⁻³, and concentration HCl = 2.50 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0220 = 0.114 mol/dm³. Convert cm³ to dm³ before multiplying — that is where most marks are lost.
  • Empirical formula, applied to a compound with 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass: divide by Ar to get 3.33 mol C, 6.67 mol H, 3.33 mol O; divide by the smallest (3.33) to get CH₂O. To find the molecular formula, divide Mr by the empirical formula mass: 180 ÷ 30 = 6, so C₆H₁₂O₆.

Common errors

  • Using cm³ directly with mol/dm³ without dividing by 1000.
  • Using 22.4 dm³ (that is at standard temperature and pressure, not room temperature and pressure). IGCSE 0620 uses 24 dm³ at r.t.p.
  • Writing an ionic formula that is not the simplest ratio, or leaving a 1:1 ratio as Mg₂O₂.

title: Statistics — Data Handling — Study Notes
content:
Statistics — Data Handling

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): averages from lists and tables, quartiles/IQR, charts, cumulative frequency, histograms.

1. Averages

  • Mean = Σfx/Σf from frequency tables. Median = middle value (ordered data). Mode = most frequent. Range = max − min.
  • Choose the best average: mode for shoe sizes, median when outliers distort the mean.

Example (table): goals 0,1,2,3 with f 5,8,4,3: mean = (0+8+8+9)/20 = 1.25.

2. Quartiles and IQR

Q₁ at n/4, Q₃ at 3n/4 (position); IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ — less affected by outliers than the range.

3. Charts

Bar charts, pie charts (angle = fraction × 360°), time series, pictograms. Compare data sets with like-for-like totals; comment on trends.

4. Cumulative frequency

Running totals vs upper class boundaries; the curve ends at (max, n). Median at n/2; Q₁/Q₃ at n/4 and 3n/4; box plot from the five-figure summary.

5. Histograms

Bar area ∝ frequency: FD = frequency ÷ class width. Recover frequencies as FD × width; unequal widths need FDs on the axis.

Exam tips: read cumulative-frequency answers with dashed construction lines; always compare spreads, not just averages, when asked to compare data.

Mean, median, mode and range

For ungrouped data, the mean is the sum of values divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value after ordering (the average of the two middle values if there is an even count); the mode is the most frequent value; the range is the largest minus the smallest value.

Frequency tables and grouped data

For a frequency table, the mean is the sum of (value × frequency) divided by the total frequency. For grouped data, use the midpoint of each class as the value and state that the answer is an estimate.

Charts and diagrams

Pie charts use angles: each sector angle is the category frequency divided by the total, multiplied by 360°. Bar charts have gaps between bars; histograms have no gaps, and for unequal class widths the height shown is frequency density.

Worked example: a full set of averages

Take the data 2, 4, 4, 7, 9, 10. There are six values. The mean is (2 + 4 + 4 + 7 + 9 + 10)/6 = 36/6 = 6. The median is the average of the third and fourth values, (4 + 7)/2 = 5.5. The mode is 4, the only value that occurs twice. The range is 10 − 2 = 8.

Stem-and-leaf diagrams

A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps every original value while showing the shape of the data. For values 23 and 27 on the stem 2, write 2 | 3 7. Always include a key such as 2 | 3 means 23, and put the leaves in ascending order so that the median and quartiles can be read directly.

Pie charts and scatter diagrams

  • In a pie chart, the angle for each category is (frequency/total) × 360°. Check that all the angles add up to 360°.
  • A scatter diagram shows the relationship between two variables. A positive correlation means that y tends to increase as x increases.
  • A line of best fit should pass close to the middle of the points. Use it to interpolate within the data, which is reliable, and be cautious about extrapolating beyond it.

Exam point: when you compare two distributions, comment on both an average and a spread, for example the median and the IQR, in the context of the data.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Study Notes
content:
Work, energy and power

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 1 (WPH11), sat at AS.

Work

  • Work done = force × displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ. Unit: joule (J), where 1 J = 1 N m.
  • No work is done by a force that acts perpendicular to the displacement, such as the normal contact force on a body moving along a horizontal surface.

Energy stores and transfers

Gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, elastic potential energy, chemical energy and thermal energy are energy stores. Work done transfers energy from one store to another.

Conservation of energy

Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred. Where only conservative forces such as gravity act, the total mechanical energy is constant. Where non-conservative forces such as friction or air resistance act, the energy they dissipate appears as thermal energy.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

  • Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy change near the Earth's surface: ΔEp = mgΔh.

Power and efficiency

  • Power = work done ÷ time = energy transferred ÷ time. Unit: watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.
  • Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. It is always less than 100%.

Worked example: a 2.0 kg object falls freely from rest through 5.0 m. Its speed at the bottom, from energy conservation: ½mv² = mgh, so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5.0) ≈ 9.9 m s⁻¹.

Exam tips: check whether the question says air resistance is negligible before using conservation of energy. Always convert minutes to seconds in power calculations. Give efficiency as a percentage.

Power, efficiency and energy transfer

Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, P = W/t = Fv for a force moving at constant velocity. Efficiency is the useful energy output divided by the total energy input, and it is always less than 1 because some energy is dissipated, usually as thermal energy from friction. When a body is raised, its gain in gravitational potential energy is mgh, and a kinetic energy change is ½m(v2 - u2). Both can be used to find the work done against resistive forces.

Exam tip: state the percentage efficiency with units, and check that it is below 100 percent.

Worked example: lifting a load

A 40 kg load is lifted through 5.0 m at a steady speed. The work done against gravity is W = mgh = 40 × 9.8 × 5.0 = 1960 J, or about 2.0 kJ. If the lifting motor is 60% efficient, the electrical energy supplied is 1960 / 0.60 ≈ 3270 J, and the rest is wasted as thermal energy. Efficiency is the useful energy output divided by the total energy input, and it can never exceed 100%.

Exam method: power and energy

Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = E/t. When a constant force moves an object at speed v, the power is P = Fv. Convert every time to seconds and every energy to joules before you substitute. Questions that give power in kilowatts sometimes ask for energy in kilowatt-hours, so check which unit the answer should use.

title: Organic Synthesis
content:
Organic Synthesis Revision Notes

These revision notes cover Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry Topic 20: Organic Synthesis, focusing on analytical deduction, carbon-chain extension via Grignard reagents, multi-step reaction planning, Core Practical 16, and advanced purification techniques.

  • 20.1 Structure Determination: Deduce formulae and structures using combustion analysis, percentage composition, functional group tests, infrared spectra, mass spectra, and both 13C and proton NMR spectra.
  • 20.2 Carbon-Chain Extension: Form Grignard reagents using magnesium in dry ether and react them with carbon dioxide to form carboxylic acids or with carbonyl compounds to form alcohols.
  • 20.3 Problem Solving and Planning: Predict unfamiliar functional group properties, plan reaction schemes of up to four steps, select appropriate practical procedures, and identify hazard-reduction control measures.
  • 20.4 Core Practical 16: Prepare aspirin (2-acetyloxybenzoic acid) through the acetylation of 2-hydroxybenzoic acid using ethanoic anhydride, followed by purification via recrystallisation.
  • 20.5 Preparation and Purification Techniques: Master refluxing, washing with water and sodium carbonate, solvent extraction, recrystallisation, drying agents, distillation, steam distillation, and melting/boiling temperature determinations.

Worked example

Plan a two-step synthesis of propanoic acid starting from bromoethane. Step 1: React bromoethane with magnesium in dry ether to form the Grignard reagent ethylmagnesium bromide (CH3CH2MgBr). Step 2: React this Grignard reagent with solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) followed by dilute acid to yield propanoic acid (CH3CH2COOH) and increase the carbon chain length by one.

Key points to remember

Always ensure anhydrous conditions when preparing and reacting Grignard reagents, using dry ether as the solvent because water destroys the reagent. When purifying organic liquids, washing with sodium carbonate removes unreacted acidic impurities such as carboxylic acids or excess acid catalysts, which are then neutralised and transferred to the aqueous layer. During recrystallisation for solids, select a solvent in which the desired product is soluble at high temperatures and insoluble or sparingly soluble at low temperatures, ensuring minimum hot solvent is used to maximise yield.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism
content:
### What earns the marks
For wires, BIL with right-angle condition earns both marks. For selectors, E/B equating the forces earns the method mark. For induction, Lenz opposition stated earns the explanation mark; power conserved in transformers earns the calculation marks.
### Traps
Error: parallel motion assumed to feel force. Correction: only the perpendicular component counts. Error: induced current aiding the change. Correction: it opposes the change. Error: particle path guessed straight. Correction: perpendicular entry gives circular arcs.
### Apply the force on a current or moving charge
For a current-carrying wire, F = BIL sin θ, where θ is the angle between the wire and the field. For a charge, F = BQv sin θ. Draw the direction with Fleming's left-hand rule and state the direction of the force.

### Use Faraday's and Lenz's laws together
Induced emf ε = −dΦ/dt, and the minus sign shows that the induced current opposes the change that produced it. Explain the sign in words, not just by writing the minus sign.

### Use the transformer equation with its assumptions
For an ideal transformer, V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p and power in equals power out. State the assumption that the transformer is 100% efficient when you use it.

title: Exam technique: Scatter Diagrams
content:
### What earns the marks
For correlation, direction (rising or falling) and strength (tight or spread) each earn a mark: comment on both. For lines of best fit, the mean point plotted first earns the method mark. For estimation questions, naming interpolation versus extrapolation earns a mark before any value, with the reliability comment credited separately.
### Traps
Error: claiming correlation proves causation. Correction: name the confounder (hot weather drives both). Error: trusting extrapolation like interpolation. Correction: outside the range is always less reliable. Error: forcing the line through the origin. Correction: anchor at (mean x, mean y). Error: calling curved association zero correlation. Correction: zero means no pattern at all.
### Worked example
A scatter diagram shows a positive correlation between hours revised and test score. The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). If x̄ = 5 and ȳ = 12 with gradient 2, the line is y = 2x + 2. Estimating y for x = 8 is interpolation if 8 lies within the data range, which makes it more reliable than extrapolating beyond the data.
### Worked example
A scatter diagram shows a positive correlation between hours revised and test score. The line of best fit passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). If x̄ = 5 and ȳ = 12 with gradient 2, the line is y = 2x + 2. Estimating y for x = 8 is interpolation if 8 lies within the data range, which makes it more reliable than extrapolating beyond the data.

title: Kinematics — Study Notes
content:
Kinematics

This note covers motion in a straight line and projectile motion for the Edexcel International A Level Physics specification, Unit 1 (WPH11), sat at AS. Kinematics describes how position, velocity and acceleration change with time, without asking what causes the motion. Most exam marks come from choosing the right tool, setting a sign convention, and reading graphs correctly.

Definitions

  • Distance and speed are scalars: they have magnitude only.
  • Displacement s and velocity v are vectors: they have magnitude and direction. Displacement is the change in position, measured from a fixed origin.
  • Velocity is the rate of change of displacement: v = ds/dt.
  • Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = dv/dt. An object moving at constant speed around a circle is accelerating, because its direction is changing.

Speed is the magnitude of velocity. An object that travels 60 m in one direction and then 20 m back has a distance of 80 m and a displacement of 40 m.

Interpreting graphs

  • On a displacement–time graph, the gradient is the velocity. A horizontal line means the object is at rest, and a steeper line means a higher speed.
  • On a velocity–time graph, the gradient is the acceleration. A straight line with constant gradient means uniform acceleration. A horizontal line means constant velocity.
  • The area under a velocity–time graph equals the displacement. Area below the time axis counts as negative, so a return journey partly cancels out.
  • On an acceleration–time graph, the area under the line equals the change in velocity.

Worked example. A velocity–time graph rises from 0 to 12 m s⁻¹ in 4 s, stays at 12 m s⁻¹ for 6 s, then falls to 0 in 3 s. The area of the triangle is ½ × 4 × 12 = 24 m, the rectangle is 6 × 12 = 72 m, and the final triangle is ½ × 3 × 12 = 18 m. The total displacement is 114 m. The accelerations are 3 m s⁻² for the first 4 s and −4 m s⁻² for the last 3 s.

SUVAT equations (uniform acceleration only)

SUVAT stands for displacement s, initial velocity u, final velocity v, acceleration a and time t. The four equations below apply only when acceleration is constant.

EquationQuantity not involved
v = u + ats
s = ut + ½at²v
v² = u² + 2ast
s = ½(u + v)ta

Choose the equation that omits the quantity you were not given and do not need. Writing down the list of known and unknown quantities first prevents most errors. Pick a sign convention at the start, normally taking the direction of motion, or up, as positive. For a body falling freely under gravity with up as positive, a = −9.81 m s⁻² (or −9.8 m s⁻² if the question uses g = 9.8).

Worked example. A car accelerates from 5 m s⁻¹ to 25 m s⁻¹ at 2 m s⁻². The time is found from v = u + at: 25 = 5 + 2t, so t = 10 s. The distance follows from v² = u² + 2as: 625 = 25 + 4s, so s = 150 m. Check with s = ½(u + v)t = ½ × 30 × 10 = 150 m.

Non-uniform motion

  • When acceleration is not constant, SUVAT cannot be used. Work from the graphs, or from a displacement function such as s = 3t² − t³, differentiating for velocity and acceleration.
  • Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Average velocity is total displacement divided by total time. These differ whenever the object changes direction.
  • The gradient at a point on a curved graph is the gradient of the tangent at that point. Estimate it by drawing the tangent carefully, and state which point you used.

Projectile motion

A projectile moves under gravity alone, with air resistance ignored. Resolve the launch velocity into two independent components:

  • Horizontal: uₓ = u cos θ. There is no acceleration, so the horizontal velocity stays constant and s = uₓt.
  • Vertical: u_y = u sin θ. The acceleration is g downwards, so SUVAT applies to this component alone.

The two motions share only the time t. At the highest point the vertical velocity is zero, so the time to reach the top is u_y/g. If the object lands at the same height it was launched from, the time of flight is 2u_y/g.

Worked example. A ball is launched at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° above the horizontal from level ground. uₓ = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m s⁻¹ and u_y = 20 sin 30° = 10 m s⁻¹. The time of flight is 2 × 10 / 9.81 ≈ 2.04 s. The horizontal range is 17.3 × 2.04 ≈ 35 m. The maximum height is u_y²/(2g) = 100 / 19.62 ≈ 5.1 m.

Exam tips

  • Write the sign convention at the top of your working. Many lost marks come from a sign error in a vertical question.
  • Check whether the question asks for speed or velocity, and distance or displacement. The words decide which quantity to give.
  • Treat the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile as two one-dimensional problems linked only by time.
  • When a graph is given, say which feature (gradient or area) gives the quantity you want before you calculate it.

Key relationships

  • Resistance R = V / I. Components in series share the voltage, and parallel branches share the current.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Study Notes
content:
Data Types and File Organisation

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 13 (Data representation), examined in Paper 3.

User-Defined Types

A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Records

A record groups related fields of different types under one identifier, for example a Student record with name : STRING and mark : INTEGER. Arrays of records are the standard structure for storing a table of items in memory.

File Organisation

  • Serial: records in insertion order; searching checks every record. Simple but slow.
  • Sequential: records kept in key order; binary search possible, but insertion needs rewriting.
  • Random (direct): a hashing function converts the key into a storage address, giving near-instant access. A poor hash causes collisions — two keys hashing to the same address — resolved by chaining or overflow areas.

Hashing

A common method is division hashing: Address = Key MOD TableSize. A good hash distributes keys evenly; load factor above roughly 70 percent degrades performance.

Exam tips: state the internal integer representation of enumerated values; define a collision before describing its resolution; compare the three file organisations in terms of search and insert cost.

File organisation and access

Serial files store records in the order they are written and suit sequential processing. Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop early. Random (direct) access files calculate a record's address from its key, using a hashing function, so any record can be reached quickly.

Exam tip: state the trade-off: sequential access is simple but slow for searching; direct access is fast but needs a hashing function and can produce collisions.

Worked example: a record definition

A record groups fields of different data types under one name. A record called Book might have Title (string), Pages (integer), Price (real) and InStock (Boolean). Each field is then referred to by the record name and the field name, for example Book.Pages. Records let a program keep related data together and pass it to a procedure as one item.

Worked example: hashing with linear probing

A hash table has 5 slots numbered 0 to 4, and the hash function is h(k) = k mod 5. Insert the keys 12, 27 and 8 in that order. The key 12 gives 12 mod 5 = 2, so it is stored in slot 2. The key 27 also gives 2, which is already occupied, so the next slot 3 is used. The key 8 gives 3, which is occupied, so it moves on to slot 4. A collision happens whenever two keys hash to the same slot, and the probing method determines where the second key is placed.

Comparing file access methods

  • Serial files store records one after another in the order they arrive, so finding one record means reading from the start.
  • Sequential files store records in key order, so a search can stop once it passes the place where the record should be.
  • Random (direct) files use a hash function to calculate the address of a record directly, which gives the fastest access for a single record.

Exam point: when asked to choose a file organisation, state the access pattern the question describes, such as frequent single-record look-ups or regular batch reads in order, and justify the choice from that pattern.

title: Organic Chemistry: Arenes
content:
Quick revision: Organic Chemistry: Arenes

Chemistry — A2 Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH15 Topic 18. This topic covers the structure and stability of arenes, electrophilic substitution mechanisms, and the reactivity differences between benzene, alkenes, and phenol.

  • Structure and stability: thermochemical, X-ray diffraction and infrared data prove benzene is a planar regular hexagon with intermediate carbon-carbon bond lengths, supported by the delocalised model involving side-on overlap of p-orbitals to form pi-bonds.
  • Reactivity difference: benzene is resistant to bromination compared to alkenes due to the delocalised ring of six pi electrons having lower electron density than the localised pi-bond in alkenes, preventing electrophilic addition.
  • Reactions of benzene: combustion with oxygen in air forming a smoky flame; halogenation with bromine in the presence of a catalyst; nitration using a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids; sulfonation using fuming sulfuric acid; Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation using halogenoalkanes and acyl chlorides with aluminium chloride as a catalyst.
  • Electrophilic substitution mechanisms: halogenation, nitration, and Friedel-Crafts reactions proceed via electrophilic substitution, which includes the vital step of generating the electrophile using a catalyst.
  • Phenol reactivity: phenol reacts readily with bromine water at room temperature without a catalyst, producing 2,4,6-tribromophenol, due to the overlapping of a lone pair of electrons from the oxygen atom into the pi system, increasing electron density on the ring.

Worked example

Describe the generation of the electrophile and the mechanism for the nitration of benzene. Step 1: React concentrated nitric acid with concentrated sulfuric acid to generate the nitronium ion electrophile: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2(+) + 2HSO4(−) + H3O(+). Step 2: The pi electrons of benzene attack the electrophile to form an unstable intermediate. Step 3: A hydrogen ion is lost to restore the stable delocalised ring, yielding nitrobenzene and regenerating the sulfuric acid catalyst.

Key points to remember

Students often forget that benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition because addition destroys the stable delocalised pi system, whereas substitution preserves it.

Always state the catalyst explicitly in Friedel-Crafts and halogenation reactions, noting that aluminium chloride acts as a Lewis acid catalyst to generate strong electrophiles.

Remember that phenol is far more reactive than benzene towards electrophilic attack because the oxygen lone pair is partially delocalised into the pi system, activating the ring.
