How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • SI base units include the metre, kilogram, second, ampere and kelvin.
  • Prefixes: milli is 10 to the power minus 3, centi is 10 to the power minus 2, and kilo is 10 to the power 3.
  • 1 m = 100 cm, 1 litre = 1000 cm³ = 10 to the power minus 3 m³, and 1 cm³ = 10 to the power minus 6 m³.
  • Estimates of a quantity should be checked against a known order of magnitude.

Common errors

When converting area or volume, square or cube the length conversion. A cm² is 10 to the power minus 4 m², not 10 to the power minus 2 m².

title: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Numerical Measures of Central Tendency

Mathematics — A2. For data x₁, x₂, ..., xₙ the mean is x̄ = (Σx)/n. For grouped data the mean is (Σfx)/(Σf), where f is the frequency of each value.

Key areas to revise

  • The mean uses every value, so it is pulled by extreme values.
  • The median is the middle value of the ordered data. For an even number of values it is the average of the two middle values.
  • The mode is the most frequent value, and a data set can have no mode, one mode or several.
  • Effects of data changes: adding a constant c to every value adds c to the mean and the median, and multiplying every value by a multiplies the mean by a.
  • Coding: if y = ax + b, then ȳ = a x̄ + b, and the standard deviation of y is |a| times the standard deviation of x.

Core facts to recall

  • Example: the data 2, 4, 6 have mean 4. Coding with y = x − 2 gives 0, 2, 4 with mean 2, which equals 4 − 2.
  • Choose the measure that suits the data: the median when there are extreme values, and the mode for categories.
  • State the formula you use before substituting values, because method marks depend on it.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

title: Electricity & Circuits — Study Notes
content:
Electricity & Circuits

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): simple circuits, current, p.d., resistance, series/parallel, electrical safety, practical electricity.

1. Circuit symbols & current

Conventional current: + → − (electron flow opposite). I = Q/t. Ammeter in series; voltmeter in parallel.

2. Current, p.d., e.m.f.

  • Current: rate of charge flow; same everywhere in series.
  • p.d.: energy per coulomb across a component; e.m.f.: electrical energy per coulomb given by the source.

3. Resistance

  • R = V/I. Ohmic conductor: V ∝ I at constant temperature.
  • Series: R = R₁ + R₂ + …; same current; p.d. shares in proportion to R.
  • Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂; same p.d.; current splits (inverse-R share).
  • Resistance ∝ length, ∝ 1/area (wires).

4. Components

Fixed/variable resistors, LDR (light ↑ R ↓), thermistor (T ↑ R ↓), diode/LED (one-way), relay, filament lamp (R grows as T rises — V–I curve flattens).

5. Power and energy

P = VI = I²R = V²/R; E = VIt. Fuse rating just above normal current; earth wire, double insulation, circuit breakers (trip quickly, resettable).

Example: 230 V, 2 A heater: P = 460 W; correct fuse 3 A or 5 A.

6. Digital electronics basics (syllabus 4.5 context)

Analogue vs digital; logic gates drive outputs from inputs (see CS link); sensors feed comparator-style circuits.

Exam tips: series: current same; parallel: p.d. same — say which before calculating; always compute total resistance first in mixed circuits.

Ohm's law and resistors

For a conductor at constant temperature, the current is proportional to the potential difference across it, V = IR. In a series circuit, the current is the same at every point and the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances. In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each branch is the same and the current divides between the branches.

For two equal resistors in parallel, the combined resistance is half the value of one resistor. A fuse or circuit breaker protects the wiring by breaking the circuit when the current exceeds a safe value.

Exam tip: state whether the circuit is series or parallel before applying a resistance rule.

Worked example: a lamp on a 6.0 V supply

A lamp is connected across a 6.0 V supply and the current through it is 0.50 A. Its resistance is R = V ÷ I = 6.0 ÷ 0.50 = 12 Ω. The power transferred is P = VI = 6.0 × 0.50 = 3.0 W, so in 60 s the energy transferred is E = Pt = 3.0 × 60 = 180 J. Give the unit with each answer, and keep power (the rate) separate from energy (the total).

Exam method: series and parallel totals

In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere and the resistances add. In a parallel circuit the voltage across each branch is the same and the branch currents add. A quick check is that adding a resistor in parallel always lowers the total resistance, while adding one in series always raises it.

title: Mechanics (M1) — Study Notes
content:
Mechanics 1: forces and motion

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Mechanics 1 (WME01), sat at AS.

M1 models particles under constant acceleration and in equilibrium. The whole subject rests on three pillars: the SUVAT equations, Newton's laws, and the turning-effect (moments) of forces.

Kinematics (constant acceleration)

  • v = u + at
  • s = ut + (1/2)at^2
  • v^2 = u^2 + 2as
  • s = (u + v)t / 2
  • A displacement-time graph has gradient = velocity; a velocity-time graph has gradient = acceleration and area = displacement.
  • Free fall: a = g = 9.8 m/s^2 downwards; a ball thrown up decelerates at g on the way up.

Dynamics: Newton's laws

  • First law: a body stays at rest or constant velocity unless a resultant force acts.
  • Second law: F = ma, where F is the resultant force on the particle.
  • Third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction, acting on DIFFERENT bodies.
  • Weight = mg, acting vertically downwards through the centre of mass.

Connected particles

Treat the system as one body first (F = total mass x a) to find the acceleration, then isolate one particle to find the connecting force (tension in a string, thrust in a tow bar).

Forces at angles

Resolve horizontally and vertically: a force F at angle theta to the horizontal has components F cos(theta) and F sin(theta). Equilibrium means the resultant force in each direction is zero.

Friction

  • F <= mu R, with limiting friction F = mu R when the body is on the point of slipping.
  • Friction opposes motion (or the tendency to motion) and acts along the surface.
  • On a rough inclined plane: R = mg cos(theta) and the component down the plane is mg sin(theta).

Moments

  • Moment of a force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot.
  • A rigid body in equilibrium has zero resultant force AND zero total moment about any point.
  • Uniform beams have their weight acting at the mid-point.

title: Exam technique: Algebra Graphs
content:
### What earns the marks
For gradient and equation questions, calculate earns marks for a correct (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1) computation with substitution shown, then the rearrangement to y = mx + c. For perpendicular lines, state earns the negative-reciprocal gradient explicitly before substituting. For curve questions, describe earns marks for roots, intercept and turning point each stated, and the axis of symmetry as an equation (x = 2, not just 2).
### Traps
Error: answering the midpoint when length is asked. Correction: re-read the final demand before computing. Error: giving the minimum value instead of its x-coordinate. Correction: label every coordinate pair fully. Error: keeping gradient 2 for a perpendicular to y = 2x + 1. Correction: flip and negate first, then substitute.
### Worked example
Find the equation of the line through (0, 2) and (4, 10). The gradient is m = (10 − 2)/(4 − 0) = 2. Because the line crosses the y-axis at 2, the equation is y = 2x + 2. Check by substituting x = 4 to get 10, which is correct.

title: Hardware & Architecture — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Hardware & Architecture

Computer Science — OL. von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

  • 1. Von Neumann model
  • 2. Registers
  • 3. FDE cycle
  • 4. Buses and performance
  • 5. RAM vs ROM
  • 6. Secondary storage

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

The Von Neumann architecture stores both program instructions and data in main memory. The processor has a control unit, an arithmetic and logic unit and registers. The fetch-decode-execute cycle loads an instruction from memory, decodes it and carries it out, then repeats.

RAM is volatile memory that holds programs and data while they are in use, and ROM is non-volatile memory that holds the start-up instructions. Cache is a small, fast memory between the processor and RAM that keeps frequently used data close to the processor. Explain the purpose of each component in terms of what it does, not only what it is called.

title: Quadratics — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Quadratics

Mathematics — AS (9709). A quadratic has the form ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Master three tools: completing the square, the discriminant, and inequalities.

Key areas to revise

  • Completing the Square
  • The Discriminant
  • Quadratic Inequalities
  • Curve and Line Intersections

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

For ax² + bx + c = 0, the roots come from the quadratic formula. The discriminant b² − 4ac decides the type of roots: positive gives two distinct real roots, zero gives one repeated root, and negative gives no real roots. Completing the square writes the expression as a(x + p)² + q, which gives the turning point at (−p, q).

To solve a quadratic inequality, sketch the graph, find where it crosses the x-axis, and read off the range where the curve lies above or below the axis. Use the discriminant to show that a quadratic is always positive or always negative. Show each step, because method marks are given for a correct rearrangement even when the final answer is wrong.

title: Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table Quick Revision
content:
Atomic Structure and the Periodic Table Quick Revision

This Edexcel International AS Level Chemistry revision guide covers atomic structure, mass spectrometry, ionisation energies, electronic configurations, and periodic trends for topic 2.

  • Atoms consist of a central nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in quantum shells and sub-shells.
  • Mass spectrometry determines relative isotopic, atomic, and molecular masses, identifying isotopic compositions and 2+ charged ions.
  • Ionisation energies are endothermic enthalpy changes influenced by nuclear charge, shielding, and sub-shell distance, providing evidence for quantum shells.
  • Electronic configurations follow the Aufbau principle, Hund's rule, and Pauli exclusion principle using s, p, and d notation across blocks.
  • Periodic properties, including melting temperatures and successive ionisation energies, demonstrate periodic trends across periods and down groups.

Worked example

Calculate the relative atomic mass of boron given two isotopes: Boron-10 with a relative abundance of 19.9 percent and Boron-11 with 80.1 percent. Step 1: Multiply each mass number by its percentage abundance. Step 2: Sum these values together. Step 3: Divide the total by 100. Calculation: ((10 × 19.9) + (11 × 80.1)) ÷ 100 = (199 + 881.1) ÷ 100 = 1080.1 ÷ 100 = 10.8 to one decimal place.

Key points to remember

Protons have a relative mass of 1 and a charge of +1, neutrons have a relative mass of 1 and a charge of 0, and electrons have a relative mass of 1/1836 and a charge of −1. The atomic number, Z, equals the number of protons, while the mass number, A, is the total of protons and neutrons. Ions have different electron numbers; positive ions have fewer electrons than protons, and negative ions have more. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

In a mass spectrometer, vaporization and ionisation produce positive ions which are then accelerated by an electric field, deflected by a magnetic field according to their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z), and detected. Ions can sometimes lose two electrons, forming 2+ ions which appear at half their actual mass-to-charge value on the spectrum. For diatomic molecules like chlorine, probability calculations for isotopic peaks must account for combinations of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 with a 3:1 ratio, resulting in relative peak heights of 9:6:1 for molecular ion peaks at m/z values of 70, 72, and 74.

First ionisation energy is the energy required to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions, and all ionisation energies are endothermic because energy must be supplied to overcome the electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron. Successive ionisation energies increase because removing an electron from an increasingly positive ion requires more energy, and large jumps in successive ionisation energies indicate the breakdown of a quantum shell, revealing the group number of the element.

Orbitals are regions within an atom that can hold up to two electrons with opposite spins. S orbitals are spherical, and p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped along x, y, and z axes. Sub-shell orbitals each take a single electron before pairing up with parallel spins. Elements from hydrogen to krypton fill 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, and 4p orbitals, noting that 4s fills before 3d and empties before 3d during ionisation. Periodic properties such as melting temperatures and ionisation energies show repeating patterns across periods 2 and 3 due to changes in bonding, structure, nuclear charge, and shielding.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Exam technique: Ethics, Security & Impact
content:
### What earns the marks
For definitions, each term stated precisely earns its mark (hacking is unauthorised access, not every attack). For discuss questions, one benefit plus one drawback plus a reasoned conclusion earns full marks. For security, the named threat matched to its countermeasure earns each mark.
### Traps
Error: one-sided discuss answers. Correction: both sides plus a verdict. Error: virus named for every malware. Correction: worms, spyware and trojans differ. Error: copyright confused with plagiarism. Correction: copyright is the legal right.### Worked example
For a question on the impact of social media, give a benefit such as fast sharing of information, a drawback such as the spread of misinformation or loss of privacy, and a conclusion that weighs them, for example that users need regulation as well as education. A one-sided answer loses the discussion marks even when every point is accurate, which is one of the most common losses on these papers.
### Recall check
Define hacking precisely, then explain why copying software without permission breaks copyright law, and why that is different from plagiarism. Name two forms of malware and give one difference between them.

title: Exam technique: Electricity and Circuits
content:
### What earns the marks
For series and parallel, current-same versus voltage-same stated earns the first mark. For power and resistance, P = VI and R = V/I quoted with substitution earn each mark. For fuses, the next rating above normal current chosen earns the mark.
### Traps
Error: voltage claimed same in series. Correction: current is the shared quantity. Error: exact-current fuse chosen. Correction: next standard rating above. Error: lamps in parallel assumed dimmer. Correction: each sees full voltage.
### Method marks
In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere and the potential differences add to the supply voltage. In parallel branches the voltage across each branch is the same and the branch currents add at the junction. Write the rule before the numbers so the method mark is visible even if the arithmetic slips.
### Explain, do not just name
A larger resistance in a series chain takes a larger share of the supply voltage. Say the current is the same through each component and the voltage is shared in proportion to resistance.
### Circuit diagrams
Draw an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel. A reversed ammeter, or a voltmeter placed in series, is one of the most common lost marks in practical questions.

title: Energy, Work & Power — Study Notes
content:
Energy, Work & Power

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): stores and transfers, KE/PE, work, energy sources, power, efficiency.

1. Energy stores & transfers

Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear, thermal. Transfer mechanisms: mechanically, electrically, heating, waves. Energy is conserved overall; transfers via work done.

2. Formulas

  • KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh.
  • Work W = Fd (force along displacement, joules).
  • Power P = W/t = E/t; P = Fv for constant speed.

Example: 0.5 kg at 4 m/s: KE = 4 J. Lift 2 kg by 3 m: PE = 60 J (g = 10).

3. Energy sources

Renewable: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biofuel, tidal — replenished. Non-renewable: fossil fuels, nuclear — finite. Discuss reliability, cost, pollution for "evaluate" questions.

4. Efficiency

Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input (×100%). Sankey diagrams show losses.

Example: motor: 150 J useful from 600 J → 25%.

5. Energy-chain problems

Equating KE loss to PE gain: v = √(2gh) for frictionless drop; braking distance grows with v².

Exam tips: define work as "force × distance moved in the direction of the force"; use g = 10 unless told otherwise; efficiency is a ratio — no units.

Work, power and energy transfer

Work is done when a force moves an object through a distance in the direction of the force, W = Fd, measured in joules. Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t, measured in watts. Energy is conserved: it is transferred from one store to another, and the total stays the same. The efficiency of a device is the useful energy output as a percentage of the total energy input, and it is always less than 100 percent.

Kinetic energy is ½mv², and gravitational potential energy is mgh, which is the energy a mass gains when it is raised through height h near the Earth's surface.

Exam tip: show the energy store changes in order, for example chemical to kinetic to thermal, when a question asks you to describe energy transfer.

Worked example: lifting a load

A 2.0 kg mass is lifted through 5.0 m at constant speed. The work done against gravity is W = mgh = 2.0 × 9.8 × 5.0 = 98 J. If the lift takes 4.0 s, the power is P = W/t = 98/4.0 = 24.5 W. Check the units at each step: joules divided by seconds give watts.

Kinetic and gravitational potential energy

  • Kinetic energy: E_k = ½mv². A 1000 kg car at 20 m s⁻¹ has 2.0 × 10⁵ J of kinetic energy.
  • Gravitational potential energy: E_p = mgh, measured from a chosen reference level.
  • Doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy, because the speed is squared.

Efficiency in practice

An electric motor takes 200 J of electrical energy and delivers 150 J of useful kinetic energy and 50 J of thermal energy. The efficiency is 150/200 × 100% = 75%. The energy that is not useful is usually dissipated as thermal energy in the surroundings, and it is never destroyed.

Exam point: in a question about the energy transfers, name each store involved, such as chemical, kinetic, gravitational potential, or thermal, rather than writing only "energy".

title: Exam technique: Algebra Inequalities
content:
### What earns the marks
For solving, calculate earns marks for each correct rearrangement step with the inequality sign carried through, and the final solution as an inequality or integer list as demanded. For integer-solution questions, list earns marks only for the complete correct set: show the solved inequality first, then enumerate. For combined inequalities, handle each side separately and intersect at the end.
### Traps
Error: forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative. Correction: circle every division by a negative and flip immediately. Error: answering x < 9 with 9 for the largest integer. Correction: step down one for strict inequalities. Error: including -1 in -1 < n <= 3. Correction: strict ends exclude, slack ends include.
### Worked example
Solve −2x > 6. Divide both sides by −2 and reverse the sign, giving x < −3. For a quadratic x² − 4 < 0, factorise to (x − 2)(x + 2) < 0. The product is negative between the roots, so −2 < x < 2.
### Reverse the sign with care
Dividing or multiplying both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality sign. Write the step that flips the sign so the examiner can see you did it on purpose.
### Show the solution set
When asked to show an inequality on a number line, use an open circle for less than or greater than and a filled circle for less than or equal to or greater than or equal to. Shade the side that satisfies the inequality.
### Test a value
Choose a value inside your answer range and substitute it into the original inequality. If it does not satisfy the inequality, the direction of your working is wrong.
### Integer solutions
When asked for the integers that satisfy a double inequality, list each whole number inside the range and no others. Include the end values only when the inequality allows equality there.

title: Exam technique: Arithmetic and Place Value
content:
### What earns the marks
For HCF and LCM, the prime factorisation of each number earns the method mark; state highest powers for LCM and lowest for HCF. For bounds, half-the-precision stated (0.05 for 1 d.p.) earns the method mark before the bound. For estimation, the rounded line (50 x 20 / 10) must be shown: a bare calculator value scores nothing. For time and money, each conversion step shown earns its mark.
### Traps
Error: 16:80 as a time. Correction: 60 minutes carry. Error: largest rounded value confused with the upper bound (6.34 vs 6.35). Correction: the bound is the first value that rounds away. Error: HCF powers used for LCM. Correction: LCM takes the highest of each prime.
### Worked example
In 4 706 325 the digit 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 700 000. For order of operations, 3 + 4 × (10 − 6)² is worked out as 3 + 4 × 4² = 3 + 4 × 16 = 3 + 64 = 67. Brackets and powers come before multiplication, and addition comes last.
### Worked example
In 4 706 325 the digit 7 is in the hundred-thousands place, so its value is 700 000. For order of operations, 3 + 4 × (10 − 6)² is worked out as 3 + 4 × 4² = 3 + 4 × 16 = 3 + 64 = 67. Brackets and powers come before multiplication, and addition comes last.

title: Complex Numbers — Study Notes
content:
Complex Numbers

Board note: complex numbers are not examined in the Edexcel International A Level main specification — they sit in Further Mathematics (FP1, WFM01). Cambridge examines them at A2 (9709); this note serves both boards.

Basics

i² = −1. A complex number z = a + bi has real part a and imaginary part b. Two numbers are equal iff both parts match.

Arithmetic: add/subtract parts; multiply with brackets and replace i² with −1.

Example: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) = 2 − 2i + 3i − 3i² = 5 + i.

Conjugates

z̄ = a − bi. zz̄ = a² + b² (real). Dividing: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

Example: 1/(3 − i) × (3 + i)/(3 + i) = (3 + i)/10.

Argand Diagram

Plot z as the point (a, b). |z| = √(a² + b²) is the modulus (distance from origin); arg z = tan⁻¹(b/a) is the argument (angle). Multiply two numbers: moduli multiply, arguments add.

Modulus–Argument Form

z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), r = |z|, θ = arg z. Useful for powers and roots.

de Moivre and Roots

[r(cos θ + i sin θ)]ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

Example: (1 + i)⁸: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so z⁸ = (√2)⁸ cis 2π = 16.

An nth root gives n evenly spaced solutions, 2π/n apart on a circle of radius r^(1/n).

Exam tips: always give arguments in the required interval; when solving equations, remember complex roots come in conjugate pairs for real polynomials.

Exam method: arithmetic and modulus

Treat i as a symbol with i² = −1 and collect real and imaginary parts separately. When multiplying complex numbers expand like brackets, then replace i² by −1. To divide, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which turns the denominator into a real number.

For z = a + bi the modulus is |z| = √(a² + b²) and the argument is the angle θ in the Argand diagram with tan θ = b/a, placed in the correct quadrant. The conjugate z* = a − bi reverses the sign of the imaginary part, and z z* = a² + b², which is always real.

Equal complex numbers have equal real parts and equal imaginary parts. Use this to solve for unknown real values, comparing coefficients on both sides of an equation.

Exam cue: State the final answer in the form a + bi, and check the sign of the imaginary part after every multiplication.

Worked example: square root of a complex number

Find z such that z² = −9 + 40i. Let z = a + bi. Then a² − b² = −9 and 2ab = 40, so ab = 20. Trying a = 4 and b = 5 gives 16 − 25 = −9, which works. So z = 4 + 5i or z = −(4 + 5i). Check by squaring: (4 + 5i)² = 16 + 40i − 25 = −9 + 40i.

Quadratic equations with complex roots

For x² + 2x + 5 = 0, the discriminant is 4 − 20 = −16, which is negative, so the roots are not real. Use √(−16) = 4i to get x = (−2 ± 4i)/2 = −1 ± 2i. The two roots form a conjugate pair, as they always do when the coefficients are real.

Loci in the Argand diagram

  • |z − 2| = 3 is the circle with centre 2 and radius 3, since it gives the distance of z from the point 2.
  • arg(z) = π/4 is a half-line from the origin at 45° above the positive real axis.
  • |z − 1| = |z + i| is the perpendicular bisector of the points 1 and −i.

Exam point: when a locus question gives an inequality, shade the correct region on the diagram and label the boundary as a solid or dashed line depending on whether it is included.

title: AS Level Chemistry: Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Introduction to Kinetics and Equilibria

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 9 joins two questions that are often confused: how fast a reaction goes, and how far it goes. Kinetics is explained by collision theory and the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies; equilibrium is described by Le Chatelier's principle and the compromise between yield and rate that industry must make. The topic rewards precise language: "faster" describes rate, "more product at equilibrium" describes position, and the two are not the same thing.

Collision theory

For a reaction to happen, particles must collide with enough energy to break the bonds that need breaking. That minimum energy is the activation energy, Ea. Most collisions do not have it, so most collisions do not lead to reaction. The rate depends on two things: how often effective collisions occur, and what fraction of collisions is effective.

  • Concentration: a higher concentration means more particles per unit volume, so more frequent collisions and a faster rate.
  • Pressure (gases): compressing a gas has the same effect as raising its concentration; the particles are closer together and collide more often.
  • Surface area: a powder exposes more surface than a single lump of the same mass, so more particles are available to collide and the rate increases. This is why powdered calcium carbonate reacts faster than marble chips.
  • Temperature: raising the temperature makes particles move faster, so collisions are more frequent, but the dominant effect is that a much larger fraction of collisions has energy greater than Ea. A rule of thumb is that a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate of a reaction near room temperature.
  • Catalyst: provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy, so a larger fraction of collisions is effective.

Measuring rate

Rate is the change in amount of a reactant or product per unit time. Two simple measurements are examined:

  • Rate = 1 / time: useful when a reaction is followed to a visible endpoint, such as the disappearance of a cross seen through cloudy sulfur, or a colour change. The units are s⁻¹.
  • Gradient of a graph: plot concentration, volume of gas or mass against time, and draw a tangent to the curve. The gradient at t = 0 is the initial rate; the gradient at any later time gives the rate at that moment. A steeper gradient means a faster reaction.

Because the rate falls as reactants are used up, the curve flattens; that is why the initial rate is usually the cleanest measurement, and why comparing experiments by initial rate removes the complication of changing concentration during the measurement.

Worked example. Magnesium ribbon is added to excess hydrochloric acid and the volume of hydrogen is recorded every 10 s. The volume rises quickly at first and then more slowly as the acid is used up. The initial rate is found by drawing a tangent at t = 0 to the volume–time curve and dividing the gradient by the molar volume; the units are cm³ s⁻¹ or, after conversion, mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution

The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution plots the number of molecules with each energy at a fixed temperature. Its shape matters as much as its position:

  • The curve starts at the origin, because no molecule has zero energy.
  • It rises to a peak at the most probable energy and then tails off to the right, because a small number of molecules have very high energies.
  • The area under the curve represents the total number of molecules, so the area is the same at every temperature.
  • A vertical line at Ea separates the molecules that can react from those that cannot; the area to the right of Ea is the fraction with sufficient energy.

Raising the temperature has three effects on the curve: the peak moves to the right, the peak becomes lower, and the curve spreads out. The area beyond Ea increases markedly, which is the main reason a small temperature rise produces a large rate increase. Increasing the concentration does not change the shape of the distribution at all; it moves a larger number of molecules into the same distribution, so the area under the curve increases while the fraction with E ≥ Ea stays the same.

Adding a catalyst moves Ea to the left. The curve does not move, but a much larger area now lies beyond the new, lower activation energy, so many more collisions are effective.

Catalysts and reaction profiles

A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by providing an alternative reaction route of lower activation energy; it is not used up, and it does not change the position of equilibrium or the enthalpy change of the reaction. It may be homogeneous (same phase as the reactants) or heterogeneous (different phase, often a solid surface).

A reaction profile plots enthalpy against reaction progress. For an uncatalysed reaction, the curve rises from the reactants to a single maximum and falls to the products. For a catalysed reaction, the curve rises to a lower maximum, and a shallow well appears in the middle representing the intermediate formed between the catalyst and the reactants. The enthalpy of the reactants and products is unchanged, so the catalysed and uncatalysed profiles start and finish at the same levels; only the height of the barrier differs.

Catalysts matter industrially for sustainability as well as speed. A lower activation energy means the process can run at a lower temperature, which saves energy and reduces carbon dioxide emissions; a catalyst can also allow a route with higher atom economy or fewer waste products, and it can make a reaction selective enough that less starting material is wasted.

Dynamic equilibrium

Many reactions are reversible. In a closed system, the forward and reverse reactions eventually occur at equal rates, and the concentrations of reactants and products stop changing. This is dynamic equilibrium, and "dynamic" is the key word: both reactions are still happening, at the same rate, so there is no net change in amounts.

  • The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction.
  • The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant, not necessarily equal.
  • Equilibrium is only reached in a closed system, because otherwise a product can escape and the reverse reaction cannot keep up.
  • A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium; it only shortens the time taken to reach it, because it speeds up both directions equally.

Le Chatelier's principle

Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose that change. The changes examined are temperature, pressure and concentration.

ChangeShiftReason
Increase temperatureIn the endothermic directionThe system absorbs the extra heat, so the yield of the endothermic side rises
Decrease temperatureIn the exothermic directionThe system releases heat to oppose the cooling
Increase pressureTowards the side with fewer moles of gasThe system reduces the pressure by occupying less volume
Decrease pressureTowards the side with more moles of gasThe system increases the pressure
Increase concentration of a reactantTowards the productsThe extra reactant is used up
Remove a productTowards the productsThe system replaces what was removed

Pressure has no effect when the number of moles of gas is the same on both sides, as in H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), because there is no side with fewer gas moles to favour.

Worked example. For the Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH is negative. Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right, because four moles of gas become two, and the yield of ammonia rises. Increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left, because the forward reaction is exothermic, so the yield falls even though the rate rises. Removing ammonia as it forms shifts the equilibrium to the right and increases the yield further.

Compromise between yield and rate

Industrial conditions are not chosen to maximise yield alone. A low temperature gives a high equilibrium yield for an exothermic reaction but an impractically slow rate; a very high pressure gives a high yield but requires expensive, energy-hungry compression equipment and thick-walled vessels. The chosen conditions are a compromise, and the examiner expects both halves of that argument.

ProcessEquationConditionsReasoning
Haber processN₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH negativeAbout 450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalystA moderate temperature balances yield against rate; high pressure favours the two-mole product side; the catalyst allows a workable rate at that temperature
Contact process2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH negativeAbout 450 °C, 1–2 atm, vanadium(V) oxide catalystHigh pressure would improve yield but is not economic because the uncatalysed conversion is already high; a lower temperature would give more SO₃ but too slowly
EsterificationAcid + alcohol ⇌ ester + waterReflux with acid catalyst, removing waterThe reaction is reversible and has no favourable pressure change, so removing a product shifts the equilibrium to the right

Data questions ask you to evaluate these choices: calculate the yield at two temperatures from a graph, or explain why a plant uses a pressure lower than the theoretical optimum. The answer is always the same shape: yield, rate, energy cost, equipment cost and safety.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying a catalyst increases the yield at equilibrium, when it only shortens the time taken to reach equilibrium.
  • Claiming that increasing concentration or pressure changes the shape of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution; only temperature does.
  • Forgetting that the area under the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve is constant, so raising the temperature lowers the peak.
  • Writing that the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal in value but not saying they are equal and opposite, or that concentrations are constant rather than equal.
  • Applying pressure changes to reactions with equal moles of gas on both sides.
  • Using "more collisions" as the whole explanation for a temperature increase, when the fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea is the dominant effect.
  • Describing equilibrium as static, or saying the reaction has stopped.

Exam-style questions

  1. Explain, using collision theory, why increasing the surface area of a solid reactant increases the rate of reaction. Answer: a larger surface area exposes more particles to collision with the other reactant, so collisions occur more frequently and the rate increases.
  2. Sketch the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution at two temperatures and use it to explain why a small increase in temperature causes a large increase in rate. Answer: at the higher temperature the curve is flatter and shifted to the right, so a much larger area lies beyond Ea; the fraction of molecules with energy at least Ea is therefore much greater, and far more collisions are effective.
  3. For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH negative, state and explain the effect on the equilibrium yield of SO₃ of (a) increasing the pressure, (b) increasing the temperature. Answer: (a) the equilibrium shifts to the right, towards the side with fewer moles of gas (three moles to two), so the yield rises; (b) the equilibrium shifts to the left, in the endothermic direction, so the yield falls.
  4. Explain why the Haber process is not operated at the temperature that would give the highest equilibrium yield. Answer: the forward reaction is exothermic, so a low temperature gives a high yield, but at low temperature the rate is impractically slow even with a catalyst. About 450 °C is a compromise that gives an acceptable yield at a workable rate.
  5. A reaction profile shows the products at a higher enthalpy than the reactants. State whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic, and describe how the profile changes when a catalyst is added. Answer: the reaction is endothermic because the products have more enthalpy. With a catalyst, the maximum is lower and an intermediate well appears, but the reactant and product levels are unchanged.

Revise by separating the two ideas in your notes: kinetics explains rate through collisions and activation energy, equilibrium explains position through opposing changes. Then move to Organic Chemistry, where the same ideas of bond strength and energy reappear in reaction mechanisms.

title: Respiration
content:
Respiration

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 12 (statements 12.1–12.3). Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans and yeast, the equations, lactic acid and oxygen debt, and fermentation.

12.1 to 12.3 Respiration

  • Respiration is the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrients and release energy. The energy powers muscle contraction, active transport, protein synthesis and keeping warm.
  • Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, releasing a large amount of energy. It happens in the mitochondria of all living cells.
  • Anaerobic respiration in humans: glucose → lactic acid, releasing a small amount of energy. The lactic acid causes muscle fatigue and an oxygen debt, which is repaid by faster, deeper breathing after exercise until the lactic acid is oxidised or converted back to glucose in the liver.
  • Fermentation in yeast: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide, used in bread making and brewing.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Equation balance, applied to the aerobic symbol equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O. Check carbon, hydrogen and oxygen counts on both sides before writing the final answer; the oxygen count is the one students most often leave unbalanced.
  • Comparison reasoning, applied to why anaerobic respiration yields far less energy: only glycolysis runs, so most of the energy locked in glucose stays in the lactic acid or ethanol molecules. State that the glucose is not fully broken down to carbon dioxide and water — that incomplete breakdown is the reason.
  • Oxygen debt explanation, applied to a sprinter recovering after a race: the lactic acid must be removed, and the extra oxygen taken in during recovery is used to oxidise it fully in the mitochondria. Answer in two parts — what the debt is, and what the extra oxygen does.
  • Gas ratio reasoning, applied to comparing organisms: aerobic respiration consumes oxygen and releases an equal volume of carbon dioxide from glucose; anaerobic respiration in humans releases no carbon dioxide, while yeast fermentation releases carbon dioxide with no oxygen used. Use those differences to design a gas-syringe experiment that identifies the pathway.

Common errors

  • Calling respiration "breathing". Respiration is cellular chemistry; breathing is ventilation.
  • Saying anaerobic respiration happens "when oxygen runs out completely". It happens whenever supply cannot meet demand in the tissue.
  • Confusing lactic acid (human) and ethanol (yeast) products.

title: Excretion in Humans
content:
Excretion in Humans

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 13 (statement 13.1). What excretion is, the excretory products and organs, and how urea is formed and removed.

13.1 Excretion in humans

  • Excretion is the removal of the waste products of metabolism, toxic substances and excess substances. This is different from egestion, which is the removal of undigested food as faeces.
  • Carbon dioxide from respiration is excreted by the lungs; urea from the breakdown of excess amino acids is excreted by the kidneys in urine; water and some salts leave in sweat and urine; heat is lost through the skin.
  • The liver deaminates excess amino acids, removing the amino group to form ammonia, which is converted into the less toxic urea. Urea travels in the blood to the kidneys.
  • The kidney filters blood, and the useful glucose, water and ions are reabsorbed; urea, excess water and salts form urine, which passes down the ureters to the bladder.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Reasoning chain, applied to why the liver is the site of deamination: amino acids come from excess dietary protein or from the breakdown of body proteins, and removing the amino group produces ammonia, which is toxic. The liver converts it to urea, which is far less toxic and can be carried safely in the blood. Name ammonia, its toxicity, and the conversion — each is a separate mark.
  • Organ identification, applied to which organs excrete which waste: lungs (carbon dioxide and water), kidneys (urea, excess water and salts), skin (water, salts and small urea). A complete answer names the product with each organ, not the organ alone.
  • Distinction reasoning, applied to a colostomy patient whose faeces contain no urea: faeces are egested, not excreted — the undigested material never entered the body's cells, so it carries no metabolic waste. State the excretion-versus-egestion distinction explicitly.

Common errors

  • Calling faeces an excretory product. Egestion is not excretion.
  • Saying the kidneys remove carbon dioxide. That is the lungs' job.
  • Forgetting that urea comes from amino acids, not from fats or carbohydrates.

title: Database Systems — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Database Systems

Computer Science — OL. limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

  • 1. File-based problems
  • 2. Relational concepts
  • 3. SQL
  • 4. DBMS features

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

### Worked example A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. A foreign key stores a primary key from another table, which links the two. For Students (StudentID, Name) and Enrolments (EnrolmentID, StudentID, CourseID), StudentID is the foreign key in Enrolments. A query such as SELECT Name FROM Students WHERE Year = 11; returns only the matching rows.

Key points to remember

A database stores data in tables made of rows (records) and columns (fields). Each table has a primary key that uniquely identifies each record, and a foreign key links a record to a related table. Normalisation removes repeated data so that each fact is stored once, which reduces errors when data changes.

In SQL, SELECT chooses the fields, FROM names the table and WHERE sets the condition. Use the exact keywords the syllabus names, and write the condition with a comparison operator such as = or >. A query question is usually answered by writing one clear SELECT statement with the correct table and condition.

title: Transport in Plants
content:
Transport in Plants

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 8 (statements 8.1–8.4). Xylem and phloem, water uptake, transpiration and its factors, and translocation between sources and sinks.

8.1 to 8.2 Xylem, phloem and water uptake

  • Xylem vessels carry water and mineral ions upwards from roots to leaves; they are dead, lignified tubes with no end walls, giving a continuous column. Phloem carries sucrose and amino acids both up and down, from source to sink; sieve tube elements are living cells.
  • Water enters root hair cells by osmosis because the cell sap is more concentrated, then moves cell to cell by osmosis until it reaches the xylem.

8.3 Transpiration

  • Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves through the stomata. It creates a transpiration stream: evaporation from mesophyll cell walls lowers water potential, water moves by osmosis from the xylem, and the whole column is pulled up under tension.
  • Rate increases with higher temperature, lower humidity, more wind and brighter light (stomata open wider). It decreases when stomata close, for example in the dark or when the plant is wilting.

8.4 Translocation

  • Translocation is the movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from sources (leaves, storage organs) to sinks (roots, fruits, growing tips). It requires energy from respiration and is not the same process as the transpiration stream.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Factor analysis, applied to a potometer experiment: the main variables are light, temperature and wind. Explain each: light opens stomata, temperature increases evaporation, wind removes humid air from around the leaf. In an investigation, name which you would control and how.
  • Structure reasoning, applied to why xylem vessels are lignified and dead: lignin strengthens them against collapse under the tension of the transpiration stream, and being dead removes barriers to continuous flow. That two-part answer is worth two marks.
  • Source and sink reasoning, applied to a potato tuber in summer: the leaf is the source and the tuber is the sink; in spring, the tuber becomes the source as stored starch is converted to sucrose and moves out. Sources and sinks change with the season — state the direction in each case.

Common errors

  • Saying transpiration is "the plant sweating". It is evaporation of water vapour, and it is a consequence of gas exchange, not a separate function.
  • Claiming water moves up xylem by root pressure alone. The transpiration pull under tension is the main mechanism at IGCSE level.
  • Confusing translocation (phloem, sugars, both directions) with the transpiration stream (xylem, water, upwards).

title: Forces and Equilibrium — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Forces and Equilibrium

Physics — AS. Draw every force on one body: weight (down), normal reactions (perpendicular to surfaces), tension (along strings), friction (opposing motion).

Key areas to revise

  • Free-Body Diagrams
  • Resolving Forces
  • Equilibrium
  • Moments and the Principle of Moments
  • Centre of Gravity

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Moment of a force = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.
  • Principle of moments: for an object in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments.
  • For translational equilibrium, the resultant force in each direction is zero.
  • A couple is two equal and opposite forces that produce a turning effect with no net force; its moment is F × d.

Common errors

The distance used in a moment must be the perpendicular distance from the line of action to the pivot. Using the length of a lever arm at an angle gives a wrong answer.

title: Probability — Study Notes
content:
Probability

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 1 (WST01), sat at AS.

Basic Rules

For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

  • P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

Venn Diagrams

Draw the universe first, then the events. Fill from the intersection outwards: if P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.25, then only-A = 0.35, only-B = 0.25, neither = 0.15. Every region must sum to 1.

Tree Diagrams

Branch probabilities multiply along a path; outcomes at the end of complete paths add. Draw one branch set per stage of the experiment. For two draws without replacement from a bag of 5 red and 3 blue: P(RR) = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56.

Conditional Probability

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) — the probability of A given that B has occurred. The condition shrinks the sample space.

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. Then P(A | B) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5, so A and B are independent since P(A | B) = P(A).

Independence

A and B are independent exactly when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B). Do not confuse independent (no influence on probabilities) with mutually exclusive (cannot co-occur). Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

Exam tips: convert every "given that" into a conditional. With trees, label the second-stage branches with conditional probabilities; they are usually different from the first stage when drawing without replacement.

Exam method: combined events

The addition rule gives P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). For mutually exclusive events the intersection is empty, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). Draw a Venn diagram to place each probability in its region before calculating.

Independent events satisfy P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Test independence by checking this equation rather than assuming it, because the question may give the joint probability and ask you to decide.

The conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A).

Tree diagrams suit sequential events without replacement. Multiply along each branch and add the branches that give the outcome required.

Exam cue: State whether events are independent or mutually exclusive, because the two are different and the formula depends on it.

Worked example: two aces without replacement

Two cards are taken from a standard pack of 52 without replacement. The probability that both are aces is (4/52) × (3/51) = 12/2652 = 1/221. Because the second draw depends on the first, multiply along the branches of the tree diagram and use the reduced totals (51 cards, 3 aces) on the second branch. If the first card were replaced, the answer would be (4/52)² = 1/169 instead.

Exam method: checking a tree diagram

The probabilities on the branches leaving any node must add to 1, so check each node before you multiply. The final probabilities at the ends of the branches must also sum to 1. For a question asking for "at least one", it is usually quicker to find the probability of none and subtract it from 1.

title: Nuclear Physics — Study Notes
content:
Nuclear Physics

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): nuclear model, radioactivity, decay types, half-life, safety, fission/fusion (Extended).

1. The nuclear model

Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with orbiting electrons (−). Nuclide notation ᴬ_Z X. Isotopes: same Z, different A. Rutherford scattering established the nuclear model; proton number Z, nucleon number A.

2. Radiation types

TypeNatureRange (air)Stopped by
alpha αhelium nucleus (2p2n)few cmpaper
beta β⁻fast electron~20–30 cmfew mm aluminium
gamma γEM wavevery farthick lead/concrete

Deflection in fields: α/β opposite, γ none. Ionising: α > β > γ. Background radiation: radon, cosmic, rocks, medical, fallout.

3. Decay equations

  • α: A −4, Z −2 (e.g. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + α).
  • β⁻: neutron → proton; A same, Z +1 (e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + β⁻).
  • γ: no change to A or Z.

Balance A and Z on both sides — that is the check.

4. Half-life

Time for half the unstable nuclei to decay (random process). Read from a decay curve or count halves: 80 → 40 → 20 over two half-lives.

Example: 800 Bq, half-life 2 h → 200 Bq after 4 h.

5. Safety and uses

Uses: medical tracers (β/γ), sterilisation, thickness gauge (β), dating (C-14), smoke alarms (α). Safety: distance, time, shielding, wear badges, store in lead. Handle with tongs; never point at people.

6. Fission and fusion (Extended)

Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron), chain reaction controlled by moderators/control rods — power stations. Fusion: light nuclei join (stellar) — needs huge T/P; releases more energy per kg; no long-lived waste.

Nuclear decay and half-life

Alpha particles are helium nuclei with two protons and two neutrons, and they are strongly ionising but have low penetration. Beta-minus emission happens when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted. Gamma radiation is electromagnetic, carries no charge and no mass, and has high penetration. Background radiation must be subtracted from measured count rates before a half-life is calculated.

Worked example: half-life from a count rate

A radioactive sample gives a count rate of 800 counts per minute. After 30 minutes the count rate is 100 counts per minute. Each half-life halves the count rate: 800 to 400, then 200, then 100. That is three half-lives in 30 minutes, so the half-life is 30 / 3 = 10 minutes. When the ratio is a power of two you can count the halvings directly; use a logarithm or the decay equation only when it is not.

Exam method: background radiation

Background radiation comes from natural sources such as rocks and cosmic rays, and from man-made sources such as medical X-rays. A measured count must be corrected for background before you use it in a half-life calculation: subtract the background count from every reading. Forgetting this step is a common reason for a wrong answer, because background sets a floor that the sample's own count never falls below.
