title: AS Level Chemistry: Energetics
content:
AS Level Chemistry: Energetics

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 6 covers the heat energy exchanged in chemical reactions: how enthalpy change is defined and measured, how calorimetry data is turned into a value per mole, how Hess's Law lets you find an enthalpy change you cannot measure directly, and what bond enthalpies can and cannot tell you. The calculations are straightforward once the definitions are exact, because most marks are lost through signs, units and the direction of a cycle rather than through arithmetic.

Enthalpy change and standard conditions

Enthalpy change, ΔH, is the heat energy change measured at constant pressure. In an open beaker the pressure is constant, so the heat exchanged is an enthalpy change; the units are kJ mol⁻¹.

Standard conditions are a pressure of 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K. A standard enthalpy change symbol has a plimsoll mark, as in ΔH⦵. The substance must also be in its standard state, which is its usual physical state at 100 kPa and 298 K: water is liquid, bromine is liquid, carbon is graphite.

  • Exothermic: heat is released to the surroundings, the temperature rises, and ΔH is negative by convention.
  • Endothermic: heat is absorbed from the surroundings, the temperature falls, and ΔH is positive.

An enthalpy level diagram shows the two states as horizontal lines: products below reactants for an exothermic reaction with an arrow pointing down, products above reactants for an endothermic reaction with an arrow pointing up. The vertical axis is enthalpy, and the arrow is labelled with the value of ΔH including its sign.

The sign convention is worth remembering in one sentence: breaking bonds always absorbs energy, making bonds always releases it, and whether a reaction is exothermic depends on which of those two totals is larger.

The five standard enthalpy definitions

These definitions are marked word for word, so learn each one with its standard state and its "per mole of" condition.

QuantityDefinition
Standard enthalpy change of reaction, ΔrH⦵The enthalpy change when the reaction occurs in the molar quantities shown in the chemical equation, under standard conditions.
Standard enthalpy change of formation, ΔfH⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states under standard conditions.
Standard enthalpy change of combustion, ΔcH⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions.
Standard enthalpy change of neutralisation, ΔneutH⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of water is formed by the reaction of an acid with an alkali under standard conditions.
Standard enthalpy change of atomisation, ΔatH⦵The enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state under standard conditions.

By definition, the standard enthalpy change of formation of an element in its standard state is zero, because no change occurs in forming an element from itself. Atomisation is always endothermic, because bonds or intermolecular forces must be broken: ΔatH⦵ of sodium is the energy to turn Na(s) into Na(g), and for a diatomic element such as chlorine it is half the bond enthalpy of Cl–Cl, since only one mole of chlorine atoms is formed from half a mole of Cl2 molecules.

Calorimetry: measuring an enthalpy change

Two experiments are examinable. In the first, two solutions are mixed in an insulated container, typically a plastic cup, and the maximum temperature reached is recorded. In the second, a fuel is burned in a spirit burner beneath a copper calorimeter containing water, and the temperature rise of the water is recorded along with the change in mass of the burner.

The energy transferred to the surroundings is calculated with the specific heat capacity equation:

energy transferred (J) = mass (g) × specific heat capacity (J g-1 °C-1) × temperature change (°C)

The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Then the enthalpy change of the reaction is the energy transferred divided by the number of moles that reacted, converted to kJ mol⁻¹ and given the correct sign.

Worked example (mixing). 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid is mixed with 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ sodium hydroxide. The temperature rises by 6.8 °C. Assume the solution has a density of 1.00 g cm⁻³ and the same specific heat capacity as water.

q = 100 × 4.18 × 6.8 = 2842 J
n(H2O) = c × V = 1.00 × 0.0500 = 0.0500 mol
ΔH = -2842 / 0.0500 = -56 840 J mol-1 = -56.8 kJ mol-1

The temperature rose, so the reaction is exothermic and the answer must be negative. The accepted value is about −57.3 kJ mol⁻¹ for a strong acid and strong alkali, so the result is close.

Worked example (combustion). Burning 0.500 g of methanol raises the temperature of 100 g of water by 20.0 °C.

q = 100 × 4.18 × 20.0 = 8360 J
n(CH3OH) = 0.500 / 32.0 = 0.0156 mol
ΔH = -8360 / 0.0156 = -536 000 J mol-1 = -536 kJ mol-1

The data book value is −726 kJ mol⁻¹. The measured value is much less exothermic, and the evaluation should explain why: heat is lost to the surroundings and to the apparatus, the combustion is incomplete because a spirit burner burns in air and produces soot and carbon monoxide, methanol evaporates from the wick without burning, and the experiment is not carried out under standard conditions.

Assumptions and error evaluation

  • The solution is assumed to have the density of water (1.00 g cm⁻³) and the specific heat capacity of water (4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹); a solution that is not mostly water makes this less valid.
  • All the heat released is assumed to raise the temperature of the solution or water; in practice the container absorbs some heat, so a plastic cup is used to reduce conduction losses. A lid reduces losses by evaporation and convection.
  • Heat loss means the measured temperature rise is too small, so the magnitude of ΔH is underestimated.
  • Temperature is read to the nearest 0.5 °C with a simple thermometer, which is a large percentage uncertainty for a small rise. Use a larger amount of reactant or a digital thermometer to improve the precision.
  • The reaction is assumed to be complete and instantaneous, and the mass of water is assumed constant.

Hess's Law

Hess's Law states that the total enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final conditions are the same. It follows from the law of conservation of energy and allows an enthalpy change that cannot be measured directly, such as the formation of carbon monoxide or the hydration of an anhydrous salt, to be calculated from values that can be measured.

An enthalpy cycle is a diagram of alternative routes. Two forms are examined:

  • From formation data: the elements in their standard states are the bottom of the cycle. Reactants and products both form from the elements, so ΔH(reaction) = Σ ΔfH(products) − Σ ΔfH(reactants).
  • From combustion data: the combustion products, usually carbon dioxide and water, are the bottom of the cycle. Both reactants and products burn to the same products, so ΔH(reaction) = Σ ΔcH(reactants) − Σ ΔcH(products).

Notice that the two expressions are mirror images. In both, you go from the reactants down to the reference state and back up to the products, which is why the subtraction reverses. Learn the direction rather than memorising a formula you may apply backwards under pressure.

Worked example (formation). Calculate ΔH for the combustion of methane: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l), given ΔfH⦵ values of −75 kJ mol⁻¹ for methane, −394 kJ mol⁻¹ for carbon dioxide and −286 kJ mol⁻¹ for water.

ΔH = [ΔfH(CO2) + 2 × ΔfH(H2O)] - [ΔfH(CH4) + 2 × ΔfH(O2)]
ΔH = [-394 + 2(-286)] - [-75 + 0]
ΔH = -966 + 75 = -891 kJ mol-1

The answer is negative, as expected for a combustion. The accepted value is −890 kJ mol⁻¹.

Worked example (combustion data). Calculate ΔH for the reaction C2H4(g) + H2(g) → C2H6(g) given ΔcH⦵ values of −1411 kJ mol⁻¹ for ethene, −286 kJ mol⁻¹ for hydrogen and −1560 kJ mol⁻¹ for ethane.

ΔH = [ΔcH(C2H4) + ΔcH(H2)] - [ΔcH(C2H6)]
ΔH = [-1411 + (-286)] - [-1560] = -1697 + 1560 = -137 kJ mol-1

The reaction is the addition of hydrogen across a double bond, so a modest exothermic value is a sensible check.

Core Practical 2: enthalpy change using Hess's Law

The enthalpy change of hydration of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate cannot be measured directly, because the anhydrous solid reacts violently with water and the hydration step cannot be isolated. It is found from two measurable dissolution experiments and a cycle.

Route 1: CuSO4(s)  + aq  → CuSO4(aq)      ΔH1 (dissolving anhydrous)
Route 2: CuSO4(s)  → CuSO4.5H2O(s) → CuSO4(aq)   ΔH(hydration) then ΔH2 (dissolving hydrated)

Both routes start with anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and end with the same aqueous solution, so the total enthalpy changes are equal:

ΔH1 = ΔH(hydration) + ΔH2      so      ΔH(hydration) = ΔH1 - ΔH2

Each dissolution is carried out in a insulated cup with a known mass of solid added to a known volume of water, recording the temperature change and calculating the enthalpy change per mole as in the calorimetry section. Since dissolving anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is strongly exothermic and dissolving the hydrated salt is slightly endothermic, the difference is large and negative. The evaluation must mention heat loss, the assumption about the specific heat capacity of the solution, and the uncertainty in reading a small temperature change.

Bond enthalpies

Bond enthalpy is the energy required to break one mole of a specified covalent bond in the gas phase. Mean bond enthalpy is the average energy required to break one mole of a specified covalent bond, averaged over a range of different compounds. The two are not the same: the O–H bond in water, in methanol and in ethanoic acid has a slightly different enthalpy in each, so data books quote averages.

For a reaction in the gas phase:

ΔH = Σ bond enthalpies broken - Σ bond enthalpies formed

Breaking bonds is endothermic (positive), making bonds is exothermic (negative). If more energy is released in forming the products' bonds than is absorbed in breaking the reactants' bonds, the reaction is exothermic and the value is negative.

Worked example. Calculate ΔH for the hydrogenation of ethene, C2H4 + H2 → C2H6, using mean bond enthalpies in kJ mol⁻¹: C=C 612, C–C 348, C–H 413, H–H 436.

Bonds broken: 1 × C=C (612) + 4 × C-H (1652) + 1 × H-H (436) = 2700 kJ mol-1
Bonds formed: 1 × C-C (348) + 6 × C-H (2478) = 2826 kJ mol-1
ΔH = 2700 - 2826 = -126 kJ mol-1

The arithmetic is simple but the bookkeeping is not: count the C–H bonds on both sides carefully, because the product has two more than the reactants. A quick check is that the number of bonds formed should equal the number broken plus one, since the double bond becomes a single bond and an H–H bond is lost.

Limitations of bond enthalpy calculations

  • The values are averages, so a calculation using mean bond enthalpies gives an approximate answer; the true value differs because the environment of a bond changes its strength.
  • The calculation assumes all species are gaseous. If the reaction produces a liquid, the enthalpy of condensation is not included, so the result differs from the standard enthalpy change.
  • Values are quoted for the gas phase, so reactions involving solids or liquids need additional enthalpy terms to be accurate.

Reversing the equation is the other examined skill: given ΔH and every bond enthalpy except one, substitute into the bond enthalpy equation and solve for the unknown. For example, if ΔH for a reaction is known and the bonds broken total 2000 kJ mol⁻¹, then the bonds formed total 2000 − ΔH.

Bond enthalpy data also gives a qualitative indication of which bond will break first in a reaction: the bond with the lowest bond enthalpy is the easiest to break, so it breaks first and the reaction proceeds more rapidly at room temperature. This is why the C–I bond in iodoalkanes breaks more readily than the C–Cl bond in chloroalkanes, and why alkanes react only slowly with halogens in the dark: the C–H and C–C bonds are strong and need ultraviolet light or heat to start the reaction.

Typical mistakes

  • Giving an exothermic enthalpy change a positive sign, or an endothermic one a negative sign.
  • Using the mass of the fuel burned instead of the mass of water heated in q = mcΔT.
  • Forgetting to divide the energy transferred by the number of moles, and reporting a value in kJ rather than kJ mol⁻¹.
  • Mixing up the formation and combustion cycles, or adding the values instead of subtracting in the correct direction.
  • Quoting a standard enthalpy of formation for an element as non-zero.
  • Treating a mean bond enthalpy as an exact value for a specific molecule.
  • Omitting the sign when writing the final answer, even when the working is correct.

Exam-style questions

  1. Define the standard enthalpy change of combustion. Answer: the enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen, with all reactants and products in their standard states at 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K.
  2. A student dissolves 4.00 g of ammonium nitrate in 50.0 g of water and the temperature falls from 21.0 °C to 16.5 °C. Calculate the enthalpy change of solution in kJ mol⁻¹. Answer: q = 50.0 × 4.18 × 4.5 = 941 J absorbed from the surroundings, so the solution is endothermic. n = 4.00 / 80.0 = 0.0500 mol, so ΔH = +941 / 0.0500 = +18 800 J mol⁻¹ = +18.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
  3. Explain why the enthalpy of combustion of methanol measured with a spirit burner is less exothermic than the data book value. Answer: heat is lost to the surroundings and apparatus, combustion is incomplete because of limited oxygen, some methanol evaporates without burning, and the experiment is not carried out under standard conditions.
  4. Use the bond enthalpies C–H 413, Cl–Cl 242 and C–Cl 328 kJ mol⁻¹, and H–Cl 432 kJ mol⁻¹, to calculate ΔH for CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl. Answer: bonds broken = 4(413) + 242 = 1894; bonds formed = 3(413) + 328 + 432 = 1999; ΔH = 1894 − 1999 = −105 kJ mol⁻¹.
  5. The standard enthalpy change of formation of ethyne, C2H2, is +227 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene, C6H6, is +49 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain what these values show about the stability of the two compounds relative to their elements. Answer: both are endothermic relative to their elements, so both are thermodynamically unstable with respect to decomposition into carbon and hydrogen. Ethyne is much less stable than benzene, which is consistent with benzene's delocalised ring and with ethyne's tendency to polymerise or decompose.

Practise by writing the cycle before any numbers: a correctly drawn cycle makes the sign obvious. Then revise Kinetics, where activation energy and reaction profiles use the same enthalpy ideas to explain rate rather than feasibility.

title: Persuasive and Argumentative Writing — Study Notes
content:
Argumentative writing sets out a clear position, supports it with reasons and evidence, and answers the opposing view. The tone should be measured and confident, not aggressive.

A clear thesis

Your thesis states your position in one sentence. It should be specific and arguable.

Weak and strong thesis statements

  • Weak: "Some people have views about school uniforms."
  • Strong: "School uniforms should be abolished because they limit self-expression without improving learning."

Building the argument

Each paragraph should develop one reason. Start with a topic sentence, give evidence or an example, and explain how the evidence supports your thesis.

Persuasive devices

  • Rhetorical questions make the reader consider a point, often expecting the answer you want.
  • Repetition of a key phrase reinforces your message.
  • A striking example makes an abstract point concrete.

Counter-argument

Acknowledge the opposing view and then rebut it. This shows awareness and makes your case stronger. Use a clear signpost such as "Some argue that... However, ..."

Register and audience

Choose a register that suits the audience and the form. A letter to the editor needs formal vocabulary, a measured tone and no contractions. Avoid slang and text-message abbreviations.

Connectives

Use connectives to show the logic of your argument. "However" introduces contrast, "consequently" introduces a result and "furthermore" adds a point.

title: Geometry — Angles and Polygons — Study Notes
content:
Geometry — Angles and Polygons

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): angle facts, parallel lines, polygon angles, circle theorems (Extended).

1. Core angle facts

  • Line 180°; point 360°; vertically opposite equal.
  • Parallel lines: corresponding (F), alternate (Z), co-interior (C, sum 180°).
  • Triangle 180°; isosceles/equilateral properties; exterior angle = sum of two remote interior angles.

2. Polygons

Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Regular polygon: exterior = 360° ÷ n; interior = 180° − exterior.

Example: regular octagon: exterior 45°, interior 135°.

3. Circle theorems (Extended)

  1. Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc).
  2. Angle in a semicircle = 90°.
  3. Angles in the same segment are equal.
  4. Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum to 180°.
  5. Tangent ⊥ radius; two tangents from an external point are equal.
  6. Alternate segment theorem.

Quote the reason in brackets every time: "∠ACB = 62° (angles in same segment)".

4. Algebra with angles

Set up equations from the theorem: cyclic quad (2x + 10) + (3x − 5) = 180 ⇒ x = 35.

Exam tips: mark every found angle on the diagram immediately; use radii to create isosceles triangles; never leave a theorem unquoted.

Angle facts you must know

Angles on a straight line sum to 180°; angles at a point sum to 360°; vertically opposite angles are equal. Parallel lines give equal alternate and corresponding angles and supplementary co-interior angles. Give a reason with every step, naming the rule (for example, alternate angles).

Interior and exterior angles of polygons

The interior angles of a polygon with n sides sum to (n − 2) × 180°. For a regular polygon each interior angle is that sum divided by n, and each exterior angle is 360° divided by n. The exterior angles of any convex polygon always sum to 360°.

Triangles and quadrilaterals

Angles in a triangle sum to 180°, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. Angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Use the properties of isosceles, equilateral and special quadrilaterals to find unknown angles.

Worked example: interior and exterior angles

A regular polygon has n sides. The sum of its interior angles is (n − 2) × 180°, and each exterior angle is 360°/n. For a regular decagon (n = 10) the sum of interior angles is 8 × 180° = 1440°, so each interior angle is 144°, and each exterior angle is 36°.

Check that exterior and interior angles sum to 180° at each vertex: 36° + 144° = 180°.

Angles in a circle

  • The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc.
  • Angles in the same segment are equal.
  • The angle in a semicircle is 90°.
  • Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.
  • A tangent meets a radius at 90°.

Example: O is the centre of a circle and the angle at the circumference subtended by an arc is 35°. The angle at the centre is 70°.

Working with unknown angles

Give a reason for every step, for example "angles on a straight line sum to 180°" or "base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal". The reason is part of the mark scheme and is often awarded separately from the numerical answer.

In an isosceles triangle with apex angle 40°, each base angle is (180° − 40°)/2 = 70°.

title: Organic Chemistry: Arenes (Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry)
content:
Organic Chemistry: Arenes - Edexcel IAL A2 Chemistry

This topic belongs to Edexcel International A-Level Chemistry WCH15, Topic 18, and covers the structure, stability, and characteristic reactions of arenes, specifically benzene, alongside activating and directing effects including phenol.

Structure and Evidence for Benzene

Benzene is an arene with the molecular formula C6H6, possessing a planar ring structure supported by multiple lines of physical and chemical evidence.

  • Thermochemical evidence: The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is approximately −208 kJ mol−1, which is significantly less exothermic than the theoretical value of −360 kJ mol−1 calculated for a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with three isolated double bonds. The difference of about 150 kJ mol−1 is the stabilisation energy, also known as the delocalisation energy, proving benzene is much more stable than the classical Kekule structure.
  • X-ray diffraction data: X-ray crystallography shows that all six carbon-carbon bond lengths in benzene are identical at 0.139 nm, a value intermediate between a typical carbon-carbon single bond (0.154 nm) and a carbon-carbon double bond (0.134 nm).
  • Infrared spectroscopy: IR data shows characteristic carbon-carbon aromatic ring stretching absorptions and aromatic carbon-hydrogen stretching bands.
  • Delocalised model: The delocalised model for the structure of benzene involves the sideways overlap of unhybridised p-orbitals on each of the six carbon atoms, forming a continuous ring of pi-bonds above and below the plane of the carbon ring. Students may represent the structure of benzene as a ring inside a hexagon or as alternating double and single bonds as appropriate in equations and mechanisms.

Resistance to Bromination and Comparison with Alkenes

Benzene displays very different chemical reactivity compared to alkenes due to the nature of its bonding.

  • Resistance to bromination: Benzene is resistant to bromination compared to alkenes because of the delocalisation of pi-bonds in benzene, which spreads the electron density over the whole ring, making it a stable region. In contrast, alkenes possess a localised electron density in their pi-bond situated between two carbon atoms, which polarises approaching electrophiles much more readily.
  • Reactivity consequence: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition reactions readily at room temperature without a catalyst, whereas benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions and requires a halogen carrier catalyst to polarise non-polar molecules like bromine.

Reactions of Benzene

Benzene undergoes a variety of chemical reactions under specific conditions.

  • Combustion: Benzene burns in oxygen in air with a smoky flame due to its high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio, indicating unburnt carbon particles.
  • Halogenation: Benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of a catalyst such as iron(III) bromide or aluminium bromide.
  • Nitration: Benzene reacts with a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acids heated to about 50 degrees Celsius.
  • Sulfonation: Benzene reacts with fuming sulfuric acid (sulfuric(VI) acid containing dissolved sulfur trioxide).
  • Friedel-Crafts reactions: Benzene reacts with halogenoalkanes (alkylation) and acyl chlorides (acylation) with anhydrous aluminium chloride as a catalyst.

Mechanisms of Electrophilic Substitution

Electrophilic substitution in benzene proceeds through the generation of an electrophile followed by attack and proton loss.

  • Generation of electrophiles: For nitration, concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid generate the nitronium ion electrophile: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+. For halogenation, bromine reacts with an aluminium halide catalyst to generate the Br+ or polarised Br-Br-AlCl3 electrophilic species. For Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation, the halogenoalkane or acyl chloride reacts with aluminium chloride, acting as a Lewis acid, to generate a carbocation or acylium ion electrophile: RCl + AlCl3 yields R+ + AlCl4−.
  • Substitution mechanism: The electron-rich pi system of the benzene ring acts as a nucleophile and donates a pair of electrons to the electrophile, forming an unstable arenium intermediate where the positive charge is delocalised over the remaining five carbon atoms of the ring. A base removes a hydrogen ion from the substituted carbon, restoring the stable delocalised pi system of the benzene ring and regenerating the catalyst.

Reactivity of Phenol

Phenol contains a hydroxyl group attached directly to an aromatic ring, significantly altering its reactivity compared to benzene.

  • Reaction with bromine water: Phenol reacts readily with bromine water at room temperature without any halogen carrier catalyst, instantly decolorising the orange bromine water and giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, accompanied by steamy fumes of hydrogen bromide.
  • Reasons for relative ease: The lone pair of electrons on the oxygen atom of the −OH group in phenol overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. This partially delocalises the lone pair into the ring, significantly increasing the electron density of the ring compared to benzene. As a result, the benzene ring in phenol is strongly activated, polarizing incoming electrophiles like bromine much more effectively and attracting them faster than benzene can.

Side-Chain Oxidation and Directing Effects

Substituents on the benzene ring affect both the position of further substitution and the reactivity of side chains.

  • Directing effects: Alkyl groups, such as the methyl group in methylbenzene, and activating groups direct a second incoming substituent primarily to the 2- and 4- positions (ortho and para). A nitro group is a deactivating group and directs incoming electrophiles to the 3- (meta) position. Hydroxyl and amino groups are strongly activating.
  • Side-chain oxidation: Hot, acidified potassium manganate(VII) solution oxidises any alkyl side chain on a benzene ring directly to a carboxylic acid group, regardless of the length of the alkyl chain, provided there is at least one benzylic hydrogen atom. For example, methylbenzene is oxidised to benzoic acid.

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Stating that benzene undergoes electrophilic addition because it has double bonds. Correction: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution to preserve the stable delocalised pi electron system.
  • Mistake: Omitting the catalyst in Friedel-Crafts equations or halogenation. Correction: Always include anhydrous aluminium chloride or iron(III) bromide as catalysts.
  • Mistake: Drawing the positive charge inside the intermediate horseshoe incorrectly. Correction: Ensure the incomplete horseshoe representing the positive charge in the arenium intermediate extends over five carbon atoms and does not touch the carbon bonded to the incoming electrophile and leaving hydrogen.
  • Mistake: Confusing the conditions for phenol bromination with benzene bromination. Correction: Phenol reacts with aqueous bromine without a catalyst at room temperature, whereas benzene requires liquid bromine and a halogen carrier catalyst.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: State the thermochemical evidence that supports the delocalised model of benzene over the Kekule structure of cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene. Answer: The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is approximately −208 kJ mol−1, whereas the theoretical value for cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene is −360 kJ mol−1. The difference of about 150 kJ mol−1 is the delocalisation energy, proving benzene is thermodynamically more stable. (Earns credit by stating both values, their difference, and naming delocalisation energy).
  2. Question: Explain why benzene is resistant to bromination compared to cyclohexene. Answer: Benzene has a delocalised ring of pi-electrons which spreads electron density, whereas cyclohexene has a localised pi-bond between two carbons. The localised electron density in cyclohexene polarises bromine molecules much more readily than the stable delocalised ring of benzene. (Earns credit for contrasting delocalised and localised electron density).
  3. Question: Write the equation for the generation of the electrophile in the nitration of benzene using concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids. Answer: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 yields NO2+ + 2HSO4− + H3O+. (Earns credit for correct reactants, products, and stoichiometry).
  4. Question: Outline the mechanism for the alkylation of benzene with chloromethane in the presence of aluminium chloride. Include curly arrows and the intermediate. Answer: CH3Cl + AlCl3 yields CH3+ + AlCl4−. The benzene ring pi electrons attack the CH3+ electrophile to form the arenium intermediate with a positive charge spread over five carbons, followed by loss of H+ to form methylbenzene and regenerate AlCl3 alongside HCl. (Earns credit for electrophile generation, curly arrows from the ring, correct arenium intermediate structure, and loss of H+).
  5. Question: Explain why phenol reacts with bromine water much more readily than benzene does. Answer: The oxygen atom in the −OH group of phenol has a lone pair of electrons that overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. This increases the electron density of the ring, activating it and allowing it to polarise bromine molecules without a catalyst. (Earns credit for mentioning lone pair overlap, increased electron density, and ring activation).

Use these notes alongside active recall of mechanisms, reagent-condition pairs, and thermochemical definitions. Revise next the chemistry of carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and esters to complete your organic chemistry mastery for WCH15.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Evidence for delocalisation, applied to hydrogenation: cyclohexene releases about −120 kJ mol⁻¹, so three double bonds would release about −360 kJ mol⁻¹. Benzene releases only about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, a difference of about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ that is the extra stability from delocalisation.
  • Nitration, applied to benzene: concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ generate the NO₂⁺ electrophile. The sulfuric acid is a catalyst and dehydrates the nitric acid. Show the electrophile first, then the arrow from the ring to it, then the loss of H⁺ to restore the aromatic ring.
  • Phenol versus benzene, applied to bromination: the lone pair on oxygen donates into the ring, so phenol reacts with aqueous bromine at room temperature without a catalyst and forms 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate. Benzene does not react under the same conditions.
  • Directing effects: an electron-donating group such as –OH or –CH₃ directs an incoming electrophile to positions 2, 4 and 6 (ortho and para). A nitro group directs to the meta position and deactivates the ring. Name the group and its effect in the answer.

title: Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles — Study Notes
content:
Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): SOH CAH TOA, exact values, angles of elevation/depression.

1. The ratios

Label sides first (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) with respect to the marked angle, then choose:

  • sin θ = opp/hyp; cos θ = adj/hyp; tan θ = opp/adj.

Example: hyp 10, angle 35°, find opposite: x = 10 sin 35° = 5.74 (3 s.f.).

2. Finding angles

Use inverse keys: θ = sin⁻¹(opp/hyp). tan θ = 3/4 ⇒ θ = 36.9° (1 d.p.).

3. Exact values (Extended)

θsincostan
30°1/2√3/2√3/3
45°√2/2√2/21
60°√3/21/2√3

4. Elevation and depression

Elevation: angle up from horizontal; depression: down. Both measured from the horizontal line at the observer.

Example: tower 20 m, elevation to top 42° → horizontal distance = 20/tan 42° = 22.2 m.

5. Pythagoras combinations

Find a missing side with Pythagoras before applying a ratio when two sides are known instead of an angle.

Exam tips: never round mid-calculation (keep full calculator accuracy); 3 s.f. for lengths, 1 d.p. for angles unless stated.

SOH CAH TOA

In a right-angled triangle with angle θ: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent. Label the sides relative to the angle you are using before choosing the ratio. Use Pythagoras to find a missing side first if needed.

Finding angles

To find an angle, use the inverse function, sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹, on the calculator. Set the calculator to degree mode and check that the answer is sensible for the triangle drawn.

Bearings and angles of elevation

An angle of elevation is measured up from the horizontal, and an angle of depression down from it. Draw a clear right-angled triangle from the description to choose the correct ratio. Round the answer to the accuracy in the question, and keep full accuracy in intermediate steps.

Worked example: finding a side

In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is 10 cm and angle θ is 35°. The side opposite θ is found with sine: opposite = 10 × sin 35° = 10 × 0.5736 = 5.74 cm (to 2 decimal places). The side adjacent to θ uses cosine: adjacent = 10 × cos 35° = 10 × 0.8192 = 8.19 cm.

Worked example: finding an angle

In a right-angled triangle the opposite side is 6 cm and the adjacent side is 9 cm. Use tan: tan θ = 6 ÷ 9 = 0.6667, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.6667) = 33.7° (to 1 decimal place). Check the answer: an angle less than 45° means the opposite side should be shorter than the adjacent side, which it is.

Choosing the ratio

  • Label the sides as opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to the angle you are given, not the angle at the right-angle corner.
  • Use the ratio that contains the two sides you know, or the side you want and one you know.
  • Keep the calculator in degree mode, and do not round until the final step.

Exam point: a bearing is measured clockwise from north, so draw the north line first and then mark the angle before using the triangle.

title: Number — Sets — Study Notes
content:
Number — Sets

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): set notation, Venn diagrams, shading, universal set, subsets.

1. Notation

  • ∈ belongs to; ∉ not in; ∅ empty set; ξ (or U) universal set; n(A) = number of elements.
  • A ∩ B intersection (AND); A ∪ B union (OR); A′ complement (NOT A).
  • A ⊆ B: every element of A is in B.

2. Venn diagrams

Fill the intersection first, then work outwards. Two sets: only A, both, only B, neither.

Example: 30 students; 18 maths, 15 physics, 7 both ⇒ neither = 30 − (11 + 7 + 8) = 4.

3. Shading

For A ∩ B′ shade where A and outside-B overlap. (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′ (De Morgan) — check every region.

4. Regions algebra

With region variables x, y, z: use the totals to form equations, e.g. n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).

5. Probability links

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) — inclusion–exclusion from the diagram.

Exam tips: "neither" sits outside both circles — subtract from the universal set last; label regions with numbers, not expressions, as you fill.

The number sets

Natural numbers are 1, 2, 3 and so on; integers add zero and negatives; rational numbers can be written as a fraction p/q with q not zero; irrational numbers, such as π and √2, cannot. Terminating and recurring decimals are rational. Prime numbers have exactly two factors, 1 and themselves.

Prime factors and HCF/LCM

Write a number as a product of primes using a factor tree. The highest common factor uses the common primes at their lowest powers; the lowest common multiple uses every prime at its highest power. Venn diagrams sort numbers by properties such as even, square or prime.

Square roots and cube roots

The square root of a number is positive or negative: √16 = 4 but x² = 16 gives x = ±4. Check whether a root is exact or needs a calculator, and give a non-exact answer to the accuracy asked.

Worked example: a two-set Venn diagram

In a group of 30 students, 18 play football (set F) and 12 play cricket (set C), and 5 play both. Fill the diagram from the centre outwards: the intersection is 5, so football only is 18 − 5 = 13 and cricket only is 12 − 5 = 7. The union has 13 + 5 + 7 = 25 students, so 30 − 25 = 5 play neither sport. Answer questions by reading from the diagram: the number who play football or cricket but not both is 13 + 7 = 20.

Notation in words and symbols

  • A ∩ B: elements in both A and B. Written as "and" in the question.
  • A ∪ B: elements in A or B or both. Written as "or" in the question.
  • A′: the complement, everything in the universal set ξ that is not in A.
  • n(A) means the number of elements in A; the total of all regions in the diagram is n(ξ).

Shading regions

To shade (A ∪ B)′, first shade A ∪ B, then leave the shaded region outside both circles. To shade A′ ∩ B, shade B and take away the part that lies inside A. A quick test: list the regions by number (1 for A only, 2 for the intersection, 3 for B only, 4 outside) and write each expression as the list of regions it covers. Expressions that match the same list describe the same set.

Factors, HCF and LCM

Write each number as a product of primes. 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 and 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. The HCF takes the lowest power of each common prime: 2² × 3 = 12. The LCM takes the highest power of every prime that appears: 2³ × 3² × 5 × 7 = 2520. The HCF multiplies to the smallest number that both divide; the LCM is the smallest number both divide into.

Surds and roots

Simplify √72 by finding a square factor: √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2. A surd is left in exact form until the question asks for a decimal. Cube roots follow the same logic: ∛54 = ∛(27 × 2) = 3∛2. Do not split a sum under a root: √(9 + 16) is 5, not √9 + √16 = 7.

Common errors

  • Writing 13 as the answer to "football only" by reading the total for football, not the region.
  • Confusing HCF with LCM, usually by taking the highest power for both.
  • Treating 0 as a natural number when a question asks for the set of natural numbers; state which convention is used if the mark scheme is strict.

title: Mensuration — Area and Volume — Study Notes
content:
Mensuration — Area and Volume

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): units, perimeter/area (incl. sectors), surface area, volume of standard solids, composite shapes.

1. Units

1 m² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³; 1 litre = 1000 cm³. Convert area/volume factors carefully (square/cube the length factor).

2. Area

  • Triangle ½bh; trapezium ½(a + b)h; parallelogram bh.
  • Circle A = πr²; sector area = (θ/360)πr²; arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.
  • Composites: split, calculate, add/subtract.

3. Volume and surface area

  • Cuboid V = lbh; prism V = cross-section × length.
  • Cylinder V = πr²h; SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
  • Pyramid V = ⅓ × base area × h.
  • Cone V = ⅓πr²h; SA = πr² + πrl, with l² = r² + h².
  • Sphere V = (4/3)πr³; SA = 4πr².

4. Problem solving

Flow/filling: volume ÷ rate = time. Packing: divide volumes (check edge alignment). Nets for surface area: label every face before adding.

Exam tips: keep π on the calculator until the final answer; for sector problems ask "fraction of the full circle?"; quote units in every answer.

Area formulae

Rectangle: length × width. Triangle: ½ × base × perpendicular height. Parallelogram: base × perpendicular height. Trapezium: ½(a + b)h, where a and b are the parallel sides. Circle: πr², and circumference 2πr. Leave answers in terms of π when asked, or round to the accuracy stated.

Volume and surface area

Prism volume is cross-sectional area × length. Cylinder volume is πr²h. Cone volume is ⅓πr²h and sphere volume is ⁴⁄₃πr³. Surface area of a cylinder is 2πr² + 2πrh. Sketch the solid and label radii and heights before you substitute.

Units and compound measures

Convert units before calculating: 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³. Density is mass ÷ volume, and speed is distance ÷ time. Keep the units with the answer.

Worked example: a cylinder

A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Volume = πr²h = π × 9 × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cm³. Curved surface area = 2πrh = 60π ≈ 188.5 cm². Total surface area adds two circles: 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr(r + h) = 2π × 3 × 13 = 78π ≈ 245.0 cm². Give the units with every answer, and keep π in the working until the final line when the question allows it.

Cones and spheres

  • Cone: volume = (1/3)πr²h, curved surface area = πrl, where l is the slant height. For r = 5 and h = 12, l = √(5² + 12²) = 13, so the curved area is 65π cm².
  • Sphere: volume = (4/3)πr³ and surface area = 4πr². For r = 6, the volume is (4/3)π × 216 = 288π cm³.
  • Find the slant height or a missing height with Pythagoras before using the formula; most lost marks in cone questions come from using the vertical height where the slant height is required.

Converting units of area and volume

Linear conversions are squared and cubed. 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m² = 10 000 cm² and 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³. A common trap is writing 1 m² = 100 cm². Remember also that 1 litre = 1000 cm³, so a tank of 2.5 m³ holds 2 500 litres.

Compound measures

Speed, density and population density are compound measures. Density = mass ÷ volume: a 600 g block of volume 200 cm³ has density 3 g/cm³. To find a mass from density and volume, multiply; to find volume, divide. Check the units match the question before dividing, for example converting litres to cm³ first.

Common errors

  • Using the diameter where the radius is required, the most common error in circle and sphere questions.
  • Leaving π out of an exact answer when the question says "give your answer in terms of π".
  • Adding the area of only one circular end when finding the total surface area of a closed cylinder.

title: Persuasive and Argumentative Writing — Quick Revision Summary

Quick revision: Persuasive and Argumentative Writing

English First Language (Cambridge) — IGCSE. Argumentative writing sets out a clear position, supports it with reasons and evidence, and answers the opposing view. The tone should be measured and confident, not aggressive.

Key areas to revise

  • Weak and strong thesis statements
  • Persuasive devices

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title:
Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI16 Topics 8 and 9. It follows the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise the topic, not to replace the notes. The topic splits into three big blocks: the nervous system and neurones, the brain, imaging and the pharmacology of the nervous system, and the plant and genetic technologies — coordination in plants, recombinant DNA and GM organisms, and bioinformatics and microarrays.

The nervous system: hierarchy and the reflex arc

The nervous system lets an organism detect a stimulus, send information quickly, and make effectors respond. In mammals it is built from the central and peripheral systems, and its fastest wired responses are the reflex arcs, which are the simplest complete circuits you study in this topic.

  • 8.1 Sensory neurones carry information from receptors toward the central nervous system; relay neurones are in the central nervous system and connect sensory to motor neurones; motor neurones carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles and glands. Schwann cells wrap many axons in myelin, an insulating fatty layer, and myelination increases the speed of conduction. The roles of the three neurone types and the reason for myelination are the core ideas here.
  • 8.2 The nervous system causes effectors to respond to a stimulus through a chain: receptor detects the stimulus, sensory neurone carries the impulse to the central nervous system, relay neurone processes the information and passes it on, motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector, and the effector responds. The pupil example is useful: the iris contains muscles that respond to the amount of light, and the wiring behind that response is the kind of autonomic coordination this part of the topic describes.
  • 8.3 A spinal reflex arc is the simplest complete pathway. The stimulus is detected by a receptor, the sensory neurone enters the spinal cord, the relay neurone in the grey matter connects to the motor neurone, and the motor neurone carries the impulse out to the effector — often a muscle. The grey matter is where the relay neurones and synapses are; the white matter is made of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord between the spinal cord and the brain. The reflex arc is fast because it is short and involves few synapses, and it is protective because it does not wait for the brain to process the information first.

The practical point is that the reflex arc is not just “a reflex”; it is the minimal circuit that shows how sensory input, central relay and motor output are wired together, and it explains why the grey and white matter of the spinal cord have different functions.

The action potential and how it travels

The nerve impulse is the action potential, a self-propagating electrical signal caused by changes in the permeability of the axon membrane to sodium and potassium ions. The sequence of events is what the exam wants, and the reason myelination speeds conduction is part of the same picture.

  • 8.4 An action potential is conducted along an axon because of changes in membrane permeability to sodium and potassium ions. At rest the membrane is polarised, with the inside negative relative to the outside. When a stimulus is strong enough, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions enter the axon, depolarising the membrane and generating the rising phase of the action potential. Sodium channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, so potassium ions leave the axon and the membrane repolarises. The sodium-potassium pump restores the resting distribution of ions over time, but the immediate repolarisation is due to potassium leaving, not to the pump. The action potential is all-or-nothing: once the threshold is reached, it fires fully; a stronger stimulus does not make a bigger action potential, only more frequent ones.
  • The propagation happens because the depolarisation of one small region of the membrane changes the voltage in the neighbouring region, opening channels there and so on along the axon. The impulse travels because each section regenerates the signal, not because the same ions travel from one end of the axon to the other. That is why the impulse is an electrochemical wave and not a current flowing the length of the axon like water in a pipe.
  • 8.5 Myelination makes this faster by saltatory conduction. The myelin sheath is interrupted by the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon membrane is exposed. Depolarisation can only happen at these nodes, so the action potential appears to jump from node to node. This is far faster than continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter, because the signal travels quickly along the insulated internodal regions and is only recharged at the nodes. The comparison is not that myelin makes the ions move faster; it is that the signal regenerates at fewer points along the way.

A frequent mistake is to say that myelination increases the speed by making the ions travel faster, or to forget that the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting conditions after the action potential rather than causing the repolarisation itself. The order of events — sodium in, depolarisation, potassium out, repolarisation, then restoration — is the secure version.

Synapses and the chemical transmission of the signal

Where one neurone meets another, the signal crosses a synapse. The synapse is the point at which the electrical signal becomes chemical for one step and then electrical again, and it is also where drugs and toxins can act. Synaptic transmission is the reason neurones can be modulated, integrated and influenced by chemicals.

  • 8.6 (i) A synapse in nerve impulse transmission has a presynaptic neurone ending with vesicles of neurotransmitter, a synaptic cleft, and a postsynaptic membrane with receptors for the neurotransmitter. When an action potential arrives at the presynaptic ending, calcium channels open, calcium enters, and vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the cleft. The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening ion channels and producing a new change in membrane potential in the postsynaptic neurone. Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction and at many other synapses, and its action is a good example of the general scheme.
  • The pupil is a useful illustration. The iris contains muscles whose contraction or relaxation changes the pupil diameter; this is under autonomic control, and the pathway involves synaptic transmission with acetylcholine and, in the relevant part of the autonomic system, noradrenaline, depending on whether the response is constriction or dilation. The point is not to memorise every transmitter at every synapse, but to understand that the synapse is where the signal is passed and where chemicals can modify it.
  • 8.7 Drugs act by influencing nerve impulse transmission, and the specification names several examples. Nicotine mimics acetylcholine at some receptors, stimulating them; lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potentials and so acting as a local anaesthetic; cobra venom alpha toxin blocks neuromuscular transmission by binding to acetylcholine receptors; L-DOPA is used in Parkinson’s disease because it is a precursor that can be converted to dopamine, which is deficient in that condition; and MDMA, ecstasy, affects neurotransmitter reuptake and release, especially of serotonin, changing mood and perception. The principle is that drugs can mimic, block, enhance or reduce neurotransmitter action, and that the effect depends on which step they influence.

A helpful way to remember the drug examples is to classify them by the step they affect: some mimic a neurotransmitter, some block a receptor, some block ion channels, some change how much neurotransmitter is released or reabsorbed, and some are supplied as precursors. If you can say which step each one affects, you can answer the typical question even if you do not remember the exact detail of every one.

Rods, rhodopsin and the detection of light

The retina is where light is detected, and the rod cell is the model system for how a stimulus is turned into a membrane potential change at the cellular level. This is the place where the idea of a receptor potential and the operation of a G-protein-linked receptor are both visible.

  • 8.8 The mammal detects light with rods in the retina. Rod cells contain the pigment rhodopsin, which is made of opsin and retinal; retinal is the light-absorbing part. When light hits rhodopsin, retinal changes shape, the opsin changes shape, and this activates a transduction pathway that leads to the closure of sodium channels in the rod cell membrane. The result is that sodium ions stop entering as much, the rod cell hyperpolarises, and the pattern of neurotransmitter release at the rod’s synapse changes. This is a case where a stimulus reduces sodium entry rather than increasing it, so the cell hyperpolarises rather than depolarising. The signal is then passed through the retinal wiring to the optic neurones, which carry impulses to the brain.
  • The important concept is that a sensory receptor converts a stimulus into a change in membrane potential, and that the direction of change depends on the receptor. In rods, light causes hyperpolarisation. If you remember that the stimulus closes sodium channels in the rod rather than opening them, you can explain why the signal is generated and why it is not the same as an action potential in an axon.

Habituation and the simple learning of stimulus responses

Not every response is fixed. Habituation is a simple form of learning in which an organism stops responding to a repeated, harmless stimulus, and the specification includes it both as a behaviour and as something you can investigate practically.

  • 8.9 Habituation is a decrease in response to a repeated stimulus that is neither rewarding nor harmful. It is not the same as sensory adaptation, which is a change in the receptor itself; habituation is a change in the nervous system’s response, often at the synapse, so that the repeated stimulus fails to trigger the full response. It is useful because it lets an organism ignore unimportant stimuli and focus on those that matter. The practical investigation is to present a harmless stimulus repeatedly and measure the response over time, looking for the decline.

The organisation of the mammalian nervous system

The nervous system is organised into central and peripheral parts, and the central part is further divided into brain and spinal cord. The structure follows the function: the central system integrates and coordinates, while the peripheral system carries information in and out.

  • 8.10 The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system, CNS, and the peripheral nervous system. The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; it integrates sensory information, coordinates responses, and can initiate behaviour. The peripheral nervous system carries sensory information into the CNS and carries motor commands out to the effectors. The division matters because it tells you which part does the integration and which part does the connecting and carrying.

The brain: structure and function of the main parts

The brain is not a single organ that does one job; its major parts have different functions, and the specification names several of them so you can map structure to role.

  • 8.14 The cerebral hemispheres are the largest part of the brain in mammals and are associated with higher functions such as voluntary movement, sensation, thought, memory, language and consciousness, with different regions specialised for different functions. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems; it is involved in homeostasis, including the control of body temperature, hunger, thirst and the release of hormones from the pituitary gland. The pituitary gland is a major endocrine gland under the control of the hypothalamus, releasing hormones that regulate other endocrine glands and other processes. The cerebellum is involved in the coordination of movement, posture and balance, and in the refinement of motor control. The medulla oblongata controls vital automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate. Knowing the role of each part means you can explain what is likely to be affected if one part is damaged.

The exam point is that the brain is a set of specialised regions, not a single uniform structure. If a question asks what function a particular region has, the answer is to name the region’s role rather than to say “it does brain stuff”.

Imaging the living brain

The living brain can be imaged in several ways, and each method gives different information. The exam wants you to compare them by what they show and how they work, not just to list them.

  • 8.15 MRI, magnetic resonance imaging, uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to build a detailed image of brain structure, and is good for showing anatomy and structural abnormalities. fMRI, functional MRI, detects changes in blood flow related to neural activity, so it shows which areas are active during a task as well as the structure; the idea is that active areas have increased blood flow and changes in oxygenation that the technique detects. PET, positron emission tomography, uses a radioactive tracer to show metabolic activity, so it can reveal which regions are metabolically active. CT, computed tomography, uses X-rays to build a cross-sectional image and is useful for detecting structural problems such as bleeding, fractures and some tumours. The common thread is that each has a different strength: some are better for structure, some for activity, some for acute structural emergencies, and none does everything.

A good comparison answer names what each method shows, what it is best used for, and the fact that they are complementary. Saying “MRI is the best one” without explanation is not enough, because the question is usually about why you would choose one method rather than another.

Imbalances, drugs and the development of new medicines

Disease can arise from the imbalance of naturally occurring brain chemicals, and understanding that imbalance is what lets drugs be developed. Parkinson’s disease and depression are the two named examples, and they illustrate different kinds of problem and different kinds of treatment.

  • 8.16 Imbalances in brain chemicals can contribute to ill health. In Parkinson’s disease, dopamine-secreting neurones in the brain are lost, so dopamine levels fall and movement control is affected. In depression, the regulation of neurotransmitters such as serotonin is thought to be involved, and drugs that affect serotonin can be used in treatment. The development of new drugs follows from understanding these imbalances: if a neurotransmitter is deficient, a precursor or a drug that affects its release, reuptake or receptor action may help. The important conceptual point is that the drug is a response to a biochemical problem, not a random intervention, and that different drugs work by different mechanisms even when they affect the same system.

A common trap is to over-simplify depression as “a serotonin deficiency” in a way that oversells a complex condition. The specification point is that serotonin is involved and that drugs that affect serotonin are used; the exam answer should say that, without pretending the biology is simpler than it is. The safe answer is to say that the imbalance is part of the explanation and that drug treatment targets it.

Coordination in plants: phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins

Plants coordinate their responses too, but they use hormones and light receptors rather than nerves. Phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins are the named examples, and they each work through effects on growth and on transcription, which connects this part of the topic to the gene-technology part later.

  • 8.11 Phytochrome is a plant photoreceptor that exists in two forms that interconvert in response to light. It allows the plant to detect light quality, quantity and duration, and it affects processes such as flowering and germination. Auxin, indoleacetic acid or IAA, is a plant hormone that promotes cell elongation and is involved in tropisms such as phototropism and gravitropism; it is distributed asymmetrically in the shoot so that the shaded side elongates more, bending the shoot toward the light. Gibberellins promote growth, including stem elongation and seed germination, and they bring about their effects partly by affecting transcription, i.e. by switching genes on and off. The link to gene technology is that phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins are not just “plant hormones”; they are part of the plant’s control system for responding to the environment and for development, and some of their effects are at the level of gene expression.

A useful practical image is the shoot bending toward light: auxin moves to the shaded side, the cells there elongate more, and the shoot curves. If you can say that, you have the phototropism story in a form that scores marks.

Core Practical 18 and the production of amylase in germinating grains

Core Practical 18 is about investigating amylase production in germinating cereal grains. The point is to connect enzyme production with germination and with the hormonal control of growth.

  • 8.12 Core Practical 18 investigates the production of amylase in germinating cereal grains. Germinating grains produce amylase to break down starch into sugars that the growing embryo can use. The practical is a way to see enzyme production during germination and to relate it to the hormonal changes that occur as the grain starts to grow. The idea is that the living embryo produces the enzyme, and that the enzyme mobilises the food store for the growing plant.

Recombinant DNA: the technology that joins genes to vectors

Gene technology is the set of methods that let scientists move genes from one organism to another. The first step is making recombinant DNA, and the key tools are restriction endonucleases and DNA ligase.

  • 8.18 Recombinant DNA is DNA made by combining sequences from different sources. Restriction endonucleases are enzymes that cut DNA at specific sequences, often leaving “sticky ends” that are complementary and can base-pair. DNA ligase joins DNA fragments together by forming the bonds between nucleotides in the sugar-phosphate backbone. So the workflow is: cut the gene and the vector with the same restriction enzyme, mix them so the sticky ends pair, and use DNA ligase to seal them together, making a recombinant DNA molecule. The point is that the cutting and joining are sequence-specific and enzyme-catalysed, and that the same enzymes are used to open the vector and to insert the gene.
  • 8.19 Recombinant DNA can be inserted into other cells. The vector is often a plasmid in bacteria, and the recombinant plasmid can be taken up by bacterial cells, which then carry the gene and can express it. Other methods include using viruses as vectors or physical methods such as microinjection or gene guns, depending on the organism and the goal. The important idea is that once the recombinant DNA is inside a host, the host’s molecular machinery can replicate and express the inserted gene, which is what makes the technology useful.

How genes are used to make products

The reason organisms are genetically modified is that they can be turned into factories for substances they would not otherwise make. The specification names the production of drugs by genetically modified organisms as a key example.

  • 8.17 Drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms — plants, animals and microorganisms. The classic example is the production of human proteins such as insulin by genetically modified bacteria: the human gene is inserted into the bacterium, and the bacterium produces the protein, which can then be purified and used as a medicine. Other products can similarly be made in microorganisms, and sometimes in plants or animals. The point is that the organism is modified once and then used to produce the product, which is why the approach is useful industrially.

Microarrays and the detection of active genes

Not every gene is active at once. Microarrays are the tool for seeing which genes are active in a particular sample, and they connect gene technology to the analysis of gene expression rather than just the sequence of genes.

  • 8.20 Microarrays can be used to identify active genes. A microarray contains many short DNA sequences attached to a solid surface, and a labelled sample of cDNA made from the mRNA of a tissue is hybridised to it. If a gene is active, its cDNA will bind to the corresponding spot, and the label reveals which genes are being expressed and at what relative level. The comparison is between samples — for example a diseased tissue and a healthy one — so you can see which genes are up- or down-regulated. The principle is that the microarray lets you look at many genes at once, rather than one at a time, and that is what makes it useful for profiling gene activity.

Bioinformatics: the computational side of this topic

Bioinformatics is the use of computational tools to handle and interpret biological data, especially large datasets. It is part of this topic because modern biology produces more data than can be handled by hand, and because tools like BLAST let you compare a sequence with everything already known.

  • 8.21 Bioinformatics is the use of computer tools to collect, store, analyse and interpret biological data, especially large datasets such as DNA and protein sequences. It includes sequence alignment, database searching, and the comparison of sequences from different organisms to find similarities and differences. A typical use is to take a newly obtained sequence and see whether similar sequences from other organisms are already known, which can suggest function, evolutionary relationships and the presence of conserved regions. The point is that bioinformatics is not a separate subject from biology; it is the way large biological data are used.

Risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms

Gene technology is powerful, and the specification asks for the risks and benefits, not just the methods. This is the part where an essay-style answer is most likely to come from.

  • 8.22 Genetically modified organisms have both risks and benefits. Benefits can include increased crop yield, improved nutrition, resistance to pests or herbicides, reduced use of chemical inputs, production of medicines, and faster or more targeted research. Risks can include effects on non-target organisms, the spread of genes to wild relatives, the development of resistant pests, and concerns about food safety, patenting and ecological stability. The important point is that the risks and benefits depend on the specific modification, the organism, the environment and the purpose; a blanket statement that GM is good or bad is not an adequate answer. The answer should weigh a concrete benefit against a concrete risk and say what is relevant to the case in question.

A good answer names specific risks and benefits rather than general ones, and it recognises that the same technology can be used in different ways with different outcomes. For example, a herbicide-tolerant crop can reduce the need for some sprays but can also encourage weed resistance; the exam rewards the balanced, specific response.

How the nervous and gene-technology parts fit together

The topic is really two linked stories. The first is how animals coordinate and respond — sensory detection, action potentials, synapses, the brain, imaging and drugs. The second is how plants coordinate with hormones and how genetic technologies let us manipulate genes and measure their activity. The link is that both are about control: the nervous system controls rapid responses, the plant hormones control growth and development, and gene technology lets us read, move and use genes, including the genes that control those responses.

  • Start with the neurone: sensory, relay, motor, Schwann cells and myelination.
  • Move to the impulse: the action potential as sodium in, potassium out, all-or-nothing, and saltatory conduction in myelinated axons.
  • Move to the synapse: vesicles, calcium, neurotransmitter release, receptor binding, and the way drugs can intervene.
  • Move to the brain: CNS and PNS, the roles of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary, cerebellum and medulla, and the imaging methods MRI, fMRI, PET and CT.
  • Move to the chemical side: imbalances such as dopamine in Parkinson’s and serotonin in depression, and how drugs are developed in response.
  • Move to plants: phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins, the link to transcription, and the practical on amylase in germinating grains.
  • Move to gene technology: restriction enzymes and ligase, recombinant DNA, insertion into host cells, production of drugs by modified organisms, microarrays for active genes, and bioinformatics.
  • End with the balanced view on GM organisms, specific benefits and risks.

Typical mistakes

  • Saying the sodium-potassium pump repolarises the membrane during the action potential: it restores the resting distribution over time, but repolarisation is due to potassium leaving.
  • Saying myelination makes ions move faster rather than explaining saltatory conduction.
  • Confusing sensory, relay and motor neurones: sensory carry in, relay are in the CNS, motor carry out to effectors.
  • Saying the rod cell depolarises in light: it hyperpolarises because sodium channels close.
  • Treating habituation as the same as sensory adaptation: habituation is a nervous-system change, not a receptor change.
  • Confusing the brain parts: the hypothalamus is not the pituitary, the cerebellum is not the medulla, and the cerebral hemispheres are not all the same function.
  • Listing MRI, fMRI, PET and CT without saying what each shows or why you would choose it.
  • Saying restriction enzymes join DNA: they cut it; ligase joins it.
  • Saying a vector is the gene itself: the vector is the carrier, such as a plasmid.
  • Treating GM organisms as either wholly good or wholly bad without specific risks and benefits.

Exam-style questions

  1. Describe how an action potential is generated and conducted along an axon, and explain the role of myelination. Answer: At rest the axon membrane is polarised; a stimulus opens voltage-gated sodium channels, sodium ions enter and the membrane depolarises; sodium channels then close and potassium channels open, potassium ions leave and the membrane repolarises; the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting ion distribution over time. The action potential is all-or-nothing. Depolarisation in one region triggers it in the next, so the impulse travels. In myelinated axons, depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse appears to jump from node to node, making saltatory conduction much faster than in an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter. (6 marks)
  2. Describe synaptic transmission and explain one way in which a drug can interfere with it. Answer: When an action potential reaches the presynaptic ending, calcium channels open, calcium enters, vesicles of neurotransmitter fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft; the neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening ion channels and changing the membrane potential of the postsynaptic neurone. A drug such as lidocaine can block voltage-gated sodium channels, preventing action potentials; or a drug such as nicotine can mimic a neurotransmitter and stimulate its receptors. (5 marks)
  3. Explain how rods detect light, including the role of rhodopsin. Answer: Rod cells contain rhodopsin, made of opsin and retinal. Light causes retinal to change shape, altering opsin, which triggers a transduction pathway that closes sodium channels in the rod membrane; sodium entry falls, the rod cell hyperpolarises, and the pattern of neurotransmitter release changes. This change is passed through the retinal wiring to the optic neurones, which carry impulses to the brain. (5 marks)
  4. Describe the functions of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum and medulla oblongata. Answer: The cerebral hemispheres are involved in higher functions such as voluntary movement, sensation, thought, memory, language and consciousness, with different regions specialised. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and helps control homeostasis, body temperature, hunger, thirst and pituitary hormone release. The pituitary gland releases hormones that regulate other endocrine glands and other processes. The cerebellum coordinates movement, posture and balance and refines motor control. The medulla oblongata controls automatic functions such as breathing and heart rate. (5 marks)
  5. Compare MRI, fMRI, PET and CT scans of the brain. Answer: MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves to give detailed images of brain structure. fMRI detects changes in blood flow related to neural activity, showing which areas are active during a task. PET uses a radioactive tracer to show metabolic activity in brain regions. CT uses X-rays to produce cross-sectional images, useful for detecting structural problems such as bleeding or fractures. The methods are complementary: some are better for structure, some for activity. (5 marks)
  6. Describe the roles of phytochrome, auxin and gibberellins in plant responses. Answer: Phytochrome is a light receptor that interconverts between forms in response to light and helps the plant detect light, affecting processes such as flowering and germination. Auxin promotes cell elongation and is involved in tropic responses such as phototropism, where asymmetric distribution causes the shoot to bend toward light. Gibberellins promote growth, including stem elongation and seed germination, partly by affecting transcription. (5 marks)
  7. Explain how recombinant DNA is made and how it can be inserted into other cells. Answer: Recombinant DNA is made by cutting a gene and a vector, often a plasmid, with the same restriction endonuclease so they have complementary sticky ends, mixing them so the gene inserts into the vector, and joining them with DNA ligase. The recombinant vector is then inserted into host cells, such as bacteria, where it can be replicated and the inserted gene expressed. (5 marks)
  8. Describe how microarrays are used to identify active genes. Answer: A microarray has many short DNA sequences attached to a solid surface; cDNA made from the mRNA of a sample and labelled is hybridised to the array; if a gene is active, its cDNA binds to the corresponding spot and the label reveals its presence and relative level. Comparing samples, such as diseased and healthy tissue, shows which genes are up- or down-regulated. (4 marks)
  9. Discuss the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms. Answer: Benefits include increased yield, improved nutrition, pest and herbicide resistance, reduced chemical use, production of medicines and faster research. Risks include effects on non-target organisms, gene flow to wild relatives, pest resistance, food-safety and ecological-stability concerns, and economic and patenting issues. The answer should be specific to the case, because the same technology can have different outcomes depending on the modification, organism and environment. (6 marks)

Use this summary to place each idea before you go into the detail in the full notes. Revise the neurone roles and myelination, the action potential sequence and saltatory conduction, synaptic transmission and the drug examples, the rod and rhodopsin mechanism, the brain regions and the imaging methods, the plant hormones and the practical, and the gene-technology tools and applications. Then check the full notes for the drug names and the microarray details, and move on to the next topic when you can do the calculations and the comparisons without prompting.

Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — Quick Revision Summary

This is the fast map of Edexcel International A2 Biology WBI16 Topics 8 and 9. It follows the same order as the full notes so you can cross-reference, and it repeats the specification numbers so you can see which paragraph exists for which point. Use it to organise the topic, not to replace the notes. The topic splits into three big blocks: the nervous system and neurones, the brain, imaging and the pharmacology of the nervous system, and the plant and genetic technologies — coordination in plants, recombinant DNA and GM organisms, and bioinformatics and microarrays.

The nervous system: hierarchy and the reflex arc

The nervous system lets an organism detect a stimulus, send information quickly, and make effectors respond. In mammals it is built from the central and peripheral systems, and its fastest wired responses are the reflex arcs, which are the simplest complete circuits you study in this topic.

  • 8.1 Sensory neurones carry information from receptors toward the central nervous system; relay neurones are in the central nervous system and connect sensory to motor neurones; motor neurones carry impulses from the central nervous system to effectors such as muscles and glands. Schwann cells wrap many axons in myelin, an insulating fatty layer, and myelination increases the speed of conduction. The roles of the three neurone types and the reason for myelination are the core ideas here.
  • 8.2 The nervous system causes effectors to respond to a stimulus through a chain: receptor detects the stimulus, sensory neurone carries the impulse to the central nervous system, relay neurone processes the information and passes it on, motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector, and the effector responds. The pupil example is useful: the iris contains muscles that respond to the amount of light, and the wiring behind that response is the kind of autonomic coordination this part of the topic describes.
  • 8.3 A spinal reflex arc is the simplest complete pathway. The stimulus is detected by a receptor, the sensory neurone enters the spinal cord, the relay neurone in the grey matter connects to the motor neurone, and the motor neurone carries the impulse out to the effector — often a muscle. The grey matter is where the relay neurones and synapses are; the white matter is made of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord between the spinal cord and the brain. The reflex arc is fast because it is short and involves few synapses, and it is protective because it does not wait for the brain to process the information first.

The practical point is that the reflex arc is not just “a reflex”; it is the minimal circuit that shows how sensory input, central relay and motor output are wired together, and it explains why the grey and white matter of the spinal cord have different functions.

The action potential and how it travels

The nerve impulse is the action potential, a self-propagating electrical signal caused by changes in the permeability of the axon membrane to sodium and potassium ions. The sequence of events is what the exam wants, and the reason myelination speeds conduction is part of the same picture.

  • 8.4 An action potential is conducted along an axon because of changes in membrane permeability to sodium and potassium ions. At rest the membrane is polarised, with the inside negative relative to the outside. When a stimulus is strong enough, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium ions enter the axon, depolarising the membrane and generating the rising phase of the action potential. Sodium channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, so potassium ions leave the axon and the membrane repolarises. The sodium-potassium pump restores the resting distribution of ions over time, but the immediate repolarisation is due to potassium leaving, not to the pump. The action potential is all-or-nothing: once the threshold is reached, it fires fully; a stronger stimulus does not make a bigger action potential, only more frequent ones.
  • The propagation happens because the depolarisation of one small region of the membrane changes the voltage in the neighbouring region, opening channels there and so on along the axon. The impulse travels because each section regenerates the signal, not because the same ions travel from one end of the axon to the other. That is why the impulse is an electrochemical wave and not a current flowing the length of the axon like water in a pipe.
  • 8.5 Myelination makes this faster by saltatory conduction. The myelin sheath is interrupted by the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon membrane is exposed. Depolarisation can only happen at these nodes, so the action potential appears to jump from node to node. This is far faster than continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter, because the signal travels quickly along the insulated internodal regions and is only recharged at the nodes. The comparison is not that myelin makes the ions move faster; it is that the signal regenerates at fewer points along the way.
