title: Continuous Random Variables — Study Notes
content:
Continuous Random Variables

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 2 (WST02), sat at A2.

Probability Density Functions

A continuous variable X is described by a density f(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and ∫f(x)dx = 1 over all x. Probabilities are areas:

  • P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx

Single points have zero probability, so strict or loose inequalities make no difference: P(X < 2) = P(X ≤ 2).

Finding Unknown Constants

Piecewise densities carry an unknown k: impose that the total area is 1 (and continuity at joins where required). One equation, one unknown.

Example: f(x) = kx on 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Total area: k·(2²/2) = 2k = 1, so k = ½.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = ∫x·f(x) dx
  • E(X²) = ∫x²·f(x) dx
  • Var(X) = E(X²) − (E(X))²

The mean is the balancing point of the area under the density. For symmetric densities the mean sits at the symmetry point — worth spotting before integrating.

The Median and Mode

The median m solves ∫₋∞ᵐ f(x) dx = 0.5 (left half of the area). The mode is the x maximising f(x). For uniform densities the median is the midpoint.

Uniform Distribution

If f(x) = 1/(b − a) on [a, b], every point is equally likely. Then E(X) = (a + b)/2 and Var(X) = (b − a)²/12 — memorise both; they are quick exam marks.

Exam tips: always verify ∫f = 1 before computing anything else. Sketch the density — area intuitions catch algebra slips. Median questions are integration-to-0.5 questions; set them up before calculating.

Exam method: density functions

A probability density function f must satisfy f(x) ≥ 0 for all x and the total area under it must equal 1, so the integral of f over its whole domain is 1. Use this to find an unknown constant before asking for any probability.

For a continuous variable, P(a ≤ X ≤ b) is the integral of f(x) from a to b. The endpoints carry no probability, so strict and non-strict inequalities give the same answer. Outside the given domain f(x) = 0.

The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is the integral of f from the lower end of the domain up to x. The median m satisfies F(m) = 0.5, and the mode is where f is largest.

Expected value E(X) is the integral of x f(x) over the domain, and the variance is E(X²) minus the square of E(X). Write each integral with its limits before evaluating.

Exam cue: Sketch the density over its domain first. A linear density is a triangle or trapezium, and the area of the shape gives the total probability quickly.

Worked example: the cumulative distribution function

Let X have probability density function f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, and zero elsewhere. The cumulative distribution function is F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = ∫ from 0 to x of 2t dt = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Then P(0.2 < X < 0.5) = F(0.5) − F(0.2) = 0.25 − 0.04 = 0.21. A probability for a continuous variable is an area under the curve, so the endpoints of an interval do not change its value.

Exam method: state the range and check the total area

Always state the range of x for which the formula applies, and write f(x) = 0 outside it. Before using the density, check that the integral over the full range equals 1; if it does not, the unknown constant has been found incorrectly. Make sure the function is non-negative across the whole range, because a negative value means the function cannot be a density.

title: Forces & Motion — Study Notes
content:
Forces & Motion

Cambridge IGCSE 0625 (2026–2028): motion (speed, acceleration, graphs); mass & weight; density link; force basics (F = ma, resultant); momentum (Extended); turning effects; equilibrium.

1. Kinematics

  • Speed = distance/time; average speed = (u + v)/2 for uniform acceleration.
  • Acceleration a = (v − u)/t.
  • SUVAT (uniform a): v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.

2. Motion graphs

  • Distance–time: gradient = speed.
  • Speed–time: gradient = acceleration; area = distance. Negative gradient = deceleration.
  • Free fall 1: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (use 10) — v = gt from rest.

3. Mass, weight, density

W = mg (g ≈ 10 N/kg). Weight acts at the centre of mass; mass is invariant. Density ρ = m/V.

4. Newton's laws and resultant force

  • Resultant: colinear addition/subtraction; perpendicular by Pythagoras.
  • F = ma. Terminal velocity: drag grows with speed until it balances weight.
  • Third law pairs: equal magnitude, opposite direction, different bodies.

5. Momentum (Extended)

p = mv; impulse Ft = Δ(mv); conservation: Σpbefore = Σpafter (explosions, collisions).

Example: 2 kg at 3 m/s hits 1 kg at rest, combined 1 m/s: 6 = 3v ⇒ v = 2 m/s.

6. Moments and equilibrium

  • Moment = F × perpendicular distance from pivot.
  • Principle of moments: Σclockwise = Σanticlockwise.
  • Equilibrium: resultant force = 0 and resultant moment = 0.

Example: 100 N at 0.3 m balances F at 0.5 m: F = 60 N.

Newton's laws in practice

Weight is the gravitational force on a mass, W = mg, and it is measured in newtons. Mass is measured in kilograms and does not change with location, whereas weight does. Newton's second law states that F = ma, so a resultant force causes an acceleration in the same direction. Newton's third law states that when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A, and the two forces act on different bodies.

Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv. In a closed system with no external force, the total momentum before and after a collision is the same.

Exam tip: the reaction force in Newton's third law acts on the other body, so it cannot cancel the force you are analysing.

Worked example: resultant force and acceleration

A 2.0 kg trolley is pushed to the right with a force of 12 N, and friction opposes the motion with a force of 5.0 N. The resultant force is 12 − 5.0 = 7.0 N to the right. Using F = ma, the acceleration is a = 7.0 ÷ 2.0 = 3.5 m/s² in the direction of the resultant force. Find the resultant force first, taking the direction of each force into account, and only then apply F = ma.

Exam method: units and wording in answers

Mass must be in kilograms and force in newtons before you use F = ma; a mass in grams gives an answer 1000 times too large. Weight is a force measured in newtons and is not the same as mass. When asked why a moving object does not accelerate, state that the resultant force is zero, not that no forces act on it.

title: Exam technique: Vectors (A2)
content:
### What earns the marks
For line equations, r = a + t b with direction from two points earns the method mark. For intersections, equating components and solving earns one mark and the consistency check earns the second. For angles and distances, the dot-product or cross-product magnitude formula quoted earns the method mark.
### Traps
Error: position vectors used as directions. Correction: subtract to get direction. Error: parameters equated across lines. Correction: different letters per line. Error: inconsistent third component ignored. Correction: verify all three or declare skew.
### Choose the right product
Use the scalar product a · b when you need an angle or a perpendicular condition. Use the vector product only when the question specifically asks for it, because the two give different kinds of answers.

### Use the vector equation carefully
For a line r = a + λb, the vector b is the direction and a is a point on the line. Make sure the two lines use different parameters, such as λ and μ, before you equate them.

### Check that the lines meet
Equate the components to give three equations in two unknowns. Solve two of them, then check that the solution satisfies the third before you give the point of intersection.

title: Binomial Distribution — Study Notes
content:
The Binomial Distribution

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 2 (WST02), sat at A2.

When Binomial Applies

X ~ B(n, p) counts successes in n independent trials when:

  • a fixed number n of identical trials,
  • each trial ends in success or failure,
  • constant success probability p,
  • trials are independent.

Check all four before using the model — "justifying a binomial model" is a real exam question.

The Formula

P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The ⁿCᵣ counts which r of the n trials were the successes.

Example: X ~ B(5, 0.3). P(X = 2) = ¹⁰C₂? No — ⁵C₂ × 0.3² × 0.7³ = 10 × 0.09 × 0.343 = 0.3087.

Cumulative Probabilities

P(X ≤ 2) = P(0) + P(1) + P(2). "At least" questions convert by the complement: P(X ≥ 2) = 1 − P(X ≤ 1). Keep one extra decimal place in intermediate steps to avoid rounding drift.

Expectation and Variance

  • E(X) = np and Var(X) = np(1 − p)

For X ~ B(20, 0.4): E(X) = 8 and Var(X) = 4.8.

Modelling Decisions

If trials are dependent (drawing without replacement from a small population) binomial is not appropriate. If p changes between trials it is not binomial. When n is large and p small, the binomial is approximately Poisson — but at A2 you usually stay exact.

Exam tips: identify n and p in words before touching the calculator. For P(X ≥ k) always rewrite as 1 − P(X ≤ k − 1). Tables give cumulative values — use them rather than summing by hand.

Exam method: binomial probabilities

If X ~ B(n, p) then X counts successes in n independent trials, each with probability p. P(X = r) = nCr p^r (1 - p)^(n - r) for r = 0, 1, ..., n. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 - p).

Check the conditions first: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant p and independent trials. If any condition fails, the binomial model does not apply.

Exam cue: Always state n and p before calculating, and say which condition you are checking. For P(X ≥ r) or P(X > r), use the complement 1 − P(X ≤ r − 1), read from the cumulative table or calculator, and state the final probability to three significant figures.

Worked example: a binomial probability

A biased coin lands on heads with probability 0.3. Let X be the number of heads in 10 throws, so X ~ B(10, 0.3). The probability of exactly 3 heads is P(X = 3) = C(10, 3) × 0.3³ × 0.7⁷ = 120 × 0.027 × 0.08235 = 0.2668 (to 4 decimal places). The coefficient 120 counts the arrangements of the 3 heads among 10 throws, and it is needed because the heads may fall in any of those positions.

At least one success

For P(X ≥ 1), use the complement: P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) = 1 − 0.7¹⁰ = 1 − 0.02825 = 0.9718. Examiners look for this shortcut, and writing the full sum from X = 1 to X = 10 is both slower and more error-prone.

Checking the mean and variance

  • Mean: E(X) = np = 10 × 0.3 = 3.
  • Variance: Var(X) = np(1 − p) = 10 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 2.1, so the standard deviation is √2.1 = 1.45 (to 2 decimal places).

Use these values to judge whether a stated answer is sensible: a mean of 3 with a standard deviation of 1.45 means most results fall between 1 and 5.

Exam point: a binomial model needs a fixed number of trials, independence, and the same probability of success on each trial. If the items are drawn without replacement from a small group, the probability changes after each draw and the binomial model is not valid.

title: Number — Indices and Standard Form — Study Notes
content:
Number — Indices and Standard Form

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): index laws, negative and fractional indices, standard form arithmetic, surds and rationalising denominators.

1. Index laws

  • aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  • a⁰ = 1; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ; a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a; a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ

Examples: 27^(2/3) = (³√27)² = 9; 5⁻² = 1/25; (2x³)² = 4x⁶.

2. Standard form

a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10.

  • 47 382 = 4.7382 × 10⁴; 0.0056 = 5.6 × 10⁻³
  • Multiplication: multiply a's, add powers. Division: divide a's, subtract powers.

Example: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) = 12 × 10³ = 1.2 × 10⁴.

3. Calculator use

Use the ×10ˣ key, not 10 ^; keep working in standard form and convert at the end. Give final answers in the form asked (often 3 s.f. standard form).

4. Solving index equations

Match bases: 2ˣ = 32 ⇒ 2ˣ = 2⁵ ⇒ x = 5. With different bases, rewrite (8 = 2³).

5. Surds

A surd is a root that cannot be written as a rational number: √2, √3, 3√5.

  • Rules: √a × √b = √(ab); √a ÷ √b = √(a/b); (√a)² = a.
  • Simplify by taking out the largest square factor: √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2; √72 = 6√2; √(9/16) = 3/4.
  • Add and subtract like surds: √18 + √8 = 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2. Unlike surds cannot be combined: 2√3 + √5 stays as it is.
  • Rationalise the denominator so no root is left below the line: 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3; 1/(3 + √2) = (3 − √2) / ((3 + √2)(3 − √2)) = (3 − √2)/7 — multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.
  • Expanding: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1; difference of two squares clears the surd.

Example: write √12 + √75 in the form k√3 → 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3.

Exam tips: check a is in [1, 10) before writing standard form; in "multiply out" questions apply the power to every factor including coefficients.

Worked example: a combined index calculation

Simplify (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁴. Add the indices in the numerator to get 2⁸ ÷ 2⁴, then subtract the indices to get 2⁴ = 16. Check by a second method: 2³ × 2⁵ = 8 × 32 = 256, and 256 ÷ 16 = 16. Both routes agree.

Fractional and negative powers

A negative index means a reciprocal: 5⁻² = 1/5² = 1/25. A fractional index with denominator n means an nth root: 16^(1/2) = 4, and 27^(2/3) = (27^(1/3))² = 3² = 9. Taking the root first and then raising the result to the power keeps the arithmetic small.

  • Any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1, so 7⁰ = 1.
  • Do not multiply the base by the index: (2³)² = 2⁶, not 2⁵ and not 6.
  • Standard form for a number between 0 and 1 uses a negative index: 0.00047 = 4.7 × 10⁻⁴.

Worked example: converting to and from standard form

Write 0.00046 in standard form by moving the decimal point four places to the right, giving 4.6 × 10⁻⁴. The number 3.2 × 10⁵ is 320 000. To multiply, multiply the coefficients and add the powers: (2 × 10⁶) × (4 × 10³) = 8 × 10⁹. To divide, divide the coefficients and subtract the powers: (6 × 10⁸) ÷ (2 × 10³) = 3 × 10⁵. The coefficient must lie between 1 and 10, so 12 × 10⁴ must be rewritten as 1.2 × 10⁵.

Exam method: checking the size of an answer

A large number should have a positive power of ten and a small number a negative one, so check the sign of the index after every conversion. If a question asks for an answer in standard form to 3 significant figures, round only at the end and keep all the digits your calculator gives while working. Rounding at each step can change the third figure and cost the accuracy mark.

title: Exam technique: Superposition
content:
### What earns the marks
For phase, path difference converted to degrees earns the method mark. For patterns, constructive versus destructive located earns each mark. For stationary waves, nodes and antinodes described earn the explanation marks.
### Traps
Error: half lambda called in phase. Correction: half lambda is antiphase. Error: nodes credited with motion. Correction: nodes stay at zero. Error: diffraction condition forgotten. Correction: gap near lambda spreads most.
### Define coherence and path difference
Two sources must be coherent, with a constant phase difference, to produce a stable interference pattern. Calculate the path difference between the waves reaching a point before you decide whether it is a maximum or minimum.

### Use the condition for maxima and minima
Constructive interference occurs when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, nλ. Destructive interference occurs when it is an odd number of half-wavelengths, (n + ½)λ.

### Explain standing waves in terms of boundaries
A node forms where the displacement is always zero, and an antinode where it is a maximum. Between adjacent nodes the phase is the same, while across a node it changes by π.

title: Exam technique: Further Algebra
content:
### What earns the marks
For modulus equations, both branches solved earn a mark each. For inequalities, the two-sided split earns the method mark with the and/or structure correct. For equal-roots problems, discriminant zero stated earns the first mark and -b/2a earns the second.
### Traps
Error: one modulus branch only. Correction: split both signs. Error: between-answers for outside-or inequalities. Correction: >= splits outward. Error: non-zero discriminants with equal roots claimed. Correction: equal roots force zero.
### Factorise before you divide
Factorise the denominator completely. Then decide whether you need to divide first, because the degree of the numerator must be less than the degree of the denominator before you split into partial fractions.

### Set up the unknown constants systematically
For each linear factor, write one constant. For a repeated factor, write one term for each power. Substitute convenient values of x to find the constants quickly, and check by substituting a value that was not used.

### Consider both cases for modulus questions
For |f(x)| = g(x) or an inequality with a modulus, solve the positive and negative cases separately, then check each solution in the original equation.

title: Exam technique: Networking & Communication
content:
### What earns the marks
For topologies, the diagram plus one benefit earns one mark each. For addresses, MAC as permanent plus IP as routable earns each mark. For security, firewall plus encryption plus passwords named in context earn full marks.
### Traps
Error: LAN and WAN swapped. Correction: LAN is local, WAN spans distance. Error: MAC claimed to change per network. Correction: MAC is burned in, IP is assigned. Error: HTTP called secure. Correction: HTTPS adds the encryption.### Worked example
Describe a star topology: every device connects to a central switch, so a cable failing removes only that device. The benefit is that faults are isolated; the drawback is that the switch is a single point of failure. A mark scheme awards the diagram and the benefit separately, so draw the switch and the spokes even when the question asks only for a description.
### Recall check
Explain why an IP address can change when a laptop moves between networks while its MAC address stays the same. Name one hardware item and one software measure that protect a LAN from unauthorised access.

title: Articles and Determiners — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Articles and Determiners

English as a Second Language (Oxford) — IGCSE. Articles (a, an, the) and determiners (some, many, much, each) tell the reader whether a noun is specific, general, countable or uncountable. Small words like these are often where accuracy is lost in writing.

Key areas to revise

  • Articles and Determiners

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Chemistry of the Environment
content:
Chemistry of the Environment

Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620, Extended route, topic 10 (statements 10.1–10.3). Water testing and treatment, fertilisers, air pollution, greenhouse gases and photosynthesis.

10.1 Water

  • Test for water: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate turns from white to blue, or anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper turns from blue to pink. Purity is tested by melting point (0 °C) and boiling point (100 °C) — impurities shift both, depression of melting point and elevation of boiling point.

10.2 Fertilisers

  • Ammonium salts and nitrates are used as fertilisers. NPK fertilisers supply nitrogen (for protein), phosphorus (for roots) and potassium (for flowers and fruit).

10.3 Air quality and climate

  • Clean dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, with noble gases and about 0.04% carbon dioxide. Pollutants include carbon monoxide (incomplete combustion, toxic), sulfur dioxide (sulfur impurities in fossil fuels, causes acid rain), oxides of nitrogen (from vehicle engines, cause acid rain and photochemical smog), and particulates.
  • Acid rain damages forests, buildings and lakes. Removal methods include flue gas desulfurisation with calcium oxide or calcium carbonate, and catalytic converters in cars that reduce oxides of nitrogen to nitrogen and oxygen.
  • Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane absorb re-radiated heat and warm the Earth. Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light and chlorophyll.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Removal chemistry, applied to a catalytic converter: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂. Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide and nitrogen monoxide is reduced to nitrogen. Name the oxidation and reduction halves separately.
  • Desulfurisation, applied to calcium carbonate removing sulfur dioxide: CaCO₃ + SO₂ → CaSO₃ + CO₂. Explain why this works: calcium carbonate is basic and sulfur dioxide is acidic, an acid–base reaction. That reasoning earns the mark.
  • Experimental design, applied to testing whether a lake is acidic: sample and compare against pure water using universal indicator or a pH meter, and state that a control sample of unpolluted water must be measured with the same method. Naming the control is often the difference mark.
  • Greenhouse reasoning, applied to why methane matters more per molecule than carbon dioxide: methane absorbs more infrared radiation per molecule, so a smaller amount produces a similar warming effect. Quantity AND per-molecule effect both count in an evaluation answer.

Common errors

  • Confusing the water tests: copper(II) sulfate is the white-to-blue test; cobalt(II) chloride is the blue-to-pink test.
  • Describing acid rain without naming its source gases (sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen).
  • Saying catalytic converters "remove carbon dioxide". They convert CO and NO, and can produce more CO₂.

title: Integration II — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Integration II

Mathematics — A2 (9709). With linear arguments: ∫ e^(3x) dx = e^(3x)/3 + c; ∫ cos 2x dx = sin 2x/2 + c.

Key areas to revise

  • Standard Integrals
  • Substitution
  • Integration by Parts
  • Partial Fractions

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Integration by substitution reverses the chain rule. Choose u as the inner function, find du/dx, and replace dx so that the integral is in terms of u only. Change the limits when you use a definite integral, or substitute back into x before you evaluate it.

Integration by parts uses ∫u (dv/dx) dx = uv − ∫v (du/dx) dx. Choose u to be the part that becomes simpler when differentiated, such as a polynomial, and dv/dx the part that is easy to integrate, such as eˣ or sin x. Partial fractions can be used first to make an integral of a rational function manageable.

title: Database Systems — Study Notes
content:
Database Systems

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): limitations of file-based systems; relational concepts; SQL (SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, INNER JOIN, SUM, COUNT); DBMS features.

1. File-based problems

Data repetition (wasted space, inconsistency), fixed queries, no concurrent access control — solved by a DBMS with shared, structured tables.

2. Relational concepts

  • Table, record, field; primary key (unique); secondary key (indexed search field); foreign key links tables.
  • One-to-many relationships via foreign keys; no repeating groups (1NF mindset).

3. SQL

SELECT Title, Year FROM Films
WHERE Genre = 'Sci-Fi' AND Year > 2015
ORDER BY Year DESC;

SELECT Genre, COUNT(*) AS NumFilms, SUM(Rating) AS TotalRating
FROM Films
GROUP BY Genre;

SELECT s.Name, f.Title
FROM Students s INNER JOIN Loans l ON s.StudentID = l.StudentID
INNER JOIN Films f ON l.FilmID = f.FilmID;

WHERE filters rows; GROUP BY aggregates; JOIN combines on matching keys.

4. DBMS features

Data dictionary (schema, types, constraints), query processor, forms/reports, access rights (read/write per user), data integrity (validation rules), backup/recovery.

Exam tips: write SQL keywords uppercase; alias joined tables (s, l, f); when asked "why relational", cite reduced redundancy + flexible queries.

Primary keys, foreign keys and relationships

A primary key uniquely identifies each record in a table, so no two records can share its value. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds the primary key of a related table, and it creates a relationship between the tables. Relationships can be one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. A many-to-many relationship is usually split into two one-to-many relationships through a linking table.

Foreign keys stop a record being added that points to a row which does not exist, which keeps the data consistent. Storing each fact once in the correct table also reduces redundancy, so an update is made in one place only.

Exam tip: when designing a table, name the primary key and say which field links it to another table.

Worked example: a two-table database

A school stores pupil details and the subjects each pupil takes. The table Pupil holds PupilID (primary key), Name and Form. The table Enrolment holds EnrolmentID (primary key), PupilID (foreign key referencing Pupil) and SubjectCode. Each enrolment row belongs to exactly one pupil, so the relationship is one-to-many from Pupil to Enrolment. The name is stored once, in Pupil, so moving a pupil to a new form needs one update rather than one per subject.

Validation and data integrity

  • A range check rejects a mark outside 0 to 100. A presence check stops a required field being left empty.
  • A type check rejects text typed into a numeric field, and a length check limits how many characters a field accepts.
  • A referential integrity check refuses an enrolment whose PupilID does not exist in Pupil.

What a database management system does

A DBMS keeps a data dictionary that describes every table and field, controls which users may read or change which data, backs the data up and recovers it after a failure, and manages concurrent access so that two users editing the same record do not corrupt it. Describe each of these with a named example from the question rather than listing the feature in general terms.

title: Electric Fields and Capacitance — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Electric Fields and Capacitance

Physics — A2. F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²). Field strength E = F/q (N C⁻¹); for a point charge E = q/(4πε₀r²).

Key areas to revise

  • Coulomb's Law
  • Uniform Fields
  • Potential
  • Capacitance
  • Charging and Discharging

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Coulomb's law: F = Q q / (4 π ε₀ r²) for point charges, and E = F / Q.
  • Radial field strength E = Q / (4 π ε₀ r²), and potential V = Q / (4 π ε₀ r).
  • Capacitance C = Q / V, and energy stored = ½ Q V = ½ C V².
  • Capacitors in series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂; in parallel: C = C₁ + C₂.

Common errors

Capacitors in series are added as reciprocals, which is the reverse of resistors in parallel. Field strength is a vector and potential is a scalar, so do not add field strengths as if they were energies.

title: Exam technique: Processor Fundamentals
content:
### What earns the marks
For the fetch stage, the register chain PC to MAR to MDR to CIR stated in order earns full marks. For assembly traces, the arithmetic shown earns one mark and the addressing mode named (direct for memory addresses, immediate for hash values) earns the second. For shifts, the bit pattern written out earns the method mark before any multiply-or-divide claim.
### Traps
Error: MAR and MDR roles swapped. Correction: address travels out, instruction travels back. Error: overflow ignored after a left shift past 8 bits. Correction: state the overflow explicitly. Error: cores credited with adding RAM. Correction: cores add parallelism; pipelining overlaps stages.
### Describe the cycle in order
Fetch-decode-execute questions require the steps in order: the program counter gives the address, the instruction is copied into the memory data register and then the current instruction register, the control unit decodes it, and the instruction runs. Write the register that holds each value.
### Registers and buses
The address bus carries addresses, the data bus carries data and the control bus carries signals. A question asking which bus carries an address must not be answered with the data bus.
### Explain the purpose
When asked why a processor uses cache, state that it holds frequently used data close to the processor, so it reduces the time spent waiting for main memory.

title: Sampling and Estimation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Sampling and Estimation

Mathematics — A2. A parameter describes the population (μ, σ²); a statistic describes the sample (x̄, s²). A statistic is unbiased if its expectation equals the population parameter: E(x̄) = μ always holds for the sample mean.

Key areas to revise

  • Populations, Samples, Statistics
  • Unbiased Variance
  • Distribution of the Sample Mean
  • Central Limit Theorem
  • Using x̄ to Estimate

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

The sample mean x̄ is an unbiased estimate of the population mean. The unbiased estimate of the population variance uses the divisor n − 1: s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1). Use the statistics mode of a calculator to find s directly, and check which of the two standard deviations the question asks for.

For a large sample, a confidence interval for the population mean is x̄ ± z σ/√n, where σ/√n is the standard error. The central limit theorem says that the distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal for a large sample, whatever the shape of the parent population. State the confidence level and interpret the interval in the context of the question.

title: Number — Sets — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Number — Sets

Mathematics — OL. A set is a well-defined collection of objects. Set notation and Venn diagrams let you describe groups and count their members precisely.

  • 1. Notation: ∈ means is an element of, ⊂ means is a subset of, ∪ means union (in either set), ∩ means intersection (in both sets), and A′ is the complement of A within the universal set ξ.
  • 2. Venn diagrams: draw the universal set as a rectangle and each set as a circle, and place each element in the correct region.
  • 3. Shading: shade the region that matches the description, and check that every region is covered or excluded correctly.
  • 4. Regions algebra: n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B), because the overlap is counted twice if you add the two sets.
  • 5. Probability links: the same regions give probabilities when each element is equally likely; P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

Core facts to recall

  • Start filling a Venn diagram from the centre, the intersection, and work outwards.
  • Check that the numbers in all regions add up to the total in the universal set.

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

title: Communication and Networking — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Communication and Networking

Computer Science — AS. `# Communication and Networking

Key areas to revise

  • Transmission
  • Packets and Protocols
  • Network Types
  • Hardware
  • Client-Server vs Peer-to-Peer

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A parity bit makes the total number of 1s even (even parity) or odd. For the 7-bit pattern 1011001 there are four 1s, so the even-parity bit is 0. If the receiver counts an odd number of 1s, it knows an error occurred. Packet switching divides data into packets that can take different routes, and each packet is checked before reassembly.

Key points to remember

Data is sent across networks in packets, and each packet is routed separately. Protocols define how devices communicate, and the TCP/IP suite is the set used on the internet. An IP address identifies a device on a network, while a MAC address is fixed to the network hardware.

Network security depends on firewalls that filter traffic, encryption that makes data unreadable to anyone who intercepts it, and user authentication that checks identity. Describe a threat, then say how the security measure prevents it, because an answer with only the name of a method gains little credit.

title: Materials: Deformation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Materials: Deformation

Physics — AS. Up to the limit of proportionality, F = kx — extension is proportional to load. k is the spring constant (N m⁻¹).

Key areas to revise

  • Hooke's Law
  • Stress, Strain, Young Modulus
  • Force–Extension Graphs
  • Breaking Stress

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Stress σ = F / A, measured in pascals, and strain ε = extension / original length, which has no unit.
  • Young modulus E = stress / strain, which is the gradient of the linear part of the stress-strain graph.
  • Within the limit of proportionality, Hooke's law holds: F = k x.
  • The area under a force-extension graph gives the elastic strain energy stored in the material.

Common errors

Strain is a ratio and has no unit. Beyond the elastic limit, the material does not return to its original length, so the Young modulus formula no longer describes the behaviour.

title: Exam technique: Sequences and Functions
content:
### What earns the marks
For nth-term questions, derive earns marks for the difference identified, the form an + c stated, and the constant found from n = 1. For function questions, order earns marks: evaluate the inner function first and write the intermediate value down. For inverse functions, show the swap (x = ... then solve) rather than jumping to the formula.
### Traps
Error: computing fg(x) when gf(x) is asked. Correction: start from the rightmost letter. Error: answering 5 + 3 x 20 for the 20th term of a 5, 8, 11 pattern. Correction: the multiplier is (n - 1), not n. Error: multiplying by the ratio once for geometric terms. Correction: the power is (n - 1).
### Find the rule first
For a linear sequence, find the common difference d. The nth term is a + (n - 1)d, where a is the first term. Check your rule by substituting n = 1 and n = 2 before you use it to answer a question.
### Read function notation carefully
For composite functions, fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then apply f to the result. Reversing the order is a common error and loses the mark even when the algebra is correct.
### Domain and range
When asked for the range of a function, consider the output values for every input in the domain. Write your answer as an inequality or a set, using the same form the question uses.

title: Exam technique: Energy Work and Power
content:
### What earns the marks
For stores, mgh and half m v squared quoted earn one mark each. For efficiency, useful over total stated earns the method mark. For power, work over time with units earns the final mark.
### Traps
Error: efficiency above 100 percent claimed. Correction: impossible; check the ratio direction. Error: mass in grams mixed with kg units. Correction: convert to kg first. Error: power and energy units swapped. Correction: watts are joules per second.
### Method marks
Use work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force, and power = energy transferred ÷ time. Quote the formula, substitute with units, and give the answer with the correct unit (J or W).
### Explain, do not just name
Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input, and it is always below 1 (or 100%). A question asking why efficiency is less than 100% needs the idea that some energy is wasted, usually as heat and sound from friction.
### Common slips
Mixing up kilowatt-hours and joules on energy bills. 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10^6 J. Check the unit of time before dividing.

title: Data Types and File Organisation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Data Types and File Organisation

Computer Science — A2. A user-defined type is derived from existing types. An enumerated type lists named values in order: TYPE Months = (Jan, Feb, Mar ...). Internally each value is an integer index starting at 0. Pointer types store a memory address; the dereference operator returns the value at that address, which is how linked structures reference their nodes. Set types store unordered collections of distinct values from an ordinal base type, supporting union, intersection and difference.

Key areas to revise

  • User-Defined Types
  • Records
  • File Organisation
  • Hashing

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example A hash function maps each key to a storage address. If the file has 100 slots and the key is an integer n, the address could be n mod 100. Two keys that give the same address are a collision, and the file must provide a method such as an overflow area to store the second record.

title: Mensuration — Area and Volume — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Mensuration — Area and Volume

Mathematics — OL. units, perimeter/area (incl. sectors), surface area, volume of standard solids, composite shapes.

  • 1. Units
  • 2. Area
  • 3. Volume and surface area
  • 4. Problem solving

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

Learn the formulas for area and volume and state the units with each answer: square units for area and cubic units for volume. For a prism, the volume is the area of the cross-section multiplied by the length. For a cylinder, use pi r squared times h for volume, and 2 pi r h plus 2 pi r squared for total surface area.

Convert units before calculating, because 1 m squared is 10 000 cm squared, not 100. Keep pi on the calculator and round only at the end. When a question gives a diameter, halve it to find the radius before substituting.

title: Organic Synthesis Revision Notes A2 Level Chemistry
content:
Organic Synthesis A2 Level Chemistry

These revision notes belong to Edexcel International A Level Chemistry WCH15, Topic 20, and cover structural elucidation, carbon chain extension via Grignard reagents, advanced problem solving, the preparation of aspirin, and practical purification techniques.

Deducing Formulae and Structure from Analytical Data

You must be able to deduce empirical formulae, molecular formulae, and structural formulae from data drawn from combustion analysis, element percentage composition, characteristic reactions of functional groups, infrared spectra, mass spectra, and both 13C and proton NMR spectra.

  • Combustion analysis and elemental percentage composition give the empirical formula by finding the simplest whole-number ratio of moles of atoms.
  • Mass spectrometry provides the molecular ion peak (m/z value) giving the relative molecular mass, alongside fragmentation patterns indicating specific structural units.
  • Infrared spectroscopy identifies functional groups from characteristic absorption wavenumbers, such as O-H stretching in alcohols or C=O stretching in carbonyl compounds.
  • 13C NMR spectroscopy reveals the number of chemically distinct carbon environments and the types of carbon environments present from chemical shift values.
  • Proton NMR spectroscopy shows the number of hydrogen environments, the relative peak areas (integration traces) representing the ratio of protons, and splitting patterns (using the n+1 rule) showing adjacent protons.

Increasing Carbon Chain Length and Grignard Reagents

You must understand methods of increasing the length of the carbon chain in a molecule by the use of magnesium to form Grignard reagents and the reactions of the latter with carbon dioxide and with carbonyl compounds in dry ether.

  • Grignard reagents are formed by reacting a haloalkane with magnesium metal in dry ether. The general formula is RMgX, where X is Cl, Br, or I. Dry ether is essential as water destroys the Grignard reagent.
  • Reaction of a Grignard reagent with carbon dioxide, followed by dilute acid hydrolysis, forms a carboxylic acid with a carbon chain length increased by one. RMgX + CO2 yields RCOOMgX, which upon acidification yields RCOOH.
  • Reaction of a Grignard reagent with methanal (formaldehyde) yields a primary alcohol with an extended chain.
  • Reaction of a Grignard reagent with other aldehydes yields secondary alcohols.
  • Reaction of a Grignard reagent with ketones yields tertiary alcohols. All carbonyl additions require dry ether followed by dilute acid hydrolysis.
  • Carbon chain length can also be increased with KCN, which turns a haloalkane into a nitrile. The nitrile can then be hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid or reduced to an amine.

Problem Solving and Planning Reaction Schemes

You must be able to use knowledge of organic chemistry contained in the specification to solve problems, including predicting properties of unfamiliar functional groups, planning multi-step synthesis routes, selecting suitable practical procedures, and identifying appropriate control measures to reduce risk based on hazard data.

  • Predicting properties of unfamiliar compounds requires applying known chemical behaviors of familiar functional groups to novel molecular structures.
  • Planning reaction schemes of up to four steps involves recalling familiar reactions and using unfamiliar reactions given sufficient information, keeping track of functional groups, reagents, and conditions.
  • Selecting suitable practical procedures involves choosing appropriate apparatus for operations such as reflux, distillation, and separation.
  • Identifying appropriate control measures to reduce risk requires interpreting hazard data such as flammability, toxicity, and corrosiveness, ensuring safe handling of volatile or corrosive chemicals.

Core Practical 16: The Preparation of Aspirin

You must understand Core Practical 16, which covers the preparation of aspirin (2-acetyloxybenzoic acid).

  • Equation: 2-hydroxybenzoic acid + ethanoic anhydride yields 2-acetyloxybenzoic acid + ethanoic acid. A little concentrated phosphoric acid or sulfuric acid is added as a catalyst.
  • Method: Mix 2.0 g of 2-hydroxybenzoic acid with 4.0 cm3 of ethanoic anhydride and 5 drops of concentrated phosphoric acid in a pear-shaped flask. Warm the mixture on a water bath for about 10 minutes.
  • Purification: Allow to cool, then add cold water to precipitate the impure aspirin crystals. Filter under reduced pressure using a Buchner funnel. Recrystallise the crude aspirin from a minimum volume of hot ethanol-water mixture. Filter again and dry the solid.
  • Yield and Purity: Determine the melting temperature to check purity; pure aspirin melts sharply at approximately 135 °C. Calculate percentage yield using actual mass divided by theoretical mass multiplied by 100.

Preparation and Purification Techniques

You must understand specific techniques used in the preparation and purification of organic compounds.

  • Refluxing heats a reaction mixture with a vertical condenser so volatile vapours condense and drip back into the flask without escaping, allowing complete reaction without losing reactants.
  • Purification by washing, including with water and sodium carbonate solution, removes soluble impurities such as unreacted acid or acid catalysts. Sodium carbonate neutralises acidic impurities, releasing carbon dioxide gas.
  • Solvent extraction transfers a solute from one solvent to another based on differing partition coefficients, using a separating funnel to isolate the organic layer.
  • Recrystallisation purifies impure solid products by dissolving them in a minimum volume of hot solvent, hot filtering to remove insoluble impurities, cooling to recrystallise, filtering under reduced pressure, and drying.
  • Drying removes trace water from an organic liquid using an anhydrous inorganic salt such as anhydrous sodium sulfate, magnesium sulfate, or calcium chloride.
  • Distillation separates liquids with different boiling temperatures. Primary alcohol to aldehyde uses distillation with acidified dichromate(VI), so the aldehyde is removed before it oxidises further. Primary alcohol to carboxylic acid uses reflux with excess acidified dichromate(VI). Aldehyde or ketone to alcohol uses NaBH4 (or LiAlH4 for carboxylic acids and nitriles). Alkene to haloalkane uses addition of HBr. Alkene to alcohol uses steam with an acid catalyst. Nitrobenzene to phenylamine uses reduction with Sn and concentrated HCl. Nitration of benzene is the first step of a route to phenylamine.
  • Steam distillation extracts organic compounds that are immiscible with water and decompose near their normal boiling points, distilling them at a lower temperature.
  • Melting temperature determination assesses purity; a sharp melting point close to the true value indicates a pure substance, whereas a broad range starting lower indicates impurities.
  • Boiling temperature determination identifies a liquid and tests its purity by checking if it boils within a narrow, specific temperature range.

Key Interconversions and Yield Calculations

Exam tip: state the reagent, the condition (reflux, distillation, heat under pressure) and the product of each step. Marks are often given for the condition, not just the reagent.

  • Percentage yield = actual mass divided by theoretical mass multiplied by 100.
  • Overall yield for a multi-step route is the product of the individual step yields. Two steps at 80% and 70% give 0.80 multiplied by 0.70 = 0.56, or 56% overall.
  • Atom economy measures the proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product: (molar mass of desired product divided by sum of molar masses of all products) multiplied by 100.

Typical Mistakes

  • Mistake: Forgetting that Grignard reagents react violently with water. Correction: Ensure all apparatus and solvents (dry ether) are strictly anhydrous.
  • Mistake: Confusing distillation and reflux conditions when converting primary alcohols. Correction: Use distillation to isolate aldehydes and reflux to make carboxylic acids.
  • Mistake: Assuming melting point ranges for impure substances are sharp. Correction: Remember that impurities lower and broaden the melting temperature range.
  • Mistake: Omitting the acid hydrolysis step after reacting a Grignard reagent with a carbonyl compound. Correction: Always include dilute acid as a second step to protonate the intermediate alkoxide.

Exam-style Questions

  1. Question: Outline a two-step synthesis of propanoic acid starting from bromoethane. Answer: Step 1: Heat bromoethane with aqueous potassium cyanide under reflux to form propannenitrile. Step 2: Heat propannenitrile under reflux with dilute hydrochloric acid followed by distillation to form propanoic acid.
  2. Question: Describe how to purify a crude solid product of aspirin. Answer: Dissolve the solid in a minimum volume of hot solvent, filter hot, cool to recrystallise, filter under reduced pressure using a Buchner funnel, and dry in a desiccator.
  3. Question: State the reagents and conditions needed to convert bromobenzene into benzoic acid using a Grignard method. Answer: React bromobenzene with magnesium in dry ether to form phenylmagnesium bromide, then react this with carbon dioxide, followed by dilute acid hydrolysis.
  4. Question: Explain why sodium carbonate solution is used during the washing stage of organic liquid purification. Answer: It neutralises any unreacted acid impurities or acidic catalysts present in the organic layer, releasing carbon dioxide gas which is vented.
  5. Question: Calculate the overall percentage yield of a three-step reaction where individual yields are 80 percent, 75 percent, and 90 percent. Answer: Multiply the decimal yields together: 0.80 multiplied by 0.75 multiplied by 0.90 equals 0.54, which is 54 percent overall yield.

Use these notes alongside active recall of reaction mechanisms and practical procedures, then practice multi-step synthesis and spectral interpretation questions next.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Grignard synthesis, applied to propanone with CH₃MgBr followed by aqueous acid: the methyl carbanion attacks the carbonyl carbon, and the alkoxide is protonated to give 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol. Count the carbons in the product to check which reagent supplies which carbon.
  • Working backwards: identify the functional group, then the reaction that makes it from a simpler group. A carboxylic acid can come from oxidation of a primary alcohol, and a primary alcohol from reduction of an acid. Plan the route from the target, then check each step's conditions.
  • Aspirin preparation: salicylic acid reacts with ethanoic anhydride, with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst, to give acetylsalicylic acid. Recrystallisation purifies the product, and a sharp melting point close to the literature value confirms its purity. A broad melting range suggests impurity.
  • Yield: calculate the theoretical yield from the limiting reagent, then divide the actual mass by it. Losses occur in each purification step, so a percentage yield below 100% does not show an error in the method.

Coordination, Response and Gene Technology — A2 Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International A2 Biology specification, WBI15 Unit 5, Topic 8 Coordination, Response and Gene Technology. It covers the nervous system — sensory, relay and motor neurones, myelination and saltatory conduction, the action potential and its conduction along the axon, the spinal reflex arc, synapses and the role of neurotransmitters, how the pupil dilates and contracts, how drugs influence nerve impulse transmission (nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and Parkinson’s disease, MDMA), how the retina detects light and forms action potentials in the optic neurones, habituation, the central and peripheral nervous systems, hormonal and nervous coordination, the structure and function of the brain (cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata), how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT are used in diagnosis and investigation of brain structure and function, how imbalances in brain chemicals contribute to ill health (dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression) and to the development of new drugs, how drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms, how recombinant DNA is produced and inserted into other cells, how microarrays identify active genes, what bioinformatics is, and the risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph, with the material set so that a student can revise from it and check themselves against the specification.

1. Sensory, relay and motor neurones, Schwann cells and myelination

The nervous system has three main types of neurone, each with a structure suited to its function. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the central nervous system; their cell body is off to one side of the axon, halfway along it, and they have a long dendron that carries the impulse from the receptor to the cell body and a long axon that carries it into the CNS. Relay neurones connect sensory and motor neurones within the CNS; their cell body is in the centre of the neurone, and they have many short dendrites and a short axon. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands); their cell body is in the CNS, and they have a long axon with many short dendrites. All neurones have a cell body containing the nucleus and many mitochondria (to supply ATP), dendrites that carry impulses towards the cell body, and an axon that carries impulses away from the cell body. Many axons are wrapped in Schwann cells, which wrap tightly around the axon in a fatty myelin sheath; the myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds conduction. The gaps in the myelin sheath are called nodes of Ranvier. The structure of each neurone type reflects what it does — sensory neurones bring information in, relay neurones process it inside the CNS, and motor neurones carry the response out to effectors.

2. The nervous system and how it makes effectors respond to a stimulus

A stimulus is a change in the environment (internal or external) that is detected by a receptor. The receptor converts the stimulus into an electrical signal (a generator potential, then if it reaches threshold an action potential) in a sensory neurone. The impulse travels along the sensory neurone to the CNS, where it is passed to a relay neurone; the relay neurone may synapse with other relay neurones and process the information, then pass the impulse to a motor neurone, which carries it to an effector. The effector — a muscle or a gland — responds: a muscle contracts, or a gland secretes its product. This is the general pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (relay neurone) → motor neurone → effector → response. The response is specific to the stimulus and to the circuitry involved, and rapid because electrical impulses travel fast along neurones.

3. The spinal reflex arc: grey matter, white matter and the withdrawal reflex

A reflex arc is the pathway of neurones that produces a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus, without involving conscious control. In the spinal reflex arc, a sensory neurone from a receptor (for example in the skin) synapses with a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which in turn synapses with a motor neurone that runs to an effector (for example a muscle). The grey matter of the spinal cord is the inner, butterfly-shaped region where the cell bodies of relay and motor neurones and the synapses between them are found; the white matter is the outer region, made up of myelinated axons that carry impulses up and down the cord, to and from the brain. In the withdrawal reflex, for example touching a hot object, a pain receptor in the skin sends an impulse via a sensory neurone to a relay neurone in the spinal cord, which excites a motor neurone that makes the arm flex (biceps contracts, triceps relaxes) and withdraws from the stimulus. The response is rapid and automatic, and happens before the brain is even aware of the stimulus, because the arc involves only the spinal cord; this protects the body from harm.

4. The action potential: how an impulse is conducted along an axon

An action potential is the nerve impulse — a rapid, transient change in the membrane potential of a neurone, from about −70 mV (resting potential) up to about +40 mV and back, caused by the opening and closing of voltage-gated sodium and potassium ion channels. At rest the inside of the axon is negatively charged relative to the outside (the resting potential), mainly because sodium ions are pumped out and potassium ions are pumped in by the sodium–potassium pump, and the membrane is more permeable to potassium ions than to sodium ions at rest. When a stimulus depolarises the membrane to the threshold, voltage-gated sodium ion channels open, sodium ions flood in, the inside becomes positively charged (depolarisation, up to +40 mV). At about the peak, the sodium channels close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, potassium ions flood out, and the inside returns towards resting (repolarisation); it rises a little too far (hyperpolarisation) before returning to resting. The sodium–potassium pump then restores the resting ion distribution. The all-or-nothing principle applies: once threshold is reached, the action potential fires at full size; a stronger stimulus does not produce a bigger action potential, it produces more of them (greater frequency). During the absolute refractory period, the sodium channels are inactivated and no new action potential can be started, which ensures impulses travel one way and sets a maximum frequency.

5. Myelination and saltatory conduction: why some axons are faster

Myelination speeds up conduction of the action potential. In a myelinated axon the myelin sheath insulates the axon so that ions cannot cross the membrane where it is covered; the action potential can only be generated at the nodes of Ranvier, where the axon is bare. The impulse therefore jumps from node to node — saltatory conduction — and this is much faster than the continuous conduction along an unmyelinated axon, because the impulse does not have to depolarise every part of the membrane. The speed of conduction also depends on the diameter of the axon (larger axons conduct faster because there is less resistance to the flow of ions inside) and on the number of sodium channels and the extent of myelination; the fastest axons in the body are large and heavily myelinated.

6. Synapses: structure, transmission, acetylcholine, and the pupillary reflex

A synapse is the junction between two neurones (or between a neurone and an effector cell) across which the impulse is passed by a chemical neurotransmitter. At a cholinergic synapse, an action potential arriving at the presynaptic neurone opens voltage-gated calcium ion channels; calcium ions enter the presynaptic terminal, causing synaptic vesicles containing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release their contents by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, opening sodium ion channels so sodium ions enter and depolarise the postsynaptic membrane (this may start an action potential if the threshold is reached). Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft breaks down acetylcholine to stop the signal and recycle the choline. Drugs and toxins can affect the synapse: nicotine mimics acetylcholine and stimulates the postsynaptic receptor; lidocaine blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and stops impulse transmission (used as a local anaesthetic); cobra venom alpha toxin blocks acetylcholine receptors so the muscle cannot be stimulated (paralysis). Meanwhile, the pupil is controlled by two sets of muscles in the iris: circular muscles and radial muscles. In bright light, the parasympathetic nervous system makes the circular muscles of the iris contract, which constricts (makes smaller) the pupil, reducing the light entering the eye; in dim light, the radial muscles contract, dilating (widening) the pupil so more light enters.

7. Drugs and nerve impulse transmission: nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA, and MDMA

Many drugs act on the nervous system by influencing nerve impulse transmission. Nicotine stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain, producing a temporary feeling of alertness and pleasure, and it is addictive because repeated use changes the brain’s reward pathways; it also raises blood pressure and heart rate, and is a carcinogen. Lidocaine is a local anaesthetic that blocks voltage-gated sodium ion channels in sensory neurones, preventing the formation and conduction of action potentials, so pain signals are not sent to the brain — it is used to numb a local area. Cobra venom alpha toxin binds to acetylcholine receptors on the muscle and blocks acetylcholine from binding, so the muscle cannot be stimulated and paralysis results, which can be fatal if the respiratory muscles are paralysed. L-DOPA is used to treat Parkinson’s disease; Parkinson’s is caused by a loss of dopamine-producing neurones in a part of the brain (the substantia nigra), so the level of dopamine falls and movement becomes impaired (tremor, stiffness, slow movement); L-DOPA is a precursor that can cross the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine in the brain, restoring the level and easing the symptoms, at least for a time. MDMA (ecstasy) causes a large release of serotonin from presynaptic neurones and blocks its reuptake, so serotonin levels in the synapse rise sharply, producing a feeling of wellbeing and empathy, but the subsequent depletion of serotonin and damage to serotonin neurones can cause depression and memory problems, and repeated use is harmful.

8. Detecting light: the rod cell, rhodopsin, and how an action potential is generated in the optic neurone

Rods in the retina of mammals detect light and allow us to see in dim light. A rod cell contains the pigment rhodopsin, which is made of a protein (opsin) and a light-absorbing molecule (retinal, a derivative of vitamin A). When light hits rhodopsin, the retinal changes shape (from 11-cis to all-trans retinal), which changes the opsin and causes the rod cell to hyperpolarise — it becomes more negative inside. This hyperpolarisation closes sodium ion channels that are normally open in the dark, so sodium ion entry is reduced and the rod cell hyperpolarises; this in turn reduces the release of the neurotransmitter (glutamate) from the rod cell’s synaptic terminal. The change in transmitter release affects the bipolar neurone, which in turn affects the neurone that runs to the brain (the optic neurone); so the rod cell’s hyperpolarisation to light ultimately leads to action potentials in the optic neurone, which travel to the brain and are interpreted as vision. This is a relatively fine point — light does not itself produce the action potential in the rod, it changes the rod’s membrane potential, and that change is passed on through the retinal circuit to generate action potentials in the optic neurone. Cone cells work similarly but are responsible for colour vision and detail in bright light.

9. Habituation: what it is and how it is investigated

Habituation is a simple form of learning in which a response to a repeated, harmless stimulus decreases over time; the organism learns to ignore the stimulus because it has learned it is not important. For example, a snail initially withdraws into its shell when its shell is tapped, but with repeated tapping the withdrawal response becomes slower and eventually disappears — the snail has habituated to the tap. Habituation is not fatigue of the muscle (if a new stimulus, such as a poke to the body, still produces a strong response, the withdrawal machinery is fine) and not sensory adaptation (the receptor still responds to the stimulus), but a decrease in the synaptic transmission at the synapse between the sensory neurone and the motor neurone that produces the withdrawal. A recommended additional practical is to investigate habituation to a stimulus — for example using the snail withdrawal response, tapping the snail and recording the time to emerge or the frequency of withdrawal, and showing that with repeated harmless taps the response declines and that the decline is not due to muscle fatigue.

10. The central and peripheral nervous systems

The mammalian nervous system consists of the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; it integrates information and coordinates responses. The PNS is the network of nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body — to receptors and to effectors; it includes the sensory neurones that bring information to the CNS and the motor neurones that carry commands to effectors. The motor part of the PNS can be divided into the voluntary (somatic) nervous system, which controls skeletal muscles consciously, and the autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions such as heart rate, gut movement and the pupils, and which is further divided into the sympathetic (which prepares the body for action — fight or flight) and parasympathetic (which promotes rest and digestion) nervous systems; these two often have opposite effects on the same organ.

11. Coordination in animals: nervous and hormonal control together

Animals coordinate their bodies by both nervous and hormonal control, and the two work together. The nervous system uses electrical impulses that travel fast along neurones and chemical signals (neurotransmitters) across synapses, giving rapid, short-lived responses targeted at specific effectors — good for rapid movements and reflexes. The hormonal system uses hormones carried in the blood, which travel more slowly and affect many cells at once, producing slower, longer-lasting, more widespread responses — good for things like growth, metabolism, reproduction and responding to stress over a longer time. In many situations they act together: for example, in the fight-or-flight response, the sympathetic nervous system acts quickly to increase heart rate, while the hormone adrenaline from the adrenal glands sustains and amplifies the response; in the control of blood glucose, hormones (insulin and glucagon) act more slowly and over longer periods than nervous control would allow. Plants coordinate only by hormones (plant growth substances such as auxin, gibberellin and phytochrome), because they have no nervous system.

12. The human brain: cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum, medulla oblongata

The brain controls and coordinates the activities of the body and is the seat of thought, memory and emotion. The cerebral hemispheres are the large, folded upper parts of the brain; they are responsible for higher functions — thought, memory, reasoning, conscious actions, language and sensation — and each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems; it controls the pituitary gland, regulates body temperature, water balance, hunger and thirst, and the sleep cycle, and it plays a central role in homeostasis. The pituitary gland, under the influence of the hypothalamus, releases several hormones that control other endocrine glands and body functions — for example growth hormone, ADH and the hormones that regulate reproduction. The cerebellum is responsible for coordination of movement and balance — it makes sure movements are smooth and coordinated and posture is maintained. The medulla oblongata controls unconscious and automatic functions essential to life — breathing rate, heart rate and the reflex centres for coughing, sneezing and swallowing — and it is where the cardiovascular control centre and the ventilation (breathing) centre are located. Damage to different parts of the brain produces different deficits, and knowing the location and main functions makes it possible to link symptoms to brain regions.

13. Brain imaging: MRI, fMRI, PET and CT — what they show and how they are used

Different imaging techniques give different kinds of information about the brain. Computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays from many angles to produce a cross-sectional image of the brain’s structure; it is good at showing bone, bleeding and structural abnormalities, and it is quick and widely available, but it uses ionising radiation and gives limited soft-tissue contrast. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses a strong magnetic field and radio waves to give detailed images of soft tissue; it shows brain structure without ionising radiation and is excellent for detecting tumours, inflammation, demyelination and injury, but it takes longer and is noisy and claustrophobic for the patient. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is MRI adapted to show brain function — it detects changes in blood flow and oxygen use that accompany neural activity, so it can show which parts of the brain are active during a task; it has good spatial resolution but poor time resolution because the blood flow change lags the neural activity. Positron emission tomography (PET) uses a radioactive tracer (for example, a labelled glucose) injected into the patient; the tracer accumulates in active tissues and its radioactivity is detected, so PET can show brain activity and metabolism, and it can show neurotransmitter receptors and help in diagnosing and studying disorders such as Alzheimer’s and cancer, but it uses ionising radiation and is expensive. These techniques are used in medical diagnosis (for example to locate a tumour, or to investigate a stroke or a degenerative disease) and in research into brain structure and function — for example to see which areas are involved in a particular task or how activity differs in a disorder.

14. Brain chemicals and disease: dopamine in Parkinson’s disease, serotonin in depression, and new drugs

Imbalances in certain naturally-occurring brain chemicals can contribute to ill health, and understanding these has driven the development of new drugs. Parkinson’s disease is caused by the loss of neurones in the substantia nigra that produce dopamine, a neurotransmitter involved in controlling movement; the resulting dopamine deficiency causes tremor, stiffness, slowness of movement and balance problems. Treatment with L-DOPA (a precursor that crosses the blood–brain barrier and is converted to dopamine) can relieve symptoms, at least for a time, and other drugs may mimic dopamine or prevent its breakdown. Depression is associated with lower levels of the neurotransmitter serotonin (and also noradrenaline) in the brain; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) block the reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic neurone, so more serotonin stays in the synapse and helps improve mood, and they are widely used to treat depression and anxiety. New drugs can be developed using this understanding of the role of brain chemicals — for example by targeting the receptors or the synthesis or breakdown of a neurotransmitter — and knowledge of the cause of a disease (such as the dopamine deficiency in Parkinson’s) is what makes targeted treatment possible.

15. Producing drugs using genetically modified organisms

Drugs can be produced using genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms. The best-known example is human insulin: the human gene for insulin is inserted into bacteria (usually E. coli) using a plasmid, and the bacteria are grown in large fermenters to produce human insulin, which is then extracted and purified. Human insulin made this way is identical to the insulin made in the human body, so it does not cause the immune reactions that some people had to the animal insulin formerly used. Other products made from GMOs include human growth hormone, clotting factor for haemophiliacs, and enzymes for washing powders; and modified plants and animals are being explored to produce vaccines and other pharmaceuticals. Using GMOs to produce drugs has advantages: the product can be made in large quantities, it can be made more cheaply than by extraction from animals or people, and it can be made identical to the human version. There are concerns, however — about the containment of the GMOs, the possibility of unintended effects, and the ethical questions of modifying organisms in this way.

16. Recombinant DNA: how it is produced (restriction enzymes and DNA ligase) and inserted into other cells

Recombinant DNA is DNA made by joining together pieces of DNA from different sources. Restriction endonucleases (restriction enzymes) cut DNA at specific base sequences, making cuts that can leave complementary ‘sticky ends’ — short single-stranded overhangs that can base-pair with each other — and these sticky ends allow a gene of interest to be joined to a vector (such as a plasmid) cut with the same enzyme. DNA ligase then seals the backbone of the sugar–phosphate chain, joining the gene to the vector to make recombinant DNA. To insert recombinant DNA into other cells, the vector (carrying the gene) is introduced into host cells: bacterial cells can take up plasmids in a process called transformation (which can be helped by making the bacteria competent — for example by calcium chloride treatment and a heat shock); viral vectors can be engineered to carry the gene into the cells they infect, using the virus’s natural ability to enter cells; and other methods such as microinjection or gene guns can put DNA directly into cells. Once inside, the host cell’s machinery may read and express the gene, making the protein it codes for (for example insulin), and if the vector also carries a gene for resistance to an antibiotic, only the cells that took up the vector will survive on antibiotic-containing medium — giving a way to select the transformed cells.

17. Microarrays: how they identify active genes

A microarray (DNA microarray) is a small slide or chip carrying thousands of known DNA sequences (probes), each in a known position. Messenger RNA is extracted from two samples (for example, a diseased tissue and a healthy tissue, or cells treated with a drug and untreated cells), converted to cDNA, and labelled with different coloured fluorescent tags (for example green for one sample and red for the other). The labelled cDNA is mixed and allowed to hybridise to the probes on the microarray: if a gene is active (expressed) in a sample, its cDNA will bind (hybridise) to the complementary probe on the chip. By scanning the chip, the colours and intensities can be read: a green spot means the gene is more active in the green-labelled sample, a red spot means more active in the red-labelled sample, yellow means similar activity in both, and the intensity reflects how active the gene is. By looking at all the spots, researchers can see which genes are active (turned on) or inactive (turned off) in a sample and compare activity between samples — for example to see which genes are active in a cancer cell that are not in a normal cell, or to see how a drug changes gene activity. This makes it possible to identify active genes and to use gene activity patterns for diagnosis and to understand disease and drug action.

18. Bioinformatics: what it is and what it is used for

Bioinformatics is the use of computer technology to collect, store, analyse and interpret biological data, especially large datasets such as DNA and protein sequences, gene expression data from microarrays, and protein structures. It depends on the availability of sequence data — the DNA sequences of genomes and the sequences of proteins — and on databases that store and organise these sequences so they can be compared and searched. Bioinformatics is used to compare sequences to find similarities and differences, to identify genes and their functions (for example by comparing a new sequence with known ones to suggest what it does), to study evolutionary relationships (by building phylogenetic trees from sequence comparisons), to predict the structure and function of proteins from their amino acid sequence, and to analyse gene expression patterns from microarrays. It depends on the work of the Human Genome Project and other sequencing projects, and on the computational tools that turn raw sequence data into useful biological knowledge. Bioinformatics is now part of nearly every area of biology — from identifying a gene, to understanding what it does, to finding targets for drugs, to tracing the evolution of a pathogen.

19. Risks and benefits of genetically modified organisms

Genetically modified organisms (GMOs) — plants, animals and microorganisms — have both benefits and risks. Benefits include: in agriculture, crops can be modified to resist pests (for example Bt crops that produce a bacterial toxin harmful to insect pests but not to people) or herbicides, to tolerate drought or salinity, to improve nutrition (for example golden rice producing beta-carotene, a vitamin A precursor), and to increase yield — which can support food security; in medicine, GM bacteria produce human insulin and other proteins for therapy; in research, GM animals and plants are used to study gene function and disease. Risks and concerns include: the possibility that the modified gene could spread to wild relatives or other organisms (gene flow) and have unintended effects; the potential harm to non-target organisms (for example whether Bt crops affect beneficial insects); the development of resistant pests or weeds; the concentration of control of food and seed in a few companies, and the effect on farmers and on traditional varieties; the long-term effects on ecosystems, which are not fully known; and the ethical questions about modifying organisms, especially animals, and about food that has been genetically modified. These must be weighed case by case: the benefits and risks of each GMO depend on what it is, how it is used, and how it is regulated. The scientific evidence about each GMO is needed to evaluate it properly, and the public has a legitimate role in the decisions because the issues are not only scientific — they include values, economics and the environment.

20. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes by working through each section and checking that you can: describe the structure of sensory, relay and motor neurones; describe the spinal reflex arc, including the roles of grey and white matter; explain how the action potential is generated, including depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, the role of sodium and potassium ions and the sodium–potassium pump, and the all-or-nothing principle; explain how myelination allows saltatory conduction and speeds it up; describe the cholinergic synapse and the roles of calcium, acetylcholine, receptors, acetylcholinesterase; explain the pupillary reflex (circular muscles constrict in bright light, radial muscles dilate in dim); describe how nicotine, lidocaine, cobra venom alpha toxin, L-DOPA and MDMA affect nerve impulse transmission, including examples; describe how rod cells detect light, the role of rhodopsin, opsin, retinal, sodium channels and hyperpolarisation, and how this leads to action potentials in the optic neurone; describe habituation and the evidence for it (the snail withdrawal practical); describe the central and peripheral nervous systems and the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions; locate and state the functions of the cerebral hemispheres, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, cerebellum and medulla oblongata; explain how MRI, fMRI, PET and CT work and what they are used for; explain the role of dopamine in Parkinson’s disease and serotonin in depression and how the drugs work; describe the production of drugs using GMOs (human insulin as the example); describe how recombinant DNA is made with restriction enzymes and DNA ligase and inserted into cells; describe how microarrays work and what they show; define bioinformatics; and discuss the risks and benefits of GMOs. After this topic, revise the rest of this unit and the related practicals, and the Biology practicals (Core Practicals 14–18) which reinforce these topics.

title: Data Structures — Study Notes
content:
`# Data Structures

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 10 (Data types and structures), examined in AS Paper 2.

Arrays and Lists

Contiguous, indexed, O(1) access; fixed size. 2D arrays: element (i, j) — rows × columns.

Stack (LIFO)

push/pop/peek at one end. Uses: call stacks, undo, expression evaluation, DFS.

Example: evaluating 3 4 + : push 3, push 4, pop both, push 7.

Queue (FIFO)

enqueue at rear, dequeue at front. Uses: print queues, schedulers, BFS. A circular queue reuses vacated slots with head/tail pointers modulo capacity.

Linked List

Nodes with data + pointer. Insert/delete O(1) at a known node; search O(n). Traversal follows next pointers until null.

Hash Table
