Hash function maps keys → index. Collisions resolved by chaining or open addressing. Average O(1) lookup, worst O(n).

Complexity

OperationArrayLinked ListHash
Access by indexO(1)O(n)—
SearchO(n)O(n)O(1) avg
Insert/deleteO(n)O(1)O(1) avg

Exam tips: trace pointers carefully in linked-list diagrams; for circular queues, show head/tail movement and overflow/underflow checks.

Two-dimensional arrays and records

A two-dimensional array stores values in rows and columns, and each element is found with two indexes, usually written A[row, column]. A table of marks for five students in three subjects is a 5 by 3 array. Indexes normally start at 0, so the last element of an array with 8 elements has index 7.

A record groups fields of different data types under one name. A student record might hold a name as a string, an age as an integer and a pass flag as a Boolean. An array of records lets a program store a whole list of students, each with several fields, in one structure.

Exam tip: an array holds one data type throughout, while a record can mix types. Say this when asked to compare them.

Worked example: a stack trace

Start with an empty stack. Push A, push B and push C, so the stack holds A, B, C with C on top. Pop returns C, and a second pop returns B. Push D, and the stack now holds A and D. A trace table with one row per operation is the method examiners expect in a trace question.

Choosing a structure

  • Use a queue for tasks processed in arrival order, such as a print queue.
  • Use a stack for reversing data, undo operations and backtracking, because the last item added is the first removed.
  • Use a hash table for fast lookup by key. A good hash gives average-case constant-time access, but collisions must be handled, usually by chaining or open addressing.

Linked list pointers

Each node holds a data item and a pointer to the next node. Inserting or deleting a node means changing pointers rather than moving elements, so the change is quick once the position is known. Finding a node by its position still means following pointers from the start of the list, which is a linear search.

Exam point: state the behaviour precisely. Describing a queue as first in, last out loses the mark; the correct description is first in, first out (FIFO).

title: Coordination and Response
content:
Coordination and Response

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 14 (statements 14.1–14.5). Nervous coordination and reflex arcs, sense organs and the eye, hormones including insulin and adrenaline, homeostasis, and plant tropic responses.

14.1 Nervous coordination

  • Neurones carry electrical impulses: sensory neurones from receptor to relay neurone, relay neurones within the spinal cord or brain, motor neurones to the effector. A reflex arc bypasses the brain for speed — the pathway is receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
  • The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord, where impulses are coordinated. Synapses between neurones allow one-way transmission because the neurotransmitter is released from the presynaptic knob only.

14.2 Sense organs and the eye

  • The eye: light passes cornea, pupil, lens, retina. The lens changes shape (accommodation) — thicker for near objects, thinner for distant — controlled by the ciliary muscle and suspensory ligaments. The retina contains rods (dim light, many, not colour-sensitive) and cones (bright light, three types, colour vision).
  • Retinal inverted image is corrected by the brain interpreting the signals as upright.

14.3 to 14.4 Hormones and homeostasis

  • Hormones are chemical messengers in the blood from endocrine glands. Adrenaline prepares the body for action: increased heart rate, more blood to muscles, dilated bronchioles, higher blood glucose.
  • Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake and conversion to glycogen; glucagon raises it. Diabetes type 1 is caused by too little insulin; type 2 is when cells respond less to insulin.
  • Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment. Blood glucose control is a negative feedback loop: rising glucose triggers insulin release, falling glucose triggers glucagon release.

14.5 Tropic responses

  • Phototropism: auxin moves to the shaded side of a shoot, causing cells there to elongate, so the shoot bends towards light. In roots, auxin at high concentration inhibits growth, so the root grows downwards — gravitropism.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Reflex arc reasoning, applied to why you move your hand from a hot plate before you feel pain: the reflex arc through the spinal cord is faster than a pathway up to the brain, so the effector responds first. Explain with the shorter pathway — that comparison is the mark.
  • Accommodation reasoning, applied to focusing on a near object: the ciliary muscle contracts, suspensory ligaments slacken, the lens becomes more curved and refracts light more strongly. State all four steps in order; each link is worth a mark.
  • Negative feedback explanation, applied to blood glucose after a meal: glucose rises, the pancreas detects it, insulin is released into the blood, cells take up more glucose and the liver converts it to glycogen, so glucose falls back to normal. Name the sensor, the effector and the response — a negative feedback answer needs all three.
  • Tropism mechanism, applied to a shoot tip exposed to unilateral light: auxin is redistributed to the shaded side, cells elongate faster there, and the shoot bends towards the light. Mention the inhibitor effect in roots for the full comparison when the question covers both.

Common errors

  • Saying insulin converts glucose to CO₂. It promotes glycogen conversion and uptake.
  • Calling the pupil the light-sensitive part. The retina detects light; the pupil is the opening.
  • Explaining tropism with "the plant wants light". Use auxin and differential growth.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation

Mathematics — A2. The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Key areas to revise

  • Range and Quartiles
  • Variance and Standard Deviation
  • Grouped Data
  • Combining and Scaling Datasets

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

### Worked example Data are 2, 4 and 6. The mean is 4 and the deviations are −2, 0 and 2. The squared deviations sum to 8, so the population variance is 8/3 ≈ 2.67 and the standard deviation is √(8/3) ≈ 1.63. The range is 6 − 2 = 4.

title: Differentiation — Study Notes
content:
Differentiation

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11), sat at AS. Differentiation finds how fast y changes with x. Most questions ask for one of three things: a gradient at a point, a tangent or normal, or the nature of a stationary point.

Start from a question

The curve C has equation y = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 1.

  1. Find dy/dx.
  2. Find the coordinates of the stationary points and state their nature.
  3. Find the equation of the normal to C at x = 3.

Part 1. dy/dx = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2).

Part 2. dy/dx = 0 at x = 1 and x = 2. When x = 1, y = 4, and when x = 2, y = 3. Next, d²y/dx² = 12x − 18. At (1, 4) this is −6, so the point is a maximum. At (2, 3) it is 6, so the point is a minimum.

Part 3. At x = 3, dy/dx = 6(2)(1) = 12, so the normal has gradient −1/12. Also y = 54 − 81 + 36 − 1 = 8, so the point is (3, 8). The normal is y − 8 = −(x − 3)/12, which gives x + 12y − 99 = 0.

The power rule

If y = axⁿ, then dy/dx = naxⁿ⁻¹, for any rational n. A constant differentiates to zero. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers first: 4√x − 6/x² = 4x^(1/2) − 6x⁻², so dy/dx = 2/√x + 12/x³.

Expand before you differentiate

Differentiation works term by term, so multiply out any brackets first. Example: y = (x + 2)(x − 5) = x² − 3x − 10, so dy/dx = 2x − 3.

A zero gradient is not always a turning point

Use the second derivative when it is non-zero at the point. If it is zero, test the sign of dy/dx on each side. Example: y = x⁴ − 4x³ gives dy/dx = 4x²(x − 3). At x = 0 the gradient is negative on both sides, so the curve keeps falling and (0, 0) is not a maximum or minimum. At x = 3 the gradient changes from negative to positive, so (3, −27) is a minimum.

Tangents and normals

Substitute x into the original equation to find y, and into dy/dx to find the gradient. The tangent uses that gradient, and the normal uses its negative reciprocal. Write both as y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and simplify.

Traps that cost marks

  • Differentiating a product factor by factor instead of expanding it first.
  • Giving the normal the same gradient as the tangent, rather than the negative reciprocal.
  • Giving only the x-value of a stationary point, rather than its coordinates (x, y).
  • Calling a point a maximum or minimum from dy/dx = 0 alone, without checking the nature.

Worked example: the chain rule

Differentiate y = (3x − 2)⁵. Treat this as an outer power of an inner linear function. The derivative of the outer function, with the inside kept as a single unit, is 5(3x − 2)⁴. Multiply by the derivative of the inside, which is 3. So dy/dx = 15(3x − 2)⁴. Forgetting the factor 3 from the inside is the most frequent error on this type of question, and it loses the accuracy mark even when the power rule has been applied correctly.

Worked example: the product rule

For y = x² sin x, let u = x² and v = sin x. Then dy/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx = x² cos x + 2x sin x. Write the two products out separately and then collect like terms. If the question asks for the gradient at a particular point, substitute only after the derivative has been simplified, because substituting first makes it harder to spot an algebra slip.

title: Enzymes
content:
Enzymes

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 5 (statement 5.1). Enzymes as biological catalysts, lock-and-key specificity, and the effects of temperature and pH that top-grade explanations hinge on.

5.1 Enzymes

  • Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions in living cells without being changed. Each enzyme has an active site with a specific shape; only a substrate with a matching shape binds, which is the lock-and-key model.
  • Rate increases with temperature because particles move faster and collide more often, up to an optimum. Above the optimum, bonds maintaining the enzyme's tertiary structure break and the enzyme is denatured — the active site changes shape permanently.
  • Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Away from it, ionic bonds in the enzyme are disrupted and the active site shape changes; extreme pH also denatures.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Graph interpretation, applied to an enzyme-rate graph against temperature: rate rises to the optimum near 40 °C for human enzymes, then falls steeply to zero. The rise is explained by collision frequency; the fall by denaturation. Both halves are needed for full marks — describing only the rise is the classic incomplete answer.
  • Reasoning chain, applied to pepsin in the stomach: its optimum is around pH 2 because of gastric acid, and at pH 7 it becomes almost inactive. Explain with the active site ionisation, not just "pH changes the rate".
  • Experimental design, applied to an investigation of enzyme concentration: the independent variable is enzyme concentration, the dependent variable the rate of product formation, and the controls include substrate concentration, temperature and pH — all held at the optimum. Naming substrate concentration as a control shows understanding that it must be in excess for enzyme concentration to be the limiting factor.

Common errors

  • Saying enzymes are "used up" or "consumed". They emerge from each reaction unchanged.
  • Saying high temperature "kills" the enzyme. Denaturation is the precise word — enzymes are not alive.
  • Explaining the fall after the optimum with "fewer collisions". Denaturation is the cause.

title: Diseases and Immunity
content:
Diseases and Immunity

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 10 (statement 10.1). Pathogens and transmission, the body's defences, the immune response, antibodies and vaccination.

10.1 Diseases and immunity

  • Pathogens are microorganisms that cause disease: bacteria produce toxins, viruses invade and destroy host cells. Transmission routes include direct contact, water and food, air droplets, and vectors such as mosquitoes.
  • Non-specific defences: skin as a barrier, mucus and cilia trapping pathogens in the airways, stomach acid killing ingested microbes, and phagocytes engulfing pathogens.
  • The immune response: phagocytes engulf the pathogen and display its antigens; lymphocytes produce antibodies specific to that antigen, which clump the pathogens for destruction and neutralise toxins. Memory lymphocytes remain, so a second exposure produces a faster, stronger response.
  • Vaccination introduces a dead or attenuated pathogen or its antigens, stimulating antibody production and memory cells without causing disease. Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Primary versus secondary response, applied to an antibody-level graph: the first exposure shows a lag of several days then a modest peak; the second shows a shorter lag and a much higher peak. Explain with memory lymphocytes already present, dividing rapidly and differentiating into plasma cells. Use all three of faster, stronger and longer.
  • Evaluation reasoning, applied to why vaccination of a high proportion of a population protects unvaccinated individuals: with fewer hosts, the pathogen cannot spread easily, so the chance of an unvaccinated person meeting it falls. That is herd immunity — name it and explain the mechanism of reduced transmission.
  • Disease control reasoning, applied to an outbreak: vaccination reduces susceptibility, isolation reduces contact, and vector control removes the route. Match each measure to the transmission stage it interrupts — that matching is the examinable skill.

Common errors

  • Saying antibiotics kill viruses. Antibiotics work on bacteria; viruses are treated by vaccines or not at all.
  • Describing antibodies as killing pathogens directly. They agglutinate and neutralise; phagocytes do the destroying.
  • Forgetting memory cells as the reason the secondary response is faster.

title: Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Number — Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Mathematics — OL. conversions between fractions, decimals and percentages; percentage change; reverse percentages; compound change.

  • 1. Conversions
  • 2. Operating on fractions
  • 3. Percentage change
  • 4. Reverse percentages
  • 5. Compound change

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

To convert between forms, use the link: a fraction multiplied by 100 gives a percentage, and a decimal multiplied by 100 gives a percentage. To find a percentage of an amount, write the percentage as a decimal, for example 35 percent is 0.35. To increase by a percentage, multiply by one plus the decimal; to decrease, multiply by one minus it.

Simplify a fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by their highest common factor. To add or subtract fractions, find a common denominator first. Give answers in the form the question asks for, and leave an exact fraction in its simplest form unless told to round.

title: Human Influences on Ecosystems
content:
Human Influences on Ecosystems

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 20 (statements 20.1–20.4). Food supply, habitat destruction, pollution including eutrophication and greenhouse gases, and conservation.

20.1 to 20.4 Human influences

  • Food supply is increased by selective breeding, fertilisers, pesticides, controlled grazing and irrigation — each carrying trade-offs such as pollution, habitat loss or cost.
  • Habitat destruction through deforestation, urban development and intensive farming reduces biodiversity and removes carbon sinks, adding to atmospheric carbon dioxide.
  • Pollution: sewage and fertiliser runoff cause eutrophication; pesticides accumulate in food chains (bioaccumulation); air pollutants include carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen; greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane enhance the greenhouse effect and warm the climate.
  • Conservation maintains biodiversity: protected areas, replanting, breeding programmes, reducing pollution, and sustainable harvesting. It is needed because species loss is irreversible and ecosystems provide services humans depend on.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Evaluation chain, applied to a proposal to build on a wetland: weigh the economic benefit against the loss of flood protection, water filtration, and habitat for migratory species. A top-band answer states a judgement and supports it with ecosystem services, not feelings.
  • Pollution reasoning, applied to DDT concentrating up a food chain: it is not excreted or broken down, so it accumulates in fat at each trophic level, reaching highest concentrations in top predators. Name bioaccumulation and biomagnification and give the consequence — thin eggshells in birds of prey.
  • Greenhouse reasoning, applied to why methane matters: it absorbs more infrared per molecule than carbon dioxide, so although there is less of it, its warming contribution is disproportionately large. Quantity and per-molecule effect both belong in the answer.

Common errors

  • Confusing the greenhouse effect with ozone depletion. They are different problems with different gases.
  • Saying pesticides "poison the food chain" without the concentration mechanism.
  • Claiming conservation means complete prohibition of use. Sustainable use is a core conservation strategy.

title: Edexcel International A Level Chemistry Kinetics Revision Notes
content:
Kinetics: Edexcel International A Level Chemistry A2 Revision Notes

This topic belongs to Edexcel International A Level Chemistry WCH14 Topic 11 Kinetics. It covers the quantitative study of reaction speeds, the factors affecting them, experimental techniques, rate equations, order of reaction, reaction mechanisms including halogenoalkane hydrolysis, catalysts, core practicals, and the Arrhenius equation to calculate activation energy.

Definitions and Key Terms

To master kinetics, you must learn precise definitions for key terminology used in exam marking points.

  • Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time, with units mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
  • Rate equation is an expression showing how the rate of reaction depends on the concentrations of reactants, given in the form rate = k[A]m[B]n where m and n are the orders with respect to specific substances and are 0, 1 or 2.
  • Order with respect to a substance is the power to which the concentration of that reactant is raised in the rate equation.
  • Overall order of a reaction is the sum of all the individual orders of the reactants in the rate equation (m + n + ...).
  • Rate constant (k) is the proportionality constant that links the rate of reaction to the concentrations in the rate equation at a fixed temperature.
  • Half-life (t1/2) is the time taken for the concentration of a reactant to decrease to half of its initial value.
  • Rate-determining step is the slowest step in a multi-step reaction mechanism, which controls the overall rate of the reaction.
  • Activation energy (Ea) is the minimum kinetic energy that colliding particles must possess for a successful reaction to occur.
  • Heterogeneous catalyst is a catalyst in a different physical state or phase from the reactants, typically providing a solid surface for gas-phase reactions.
  • Homogeneous catalyst is a catalyst in the same physical state or phase as the reactants.

Experimental Techniques and Monitoring Methods

Choosing and justifying the correct experimental technique to obtain rate data is essential for both practical endorsements and written papers.

  • Titration involves quenching reaction aliquots at timed intervals and titrating against a standard solution, suitable for slow reactions like the acid-catalysed iodination of propanone.
  • Colorimetry measures the absorbance of light by a coloured species over time, ideal for reactions involving iodine or transition metal ions.
  • Mass change uses a sensitive balance to track mass loss over time as a gas evolves, suitable for reactions producing carbon dioxide.
  • Volume of gas evolved uses a gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder over water to measure gas collected per unit time.
  • Initial-rate method involves carrying out separate experiments where different initial concentrations of one reagent are used while others are kept constant, measuring only the initial rate to avoid complications from reactant depletion.
  • Clock reaction is a convenient approximation of the initial-rate method where a single measurement is taken of the time taken for a specific visual change (such as a sudden colour change) to occur, assuming initial rate is proportional to 1 / t provided less than 15 percent of the reaction occurs.
  • Continuous monitoring method generates data over the entire course of a single reaction run to enable concentration-time or volume-time graphs to be plotted.

Deducing Reaction Orders and Calculations

You must be able to deduce the order with respect to a substance using different graphical and numerical representations.

  • Concentration-time graphs show how reactant concentration changes over time. A straight-line downward slope indicates a zero-order reaction with a constant rate. A downward curve with a constant half-life indicates a first-order reaction. A downward curve where the half-life increases as concentration decreases indicates a second-order reaction.
  • Rate-concentration graphs plot rate on the y-axis against concentration on the x-axis. A horizontal straight line parallel to the x-axis indicates zero order (rate is independent of concentration). A straight line passing through the origin indicates first order (rate is directly proportional to concentration). A curve with an increasing gradient (parabola) passing through the origin indicates second order (rate is proportional to concentration squared).
  • Initial-rate calculations compare how changes in initial concentration affect initial rate to find integer orders of 0, 1 or 2.
  • Half-life calculations use data from concentration-time graphs. Identifying a constant half-life is definitive proof that a reaction is first order with respect to that reactant.

Mechanisms and Rate-Determining Steps

The rate equation provides direct evidence for the composition of the rate-determining step and helps deduce reaction pathways.

  • Deducing rate-determining step from a rate equation means any species appearing in the rate equation with a non-zero order must be involved in the rate-determining step or in preceding fast steps that equilibrate before it. Stoichiometric coefficients of reactants in the rate-determining step match their orders in the rate equation.
  • Deducing reaction mechanism uses the rate equation alongside the overall stoichiometric equation. Fast steps before the rate-determining step introduce intermediate concentrations that can be substituted using equilibrium expressions.
  • Hydrolysis of halogenoalkanes provides classic evidence for mechanisms. Primary halogenoalkanes undergo SN2 hydrolysis, which is second-order overall (rate = k[halogenoalkane][OH−]), involving a single concerted step with a transition state. Tertiary halogenoalkanes undergo SN1 hydrolysis, which is first-order overall (rate = k[halogenoalkane]), where the slow rate-determining step is the heterolytic fission of the carbon-halogen bond to form a carbocation intermediate before rapid attack by the nucleophile.
  • Acid-catalysed iodination of propanone involves obtaining data to calculate the order with respect to propanone, hydrogen ions, and iodine. Iodine is found to be zero-order, while propanone and hydrogen ions are first-order. This data proves that neither iodine nor the second step is in the rate-determining step, leading to a mechanism featuring a slow, acid-catalysed tautomerization step forming an enol, followed by rapid reaction with iodine.

Heterogeneous Catalysis in Industry

Solid catalysts function by physical and chemical adsorption of gas-phase reactants.

  • Solid heterogeneous catalysts provide an active surface where reactant molecules are adsorbed.
  • Adsorption weakens internal covalent bonds within the reactant molecules, lowering the activation energy.
  • Reacted species subsequently desorb from the surface, freeing active sites for further catalytic cycles. Examples include iron in the Haber process and platinum, palladium, and rhodium in catalytic converters.

Core Practicals and Activation Energy

Experimental determination of activation energy links rate constants at different temperatures.

  • Core Practical 9a involves following the rate of the iodine-propanone reaction by a titrimetric method, quenching reaction samples with sodium hydrogencarbonate at timed intervals and titrating remaining iodine with standard sodium thiosulfate solution.
  • Core Practical 9b involves investigating a clock reaction, such as the Harcourt-Esson hydrogen peroxide-iodide reaction or the iodine clock, measuring time t for a colour change to appear using varying initial volumes of reagents.
  • Core Practical 10 involves finding the activation energy of a reaction by measuring reaction rates at different temperatures, calculating rate constants k, and applying the Arrhenius equation.
  • Arrhenius equation is given as k = A e^(−Ea / RT), where R is the ideal gas constant (8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) and T is temperature in Kelvin.
  • Taking natural logarithms yields ln k = (−Ea / R) × (1 / T) + ln A.
  • Plotting ln k on the y-axis against 1 / T on the x-axis produces a straight line with gradient equal to −Ea / R, allowing Ea to be calculated from gradient × (−R).

Typical mistakes

  • Mistake: Assuming the orders in a rate equation match the stoichiometric coefficients in the overall balanced equation. Correction: Remember that rate equations must be determined experimentally, as overall equations show only reactants and products, not the step-by-step mechanism.
  • Mistake: Stating that the rate constant k changes when reactant concentrations are altered. Correction: The rate constant k is only affected by changes in temperature and the addition of a catalyst. Changing concentration alters the rate, not k.
  • Mistake: Forgetting temperature must be in Kelvin when using the Arrhenius equation. Correction: Always convert Celsius to Kelvin by adding 273.15 before calculating 1 / T or using ln k.
  • Mistake: Confusing the units of k for different overall orders. Correction: Derive the units dynamically by rearranging the rate equation: units of k = (units of rate) / (units of concentration) raised to the power of the overall order.

Exam-style questions

  1. Question: The reaction between nitrogen monoxide and hydrogen has the rate equation rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. State the order with respect to NO, the order with respect to H₂, and the overall order of the reaction. Answer: Order with respect to NO is 2; order with respect to H₂ is 1; overall order is 3 (obtained by summing 2 + 1).
  2. Question: Deduce the units of the rate constant k for a third-order overall reaction where rate is measured in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ and concentration in mol dm⁻³. Answer: Rearranging gives k = rate / [concentration]³. Units = (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) / (mol dm⁻³)³ = s⁻¹ mol⁻² dm⁶.
  3. Question: In an experiment, a student plots a concentration-time graph for a reactant and finds that successive half-lives are constant at 45 seconds. Deduce the order of the reaction with respect to this reactant. Answer: A constant half-life is the defining characteristic of a first-order reaction.
  4. Question: Explain why tertiary halogenoalkanes undergo hydrolysis via an SN1 mechanism whereas primary halogenoalkanes undergo an SN2 mechanism. Answer: Tertiary halogenoalkanes form a relatively stable tertiary carbocation intermediate due to the electron-releasing inductive effect of three alkyl groups, favouring SN1. Primary halogenoalkanes cannot form stable carbocations, so the attack by the nucleophile must occur simultaneously in a concerted SN2 transition state.
  5. Question: A graph of ln k against 1 / T for a reaction gives a straight line with a gradient of −12400 K. Calculate the activation energy Ea in kJ mol⁻¹. Use R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Answer: Gradient = −Ea / R, so Ea = −(gradient) × R = −(−12400) × 8.31 = 103044 J mol⁻¹ = 103 kJ mol⁻¹ to 3 significant figures.

Use these notes alongside active recall of definitions, rigorous practice of initial-rate data tables, and past paper calculations on the Arrhenius equation. Next, revise Equilibria (Topic 12) to connect reaction kinetics with thermodynamic and dynamic stability.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Order from initial rates, applied to data showing the rate quadruples when [A] doubles with [B] constant: the order with respect to A is 2, because 2² = 4. Read the orders from the experiments, not from the coefficients in the equation, because the orders are found experimentally.
  • Rate constant units, applied to rate = k[A]²: rate is in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ and [A]² is in mol² dm⁻⁶, so k is in mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹. If rate = 2.4 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ at [A] = 0.20 mol dm⁻³, then k = 2.4 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.040 = 0.060 mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹.
  • Rate-determining step: the slowest step sets the rate, so the orders in the rate equation contain only the species up to and including that step. Catalysts appear in the rate equation if they take part in the rate-determining step.
  • Activation energy from Arrhenius data: a plot of ln k against 1/T gives a straight line with gradient −Ea ÷ R. Use the gradient, and convert the temperature to kelvin before you plot.

title: Probability — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Probability

Mathematics — A2. For an event A with P(A) = p: 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A). For mutually exclusive events, probabilities add: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B). For events that can occur together, subtract the overlap:

Key areas to revise

  • Basic Rules
  • Venn Diagrams
  • Tree Diagrams
  • Conditional Probability
  • Independence

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key points to remember

For any two events, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Conditional probability is P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Events A and B are independent only when P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), so test this before you multiply probabilities.

Use a Venn diagram or a tree diagram to organise the information. On a tree diagram, multiply along each branch and add the branches that give the outcome you want. Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen, so P(A ∩ B) = 0 for them, and this is a different idea from independence.

title: Materials: Deformation — Study Notes
content:
Materials: deformation

Edexcel International A Level Physics — Unit 1 (WPH11), sat at AS.

Stress and strain

  • Stress = F ÷ A, where A is the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. Unit: pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻².
  • Strain = extension ÷ original length. It has no unit.

Young modulus

Young modulus E = stress ÷ strain, measured in the region where stress is proportional to strain. Unit: Pa.

Force–extension behaviour

  • Up to the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force (Hooke's law), and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
  • Up to the elastic limit, the material returns to its original length when unloaded. This is elastic deformation.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, the material is plastically deformed and does not return to its original length. The graph curves, and the energy in the extension is not recovered.

Energy stored

The elastic energy stored in a stretched material equals the area under its force–extension graph up to the point of interest. For a spring obeying Hooke's law, E = ½Fx = ½kx².

Worked example: a wire of cross-sectional area 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is pulled by 500 N. Stress = 500 ÷ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.5 × 10⁶ Pa. If it extends by 1.0 mm from an original length of 2.0 m, strain = 0.001 ÷ 2.0 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, so E = 2.5 × 10⁶ ÷ 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.0 × 10⁹ Pa.

Exam tips: convert the area to m² and the extension to m before calculating. Strain has no unit, so do not write a unit for it. Say "the limit of proportionality" and "the elastic limit" as separate ideas.

Stored elastic energy and Hooke's law

Within the limit of proportionality, extension is proportional to force, F = kx, and the stiffness k depends on the material and its dimensions. The elastic strain energy stored in a stretched wire is equal to the area under the force-extension graph, E = ½Fx. For a material, the Young modulus E = stress / strain. Beyond the elastic limit the material deforms plastically and does not return to its original length.

Exam tip: state the limit of proportionality on the graph, because the energy formula only applies while the material obeys Hooke's law.

Worked example: a stretched wire with a load

A steel wire 1.5 m long and 0.80 mm in diameter is loaded with a 20 kg mass. The cross-sectional area is π(0.40 × 10⁻³)² ≈ 5.03 × 10⁻⁷ m². The force is F = mg = 20 × 9.81 = 196 N, so the stress is 196 ÷ (5.03 × 10⁻⁷) ≈ 3.9 × 10⁸ Pa.

If the wire stretches by 1.1 mm, the strain is 0.0011 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 7.3 × 10⁻⁴, and E = stress ÷ strain = 3.9 × 10⁸ ÷ 7.3 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 5.3 × 10¹¹ Pa. Quote the Young modulus with its unit and to two significant figures, and check that the value is in the range expected for the material: steel is roughly 2 × 10¹¹ Pa, so a result far from that points to an area or unit error.

Comparing materials

  • A stiff material has a large Young modulus: for a given stress, it produces a small strain.
  • A brittle material fractures soon after the elastic limit, with little or no plastic deformation, so its graph stops abruptly.
  • A ductile material, such as copper, undergoes large plastic deformation before it breaks, so its graph shows a long curved section after the elastic limit.

Area under the graph

For a non-linear force–extension graph, the energy stored is still the area under the curve. Count the squares, or split the region into a triangle and a rectangle, and convert the result to joules using the scale factors. Only the energy up to the elastic limit can be recovered when the load is removed; the rest is dissipated as heat.

Hysteresis and loading cycles

When a material is loaded and then unloaded, the unloading curve may not retrace the loading curve. The region enclosed between the two curves is energy dissipated per cycle, often as heat. Rubber bands and car tyres show this, which is why they warm up when repeatedly deformed.

  • Strain is extension divided by the original length, so do not use the stretched length.
  • Young modulus has the unit of pascal, the same as stress, because strain is dimensionless.
  • Only a sample loaded within its elastic region returns to the same length; a permanent set after unloading means plastic deformation has occurred.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the diameter as the radius in the area formula, which quadruples the area.
  • Calling the gradient of the stress-strain graph the "stiffness". Stiffness belongs to the force-extension graph; the gradient of stress against strain gives E.
  • Quoting Hooke's law as valid beyond the limit of proportionality, where extension is no longer proportional to force.

title: Gas Exchange in Humans
content:
Gas Exchange in Humans

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 11 (statement 11.1). The breathing system, ventilation, alveolar adaptations, and the comparison of inspired and expired air.

11.1 Gas exchange in humans

  • The breathing system: trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli, supported by cartilage rings and moved by the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.
  • Ventilation: inhalation — the diaphragm contracts and flattens, the external intercostal muscles contract lifting the ribs, volume increases, pressure falls below atmospheric, air flows in. Exhalation is the reverse, mostly passive at rest.
  • Gas exchange in the alveoli happens by diffusion down concentration gradients: oxygen from alveolar air into the blood, carbon dioxide from the blood into the alveoli to be exhaled.
  • Alveoli are adapted by an enormous surface area, a one-cell-thick wall, a dense capillary network, and a moist lining in which gases dissolve.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Air composition reasoning, applied to expired air compared with inspired: oxygen falls from 21% to about 16%, carbon dioxide rises from 0.04% to about 4%, and water vapour is saturated. Explain both changes: oxygen was taken up by blood in the alveoli and carbon dioxide added by the same diffusion gradient in reverse.
  • Pressure reasoning, applied to inhalation: the key link is that an increase in volume decreases pressure, so air rushes in to equalise. Answer in the order diaphragm contracts → volume increases → pressure decreases → air enters. Examiners mark each link.
  • Smoking effects, applied to explaining why long-term smoking reduces gas exchange: tar damages cilia so mucus is not cleared, emphysema destroys alveolar walls reducing surface area, and carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin reducing oxygen carriage. Name the three separate mechanisms — each is its own mark.

Common errors

  • Saying the diaphragm "moves down to let air in" without the muscle contraction and pressure links.
  • Confusing ventilation (breathing) with gas exchange (diffusion across the alveolar wall).
  • Claiming carbon dioxide is "toxic". Its main measured effect is on blood pH, and it is the level of carbon dioxide that drives the breathing rate.

title: Descriptive Writing — Study Notes
content:
Descriptive writing succeeds when the reader can see, hear, smell or feel the scene. It is built from precise detail, controlled sentence rhythm and a clear sense of focus.

Sensory detail

Use all five senses where they fit, not only sight. Specific nouns and verbs do more work than general adjectives.

Precision

  • Replace weak words such as "nice" or "went" with exact ones: "gleaming", "stumbled".
  • Use concrete nouns: "rust-flecked railings" rather than "old fence".
  • Choose one striking image and develop it, rather than listing many.

Show, do not tell

Show a feeling through action and detail rather than naming it. "She was furious" tells the reader. "Her jaw tightened and she slammed the cupboard door" shows it.

Sentence variety

Varying sentence length controls pace. Long sentences can build a scene slowly, and short ones can cut the mood or create a jolt. Vary your openings too, rather than starting every sentence with the subject.

Structure

Organise the piece around a clear focus. Options include:

  • A close-up that moves outward, from a detail to the wider scene.
  • A changing viewpoint, following a person through a place.
  • A fixed point in time that shows change, such as dawn to dusk.

End with an image or a reflection that returns to your focus. Avoid ending on a plain statement of fact.

title: Redox Equilibria Revision Notes A2 Chemistry
content:
Redox Equilibria A2 Level Chemistry

This revision note covers Edexcel International A Level Chemistry — Unit 5 (WCH15), Topic 16, exploring redox equilibria, standard electrode potentials, electrochemical cells, thermodynamics of redox reactions, cell diagrams, advanced redox titrations, uncertainty analysis, and fuel cells.

Oxidation and Reduction in s-, p- and d-Block Elements

Redox processes involve electron transfer and shifts in oxidation numbers, applying seamlessly across s-, p-, and d-block elements.

  • Oxidation is defined as loss of electrons and an increase in oxidation state. Reduction is gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation state.
  • The reducing agent is oxidised by losing electrons, whereas the oxidising agent is reduced by gaining electrons.
  • These rules apply whether dealing with simple s-block metal ions, p-block non-metals, or complex d-block transition metal ions showing multiple stable oxidation states.

Standard Electrode Potentials and the Standard Hydrogen Electrode

Standard electrode potentials provide a quantitative measure of a species' tendency to be reduced.

  • Standard electrode potentials, E-zero, are measured strictly at 298 K temperature, 100 kPa pressure of gases, and 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration of ions.
  • The standard hydrogen electrode serves as the universal reference electrode with an E-zero value defined as exactly 0.00 V.
  • A reference electrode is necessary because absolute electrode potentials cannot be measured in isolation; only potential differences can be determined.
  • The standard hydrogen electrode uses platinum foil coated in platinum black, immersed in 1.00 mol dm-3 hydrogen ions, with hydrogen gas bubbled at 100 kPa and 298 K.

Measuring Electrode Potentials and Electrochemical Cells

Different half-cell assemblies are required depending on the physical states of the species involved.

  • For metals or non-metals in contact with their aqueous ions, a metal rod is dipped into a 1.00 mol dm-3 solution of its ions, or an inert platinum electrode is used for non-metals like chlorine gas bubbling over chloride ions.
  • For systems involving ions of the same element with different oxidation numbers, an inert platinum electrode is immersed in a solution containing both species at 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration.
  • CORE PRACTICAL 12 involves investigating electrochemical cells by measuring cell potentials for various metal-metal ion combinations and redox systems.

Cell Diagrams and Standard Cell EMF Calculations

Electrochemical cells can be represented concisely using conventional notation and evaluated mathematically.

  • Cell diagrams use a single vertical line to represent a phase boundary and a double vertical line to represent a salt bridge.
  • Oxidised forms are written closer to the salt bridge in conventional half-cell representations, with the more negative half-cell conventionally written on the left.
  • Calculate standard cell emf, E-zero-cell, using the formula: E-zero-cell = E-zero(reduction) - E-zero(oxidation).

Thermodynamic Feasibility, Entropy, and Equilibrium Constants

Standard electrode potentials connect directly to thermodynamic feasibility, entropy changes, and equilibrium constants.

  • Standard electrode potentials are also known as standard reduction potentials and are listed in an electrochemical series.
  • A positive E-zero-cell value indicates that the forward reaction is thermodynamically feasible under standard conditions.
  • E-zero-cell is directly proportional to the total entropy change, delta-S-total, and to ln K for a reaction, meaning larger positive E-zero values correspond to larger equilibrium constants and greater spontaneity.
  • Standard electrode potentials can predict the thermodynamic feasibility of disproportionation reactions, where a species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.

Limitations of Standard Electrode Potentials

Thermodynamic predictions do not always match real-world outcomes due to kinetic and condition factors.

  • Predictions made using standard electrode potentials have limitations due to the kinetic stability of systems; a reaction may be thermodynamically feasible with a positive E-zero-cell, but have an activation energy so high that the reaction rate is negligibly slow.
  • Departures from standard conditions, such as non-standard concentrations or temperatures, alter actual electrode potentials according to the Nernst equation, potentially reversing feasibility.

Redox Titrations and Uncertainty Analysis

Volumetric analysis using redox titrations allows accurate determination of concentrations in structured and unstructured problems.

  • CORE PRACTICALS 13a and 13b involve carrying out redox titrations with iron(II) ions and potassium manganate(VII), and with sodium thiosulfate and iodine.
  • Manganate(VII) titrations are self-indicating, turning from purple to colourless at the end point when excess MnO4- ions react to form colourless Mn2+ ions.
  • Iodine-thiosulfate titrations use starch indicator, which forms a deep blue-black complex with iodine and turns colourless at the end point when all iodine is consumed.
  • Discussing the uncertainty of measurements requires evaluating percentage errors of apparatus like burettes and volumetric flasks, and their implications for the validity of final results.

Fuel Cells

Fuel cells convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy through redox reactions.

  • Fuel cells use the energy released on the reaction of a fuel with oxygen to generate a voltage, utilising hydrogen-rich fuels like hydrogen and methanol.
  • In an acidic electrolyte hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode: H2 yields 2H+ + 2e-, and oxygen is reduced at the cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- yields 2H2O.
  • In an alkaline electrolyte hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, hydrogen reacts at the anode: H2 + 2OH- yields 2H2H2O + 2e-, and oxygen reacts at the cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e- yields 4OH-.

Typical Mistakes

  • Mistake: Confusing the left and right sides of a cell diagram. Correction: Remember reduction always occurs at the right-hand electrode and oxidation at the left-hand electrode in conventional notation.
  • Mistake: Omitting the inert platinum electrode in half-cell descriptions containing only aqueous ions. Correction: Always include platinum in phase boundaries if no other solid conductor is present.
  • Mistake: Forgetting that E-zero-cell values are independent of the stoichiometry multipliers used to balance half-equations. Correction: Never multiply E-zero values by balancing coefficients when calculating E-zero-cell.
  • Mistake: Assuming a reaction with a positive E-zero-cell will occur rapidly at room temperature. Correction: Always consider kinetic stability; a positive E-zero only proves thermodynamic feasibility, not reaction rate.

Exam-Style Questions

  1. Question: State the standard conditions required for measuring standard electrode potentials. Answer: 298 K temperature, 100 kPa pressure of gases, and 1.00 mol dm-3 concentration of ions.
  2. Question: Write the conventional cell diagram for a cell formed by Zn(s) / Zn2+(aq) and Cu2+(aq) / Cu(s). Answer: Zn(s) | Zn2+(aq, 1.00 mol dm-3) || Cu2+(aq, 1.00 mol dm-3) | Cu(s).
  3. Question: Calculate the E-zero-cell for zinc and copper given E-zero(Zn2+/Zn) = −0.76 V and E-zero(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V. Answer: E-zero-cell = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V.
  4. Question: State the colour change at the end point in a titration of potassium manganate(VII) with iron(II) ions. Answer: From colourless or very pale pink to permanent pale pink.
  5. Question: Write the anode half-equation for an alkaline hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell. Answer: H2 + 2OH- yields 2H2O + 2e-.

Use these notes alongside active practice of past paper calculation questions, ensuring all standard conditions and half-equation balancing steps are memorised. Revise transition metal chemistry next.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Cell EMF, applied to a zinc and copper cell: E(cell) = E(cathode, reduction) − E(anode, oxidation) = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. Zinc is the anode because it has the more negative potential, and it is oxidised. Always identify the anode and cathode before you subtract.
  • Feasibility: ΔG = −nFE, so a positive E(cell) gives a negative ΔG and a feasible reaction. Under non-standard conditions, E changes with concentration, so a reaction can be feasible even when E(cell) under standard conditions is small.
  • Redox titration, applied to Fe²⁺ with acidified MnO₄⁻: 5Fe²⁺ + MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ → 5Fe³⁺ + Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O. The ratio is 5 : 1. The permanganate is its own indicator, so the end point is the first permanent pale pink colour.
  • Limitations of E° values: they apply only under standard conditions and say nothing about the rate. A reaction can be thermodynamically feasible but kinetically slow, so a metal can appear reactive from its potential yet react slowly in practice.

title: Quick Revision: Organic Chemistry
content:
Quick Revision: Organic Chemistry: Carbonyls, Carboxylic Acids and Chirality

Chemistry — A2. Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH14, Topic 15, covers carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, and chirality, including optical isomerism, reactions, and tests.

  • Carbonyl compounds: aldehydes and ketones contain the carbonyl group, C=O, and undergo nucleophilic addition reactions.
  • Reactions and tests: Fehling's, Benedict's, Tollens' reagent, acidified dichromate(VI) ions, and 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) are used to identify carbonyl compounds.
  • Carboxylic acids: contain the carboxyl group, COOH, and can be prepared by oxidation of alcohols or aldehydes, and hydrolysis of nitriles.
  • Chirality: optical isomerism results from chiral centres in molecules with asymmetric carbon atoms, and optical activity is the ability of a single optical isomer to rotate plane-polarised light.

Worked example

Draw the structural formula of the optical isomer of 2-bromobutane. Answer: (1) CH₃CH(Br)CH₂CH₃ and its non-superimposable mirror image.

Key points to remember

Optical isomerism is a result of chirality in molecules with a single chiral centre, and racemic mixtures contain equal amounts of enantiomers. Carboxylic acids can form hydrogen bonds, affecting their physical properties, and can be prepared by oxidation and hydrolysis reactions.

How to use this: skim the key points, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Acyl Chlorides and Esters

Acyl chlorides contain the functional group −COCl and are highly reactive derivatives of carboxylic acids. They undergo addition-elimination reactions with water to form carboxylic acids, with alcohols to form esters, with concentrated ammonia to form primary amides, and with primary amines to form secondary amides. Esters contain the −COO− group and can be hydrolysed under acidic conditions to give a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, or under alkaline conditions to give a carboxylate salt and an alcohol. Polyesters like Terylene are formed via condensation polymerisation between a dicarboxylic acid (or diester) and a diol, eliminating small molecules such as water.

Spectroscopy and Analytical Techniques

Mass spectrometry provides accurate relative molecular masses to four decimal places, allowing chemists to determine molecular formulae. Carbon-13 NMR spectroscopy indicates the number of carbon environments and their chemical shift values in a molecule. Proton (1H) NMR spectroscopy reveals the types of hydrogen environments, their relative peak areas corresponding to the ratio of hydrogen atoms, and splitting patterns governed by the (n + 1) rule for adjacent non-equivalent protons, where n is the number of adjacent protons. Chromatography techniques, including paper chromatography, thin-layer chromatography (TLC), high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), and gas chromatography (GC), separate mixtures using stationary and mobile phases, relying on differential retention times or Rf values for analytical identification.

Advanced Worked Example

Determine the splitting pattern and relative peak areas for the proton NMR spectrum of pure ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH). Answer: The methyl protons (CH₃) are adjacent to two protons, so they split into a triplet with a relative peak area of 3. The methylene protons (CH₂-O) are adjacent to three protons, so they split into a quartet with a relative peak area of 2. The hydroxyl proton (OH) typically appears as a singlet with a relative peak area of 1 that exchanges with deuterium oxide.

Further Key Points to Remember

Acyl chlorides react vigorously with nucleophiles through addition-elimination mechanisms due to the strongly electron-withdrawing chlorine and oxygen atoms attached to the carbonyl carbon. Spectroscopic data must be cross-referenced: high-resolution mass spectra provide accurate molecular masses, 13C NMR identifies carbon frameworks, and 1H NMR determines hydrogen connectivity and neighboring environments. Chromatographic Rf values depend on the relative solubility of components in the stationary and mobile phases, and modern analytical procedures frequently couple gas chromatography with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) for forensic and doping analyses.

title: Information Representation — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Information Representation

Computer Science — AS. Computers store everything as binary patterns. The same pattern means different things depending on the data type, so the representation must be known to read it correctly.

Key areas to revise

  • Number systems and ranges: binary, denary and hexadecimal convert between each other. An 8-bit unsigned value ranges from 0 to 255, and two's complement ranges from −128 to 127.
  • Binary arithmetic: add bits in columns and carry where needed. Overflow occurs when the result needs more bits than are available.
  • Text: ASCII uses 7 bits for 128 characters, and Unicode uses more bits to represent many more characters.
  • Images and sound: an image file size is width × height × colour depth; a sound file size is sample rate × resolution × duration × channels.
  • Compression: lossless compression, such as run-length encoding, can restore the original exactly, while lossy compression discards data that is hard to notice.

Core facts to recall

  • Example: an image of 800 × 600 pixels with 24-bit colour needs 800 × 600 × 24 bits, which is 11 520 000 bits or about 1.44 MB.
  • Increasing the sample rate or the colour depth increases the file size but improves quality.
  • Name the compression type and give one reason for choosing it.

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

title: Measures of Variation and Standard Deviation — Study Notes
content:
Measures of Variation

Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Statistics 1 (WST01), sat at AS.

Range and Quartiles

The range is max − min — quick but destroyed by a single outlier. Quartiles split ordered data into quarters: Q₁ at position (n + 1)/4, Q₃ at 3(n + 1)/4 (raw data). The interquartile range, IQR = Q₃ − Q₁, is the spread of the middle 50% and resists outliers. Outliers are commonly flagged as values beyond Q₁ − 1.5·IQR or Q₃ + 1.5·IQR.

Variance and Standard Deviation

For raw data:

  • variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n (the definitional form)
  • equivalently s² = Σx²/n − x̄² (the computational form)
  • standard deviation s = √(variance)

The standard deviation shares the units of the data; the variance does not. For frequency tables use Σf(x − x̄)²/Σf, or Σfx²/Σf − x̄².

Grouped Data

Use class midpoints as x. The result is an estimate — grouping discards within-class detail.

Combining and Scaling Datasets

Multiplying every value by b multiplies s by |b| and the variance by b². Adding a constant changes nothing in the spread. Two merged datasets: compute combined Σx and Σx² from each part, then apply the computational formula.

Example: data 1, 3, 4, 5, 7: mean 4, Σx² = 100, so variance = 100/5 − 16 = 4 and s = 2.

Exam tips: state units for s. When comparing consistency, the dataset with the smaller standard deviation (relative to its mean) is the more consistent. Always give the comparison sentence, not just the two numbers.

Exam method: variance and standard deviation

The variance is the mean of the squared deviations, or equivalently Var(x) = Σx²/n − x̄². The standard deviation is its square root, and it is in the same units as the data. Using the second form is quicker when the mean is already known.

Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean by that constant but leaves the standard deviation unchanged. Multiplying every value by a constant k multiplies the standard deviation by |k| and the variance by k². Use these rules to avoid recalculating from scratch.

For grouped data, use the class midpoints and the frequencies. The variance is Σfx²/Σf − x̄², with x̄ = Σfx/Σf.

The standard deviation is a measure of spread. Compare two data sets by stating which has the larger spread and linking that to the context of the data.

Exam cue: Show the sum of the values and the sum of squares before dividing, because the method marks depend on those totals.

Worked example: standard deviation from raw data

For the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 there are n = 8 values with mean 5. The sum of the squares is 4 + 16 + 16 + 16 + 25 + 25 + 49 + 81 = 232. The variance is Σx²/n − (x̄)² = 232/8 − 25 = 29 − 25 = 4, and the standard deviation is √4 = 2. Using the formula with the sum of squared deviations gives the same answer and is a useful check on your working.

Exam method: outliers using the interquartile range

The interquartile range is Q3 − Q1. Under the usual rule, a value is an outlier if it lies below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Use the definition given in the question if one is stated, and show the two boundary values in your working. Writing a conclusion in context, such as "the value 40 is an outlier for these hours", gains the communication mark.

title: Programming Concepts — Study Notes
content:
Programming Concepts

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): variables/constants, data types, selection/iteration, arrays, file handling, subroutines, scope, IDE tools.

1. Basics

Constants vs variables; types: INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE; casting between them. Declaration with meaningful names.

2. Selection and iteration

IF score >= 50 THEN
  grade ← "pass"
ELSE
  grade ← "fail"
ENDIF

CASE OF grade
  "A" : OUTPUT "excellent"
  OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "keep going"
ENDCASE

REPEAT
  INPUT pin
UNTIL pin = storedPin

FOR i ← 1 TO 10 STEP 2 ... NEXT i

WHILE: condition first (may not run); REPEAT: runs at least once.

3. Arrays

Fixed size, indexed (0- or 1-based per spec); 2D arrays: row, column. Bounds errors when index leaves range. Traversal with FOR loops.

4. Files

OPENFILE "data.txt" FOR READ
READFILE "data.txt", line
CLOSEFILE "data.txt"

OPENFILE "log.txt" FOR APPEND
WRITEFILE "log.txt", record

Modes: READ, WRITE (overwrites), APPEND (adds).

5. Subroutines

Procedure (no return) vs function (returns value). Parameters by value (copy) vs reference (original). Local scope inside; global shared — declare deliberately, avoid overuse.

6. IDE tools

Syntax highlighting, autocompletion, breakpoints, single stepping, variable watch — name the tool and its debugging benefit.

Exam tips: use the exam pseudocode style exactly; for 2D arrays, loop rows outer/columns inner; choose WHILE vs REPEAT by "must it run once?"

Selection and iteration in practice

Selection uses IF and CASE structures to choose between paths, and a branch runs only when its condition is true. Iteration repeats a block of code. A count-controlled loop, such as FOR, runs a known number of times. A condition-controlled loop, such as WHILE or REPEAT, runs until a condition changes. A WHILE loop may run zero times, but a REPEAT loop always runs at least once.

A well-written program uses meaningful identifiers, indents its code to show structure, and includes comments that explain why a piece of code exists. Subroutines split a large problem into smaller tasks that can be tested separately.

Exam tip: choose the loop type from whether the number of repetitions is known in advance.

Worked example: a loop that totals marks

Suppose a program must add up five test marks and print the average. Set a total variable to 0 before the loop. Repeat five times: read a mark, add it to the total. After the loop, divide the total by 5 and output the result. Tracing the variables on paper with marks 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 gives totals of 60, 130, 210, 300 and 400, so the printed average is 80. Exam answers are marked on the logic, so write each step even when a shorter program would work.

Choosing between selection and iteration

Use selection (IF or CASE) when the program must choose one route. Use iteration (FOR, WHILE or REPEAT) when the same steps must run several times. A FOR loop suits a known count, while a WHILE loop suits a count that depends on input, because its condition is checked before each pass.

title: Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7 — Study Notes
content:
Redox Chemistry and Groups 1, 2 and 7

Edexcel IAL Chemistry WCH12, Topic 8. Every statement 8.1 to 8.28 is covered below, with its code in the heading. Three ideas run through the whole topic: oxidation numbers track electron transfer, the Group 1 and 2 trends follow from atomic size and nuclear charge, and the Group 7 trends are the same ideas applied to halogens.

8.1 to 8.4: Oxidation numbers

  • Rules: an element is 0; a monatomic ion equals its charge; the sum of oxidation numbers equals the overall charge. Oxygen is usually −2 (but −1 in peroxides such as H₂O₂), hydrogen is usually +1 (but −1 in metal hydrides such as NaH), fluorine is always −1, Group 1 is +1 and Group 2 is +2.
  • 8.2: in MnO₄⁻, manganese must be +7, because four oxygens contribute −8 and the ion has a charge of −1.
  • 8.3: write the oxidation number as a Roman numeral in the name: manganese(VII), iron(III), copper(II).
  • 8.4: work backwards from oxidation numbers to a formula. Iron(III) sulfate is Fe₂(SO₄)₃, because Fe³⁺ must balance SO₄²⁻ in a 2:3 ratio.

8.5 to 8.9: Oxidation, reduction and disproportionation

  • 8.5: oxidation is loss of electrons, and it appears as an increase in oxidation number. Reduction is gain of electrons, a decrease in oxidation number. In 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl, sodium is oxidised (0 to +1) and chlorine is reduced (0 to −1). The same idea covers reactions of s-block metals and p-block non-metals.
  • 8.6: an oxidising agent gains electrons and is itself reduced. A reducing agent loses electrons and is itself oxidised.
  • 8.7: disproportionation is when one element in a single species is both oxidised and reduced at the same time. Chlorine in water is the standard example: Cl₂ → Cl⁻ (0 to −1) and HClO (0 to +1).
  • 8.8: oxidation numbers classify reactions. A reaction is redox if any oxidation number changes, and it is a disproportionation if the same element goes both up and down.
  • 8.9: metals form positive ions by losing electrons, so their oxidation number increases. Non-metals form negative ions by gaining electrons, so their oxidation number decreases.

8.10: Half-equations and full ionic equations

  • Write the oxidation and the reduction separately, balance atoms, then balance charge with electrons. For magnesium with chlorine: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.
  • Add the half-equations so the electrons cancel, then cancel any spectator ions to give the full ionic equation.

8.11 to 8.13: Group 1 and Group 2 trends and reactions

  • 8.11: ionisation energy falls down Groups 1 and 2. The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded by inner shells, so less energy is needed to remove it.
  • 8.12: reactivity rises down Group 1 (Li to K) and Group 2 (Mg to Ba), for the same reason: the outer electron is removed more easily.
  • 8.13: Group 1 metals burn in oxygen and react vigorously with chlorine and water. Group 2 metals react with oxygen and chlorine to form oxides and chlorides. Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water and readily with steam, while calcium reacts steadily with cold water to form Ca(OH)₂ and hydrogen.

8.14: Reactions of oxides and hydroxides

  • Group 1 oxides dissolve in water to give alkaline hydroxides. Group 2 oxides react less vigorously, and CaO gives a limewater-type solution, Ca(OH)₂.
  • Oxides react with dilute acid to form a salt and water, for example MgO + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂O.
  • Hydroxides neutralise dilute acids: Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O.

8.15: Solubility trends of Group 2 hydroxides and sulfates

  • Hydroxides: solubility increases down the group. Magnesium hydroxide is almost insoluble, calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble, barium hydroxide is quite soluble.
  • Sulfates: solubility decreases down the group. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, barium sulfate is insoluble, which is why acidified barium chloride gives a white precipitate in the sulfate test.

8.16: Thermal stability of nitrates and carbonates

  • Stability increases down each group. A larger cation has a lower charge density, so it polarises the carbonate or nitrate ion less, and the anion breaks down less easily.
  • Carbonates: MCO₃ → MO + CO₂. Group 2 nitrates: 2M(NO₃)₂ → 2MO + 4NO₂ + O₂. Group 1 nitrates (other than lithium) give the nitrite and oxygen: 2NaNO₃ → 2NaNO₂ + O₂.
  • Lithium is the exception: its nitrate decomposes like a Group 2 nitrate, because the small Li⁺ ion polarises the nitrate strongly.

8.17: Flame colours

  • Heat excites outer electrons to higher energy levels. When they fall back, they emit light of a specific wavelength. Lithium is crimson, sodium is yellow-orange, potassium is lilac, calcium is brick red, strontium is red and barium is green.

8.18: Experiments on thermal decomposition

  • Heat a small sample of nitrate or carbonate in a test tube and test the gas. Brown NO₂ shows a nitrate; a glowing splint relit by O₂ shows oxygen. A carbonate gives CO₂, which turns limewater milky.
  • Compare the temperatures needed for decomposition down a group to show the trend in 8.16.

8.19: Identifying ions

  • Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) or hydrogencarbonate (HCO₃⁻): add dilute acid. CO₂ is released and turns limewater milky. Ionic equation: CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
  • Sulfate (SO₄²⁻): add acidified barium chloride. A white precipitate of BaSO₄ forms: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄. The acid stops carbonate and sulfite interfering.
  • Ammonium (NH₄⁺): add sodium hydroxide and warm. Ammonia is released, turns damp red litmus blue, and gives white fumes with HCl.

8.20 to 8.23: Concentrations, titrations and uncertainty

  • 8.20: concentration in mol dm⁻³ = moles ÷ volume in dm³. To convert to g dm⁻³, multiply by the molar mass.
  • Indicators: methyl orange changes from red to yellow at about pH 3–4, suited to strong acid against weak base. Phenolphthalein changes from colourless to pink at about pH 8–10, suited to weak acid against strong base.
  • 8.21 (core practical 3): titrate hydrochloric acid against a standard alkali, record the titre and use the balanced equation to find the acid's concentration.
  • 8.22: reduce uncertainty by rinsing the pipette and burette, reading the meniscus at eye level, and repeating until two titres agree within 0.10 cm³. A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³, so a titre has ±0.10 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty as uncertainty ÷ reading × 100.
  • 8.23 (core practical 4): weigh a solid acid such as hydrated ethanedioic acid accurately, dissolve it, make it up to 250 cm³ in a volumetric flask, and use it as a standard solution to find the concentration of sodium hydroxide.

8.24: Trends in Group 7

  • Melting and boiling points rise down the group, because the molecules are larger and have stronger London forces. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, iodine is a solid.
  • Electronegativity falls down the group, because the bonding pair sits further from the nucleus and is shielded more.
  • Reactivity (oxidising power) falls down the group, because the atoms are larger and gain an electron less readily.

8.25: Displacement reactions and colours

  • A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂, and Cl₂ or Br₂ + 2I⁻ → I₂ + halide.
  • Colours: in water, chlorine is pale green-yellow, bromine is orange and iodine is brown. In a non-polar organic solvent such as cyclohexane, bromine stays orange and iodine turns violet.

8.26: Reactions of the halogens, including disproportionation

  • (i) Halogens oxidise Group 1 and 2 metals to halides, for example 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
  • (ii) Chlorine with water is a disproportionation: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO. The HClO is the basis of chlorine water treatment.
  • (iii) Chlorine with cold, dilute NaOH gives bleach: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H₂O.
  • (iv) With hot concentrated alkali, chlorine disproportionates to chlorate: 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O.
  • (v) Bromine behaves in the same way with cold alkali. Use the oxidation number of each chlorine to check each product.

8.27: Reactions of halides and hydrogen halides

  • (i) Solid halides with concentrated H₂SO₄ show the reducing trend. NaCl gives HCl only. NaBr is oxidised further to Br₂ and SO₂. NaI is oxidised to I₂ and H₂S. The reducing ability is HI > HBr > HCl.
  • (ii) Silver nitrate with the halide ions in nitric acid: AgCl is white, AgBr is cream, AgI is yellow. AgCl dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia, AgBr only in concentrated ammonia, and AgI does not dissolve.
  • (iii) Hydrogen halides with ammonia give ammonium halides (NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl). With water they give acids.

8.28: Predicting fluorine and astatine

  • Fluorine is the most electronegative element and the strongest oxidising agent in the group. It reacts violently with water, displacing oxygen from it.
  • Astatine is at the bottom of the group, so by the trends it should be a dark, solid, less reactive halogen than iodine, with a lower electronegativity. It is radioactive, so its chemistry is hard to study directly, and predictions come from the trends.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Half-equations in acid, 8.10 applied: dichromate(VI) reduced by iron(II). Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O, and Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (multiply by 6). Adding gives Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. Check atoms, then charge: both sides total +24.
  • Titration calculation, 8.20 and 8.22 applied: 25.0 cm³ of an iron(II) solution needs 18.0 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ K₂Cr₂O₇. Moles of dichromate = 0.0200 × 0.0180 = 3.60 × 10⁻⁴ mol. Each dichromate needs six Fe²⁺, so Fe²⁺ = 2.16 × 10⁻³ mol. Concentration = 2.16 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0864 mol dm⁻³. An A* answer shows the ratio from the balanced equation before any arithmetic.
  • Disproportionation, 8.7 and 8.26 applied: chlorine with cold dilute NaOH gives Cl⁻ (0 to −1, reduction) and ClO⁻ (0 to +1, oxidation) in one reaction. Name both oxidation numbers when explaining why a reaction is disproportionation.
  • Group 2 hydroxide solubility, 8.15 applied: solubility rises down the group because hydration enthalpy falls more steeply than lattice enthalpy as the cation grows. Lattice enthalpy depends on the ion sizes and charges; hydration enthalpy depends on how strongly water molecules bind the cation. Both are needed for full marks.
  • Thermal stability, 8.16 applied: a small, highly charged cation such as Mg²⁺ polarises a carbonate ion strongly, which weakens its C–O bonds, so MgCO₃ decomposes at a lower temperature than BaCO₃. Use the word polarisation, not just "smaller ions decompose more easily".
  • Halogen displacement and redox direction, 8.25 and 8.27 applied: chlorine oxidises bromide and iodide, bromine oxidises iodide, but iodine oxidises neither. Read the direction from the reducing trend: iodide is the strongest reducing agent among the halides, which is why concentrated sulfuric acid reduces HI to H₂S.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Using the wrong oxidation number for oxygen in a peroxide or hydrogen in a metal hydride.
  • Confusing reducing ability with reactivity for the halogens: reactivity falls down Group 7, but the reducing ability of the halide ions rises.
  • Writing the test for sulfate without acid. Without acid, carbonate would also give a white precipitate.

title: Functions — Study Notes
content:
Functions

This note builds the functions work used throughout the Edexcel International A Level Mathematics — Pure Mathematics 1 (WMA11) course. A function maps each input in its domain to exactly one output in its range. Notation such as f(x) = 2x + 1 names the rule, and the examiner expects you to state domain, range and inverse clearly.

Domain, range and notation

The domain is the set of inputs the function accepts. Restrictions usually come from denominators (which cannot be zero), square roots (which need a non-negative argument) and logarithms (which need a positive argument). The range is the set of outputs the function actually produces over that domain. For f(x) = x² on all real numbers, the range is f(x) ≥ 0. Writing the domain as x ≥ 0 gives the same range but changes whether an inverse exists.

A many-to-one function, such as x² on all reals, sends two inputs to the same output. A one-to-one function never does. Only one-to-one functions have inverses.

Composite functions

The composite function fg(x) means f(g(x)): apply g first, then f to the result. Order matters, so in general fg(x) and gf(x) are different functions.

Example: f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x².

  • fg(x) = f(x²) = 2x² + 1
  • gf(x) = g(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1

When a restriction is involved, check the range of the inner function against the domain of the outer one. If g(x) = x − 3 with domain x ≥ 0 is followed by f(x) = √x, the range of g is x ≥ −3, which is wider than the domain of f, so the composite fg(x) = √(x − 3) needs x ≥ 3 to be defined. The exam often asks for this domain explicitly.

Inverse functions

The inverse f⁻¹ reverses the action of f, so f⁻¹(f(x)) = x. To find it, write y = f(x), swap x and y, then rearrange to make y the subject.

Example: f(x) = 3x − 2. Write y = 3x − 2, swap to x = 3y − 2, then y = (x + 2)/3. So f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3. Check by substituting: f(f⁻¹(x)) = 3 × (x + 2)/3 − 2 = x.

An inverse exists only if f is one-to-one on its domain. If it is not, restrict the domain to make it so. For f(x) = x² with domain x ≥ 0, the inverse is f⁻¹(x) = √x with domain x ≥ 0. Without the restriction, x² would have no single inverse, because both 3 and −3 square to 9.

The domain of f⁻¹ is the range of f, and the range of f⁻¹ is the domain of f. The graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of y = f(x) in the line y = x, so a point (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹. Use this to check an answer: if (2, 5) is on the graph of f, then (5, 2) must be on the graph of f⁻¹.

Transformations of graphs

Each change to the rule moves or stretches the graph in a predictable way. Learn these as a table:

Transformed graphEffect on the graph of y = f(x)
y = f(x) + atranslation by a units up (a < 0: down)
y = f(x + a)translation by a units left (a < 0: right)
y = a f(x)vertical stretch, scale factor a
y = f(ax)horizontal stretch, scale factor 1/a
y = −f(x)reflection in the x-axis
y = f(−x)reflection in the y-axis

The horizontal translation runs against the sign: y = (x − 3)² is the graph of x² moved 3 units to the right. A common error is to move it left. For a sequence of transformations, apply them in the order the question gives, tracking a few key points such as the vertex or the intercepts.

Method for exam questions

  • For a composite function, write out fg(x) and gf(x) separately whenever the question names two functions, and simplify each.
  • For an inverse, state both the rule and its domain. A correct rule with the domain missing loses marks.
  • To show a function has an inverse, argue that it is one-to-one on the stated domain, usually because it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing there.
  • When sketching y = f⁻¹(x), reflect the graph of f in y = x and mark where the line crosses it, since that point lies on both graphs.

Exam cue: whenever a question says "hence" or "using your answer to part", the composite or inverse from the earlier part is usually the route to the answer, so keep it in simplified form.

title: Robotics & AI — Study Notes
content:
Robotics & AI

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): AI characteristics, machine learning basics, robotics/simulation contexts, automated systems.

1. AI characteristics

Systems exhibiting: planning, learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, knowledge representation. Narrow (task-specific) vs general AI distinction for discussion answers.

2. Machine learning

Supervised (labelled data — spam filters), unsupervised (clusters — segmentation), reinforcement (rewards — game agents). Training/evaluation loop: train on a set, test on unseen data; overfitting = memorising rather than generalising.

3. Robotics

Components: sensors (input), processors (decision), actuators/motors (output), power. Examples: manufacturing arms, delivery drones, autonomous vehicles (LIDAR + vision). Benefits: precision, 24/7 operation, dangerous jobs; concerns: job displacement, safety, cost.

4. Automated systems & simulation

Sensors → processor → actuators loops (greenhouses, traffic lights, self-checkouts). Simulation models real systems cheaply and safely (flight training, weather, crash tests) — limitations: model quality, missing variables.

5. Ethics of AI

Bias from unrepresentative training data; opacity of decisions; accountability for errors; privacy of training data; effect on employment.

Exam tips: for "describe how AI could be used in X" — tie each AI characteristic to a concrete step in the scenario; for evaluations, give both sides then a justified conclusion.

Sensors, actuators and feedback

A sensor converts a physical quantity, such as light, temperature or pressure, into an electrical signal. An actuator does the opposite: it converts an electrical signal into physical movement, for example by turning a motor. A robot or automated system uses sensors to read its environment, a processor to decide what to do, and actuators to act.

A feedback loop compares the measured value with the required value and adjusts the output to close the gap. A thermostat is a simple example: it switches the heater off when the room reaches the set temperature. Feedback allows a system to correct itself, but a poorly set loop can overshoot or oscillate.

Exam tip: name a sensor and an actuator in any automated system you describe, and explain what the feedback corrects.

Worked example: a sensor-driven robot

A robot moves forward while an ultrasonic sensor reports distances greater than 20 cm. When the reading falls to 20 cm or less, the robot stops and turns right, then resumes. Describe this as input (distance reading), process (compare the reading with the threshold) and output (motor commands). Mark schemes reward naming each part of the control loop: sensing, decision and actuation.

Sensors, actuators and feedback

  • A sensor converts a physical quantity such as light, temperature or distance into a signal. An actuator converts an electrical signal into motion, such as a motor or servo.
