6. Core Practical 7 — transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves

Use a light microscope to make observations, draw and label plan diagrams of transverse sections of roots, stems and leaves, and to observe and label cells of plant tissues, identifying sclerenchyma fibres, phloem, sieve tubes and xylem vessels and their location. To make a transverse section, cut a very thin slice across a stem or root with a razor blade (a sharp blade and a steady hand or a sectioning technique), float the section onto water on a slide, lower a coverslip at an angle, stain if needed (for example with toluidine blue or iodine) to distinguish lignified xylem, sclerenchyma and phloem, and observe under the microscope at several magnifications. In a stem transverse section, note the positions of the epidermis, cortex, the vascular bundles (with xylem toward the inside and phloem toward the outside, and sclerenchyma fibres often outside the phloem in a bundle cap), and the pith in the centre; in roots the vascular tissue is central. Draw a plan diagram (an outline of the whole section showing the arrangement of tissues, not the cells) with the correct relative sizes and positions, label the tissues, give a title and magnification. Then observe and label the cells: look for the thick lignified walls of xylem and sclerenchyma, the sieve plates and companion cells of phloem, and the thin-walled cells of the cortex and pith.

7. Plant fibres and starch in sustainability

Plant fibres and starch can contribute to sustainability and to replacing oil-based plastics. Plant fibres (from sclerenchyma or from phloem fibres) are strong, renewable and biodegradable, and they can be used in textiles, paper, building materials and composites that replace oil-based plastics and synthetic fibres; water transport in plants today parallels the transport of sap and provides a model for how plants already do this. Starch can be used to make bioplastics — for example, starch can be processed into film-forming materials suitable for packaging, plates and disposable items — and because starch is a renewable, biodegradable material made from crops such as potatoes, maize or cassava, it can replace oil-based plastics in some uses. Using plant fibres and starch reduces reliance on oil, is renewable and can be more sustainable if the crops are grown responsibly; but there are trade-offs: land, water and energy for the crops, possible competition with food production, and the need to assess the whole life cycle. The use of plant products to replace oil-based plastics is a topic that connects plant structure (cellulose and starch), to sustainability, to human decisions informed by science.

8. Water and inorganic ions to plants, and mineral deficiency

Plants need water for photosynthesis (a reactant and the medium in which it happens), for transport (water is the solvent for minerals and for sucrose in the phloem), for support (turgor pressure keeps non-woody parts rigid), and for cooling (transpiration). Water enters the roots by osmosis from the soil and moves up the xylem. Inorganic ions are essential: nitrate ions (NO3-) are needed for making amino acids, proteins, DNA and chlorophyll — a deficiency causes stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves (chlorosis); calcium ions are needed for the middle lamella (pectin in the cell wall) and for cell membranes — a deficiency gives stunted growth and necrosis of the growing point and young leaves; magnesium ions are the central atom in chlorophyll — a deficiency causes chlorosis of the older leaves. A recommended additional practical is to investigate plant mineral deficiencies: grow plants in a solution with all minerals (complete) and in solutions missing one of nitrate, calcium or magnesium, observe and measure the effects on growth and leaf colour over weeks, and explain the results in terms of the roles of the missing ion.

9. Core Practical 8 — tensile strength of plant fibres

Determine the tensile strength of plant fibres — the force a fibre can take before it breaks. A typical method: take strands of a plant fibre (for example the fibres from celery stalks or nettle stems, or a piece of a plant stem with visible fibres), clamp one end, hang weights from the other, and add weights until the fibre breaks; record the mass (converted to a force, weight = mass × g) needed to break the fibre. Repeat for several fibres, present the results, and compare fibres from different plants or different parts of a plant. Safety: sharp blades and falling weights. The practical shows how the arrangement of cellulose and lignin gives the fibre its strength, and connects the cell-level structure to a macroscopic useful property.

10. Conditions for bacterial growth

Bacteria need certain conditions to grow: a supply of nutrients (carbon, nitrogen, minerals and, for some, specific organic factors), water, a suitable temperature (most pathogenic bacteria around 37 °C, though many grow across a range), oxygen (some need it — aerobic bacteria — some do not — anaerobic bacteria — and some can manage with or without), a suitable pH, and, for many, time to multiply. In the laboratory these conditions can be met and controlled: cultures are grown in nutrient broth or on agar plates, at a set temperature (often 25 °C for environmental organisms and 37 °C for those that grow at body temperature), with or without oxygen, and in sterile conditions so that only the desired organism grows. Aseptic technique is essential to avoid contaminating the culture or releasing harmful bacteria into the environment — sterilise equipment (by flame or autoclave), work near a flame to create an upward air current, work quickly and cover the plates, and dispose of cultures by sterilising before disposal.

11. Antimicrobial plant substances and the aseptic practical

Substances derived from plants can have antimicrobial and other therapeutic properties. Some plant extracts inhibit the growth of bacteria or fungi — for example, garlic has been traditionally used and does have some antibacterial effects; other plants yield useful compounds (aspirin from willow bark, morphine from poppies, and many modern drugs are derived from plants). A recommended additional practical is to investigate the antimicrobial properties of plants, including aseptic techniques for the safe handling of bacteria: prepare agar plates, use sterile swabs or paper discs impregnated with different plant extracts, incubate and measure the zones of inhibition around the discs — the diameter of the clear zone where bacteria did not grow — and compare the effectiveness of different extracts or the same extract at different concentrations. Use aseptic technique: sterilise the discs and loops, work near a flame, spread the bacteria in a controlled way, seal the plates with tape (but do not seal all the way so they do not become anaerobic), and incubate at a safe temperature. Measure the zones of inhibition and record them, including in a table, and draw a conclusion about which extract is most effective and about concentration.

12. Drug testing: from Withering''s digitalis soup to modern trials

The development of drug testing has moved from historic, uncontrolled methods to contemporary, rigorous protocols. William Withering''s digitalis soup in the 18th century was an early use of a plant-derived medicine — foxglove (Digitalis) — for dropsy (oedema), tested by trial and observation on patients, but with no controls, no placebo, no blinding and no large sample, so the evidence was weak and mixed with other treatments. Modern drug testing uses a sequence of phases: pre-clinical testing in the lab and on animals; clinical trials in humans in three phases — Phase 1 tests safety in a small group, Phase 2 tests efficacy and side effects in a larger group of patients, and Phase 3 tests the drug against the current treatment or a placebo in a large group, in a double-blind trial (neither the patient nor the clinician knows which treatment is being used) so that expectations do not bias the result. Placebos are used to control for the placebo effect (improvement from the belief of being treated). The modern protocol — double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-centre, large trials — is far more reliable than Withering''s soup, and it protects patients and produces trustworthy evidence. Students should be able to describe this progression and evaluate the designs.

13. Classification: organising life, the species concept and the three domains

Classification is a means of organising the variety of life based on relationships between organisms, using differences and similarities in phenotypes (observable features) and in genotypes (the DNA and the proteins the DNA codes for). It is built around the species concept — a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring — and a hierarchy of groups above it: genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom, with organisms grouped because they share common ancestry. The classification has changed as new data — especially molecular evidence from DNA and protein sequences — have come in, leading to critical evaluation of existing groupings and new taxonomic groupings. The three-domain system, based on molecular evidence, divides life into the Archaea, the Bacteria and the Eukarya (which includes all eukaryotes, plants, animals, fungi and protists); the Archaea are distinct from the Bacteria and include organisms that often live in extreme environments, and the evidence from ribosomal RNA sequences and other molecular data led to this reclassification, replacing the older five-kingdom system. The process of critical evaluation of new data by the scientific community — comparing, testing and debating — is what leads to new groupings and to science being self-correcting.

14. Biodiversity, endemism and threats from human activity

Biodiversity is the variety of life — the variety within a habitat, within a species or across the whole planet; it can refer to species richness (the number of different species in a habitat) or to genetic diversity within a species. Endemism is the state of a species being found only in one particular place (an endemic species, such as a plant found only on a particular island). Over time the variety of life has become extensive through evolution, but it is now being threatened by human activity — habitat destruction (deforestation, drainage, conversion to agriculture), over-exploitation (hunting, fishing, logging), pollution, the introduction of invasive species, and climate change, all of which can reduce biodiversity and cause extinctions. Biodiversity matters because it provides ecosystem services, genetic resources for medicines and crops, and is itself valuable; its loss affects ecosystems, food security and human health. Understanding the causes of the loss is important so that conservation measures can be designed to address them.

15. Measuring biodiversity: species richness, genetic diversity and heterozygosity

Biodiversity can be measured in different ways. Species richness — the number of different species in a given area — is one simple measure of biodiversity within a habitat; a habitat with more species is generally more diverse, though this ignores the abundance of each species (a habitat dominated by one common species and several rare ones may have the same species richness as one where all are equally common). Genetic diversity within a species can be measured by the heterozygosity index (also called heterozygosity): the proportion of individuals in a population that are heterozygous at a locus. It is calculated as the number of heterozygotes divided by the number of individuals in the population (for a single locus); a higher heterozygosity means more genetic diversity within that population. This matters because genetic diversity helps a population adapt to changes, resist disease and avoid the problems of inbreeding; loss of genetic diversity raises the risk of extinction.

16. Comparing habitats with the index of diversity

Biodiversity can be compared between different habitats using the formula for the index of diversity, D: D = (N(N−1)) / (Σ n(n−1)), where N is the total number of organisms of all species in the habitat, and n is the number of organisms of a particular species. Calculation: for each species, work out n(n−1); sum these to get Σ n(n−1); then divide N(N−1) by that sum to give D, the index of diversity. Worked example: in a habitat with species counts 10, 15, 5, 2 (N = 32): Σ n(n−1) = (10×9)+(15×14)+(5×4)+(2×1) = 90+210+20+2 = 322; N(N−1) = 32×31 = 992; D = 992 / 322 ≈ 3.08. A larger D means a more diverse habitat, because it reflects both the number of species and how evenly the individuals are distributed among them. To compare habitats, calculate D for each and compare the values, stating which is more diverse and what that suggests. The formula must be applied correctly: calculate n(n−1) for each species, sum them, and divide N(N−1) by the sum.

17. Niche and adaptations: behavioural, anatomical and physiological

A niche is the role of an organism in a habitat — the conditions in which it lives and the resources it uses, and how it interacts with other organisms; it is more than just the physical place (the habitat) where it lives, and no two species can occupy exactly the same niche for long because of competition. Adaptations are features that help an organism survive and reproduce in its niche, and they can be behavioural, anatomical or physiological. Behavioural adaptations are things the organism does — for example migration to avoid harsh conditions, hunting in packs, basking to warm up, or the specific foraging behaviour of a bird. Anatomical (structural) adaptations are physical features of the body — for example the shape of a bird''s beak for its food, the camouflage colours of a prey animal, the thick fur of an arctic mammal, or the long beak of a nectar-feeding bird. Physiological adaptations are internal functions — for example a camel''s ability to tolerate dehydration and to conserve water, the production of venom by a snake, the production of antifreeze proteins in some polar fish, or the specialised nitrogen excretion of desert animals. The concept of niche and the types of adaptation help explain how different organisms fit into their environments and how competition and adaptation shape communities.

18. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can identify plant cell ultrastructure and organelles in an electron micrograph and state their functions, explain how starch and cellulose differ in structure and role, describe the secondary thickening and the properties of xylem vessels and sclerenchyma fibres, compare sclerenchyma fibres, xylem vessels and phloem in structure, position and function, carry out the transverse section and tensile strength practicals and explain the variables and safety, describe the conditions for bacterial growth and the aseptic practical, describe the development of drug testing from Withering''s digitalis to modern three-phased trials and evaluate the designs, define classification and the species concept, describe the three-domain system and the molecular evidence for it, define biodiversity and endemism and the threats from human activity, carry out the species richness and heterozygosity and index of diversity calculations, and define niche and give behavioural, anatomical and physiological adaptations. After this topic, revise Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development (plant and animal cells, division) and Topic 5 Energy flow, ecosystems and the environment, because classification and biodiversity sit within ecology.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Simpson's index, applied to a quadrat with 10 daisies and 5 dandelions: N = 15, D = 1 − Σ(n ÷ N)² = 1 − [(10 ÷ 15)² + (5 ÷ 15)²] = 1 − (0.444 + 0.111) = 0.556. Use the index to compare two sites; a higher value means greater diversity.
  • Xylem and phloem: xylem transports water and minerals upwards and is made of dead, lignified cells with no end walls, so the water column is continuous. Phloem transports sucrose and amino acids in both directions and is made of living sieve tube elements with companion cells. Name the direction of transport and the living or dead state of the cells.
  • Cellulose versus starch: cellulose is made of β-glucose units linked alternately, which allows hydrogen bonding between chains, forming strong microfibrils. Starch is made of α-glucose, is coiled and is used for storage. The different glucose isomer explains the different shapes and functions.
  • Conservation: a protected area works only if the populations inside it are large enough to be viable. Name the factor, such as a wildlife corridor, that connects populations, because isolated populations lose genetic diversity over time.

title: Work, Energy and Power — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Work, Energy and Power

Physics — AS. W = Fs cos θ — force × displacement in the force's direction. Unit: joule (J).

Key areas to revise

  • Work
  • Energy Forms
  • Conservation of Energy
  • Power
  • Efficiency

How to use this: skim the list above, then read the full study notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic quiz to check yourself.

Key relationships

  • Work done W = F s cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement.
  • Power P = W / t = F v for a constant force moving at speed v.
  • Kinetic energy = ½ m v² and gravitational potential energy change = m g Δh.
  • Elastic potential energy = ½ F x = ½ k x² for a spring obeying Hooke's law.

Common errors

Forgetting the cos θ term when the force is not parallel to the displacement gives a wrong work value. Efficiency is useful power output divided by total power input, and it is always less than 1.

title: Exam technique: Differentiation
content:
### What earns the marks
For differentiation, every term handled earns credit: show each power lowered. For stationary points, setting dy/dx = 0 earns one mark and the second-derivative (or sign) test earns the next. For always-increasing proofs, the discriminant shown negative with positive leading coefficient earns both marks.
### Traps
Error: constants surviving differentiation. Correction: constants vanish. Error: tangent gradient used for normals. Correction: negative reciprocal first. Error: claiming increase without the discriminant. Correction: no roots plus positive shape proves it.
### Differentiate term by term
For a term ax^n, the derivative is a n x^(n - 1). Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers before you differentiate, since a term left as a fraction is often differentiated incorrectly.
### Stationary points
Set dy/dx equal to zero and solve for x, then find the matching y value. To decide whether a point is a maximum or a minimum, check the sign of dy/dx either side of it or use the second derivative.
### Gradient at a point
Substitute the x value into dy/dx to find the gradient, then use the point and the gradient to write the equation of the tangent. Write the equation in the form the question requests.
### Common slips
Forgetting to differentiate a constant to zero, and forgetting that the chain rule is needed when a bracket is raised to a power.

title: Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding — Study Notes
content:
Algebra — Simplifying and Expanding

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): substitution, collecting like terms, expanding brackets, factorising (common factor, quadratics, difference of two squares), algebraic fractions.

1. Substitution

a = 3, b = −2: 2a² − b = 2(9) + 2 = 20. Always bracket substituted negatives.

2. Collecting like terms

5x + 3y − 2x + y = 3x + 4y. Terms need identical letter parts (x² and x are not like terms).

3. Expanding

  • Single: 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
  • Double: (x + 3)(x − 4) = x² − x − 12 (grid or FOIL).
  • Cubic products: (x+2)³ = x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.

4. Factorising

  • Common factor: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y).
  • Quadratics: x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3) (two numbers ×6, sum −5).
  • Harder: 6x² + 7x + 2 = (3x + 2)(2x + 1) — split the middle term.
  • Difference of two squares: 9x² − 25 = (3x − 5)(3x + 5).

5. Algebraic fractions

Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x − 3). To add, use a common denominator: 1/(x+1) + 2/(x−1) = (3x + 1)/((x+1)(x−1)).

Exam tips: always factorise out the highest common factor including the number; check expansion by substituting x = 1 into both forms.

Expanding brackets

Each term outside a bracket multiplies every term inside it. For a double bracket, multiply each term in the first by each term in the second, then collect like terms. Expanding (x + 3)(x − 5) gives x² − 2x − 15. Keep track of signs carefully, since most lost marks come from negative terms.

Factorising

Take out the highest common factor first, then look for a pair of brackets. For a quadratic x² + bx + c, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. For the difference of two squares, a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). Check by expanding your answer.

Algebraic fractions

Simplify by factorising the numerator and denominator and cancelling common factors. Add or subtract fractions by writing them over a common denominator. Never cancel terms that are added, only factors that multiply.

Worked example: expanding and collecting terms

Expand (2x + 3)(x − 4). Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second: 2x × x = 2x², 2x × (−4) = −8x, 3 × x = 3x, 3 × (−4) = −12. Collect the like terms: 2x² − 5x − 12.

A quick check is to substitute x = 1: (5)(−3) = −15, and 2 − 5 − 12 = −15. The two agree.

Factorising quadratics and the difference of two squares

Factorise x² + x − 12. Find two numbers that multiply to −12 and add to +1: +4 and −3. So x² + x − 12 = (x + 4)(x − 3).

The difference of two squares gives 4x² − 9 = (2x − 3)(2x + 3). Recognise it whenever there is no middle term and both terms are squares with a minus sign between them.

Simplifying algebraic fractions

Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + x − 6). Factorise the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3) and the denominator as (x + 3)(x − 2). Cancel the common factor (x + 3) to get (x − 3)/(x − 2), with the restriction x ≠ −3 stated because the original expression is undefined there.

Common errors that lose marks

  • Writing (a + b)² = a² + b², which drops the middle term 2ab.
  • Cancelling a term rather than a factor, for example simplifying (x + 3)/(x + 2) to 3/2.
  • Expanding a negative bracket without changing the signs inside it: −(x − 4) = −x + 4.

title: Proof — Study Notes
content:
Proof by induction and other formal arguments

Board note: mathematical induction is not in the Edexcel International A Level main specification — it sits in Further Mathematics (FP1, WFM01). Cambridge examines it at A2 (9709).

A2 proof extends the AS toolkit with mathematical induction — the standard method for statements indexed by the positive integers (series formulae, divisibility, inequalities).

The structure of induction

1. Base case: verify the statement directly for n = 1 (or the stated starting value).

2. Inductive step: assume the statement true for n = k (the inductive hypothesis). Prove it true for n = k + 1, using that assumption.

3. Conclusion: by induction the statement is true for all positive integers n >= starting value.

Divisibility inductions

To prove "expression is divisible by m": the base case must divide exactly, and the inductive step writes P(k + 1) = P(k) + m x (something), so divisibility passes from k to k + 1.

Series inductions

To prove a sum formula: write S_{k+1} = S_k + a_{k+1}, substitute the assumed formula for S_k, and simplify to the claimed form with n replaced by k + 1.

When induction is NOT appropriate

  • Statements about all real numbers (use direct proof or contradiction).
  • Finite case lists (use exhaustion).
  • Disproving a universal claim (use a counter-example).

Contradiction and contrapositive

  • To prove "if P then Q" by contradiction: assume P and not Q, and derive nonsense.
  • Contrapositive: prove "if not Q then not P", which is logically equivalent and often cleaner — e.g. "if n^2 is even then n is even" is proved by "if n is odd then n^2 is odd".

title: Exam technique: Oscillations and Waves II
content:
### What earns the marks
For Doppler, approach raising pitch stated earns the mark; v/c quoted earns the calculation marks. For standing waves, half lambda in L for the fundamental earns the method mark. For coherence, constant phase difference stated earns the definition mark.
### Traps
Error: receding claimed to raise frequency. Correction: approach raises, recession lowers. Error: fundamental taken as lambda = L. Correction: L holds half a wave. Error: EM waves given a medium. Correction: they travel through vacuum.
### Distinguish free, damped and forced oscillations
A free oscillation has a natural frequency. Damping reduces the amplitude over time, and a driven system oscillates at the driving frequency. Name which type the question describes before you explain it.

### Describe resonance from the graph
The amplitude peaks when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency. Explain that the peak becomes sharper and higher when the damping is reduced.

### Use the stationary wave conditions
For a string or pipe, the harmonics are integer multiples of the fundamental. Use the boundary conditions to decide whether a node or antinode is needed at each end, and state the harmonic number.

title: Exam technique: Congruence and Similarity
content:
### What earns the marks
For similarity lengths, calculate earns marks for the scale factor stated (larger over smaller, matched pairs) and then applied. For area and volume, the squared and cubed factors stated earn the method mark before any multiplication: write k squared or k cubed explicitly. For symmetry, count earns marks per correct count with the reasoning (vertices, rotation step 360 / n). For congruence, name earns the test (SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS) with the matching parts listed.
### Traps
Error: adding the length difference instead of scaling. Correction: similarity always multiplies. Error: using k instead of k squared for area or k cubed for volume. Correction: write the power first. Error: equal angles claimed as congruence. Correction: angles alone prove similarity; a matching side upgrades it.
### Worked example
Two triangles have sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, and a second triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. The second triangle is an enlargement with scale factor 2. Each length is multiplied by 2, so each area is multiplied by 2² = 4. If the lengths are scaled by 2.5, the areas are scaled by 6.25.

title: Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving — Study Notes
content:
Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618: section 19 (Computational thinking and problem-solving), examined in Papers 3 and 4.

Thinking Ahead, Abstractly, Systematically

  • Abstraction: keep essential features, drop detail — a metro map ignores street geometry.
  • Decomposition: split the problem into sub-problems solved independently.
  • Thinking ahead: pre-plan inputs, outputs and reusable components; pre-calculate tables where possible.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself with a smaller input and a base case that stops the recursion. Elegant for trees and divide-and-conquer, but each call consumes stack space — deep recursion can overflow. Any recursion can be rewritten with a loop and explicit stack.

Searching and Sorting

  • Linear search: O(n), works unsorted.
  • Binary search: O(log n), needs sorted data.
  • Bubble sort: O(n²) average; simple; detects a sorted pass.
  • Insertion sort: O(n²) average; fast on nearly-sorted data.
  • Merge sort: O(n log n) always; needs extra memory.

Testing

White-box tests trace internal paths; black-box tests check specification behaviour. Choose normal, boundary and erroneous data. Dry runs use trace tables recording variables line by line; a trace of recursion should log each call and its return.

Exam tips: write the base case before the recursive call in pseudocode; give the Big-O with a one-line justification; construct a trace table for a small loop or recursive call.

Recursion

A recursive routine calls itself on a smaller version of the problem. It needs a base case that stops the calls and a recursive case that moves towards the base case. Without a base case the routine never terminates and the call stack overflows.

Example: factorial(n) = 1 if n = 0, otherwise n × factorial(n − 1).

Recursion and iteration can solve the same problems. Recursion is often clearer for tree-shaped problems; iteration uses less memory because it does not build up stack frames.

Worked example: binary search on sixteen items

A sorted list has 16 items. Each comparison with the middle item halves the search range: 16 to 8, 8 to 4, 4 to 2, 2 to 1. At most ⌈log₂16⌉ = 4 comparisons are needed to find the item or confirm it is absent. A linear search on the same list may need 16 comparisons, so binary search is much faster, but only when the list is sorted.

Recursion: factorial

A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. For factorial, fact(n) returns 1 when n is 0 (the base case), and otherwise returns n × fact(n − 1). Each call waits for the next one to return, so the calls build up on the call stack. Without a base case the recursion never ends.

Testing a solution

  • Normal test data checks the typical case.
  • Boundary test data checks the limits, such as the first item, the last item and an empty list.
  • Erroneous test data checks that invalid input is rejected, for example a letter typed where a number is expected.

Exam point: a test plan lists the input, the expected output and the reason for each test, so that the result can be checked against the design.

title: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Mensuration — Bearings and Loci

Mathematics — OL. compass bearings, scale drawings, constructions (perpendicular/angle bisectors), loci regions.

  • 1. Bearings
  • 2. Scale drawings
  • 3. Constructions
  • 4. Loci

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from north, written as three figures, such as 045 degrees. Draw the north line at the starting point and measure the angle from it. The back bearing differs from the bearing by 180 degrees, so add or subtract 180 to find it.

A locus is the set of points that satisfy a condition. A locus equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining them, and a locus equidistant from two lines is the angle bisector. Use a ruler and compasses for construction questions, and leave the construction arcs visible so the examiner can see your method.

title: Hardware & Architecture — Study Notes
content:
Hardware & Architecture

Cambridge IGCSE 0478 (2026–2028): von Neumann model, FDE cycle, registers, buses, RAM/ROM, secondary storage, embedded systems.

1. Von Neumann model

CPU (ALU, control unit, registers) + memory + I/O on shared buses; instructions stored as data (stored program concept).

2. Registers

RegisterRole
PCaddress of next instruction
MARaddress being read/written
MDRdata/instruction in transit
ACCALU results accumulator

3. FDE cycle

Fetch: PC → MAR; memory → MDR → CIR; PC + 1. Decode: control unit interprets opcode. Execute: ALU/registers act. Interrupts can pause between cycles.

4. Buses and performance

Address bus (one-way, width ⇒ addressable memory), data bus (two-way, width ⇒ bits per transfer), control bus. Performance factors: clock speed, cache size, core count — explain the effect, not just the name.

5. RAM vs ROM

RAM: volatile, read/write, holds running programs + data. ROM: non-volatile, read-only, bootstrap/firmware. Embedded systems: dedicated microprocessors inside devices (washing machines, engines) — one function, low cost, hard to update.

6. Secondary storage

  • Magnetic (HDD): platters, read/write heads; high capacity, cheap per GB, moving parts (shock-sensitive).
  • Optical (CD/DVD/Blu-ray): laser pits/lands; cheap, portable, slow, small capacity.
  • Solid state (SSD/flash): NAND cells; fast, silent, robust, no moving parts, more expensive per GB, finite write cycles.

Choose by use case: video editing (SSD), archive (optical/magnetic), tablets (flash).

Exam tips: trace FDE with register values; compare storage on capacity, speed, cost, durability, portability; always tie a performance factor to its effect.

Worked example: clock speed and throughput

A processor runs at 2.0 GHz, which is 2.0 × 10⁹ clock cycles per second. If each instruction takes four cycles on average, the processor completes 2.0 × 10⁹ / 4 = 5.0 × 10⁸ instructions per second. Clock speed alone does not decide performance: a faster clock with more cycles per instruction can still be slower overall.

Cache memory

Cache is small, fast memory between the CPU and main memory. It holds copies of recently or frequently used data and instructions. A cache hit avoids a slow RAM access; a cache miss forces one. Cache is faster than RAM but much smaller, which is why it holds only the data most likely to be needed next.

The ALU and the control unit

The ALU performs arithmetic and logic operations. The control unit fetches and decodes instructions and sends control signals around the system. A comparison such as A > B is evaluated in the ALU, while the decision about which instruction runs next is made by the control unit.

  • Pipelining overlaps the fetch, decode and execute stages of successive instructions to raise throughput.
  • Multi-core processors run several fetch-decode-execute cycles at once, but one program gains speed only if its work can be split into parallel tasks.
  • A 16-bit address bus can address 2¹⁶ = 65 536 locations.

title: Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles — Quick Revision Summary
content:
Quick revision: Trigonometry — Right-Angled Triangles

Mathematics — OL. SOH CAH TOA, exact values, angles of elevation/depression.

  • 1. The ratios
  • 2. Finding angles
  • 3. Exact values (Extended)
  • 4. Elevation and depression
  • 5. Pythagoras combinations

How to use this: skim the list above, then open the full revision notes for any area that feels shaky, and finish with the topic questions to check yourself.

Key points to remember

In a right-angled triangle, label the sides as opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to the angle you are using. Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite over adjacent. Use SOH CAH TOA to choose the correct ratio, then rearrange to find the unknown.

Pythagoras' theorem finds the third side when two sides are known: the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the other two squares. Make sure your calculator is in degree mode, and round the final answer to the accuracy the question asks for, usually to three significant figures.

title: Number — Arithmetic and Place Value — Study Notes
content:
Number — Arithmetic and Place Value

Cambridge IGCSE 0580 (2025–2027): 1.1 integers & place value; 1.2 fractions/decimals/percentages context; 1.3 powers & roots; HCF/LCM.

1. Types of number

  • Integers: … −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 … Primes: exactly two factors; 2 is the only even prime; 1 is not prime.
  • HCF = product of common prime factors (lowest powers); LCM = all prime factors (highest powers).

Example: 60 = 2²×3×5 and 84 = 2²×3×7 ⇒ HCF = 2²×3 = 12; LCM = 2²×3×5×7 = 420.

2. Place value

In 47 382 the digit 7 has value 7000. Rounding to significant figures: keep n digits, round using the next digit (≥5 up).

Estimation: round inputs to 1 s.f. first — 39.2 × 5.98 ≈ 40 × 6 = 240.

3. Order of operations

BIDMAS. 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 16 = 19. Insert brackets yourself when translating words: "3 added to the product of 4 and 2²" = 3 + (4 × 2²).

4. Negative numbers and calculators

Bracket negatives when substituting. Know the ×10ˣ, x², √, ˣ√ and fraction keys; give answers to 3 s.f. unless told otherwise.

5. Bounds (Extended)

Measured to nearest u: UB = +u/2, LB = −u/2. Division p/q: max = UBp ÷ LBq.

Example: 45 cm (nearest cm) in 6 s (nearest s): max speed = 45.5 ÷ 5.5 = 8.27 m/s (3 s.f.).

Exam tips: show prime-factor trees for HCF/LCM; always state rounding units (3 s.f., 1 d.p.); bounds answers quote both limits.

Place value and ordering

Each digit is worth ten times the digit to its right. To order decimals, compare digits from left to right, padding with zeros so every number has the same number of decimal places. Rounding to a given number of decimal places or significant figures looks at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up.

Written methods

Long multiplication and division are set out in columns with place value kept aligned. Estimate first by rounding each number to one significant figure; the estimate shows whether the exact answer is reasonable. Check using the inverse operation.

Order of operations

Brackets, then indices, then division and multiplication from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. For example, 3 + 4 × 2² = 3 + 4 × 4 = 19. Use a calculator's brackets key to enter long expressions in one go.

Worked example: signs in multiplication and division

Two negatives multiply to a positive, so (−3) × (−4) = 12. A negative times a positive gives a negative, so −24 ÷ 6 = −4. Subtracting a negative is the same as adding, so 3 − (−5) = 8. Apply the order of operations first: in 2 + 3 × (−4), the multiplication gives 2 − 12 = −10, not (2 + 3) × (−4) = −20.

Exam method: estimating before calculating

Round each number to one significant figure to estimate the answer before you use a calculator. For 4.9 × 21.8, the estimate 5 × 20 = 100 tells you that an answer of 10.68 or 1068 is wrong and that the true value, 106.82, is sensible. Writing the estimate down also gives you a check when a key is pressed incorrectly. When a question asks you to show working, write each step on its own line so that method marks can be awarded.

title: Movement into and out of Cells
content:
Movement into and out of Cells

Cambridge IGCSE Biology 0610, Extended route, topic 3 (statements 3.1–3.3). Diffusion, osmosis and active transport, with the water-potential reasoning that separates the top grades.

3.1 Diffusion

  • Diffusion is the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient until evenly spread. It is passive: no energy is needed. Oxygen moves into cells and carbon dioxide out by diffusion.

3.2 Osmosis

  • Osmosis is the net movement of water molecules from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution, through a partially permeable membrane, down a water potential gradient. Pure water has a water potential of zero; all solutions have negative water potential, and more negative means more concentrated.
  • Animal cells in pure water gain water and burst (lyse); in concentrated solution they lose water and shrink (crenate). Plant cells in pure water become turgid — the wall resists further entry; in concentrated solution they become plasmolysed, the membrane pulls away from the wall.

3.3 Active transport

  • Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, from dilute to concentrated, using energy from respiration. Root hair cells absorb mineral ions this way; the small intestine absorbs amino acids and glucose when concentrations are lower inside than outside.

A* extension: worked reasoning and calculations

  • Explanation chain, applied to why root hair cells take in water by osmosis but mineral ions by active transport: water moves down its gradient automatically because the cell sap is more concentrated; minerals must be moved from dilute soil solution into a more concentrated cell, which needs energy from respiration. Name both gradient directions — that contrast is the mark.
  • Practical interpretation, applied to potato cylinders left in a series of sucrose solutions and plotted as percentage change in mass: the solution where the line crosses zero change is isotonic with the tissue. Explain the shape: below that concentration cells gain water by osmosis, above it they lose it.
  • Experimental control, applied to a diffusion investigation: the independent variable is the distance or concentration, and the control variables include temperature and the particle size of the agar. Naming temperature as controlled shows you know diffusion rate depends on it.

Common errors

  • Omitting "partially permeable membrane" from the osmosis definition — it is a required phrase.
  • Saying water moves to the "salty side". Use dilute to concentrated solution and water potential.
  • Claiming active transport needs a concentration gradient to be followed. It works against the gradient.

title:
Molecules, Transport and Health — AS Level Biology

This revision note belongs to the Edexcel International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) Biology specification, WBI12 Unit 1, Topic 1 Molecules, Transport and Health. It covers water as a solvent and its structure, carbohydrates and lipids, proteins and their structure and function, gas exchange surfaces and Fick's law, the mammalian circulatory system and the cardiac cycle, haemoglobin and the oxygen dissociation curve, atherosclerosis and blood clotting, the risk factors for cardiovascular disease, diet, cholesterol and antioxidants, how people use scientific knowledge to reduce risk, the benefits and risks of treatments, and data analysis and evaluation in health studies — plus the gas exchange surfaces and enzyme practical work that support the topic. Every statement the topic is responsible for is covered in its own section or paragraph.

1. Water: structure, properties and why it is the solvent of life

Water is a small molecule with two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom; because the oxygen atom is much more electronegative than hydrogen, the shared electrons spend more time near the oxygen, so the molecule is polar — the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen end slightly positive. This polarity lets water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which gives water its high specific heat capacity, its high latent heat of vaporisation, its cohesion (important for the transpiration stream in plants) and its solvent powers. Water is an excellent solvent because its polarity lets it surround and dissolve ions and polar molecules; ions become hydrated with water molecules around them, and polar molecules such as glucose dissolve readily. In transport, water's solvent nature lets it carry dissolved substances in blood and in plant tissue fluid and sap, and its dipole nature explains why it can do that — the partial charges interact with the charges of ions and the polar groups of molecules like glucose and amino acids.

2. Carbohydrates: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides

Carbohydrates are made of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, with hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio as in water (2:1). Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates and are the building blocks — glucose, fructose and galactose are hexose monosaccharides with the formula C6H12O6. Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction, losing a water molecule and forming a glycosidic bond; the common ones are maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Polysaccharides are long chains of monosaccharides; starch in plants is made of two polymers — amylose, a long unbranched helix of glucose, which is compact for storage, and amylopectin, which is branched so that glucose can be added or removed quickly from the ends. Glycogen is similar to amylopectin but more branched, and it is the storage carbohydrate in animals, mainly in liver and muscle cells. Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide of beta-glucose chains forming long, straight fibres that cross-link by hydrogen bonds into strong microfibrils; it forms plant cell walls. Carbohydrates provide and store energy: starch and glycogen store glucose in a compact, insoluble, osmotically inert form, so they do not affect the cell's water potential, and they can be hydrolysed back to glucose when needed for respiration.

3. Core Practical 1 — semi-quantitative tests for reducing sugars and starch

Use Benedict's reagent to estimate the concentration of reducing sugars and iodine solution to estimate the concentration of starch, using colour standards. Benedict's reagent (copper(II) sulfate, sodium carbonate and sodium citrate) turns from blue to green, then yellow, then orange, then brick-red as reducing sugars are heated with it — the colour depends on the concentration of reducing sugar. For a semi-quantitative estimate, prepare a range of known reducing sugar concentrations (for example glucose solutions), heat each with Benedict's, compare the colour with a colour standard chart, and record the colour or its code for each; then use the standards to estimate the concentration in an unknown. For starch, add iodine solution (iodine in potassium iodide) to the sample; a blue-black colour shows starch, and the intensity of the colour relates to the concentration — compare with colour standards to estimate. State the variables: the independent variable is the sugar or starch concentration, the dependent variable is the colour or colour standard, and controlled variables include the volume, temperature and time of heating.

4. Glycosidic bonds: condensation and hydrolysis

Monosaccharides join by condensation reactions to form disaccharides and polysaccharides, with a glycosidic bond formed between them and a water molecule lost each time. Conversely, polysaccharides and disaccharides can be hydrolysed — split by the addition of water — into their monomers; hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic bond and needs a water molecule for each bond broken. Glucose, fructose and galactose join to make maltose (glucose + glucose), sucrose (glucose + fructose) and lactose (glucose + galactose). Amylose and amylopectin are formed from alpha-glucose units; cellulose is formed from beta-glucose units, and because beta-glucose has a different orientation the chain is straight rather than coiled, so the hydrogen bonds between adjacent chains form strong microfibrils. Hydrolysis of starch gives maltose then glucose; hydrolysis of sucrose gives glucose and fructose; hydrolysis of lactose gives glucose and galactose. This matters in the body: dietary starch is hydrolysed to glucose in the gut by enzymes, and that glucose is used in respiration or stored as glycogen; lactose intolerance is caused by a deficiency of lactase, the enzyme that hydrolyses lactose, so lactose stays in the gut and causes problems.

5. Triglycerides: structure and saturated and unsaturated lipids

A triglyceride is made from one glycerol molecule and three fatty acids, joined by three ester bonds formed in condensation reactions; it is insoluble in water (hydrophobic). Fatty acids have a carboxyl group at one end and a hydrocarbon chain that may be saturated — no double bonds in the chain, so the molecule is straight and packs tightly, and saturated fats (and the triglycerides made from them) are usually solid at room temperature — or unsaturated, with one or more double bonds that kink the chain and prevent tight packing, so unsaturated fats are usually liquid at room temperature (oils). Lipids have several roles: they store energy in a compact, insoluble form (1 g of fat stores more energy than 1 g of carbohydrate), they form the phospholipid bilayer of all cell membranes, they form the myelin sheath around nerve fibres, they form a protective waterproof layer in the skin (subcutaneous fat), and they form steroid hormones. In membranes the phospholipid bilayer controls what enters and leaves the cell; the membrane also has proteins, cholesterol and glycoproteins.

6. Why animals need a heart and circulation

Many animals need a heart and a circulatory system because as an organism grows, diffusion alone is too slow to supply its cells with oxygen and nutrients and to remove waste — the surface area to volume ratio falls as size increases, and diffusion is only effective over short distances. A mass transport system (heart, blood vessels and blood) moves substances rapidly around the body, overcoming the limitations of diffusion. Blood carries oxygen, nutrients, hormones, waste products and defence cells and molecules. In simple organisms (small ones, or those with a large surface area to volume ratio or a thin body wall) exchange can happen directly by diffusion with the environment; larger or more active animals need a specialised exchange surface and a circulation system to move materials there and back.

7. The structure of arteries, veins and capillaries

Blood vessels relate their structure to their function. Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; they have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand and smooth the pressure and to help push the blood on, and a narrow lumen relative to wall thickness; they have no valves (except at the heart). Veins carry blood back to the heart at low pressure; they have thinner walls (less muscle and elastic tissue) and a wide lumen, and they have valves to prevent backflow, helping return blood when pressure is low. Capillaries are the exchange vessels; they have walls only one cell thick, a very narrow lumen just wide enough for red blood cells to pass in single file, slowing the blood and maximising the surface area for the exchange of substances. The structure of each vessel matches the pressure and role it plays.

8. The cardiac cycle and the structure of the mammalian heart

The mammalian heart is a muscular pump with four chambers — two atria (thin-walled, receiving chambers) and two ventricles (thick-walled, pumping chambers), with the left side pumping oxygenated blood to the body and the right side pumping deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The cardiac cycle is the sequence of events in a heartbeat: atrial systole (the atria contract, pushing blood into the ventricles), ventricular systole (the ventricles contract, pushing blood out into the pulmonary artery and aorta, and the atrioventricular valves close to prevent backflow, making the first heart sound), and diastole (the heart relaxes, the ventricles fill, the semilunar valves close, making the second heart sound). The valves ensure one-way flow: the atrioventricular valves (between atria and ventricles) and the semilunar valves (in the aorta and pulmonary artery). The left ventricle has a much thicker wall than the right because it must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body, whereas the right ventricle pumps only to the nearby lungs. The structure of the heart and its operation are shown by dissection (a recommended additional practical), and the heart's own rhythm is myogenic, starting at the sinoatrial node, though details of that are not needed at IAS.

9. Haemoglobin, oxygen transport and the oxygen dissociation curve

Haemoglobin transports oxygen in red blood cells. Each haemoglobin molecule has four polypeptide chains, each with a haem group that contains an iron ion that can combine with one oxygen molecule, so one haemoglobin can carry four oxygen molecules. The oxygen dissociation curve shows how much oxygen haemoglobin takes up at different oxygen tensions: at high oxygen tension (in the lungs) it becomes almost fully saturated, and at low oxygen tension (in respiring tissues) it releases oxygen; the shape of the curve means a small drop in oxygen tension in the tissues releases a lot of oxygen — this is important. The Bohr effect: as carbon dioxide concentration rises and pH falls, haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen falls and it releases oxygen more readily — so where respiration is high and CO2 is produced, haemoglobin unloads oxygen. Adult haemoglobin has a lower oxygen affinity than fetal haemoglobin, which has a higher affinity — this lets the fetus pick up oxygen from the mother's blood across the placenta, because fetal haemoglobin can take oxygen from adult haemoglobin. Carbaminohaemoglobin carries some carbon dioxide as well, so haemoglobin transports both oxygen and carbon dioxide.

10. Atherosclerosis: how it develops and why it matters

Atherosclerosis is the narrowing and hardening of arteries by plaques. The process begins with endothelial dysfunction — damage to the lining of the artery, by high blood pressure, by smoking chemicals, or by immune responses — then an inflammatory response follows, white blood cells (including phagocytes) move into the artery wall, LDL cholesterol is taken up and oxidised, smooth muscle cells multiply and fibrous tissue forms, and a plaque builds up (a fibrous cap over a lipid core). As the plaque grows it narrows the artery, raising blood pressure further and reducing flow; eventually a plaque may rupture, triggering blood clotting and a thrombus, which can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction (heart attack). The main risk factors — genetics, diet, age, gender, high blood pressure, smoking and inactivity — act through these mechanisms, and the disease shows why passive transport and diffusion alone cannot supply the larger, more active human body and why the heart and blood vessels are needed.

11. Blood clotting and its role in cardiovascular disease

Blood clotting forms a network of insoluble fibrin threads that traps platelets and red blood cells to form a clot and seal a wound. The process: damage to a blood vessel exposes platelets to the collagen in the wall, and they are activated and release thromboplastin; thromboplastin, in the presence of calcium ions, converts prothrombin (an inactive plasma protein) to thrombin; thrombin then catalyses the conversion of soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, which forms a mesh that traps platelets and red blood cells into a clot. Clotting is needed to prevent blood loss and to stop pathogens entering, but in cardiovascular disease a clot formed on a ruptured plaque can block a coronary artery and cause a myocardial infarction, or travel to block a cerebral artery and cause a stroke. Treatments to reduce clotting include platelet inhibitors such as aspirin, and anticoagulants such as warfarin, which slow the clotting cascade.

12. Risk factors for cardiovascular disease

Many factors increase the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), and most act through the mechanisms above. Diet high in saturated fats and cholesterol raises LDL levels and contributes to plaques; high blood pressure damages the endothelium and raises the risk of both atherosclerosis and clotting; age increases risk because damage accumulates and repair is less efficient; males are at higher risk at younger ages than females; smoking introduces chemicals that damage the endothelium and raise blood pressure and heart rate and reduce oxygen carried by haemoglobin; inactivity contributes to high blood pressure, obesity and high cholesterol; and genetics/family history affects a person's baseline risk. Risk is often the result of several factors combined, and reducing one can help even if others remain. People's perception of risk is often different from the actual risk — they may underestimate or overestimate the risk from diet and other lifestyle factors, and scientists work to clarify the real risks through studies.

13. Diet, cholesterol and antioxidants and the evidence for them

Dietary antioxidants (such as vitamins C and E from fruits and vegetables) may reduce the risk of CVD by preventing the oxidation of LDL cholesterol — oxidised LDL is taken up more readily by artery walls and contributes to plaque formation. Blood cholesterol level is an important indicator: total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol are linked to CVD, and HDL cholesterol helps remove cholesterol from the artery wall, so high HDL is protective. The evidence that cholesterol causes CVD comes from studies showing a causal relationship between blood cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease, and from trials of the statins, which lower cholesterol and reduce CVD events. People use scientific knowledge about diet, body mass index (BMI = mass (kg) / height (m) squared) and waist-to-hip ratio (a measure of central obesity), exercise and smoking to reduce their risk of coronary heart disease — and they should distinguish between correlation and causation when interpreting the data, because two things occurring together does not by itself prove one causes the other.

14. Data analysis in health studies: correlation, causation and study design

Health studies use quantitative data on illness and mortality rates to determine health risks. Two things can be correlated without one causing the other — a third factor may cause both, or the relationship may be coincidental — so a key skill is distinguishing correlation from causation. A causal relationship for cholesterol and CVD is supported by mechanistic evidence (the biology above) plus the results of trials. When evaluating the design of studies used to determine health risk factors, consider the sample selection (is it representative, or biased, as in a sample of only one type of person or only volunteers) and the sample size (small samples are less reliable and more easily swayed by chance). Conflicting evidence exists because studies differ in design, in the populations studied, and in the measures used, and scientific decisions draw on the whole body of evidence, not one study.

15. Perceived and actual risk and why people's views differ

People's perception of risks is often different from the actual risks — they may underestimate risks due to diet and lifestyle because those risks feel distant and small, or overestimate them because of vivid or recent examples, or because of personal experience, cultural beliefs or poor understanding of the probabilities. Scientific knowledge can clarify the actual risk: for example, many people underestimate the risk from diet and inactivity for coronary heart disease even though the evidence is strong, and the gap between perception and reality is itself a reason to communicate the science clearly. Understanding that perception and reality can diverge is part of evaluating the use of scientific knowledge in making decisions about health, and it explains why public health messages must be carefully designed and evidence-based.

16. Treatments for cardiovascular disease: benefits and risks

Several treatments are used for CVD. Antihypertensives lower blood pressure, reducing the risk of endothelial damage and of heart strain. Statins lower blood cholesterol, reducing plaque formation and the risk of atherosclerosis. Anticoagulants (such as warfarin) and platelet inhibitors (such as aspirin) reduce clot formation, lowering the risk of a clot on a ruptured plaque causing a heart attack or stroke. Each has benefits and risks: antihypertensives can cause dizziness, fatigue or kidney effects and may over-lower pressure; statins can cause muscle pain, digestive upset and, rarely, liver effects; aspirin can cause bleeding, especially in the gut, and is not suitable for everyone. Decisions about treatment balance the degree of risk against the benefit, take the person's overall risk factors into account, and should be supported by the evidence — and by the science behind the disease, so that treatment targets the actual risk factors.

17. Core Practical 2 — vitamin C content of food and drink

Investigate the vitamin C content of food and drink, using DCPIP (2,6-dichlorophenolindophenol), which is blue when oxidised and colourless when reduced. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) reduces DCPIP, so as vitamin C is added from a food or drink sample, the blue colour fades; the volume of a known concentration of vitamin C solution needed to decolorise a fixed volume of DCPIP gives a calibration, and the volume of the food or drink needed to decolorise the same DCPIP lets you estimate its vitamin C concentration by comparison. Carry out the test for several drinks (for example fruit juices, boiled and unboiled samples) to compare vitamin C content, and note that heat (boiling) destroys vitamin C, so boiled samples contain much less. Record volumes, identify the independent (volume of sample) and dependent (volume needed to decolorise DCPIP) variables, and control temperature, DCPIP volume and end-point judgement.

18. Proteins: amino acids, peptide bonds and the levels of structure

Amino acids are the monomers of proteins; the basic structure is an amino group, a carboxyl group and a variable R group attached to a central carbon. There are around 20 amino acids, differing in their R group, and the sequence of amino acids in a protein (primary structure) determines its folding and function. Amino acids join by condensation reactions to form peptide bonds, making dipeptides and polypeptides. Secondary structure is local folding into alpha-helices and beta-pleated sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between peptide bonds. Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions; it determines the protein's function. Haemoglobin is a globular protein with four chains and four haem groups each carrying one oxygen; collagen is a fibrous protein of three polypeptide chains in a triple helix, strong for tendons and skin. Biuret reagent (copper(II) sulfate and sodium hydroxide) turns purple in the presence of peptide bonds, and a semi-quantitative method using it and colour standards can estimate protein concentration — that is a recommended additional practical.

19. Gas exchange surfaces and Fick's law

An effective gas exchange surface has a large surface area to volume ratio, a thin surface (short diffusion distance) and a difference in concentration between the two sides — the three properties that make diffusion rapid. The rate of diffusion is described by Fick's law: rate of diffusion = (surface area × concentration difference) / thickness of the surface, so increasing surface area or concentration difference, or decreasing thickness, increases the rate. The mammalian lung is adapted for rapid gaseous exchange: the alveoli provide a huge total surface area (about 70–90 m² in an adult), they are thin-walled (one cell thick, with a shared basement membrane) so the diffusion distance is very short, the air in the alveoli is highly oxygenated while the blood arriving is deoxygenated, so there is a steep concentration gradient, and the constant ventilation and blood flow maintain that gradient. Fick's law explains why these adaptations matter quantitatively.

20. Enzymes: specificity, catalysing reactions and factors that affect rate

Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy needed. Their mechanism of action is explained by their three-dimensional structure: the active site has a specific shape that fits the substrate (the lock-and-key model) or changes shape to fit it (the induced-fit model), and specificity comes from the exact shape of the active site — each enzyme works on one or a few substrates. Enzymes are proteins, and heat, pH and the concentrations of enzyme and substrate affect their rate: each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; above or below the optimum the rate falls, and extremes denature the enzyme (irreversibly changing the shape of the active site, so it no longer works). Enzyme concentration increases the rate when substrate is in excess, and substrate concentration increases the rate up to a point, after which the enzyme's active sites are saturated and the rate levels off (maximum rate, Vmax). These effects are investigated in Core Practical 4.

21. Core Practical 4 — factors affecting enzyme rate

Investigate the effect of temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate concentration on the initial rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. For each factor, choose a suitable enzyme and substrate (for example amylase and starch, or catalase and hydrogen peroxide) and measure the initial rate — the rate in the first part of the reaction, before the substrate is used up or the enzyme denatures. Change the factor being tested in steps, keep the other factors constant (control variables), take several measurements, and calculate the initial rate from the slope of the graph of product formed (or substrate used) against time. For temperature, the rate rises with temperature to an optimum, then falls as the enzyme denatures; for pH, rate is highest at the enzyme's optimum pH; for enzyme concentration, rate rises linearly with concentration; for substrate concentration, rate rises and then levels off at Vmax. Plot graphs and explain the patterns in terms of collisions, activation energy and denaturation.

22. How to use this note and what to revise next

Use these notes section by section, checking that you can state the structure of a water molecule and explain its polarity, draw the structures of alpha-glucose and beta-glucose and state the difference, carry out the Benedict's and iodine semi-quantitative tests and explain the variables and the colour standards, draw a triglyceride and distinguish saturated from unsaturated, state the structure and function of arteries, veins and capillaries, describe the cardiac cycle and the structure of the heart, sketch the oxygen dissociation curve and explain the Bohr effect and fetal haemoglobin, describe the stages of atherosclerosis and blood clotting, list the risk factors for CVD and state how each acts, carry out the DCPIP and biuret practicals, describe the properties of a gas exchange surface and apply Fick's law, and explain enzyme specificity and the effects of temperature, pH and concentrations. After this topic, revise Topic 2 Membranes, proteins, DNA and gene expression, and Topic 3 Cell structure, reproduction and development — the transport and exchange ideas here underpin the circulatory and gas exchange systems in later topics.
